I first heard of stellaris from youtube and i first that it was just like any other 4x strategy game, however i was wrong. When i first bought it i thought i would be very hard to learn but took only five mins to learn how play the game, after that i quickly created my species and began to conquer the galaxy, now the AI is not perfect as there are some problems like the AI getting a head start in technology and more resources but i find it to be a fun challenge because if this was real life we would likely be in a similar position.
My final thoughts are that is a really fun game and it can somewhat help you to negotiate with real people and so you that war is not something that you can just win over night. Overall there are some bugs and glitches that are in the game but it doesn’t affect me that much, i just find it to be another challenge in the game that you have to master, i would go over the multiplayer but i haven’t played it yet so i won’t give my opinion on it yet.

Wildstar has hit the mark so far for me, but I have yet to reach the "elder game", as I believe the end-game is referred to here.
I have played all classes far enough to get a feel for them, and am pushing on with the Esper. Engineer was also a lot of fun. All classes seem viable.
The leveling experience has been engaging, I am not watching the experience bar percentage counter because the journey is so fun. Thanks to WOW's hierloom system, and progressive changes to the game difficulty, I had forgotten what it was like to have to exercise caution when doing leveling quests. While I am not dying constantly, Wildstar is refreshingly challenging in this regard.
The combat system took me a couple of levels to get used to. However, now that I have, it feels very natural. Figuring out the right set-up of abilities on my action bar has been a pleasant challenge too. The lack of up-to-date guides has made me think for myself in a way I haven't had to for a while.
The amount of lore objects out in the world was a bit overwhelming at first. I cannot just run past an object without clicking on it, I really should work on that. Until I get that under control though, I will keep clicking and enjoying the story as it unfolds.
The level announcer hasn't gotten old yet. It has made me jump a couple of times though lol, not realising how close I am to leveling then some dude yells in my ears "that was f@#$%n awesome!"...
Hats off to the housing and holo-wardrobe features too. Particularly the latter, where I can pick an outfit and not have to reset it every time I equip a new item. Also, the dye system for recolouring my kit, this adds another level of personalisation to the feature.
I also enjoy the art style, although I recognise that it is a polarising subject for many. It seems to compliment the other irreverent aspects of the games humour and narrative style nicely.
Anecdotally, I am noticing more people in the levelling zones too. Hopefully that is a good sign.
On that note, I am not one that dons rose-tinted glasses for Vanilla WOW, but one thing I do miss is the way that single-realm set-ups make people accountable for their actions. If you get a bad rep, no groups for you. Wildstars community seem to be very helpful and welcoming in my experience to-date. Without the nonsense that pollutes chat in WOW, and the poor behaviour exhibited by so many when joining random groups.
The jury is still out for me on the crafting system. I haven't really delved into that aspect too much yet as it doesn't seem all that intuitive. Particularly the cooking skill, which is very hit'n miss in my opinion. Still prefer it to Nomi though. This is not a deal breaker however, as it doesn't seem to  affect the levelling experience.
Paths, not sure about the "value" of these. Settler and Scientist have been pleasant diversions, which is enough of a reason for me to push on with them. Explorer just had me stumped a couple of times, and I gave up. Soldier just seems to be "kill more stuff", which stands to reason I guess, but doesn't bring a new dimension the way the others do.
Challenges. I wish I had more control over these. I am not a fan of them just popping, and forcing me to scramble. I am too competitive to just ignore them so it can make everything seem a bit frantic and stressful at times.
The game-world seemed really hectic too until I figured out how to turn off a lot of the markers to declutter my view.
All-in-all, I am having a lot of fun on Nexus. I would recommend it to fans of MMORPG's looking for a new challenge.

An absolute classic of the Total War series, I would still highly recommend the game to anyone who enjoys historical, strategy games, be that grand strategy or RTS. This edition really put Creative Assembly and the Total War franchise on the map, and drew in many fans for it's rich historical setting, diversity of challenge and sheer depth that means any campaign can take weeks to fully play through.
I highly recommend the Kingdoms expansion, all four of the more story-driven mini-campaigns are highly compelling, as you can fight for power, wealth, religion or just for kicks across the various intricate settings. I do recommend installing mods: particularly the Stainless Steel mod as this expands the campaign map significantly and adds more historical resonance to the gameplay.

Alright, so I've played the Total War series from the original Shogun: Total War, Rome: Total War, the Barbarian Invasion and Alexander Expansions, and when this game came out, I let out a hardy war cry of joy (not really, because people would think I was a bloody lunatic). I even played Empire and Napoleon (but they didn't feel as good to me). But trying to be as unbiased and from a modern perspective, I'm going to make a stab at reviewing this game.
Graphics: The graphics of this game isn't all that bad, but doesn't hold up to more modern titles and can appear a bit dated. Even so the graphics have aged surprisingly well and while not as smooth as some newer titles, it's servicable and really isn't all that bad for a decade-old title.
Sound Design: The sound effects in this game aren't bad. I thought that the sounds might not hold up all that well, but I was glad to find I was mistaken. Everything from the sounds in the menu to the sounds of a firing cannon, crossbowmen winding up their weapons, or the sounds of a pitched melee, the sound design is still very good.
Music: Perhaps one of the parts of the game that really holds up well. The rendition of Ailein Duinn for the Britannia expanion is very well done. Honestly the OST is something I occasionally listen to from time-to-time. The music is very well composed, even impressive for a game, many of the tracks feel truly timeless and manage to fit in well with the period without being cheesy or feeling jarring. The orchestral work here is well worth a listen.
Gameplay: Don't let the amount of time I played on Steam fool you. I've probably 'wasted' an entire year or so of my life in game-hours on this game's cd version. After I lost the box and CD for a while, I re-purchased the Steam version to get my fix... and it's all because of the gameplay, that beautiful, sweet, delicious gameplay. Controls may be a bit odd for newcomers to the series, but after you get used to them it's like second-nature. Controls in battle are smooth, intuitive, and engaging. This game features both a world-map for grand strategy, but then breaks down into a tactical battlefield map in which you control units attempting to win individual battles with your guile. It's a great mix and I really wish other grand strategy titles would take up a similar formula.
Factions: Holy s*** does this game (and the expansions) have a good selection of factions. The core game only centers around Europe and North-most Africa, but the expansions do include the Americas.
Mods: A section in its own right. Some modders have done amazing work adding in China, Japan, and the Warhammer fantasy mod on mod DB is freaking fantastic when you consider that the game engine is over a decade old now. Honestly I really wish I knew how they did it.
Overall: I was surprised to find that this game, after all these years, is still a timeless classic that's fun and engaging. For me this game ranks higher for playability and fun-factor than other, more popular titles. While Starcraft 1 and Dark Reign are still solid games nowadays, they feel dated and old when I play them, somehow Medieval II: Total War is immune to being dated. This is the game (that at least for me) sold the series, and has been a cherished title I return to again-and-again after all these years, if that isn't the hallmark of a great game, I don't know what is.

Before buying or playing this game, consider stabbing yourself in the eye first. At least you'll die quickly.
In a phrase: This game is a HORRIFIC version of Minecraft. Imagine if, in Minecraft, in order to chop down trees you had to increase a skill called Woodcutting. And increasing that skill would take you several HUNDRED hours of grinding, to get it to a reasonable level of tree-chopping-intensity. Now multiply that for everything in the game. Dirt? Digging. Stone? Mining. Planting crops? Farming. Fighting. Blacksmithing. Yo-yoing. Yes, you're going to spend more time grinding one skill in this game than it took you to finish Final Fantasy 7, unlock all the final limit breaks, get a gold chocobo, kill Emerald and Ruby weapon, and get the Knights Of The Round summon.
The graphics are horrible. Constant screen clipping, no third person mode, static animations, and characters that attempt to appear lifelike but are actually more static than the blocky characters in Minecraft. Little character customization means you can either spend 10,000 hours of your life to make your character look different (not exaggerating), or you can look like everyone else. So everyone looks the same.
The monsters are uninteresting and they all behave the same. Cat, Dog, Rat, Scorpion, Bear, Spider --- I just named half of the monsters available in the game. They are all the same thing - a static animal with minor animation and a hit box.
The sounds are terrible. Opening a treasure chest sounds like an overweight neckbeard full of cheese just farted inside your hoodie. You can actually fart on other characters -- which normally would be funny and awesome, but this game somehow takes what should be a universally funny thing and makes it actually bad. All of the characters can emote to each other and the emotes are FAR louder than any of the other sounds in the game, and are actually rather scary when you hear them for the first time.
The combat system is horrific. The game starts you out with a sword and shield, but you really won't even be able to kill a SINGLE rat without getting completely wrecked. If you do manage to die, then congradulations, you've just lost 20 or more hours of the skill grinding that you completed to get to where you are now. Yes: When you die, you actually LOSE SKILLS that you gain, AND all of the items you were carrying. The death penalty in this game is so harsh that I'd rather die in Hardcore mode in Diablo 3 and lose my character forever than die in this game -- making a new character in Diablo 3 would actually take less time to gear up than trying to regain the skill loss in Wurm.
The main attraction of this game is that you can claim land "a deed" and make it your own, build a house on it, etc. Unfortunately, you have to pay upkeep on this deed, and all the stuff you build on this deed will decay over time. You stored your weapons in a container so you could use them later, and it's been a few weeks? SORRY, they are probably decayed too much now and they are GONE. If you're lucky they are only damaged, and you'll have to spend a few HOURS repairing them and improving them back to their former glory.
The worst part is that other players can "deed up" land next to yours and set you to a "kill on sight" list on their deed. Even on PvE servers, there are so many ways that other players can grief you it's not even funny. Oftentimes, the server admin will allow this because it is "legal play". If you've bothered to improve land off your deed, then other players can come by and stake your hard-worked land, ruin it, or do whatever they want to it.
If you or your friends even think you like this game, STOP NOW and go play Minecraft. Or inject yourself with heroin in the eyeball, because that will actually be a better experience.
This game belongs on a list with Daikatana, Superman 64, Shaq Fu, and crystal meth.

I've had to revise my previously glowing review...
Sadly this largely comes down to technical issues with the game and the hosts. Lagg spikes are common, but server capacity is a major limitation.
I should forewarn you that servers such as this sell services ie clay spawns, various in item advantages etc. Servers all seem to suffer a common issue with coastal crowding, but despite the ladnscape being plastered with buildings along the coast, as far as the eye can see, there are very few players online. It's like a ghost town in most cases.
When you select the server you'll see how many are online, and it won't be many. You'll likely feel amazed when a rare visitor drops by once a week. The lack of NPCs and life in between make the game feel very much deserted. Though you can satisfy some of your design needs with the game, it won't go much further in it's current state.

As of writing this, my game save says 20.5 hours played.
Love this game. I didn't hesitate to buy it despite the reviews as I can't control myself.
Had one crash about 4 hours in, however no other issues since. I purchased the $4 Borderless Gaming mod via steam store and play the game in borderless windowed (looks no different to fullscreen), and haven't had any issues apart from the first time loading the game:
1) Opened game with BG, messed around a bit to figure out BG mod.
2) Screen was white, google fix was Alt+Enter, didn't need to do it again.
3) Game worked fine.
Once you're in game, you can save a lot more than you might think, access points all over the place and quick save menu whenever you have the topright hand corner option to do so.
Gameplay is amazing, combat is fluid, story is great, and the soundtrack is from another world.
Would highly recommend if you just have the patience to look past the minor issues. I'd also recommend playing with a controller (I bought the xbox one controller and it works great).  I am sure they'll fix it up either way considering the amount of bad reviews. Just don't board the hate train to follow the trend, figure it out and you'll have the time of your life immersed into this incredible story.
EDIT: 45.5 hours on game save now, no crashes or any other issues since the few at the very beginning (detail above).

I would like to preface this by saying both that this is my first real Steam review and I'm most likely the least qualified person on the planet, and that NieR: Automata is one of the most beautifully symbolic and artistic games of all time, and it most definitely kept me gripped through the entire experience, Yoko Taro's form of storytelling made the games themes and narrative structure undeniably one of it's strongest areas, the story is thoughtful and most definitely impactful, and the way that the environment and character designs support the games ideas is perfect. I do not want to get into spoilers because I feel it is something that every person who enjoys video games should play for themselves. The
majority of the gameplay mixes the typical Platinum Games' character action style of fighting with RPG elements, a lot of the gameplay also transitions into bullet hell style Shoot 'em ups, side scrolling hack and slash's, and top down fighting sections, the transitional gameplay really allows for an experience that stays fresh and engaging for the majority of the gameplay. NieR's music is another one of it's strongest area, to the point where most would say that there is not a single weak track in the game, I'd certainly agree with this as I find myself listening to it constantly even after finishing the game up.
The only real issue I have with NieR lies not in the game itself but rather It's horribly optimized port. It doesn't make the game unplayable by any means, but tinkering will have to be done for sure.
I don't know if It would be proper of me to call NieR: Automata a flawless game, as I am sure that someone out there will have issues with it (Outside of the poor optimization.) But in my case at least it was a flawless experience, it's everything I could want from a gaming experience and far better than I could ever have expected. I highly recommend this game to anybody who REALLY enjoys video games, when people call video games art, things like this are shining examples of it.
So IN MY OPINION-- I have to give NieR: Automata a 10/10

A spoiler-free review for all of you who don't know this game:
The game took me roughly 75 minutes to play through, but it is a solid, and well made game. The game costs only 10€, so please don't expect too much of it.
Graphic:
Everything in this game looks beautiful in it's own way. It's very simplistic and colorfull, that's something I like about it.
Music:
The music was well chosen, atmospheric, and fitted the simplistic style of the game.
Story:
The story does not explain a lot, and let's you speculate about the things that happened in the past. Like the rest of the game, the story is simplistic, but it's still well written.
Difficulty:
The puzzles aren't that difficult, it won't take long to solve them, but that shouldn't hinder anyone on playing this game.
World:
The world is rather narrow, you don't have much to explore, only a few secrets lurk in the shadows.
My conclusion:
The game isn't that expensive, and it's worth every cent of it's price. If you don't mind paying 10€ for one to two hours of beautiful gameplay, you should give it a try, I believe you won't regret it.

This game is not completely unpleasant but I cannot recommend it at its full price of $9.99 or even half price at $4.99.  I got this game included in a Humble Monthly Bundle and so I'm not angry at what I paid for it to play it.
I beat this game in two play sessions. I will list some pros and cons and then TL;DR it all up.
Pros:
+Decent soundtract, at points even catchy.
+The graphics are not technically impressive but they do match the games setting and general tone. There is some novelty in the enemy design. Knowing Illustrator as I do, I'm not incredibly impressed... you could whip up the games graphical assets in a weekend if provided enough coffee and cigarettes.
+The puzzles are well paced and remain challenging but nothing is too hard, there is nothing to make you rage here, you will rise to the challenge.
+It is novel that this is basically a refreshingly simple d-pad and 2 button game. There is no true combat, just some clever puzzles wrapped up in platform packaging.
+The controls are TIGHT, they feel good and are quite responsive.
Cons:
-This game completely lacks a plot... you just keep going forward. You are a mute robot and the enemies dont speak. The only speech in the entire game is this guy (who has a great gravelly voice) who talks to you via cassette tapes you find throughout the game. This lack of plot failed to motivate me to care about what was happening in the game.
-The end "boss" is a very simple tile puzzle that shouldve been placed in the first half of the game. In fact the ending is the real insult of this game. I feel like the ending was rushed and meaningless.
-The biggest issue: This whole game seems meaningless. The developers did not do enough to force the player to become invested in the story and progress. It's just an empty wasteland littered with puzzles and bizare stuff that never becomes cohesive.
When I finished the game, I felt empty and a little cheated. I kind of wanted my time back... could've invested that two hours into much more fulfilling endeavours. I rarely feel this way about any game, let alone a game with great art direction and tight controls like Planet.
TL;DR=====> You can nail the controls, art, soundtrack and puzzles but if you don't craft an inviting world and motivate the player to actually care about the game or its protagonist then the player can't recommend your game. This is my first negative review on Steam and if the game was around $2-3 or Humble Bundle only I might recommend it but at $10 I feel I should warn people.

As someone that actually really likes Warmachine and Hordes as well as all the Iron Kingdoms stuff, this game just makes me sad. So much wasted potential an numerous bugs just sucks the fun out of it.

Interface is difficult to use, movement is bizarrely random at times, cutscenes are basically still frames with voice over. Overall if the game plays the way the Demo does it is unpolished & clunky. This game needs alot of work to make it enjoyable to play,

The big problem with Warmachine Tactics is that I kept finding myself ask 'who thought this bit was a good idea?' while playing it. While there's a whole host of performance and mechanical issues with the game, the reason why I keep uninstalling it is because far too many design choices are simply self-defeating.
Here's a few of them:
-No saving in single player missions.
-seemingly unskippable cutscenes (which can easily last 5 minutes, making replaying a mission truly obnoxious).
-no way to leave multiplayer quick match without force quitting.
- the utterly bizarre decision to fill cutscenes with frozen characters. Descends into farce when the camera zooms into motionless characters' faces when delivering exposition.
-The conversion of the Warmachine ruleset into something where it feels like absurd effort has thrown at the simplest of enemies.
None of these seem to be design features that should have escaped QC, let alone early access. In particular, the unskippable, farcical cut-scenes smacks of a hole in the budget that got filled in an 'arty' fashion. Game balance feels truly out the window, simply because everything feels extraordinarily pillow-fisted, so massive effort has to be hurled at largely inconsequencial enemies.
The main gameplay feels like a kludgy, sticky mess where you often feel like you're fighting the controls more than the enemy. The AI is pants-on-head dumb, making Skirmish mode some what akin to shooting fish in a barrel. The conversion of the Warmachine ruleset often feels extraordinary restrictive and often poorly signalled (it is often hard to tell a unit's facing, which makes the facing rules a frequent pain). Knowledge of the tabletop game feels essential to making the game playable, yet the game doesn't clue you into the changes it's made to units' abilities so even that knowledge is often wrong. Mechanics and effects often feel wonky or unpredictable (I've watched an electro-leap leap to an enemy a screen away, which basically the opposite of what it's supposed to do). It often feels like the camera is deliberately annoying you, hiding itself behind terrain when you're trying to see what's going on.
Multiplayer feels extraordinarily hampered by a limited pallette of options as well as the aforementioned Quick Match issue. Frankly, I've gotten one game of multiplayer in the year I've owned the game. Apparently, multiplayer missions have flags and killboxes, but I've no idea what either looks like because the game doesn't seem to show them.
The core campaign is little better. It's your bog-standard 'discover macguffin, fight to macguffin, fight off people who want it, then destroy it' plot that seems to be the default RTS plot design and Sturgis might as well be called 'Arthas' for the originality in his contribution. Due to Jakes being as pillow-fisted as the rest of the units, the missions often feel like they've got a reversed difficulty level, with some of the toughest missions coming at the start and the late game missions feeling much easier. Again, the AI is dumb as a box of bricks, often letting you dictate the pace of missions because enemies often won't activate until you attack them (the sterling winner has to be a late mission, where the Butcher will gleefully run around in front of your guns like a headless chicken). Mission design itself often feels profoundly unfun, with many missions with multiple fronts, something that just doesn't work with the Warmachine game mechanics. The game often doesn't signal the arrival of enemy reinforcements, leading to you often just spotting reinforcements by accident halfway through a turn. I shouldn't have to play 'hunt the mechanithrall' at the start of the turn, but there's no better way to check you know what's going on. Missions often require you to keep a number of character units alive, but this often causes auto-wipes half-way through missions as they're profoundly squishy. Special marks have to go to the second longest running character in the campaign, known either as Sarge or 'Trencher Sergeant'. Looking identical to his fellow Trenchers, he's easy to lose to enemy attacks and suffers the indignity of never being given an actual name.
The unit selection feels a lot like someone went through the minature game, picked their favourite models and stuck them in. In particular, once you've unlocked Jakes' feat, it really doesn't feel like it works well with the rest of the Cygnaran army. It's a close combat buff, but there's only two melee infantry available and one of them already has all the buffs she hands out. There's also a paucity of repair units, which only makes the campaign harder. The 'alternate weapon' variants of infantry (like the Trencher Grenadier and Winter Guard Rocketeer) have almost identical (if there is a difference, I haven't noticed it) appearances, which means you often have no idea what the enemy troops are armed with until they fire it at you.
So the big question is 'can this be fixed?' I really don't think so. The game cries out for a complete overhaul of the mechanics, but that'll take ages and if it hasn't been done yet, I doubt it's ever going to happen. Fixing the awful cutscenes would cost a ton. Realistically, the only things that can be overhauled are the array of bugs and poor design choices. An option to save during missions and skip cutscenes would be a nice start to making this a lot more user friendly.
So in the end do I recommend this game? No. It simply never feels fun to play. While it has a few bright spots (a late game stealth mission is surprisingly fun for a stealth mission) the single player has a difficulty curve more akin to a roller-coaster, terrible cut-scenes and profoundly bad mission design. Skirmish mode is as challenging as beating a puppy and just as much fun. Multiplayer seems to be completely dead. It's a shame, but that's the truth.

As a fan of the Tabletop and a KS Backer, this review kind of pains me to write.
All the framework of a good game is there, and for the most part, actual gameplay animations run really smoothly and look amazing. A focus on smaller skirmishes as opposed to the large sclae battles seen on a tabletop has the potiential for an interesting game.
Where everything falls apart however is the UI. It is so clunky, so user-unfriendly that it borders on ridiculous. Having to fiddle with a units facing just to get it to look in the correct direction as the thing you want it to kill, and then take 3-4 clicks from there just to make your attack feels frustrating and takes absolutely forever. Movement is a chore, having to constantly rotate the camera so that you can click the exact spot you want to move to, because a small rock was blocking it from vision, and hope to god you don't misclick anything and send your unit off in the wrong direction, with no option to undo (Which can happen freuquently because...) Selecting units is a huge pain. You can of course click on their name in your army list on the side of the screen... which is hidden from view most of the time while controlling a unit, or you can click the actual unit, which is as fiddly as it gets, if you accidentally select the wrong unit, you can proceed to accidentally move it where you didn't want it to go as you try to pick the right one.
Ultimately, Warmachine: Tactics is a game that could be great, it just needs more time and polish than even devoted fans are willing to give it.

I can't recommend this game, which is a shame, because the concept is excellent. I was compelled to buy Of Orcs & Men by the idea of your typical fantasy setting being inverted to the point where the orcs are the heroes and the humans are the barbaric oppressors/invaders. Unfortunately, the game tries WAY too hard to be funny, edgy, and gritty when all it really needed to do was be epic in the literal sense. I don't typically mind profanity, but the dialogue is so frought with cursing, sexual innuendo, and poor attempts at wit that it alternates between feeling forced and being downright juvenile. When it isn't being juvenile, the game is constantly going out of its way to remind you that this is the F--king GRIMDARK, and everything sucks. The humans are EVIL, man. The orcs are BADASS, dude. Essentially, everything in this game seems to be a charicature with little in the way of depth. This is extremely unfortunate given the incredible potential of the setting.
Less than an hour in, and I just can't play anymore. I really want to like this game, but I've seen enough. I might be willing to soldier on and hope that the dialogue and plot/character development improve, but the controls and gameplay also leave quite a bit to be desired. At the end of the day, this game just wasn't for me. There may be someone out there that would enjoy Of Orcs & Men...but I can't imagine them being older than twelve.

The visuals are great considering the original game was on the Nintendo 3DS, the campaign clocks in at about 5-7 hours, depending on skill/difficulty, the sound design is supurb, the atmosphere is spooky and the gameplay extremely challanging, which is a problem I found all the latest Resident Evil games were lacking, my main complaints would be the lack of puzzles, which is a main staple of Resident Evil games, the original trilogy were full of them and as the series continued you see less and less... and Zombies.. where the hell are the zombies?! and finally... the lack of Co-Op, you are followed 90% of the time by a partner... whos AI is terrible and pretty much useless, was Co-Op really that difficult to implement?
No Co-Op.. but we do have RAID mode, which is actually pretty awesome, lots of characters, weapons, mods and levels to gain on over 20+ stages, extremely fun with a friend and very challanging at times, lots of time will be spent in this mode, considering over 1/2 the achievments are for it.

When I first saw this, I thought it’d be just another cheap “Bullet Hell” game that doesn’t add anything to the genre. However, after playing it for the first time, I couldn’t stop and here’s why:
Pros:
♦ No bugs (Despite some reviews saying the game has bugs, I have played three hours and have not come across a bug)
♦ Awesome TV Effect that can be turned on and off (This is amazing for those who want to play Arcade Machine Retro Style, there is the choice to do so or not)
♦ Amazing Voice Overs (Every game should have Voice Overs and the Voice Overs in this fit the genre perfectly)
♦ Music and Sounds are eargasmic (The music isn’t distracting and really adds to the feel of the game and the sound effects also fit really well with the genre and game)
♦ Hitbox is on point (This has to have one of the best hitboxes I’ve seen in a “Bullet Hell” game)
♦ Graphics are awesome (Has that Retro, Arcade Machine, old-school look and feel to it which I find amazing in “Bullet Hell” games)
♦ Has Steam Trading Cards and Achievements (For the price of the game, the cards almost pay for the game and the achievements are easily gotten for just playing the game, there is no rocket science behind unlocking them)
♦ Worth the Price (You’ll get your monies worth easily if you enjoy classic “Bullet Hell” games and if you don’t the Steam Trading Cards will almost pay for the game)
♦ Decent number of game modes (If you want to play with lives you can, if you want to play with no lives you can, just versing bosses you can, easy or hard?, there’s a game mode almost for everyone)
♦ Randomness done well (Every time you play you’ll rarely get the same set of enemies, powerups or bosses twice in a row. For example, you play and die, then play again, you’ll have a different set of enemies, powerups and bosses etc)
♦ Number of powerups and enemy varients are great (Never know what you’re going to verse or get powerup wise each playthrough, which is decent)
♦ Mad Events keep the game interesting (Mad Events randomly happen and adds a whole new aspect to the game from just shooting enemies and killing bosses. These keep the game interesting)
♦ Controls seem responsive (From what I've played, I haven't noticed an issue with the controls not responding or feeling jerky)
Cons:
♦ Slow game launcher (Takes a long time to open the game client after clicking play)
♦ No in-game options (Can’t alter resolution, sound, graphics or change controls)
♦ Must use a controller to be able to player any sort of local co-op (This is annoying because you should be able to use the same keyboard, a second keyboard or anything. It shouldn’t be forced to a controller)
♦ Can’t change controls (I found the pre-set controls to be decent, however for those who want to change them for whatever reason can’t)
♦ Help menu could be improved (The help menu is bad as it doesn’t describe any of the in-game powerups, bosses, enemies, mad-events or anything except controls. Therefore, you must go in and figure everything out for yourself. Some people like figuring it out for themselves, others like to know before they go in. There should be the option)
♦ Some Mad Events are way harder than others (This is bad because there is no difficulty scaling of Mad Events. This means despite the mode chosen, for example, “Easy” mode rather than “Hard, you could get a really difficult Mad Event for your first Mad Event on “Easy” and a really easy one for your first Mad Event on “Hard” mode. Mad Events are random, but they should scale depending on the mode, level etc)
♦ Sometimes things blend into the background (This doesn’t happen too often, but it can happen depending on the spawns and how crazy the game gets)
Overall, despite there being a few cons, they are only minor and there are more pros. Therefore, this is one of the best Retro, Arcade Machine and Old-School styled “Bullet Hell” games with one of the best hit boxes that I’ve seen in a long time. Also, as you’ll get your monies worth whether you play it or just get the cards, I can recommend picking up a copy of this game at any price.

Been looking for a MMO that stands out for year and i have to say i finally found it.
PERKS of WildStar:
1) As a Free-To-Play player i found it really nice that i am able to buy items from the cash shop using omnibits currency (earned by jus playing the game and doing quests).
2) Also, there is a ton of content with each and every zone having a unique storyline that keeps you drawn to the game. There are also cutscenes and voiceovers for NPCs which make the game more immersive.
3) What i like most would definitely be the game interface as everything is very beginner friendly (from the quest markers that guide you to the npc and mobs to the mentoring system to allowed veteran players to play with newbies) Calling system from NPCs also saves u time so you wont have to travel back and fro to turn in quests.
4) The trading system in the game is also well thought out with the auction system to allow efficient and quick selling/buying of items without the need to spam the chat.
5) Players who like to decorate their houses will also find that there is a wide variety of commodities to choose from to create their dream home.
6) Crafting system ( TradeSkills) is also pretty decent with lots of variety to choose from, but i have yet to dwell into it.
7) Addons that are downloadable from web to allow customizations to interface or save time while grinding which is a really nice perk to the game.
10/10 would recommend this game to anyone who is searching for a F2P MMO to commit to as this is the one you are looking for. Its really sad that bcoz of it's bad start at launch, this caused the game to be underrated and overlooked by many. On a side note, looking forward to level up to 50 and start on world boss raids soon :)

Tldr: Great potential ruined by terrible decisions.
// In terms of progression, I finished the first playthrough and did one third of the second, which I think is enough to give my opinion. Even though the 3rd playthrough might be better, I shouldn't have to play two thirds of a 60 hours game to enjoy it \\
I'm not going to talk about the PC port, since I haven't run into game breaking problems myself, aside from the fact that I have to play it in windowed mode in order to reach 60 fps, which doesn't bother me anyway, and those who have actually had problems will talk about them better than I could.
However, I still would not recommend this game. if only for its very poor decisions in terms of gameplay and character narratives, but I'll come back to that, first let's review the positives:
Amazing Soundtrack, this has got to be the game's best attribute, and honestly it has some of the best video game musics I have heard in a while (and I've played Furi/Undertale recently, just to give you an idea). Not much else to say about that, if anything you should buy the soundtrack if they ever release it solo. The voice acting is also pretty good, even in English.
Graphically the game holds up pretty well, design-wise the machines are outstanding, they each have their own little tweeks which makes them unique, and they feel alive, which is the whole point of the game, so that's a resounding success on the part of the devs. I don't like the androids, I don't like the oversexualization of 2B, and I don't like the design of the two antagonists at all, but that's a matter of personal tastes, so I guess if you're into weab stuff you won't mind. The environments would gain to be a bit more original, but it still works, and that's fine by me.
And that's about it for the positives, as you can see, on the outside, it's great, but that's when you dive into details that you can feel the poor decision making that makes what could've been a masterpiece an overall mediocre game at best.
The gameplay: Nier can't seem to decide if it wants to be an A-RPG or a beat'em all, and it ends up being neither. On the RPG side it's got a leveling system and chips that you can insert into your character to modify the gameplay a bit and give you that little power boost you might need, but it all feels like power creeping. I like the idea of being able to take away informations from your HUD to gain more power, but the chips all feel like the same. Aside from a few useful ones that will actually affect the gameplay like the deadly heal, the shockwaves, the overclock or the auto use item, the rest is just "more damage", "more defense", "more speed" and things like that, which feels kind of underwhelming. On the other hand, the beat'em all part is really basic, two buttons (one with 9S), 2 combos depending on your weapons (literally, nothing more) and a shoot mechanic that feels like it could've been automatic considering how little it asks of the player gameplay wise (just press the button and lock the enemies with the camera while hitting them, woooh, so subtle), a dodge, and that's it. No crazy combos, no chains like in Bayonetta, nothing subtle, just basic button mashing and dodging until the enemies die. By the way in normal difficulty, the game is incredibly easy, so if you're used to these types of games, you might want to try the harder settings from the start.
9S: Oh boy, this guy deserves an entire section altogether. His gameplay is basically everything I said above minus one button and with a hacking minigame that feels like it's been taken out of a game from the 90s and patched on to Nier Automata because they didn't have any idea on how to actually make a hacking game feel compelling. And that wouldn't be a problem if the hacking was secondary, a few sessions here and there just to diversify the game, but it's not. Considering how weak 9S is in combat, you actually have to hack your way into almost every single pack of enemy in the game, which can really be a pain. Don't get me wrong, the minigame isn't hard, in fact it's almost too easy, but it's just soo boring and cuts out the action entirely. Too bad, considering that the consequences of that game (controlling the machines, making them blow up...) were actually a pretty nice addition to the gameplay.
The rythm: That is for me the biggest fault of the game. It doesn't know how to create tension or anything really when it comes to storytelling. Everytime I feel like it's finally going to become interesting, like the story might actually make me think about deep philosophical problems, it throws a giant robot or a cliché villain to my face to remind me that I'm playing an anime ripoff, it's exhausting, and frustrating. It's almost like the game tried to hide what it really is because it was ashamed of itself, or afraid that cynic people might think it's not deep enough. Please, I want more Jean-Paul, I want more existentialism, and I don't want to have to play 30 hours of boring gameplay just to get that in the 3rd playthrough, which apparently is better.  I might as well read Sartre directly, it'll be easier.
Overall I don't think Nier is a bad game, I just think it's an alright game that could've been great, and that is maybe the worst crime of all for a work of art: ruined potential.

It is immediately evident that Cococucumber’s Planet of the Eyes is indebted to the success of Limbo. The cold open, the parallax art style, and the first puzzle involving a runaway boulder, are all indisputably intended to conjure comparisons to Playdead’s pivotal release. What isn’t as apparent from the beginning, though, is that Planet of the Eyes is not a response but a reflection; the other side of Limbo’s macabre coin, only fully recognizable when both are placed in context with one another.
In all matters concerning play, Planet of the Eyes is a direct replication of Limbo’s death-obsessed puzzle platforming. Movement is weighty and momentum driven, with shallow jumps and harrowing ledge grabs giving way to a feeling of intense gravity and powerlessness. The fragility of Limbo’s protagonist is also echoed in Planet of the Eyes through how relentlessly the environment attempts to kill you (and often succeeds at doing so in brutal fashion). Here, however, is where Planet of the Eyes began to feel odd, the reproduction showing flaws and dissimilarities that couldn’t be accounted for when viewing it as directly analogous to Limbo.
Limbo, at its more fundamental level, is about death. Death is everywhere, a horrific inevitability that can be circumvented for a time but is ultimately circulatory and perpetual. Progress can often only be made through death, as many obstacles are impossible to perceive until they have taken your life at least once. Even to the end, Limbo makes no illusions to hope or even relief through death’s finality. In Limbo, you live to die, a cycle with no branches or purpose. It is aggressively bleak, and the horrors inflicted upon its young boy protagonist unrelenting.
Planet of the Eyes, for as much as it mirror’s Limbo’s mechanics, is wholly antithetical to that game’s hopelessness. Death is still prevalent and unpredictable, but Planet of the Eyes doesn’t fixate or even really recognize it has occurred. The narration doesn’t stop, the upbeat techno soundtrack keeps playing, and the marvelous alien colors become no less vibrant. This may seem a small distinction, perhaps even an excusable oversight, but there is an inherent optimism throughout Planet of the Eyes which seems to affirm its contrasts with Limbo are intentional. You are not Dante descending into the Hell, but Indiana Jones marveling at a lost civilization. Planet of the Eyes is meant to be beautiful and enthralling, wondrous in its peculiarities and otherworldliness as deadly as it is captivating.
Planet of the Eyes even begins to recognize its tonal divergence from Limbo in its final act, in which the narrator effectively states outright what has been implied up to that point. I would argue against such an overt sub-textual acknowledgment, but given the video game industry’s tendency toward surface comparisons and generalizations, it almost feels necessary that Planet of the Eyes make plain that it is not attempting to repeat Limbo but deconstruct and invert its themes. It is not uncommon for games to take cues from the successes of others, but these often take the form of gameplay conventions or genre choice. It is much rarer to see a game like Planet of the Eyes, which rather than try to usurp its inspiration by recreating it wholesale, finds a way to meaningfully alter its thematic framework and in doing so turn the experience and our understanding of it on its head.

Warmachine Tactics has a lot going for it, and a lot holding it back.
First, the negative: production values are inconsistent. A lot of still portraits, and in many cases, still models in cutscenes whose mouth's don't move while they talk. Various UI glitches that may force you to skip unit activations. Scripted events throughout the campaign make it less about tactics, and more about just getting through the mission. No saving mid-level (this means if you don't have at least an hour or so each mission, you are likely to lose a lot of progress if you have to stop playing).
Despite all of that, there are a lot of good things about Warmachine Tactics. A unique world, setting and units based on the award winning tabletop game: WARMACHINE. The rules and interactions are very deep with many different things to consider throughout a match. There is an unlimited amount of replayability as unit selection and opponent choices make it so no two matches are exactly alike.
If you are willing to look past various annoyances in the production of the game, this title has a lot of excellent tactical wargaming to be had. Anyone who is a fan of grid-based strategy games would be remiss to not give this game a chance.

The story is tight, well paced (for the most part), and interesting: I've killed thousands of orcs and goblins over the years, and so it was fun to play as two of the "bad guys" on a mission to kill the human emperor.  The main characters are well written (despite the unnecessary profanity) and their reluctant team dynamic is fun.  The gameplay is the best part: building out both characters into the rolls I chose for them (it's clear there are several viable combinations of builds) was satisfying.  Neither character can succeed on its own so designing and implementing a team strategy was rewarding, and the challenge on normal was just right.  Each encounter felt like a discrete combat puzzle, and so I didn't mind that the levels were, almost without exception, linear pathways from one encounter to the next because I looked forward to the next encounter.  The graphics do the job: sometimes pretty, sometimes ugly, usually just fine.  The music is sparse, but has character.  The supporting cast is, for the most part, poorly acted, which is the only truly disappointing aspect of the game.
In sum, if you want a combat focused RPG with two likable characters and an interesting story, and can excuse the small budget presentation, this game is definitely worth the 12-15 hours it takes to finish.

The core gameplay is battle heavy,  and relies on you selecting skills to use in a Baldur's Gate/Dragon Age kind of way, which is awkward since the rest of the game sets it up to be a third-person beat 'em up. Since you have to pick every skill by hand (or set up to 9 to a hotkey), each battle wears on your nerves. On harder difficulties, it's not clear what tactic to use against who, basically making you use all of the skills and hope something sticks. Of Orcs and Men tries, but doesn't quite get its main aspects right. And that makes it quite a disappointment.

Criminally underrated RPG, but then I can't say it's for everyone.
What I loved: The story, the setting, the character interaction. It has a very captivating world with a pretty good mythology, and the two main characters are among the most memorable in any recent game I've played. The relationship between Arkhail and Styx feels very genuine —you really get to care about those two.
The downside: The combat system is quite a bit loose, the AI is stupid. The combat mechanics consist in pausing, choosing targets, queueing attacks and abilities, and constantly switching between Arkhail and Styx, making sure their actions complement each other. It works for the most part but it's not very refined and you can bump into some pretty frustrating moments as a result. The way certain fights are designed doesn't help too much either, and if you leave the AI to make its own decisions (by only focusing on one character, that is), you'll be screwed most of the time. It's far from being unplayable, but I can see these problems turning off a lot of people.
It's a flawed game, but a very charming one. Recommended if you think you can get past the somewhat flimsy combat and you don't mind its linear, basic design.

This game is one of the greatest underappreciated gems I have had the pleasure of finding in a long time. There are obvious things that sully the experience a bit, but given this is the effort of small studio on a tight budget these aren't hard to look past.
The story takes a twist on typical fantasy by having orcs being oppressed and subjegated by humans, and in light of this, your main character is on a quest to kill the emperor who seeks to unite elves and dwarves against "the greenskins."
The main character is Arkail, or the "butcher" as he has been dubbed after a bloody masacre in his past. What's great here is that this story element actually works into the gameplay. As you take damage your rage meter builds, and if you don't use skills to keep your calm he becomes enraged. In this state, he more powerful but reckless and uncontrollable, attacking foes in random order.
Evening this out is his original odd couple partner in crime, Styx. He is a goblin assassin, the only one of his race who can speak or display any intelligence at all. He causes bleeds, poisons and lowers defense in combat, and out of combat he small stealth sections where he dispatches as many soldiers as he can before things eventually fall to pieces.
The story is well surprisingly well written considering every other line of dialogue has a swear word, because it fits into the narrative and general feeling of the story. I was honestly surprized at myself when I started the characters, admiring the way the duo chirped eachother and eventually grew into a like-minded friendship. Combat slows down when you pause so you can plan each of their actions, and everything works quite well. The graphics are nice enough and the game has a surprizingly good soundtrack that hits all the right notes when a sad or intense situation takes rise.
Sadly, there are some issues, though they are just a lot of nitpicks that don't effect the solid feel of gameplay. Character models don't sync up in most cutscenes, a weapon constantly floats in air against Ark's back, voice acting apart from the main duo is largely sub-par. You are told of great battles going on in other places due to what's happening in the story and can't be there because the game's budget wouldn't allow it, and some people might not like how the stealth sections work. You essentially sneak around and kill guards in order of which would be able to see the act from their FOV, the ai will walk past dead bodies without raising alarm which seems silly but is also necessary to that element of gameplay. This is a stop motion turn based rpg first, the stealth is more like a small minigame that you are never actually forced to do that makes fights easier.
Past that, there are a bunch of sidequests which never feel pointless as the duo banter and you find out more meaningful things about the story. I'm not usually someone who likes sidequests but it worked well for me. You have a mission hub in different zones and when you pick a mission it is generally linear except for a few hidden treasures. There's a couple of choices to be made in the game that have small outcomes on story, but nothing with permanance.
All and all, the flaws take you out of the experience in a small fathom but do little to stop this extremely charming game from taking your heart. The prequel, Styx:Master of shadows is out soon, and I can't wait to delve again into this world again, and see how much the studio has grown since their time between the titles.
9/10   There's nitpicks, but the story, the gameplay and the pacing are all great and a low budget doesn't change that.
Edit: Fixed a couple errors, special thanks to Snapfit for calling me out on goofing the main character's name and thanks for all the positive feedback on my review.

"Of Orcs and Men" puts you in the shoes of the traditional bad guys, for a surprisingly gripping game. The linear progression wasn't particularly noticeable, to me, because of the excellent/difficult combat and the witty banter.
It did take me a little while to get into it, but it's worth persevering. This isn't a game where you can button mash, you have to pay attention to what is happening in combat and switch tactics on the fly. There is a handy pause feature, allowing you to queue skills, but it doesn't slow down the feel of the action.
If you enjoy stories from a different perspective (Orcs series by Stan Nicholls for example), or enjoy tactical combat, give this a try. Once you get past the initial learning curve, you are sure to love this game as much as I do.

Excellent graphics, fluid movement, a great combat system, but an over-complicated UI and poorly explained quests leads to frustration instead of fun.  I have to say I didn't get very far in to the game, because of the constant frustration with the quests. Now, it's true to say that I don't like games with a steep learning curve, but I found that Wildstar redefined steep. Time and time again you are left confused as to what it wants you to do. It repeatedly fails to explain the most basic information and the over-complicated UI just serves to confuse even more. It completely destroys the flow of the game and constantly interrupts the action, because you have to try to find a safe area to work out what on earth you are supposed to be doing next. A few simple quests can take a silly amount of time because you are constantly running in and out of safe/danger areas to sort out what's going on. Even in training missions it often completely neglected vital information that left you guessing.
Another really annoying point is that the auto-compass ( the thing that points to a quest target for you ) switches off after a few seconds, so you have to keep stopping to activate it again. Again, not a good idea when you are in a combat zone.
I would recommend you try it, because everything else about the game is great, and you may find the quest system OK, but for me I am afraid that it was a very short-lived game. A game either grabs you or it doesn't, and I am afraid, for me, Wildstart didn't.  I'm eally disappointed, becuase it look glorious, and the mechanics of the game really are excellent.

I don't play new games very often, and one's that cost $60 even less. Having read the reviews, I thought that this one might meet my expectations for a solid and unique storyline, with some fast paced gameplay and RPG elements thrown in. Unfortunately, I was dissapointed yet again. This game was nothing more than a gimicky 50 hour timesuck that left me feeling ripped off.
On the plus side, I think the combat was fairly engaging and fast paced, and that didn't really chang throughout the game, which I think is a credit to the developer. Additionally, the graphics fit the gameworld well, and were wello complimented by an oustanding musical score which I thoroughly enjoyed. Unfortunately, the cons far outweigh the pros for me.
First, let's start with the gimicks which add a fair chunk of time to the game.
Gimick #1: Late 1980's Arcade Style fighter pilot gameplay
You'll spend probably about an hour's worth of gametime flying around in a linear box as enemy fighter pilots come at you shooting little balls of energy from a variety of angles. Not only is it completely boring and incredibly outdated, but it is also not at all challenging. You have to be a complete moron to die during any of these scenes no matter what the difficulty is. Waste of time that adds nothing to the game.
Gimick #2: Early 90's SNES ShadowRun inspired Hacking minigames
Hacking is always an interesting element to add to gameplay, but by and large, the hacking requirements in this game didn't even make sense. There are only a handful of enemies in the game you would really want to hack, and 90% of the hacking in the game will involve you "hacking" treasure chests that have chains on them. How does that begin to make sense? More importantly, the hacking mini-games require no brains or ingenuity at all. Instead, you are EXPECTED to die over and over again, because its impossible to know where enemies are until you've gone through the minigame several times.
Gimick #3: 26 different endings, most of which last 5 seconds and are junk
While it sounds good, multiple endings in this game consist of gimicky nonsense. I'm all about the fine details in a game, so although I think it's cool that you can kill your character by removing their Operating System chip and get an "ending", its also pure fraud to tell anyone this game has 26 real endings. Additionally, this leads people to believe that they actually have choices that impact the ending of the game. This is not the case.
Gimick #4: Multiple playthroughs
I think its great when games allow you to play through again with maxed out equipment and levels. This is something that many games have done well, allowing you to unlock new game elements, if you want to. In the case of Nier Automata, you are REQUIRED to play the game all over again in order to unlock critical elements of the storyline. That's just altogether cheap.
Other issues I had with this game:
This game gives the sense of an open world, but is actually very linear. I'll give credit to the developers for creating a stunning environment, but it is also entirely too small, and the tiny environment doesn't lend itself well to a storyline which involves the entire planet.
The variety of weapons is abysmally small, and frankly you can go through the entire game with your starting weapon just fine. There is little incentive to swap weapons. Additionally, the crafting system is plain weird. Why would I need items like tree sap and plant seeds in order to upgrade my robot drone? How does that even begin the make sense? Upgrading weapons is equally nonsensical.
The game doesn't reward the player for searching around the environment. There are treasure chests all over the place, but 90% of the time they contain minor healing items. And because you have to go through an annoying minigame each time you want to open one,  you just stop bothering altogether.
Character development in the game is weak, but that is attributable to the multiple playthrough aspect involved with unlocking the storyline. If you were to play through the game 3-4 times, you would have a much deeper understanding of what's going on, but that is a really cheap and gimicky way of bringing a game to life.
Finally, when you're done with the game, it just leaves you feeling empty. You realize that, by the very nature of the story, everything you just did was completely purposeless. If the first game was anything like this one, I can't think of a reason it ever had a following. The crap philosophy of the primary developer is very obvious from the story.
All in all, I would say this game is worth $20 based on its good elements.

Preamble: I have personally not really been bothered by any of the issues i've heard about the PC port. I usually play my games in windowed (effectively borderless in this) all the time, so I haven't noticed the odd banding or resolution issues mainly.
That being said... oh my god. This game is beautiful. And I don't mean in a sense that the images on the screen have high fidelity... I mean that this game, as a piece of art, is truly the most beautiful game I have ever played. Words cannot exactly describe this game in enough detail, nor can it do it justice - which is exactly why it succeeds as a video game and not some other form of media. This would not work as a book or a movie... you simply go on an emotional rollercoaster along with this tragically beautiful world of NieR: Automata, while traditional gaming standards are challenged and broken.
The gameplay itself is fun, fluid and fast-paced. A nice thing to point out is literally anyone of any skill level can play this game and enjoy it. Easy gives you access to special upgrades that essentially give you a hand in controlling your character (auto-evading and auto-attacking), normal and hard are fairly challenging (though not in a frusterating way), and very hard exists for those hardcore players who aim to fight enemies without getting hit at all. The game has a clever way of tieing mechanics into the narrative as well. You always have the ability to attack NPCs just as fluidly as you always fight, even during semi-cinematic moments where they beg for mercy, but choosing to stay your hand in the face of non-hostiles sometimes yields interesting results. Sometimes, it is not even that obvious that an NPC is friendly or non-hostile. Then the question arises, should you even spare these non-hostile enemies? Your companion will point out that leaving some of them around can be dangerous. And they might just be.
You may hear of the various endings/playthroughs of the game and think (do I really have to beat this game x many times to see the whole story?). I'd challenge the wording of "playthrough" however, and instead suggest you look at them as "chapters" or "acts" of the game. It is MUCH more than just a New Game+ mechanic. After you load your game following the initial ending and credits, you will quickly see that things are much different. Yes, you are seeing the same story through another character and some things may repeat, but you will also see and have access to many things you didn't your first run through. And by the way, your third "playthrough" will not even be the same story at that point. Yes... you essentially are playing an entirely new storyline at that point, so even if you think you know what is coming... you don't. This sense of "oh... there's more?" ended up extending the game another 40 hours for me. And I don't just mean in side content. The main story is honestly rich and worthwhile, while side quests are not overbearing and even serve to enhance the main quest.
tl;dr
If you aren't into narrative... well this game isn't for you. Otherwise... prepare for a really weird... and really satisfying ride.

This could become a great game. The ships are fairly realistic, and the maps, despite lacking true distinctions, are easy to navigate and understand from a strategic point of view. There are a couple modes to choose from: capture the objective, deathmatch, and single-player vs. AI. The maps diversify this rather dearth selection by varying the amount of objectives among the CTF maps and matches, but not by any appreciable degree.
Unfortunately, the game is marred by some major problems: a poor balancing system, long wait times to get into a match, and a confusing ranking system. Matches usually involve a great deal of trying to outmaneuver ships bigger and more powerful than your own (mostly the BBs including higher tier destroyers and cruisers) while also attempting to swat away smaller destroyers and subs chasing you. Sometimes you'll get placed on a server where the players work together, but most of the time teamwork is constrained to the people who you play with and constrained to the layout of the map. The great thing about the game is the radio feature where you can just talk to your teammates without the need to hook up on teamspeak (or equivalent service). Yet, even cooperative play sometimes is a moot value due to the ships you choose and the ships go up against and, unfortunately, connection problems.
The time to get onto a server can take as little as a few seconds, or, in some unlucky circumstances, upwards of five minutes. Despite that, the wait time isn't so much long as it is unpredictable. If you aren't part of a fleet (squad), you will have a difficult time pairing up with friends in matches. The matches are assembled based on the types and the amounts of ships in que, so this affects the wait time for matches.
Unfortunately, the "ranking" system is rather unintuitive, fragmented and disconnected from the acquisition of better ships and equipment. Player rank, or renown, relies on a consistent play time to calculate. Basically, if you only play the game sporadically, your renown won't increase very much or at all, and every so often the game resets player rank. This can be helpful in gauging your efficiency, but it can also be misleading in the long run if you play well yet play infrequently.
The game does have an "EXP" awarded feature, which is thankfully a good aspect of the ranking system to have since it is based on the work you put into a battle. You can use it to unlock new ships. However, it has a separate currency system used to pay for unlocking new ships.
Silver is one of those currencies. Gold and merits are two other types as well. Silver and merit are understandable features. They are used to resupply and repair your ships (silver), and level up your commanders, among other things (merit), but gold is just a fancy credit system using your own money. I understand that some players are more than willing to pay a little something for a free-to-play game, and I understand that it's awesome to help developers out this way when they don't ask for much. However, if you are truly dedicated to ranking up and acquiring better ships in the game, I think that players should be given the opportunity to earn those features by actually playing the game, not paying for it. If the devs need money, they should probably put a price on the game. Paying to win is rather cheap, in my book. Really didn't plan on reviewing, but noticed a lot of people asking if this is worth $15 on sale. Short version - definitely yes. Now onto specifics...
Offline modes are very much improved. Expansion teams for MyGM/MyLeague, with expansion draft of course, and customization options for those are really cool, for example if you're looking to create a legitimate historic team court and things, you can actually get pretty close using just in-game editor. Only bad part is that you can only create 2 custom jerseys (home and away) per team. MyCareer is a vast improvement over last year, specifically due to absence of the Spike Lee story. There's a new "story" so to speak, it irks some people, but it's not too bad and you still have control over the entire season. One downside is due to new player archetypes, you're effectively reduced to a role player even when you reach your maximum. Personally I can still hit triple-double average on Hall of Fame difficulty with my primary player, but the new stat caps severely limit the player potential. Ironically, you can't at all play some of the iconic player archetypes such as true all-around, 3 and D, or Dunker/Defensive Specialist.
Online modes on PC are... disgusting. First off there's a smaller player base, so you're bound to run into some queue times, or a completely dead queue very late in the night. Also, the game is susceptible to cheats, for example, only couple of months ago they blocked one particular cheat from MyTeam auction house, which was blatantly obvious and apparent and had very bad impact on economy. I won't go into details here as I don't want to be seen as advertising cheating, but I think it's very obvious they are weak on the ban hammer side, and the game itself is weak on protection. Also there is the unavoidable server lag for online modes, couple of sources close to the company explained that all servers are in Virginia, US, even the EU or Asian servers.
Gameplay is improved over the last year, primary addition being various types of Pick and Roll defenses, you can literally see different teams using different defenses and things like that. However I feel it's important to note that stock difficulty settings are sorely lacking in realism/simulation aspect. They are all very much arcade. However, there are lot of simulation slider settings listed at OperationSports for example, and once you tweak them, the game really shines. Of course, there are still couple of bad animations that can't be completely avoided, but custom sliders help out a lot in this regard. I should note that by default MyCareer doesn't allow custom slider settings, but there's a mod tool that can be used to accomplish this.
Graphics of course you can easily see in any random gameplay video - they are obviously improved over last year(s). One part that sort of falls into this category that is dramatically worse are the replays. About 50% of the time, the replay will use the silly rim camera, and you won't be able to see the play at all.
In summary, as you can probably tell from the hours I played, I find this to be a great game, not like we really have a choice on PC when it comes to basketball. After thoroughly playing most of the game modes (except Play Now Online & All Star Team-Up), I'd easily recommend this to any basketball fan. However, keep in mind that online modes can be very frustrating, and if that's your primary reason for purchasing, it might be wise to wait and see how 2k18 turns out in that regard.

Pretty decent game. The artwork and environments are beautiful, but level design doesn't seem too well thought out. There's a lot of walking down hallways without much to do lacking even character dialogue to entertain you.
Combat is very good. I really enjoyed the different skills that were available and the strategy that came into play in most battles. And you have to employ the strategic menu during battles or you will fail.
Which is where combat was annoying. Most of the difficult battles occure immediately after a long cutscene which means if you die (and you very likely will again, and again, and again) you have to go through the cutscene (again and again and again). You can skip by pressing Esc repeatedly, but it's just incredibly frustrating. Also, the battles aren't very well balanced. I breezed through most of the game on easy so that I could enjoy the story, but then cam across maybe 3 battles that took me forever to get through. I almost just quit the game and gave up it was that frustrating.
Anyway, voice acting was good and engaging but the script seemed quite stilted at points. The characters swore a lot, which I don't mind, it just seemed overdone to me and came across as the writers using swear words more as a publicity stunt rather than for dramatic emphasis. Maybe that's just me.
The storyline and characters were great. Kept me interested for the duration of the game and I really enjoyed watching how the main two characters developed and got to know eachother as the game progressed.
AI was a little messed up (which was also frustrating). If you ever leave one of the characters to do their own thing for a bit during combat, they are bound to do something stupid, like target the guy furthest away so they run past every other enemy and get killed on the way. Or sometimes they'll just stand there and you can't tell why. You've given them commands to carry out, you're pretty sure they haven't been stunned, but they're not responding to anything.
Also, the still warm corspe of a soliders friend is apparently an everyday sight, cause they won't do anything about it. You can kill 10 people and then watch a patrol just walk over their bodies and go on their way without raising an alarm or even breaking stride. Not a game breaker, but weird for a modern game. It does make stealth assassinations a piece of cake.
My recommendation. Play it on easy just for the sake of the story, otherwise the long hallways, frustrating battles and inconsistent AI aren't worth the effort.

After playing some Endless Space 2, I came into this game expecting an improvement. I've never played any Paradox games, but I know they are widely regarded as cohesive and rich 4X-style grand strategy. However, I was pretty disappointed by this experience. The lack of intuitive UI combined with a clunky, unclear tutorial made the initial rounds feel confusing and slow. It started to speed up a bit towards the middle, but after 30 hours I had to quit when faced with a large-scale war between myself and a 4-faction federation. It would have taken eons. The whole late-game is just a frustrating grind. Fleet development is incredibly arduous, and the management is not much better, especially with the stupid AI decision-making during wars. The battles look good and feel fair within a system, but the inter-system movement system is just clunky. The research upgrades often felt useless, particularly weaponry, and the traditions should probably just reallocated to be research upgrades. Also, the outposts system is annoying to use, because you often need to get rid of them to recuperate your tiny influence income, but guess what? It will silently knock out any system that is now outside your reach, eliminating all your stations there! There's no way to tell how much reach you'll lose, so you better spam the save button!
The worst part of all is the inconsistent, poorly labeled UI makes it damn near impossible to play smoothly. You can't easily select an inhabited planet (only by mapping a specific planet to your numeric hotkey, max 10). You can't manipulate open windows. It's not always clear what's selected, or if there are free slots to build more. Half the learning experience is a toss-up of right-clicking, hovering and looking at the complaints of similarly confused players on the Paradox forums.
I imagine the UI is very close to how it is in CK / EU. Might work fine there, but honestly creates an experience of horrid tedium. Overall, didn't have fun. I'd recommend Endless Space 2 if you really need to play a space 4X.

You don't need to try anything more than the game's demo on Steam to see how bad the game is. By default the graphics are set to "medium" or something, which means all characters, the terrain and the characters' portraits are extremely blurry which stands in stark contrast with the pixel-crisp GUI. The game was probably optimized for tiny screens, like 640x480 or something, as on my 1920x1080 the GUI elements are tiny and are scattered in the edges of the screen. The level minimap, for example, is smaller than a single soldier when viewed from max zoom out.
Even after I set all graphical settings to maximum and restarted the game, everything was still blurry. There might be something wrong in their shaders code or whatever, but all objects are too glossy and too bright, with large spots of plain white on many objects. The tutorial text is written in huge blurry font. Tutorial messages tell about what on-screen buttons do but at the same time the whole GUI is hidden, so you don't know what they are talking about. You will stop understanding the explained game mechanics about 1/3 into the tutorial. After that you will keep clicking the highlighted areas/buttons with no clue what's going on. Obviously the developers never tested the tutorial on anyone except themselves. The cutscenes are ugly and some of them can't be skipped. E.g. I wanted to exit the game during an endless cutscene, and the dialog to confirm exiting was there, but when you press "Yes" (yes, please exit) it just hangs. This was the last straw for me.
My guess is that 90% of people who try the demo will exit it and uninstall it right after the tutorial stops showing its messages and lets you finish the first mission by yourself. Or rather, most will exit even before the tutorial shows anything, after seeing the super-blurry font.
All that said, the combat system seems to be pretty interesting (from what I could understand) and feels like something between XCOM Enemy Unknown and The Banner Saga. It's a pity that this promising system got such an atrocious implementation.

That's when I knew that this game is truly a masterpeice and my personal favorite of all time. That's really all I have to say for now. Keeping this as short as possible:
First of all, there are multiple story routes in the game, so once you finish the first one, A route, you'll get access to the rest of the routes. So far I've only finished the A route and it took me roughly 18 hours to finish the first route, so the game has quite a lot to offer. However, the main mission part in the route A was a little bit too short, meaning that once you start to have fun with it, it suddenly ends.
As for the gameplay itself, there's really nothing to comblain. Platinum Games knows how to make good battle mechanics and they don't let you down this time either.
For the other gameplay mechanics, there are several different weapon types that you can obtain and each weapon type changes the way you fight. You can also find loot from the world or item drops from the fallen enemies, which you can then use to upgrade your weapons, skills and pods. Pods are basically your second half in the game, allowing you to use range attacks and different variety of powerful skills.
Graphically the game looks decent, though the color scheme makes it sometimes hard to graps your surroundings.
Pros:
+ Gameplay/Battle mechanics
+ Beautiful to watch and listen
+ No autosave function
+ Multiple storylines
+ Characters
Cons;
- Main mission in the "A Route" is little bit too short
- Small delay in subtitles (annoying if you play with Japanese voice acting like I did)
- Boss mechanics little bit too easy and predictable for my taste
- Color scheme
- Makes you desire for sequel
Do I recommend:
Yes. If you've ever played the previous games from the Platinum Games and liked them, you'll like this one too. And even if you're new to Platinum Games titles, this game is a good start to make your acquaintance on them.
