So AMD finally got around to updating their drivers to fix the issues with this game, right after I write a review (totally not a rant) about their problems of course. Now there is no reason not to get this game, unless you have a GTX 780 or 780ti, because those cards still have problems.
This is probably my favorite singleplayer game of all time. The story is enthralling, the characters develop in interesting ways throughout the story, the music is phenomenal, the combat is satisfying, and the locations are stunning.
To start with, the story. This game is technically a sequel, but no knowledge of the original is required to appreciate this game, and beyond a couple of references there aren't many links between the two. Automata takes place thousands of years after the original, in fact. In NieR:Automata you play as an Android that is fighting endless numbers of robots to reclaim the Earth so humanity can come back from the moon. Why is humanity on the moon? Aliens. But seriously, humanity fled to the moon when the aliens created robots to wipe them out. Sounds a little complicated? It gets better, but I am not going to spoil anything here. As a sidenote, if you get this game, and you get to an ending, it isn't the end of the game. In reality, both Ending A and B are breaks in the story, while Endings C, D, and E are the alternate actual endings. F through Z are either jokes of some sort or because of a mistake you make in the story. Each time you get an ending, it will put a letter on your save file then let you go back to your last save, or in A and B it will start the next section of the story.
Next, the character development. This is obviously a byproduct of events in the story, so anything specific would be a pretty large spoiler. Lets just say that some pretty major changes happen in the way characters behave both to eachother and overall. The side characters from various quests are interesting as well, one example being some characters that link to the original. These plots are still good without playing the original NieR though.
The music is another mind-blowing element of this game. This soundtrack has such a wonderful variety of tracks that I think fit with every part of the story. NieR:Automata is one of the few games that I have stopped to listen to the area music, and some songs are so dazzling that I bought the soundtrack and listen to them even when i'm not playing the game. The various boss songs and character themes are superb as well.
Admittedly the combat is probably the weakest part of this game. I personally think it is satisfying, but I can understand if someone doesn't like it. It is simple, compared to a game like Bayonetta or others in this class. There aren't tons of unique combos, and even the number of weapons is somewhat small. What it falls behind on in combos is the crispness of animation and the gratification that comes with that. The few weapon types that are in the game do provide some variety of attack set as well.
Finally, the locations. They aren't very specifc about what they are, so there isn't any connection to a present day setting. They are beautiful though, and there are enough of them. Though the first 2 endings take place in the same area with enemies being similar, the third set of endings adds some new areas for the story to progress in, with the final area being my personal favorite in the end, even if the story is a bit sad.
Now that the driver issues have been fixed, there is no reason not to buy this game. My last serious issue is gone, and yours should be too. If you can't be convinced to buy a game based on its merit in the categories that actually matter like story and gameplay, what is the point of reading reviews? Go buy NieR:Automata.

One of the best and original games I´ve played in  a long while. The story was captivating, the music gave me chills, the combat, well, I would describe it as the thinking mans dragon age. It obviously had flaws, the biggest was that there was too little of everything. I finished it in about 13 hours and am left dreaming of a sequel.
I noticed this game just around the time it came out, but  waited with a buy until it was discounted and sat on it for even longer as I had read so much negative feedback beforehand. I wish I could go back in time, buy it at release to support the studio, and get on the barricades to defend it against all the flaming. I can understand a lot of the critisicm, however I think it all boils down to this game being unaccessable to a lot of people due to the challenge of the combat system, and the game being marketed in a way that perhaps fooled people it was a more action-oriented game with a bigger budget. The trailer kind of looked like gears of war with orcs, to be honest.
I could write a lot about this game but will just summarize the main points;
I enjoyed the combat, allthough a little unforgiving at some points, it did let me think up different tactics for different battles. The skills were fun and there were a few easier patches that let you feel powerful. Gear managment was a little thin but worked okay. Leveling your characters was business as usual with stat and skill points, with some new intresting bits such as deflection and stability. The game looks and plays beautifully. Encountered only a few minor glitches (perhaps it has been patched a bit?). Voice acting quality varied throughout the game from excellent (main characters) to crappy, but I only disliked a few of the actors.
The bad? "Corridor running" which I did not really mind, as I enjoyed the combat and the quests.
Slow paced combat, so be prepared if you don´t like that sort of thing. Lack of in-game cinematics or at least more cinematic finishes to some of the more epic events, which left some anti-climatic feelings at parts. And in the end, a lack of budget? If there would have been some more time and resources to flesh more stuff out, this could have been a dragon age killing tripple A.
I can´t help but picturing a sequel of magnitude, with deeper tactical combat, different character choices, a more open world with continuation of the story.
If you enjoy tactical RPG´s - a must play, if you came here looking for an action game, you should probably head back.
As for me?  Would marry/10.

Purely from a writing standpoint, this is one of the most overlooked gems in the RPG genre. If you love story driven RPGs, I highly suggest considering this game. Tons of games talk about "Mature Themes" but this one really hits that nail on the head, and not just from the adult language (which there's a lot of). It covers racism, slavery, political ambition, violence, and betrayal. I felt both of the main characters were well written and it was interesting to see how their interactions with each other evolved as the story progressed.
Now onto the actual game systems.
The combat system isn't going to be everyone's cup of tea. It's just like Game of Thrones, super slow mow where you can queue up 4 moves for each character. If you haven't played GoT, it's like KOTOR but without the actual pause. Difficulty of combat spikes a bit too and can be pretty hard when you don't get assassinations done before hand.
The game is really linear and there's almost no exploration. There's a handful of side quests but, they need to be done right then and there. Maps are very railroady with minimal hallway detours to find an occasional goody.
Each hero has 2 full trees and another tree split in half to work together/class specialty. It's by no means one of the most flexible systems in the genre but, it is far better than many others.
Game also isn't a huge, 40+ hour epic. I would expect 10-25 hours depending on difficulty with combat.

Steel Ocean is my favorite game. Prior to this, I played numerous first person shooters.
To become great at this game will require skills which you will build upon as soon as you begin sinking enemy ships. The ships are modeled after warships built from the early 20th century to the end of World War II, including submarines, aircraft carriers, destroyers, light cruisers, heavy cruisers, and battleships.
One of the worst problems with other shooters is that new players do not stand a chance against veteran players. Steel Ocean has made numerous changes which greatly benefit new players, such as eliminating much of the grind to build up your ships and their crew. Less grind makes it easier than it's ever been for any new player to acquire the ships, equipment, captains and crew needed to become a veteran player and compete against the best.
The biggest problem with the game is that despite its' superiority over similar games there is little to no advertisement, so the player base is small. However, despite having a low population, waiting for a match to get underway is usually anywhere from 2 seconds to 4 minutes depending on the tier (level) of the ship, and the ship type. As you build up your personal fleet of ships, you'll be queueing for higher level matches which might take longer depending on the time of day/night, but by then you will know how to queue for faster matches.
Learning how to play is a bit difficult, but not intimidating. The playerbase has created guides and videos, and many veteran players are helpful, and the discussion forum on Steam is also a good source of information.
Learning how to play like a pro will be much more challenging, and that is one of the best reasons to play this game. You can do it! To become GREAT at this game, you're going to have to learn how to handle extremely difficult situations, such as being bombarded by artillery from ships that can see you but you can't see them.  No, it's not hackers, it's skilled players who just sunk you! Learn about scouting ranges, use of camo for disguise, hiding factors of different ships, and how customizing your crew can help. You will also need to help each other as a team in order to attain VICTORY!

If you are thinking of giving this game a solid chance, do so, it will cost you nothing and if you like it great, you get all sorts of useful free stuff to get you going, and if you don't like it, well then you lost no money at all.

Instead of creating Borderlands 3, the developers decided to narrate a little more about what happened before Borderlands 2, just to re-use the beloved villain Handsome Jack. The story however is actually good. Some people say the game is boring and it is true there are weird Australian jokes that I don't understand as a foreigner... But it is still enjoyable with typical Borderland style comedy scenes, and the character in which you play actually interacts with the NPCs. That's not bad? The low-gravity system is very fun and addicting that has brought the combat system to the next level.
The best part is you can play as CL4P-TP. What could be better than this? Now you are officially an outcast. Literally no one is going to like you; the NPCs and your friends as well. If you want to get punched in the face and kicked in the balls by your fellow neighbors, this is the perfect choice for you! Feel the endless solitude in your hearts as no one accepts your high-five request!

Character breakdown (IMHO):
- Athena: ARE YOU NOT ENTERTAINED?! (in all seriousness, Aspis is bae)
- Nisha: What's an aimbot? (like really, I just have really good aim)
- Wilhelm: (replace all aspects of your life with robots and machines)
- CL4P-TP: ...I didn't ask for this. (random =/= funny)
- Jack Double: Who needs friends, right? (Inspired~!)
- Aurelia: Snipers need spotters and meat shields (greatly under-utilized if playing alone ;-;)
For what it's worth, I had a fun time playing through and learning more about what happened before and after Borderlands 2. Unlike Borderlands 2, I didn't feel as compelled to run through as each character to lvl 72 on Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode.

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel tells the story of how Handsome Jack progressed from being a corporate lackey to becoming the villain we know in Borderlands 2. It’s not a journey I asked to take, but since it’s here, I played it and had a good time – but with no camraderie, no Angel, minimal Claptraps, and little environment variety, much of the charm is missing. Gameplay is the same as previous games in the franchise, but now with oxygen tanks and low gravity. Worth a purchase for fans of the series and its co-op loot-and-shoot gameplay (which is as good as ever). New-comers to the franchise should look at Borderlands 2 instead; it is the better game.
Total size installed on my hard-drive (base game + Season Pass): 10.4 GB
The story tells the tale of Athena, an assassin encountered in the first Borderlands game, and how she was employed by Jack to save Pandora’s moon from the evil Captain Zarpedon who has taken over the Helios space station and is firing the station’s laser at the moon to destroy it because reasons (whew, that was mouthful). Zarpedon actually does have reasons, and you can find some Echoes lying around that tell more of her story; she’s actually a really interesting character.
But like so many of the characters in the Pre-Sequel, she’s barely there. Mordecai and Brick only appear in cut-scenes, while Roland and Lilith stand around in the Up Over Bar doing nothing (with two lines of dialogue apiece when clicked upon). Tiny Tina provides some voice-over in True Vault Hunter mode, but otherwise only has one or two lines. Jack tells jokes constantly, but is never funny – not even in a “I’m ashamed of laughing but I’m laughing anyway” approach. And apparently it’s impossible to have a Borderlands game without Moxxi or Crazy Earl. Marcus is NOT present, but his vending machines are everywhere, even in the most unlikely of places. In place of Scooter is Janey Springs, and she is a bright, cheerful addition to a cast that is frequently far too glum. Unfortunately, the Pre-Sequel’s attempts at fun and funny is mostly meh.
The areas feel smaller. Unlike Borderlands 2, which featured a great variety of environments, the Pre-Sequel features one style of terrain – the rocky surface of Pandora’s moon – and any variety happens in the in-door levels. The low-gravity was fun, and allowed for some really creative jumping puzzles. The oxygen requirement was limiting, though. It discouraged random exploration, because I was frequently checking my air amount to make sure I didn’t run out. This concern is somewhat mitigated by plentiful air pockets in every level, but still annoying. Most enemies are recycled from other games (and re-spawn very quickly). Now we have Torks instead of Skags, and they’re animated differently, but their function and hitpoints feel the same. There are fewer bosses than in previous Borderlands games, but the final boss is awesome, taking place in more old Eridian ruins. Design and atmosphere is great, even if it was easy to slice through all the enemies (I finished my first run at Level 26).
As in previous Borderlands games, there are tons of things to loot, but few of them are useful. All the beam weapons are OP; they even helped me to wipe out the Zarpedon boss in less than five minutes – SOLO. Find one (or more!), organize your build around it, and proceed to plow through enemies. A nice addition to the gameplay is the ground-slam. Suddenly, facing hordes of creatures doesn’t seem like a fruitless endeavor. Jump, boost to a greater height (which uses oxygen!), then slam back into the ground for area-of-effect damage. The slam can be customized and upgraded like everything else. I found myself avoiding fire-based elemental weapons because fire needs an atmosphere in order to burn – making their use situational at best. Ice weapons + ground-slam (which shatters frozen enemies) was a more than viable substitute.
At the heart of any Borderlands game is the co-operative experience, and that is as good as ever. Getting four people together to save Pandora’s moon makes for a great time, with easy drop-in, drop-out. Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is easily the lesser game of the trilogy, but it’ll scratch that loot-and-shoot itch. Recommended if you’ve just got to have more Borderlands.

Amazingly fun MMORPG. While the cartoonish graphics can feel odd looking at videos, you need to get in game to see them. They feel much more at place, and more "natural" in game (though they are still definitely cartoony). Combat is tight, and fluid, while alowing you actual choice in how you manage your builds, of which there are numerous options.
Pros:
Cash shop is EXTREMELY FAIR for a F2P game, even better than some B2P games like ESO. If you are worried about any Pay to win junk, don't be, the closest you get to P2W is XP leveling boost, which is irrelevant once you hit max level!
It boasts one of the best housing systems, hands down, in the MMO world. Utility with modules that you can install, but completely freeform placing of tons of housing items, any way you want. Customise your floor, ground, roof, ceiling, sky, and even the atmosphere and lighting of your home....not to mention the infinite things people can do. This isn't cookie cutter housing like FFXIV or ESO. If nothing else, install this game just to explore the amazing homes people have created.
Combat is tight, and fluid, with lots of customisation choices!
Dungeons are mechanically challenging, and take skill
PVP is fun, and action packed!
Every zone has a different atmosphere
The transmog/wardrobe system is top tier! You can transmog any gear, and 98% of gear can be dyed as well.
The lore is very well fleshed out, and there are tons of lore books lying everywhere!
Dungeons and raids are top notch in Wildstar, and few games can compete (WoW is probably biggest competitor for good dungeon & raid experience)
Race minigames are fun! (Make this a side game like pet battles in WoW Carbine! Racing can be big as a side attraction!)
Cons:
Leveling is a bit of a slog.....seriously, fix this Carbine!
Queues for PVP can take a bit sometimes
Other games definitely do quests better (this ties in with the leveling experience)
There isn't much to do outside of combat oriented gameplay, especially at max level.
While faction restrictions are mostly non-existant, it is difficult to find someone to do faction specific scenarios as a Dominion character.
Overall, if you are looking for a F2P game with high polish, fair cash shop with no P2W of any kind, good dungeons, and awesome combat, I'd say give this game a try. Definitely better than 90% of the F2P MMOs on Steam

The decision to take direct fleet control off the player in a space exploration / combat game relies heavily on how good the combat AI is as it can quickly become frustrating for the player if the AI makes poor and possibly game changing choices. This is unfortunately the case currently with Stellaris as the AI repeatedly ignores wounded and almost dead enemies to target fresher enemys to reduce incoming fire, the only way to therefor reliably win the combat which depending on playstyle is a relatively small yet important part of the game is to constantly bring overwhelming force to bear to overcome the AI shortcomings which unfortunately removes any tension and nuance to either ship design or combat tactics and results into a grind until the opposing fleets are outnumbered at least two to one.
Otherwise it is an excellent space empire builder and exploration game which will be enjoyed by fans of the genre.

Every Resident Evil game cannot be considered complete without those moments of fear, anxiety, suspense, pressure, and relief, and Resident Evil Revelations delivers them. There is nothing like being in the middle of the ocean on a tightly confined cruise ship with infected monsters seeking blood. With each turn down a corridor or opening of a door you always be thinking to yourself about what could be waiting for you there. You will also find yourself checking every nook and cranny just to make sure you have killed everything, only to find that all of a sudden out from the depths of an elevator shaft or air duct comes a slimy eight foot monster reaching out to lend you a hand. While I was surprised by, and at times felt some of the pressure of, too many enemies, I quickly realized that they tend to be rather dumb and sluggish and that I could just run away.
Revelations looks incredibly good considering this is a DS port.  Graphics are not grounbreaking but are nice and have decent effects that are utlitized well on the PC.  I really enjoyed the character models myself and thought that Jill looked good as well as the rest of the cast. The sound and music are typical RE flare and add a great sense of ambience and spooky moods.
What is consistent throughout all Resident Evil games is the sense of anxiety when blowing through a ton of ammo and feeling like you are on the verge of not having enough, when low and behold the ammo gods bless you with more. One of the new ways the game has you searching for ammo and health outside of the usual opening of lockers and smashing of boxes is by using the Genesis.  The Genesis is a scanner that detects items around the environment that wouldn't normally be seen with the naked eye. The scanner can also be used on the enemy, and with each successful scan you accumulate a percentage number; when the numbers total up to 100% you are rewarded with a health potion.
Yes this is not RE6, which I have not played but it is very fun and has decent story length of gameplay.  There is replayability also with New Game modes and Multi/CoOp play.  Remember that flashy graphics and latets tech does not always equal a stellar game usually it is the gameplay that makes ot breaks it... again RE6 seems to have been disappointing from what I have read, so I opted for this game instead and am gald I did.  It brings back that old school Resident Evil feeling and that I have missed lately.
Had a lot more fun with Revelations than I did with 6. Felt like I could play thought it again.

I got this game as part of the August Humble Monthly, and I'm usually a huge fan of puzzle platformers, especially 2D side-scrollers. However, this game I found to be pretty lack-luster, and I technically only paid around $2 for it because of my monthly subscription. To start, I know the game is tagged as short, but I felt like the majority of "puzzles" for the first half of the game weren't tricky at all, almost too easy or just plainly obvious, really making this game feel even shorter than it is. Though there were some puzzles that were more difficult once you were more than halfway through the game, I became bored by that point just because of how easy everything else had been.
The art-style was decent, but I don't think it worked in favor of this game. There were a handful of times I found myself confused on what I could or could not interact with because it blended too much with an object's surroundings.
Also, I had the same problem others were having when trying to use a Xbox One controller, forcing me to use my keyboard, which made everything feel stiff.
I can't recommend this for $10, which is the current full price, and I'm honestly surprised a lot of people do. If it's on sale for maybe less than $5, and you're really dying for another puzzle platformer for about an hour because you've played every other one...sure. This game is just not worth $10.
TL;DR If you like Limbo, just play Limbo, or buy Limbo for your friend and watch them play it.

Loadout is an extremly fun and arcady third-person shooter, mobility is key to winning aswell as your guns. As I said earlier mobility is key to winning as they give you a combat roll, jumps that can be effected by ramps, and jump boots which gives you a double jump, but mobility is only a way of dodging the tons of bullets, beams, rockets, grenades, cannonballs, and more it also allows your team to get around the map quickly. Suprisingly for an arcady shooter like itself another even BIGGER key to winning is your team the game requires good team co-operation, and even if you don't for say have the best team and you lose it doesnt matter at all because you still will gain XP and BLUTES this system of making losing not so bad is also reflected in Loadout's combat, in this game you will die alot its a good thing though that the games has a very small respawn timer of at its most 2.5 seconds long, so you will be back in the action faster than you can blink, but this respawn timer can be the difference between winning and losing in that extra 2.5 seconds of time a team can get across the maps using certain routes and well timed mobility skills (OFF TOPIC: The maps are pretty big aswell Im just saying the tools and the expertly crafted maps give the player a so called playground of parkour) the game requires much skill because of this however it is easy to get into by new players and new players to the genre, Those are the game features the game also comes with multiple TENSE and FUN AS HELL gamemodes each completly changing the game's pace, the game's art style is somewhat alike TF2 but only in asthetic it feels like its own thing even though it's art style is remenisent of cartoony CGI styles. OVERALL Loadut is an extremly fun game to play with friends and without them I found myself returning to the each day I had it and it is extremly satisfying to shoot a freaking hole through your enemy's stupid corpse haha, the game is hilarious with crass language and slap stick if you will the multiple over-the-top death animations had me chuckling and  customizing guns is easy and fun it ALSO helps that the game is not free to play ergo no gameplay features are blocked by microtransactions so yeah, go out and get it afterall it is FREE TO PLAY. As a backer of the Kickstarter, I'm very disappointed in this game.  I have a 6-core 3.5Ghz processor, and while my graphics card isn't all that hot, it is an Nvidia gaming card... and this is not a real-time FPS.  It's a table-top game with "flavor" animations... most of the game, very little on the screen is moving, yet I have to turn the video settings way down to keep the audio from being choppy, and I still get terrible frame rates.  There is no reason a game that is presenting a mostly-still image should get such terrible performance, even with a cheap video card.  I was really surprised to see the game released and it still be hardly any better when I tried it out shortly after it went into beta.  The developers shouldn't have started working on DLC, they should be working on fixing the problems with the game.
As others have noted, the UI is very clunky, and the number of times I move a unit to the wrong location because the UI interpreted my click wierdly is annoying (and I've only played 4 hours!), and accidentally entering melee with a unit you meant to shoot at can mean the difference between winning and losing a battle.  The camera is difficult to maneuver, it's hard to find all your foes (you can't see the mini-map during focus allocation), and it's easy to lose track of active enemy units among all the dead enemies and visual clutter.
This game had lots of potential, and it could still be fixed... I'm just afraid that the developers don't see the problems here.
The reproduction of the tabletop game is, as far as I've seen, rather good.  If you enjoy Warmachine on the tabletop and don't get to play enough, and you can put up with a poorly made game, it might be worth it.

The selection of units they provide for the base price ($40 USD) is incredibly restrictive. Then they want you to buy all the DLC units to compensate for the fact that they've sold you an engine, but not a game.
I'm not sure why I expected anything else out of a product based on a table top miniatures came, but it's absolutely shameful.

The Iron Kingdoms are a great intellectual property to build a game from, and WARMACHINE: Tactics is a reasonably faithful interpretation of the Warmachine and Hordes ruleset. It's hard to transition a good tabletop game into a good video game, but Whitemoon Dreams and Privateer Press have managed to make it work.
What they haven't managed, unfortunately, is to make the game run. Even at minimum settings, my framerate has been absolutely awful, the action is choppy at best, and textures don't load until halfway through a given scene. The controls suffer, too, from the close resemblance to XCOM's grid-based movement, and more than once I found myself moving a unit into harm's way simply because I clicked what I thought was a safe square but was actually somewhere else.
The game is still not to release quality, and I'm heartened by the fact that WMD and PP recognize this. I'm excited to see what improvements and additions they make to this game which has so much potential.

Warmachines: Tactics is just what I thought it would be. A solid indie game with a lot of heart - and some awkward choices. The UI looks like it was done by the coders who have become so use to its appearance that they have just accepted it. Which is a shame because it is the game’s biggest flaw. However, once you accept it yourself the game is just what I hoped it would be.
The game creates an excellent representation of playing a table top game (TTG). I myself was not a Warmachines veteran, but I have played other TTGs. So not being able to judge the mechanics – only the experience it is very successful. Part of how this is done comes from the lack of mechanization a significant amount of what you do is left completely up to you. So if you move a character and he is facing the wrong way and you forget to adjust his direction (there is a button for this) that’s too bad. A HUD will not prompt you or attempt to fix it automatically. Do you see what I mean just like a TTG. This sort of infraction during a traditional game happens and can be exploited.
I found the best way to understand the strengths of the various factions was to use the skirmish mode. This is the heart and soul of Warmachines: Tactics after you finish the campaign and is the only repayable portion of the game. There is no option the replay the campaign under a different faction, or other campaigns for other factions. Oh well, I’m sure the developer will offer them as DLC (which is no worse than buying campaigns of physical models) but for some reason the fan boys are crying over this idea. Whatever. I like that they are offering more models, more environments etc. It means they are still involved and looking to grow the idea. Well done fellas.
Though there are bugs, the main storyline was a fun playthrough. Once you get to the point where you can customise your army it gets really fun, but I would have liked more options.

Game is really great fun, has moved along fairly well in its competitiveness compared with WoW.
Key Points:
1. A lot of people despise the game over the graphics compared with WoW (If your problem with this is the graphics then you can either get a better computer, go and use clipart instead or just play the game because it ain't about the pretty it's about the play), to be honest, the graphics aren't that bad, you have various graphic detail settings available for you to tailor to your computer's limits without it looking like something you could achieve from an iPad/tablet.
2. The tier system is pretty balanced overall (pro) with the occasional (con) OP ship in some tiers such as the CL Atlanta or DD/DC Laforey. On top of that, despite the insane scouting range on some BBs in tier 6+, all of these factors encourage you to play smarter on the open seas and rather think through your options without being spotted.
3. Heated topic around this game in comparison with WoW is the player base. This game really does deserve more players than it currently has and I understand why there is only US servers and the proxy servers. There really isn't much you can do about the sheep that follow the WoW franchise when there is a perfectly more enjoyable and entertaining game right here needing its global support - I sympathise with you.
4. Alike in Battlefield where there are "only in Battlefield moments", Steel Ocean (SO) has its own moments as well. Again, let down with its player base (low population), these "Steel Ocean moments" only occur every once in a while, however almost all the time in either a large battle or during Submarine warfare (dependent on your experience and play style in SS as well as any other ship class).
5. Only really frustrating thing I have with the game is the fact that, despite the in-game scaling of the environment, where in real life you could see an enemy ship off the horizon - obvisouly for game mechanics to work there is what is known as 'scouting range/visual', I really dislike the fact that an enemy ship can see you whilst you cannot see them if they're only a couple of meters ahead (say somewhat 300m). I have encourtered battles where I am a cruiser and cannot see an enemy destroyer in the open water that was only a few meters ahead of me and yet I am getting pounded by artillery with no hope - even with smokes they still see sometimes. (gotta fix this, the only real kickback)
6. Absolutely love scenario mode and I wish there were other game modes alike that within normal matchmaking - it would really enhance the whole WWII tier structure and encourage players to use their ship class as designed. This would also enphasise teamwork and, as seen within scenario mode, have all ships on one team be of the same country of origin (US vs JP).
7. Matchmaking is another heated topic as a lot of people in the reviews bag on about how it took them 30mins to find a game. This happens for a few reasons and the person at fault is usually themselves. After the first few minutes after you have initiated to find a game and haven't found one, you are given a message to advise you to perhaps change your ship or tier in order to get better results. Another factor is that you can see how many people are within your tier group that are also finding a match, if there are less than 4 per 15seconds, it's a pretty good indicator that you need to change tier. Finally, if you're finding a game and there are say 14 players within that team and 12 disappear and you and another person are the 2 left on the match making screen, it's a fairly good indicator that you chose a ship that was either too popular within that tier or wasn't popular enough in order to have a fair game. (What could really help is instead of showing all the ship classes that are searching for a game, only show the ship classes that are active within the tier you are searching for in order to adhere this issue)
8. The community is great and really enforces a more enjoyable experience for newcomers. Like every game, you can't just judge it by your first few hours of playing, especially a strategy shooter such as this one as it takes time to accumulate enough skill/experience in order to fully understand and appreciate the game and how the ships work individually, catering for your own play style.
9. Perhaps bringing in bots in higher tier games (where few players ever reach because of the grinding, alike in WoW, to get high tier ships) is an option and work them like how they operate in other games where if your player dies, they can choose to either leave or keep playing by taking command over a bot ship and the points earned from the bot ship will only be rewarded in silver instead of xp. This will increase and support the larger sea battles and help new players get their hands dirty while playing (bot difficulty increases within the tiers obviously).
It's a wonderful game and deserves more than what it get, it takes a lot to create a game such as this one. As much as I would love all the issues addressed by negative reviews, I've tried to keep these key points as open as possible in order for you to understand the game a little better without bias. I do hope the devs sort out those issues indicated within those reviews but alas, it is still a game worth giving a second chance and spending your time on.

This game is okay, but not better than Borderlands 2.
If you REALLY liked Borderlands 2 and did everything you could there, but still want more, get this, otherwise stick to BL2.
The Good:
+ New characters with new fun to play styles.
+ New kind of weapon: Lasers. They also come with variants as Railguns and Continuous Beams, aside some unique variants for Legendaries.
+ Low gravity, air boosting and some other features are fun.
+ Cold/Cyro damage, something that should have been here since the first game. Replaces Slag damage (which makes sense)
+ You can play as Claptrap and Jack (Sort of)
+ Enemies are balanced to not be that much of bullet sponges like BL2.
+ Its more Borderlands. More stuff to shoot, more stuff to loot.
The Meh:
+/- Not a lot changed from BL2, even with the new place, everything feels the same.
+/- Several reused assets.
+/- The level design gets annoying when you are forced to boost/slam everywhere to get somewhere.
+/- The game is what happens when you kill a character but then wanted to do a new game with said character. You have no other choice than to make a prequel or pull one cliche like 'there is a clone' or 'his mind is on a computer now'
The Bad:
- EVERY single mission is filled with ludicrous amounts of dialogue.
Unskippable dialogue that blocks the mission progression or hides objectives until the dialogue ends.
Sometimes a secondary objective tells you to do or dont do something, but since the dialogue is hiding it, you pretty much fail the objective without knowing.
- 99% of the missions are either 'fetch item' or 'kill thing'. Sometimes its a mixed objective, 'kill things until fetch item shows up'
- Missable or failable Badass Challenges.
Local Specific challanges can now be tied to something that happens in a mission, if you dont check the challanges menu every 10 steps or watch a video before playing the mission, you wont know about it until its too late. You missed/failed it? Either gotta wait until New Game+ or mod your game to replay the mission.
Some are pretty much impossible to do on your first time and some are easy to fail by accident.
For example, the 'kill this surprise mob in less than a second before he explodes' or the 'dont let the instakilling robot score a kill on mobs that spawn right in front of it' require you to know that would happen AND know where every single enemy will spawn.
- All the maps are BIG and takes a lot of time to walk around, even on cars.
- Most of the missions require you to backtrack to previous areas SEVERAL times, sometimes a single mission requires you to go back to other 3 areas before making to go back to finish it.
- Most missions go like this: Go this way -> Oh path is blocked, go the other longer way -> Oh also blocked, go to the near start of the map to get an item to unlock this way.
- Most side missions are boring, long and reward you low exp/money/stones and a bad weapon, you are better off skipping every secondary mission that rewards you anything under blue quality.
- Every character has little to no personality.
The most they have are one or two 'traits' that make up their whole personality.
For example, Springs is 'crazy' and 'gay', Pickles 'likes stealing' and 'is british'.
All dialogue of secondary characters will be about reminding you about their "personality".
Ironically, Claptrap turns to be the character with the most personality in the entire game.

I said all that to say I have been waiting to play this game for quite a while now and was eager and convienced I would enjoy it. The story is pretty good. The dialouge options are really nice. It's great to hear your character actually say your dialouge choices instead of the silent avatar syndrome. Combat is meh. It's exactly the same as Game of Thrones. It's a mix of real-time/Turn-based combat that has you switching your attention between controlled characters. The problem I have with combat in Of Orcs And Men is the same problem I had in Game of Thrones. All encounters seem to have a slim margin of victory. You will focus on one characters attacks and after issuing 2 or 3 skills, you'll notice the other character is about to die. I don't understand how both of my characters seem to always be near death everytime I change focus. As well the skills you choose in combat aren't all that varied and I found myself sticking to a one two punch combo with my Orc and leaving the goblin as fodder since he's worthless in combat.
Combat can be forgive though. I don't mind a challenge as long as the story is good. The reason I do not recommend Of Orcs And Men is FOV!!! That's right! The field of view for this game has to be about 30. Your Orc takes up 45% of the screen. If you choose to switch to the Goblin you're presented with a super zoomed in view. The graphics are great, the set pieces are nice, why they chose to make the view so damn limited and not show off their work defies logic. Game of Thrones had the same issue, but there was a work around. This game has none. It feels like you're trying to play a game while wearing your creepy uncle's coke bottle glasses. Pros (Ranked in terms of strength):
#1. The game's art style and aesthetics are amazing. One of French Bread's main goals with UNIB was definitely style, and they succeeded undoubtedly. Compared to most anime fighters, it's simple, yet very sleek. As the title suggests, UNIB's world is in a state of seemingly perpetual nighttime, yet the designers kept the lighting strong with bright moonlight and cool color tones, all contrasted with hard strikes of red throughout. UNIB also aims for a "modern fantasy" look, which it does very well, making its universe fit snug into the look of the new millennium. It may not be as beautiful as Guilty Gear Xrd's spot-on anime cell shading, nor as complex and excruciatingly detailed as BlazBlue, but its looks send a strong message regardless, so maybe it doesn't need it in the end.
#2: The fighting system is very solid, appearing quite accessible and easy to learn at first, but it masks much deeper systems for more hardcore players to sink their teeth into, as any good fighter does. While things like long, hard-to-execute combos and deceptive mixups and setups are apparent, UNIB's main focus seems to be poured into the neutral game, encouraging the player to get better at being patient, finding openings, and making the opponent respect you. No fighting game is ever easy, and those who say they are are lying to your face, but UNIB is likely one of the more accessible fighters out on the market.
#3. The game's unique "GRID" system is something I haven't encountered before, but it offers a new level of gameplay to the table, and enforces the points I made in Pro #2. Put very simply, it's a tug-of-war mechanic between you and your opponent, plainly telling you who has the advantage and disadvantage in the fight, and rewarding the one who can keep up the advantage. It rewards and punishes you for doing various actions both offensively and defensively, playing into UNIB's encouragement of learning the neutral game. You are free to ignore the GRID system and play how you like, but considering it can give you buffs such as a straight damage increase, as well as the ability to instantly cancel practically anything for both offensive and defensive reasons, you might as well learn it.
#4. What UNIB lacks in character quantity, it makes up for in quality. Everyone in the cast plays differently and has their own systems to learn. Of course some characters are easier to learn than others, but that doesn't make trying out the more complicated ones any less fun. The characters' looks and personalities are also diverse, while simultaneously fitting into the game's world. Want to feel like a boss? Pick up Gordeau or Linne. Prefer the edgier types? Try Seth or Carmine. Don't like being human? Merkava's right there. Not interested in UNIB's main cast at all? Mess with Eltnum or Akatsuki, the guest characters.
#5. The soundtrack is pretty good. Excluding a few tracks, I have heard better, but all the songs fit the game's universe and characters quite well. If you like rock, electronica, piano tunes, and/or a mixture of the three, you'll enjoy this soundtrack. If you like anime soundtracks in general, you might just have to add this one to your collection. I can see the potential of the game's music really coming into its own in future installments, especially from what I'm hearing in the series' latest iteration, Late[st].
Cons (Ranked in terms of woe):
#1. The online netcode can be choppy and inconsistent. While actual matches rarely ever lag, I've had trouble connecting to some player lobbies, as well as instances where everyone would suddenly disconnect from the lobby, leaving the host alone. It's certainly not the worst netcode out there, and you can chalk up most of the netcode problems to usual stuff like distance lag or computer performance, but the game could use a few more patches to refine it and make things more stable.
#2. UNIB is an anime fighter, and not the most popular anime fighter out there, so don't expect a 24/7 steady flow of player lobbies and ranked matches. The game is ~4 years old if you count arcade releases, but only ~2 years old in terms of mainstream console releases. UNIB as a whole is still a budding flower in a land of old, experienced veterans, so the population surrounding the game is still gaining traction. Some people are fine with that and like growing along with a series, but for those who want a large community to jump into, you'll struggle a bit. You can take comfort in the fact that what community is here is largely friendly and helpful, however.
#3. There is no in-game formal tutorial to teach you the in-and-outs of the game's mechanics. The available practice mode is rather extensive and customizable, but there's nothing to directly tell you how something works, something that BlazBlue and Guilty Gear Xrd have an edge over UNIB about. A bit of Googling and reading/watching, or consulting someone who's knowledgeable of the game, will fix that issue pretty fast, but for those spoiled by the recent inclusion of extensive tutorials in more popular fighters nowadays, this might prove as a minor annoyance for them.
#4. It's not immediately obvious, but the game's character balance in this edition of the UNIB series is a bit polarized. Nothing broken by any means, but some characters struggle to be a huge threat in a match, and others dominate the tiers with an iron fist. Characters like Gordeau, Merkava, and Waldstein will have players rubbing their temples in frustration trying to figure out how to get past their amazing tools, and characters like Seth, Chaos, and Akatsuki are a game in of themselves in optimizing their effectiveness. It's not the worst and most confusing balancing out there, though, and you can learn how to handle anyone with time and effort. It's just more of a struggle compared to the balance of UNIB's latest edition, Late[st], which is arcade-exclusive currently.
#5. For those wishing to seek good stories in fighting games, well... 1. You're a trooper, and 2. UNIB's story can be hard to get into without a wiki handy. There isn't really a gradual introduction into the game's universe and terminology, and while playing through every character's arcade path can give you a better idea of what's going on, you might be left wondering what the heck you're reading initially. When you do understand, though, the story is actually pretty interesting, and has a lot of potential. What's currently here in UNIEL offers more of an establishment of setting and characters, and leaves a lot of the bigger plot points, backstories, and developments in mystery.
There's some other minors things I could praise or gripe about, but this should cover the main points of interest. Plus I believe I've gone on long enough, lol. Personally, I'm making this game one of my main fighters along with Tekken, just because there's so much this game has that appeals to me. I highly recommend that you at least give this a try, whether you do or don't like fighters, and I'm very eager to see the future developments of this series.

What do I say about this game? Well, first off, let me preface with: I am not a fan of anime. I am not a fan of anime fighting games. However, I am a fan of fighting games and I always thought this game had some solid mechanics, a diverse roster and was made by French Bread, the company that made the Melty Blood series. I first played this game in a JPN arcade in my travels about 3 years ago now and fell in love with Merkava like, instantly. When I got back home, I found out it had a PS3 release and so, I quickly scooped that up on a JPN PSN account. I got some friends into the game and damn was it fun. Unfortunately, it died out rather quickly on PS3 but I definitely had some good times with it. I had a purple square (the highest player rating) and everything.
Fast forward to 2016 and I find out this game is now on steam. With nostalgia in my pocket, I quickly got the game again. The rust is definitely there but I am working out those kinks and am currently up to an orange square (2nd best player rating) and keep on training in this game with little more purpose than the love of the game.
So, as you can see, I definitely have a history with UNIB/UNIEL and I have many, many more hours than what my steam says. So, why do I like this game? What do I dislike? Let me make a quick rundown of both:
+Pros
*Easy to pick up and play. It's very user-friendly if you played fighting games before.
*Diverse roster. There aren't any clone characters in the game.
*Merkava. My bae. <3
*Good netcode... when 2 bars or higher.
*High skill ceiling. There's a lot of tech to this game, a lot of which you have to figure out yourself. This promotes the notion of player growth wherein as they get more skilled, they really have something to show for it.
*Has an actual story mode... unlike a certain other fighting game that was released this year that didn't get a story mode for several months...
-Cons
*This game isn't particularly balanced. You will have to work much harder with a low tier character than a top tier one. That being said, there are plenty of viable characters and, as stated before, you can win if you are a skilled player; you just will have to work harder.
*When it rains; it pours. This game's netcode, when you're playing against someone with poor ping to you, is reaaally hard to play in. This can be circumvented by only playing people 2+ bars or higher to you though.
*Not a large community. Since this game is fairly obscure, there isn't a large playerbase. This isn't the game's fault but it can be frustrating to find matches, especially if you beat a player and they refuse to rematch you.
All in all, I highly recommend this game if you're a fan of fighting games or anime or whatever floats your boat. If you want to learn the mechanics of the game and whatnot, I suggest looking to dustloop or the mizuumi wiki to learn more about the game, your character and tech for UNIEL. It's helped me immensely to learn how to play UNIEL.

Originally released for the 3DS early last year, Revelations was an incredible game for the system and the series. A little over a year later, Capcom decided to release it on the consoles and PC.
Story
Set between Resident Evil 4 and 5, this game will have you playing as Jill Valentine, as she and her partner are sent to discover the source of creatures that have been washing up on shore. They soon discover a cruise ship filled with dead people and various monsters. Their day goes down hill from there.

Presentation
While not as pretty as Resident Evil 6, the visuals in this game are quite nice, and its easy to forget that this was original made for a screen only a few inches big. Some textures are a little blurry. Character models for both you and enemies look great though.
The voice acting in this game works well, with there never being any problem understanding what characters are saying. No faults here. Music works well to set the mood of the locations, adding to the atmosphere. The sound effects are also great, with plenty of small things to enhance the scares.
Controls
You won't have any problems with controls, no matter if you prefer a gamepad like me or a keyboard and mouse. Both work well, using the standard controls for a third person shooter.
Gameplay
Well the controls may have shifted to the standard for a third person shooter, you don't need to worry that this is all action and explosions like Resident Evil 6 was so fond of. This game frequently has you searching for just a bit more ammo and dodging monsters rather than destroying them. It even has some of the old fetch quest puzzles to keep you busy. You are simply able to move around better while dealing with the swarms of foes. The shambling monstrosities can still get in your way often enough, but its easy enough to take them down. Just don't forget to keep an eye on your ammo, and the other on your surroundings, as there are always more beasts looking to take you down. Many of the fights will involve numerous creatures looking to nibble on you.
This game has streamlined the inventory. Now, you can hold at most three weapons and some grenades, several green herbs, and any key items as you find. The only time you will need the storage box is to switch between various weapons and upgrade them. These are one of the new changes, where you can find various parts to try out on your gear. Some will boost damage, others increase clip size or reload speed, and others will be able to boost other stats or add additional abilities to your favourite weapons.
The last major addition to this game that should be mentioned is the Genesis. This device allows you to scan your surroundings and the enemies you come across. Enemies will boost the Genesis scan percentage, with it giving you an additional herbs, which scanning the landscape will reveal hidden items such as ammo or weapon parts.
This game is incredible fun, but being a Resident Evil title, and one made for a handheld to boot, the game can be finished rather quickly if you are focused on just beating the story mode. My own playtime for the story was just over 6 hours.
Lifespan
Fortunately, there is no reason you have to stop there. If playing the story over in New Game Plus mode while on a higher difficulty isn't enough to tempt you, perhaps the Raid mode will. This is a series of levels based on the story mode, where you will need to reach the end of each level while taking down the enemies in your way, either while playing solo or with a friend online. As you go through each area and accomplish goals, you will earn additional weapons, weapon parts, costumes and experience. Your character will be able to level up and become more powerful, which will be wanted for the later Raid levels.
Closing
This is, in my opinion, one of the best Resident Evil titles available, and easily the best released in the last 8 years. Good story, great gameplay and an extra mode for you and a friend to continue enjoying well after you have tired of beating the main mode.

Planet of the Eyes is a very short 2D platformer game. It takes less than an hour and a half to complete this game and acquire all the achievements – indeed, I did so on my first run-through.
So what is it like?
Unlike a lot of 2D platformers, the protagonist of this game – a robot – cannot jump very high or very far. There is no parkour in this game. Indeed, I would say that the robot’s physical capabilities are almost realistic. This means that your jumps are not exactly spectacular. You swim some, there are some bouncy pads, and you pull stuff around and stand on buttons at times. There are some timing elements, and some moving platform elements in a few places, but not many.
That said, the platforming is not dissatisfying; it is okay. But that’s really the problem with this game; it is… okay. It isn’t anything special. It never really goes above and beyond. You find some voice logs over the course of the game which have fairly decent voiceovers and which gradually hint at some sort of plot, but in the end, you are just trying to get from point A to point B, and there’s not much more to it than that. The visuals of the game are clean and attractive, and don’t look cheap, instead having an almost art deco quality to them.
But all of the game is adequate; it never makes the jump to the extraordinary. I can’t say that it wasted my time, but I can’t say that it particularly felt fulfilling either; it was just kind there.
I would not buy this game. But if you happen to already own it, as part of a bundle or something, it isn’t a terrible thing to play through. But it isn’t something you should go out of your way to pursue, either – it is basically a “replacement level platformer”, for want of a better term. It is okay. Unexceptional. Mediocre.

First off this game is nothing like WoWS and is not pay to win as I can personally attest being one of the top players and having not spent a dime.
The aim mechanics are entirely different both for guns (aim in time vs point and shoot) and torpedoes (single shot capable vs autospread). Secondary guns, AA, and planes (yes even on non carrier ships) are all manually controled. The roles of ships are far more defined and have to work together to provide scouting (more discription on this at the end). All this makes the game play entirely differently than WoWS and means that if your team knows their role and knows how to support eachother you can beat far "better" players or ships that don't work together.
Some of the complaints about the game some are valid some aren't. The graphics aren't great but they aren't as bad as some say, there is only the NA server (and a European proxy), the population is pretty low though not as low as some reviews say since they are looking at the currently waiting for a game count, partly because of the former the matchmaker can give badly setup games, and the tutorials are lacking and many things go unexplained. People who complain about cheaters who can always see them don't understand the scouting system and how you use commanders to buff your scouting and that you can buy camoflauge for your ship (you can buy it with the non-premium curency which many don't know) because these things are not explained which is my biggest problem with the game itself unrelated to the size of the player base.
As to pay to win accusations people like to say that the commander system is pay to win but you would have to spend hundereds of dollars on commanders to get anything resembeling a gamebreaking advantage. Completing all the events of one week means you get one 36 dollar commander pack a though this requires playing in a fleet and tier 5 ships which can all be had within a week. And this dosen't include the monthy 20 days login event (worth 1/2 a pack) and the monthly fleet rankings. You can get gold items (excluding ammo which would be ludicrously expensive to use) from events and rankings and the 5v5 ranking even gives gold.
For ship types; destroyers function as scouts formost while killing subs and DD and as dropping torps to kill larger ships being secondary roles, light cruisers are larger less maneuvarable DDs with more/better guns, heavy cruisers have fast firing long range guns to kill lighter ships,  battleships are your heavy long range hitters for taking punishment and dishing it out to other battleships and heavy cruisers, and carriers act as AA to protect against other CVs and using planes as scouts while only occasionally attacking ships unless the enemy has fewer CVs than yours, and subs can function as stealth scouts and assasins or they can draw the enemy destroyer back so he can't scout while harrassing the BBs so they have to turn and can't fire.
Continually just matches the game. Never actually plays.

text:
So AMD finally got around to updating their drivers to fix the issues with this game, right after I write a review (totally not a rant) about their problems of course. Now there is no reason not to get this game, unless you have a GTX 780 or 780ti, because those cards still have problems.
This is probably my favorite singleplayer game of all time. The story is enthralling, the characters develop in interesting ways throughout the story, the music is phenomenal, the combat is satisfying, and the locations are stunning.
To start with, the story. This game is technically a sequel, but no knowledge of the original is required to appreciate this game, and beyond a couple of references there aren't many links between the two. Automata takes place thousands of years after the original, in fact. In NieR:Automata you play as an Android that is fighting endless numbers of robots to reclaim the Earth so humanity can come back from the moon. Why is humanity on the moon? Aliens. But seriously, humanity fled to the moon when the aliens created robots to wipe them out. Sounds a little complicated? It gets better, but I am not going to spoil anything here. As a sidenote, if you get this game, and you get to an ending, it isn't the end of the game. In reality, both Ending A and B are breaks in the story, while Endings C, D, and E are the alternate actual endings. F through Z are either jokes of some sort or because of a mistake you make in the story. Each time you get an ending, it will put a letter on your save file then let you go back to your last save, or in A and B it will start the next section of the story.
Next, the character development. This is obviously a byproduct of events in the story, so anything specific would be a pretty large spoiler. Lets just say that some pretty major changes happen in the way characters behave both to eachother and overall. The side characters from various quests are interesting as well, one example being some characters that link to the original. These plots are still good without playing the original NieR though.
The music is another mind-blowing element of this game. This soundtrack has such a wonderful variety of tracks that I think fit with every part of the story. NieR:Automata is one of the few games that I have stopped to listen to the area music, and some songs are so dazzling that I bought the soundtrack and listen to them even when i'm not playing the game. The various boss songs and character themes are superb as well.
Admittedly the combat is probably the weakest part of this game. I personally think it is satisfying, but I can understand if someone doesn't like it. It is simple, compared to a game like Bayonetta or others in this class. There aren't tons of unique combos, and even the number of weapons is somewhat small. What it falls behind on in combos is the crispness of animation and the gratification that comes with that. The few weapon types that are in the game do provide some variety of attack set as well.
Finally, the locations. They aren't very specifc about what they are, so there isn't any connection to a present day setting. They are beautiful though, and there are enough of them. Though the first 2 endings take place in the same area with enemies being similar, the third set of endings adds some new areas for the story to progress in, with the final area being my personal favorite in the end, even if the story is a bit sad.
Now that the driver issues have been fixed, there is no reason not to buy this game. My last serious issue is gone, and yours should be too. If you can't be convinced to buy a game based on its merit in the categories that actually matter like story and gameplay, what is the point of reading reviews? Go buy NieR:Automata.

First of all, I installed Stellaris not a while ago. Being a huge fan of the GalCiv series, I installed this game with a high bar of standards set by the GalCiv games. Also, I might add, I've played other Paradox games extensively (HoI series, CK2, EU 3 and 4). So, here's my result:
Pros:
- The Clausewitz engine that Paradox uses on other games such as HoI 4 and EU 4 work incredibly well with Stellaris. Fans of those games might be able to pick mostly everything up from the start. The learning curve isn't that bad, though I recommend watching a video or 2 on YouTube to grasp the basics.
- The tech system: one thing that bothered me from other 4X games was that tech was mostly always limited by a visible, static tech tree. So, after a few games in, you would know what to research first always. Well, not this time, chump! Stellaris uses a clever deck system, so whenever you wish to research something, it'll "deal" you 3 random techs, which might or might not appear once you finish researching the current one! This means you need to choose intelligently and meaningfully which option to research, knowing that the other options might not be at your disposal in a few years. This gives the game a good deal of unpredictibility and actually makes you think about your tech choices rather than blindly follow a tech branch.
- The galaxy: Yep, it's big. More than that, its populated with randomly generated species, either pre-sentient, primitive, FTL or fallen. This gives for a lot of replayability, since no two games are the same.
- Less micromanagement: I must admit, I'm a control freak. I have to control everything, min/max everything. With other 4X games I usually had a hard time; managing 30+ planets was no laughing matter. I know, many of them had automated governors that in my opinion were pretty bad. Stellaris managed to "unbog" this by adding sectors. Yes, it's the same concept as an automated governor but for several systems. The thing is, that with proper management and smart thinking, you can make these sectors amazingly productive without the extra work of micromanaging. Many people here tend to hate this system: I personally love it and it makes my late game less muddy.
- Mods: Lots of good mods out there, and the engine allows for rather easy and powerful modifications.
- Real-Time Pausable: Although most 4X are turn based (which isn't a bad thing), I've found that being able to speed up the game especially early in the game works wonders and keeps the game's pace constant.
- Solid race creation process: Yes, you can make a space cockroach empire where your cockroaches are religious zealots. Or a space fox megacorporation. The ethos/civics system works pretty well in defining your government type and the general flavour of your empire.
Cons:
- Like with the other games using the Clausewitz engine, once you know a bit about how it behaves, you can start "gaming" it for your benefit. Might ruin some of the inmersion.
- Few diplomatic options: actually, there are not few, but with the richness of the engine, they could've add even more options (Trade Agreements, I'm looking at you!).
- Rock, paper, scissor: Like everyone else, but at least Stellaris gives us a few options that go beyond the tipical laser-kinetic-missile weapons. Also, combat is usually determined by biggest fleet unless you have a huuuge tech advantage. Still, battles are beautiful (even more so with mods!).
TL;DR
It's a great 4X game that will offer you a lot of replayability and fun. Oh, and try to get the DLCs as well, they both add more events and cool stuff to do in-game.

I finished this a while back so this isn't as fresh in my memory as it should. Also I have to be honest here, cyanide games are a guilty pleasure of mine. I always think there are some good ideas floating in their games but they don't manage to make the best out of all those ideas. That being said on to the main event.
Gameplay:
You play as 2 characters here and you can switch between them at any time once you get the second one. The first is the orc, Arkhail, and the second is the goblin, Styx.
Each of them has 3 skill trees in which you can add points to get new abilities or improve an ability in 1 of 2 different ways that adds an effect like stun or lifesteal to that ability . Arkhail has a berserker and a tank tree and the 3rd has some actions that include Styx like throwing him towards enemies and later on when you choose a specialization class(story event) you get some more skills here. Styx has an assassin tree and ranged dagger throwing tree and the 3rd again has combo actions such as throwing a heal potion to Arkhail. These skill trees/wheels also count as stances that give different bonuses.
Speaking of potions there are none :P You have to keep your HP up by using skills, items with lifesteal and good planning before going into the fight.
Both characters can equip gear that drops or is found in chests and is specific for each character. While there isn't a whole lot of gear each new item you find will be different and sometimes they will be sidegrades instead of upgrades so they can be useful to the build you are using for them.
The fights can get rather challenging at times but all of them can be overcome with some good planning. The main thing to take into account is that Arkhail has a rage meter that can build up pretty fast and sends him into berserker mode where he is faster and stronger but you cannot control his actions and he sometimes takes pauses just to roar at the enemies in which time he gets pummeled. It's up to you if you want to go the berserker route and try to survive fights counting on his rage or go the tank way where you can control his rage and diminish with certain skills. Personally I went berserker for Arkhail and assassin for styx with a few skills from the other trees just enough to cover all my bases and it was fine though there were some fights that I had to restart quite a few times. It is by no means an easy game.
Graphics:
From a distance they graphics look OK but when the camera zooms in for conversations the textures are really bad and blurry. A high res texture pack would to wonders for the game but I doubt we'll ever see anything like that. There is variety in the locations you go as far as design but the overall color palette is pretty bland with a lot of browns and greys.
Sound:
I'm not really good at this part. Thesound seems ok to me but maybe someone with a better ear will tell you differently. The music is good and the volumes are well implemented (as opposed to viking battle of asgard). My only issue here is that half the voice actors are bad. Arkhail and Styx are ok though and it's their banter that you will be hearing for most of the game anyway.
Story:
At the beginning the human empire is waging a massive war against all greenskins and is winning. The chief of the clan tasks Arkhail with killing the emperor as to finish the war. Arkhail needs help getting to the emperor so a guide is hired and this is where Styx comes in. From there the story has all sorts of twists and turn, some that you will expect and others that you won't. I really enjoyed the story but what I enjoyed more was Styx. He's just one of those characters that you either love or hate and if you love him you can't get enough of him.
Bottom line:
While there could be improvements done to all sorts of things it was an enjoyable RPG that has replay value at least for the way you can customize the play style of the 2 characters. Also take note that a lot of F-bombs are dropped, and I mean a whole lot (just in case you wanna give this to your kids to play and you're worried about that sort of thing).

Listen up Cupcake! If you were shrunk to the size of a Jabbit and put into a  Discombobulator how would you get out?!
If that means nothing to you you haven't played Wildstar, and if you have what are you reading this review for? Nexus needs saving!
Wildstar is a Multi Player Online Mash up with a line of humour running through it and copious book and film references, along with some awful puns – example A mission where you have to find the underground lair of a bunch of free robots (called simply Bots in the game). What's the mission called? 'To the Bot cave!' I mean what else would you call it? (probably plenty of things).
The main plot involves a mysterious race called the Eldan who used Nexus, where the game is based, as a home and laboratory. Most if not all of the wildlife you meet is a result of their tinkering and there are a lot of critters. Things walk, run hop, fly etc. with surprisingly realistic animations given the general style of the game is a bit cartoon like. There are pets which you can buy, get as a drop, or just find by scrabbling in the ground – you'll also find buff stations and secret teleporters to instances this way. Sadly pets don't do much, you can't feed 'em or heal 'em – they don't take damage - and with the exception of the engineers constructs they don't fight for you.
You can choose your gender – other games take note! You play either an Exile (yey!) or part of the Dominion (boo!) and can select from 4 races in each, ranging from the usual Human, rock creature, robot etc. Some races are excluded from certain classes, though you can purchase an excluded one on a few. Wildstar is free to play with very few restrictions. I haven’t put any real money in so far, yet I have a house and a hover board (think Back to the Future Pt2) and am at level 46.
There are 6 classes ranging from Engineer (tank & ranged with fighting bots), Esper (telepathic healer & ranged),Healer (healer -no! - and ranged), Spellslinger (duel pistol toting healer and ranged), Stalker (assassin, tank and mele) & Warrior (Huge sword and gun toting tank and mele). The type of armour (light, medium or heavy) you can wear depends on your class.
Finally you can pick from 4 paths: Explorer, goes looking for stuff and spies on the other side; Scientist, has a scan bot that find info about the planet Nexus, its geology, wildlife etc.; Settler, builds new items on the surface, buffs, housing etc. & Warrior – basically if it moves they kill it.
Combat is fluid, you can jump, dodge etc and cast at the same time with enemy specials shown with a red area - stay out of that!
Add to this a deep set of crafting systems and you have a game that'll keep you busy for a long time... if you like it. Its a bit like Marmite (or Vegemite) if you like it and can get past a stupid set of bugs (more on those shortly) its a great game. If not (and you can see from some reviews some folk just don't -  check how long they spent in the game) then look elsewhere.
Quests include the usual kill stuff, collect stuff type but unlike other mmorpgs you don't kill or collect a number of things but a percentage, kill easy stuff and the percentage goes up slowly, kill tough stuff and it rises quicker. Escort missions don't really exist once you've rescued someone they tend to look after themselves. There are also hack missions (a bit like the old electronic Simon says thing – Google it) and a few other that escape my memory for the moment. Wildstar tends not to send you back to the same place repeatedly. You know the kind of thing:
'Oh help me wonderful person while I was on my way to this place in the middle of nowhere I was attacked by a bunch of beasts, I'll pay if you go and kill some of them' – when you return – 'Oh thank you wonderful person while I was running from the beasts I dropped my thingys can you collect them for me?' - so you go back and on your return... 'Oh thank you wonderful person while I was running from the beasts I noticed that they all wore wigs, I'm sure these are valuable – please go and get some for me.' -WHAT! You want me to go back where I have just been twice AGAIN! And I'm looking at you here Lord of the Rings Online!
In Wildstar you have a communicator and npc's mostly contact you on this if you are in the vicinity of one of their quests even if you've never met them and again once you have completed the quest. You can also fire off a challenge at any time, this could be kill or collect the same stuff you are already doing but in a limited time, get from one place to another in a time limit etc.
You naturally level by completing quests, but also by completing path quests – which are different from your main exp and drop useful stuff for your class – and by completing challenges (where you get bronze, silver or gold points which add up to more useful drops). Wildstar is pretty generous in the drops, money, items specific to your class, very rarely another, you can sell the junk or strip stuff you don't want into its component parts for crafting. Levelling is quick and the only grind I have found is in the crafting – particularly where you have to go out and collect stuff. Many items can be buffed with runes which you can either craft or get as drops.
The humour makes me chuckle, particularly when I die (which I do a lot) and the resurrecting thing say 'You again? If you don't like dyeing why do you do it so much? Or 'The next time you come here I'm going to take away your shoes' and so on. There are a bunch of profit mad cloned reps from the Protostar corporation, who's scripting is also fun and where that quote at the top of this review comes from. Add to this the general npc interactions – kidnappers worried about their weight, boy beings failing to chat up girl beings under the silvery light of the moon, which then explodes for no apparent reas... oh hang on. Remember the film and book reverences? Well Hitchhikers is there, but you have to go a long way into the game to find it. There's also the red wire blue wire conundrum from Juggernaut and an unbelievably obscure Doctor Who reference from the John Pertwee years. Large areas steal.. sorry are influenced by classic novels and well its a lot of fun.
The player footprint is low, so you will have to queue a long time for multi player instances and may never get to do some of 'em. Some are possible to solo if you have a high enough level but not all. Multi player world events happen and tend to get left as there are few folk to do 'em. Joining a guild helps greatly.
If your pc has a dynamic IP address you will be plagued by a login failure that says you are not registered and sends a code to your registered email, copy the code out it in the box and it'll let you log in – until your pc changes it's IP again...
There are bugs. I have had all of the following, missing npcs, (you can get an arrow pointing to where an npc, or quest is - key f by default - but it's not good if they ain't there!), npcs refusing to talk to you, movement keys suddenly swapping around so strafe becomes turn and visa versa. All these can be fixed by re-logging but - the most maddening of all if you are a scientist – if you log out with your scan bot active logging in will still have it active but the scan button is missing and you cannot dismiss it. The only way to regain control of your scan bot if for either it (they do take damage) or you die.
These are a massive shame. Wildstar is a great game with a good community and does not deserve its current low foot print. Logging on for the most part is a cinch as it links to your steam account so you don't have to enter a password and you'll loose that stupid verification problem if you set your pc the have a static IP address. Its generous with its drops and really is free to play, no stupid weekly rent for housing for example.
If you haven’t tried it give it a whirl, but stay longer than a couple of hours before you make your choice. See you there!
