First of, I've seen A LOT of downtalk and "DON'T BUY THIS" warnings from other reviews.
Which is why I've been hesitant to try this game untill recently, despite having thoroughly enjoyed Borderlands 2.
But after having played it for 30 hours, and completed the entire campaign + side missions and DLC, which only took roughly around 30 hours... I honestly found it
as Borderlands 2.
Story missions feel more interconnected and relevant to one another. Gives a proper feeling of necessity.
Unlike some of BL2's missions which felt like they were dragging out the story as much as possible for gamelength, as well as sending you on sidetracked tasks when there is a very obvious and easier alternative.
However that does not necessarily mean the story was more well-made. Honestly I cannot say which was the better of the two, as I enjoyed both games equally.
Which should not be a surprise, as the Pre Sequel's template is literally a copy+paste of BL2.
Though solo-play suffers from the same downsides that every Borderlands game has. Far more difficult (or far too easy) with certain classes and/or builds than others. Singleplayer combat is sometimes very unfair.
As is the utterly contrived player-on-player duel system.
I consider this game to be neither a step-down nor a step-up from BL2. It is simply the same game, but a different setting, different--and to me, slightly better--story and with a tiny few extra mechanics.
Like the oxygen management, gliding and slamming, and cryo element are introduced exclusively in this game and makes things a little more interesting. But ultimately irrelevant to making it the game it is. Would still like the game without it.
But I must urge people to avoid buying it (or the season pass) at full price. Though it is just as good as BL2, it is noticably lacking in terms of side content and DLC. Regrettably I did pay the full price of the basegame + season pass.
On the subject of season pass, I must once again iterate that it is not worth the full price.
The two additional characters were not all that interesting to me. Especially the Doppelganger which feels like just a way to get quick cash from making a popular character playable.
And 2 of the 3 playable DLCs are just repetitive 5 rounds Arenas identical to BL2's Fink Slaughterhouse. Which were featured in the game as sidequests, part of the basegame, not an overpriced DLC.
The final DLC however,
was fantasticly entertaining with a story that connects with its chronological sequel. But as expected, it was also disappointingly short. Buying it standalone however is worth it, unless you already got the season pass.

Yes, I have a limited amount of time on this game, and from my limited amount of time, I actually enjoyed it. However, there is one reason why I cannot recommend this game: There is no save feature. I love rogue-likes and permadeath, but not having a save feature does not impact the difficulty of the game, only the functionality.
This is especially annoying when it comes to multiplayer. Rarely do I have 1+ hours to sit at my computer playing a game nonstop. For this game, you would be forced to work this out between yourselves, limiting what you could actually accomplish. It doesn't make sense that you wouldn't include such a feature, since the game has prebuilt towns that would make a perfect save point.
All-in-all, if you have the time to invest multiple hours in succession, this game seems to be very enjoyable. If you are like me, however, and do not have such freedom with your time, it would be a shame to invest in this game.

Loadout is a Free to Play game with arguably the fairest free to play game at the time of writing. It's "design-your-own-ubergun" mechanic is generally well balanced (with some problems at the moment being addressed), with literally no pay to win at all. The only things you can buy are cosmetics which don't affect the game, and 2x XP/Money earning boosts, meaning that you have to play to improve your gun.
Because of this, earning money to buy parts with is given at a reasonable rate, as the amount earnt is worked out via your experience gain, with a level netting you a bonus 2000 "blutes". The part variety is also good, with four main types (rifle, launcher, pulse and beam) and many modifications such as Electrical and Fire type shots, different barrels such as gatling gun to suppressor (although why you would want that I don't know...), and much more. It's definitely enough to keep you interested, with different combinations to tailor your playstyle with.
As for the map variety, there are around 5 to 6 maps, which doesn't particularly sound much. However, the sheer variety within these maps more than makes up for it. As for the game modes, the game offers interesting twists on old classics. Jackhammer is a game mode similar to CTF, but wih an Instakill Hammer that increases the amount of points you earn for every kill earnt with it at the point of capture. There's Death Snatch, a Kill Confirmed style mode, a Blitz mode which is inspired from domination,  and an Extraction mode where a random player from each team is selected to be a collector, whose job it is to collect Blutonium and to put it into a shredder. There's also an Annihilation mode which combines the majority of these together, but is also the weakpoint of the selection, as it can feel like there's just too much to do at any one point.
There's not much wrong with this game to be honest. There are problems, such as the major disadvantage to losing a player due to the 4 vs 4 system, and the arguable low skill ceiling due the tactic of "instead of using dodge, jump around because you can actually shoot", but the good indefinitely outweighs the bad. The sheer fun of annihilating everyone at the start due to everyone starting in a circle together and seeing the damage you've done to people such as putting holes through their chests is just a total blast. And for those thinking that the gun mechanic is a gimmick - it most certainly isn't

An elegant game that fully embraces the idea that less is more. Despite being a 3DS port, Resident Evil: Revelations manages to surpass the big-budget Resident Evil 6. Though the story is the standard Resident Evil bio-terrorism/global conspiracy nonsense, Revelations introduces some new and likable characters and thanks to excellent pacing and a tighter scope, it never outstays its welcome. The game also features excellent gunplay, combined with the best upgrade system in the series. In addition to the single-player campaign, the game also features a score-attack mode called 'Raid', which is easily as compelling. It throws in some ARPG features, such as drops of various rarity and special enemies, and can be played alone or with a friend.
If you miss classic Resident Evil, this game is for you.

This is definitely one of the lesser RE games. The visuals, combat, and enemies all seem watered down from proper numbered entries in the series. This one has a lot of the same problems as RE5. Most of the action takes place on a cruise ship, that's shiny, sterile, and empty. A cruise ship is a very unscary place. Don't make me go to the casino, NO! There's also a LOT of tight corridors to fight and run through. And there's only really one room in the entire game that has creepy monster stuff adorning the walls and floor. It's the only room with an ounce of atmosphere and there weren't even any enemies in the room. Everywhere else could be a part of any other cookie-cutter action game. Put a freaking spider web up somewhere! There are not a lot of different enemy types. A lot of them look like slight variations of each other. What I did like was that the game kind of has the format of the older style RE games where searching around and solving puzzles is necessary to advance. The map does has an objective marker at some points, but it's a good compromise between the more difficult, slower-paced original RE games and newer action-oriented entries. The story is classic RE rubbish. You know all the words to that song so feel free to sing along while you're playing. The campaign takes around 11 hours. When comparing this to RE6 which came out around the same time, there really is no comparison. RE6 is better in every way. It's baffling that Capcom is charging more for this than the much superior RE6. Do not under any circumstances pay full price for this 3DS port. Wait for a severe discount if you really must play this.
I recommend you play this game over RE6. Actually, I recommend that you don't play RE6 at all.
It might be the best RE game we'll see for a while, so you might as well get it.  If you missed it on 3DS, it works great here.

DLC consists of a couple units here and there, or sole units. This has been done to the point where the DLC outcosts the base game. Warhammer 40k seems to have found a good route, where each expansion has the full set of units available, without microtransactions. This doth herewidth be the account of the life of Admiral Yurulek, the Mighty Dragonslayer, destructor of the Mesh'been Reconquers, Leader of The Fleets of the Draconis Theocracy for over 100 years-May His Name Live Forever.
Starting out as a lowly Destroyer captain with a fleet of 3000 at his disposal Yurulek kept the space lanes free of pirate scum in the budding empire of Draconia. While sweeping aside another pirate raiding-band his great skills are realised and he is promoted on the spot to Admiral for his great courage and leadership skills in the face of critical danger and men with eyepatches. He immediately set about focusing resources into growing the fledgeling fleet...for space is dark and full of terrors. He kept one beady eye on the Tyrathian Confederacy,never wholly trusting their outwardly democratic face, feeling their jealous eyes rove over our rich planets.
His experience grew while ridding the systems under our sway of ancient enemies such as the dastardly Void Clouds and Dimensional Instabilities, all the while duelling with any pirates that dared our shores with one hand,while rolling cigarettes with the other. With narrowed eyes he gazed into deep space, swearing that one day the Draconis Theocracy would know freedom and peace.
RAID! The Tyrathians have come in force, claiming our colonisation of a star near their borders as a clear threat. Gathering his scatterred forces from the four corners of known space, Yurulek hatches an ingenious plan to smash the vastly superior Tyrathian Federation Fleet. Cutting in behind them he savagely strikes their supply lines. System after undefended system has its lights turned out by the Dashing Admiral who,with amazing skill, outmanouveres every attempt to catch him. He drags the war out for 14 years,crippling the Tyrathian Economy and capturing planets when possible until finally they relent and withdraw, leaving some of their most valuable planets in our hands. VICTORY! Cries the people...but Yurulek has already turned away from the charts table to gaze again into the abyss beyond the window, searching for the next threat.
Through constant demands for more resources the Fleets continue to grow, amassing 35k when drawn together under a single banner-that of Yurulek The Admiral. And one threat stands above all presently. A ghastly creature of unknowable presence-The Interdimensional Horror of Rikkars Maw. Even the wisest Draconian knows little about this creature,every attempt to study it has resulted in the immediate and total destruction of any vessels involved. The most complete study to this day was as follows
"We have entered the Rikkars Maw system and..whatisthatnonono..ARRGHHcracklecrackle..hiss"
This led the Good Admiral to the doors of the Curators, beings of little power but great wisdom who had, on occasion, rendered assistance to the Draconis. With pride begetting his station Yurulek approached the gross slug atop his Scientific Monolith, and asked for his help. Weighing Yurulek in his gaze, the Curator Of The Alpha Enclave found him worthy and passed along all they knew of the Horror,including a potential weakness in its seemingly impervious armour.
Grimly Yurulek gathered his Armadas together,giving out final orders and bellowing instructions across the vast distances of space to organise the ungainly might of Draconia.
*FLASH* The fleet arrives in Rikkars Maw, as close to the dimensional Instability as possible, but still almost half a system away...and the fleets engines seem to be affected by the rift, giving no more than 50% speed. Yurulek harangues his engineers and mechanics, but to no avail. With the light of horror growing in his eyes he sees the Violet and Ebony Nemesis turn towards them, an epic siluette against the majesty of the systems star. A noise like the rushing of all the oceans in all the worlds echos through the ship,and one of the Drake Battlecruisers shatters soundlessly off of the port bow. "Charge" says The Admiral,his quiet,clear tone cutting through the stunned silence of his staff officers,who erupt into activity, relaying orders,engaging shields and throwing out a skirmishing screen of Gecko Corvettes and their torpedoes. The fleet closes in agonising slowness, the roar of the engines interspursed with the Admirals terse commands squeezing the most from each ship as they closed.
An energy blast washes over the bow of the ship as the Kinetic artillery open up on the deck of each Battleship, sending a rattling broadside toward the Horror. its screams ring out across empty space, by what means none know, as the empty void of space should be silent, but it drives spikes of ice into each mans brain. The only man not on his knees-Yurulrk. Wiping away a smear of blood from his nose he takes the helm and brings the fight to the creature.
A final earth-shatterring barrage, one last scream, and a violet caucophany leaves every man still breathing in the fleet reeling, with sight, sound and touch numbed by the onslaught,silence gradually returns to the fleet. As the men pick themselves up amid the wreckage of the command room,gazing out of the windows at the detritus surrounding them in space-men, torn apart and tossed into vaccum,ships,once graceful and delicate things of power, now kindling and scrap metal floating in the void. But the horror is destroyed, and through its study the Draconis will rise greater than ever before. The Draconis cheer themselves hoarse,chanting the name of the Draconain hero. Yurulek! But he was not ready to rest on his laurels yet. He knew his greatest challenge ever still awaited him...
The DRAGON.
Coming from a dragonian background themselves, the legend of a great Firebreathing beast is one found in all Draconis histories, and a reverance for the great leviathian was instilled at a young age. Despite this Yurulek knew that the beast must fall for the Draconis to truly rise as they could. He sought its layer across all the systems of space,eventually finding the creature wrapped nose-to-tail around a world of unimiginable richness-the Dragons Hoard. Girding his loins, he launched his attack (accounts therof are held within scribe Dellivin's "An Ode To The Dragonslayer", great library Of Vax-Raxxa, Raxx-anos)
The nations of the Draconis Technocracy went through a period of great peace following the slaying of the Dragon, with many Great Victories against many enemies, from the Tricksy Enigmatic Fortress to the Underhanded Cygannian Confederancy; too many to tell in this brief (ha) obituary. But the greatest challenge ever faced came in his twilight years. At the age of 101, after nearly 70 years of command of the fleets of Draconia, the Mesh'been, a Stagnant Empire, Awoke without warning. And attacked.
Gathering the great strength he had overseen the growth of all these years,Yurulek drew 145k of fleetpower together for one decisive battle...only to enter their system and see their fleet. 450k strong. The blood draining from his face, his voice for once forsaking him, his hand groped for the "recall" button...too late. the first broadside anniahlates the front ranks; years; decades of ship building disappear in a blinding titannic flash...and beyond...The TITAN. A ship easaily doubling in size and massively outranking in firepower anything we could bring. Only one course of action."retreat" says the Admiral, his hoarse whisper sounding like a klaxon of doom over the ships speakers. Limping, dragging its half destroyed and wholly disheartened fleet away, Yurulek broods on his next step. How to defeat a fleet of that size and strength? It haunted his nights for the two weeks it took to travel to Vax-Raxxa. Then he remembered the Tyrathian invasion, so many years before. Did he still have the nerve, the ability, the dashing recklessness of youth he needed to repeat the results? Yurulek squared his shoulders and went to work.

First of all, I installed Stellaris not a while ago. Being a huge fan of the GalCiv series, I installed this game with a high bar of standards set by the GalCiv games. Also, I might add, I've played other Paradox games extensively (HoI series, CK2, EU 3 and 4). So, here's my result:
Pros:
- The Clausewitz engine that Paradox uses on other games such as HoI 4 and EU 4 work incredibly well with Stellaris. Fans of those games might be able to pick mostly everything up from the start. The learning curve isn't that bad, though I recommend watching a video or 2 on YouTube to grasp the basics.
- The tech system: one thing that bothered me from other 4X games was that tech was mostly always limited by a visible, static tech tree. So, after a few games in, you would know what to research first always. Well, not this time, chump! Stellaris uses a clever deck system, so whenever you wish to research something, it'll "deal" you 3 random techs, which might or might not appear once you finish researching the current one! This means you need to choose intelligently and meaningfully which option to research, knowing that the other options might not be at your disposal in a few years. This gives the game a good deal of unpredictibility and actually makes you think about your tech choices rather than blindly follow a tech branch.
- The galaxy: Yep, it's big. More than that, its populated with randomly generated species, either pre-sentient, primitive, FTL or fallen. This gives for a lot of replayability, since no two games are the same.
- Less micromanagement: I must admit, I'm a control freak. I have to control everything, min/max everything. With other 4X games I usually had a hard time; managing 30+ planets was no laughing matter. I know, many of them had automated governors that in my opinion were pretty bad. Stellaris managed to "unbog" this by adding sectors. Yes, it's the same concept as an automated governor but for several systems. The thing is, that with proper management and smart thinking, you can make these sectors amazingly productive without the extra work of micromanaging. Many people here tend to hate this system: I personally love it and it makes my late game less muddy.
- Mods: Lots of good mods out there, and the engine allows for rather easy and powerful modifications.
- Real-Time Pausable: Although most 4X are turn based (which isn't a bad thing), I've found that being able to speed up the game especially early in the game works wonders and keeps the game's pace constant.
- Solid race creation process: Yes, you can make a space cockroach empire where your cockroaches are religious zealots. Or a space fox megacorporation. The ethos/civics system works pretty well in defining your government type and the general flavour of your empire.
Cons:
- Like with the other games using the Clausewitz engine, once you know a bit about how it behaves, you can start "gaming" it for your benefit. Might ruin some of the inmersion.
- Few diplomatic options: actually, there are not few, but with the richness of the engine, they could've add even more options (Trade Agreements, I'm looking at you!).
- Rock, paper, scissor: Like everyone else, but at least Stellaris gives us a few options that go beyond the tipical laser-kinetic-missile weapons. Also, combat is usually determined by biggest fleet unless you have a huuuge tech advantage. Still, battles are beautiful (even more so with mods!).
TL;DR
It's a great 4X game that will offer you a lot of replayability and fun. Oh, and try to get the DLCs as well, they both add more events and cool stuff to do in-game.

Of Orcs And Men has all the qualities of a great book: it lures you into its story and you are constantly interested in what will happen next. Character interaction isn't forced by putting them around a campfire at night and boasting stories over roast pig. We hear little of their stories, and we learn of the main characters by how they talk to eachother and to others, and you learn more about them in a good pace across the game.
Sadly, it also has flaws that comes with trying to simulate a good book in a videogame: the level designs and progress through the game are very linear, where the few stray paths are there to provide a little more gear, experience and sometimes a bit of story. The combat itself reminds me of Dragon Age 2, where you can queue up abilities in a slow-motion menu, where it is then executed in real-time. There's no shortage of abilities, but beyond the Rage and Concentration system, there isn't a very unique combat style. (In fact, on harder difficulties, certain abilities and builds are so much more effective than others, that combat itself can become repetitive).
The blend of shallow RPG-elements but great story elements does make it fun to play however. If you take all the optional sidequests, routes and talk with every NPC, the game has a surprisingly large amount of content. With only three achievements dependant on multiple choice, it's possible to get every achievement in the game with two instances of reloading to a previous save.
A few last special notions to some of the more memorable notions of the game: it's graphics, it's world and it's soundtrack.
The graphics aren't very high-end, and with some ofthe more advanced games around, you won't be impressed. But it does a good job at imitating them, without being very demanding on your hardware.
The world it plays in is different from other fantasy RPGs - that much should be clear by the title alone! It's one of the few recent RPG-releases that's more interested in painting morals gray than black-and-white.
The soundtrack is from the Boston Cello Quartet, and is an absolute gem. It's also implemented into the game to play/loop certain parts of a soundtrack at certain points of combat/cutscenes; the soundtrack itself syncs with your level progression.
Of Orcs And Men is a good recommendation, and it's a shame that Spiders Studio confirmed there are currently no plans for a much desired sequal. I personally found the price a bit too steep, but thankfully, Steam regulary allows sales and I managed to get Of Orcs And Men for a considerable discount.

Now, the small scope makes me think of this game as sort of like a B-list movie. That's
actually. It's almost like an indie RPG but it's definitely not since they've got big Publisher support. It makes the game feel well rounded and solid. The devs knew what they wanted to make and they did so splendidly. It's a budget title so to speak.
The game uses my favorite combat style of queuing up actions and attacks either in real-time or in paused time (but in this game's case - slowed time) much like Knights of the Old Republic or Neverwinter Nights. And the combat is fantastic by the way. It's definitely challenging since every attack is deliberate and damaging to both your characters and the enemies. What I mean by that is the enemies usually come in packs and can easily interrupt, stun, and then kill your party if your not careful. The levels actually reinforce the idea of planning. The levels are mostly straight corridors that are dotted with wide open arenas. You can approach them stealthly or guns blazing.
Now, I should mention that you've only got
playable characters, Arkail the big orc and Styx the obviously rogue goblin. The customization is kind of limited. The game's got small skill trees, obvious shiny loot sacks, and (to the devs credit) upgradeable gear. It's obvious that your party is going to turn out with the orc as your tank and the goblin is either your range or melee DPS. But an interesting thing about the orc is you can lose control of him since he has a rage meter. The rage meter also acts as the orc's "mana" to activate certain skills though. So you can imagine how your going to plan out your fights with that in mind.
Their story and that of the game's story is actually your typical fantasy. You got your orcs, goblins, mages, fanatical religious orders, and later on a brief appearance by the Elves and Dwarves. Basically, the story is that the orcs are being enslaved by a cruel human empire. Your story is to lead Arkail and Styx on a suicide mission to kill the human emperor. It's a nice story and the world is really interesting. It's got this typical western european medieval look to it. But the Orcish perspective help in sucking me in to the game's world. However, the dialogue and the voice acting is pretty bad. The swearing is so out of place. It's like the devs were trying to be edgy but just failed with the translation from the original french script. There is a dialogue system. But it's there to either get more lore to choose which side quest to take.
The graphical fidelity is also pretty great. The character models of the orcs & goblins plus the later levels look stunning especially with an obvious budget title. And the soundtrack is also great. I would definitely buy it.
All-in-all, the game's a fairly decent RPG from two studios who would later on make some fairly decent RPG's with the same combat system. I love the combat and the Orcish perspective on a typical fantasy world is refreshing experience. And if your aching for a solid and almost indie like RPG, then
. If your on the fence, then buying at a discount is always a good idea.

I rewrote this review from scratch as it was beginning to be a pile of never-ending edits.
Here's the simple/short version:
Wurm Unlimited is like having a dedicated server-based version of the MMO Wurm Online. For those who don't know - Wurm Online is kinda like Runescape back when it actually had challenge/point, you start with a specific set of gear and work for what you get beyond that.
Here's the Details:
Tools are a very basic and integral part of the game and you will NOT recieve the entire set when you first start (or anywhere close to it). The Combat System and Graphics aren't exactly "up-to-date" but if you are like me and a significant majority of my friends that won't matter as much as gameplay; which Wurm Unlimited provides in Spades. This is NOT a game of instant gratification or quick easy playstyles - you will very much have to put work into this game to get any enjoyment out of it.
The major difference in the scheme of Wurm Unlimited compared to Wurm Online ( which isn't available on Steam - you have to goto
) is that Wurm Online is free-to-play with a severe skill cap and several restraints on gameplay resulting from it - unless you choose to pay for a subscription. Now Wurm Unlimited will be a purchase - but it's a one-time purchase with no subscription required to play for the rest of the time with full features.
Furthermore Unlimited true to it's name has several options that do not exist in the "Hardcore" MMO world of Wurm Online - chief among them the ability to have somewhat accelerated growth and relaxed style; these things depend on the server(s) you choose to play on naturally but in general most servers allow for atleast 2 - 10 times the skill gain rates of Wurm Online at their most basic form, often having several other "time-related" modifications to the rates. As well as these "tweaks" a server admin of Wurm Unlimited may opt to install mods or enhancements onto the server as a whole.
All in all I recommend you try Wurm Online as a sort of "Test Drive" before buying this with the understanding that the free-to-play experience is a "trial" and this would be the "full version".
Also to help allievate any concerns about single-player - while it is not /exceedingly/ hard to register your own server - it will require port forwarding and the like in order to allow OTHER people to play on it.
The Dedicated Server Software itself is available as a seperate download under "Tools" of the library submenu on Steam - be aware this will NOT allow you to play the game - only host a server from that machine hence why it is publically available. You will need to purchase Wurm Unlimited to actually be able to play on said server; that said this is also a good chance for you to experiment with the options if you have an interest in doing some hosting or single-player as many of the things in this software revolve around the "tweaks" between Online and Unlimited.
The Game is good - but it's not for everyone - keep in mind that I have said that the graphics and combat system are not the best - and if you are OK with that then you should get along fine.
I have never played Wurm Online, but am now addicted to Wurm Unlimited.  It will test your patience, but it is well worth it.

Port of a 3DS game, and yet it leaves me wondering: why? Not to mention that it is actually priced *higher* than Resident Evil 6 (despite 6 having more content, higher production value, and (arguably) more thought behind it).
Okay, some things I liked. Keeping in mind that it was a port of a mobile game, it actually looks pretty good at times. The weapon customisation, while not stellar, was still pretty nice. Raid mode is also pretty nice, if you like grindfests (I do).
But really, people tout this game as returning to the roots of the series, which I certainly think it tried to do, but it just falls short. Why? Ammunition is plentiful, sense of dread and the fear of what lies around the corner is gone, puzzles are pretty much nonexistant, no inventory management to speak of and decisions of fight or flight are never really made.
That's just comparing it to the classic games, mind you.
On top of that, I think there's a lot of wasted potential here. I was excited for the game mainly because of two things: the setting and the enemies. I thought the setting would be perfect, combining survival horror with dreaded underwater segements, creating a truly fiendish monster of a game. I also thought the enemies were kind of wierd and abstract looking, and I thought a lot could be done with underwater creatures affected with a new kind of virus.
What you get instead is a very straightforward corridor shooter. The enemies are basically reskinned zombies (regular zombies, strong zombie, zombie with a gun, fat zombie etc.) and the underwater segments are actually few and far between. Not to mention the underwater segments are *less* scary than the dry segments, thanks to a "Mario 64"-like water-surfacing-health-regeneration system.
The plot, like most RE games, is silly. But not only that, its just not entertaining. The voice acting is pretty questionable too. It's nice to see Chris Redfield back, looking & sounding like he does in RE5 and 6 (although it sounds a little like hes just phoning his performance in this time), but unfortunately Jill has received a visual and audible makeover, making her just a stranger in the room. The other characters are pretty bland and uninteresting, and the emotional 'high point' of the story amounts to an anti-climax, where it turns out a guy that was meant to die just got a crippy leg.
Anyways, mostly just a big dissapointment in the untapped potential that a sea-based isolated setting could provide for a game like this. And, okay, I appreciate that they ported the game to other systems so a wider audience can play it, but I really question the decision to price a port of a mobile game as high as a regular AAA title.

So AMD finally got around to updating their drivers to fix the issues with this game, right after I write a review (totally not a rant) about their problems of course. Now there is no reason not to get this game, unless you have a GTX 780 or 780ti, because those cards still have problems.
This is probably my favorite singleplayer game of all time. The story is enthralling, the characters develop in interesting ways throughout the story, the music is phenomenal, the combat is satisfying, and the locations are stunning.
To start with, the story. This game is technically a sequel, but no knowledge of the original is required to appreciate this game, and beyond a couple of references there aren't many links between the two. Automata takes place thousands of years after the original, in fact. In NieR:Automata you play as an Android that is fighting endless numbers of robots to reclaim the Earth so humanity can come back from the moon. Why is humanity on the moon? Aliens. But seriously, humanity fled to the moon when the aliens created robots to wipe them out. Sounds a little complicated? It gets better, but I am not going to spoil anything here. As a sidenote, if you get this game, and you get to an ending, it isn't the end of the game. In reality, both Ending A and B are breaks in the story, while Endings C, D, and E are the alternate actual endings. F through Z are either jokes of some sort or because of a mistake you make in the story. Each time you get an ending, it will put a letter on your save file then let you go back to your last save, or in A and B it will start the next section of the story.
Next, the character development. This is obviously a byproduct of events in the story, so anything specific would be a pretty large spoiler. Lets just say that some pretty major changes happen in the way characters behave both to eachother and overall. The side characters from various quests are interesting as well, one example being some characters that link to the original. These plots are still good without playing the original NieR though.
The music is another mind-blowing element of this game. This soundtrack has such a wonderful variety of tracks that I think fit with every part of the story. NieR:Automata is one of the few games that I have stopped to listen to the area music, and some songs are so dazzling that I bought the soundtrack and listen to them even when i'm not playing the game. The various boss songs and character themes are superb as well.
Admittedly the combat is probably the weakest part of this game. I personally think it is satisfying, but I can understand if someone doesn't like it. It is simple, compared to a game like Bayonetta or others in this class. There aren't tons of unique combos, and even the number of weapons is somewhat small. What it falls behind on in combos is the crispness of animation and the gratification that comes with that. The few weapon types that are in the game do provide some variety of attack set as well.
Finally, the locations. They aren't very specifc about what they are, so there isn't any connection to a present day setting. They are beautiful though, and there are enough of them. Though the first 2 endings take place in the same area with enemies being similar, the third set of endings adds some new areas for the story to progress in, with the final area being my personal favorite in the end, even if the story is a bit sad.
Now that the driver issues have been fixed, there is no reason not to buy this game. My last serious issue is gone, and yours should be too. If you can't be convinced to buy a game based on its merit in the categories that actually matter like story and gameplay, what is the point of reading reviews? Go buy NieR:Automata.

After playing through the game and observing where it has been going since beta, I can say I would not reccomend this in the state it is currently in, and do not feel it will get to a point where I would in the near future.
For people who enjoy the table top game this game is an awesome idea to experience more story in the Iron Kingdoms, and to play the game in a way that requires less clean up and even try out different factions.
For a project like converting a table top into a PC game, there were of course its share of bugs that would be expected from a relatively new studio. I was perfectly fine with that, they were trying to get the game fully released so all its kickstarter backers could enjoy what they paid for.
Unfortunately, the game ended up feeling hacked together when it was officially "released".
The single player campaign, although it was enjoyable to be given different scenerios to overcome, there were just a lot of things wrong with it. The camera was, and still is pretty unbarable, the UI would not always play nice with the map you were on, and the AI was not very challenging and followed a very specific sequence of moves unless you put a target right in their face.
The cutscenes were something out of a launch Playstation 1 game. Completely still models with the camera panning to whoever was talking, and even then you had a hard time seeing who it was because of the lighting. With how much work that was put into the in game models, you think they could have animated the scenes. That said, the in game models are pretty nice, fans of the table top will appreciate how the characters and warjacks look animated.
The multiplayer was meant to be the bread and butter for this game, a way for people who enjoy the table top, or even new comers, to come press a button and be put into a game of warmachine instantly. The multiplayer feels like its lacking A LOT. Yes you can be matched with another player, most of the time. It is not uncommon for the "quick match" option, to not be quick at all. The multiplayer as a game functions, bugs excluded, but it not very enjoyable because of the problems the overall game has, as well as very simple win conditions.
The UI is just awful. Actions feel unresponsive, it is arranged in an unappealing matter, text can be hard to read, and it difficult to traverse the playing map. Getting information to appear on your spells and abilities usually requires you to click the button for it, thus committing to the action.
The grid system is also not executed as well as it could have. It feels clunky and sometimes even inconsistent.
What is worse about knowing all these things is the price tag that has been on it. The DLC model is also kind of a turn off, especially in the state the game is still in. If the game were in a relatively bugg free state, charging DLC is reasonable.
Developing the DLC seemed to be as high, or perhaps an even higher priority than making the game as functional as it could be.
TLDR: Game is no where near as functional as it should be. UI is unbarable, camera is wonky, gameplay is not strong enough to hold it all up. DLC seems to take a place above fixing bugs and improving overall functionality.

This game, when playable, is a rather enjoyable naval warfare game.  However, should you not have a dedicated fiber optic line that runs right to whatever hampster-powered servers they possess, you will not be able to maintain connection whatsoever.  I played for about 8 hours without a hitch, however the moment a roommate came home and opened Youtube, the strain on the network (that still supporst flawless connection to -numerous- other MMO style games) was enough that I could not maintain a constant connection and was disconnected from the game servers every 15 seconds or so.
So, if you enjoy repeatedly relogging into the game to see a grey-filtere over your sinking ship, this is the game for you.  If you have the resources available to have the dedicated laser-satellite rig required to have a ping of less than 21 to the servers, then by all means, enjoy pelting ships with cannonades and torpedos; the rest of us will just sit back and play something better.
Never have I played a naval game quite so poor of quality.

I do not often review games, but in this case I will make an exception.
I grabbed it, looking for a fun, free MMO just to mess around with, not expecting much, and have been very pleasantly surpried by it.
The game play, while not groundbreaking, is quite a lot of fun.  The graphics might be a bit cartoony, but it actually fits the aesthetic of the genre.  Combat is a nice mix of traditional MMO click and power use, and a more active combat system that encourages and in some cases requires you to get the heck out of the way of incoming attacks.
Story wise, it has been interesting so far, though I've barely scratched the surface.  There are the traditional quests, dungeons and pvp, but also raids, adventure areas for 1-5 people, crafting, and housing.
The Path system adds a nice social aspect to things, if you desire it (being able to set up boost kiosks and vendors for other people is fun).
And best of all, it is free.  Not only free, but the game rewards you for playing. To be honest I hesitated for a long time before I bought the game. I have played Borderlands 2 a lot and it is still one of my favorite games, so I was afraid The Pre-Sequel was gonna be a cheap follow-up game. After my first playthrough I have to say that all in all I was pleasantly surprised.
Adding the features of low gravity in certain areas of the game (and yes, there are still areas like facilities that have "regular" gravity as known from Pandora) was a great idea and it is really lots of fun. You can even smash down on enemies with effects according to your O2-kit. In addition to providing you with awesome smash-affects, that burn, corrode, shock or freeze away your enemies, the O2-kit also provides you with - yes, you guessed it - O2, that you need to breathe when outside of facilities. I was a little afraid that this might be a problem, but there are usually plenty of ways to recharge your O2.
The story basically tells how Handsome Jack became to be the Handsome Jackass (badum-ts) that he is in Borderlands 2. I don't wanna spoil anything now, but basically you're playing a Vault Hunter again (duh!) and you're at Jack's service, following his command. So while I expected this game to be just a quick prequel/sequel to the first 2 games it turned out to be a lot of fun and while the graphics and gameplay didn't really change a lot, there are a lot of new elements in the game, that you can explore and try out.
The only thing that bothered me a little was a lack of diversity in the various levels. In my opinion that was done a lot better in Borderlands 2, where there is really a little bit of everything, whereas in the Pre-Sequel everything looks kinda gloomy, dark, cold and ... "boring". I heard that the DLCs bring in a bit of diversity, but I still don't have them, so can't really comment on that.
Still, I enjoyed the game a lot and can't wait to play through it over and over again with all the characters and in True Vault Hunter Mode.

Let's get this out of the way. The Pre-Sequel is easily the worst game in the Borderlands series. Design so often falls short of what it set out to do or works against itself. Despite that, it does enough things well enough to give it a cautious recommendation.
If you know the gist of the series, you know what to expect here. (If you don't, start with Borderlands 2.) Pre-Sequel makes some changes from 2 but so many of them don't live up to expectations. Class builds are *extremely* synergy-oriented, which allows for some really cool, highly differentiated ways to play when you get them off the ground, but it takes a long time to get those Rube Goldberg machines working, to the point that you're probably most or all of the way through the first run of story mode before your character really "clicks" and you play meaningfully differently from anyone else. That's a long time to wait and pretty much pre-supposes that you're going to stick around for True Vault Hunter Mode (new game +) to see how the game is really meant to be played.
These kinds of well-meaning design screwups are the norm. It sounds nice not to force each class into a particular gun type, for example, but when everyone on your team wants that cool new legendary that just dropped, you begin to see the wisdom of pigeon-holing each character into a different weapon group. It also causes problems in investing moonstones (TPS's counterpart to Eridium) to upgrade max ammo capacity. Athena, for example, doesn't care about the weapon type as much as the damage type, so you can easily find yourself spending moonstones upgrading shotguns, SMGs, assault rifles, AND lasers, needing a giant heap of stones every time you find a good gun in a previously unused family.
The oxygen/slam system feels bolted on. Oxygen kits give you air that rarely matters in a vacuum and make it possible to make large jumps and powerful ground-slams that rarely work in atmosphere. The same vacuum/atmosphere split also makes incendiary weapons a lot more disappointing.
And finally, the campaign is a dull slog and loot drops have been tuned to only really be rewarding when you defeat bosses, which makes discovering loot pretty disappointing and kitting out a high-quality murder machine mostly a game of boss-grinding. Lame. The "loot grinder" machine was supposed to add some more consistency to it but other than reliably getting you your legendary class mod, it mostly just eats purples for no reward.
All that said, TPS shows off the best writing in the series, with a lot to reward attentive players who keep coming back. It does a great job of showing a sympathetic side to Borderlands 2's main foe Handsome Jack without muddying the waters; it's clear he's a bad guy, but we have a better understanding of how he got there.
And while synergy-centered builds take *entirely* too long to get off the ground, they can be immensely rewarding. The pure anarchic joy of playing a Claptrap who explodes every time he shoots, hits a target, loses his shields, falls to the ground, or does pretty much anything at all, for example, is something that should delight powergamers and funhavers alike.
Overall, TPS is a deeply flawed game but there's enough moments of true greatness to justify giving it a try. Wait for a sale.

N00b review coming up.  So I am completely new to Wurm and I already love  it.  Evidently this game is the long lasting Wurm Online game (well over a decade and running strong).  The graphics and animations are way below today's standard but the game play is engaging and addictive.  If you love the First Person Shooter game, this is not for you however.  You enter the game weal and jelpless and have to slowly, slowly, painfully at times slowly work your way up.
The first few times I attempted to play I had the misfortune to spawn at night amongst ghosts and was killed off immediately.  D:  No worries though, nothing yet gained so nothing lost.  Then I had the good start.  Found a friendly server, started in daylight, got a few quests assigned from an NPC that taught me some of the basics.  I was off and running.  The slower pace was refreshing and it made what I achieved all the better.  I lucked out and my extremely shallow mine hit an iron vein right away.  Then I came across a town guards corpse and got a full set of armor and a nice spear... of course it weighs so much I can hardly move in it so I just keep it in a locked chest for emergency use.  I leveled some ground and built a crude fence with gates and locks to protect me from my enemies.  And well that was it for the first day.  :|  Yep that was it for day one, real life day mind you, it was several game days that had passed and all I have is a small foothold.  Now I need to mention that the server has an excellerated craft and experience timer as well and that is all I accomplished... but do I have plans!  I shall build from here a home then a village and establish myself.  It shall take real days, weeks, and months, and even years.  I shall enlist friends and work hard at it and slowly it shall be.
In my humble opinion this game is for the casual player that can take his time and make something that will last.  There is no race for the top level or to kill the ultimate boss.  It is a survival game that is realistic to the point of pain.  Expect to die a lot and in unspectacular ways.  The game will be painfully slow at times, it takes several minutes to fish and expect to fail until your level goes up.  Same with finding and making medical supply.  Expect to run more often then you stand and fight for quite sometime.  Realisticly if you were in the woods and a bear came along and all you had was a stick would you be able to stand and fight it succesfully?  Wounds do not automaticly heal and bad wounds actually get worse and harder to heal as time passes until you either get a high enough level of healing cover (hard to do when new) or die from them.
The gameplay is NOT intuitive and must be learned.  Tutorials if any, barely scratch the surface.  I highly recommend the Youtuber Gamester4life and his tutorial.  Without it I would have likely raged and given up.  His videos are paced similarly to the game and you must watch the whole video because you never know when he will drop that key bit of information that you needed to enjoy what you were doing.  I often have him playing on the laptop while I am playing Wurm on the desktop.  His voice can be calming.  XD  He has also been a tremendous help.  If you are sitting on the fence about purchaseing this game I would go and watch a few of his videos, more then the first one as they do get better.  After two or three you will know what you are getting into.
Now go, learn, buy, and have fun being addicted to this game!

--------Intro--------
I bought a copy of Wurm Unlimited (WU) mostly out of curiosity as to what exactly is the difference between this and Wurm Online(WO). From what I've seen so far, it is essentially exactly the same game except you the servers are run by the community. The fact that you get the "dedicated server" software enables you to set up your own Wurm server, to play locally in "singleplayer" or you after the initial set up (Port forwarding or peer-to-peer tunneling) you can play the game with your friends! The server allows you to set up "Adventure" mode, which is pretty much same as your normal WO with the option to tweak some variables such as skill gain, monster count player set up etc. Then there's "Creative" mode which I haven't tried, but supposedly it loads up a blank map on which you can then build upon.
--------Would I recommend it?--------
Hard to tell. I mean if you already played Wurm Online, and you ever wanted to host your own server for you and your friends to play with, without having to worry about monthly subscribtion, Wurm Unlimited might be for you. It's essencially the same game or at least I haven't noticed many differences.
If you haven't played Wurm before, I suggest you to try the Wurm Online (MMO version) first, learn to get around, maybe find some friends to find out if this is the kind of game for you. It's free to play, with the optional "premium" version which grants you exp. boost. and some other benefits for monthly subscribtion of $10 or your regional equivalent.
ADHD Version: If you want a demo, try the MMO version first.
This is everything Wurm online should have been.

I tried to like this. I couldn't. I like sandboxes and love them when they have the potential for long term persistent change.
This had some micromanaging at the start just to survive your first few nights. That in itself was extremely time consuming and difficult but I like a little challenge.
Made a server, slightly inflated rates. Ok let's do this.
I eventually found out this relationship wasn't going to happen.
User vs UI: You have to right click or go into menus for nearly everything. There is no left-click = use tool. You have to queue up several actions and your character statistics throttle this. It also doesn't help that the game has a built-in wiki that it encourages you to use for every single item.
There is no tutorial.
Fighting a wild cat of really low level took half an hour and 3 retreats to heal up. Even then the combat log was saying "barely poked" or "hardly scratched" which wasn't very reassuring.
Trying to get started with the 'first night essentials' was taking the greater part of two hours.
Could hardly make tools as you have a percentage based failure rate in proportion to low crafting skill.
On top of that Java loved to hang and crash.
This game is meant for a large persistent community with people religiously returning on a daily basis to get things done. You would only begin to experience what the game has to offer when you have a constant flow of over 16 people working together. There is no going lone wolf and expecting to get a small start to eventually bring people on or become accepted to a group. You need a team and you need people as a single person at starting rank cannot do anything within a reasonable time frame.
Tales of other players explain that they spent months or even years of repeated returns to the game just to spend a lot of time and feel 'rewarded'. It's at this point where the game seems more like a second job than just having fun for a little bit.
So for a short pick up and go this is definitely not the game you are looking for.
If you like convoluted UI with tons of clicking and days or weeks waiting from queued up actions then this is it.
I don't mind a bit of a grind but this was way too much for my patience, so I can't recommend this title.

Newcomers, to not get fooled, as this is nothing but a lazy port from a 2012 game. Of course, if you're nostalgic of the PS3 version, go for it, but here's what, as a newcomer, the game feels like:
Pros:
-Good netcode (no lag)

-Very good OST

Cons:
-New players are absolutely not welcome (only experienced players are to be found online)

-Combos are annoyingly long and the game doesn't have any burst mechanic to escape them

-Some combined inputs have a shortcut, some don't (ie: you have to use JoyToKey to get a A+B button, which is really useful to Seth players)
Overall, the most fun you'll end up having is in training mode, trying to do what you see in youtube combos videos

A cute, cheerful, dark, depressing rogue-like puzzle game. It has interesting characters and some neat ideas (proceduraly generated NPC and character designs). Road Not Taken is a game of thoughtful puzzles, intimate and personal relationships, and a strong but subtle story of the deeply flawed town you are protecting. The dialog is well-written, the puzzles hide a robust crafting system, and your mastery of the game and its systems builds up naturally across multiple playthroughs.
Road Not Taken is *also* a game with frustrating randomness in both the story and the puzzle levels. Your friends and loved ones will abandon you at the flip of a coin, it's easy to render certain puzzle rooms impossible to complete, and the first time you learn the crafting system is probably by summoning an immortal demon.
After 2 full playthroughs I think I've seen most of what there is to see, but I've enjoyed my time with Road Not Taken. The myriad ups and downs are the point of the game - it's a game about life, and life always has its ups and downs. This game is bittersweet, and it won't last you forever, but I think it's a game worth experiencing.

The game is a mix of light rpg mechanics, a startdard Platinum character action game and a decent amount of bullet hell for good measure. The combat at first is little bit less fun than other platinum games, but as you progress you will get upgrade chips that give you abilities like witch-time and counters.
I love just about everything about the game but, the combat feels a little more loose than most of Platinum's other titles. I assume that it was deliberately designed this way to accommodate the bullet mechanics. I reccomend you play with a claw grip on your controller so you can hold down RB for your pod's gun.
The soundtrack is beautiful. There is a long list of songs and just about all of them have multiple versions that play during major events.
To me the flaws in the game are so minor I would actually call Nier Automata perfect, too bad the same can't be said about how it runs.

There is false information in a lot of reviews, so I just wanted to set the record straight.
1. Many reviews claim there is NO singleplayer. This is not true. There is an offline mode with three difficulty settings for AI. You can use any of the premade teams in this mode at least.
2. This game doesn't get enough credit for its dungeon designing system. This elevates the game in my opinion.
3. This game is still online-capable if you set up a game with someone, and it can be played on LAN.
4. It is a perfectly competent addition to the Blood Bowl games, but it doesn't replace either of the other digital options (BB or BB2). Instead, it's just a supplement to mix things up.
I can't find out in the short amount of time I've spent testing the game if leveling up players and teams occurs when you play singleplayer or not. I'd guess probably not. Also, didn't see a way to create your own teams yet, but the prebuilts are pretty varied and interesting.
Anyway, I'd say for true BB fans this game is a must-buy, and if you're savvy you'll be able to find it for very cheap by waiting for the right time or asking around on Steam trading forums. I got mine for about a buck. Worth it, for sure.

Fun but short puzzle platformer.  It's fairly easy, but not too easy; I really liked the difficulty level.  A couple of the puzzles took me some effort to figure out, and some of the platforming was a bit challenging, mostly due to timing.   Nothing that made me want to walk away from the game.
The art style is sharp and original, and I liked the little robot, especially its swimming and dance animations.  The game reminded me a bit of The Fall; the story and narration (which is very well done) give this game a similar melancholy feel.  Some of the puzzles also brought to mind Amanita Design's games (Samorost, etc.).  But there are a few elements in this game that I haven't seen before.  My favorite moments were using a surfboard-like thing to glide over certain areas, and riding the cart-like thing in the area with all the lava.  Those parts felt like a fun challenge, since I had to use both logic and reflexes.
My one complaint is that it only took me 3 hours to beat, and I'm slow at action games.  The regular price ($9.99 us) seems a little high for such a short game.  But it was a really nice way to spend an evening, and this game is definitely worth playing.

I bought this on sale for a very low price (75% off). It might be the best value for money I've experienced in a Steam game.
This little gem of a game kept me hooked, curious, entertained and amazed by its beautiful aesthetics, vector graphics and soundtrack for a couple of hours. And the puzzles: fun, not too hard, and when you die, the game designers don't go all-sadistic on you. The timing-based puzzles usually reset to a point where you can just move straight on to the next step of the puzzle (which is great!) - instead of making you wait for a tedious, exact moment where you can resume (many diabolical puzzle designers do this).
Excellent design overall. Even though I must have died a hundred times or so, it was totally worth it. Amazing experience. Recommended for fans of the platformer genre that want to soak up atmosphere, a decent story, easy-ish puzzles and beautiful, beautiful visuals and sound.
I just wish it could have lasted longer, but at least there was no filler and no crap. Short and sweet.

A diamond on the rough! Of Orcs and Men is nothing short of a compelling tale of a reverse good-vs-evil plot. Although not necessarily a style only seen under fantasy, high or low, storylines, OO&M tackles those elements and tackles them HARD. Be ready to have some of your pre-conceived notions of fantasy twisted in a way that not even Shrek could come up with - and with a much more serious tone. Watch out for foul language (there is a LOT) if you'd like to avoid it. If you don't mind it like me, this will just bring much more life to this already vibrant world (after all, a rough orc and a shifty goblin aren't old ladies nor are their usual repertoire).
Nevertheless, there are some flaws: animation is pretty damn bad (the persistent use of the blatant same animations reminds me of KotOR of all things, in a sense that you can tell which animation is being used - for the 100th time), so is voice acting for anyone outside the main cast (although Arkail and Styx, the protagonists, sound perfectly as they should) and graphics are okay, at best - a medium-end machine or lower can play it maxed and indeed enjoy some good visuals. I also dislike how pretty much every section of the game is structured as a "corridor": you have optional pathways, but it really works as a road with just one blatant way to go - instead of a dungeon-crawler, this is a corridor-crawler.
The fascinating story, the likeable characters (despite sometimes feeling too one-dimensional, until late chapter 2, when things begin heating up) and the intriguing, almost turn-based, and simple (if played on easy) yet complex (on hard and *gasp* the frustratingly challenging Extreme difficulties) combat kept me going despite the flaws.
Really enjoyed playing the game and I'm definetly playing it again sometime in the future. As well as keeping an eye out for future games from these devs.

Medieval II: Total War is one of the best strategy games I've played. It's both enjoyable in a strategical and personal sense.
Lets just straight get into why.
- The game manages to be detailed with their strategy, forcing you to actually flank and position your troops. It doesn't just account to how large your force is or whose troops are more disciplined, though, those two are factors to consider as well. In multiplayer, you might even be able to factor in Psychological Warfare! It gets pretty in-depth. And I love that.
- In the Campaign, your Generals, Merchants, Spies, Diplomats and Assassins can gain, lose, enhance and diminish traits. It forces you to treat them as actual people to win the war, not the game. Your General is too hot-headed? Have him take up an Administrative Role for a while...Oh, he's too scary? Have him spare the peasants. He's a good guy, despite all the villages he burned...Probably.
- The building and unit descriptions are just superbly fun to read, I find myself spending minutes reading the buildings and units on the queue. As well as the trait descriptions..It makes the game more immersive.
- General Speeches are just the best thing ever. They can either be very good, like "Pray now for the intercession of Saint Michael in our Imperial Cause..If you ride a horse, add a prayer to Saint Martin for your devotions!" Or they can be extremely savage, "They say that the French are better loves than fighters, this is true: Ask any goat, pig or other farmyard animal." And, my favorite, can be hilarious, "Well, here's the thing. I look at our foes, and all I see are a bunch of♥♥♥♥♥♥weasels!" These things don't matter. They don't. But they're so good. And the fact that the later Total War games remove this makes it feel like something was missing in their core.
- If you're ever bored with native gameplay, the modding community is ready to make you waste more hours on their mods like Stainless Steel, Third Age, DarthMod, etc.
- The dead bodies don't despawn. The unit sizes are 80-160 men per unit. Maybe even more. I think that speaks for itself. It does? Of course it does.
- While the campaign is great, I can't deny, nor can anyone deny, the fact that the AI is bad. I'd like to take this short moment to just be thankful that it's not as dumb as Empire: Total War's..
- The unit variety is very large at first, but after a few hours of gameplay, you'll start to realize how little it is..
- The Community isn't very bad, but not very good either. From my experience, the people are usually nice, and everyone follows the rules given by the host. (And apologize if they accidentaly don't.) Though, you will still occassionaly run into rude people, cheaters, campers, etc. Still, I still find a lot of fun in Multiplayer.
- The Graphics in Medieval II isn't very impressive, but it's not bad either. But hey, it's an old game, so the lack in graphics is justified. Besides, charging knights will still look epic in any Total War game, no matter the graphics.
- The best thing about any total war game, or any game, is the experience. I have so much misadventures and adventures in this great game. I had a great general who died in defense of our Great Capital. (His name was Richard the Fearless.) I had an Assassin who assassinated every Pope that was elected until only the Cardinal from my nation was left to be elected. (His name was
Borgognion the Killer.) I had a faithful unit of Mailed Knights that I brought to in every single campaign since the moment they were recruited early into the campaign. It's just..It's great. To be honest, this is probably why Medieval II is considered one of the best strategy games, and one of the best Total War games. It's the adventures you get through this.

I've played Wurm Online on and off since about 2006. My only gripe with the online version back then was the absolutely horrific graphics and the fact that a good 80-90% of the map was populated with people's old♥♥♥♥♥♥ so it was very difficult to carve out a niche for yourself in all that.
What Code Club AB have done by releasing Wurm as a standalone version is nothing short of amazing. This game planted the seed in Notch's mind for Minecraft, and in itself is a much more complex, deep and time consuming game with much the same premise: exist and thrive in an empty world.
But the only real similarity that Minecraft and Wurm share here that I want to bring attention to is the core principle of the entire game: Teamwork and creativity.
You can terraform, build a house, tame animals, fight monsters, craft armour and weapons, and even commit yourself to one of the two religions in the game, but it does take a lot of time and a lot of teamwork. Whether that's something you find appealing or cannot stand, there is grinding in this game. But it's a grind that pays off with legendary tales and a real world that you strived to construct from nothing.
If one were to take even a cursory glance at Wurm Online's colourful history, they would find a completely player driven lore comprised of the rise and fall of empires, epic constructions of vast cities and trade highways, and to me, that highlights what Wurm is: stories. Being a part of something bigger. Helping to construct something lasting that you know took a lot of time and effort between friends.
With the release of the standalone version comes the chance for everyone to be a part of their own player driven history. While the MMO version has only a limited amount of resources and space for only so many cities and empires, this is not so for Unlimited. There's also the potential for mods and an ever increasing skill set for even more stuff to build and do in the game.  The possibilities truly are unlimited.
While I hesitate to draw more comparisons to Minecraft, I think for the benefit of the layman it'd be fair to say something like: In Minecraft you can create a house and perhaps even a town in the span of a day; it's really not a big deal and even less of an accomplishment. In Wurm, when you crest a hill and find a city that is truly impressive, you can count on the fact that a lot of people were here and they worked very hard to create it. That itself lends appeal to people who find enjoyment in coming together and working to build something cool. And whether it's a lone shack in the middle of the woods or an epic castle that you've just completed, the satisfaction of striving to build something from nothing is what keeps people coming back.

AdVenture Capitalist, as well as many other games encapsulated in the "clicker genre" are now, albeit slowly, appearing on steam. There's no denying that these games have a particularly addictive element to them. In AdVenture Capitalist, you start with your very own lemonade stand, you click enough times until you can automate the process and save up enough money to purchase a newspaper delivery service, and so on, until you're the owner of your own oil company.  But wait, you don't need to just own one lemonade stand, you can own THOUSANDS: you can hire managers, you can get investors, and you can upgrade your business!
That sounds great, right?
No, not when you really look at what you're playing. To get straight to the point: these games have a painfully linear system of progression that targets addictive personalities and shackles you into the constant want for more until you beat the game, but you never really beat the game. This is the perfect example of a "waiting" simulator; you wait until you have enough money to upgrade your businesses, you upgrade your business, and then you wait some more. What IS the actual gameplay? The starting blocks of the game are fun, because you're a bigger part of what you earn. Once you get into the septenvigintillion amounts, your gameplay will consist of constant upgrading, resetting, some more upgrading, some more resetting, sigh..
This game alludes you into thinking that you're constantly progressing, the truth is that the gameplay becomes slower the more money you earn. If you value your time, you'll stay away from this game. It's okay-ish when you like something running in the background, something that you can check once in a while, but the game is desired to entice you into the micro-transactions. It's a tool for exploiting addictive personalities whilst eagerly tempting you to spend money.
Stay far, far away.

In my opinion this is the total war golden age, before sega started the DLC greed.
The game feels polished unlike most of the newer additions. Despite being old, it is still a very deep game, there are a lot of details in relations and trading that you can't see at first sight. The unit diversity is great, when I play shogun total war nowadays I feel like every faction is way to similar, wich is understandable because the all share japanese culture, but I don't feel like restarting shogun as another faction because of this, whereas in Medieval there is a bigger variety of cultures.
The battles are great, using units correctly is really rewarding, even if at first cavalry can seem op. Not going for the full stack cost efficient feudal knights into autoresolve is way more fun.
The feeling you get when you use those stacks of gold to recruit a massive army to fare into crusade, then get cushed by some mongols and rebellions, not great at first, but when you finaly succeed to establish yourself in the holy land as christian factions, it is really awesome awesome. Or the times you get excomunicated and get 10 full stacks armies from all over Europe knocking at your door. And finaly when you manage to get your Cardinal elected Pope and are basicly imune of any repercussion..
Also the factions power curves can be very rewarding or punishing if you play them correctly or not (E.G. byzantines only have acces to rock cannons).
Plus for begginers you can only start with 5 factions wich helps getting started faster play and then conquering the factions you want to play is fun imo.
The AI might be stupid at some times and there are exploits, but I have not encountered as much big flops as in the newer TW games.
One thing I dream about at night are medieval 2 online campaigns. Also I would love there to be a technology tree to be able to have some kind of deeper race to America, there may be a mod for this I don't know.
The expansions of this game are also pretty cool, especially teutonic and americas in my mind.
By the way there are some great mods out there (Middle earth).
I probably had some more bad things to say about this game but really I forgot them all playing other total wars, I have been playing this game for years now (not shown on record I only moved to steam license recently because of a scratched disc), and I still enjoy it and I even manage to get surprised sometimes.
The only really bad bugs I can remember is the first time I got trapped in a battle map because I didn't set any time limit and the AI stopped sieging me, thus I was forced into a defeat while I didn't even start the fight in the first place. And the time I got stuck while fighting in the Alps my spawning zone was surrounding by unpassable terrain lol.
I only hope that, if CA and Sega decide to make a Medieval 3, they will dully understand what they have to live up to and deliver and stop stealing us with overpriced DLC's, ffs having to play for blood in a war game I still can't believe this.

If you can look behind the game, which is not THAT bad as people claim, you have a solid fun and simple backstory, a good unscrolling of events and for me, one of the best Goblins ever to grace a computer game: STYX.
