Stellaris is not a game that I would reccomend. While it seems to offer a wide universe to play in with many different options, this is not really the case.
There is a really fundamental problem in the game's design. The most obvious symptom of this is "doomstacks". Doomstacks are how most wars go, there is one battle with all your ships vs all the enemy's ships and once that rather boring slap fight is done, you win the war. The only thing that matters is that your numbers were bigger than the enemy's. Ship design has a MINOR role in this. Unless designs are massively skewed, and they never are, it's just numbers of homogenous fleets.
But why? Lets look at where the game's complexity. It appears to be in its in ethics and government system, you have factions and influence and such. But apart from that?
Military, economy and even diplomacy are extremely simplistic and homogenised. Is it any surprise fleet combat is such? It's big numbers v numbers because that's all that matters. Only things that either have a big number or are in large numbers matter. Look at planets, losing one doesn't matter that much in mid or late game. The only thing that gives planets value is what fraction of your empire's energy, minerals, or science they produce. Large empires can easily absorb the loss of multiple planets without really much consequence because they represent a small fraction of their 500 mineral per second income. There's no depth. For such a large game I think Stellaris is actually rather shallow. Things like the endgame crises and War in Heaven (for those with that DLC) are fun, but what are they sitting on? Nothing much really. It almost feels like they're there to distract from the blandness of the normal gameplay.
There were some major complaints with the game a number of patches ago. There was nothing to do. There were no mid game events worth talking about. The game was really hollow apart from the early game rush to colonise, the late game crisis, and final empire steamroll.
But that just made me think about how the game is so shallow that it needs such events to remain interesting. Somewhere on the paradox forums the developers have said that they're not interested in making the economy deeper. That has really dampened my interest in the game, as it should yours, because it means this problem will never be fixed.
Other paradox titles like the Europa games game mechanics that aren't massively complex but there's other non-event features that provide depth. In the EU games just having terrain creates actual choices because you need to choose how to deal with it. While income is just ducats you do have choices in how you acquire and spend it. Trade, production, and taxes are all different ways and are still important. You can focus on one, make choices in how you spend your resources to enhance it. Even if you're not focusing on say, trade it's still a good idea to put a little bit of effort into interacting with that system during the game. You can take into account things like the trade goods of resources, how they change in value. You can interact with it with armies, you can scorch the earth and loot places. There's various in-game events that change their values, which change the 'trade landscape.'
Stellaris has none of these things. Planet colonisation is very simple; you colonise, you build one of the three production buildings over the entire surface plus a unity building. In the early game you might take tile resources into account but later in the game the production bonus buildings, and things like assist research mean that you should make your planets produce one resource so you can apply the planetary bonuses to as many production buildings as possible.
You have a farm planet(s) too of course but those barely need touching and in any case sectors will ensure that you have more than enough food. Energy credits are near worthless past early game, they exist to be converted into minerals and that's basically it. I'm quite sure you could remove energy credits from the game entirely and there wouldn't be a fundamental shift in the gameplay of Stellaris.
Diplomacy is very simple, and has little choice. There's standard pacts, there's federations, but can you demand a planet diplomatically? Can you demand anything, or offer something in support? Can you buy or sell ships? No.
Combat is quite simple as we know, but even worse than that is the meaninglessness of ship designs. There are a few designs that are the best and we all know, or soon will, what those are; mono-composition fleets of corvettes or artillery/lance battleships (or whatever the current hotness is). Why build anything else? Why research anything else? Fleet combat is so simple to boil down. The whole game is.
There's very little actual choice in Stellaris. There's no terrain, so you don't need to chose which way to reach your enemies. There's no trade routes so you never choose where to provide value, or what trade good to take control of, and you can never raid trade routes unlike HOI and EU. There's no economy to speak of so you can never choose to focus on this product/component/whatever over another. Even Hearts of Iron has that. As I just said, ship design is an illusory choice. You think you have options but you don't really have meaningful choices. Planetary management has very little in the way of choice, if any. In fact the choices for planets are so non-existent that sectors exist, taking those choices away from you.
Shallow gameplay, do not reccomend. The game looks nice, pity there's nothing worth seeing, certainly not for its price.
Just a great, real time, 4x space game. Definately worth it.

Easily one of my favorite fighters in the past few years. If you're a fan of French Bread's "Melty Blood" franchise, you'll most likely love this game.
Each character is very diverse and plays dramatically differently than the others, so there is no fear of "clone" characters like in a lot of fighters nowadays.
It has your basic modes, Arcade, Time Trial, Score Attack, Survival, Training and Online.
The Online, I've only played a few matches, but the netcode seems very stable. Each match went with very little, to no lag whatsoever. (And these were on 2 and 3 bar connections)
Only thing I was hoping they would decide to add in, would have been a challenge or trial mode. This way it would help to guide newer players into the game by teaching them basic BnB combos, and other things. But, this is a port, and not a remake so its understandable that it wouldn't have any additional content.
Overall, I love this game. And was so happy to see it was making its way onto Steam.
10/10

So I have had an intresting relationship with the Arc Systemworks games that have been coming out recently. In conclusion I can easliy suggest UNIEL to ANYONE who as a intrest in the anime fighting game genre.

Pros:
- nice graphics
- gameplay is pretty cool, it's less air based than most anime fighters and combos are slightly less overwhelming than usual.
- interesting character design
- netplay is totally fine for me with no really noticeable input lag or network delay, although many people report issues. I think if you play it on a good PC and against people who aren't on the other side of the world you'll be fine.

Cons:
- this is basically a lazy 1:1 port of a PS3 title released 3 years ago and they're asking 30 bucks for it. They even left PS buttons in some menus, come on.
- absolute lack of any kind of tutorial inside the game, which is a shame for a relatively technical fighter in 2016.
- single player content is much poorer and more boring than in other titles published by ASW.
- on day 2 there is already almost no one playing it online whether in ranked or in player matches...
- ...and the only opponents you'll find clearly already have a ton of experience in this type of games or even in this game in particular. They won't hesitate to counterpick your character and steamroll you to show that you're not welcome.
I'd really like to recommend UNIEL as an introduction to anime fighters, but as it is it can only interest seasoned FG players. If you want more and better SP content as well as flawless netplay (sadly without players), buy Skullgirls. If you're new to fighting games and you wanna play online against a lot of opponents around your level, you'd better pick Street Fighter V which may cost you more but at least won't be dead in a week.

Thanks to this I can play Wurm again. It's a perfect solution for people who don't want to pay the monthly subscription and giving people the ability to run their own servers fixes the problems that Wurm Online had. The majority of the servers speed up the xp and building rate which is a god send since Wurm Online's xp rate was deathly slow which probably killed off the playerbase in the first place. And speaking of playerbase you now actually do have a ton of people playing. There are servers that have at least 100 people playing which really is a good amount for this type of game. Though I'm not sure if new players would enjoy this since the whole game is literally just grinding. But it's about the joy of progression and watching everything slowly coming together. Having played Wurm Online (WO) since 2009 I am very familiar with how things work in Wurm. So I did not encounter a learning curve when I tried Wurm Unlimited (WU). So for me the transition was smooth and effortless. The rewards I saw for stepping into WU where everywhere, beginning with modifiable skill gain helping to make the advancement of skills easier all the way to having ultimate GM powers. The server setup was simple and intuitive in my opinion. There is currently a lot of forum activity and advice if you do get stuck and need help. The overall WU experience was extremely positive for me.
That being said, Wurm is truthfully not for everyone, but for those that can get by the learning curve of the vast crafting system and want to create a world around you from your own imagination the rewards are great. Now with WU you can play with friends or decide to go it alone. Like I said before the extensive Wurm community is there to help when you need it or you can try working things out on your own if you enjoy more of a challenge.
I cannot say enough about this game, challenging, addicting, rewarding, seemingly limitless ability to create and change the world to suit your own pleasure. I would highly recommend this game to anyone that wants to create and build, explore (careful out there, you could get eaten) or just rest and relax in the ambiance of your own created village, Wurm has it all if you are willing to spend some time to find it.
My recommendation would be if you are unsure of whether this game is for you, try it first with Wurm Online, it is free to play. That way you get a feel of what Wurm has to offer before you jump in and buy it.

I am of the rare breed that prefers Dungeonbowl to Blood Bowl; after extensively playing and enjoying the tabletop game, I waited for this game to be on sale.  Purchasing it I was initially impressed with the game play but frustrated with the difficulties in finding an opponent.  I made teams to match my tabletop ones which won consistently but here this was not the case.  I pressed on assuming that I did not have the skill and it took me time to get used to the interface.  I eventually realized that my gameplay had little to do with it: the rules were subtlety different and at times broken, such as game duration limit and no blitzing off a teleport.  The final blow for me was the Dwarven Deathroller which in my opinion is so broken that I have caught myself swearing at my monitor at least forty times.  All other "big guys" have a detriment skill like take root, really dumb, etc. but not this beast.  I calculated that teams I played against that did not have a Deathroller, I won >65% of games while if they did have one, I would win less than 20% of the time.
Why not make a team with a Deathroller, Trou?  My answer: why not make a game that is at least reasonably balanced?
I am able to look passed a lot of this game's flaws that are stated here in these accurate reviews but combined together with this diarrhea on top, I would not recommend this game even if you love the table top version like I do.
Jepumk said it best: it is a poorly realized version of the table top game.

Resident Evil: Revelations tells the story of what happens between Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 5 and is an extended remake of the Nintendo 3DS handheld game, which adds HD textures.
Jill Valentine is on a mission to find her missing partner Chris Redfield, who was last heard from on the cruise ship Queen Zenobia.
The Queen Zenobia is one of the best settings in a Resident Evil game since the Arklay mansion.
Now stranded on board in the middle of the Mediterranean, Jill and fellow BSAA agent Parker Luciani soon discover they are not alone.
Whereas the earlier Resident Evil games prioritized zombies, and recent entries revolved around the Las Plagas parasites, Revelations makes use of a new angle: freakish human/sea-creature hybrids.
Along the way you will also play as Chris Redfield and a variety of other newer cast members. Jill’s sections are the main course containing all the exploration, key finding and item management as is expected.
There is no co-op for the campaign; your only option in the way of multiplayer is Raid Mode. Raid Mode is a two-player cooperative gauntlet through small sections of the game that feel like small-scale, time-attack sessions of horde mode. It is fun for a while, but it quickly turns into a grind for XP and new items.
The facial animations are a little stiff, and overall the visuals naturally are not as nice as Resident Evil 5 or 6.
In my opinion is Revelations the best Resident Evil game of the past few years and the one that is the most true return to classic-style horror action.
Resident Evil: Revelations is very much worth playing in its HD form for its atmosphere and scares alone.

Richard Walter Zisk (born February 6, 1949) is a retired Major League Baseball player currently in charge of pro scouting in Florida for the Chicago Cubs.[1]Zisk was drafted by the Pittsburgh Pirates out of Seton Hall University in the third round of the 1967 Major League Baseball Draft, and made his major league debut on September 8, 1971 replacing Roberto Clemente in right field in the eighth inning of Pittsburgh's 10-1 victory over the Chicago Cubs, and got a single in his first major league at-bat.[2] Zisk also made seventeen appearances with the 1972 Pirates, however, he was not on either team's post-season roster.
In Zisk's rookie season, 1973, he batted .324 with ten home runs. On June 9, 1974, he hit for the cycle in a 14-1 victory over the San Francisco Giants at Candlestick Park.[3] For the season, he led the Pirates with 100 runs batted in while also clubbing seventeen home runs. He made his only post-season appearances with the 1974 and 1975 Pirates. While batting an impressive .400 in the post-season, Zisk only scored one run and had no RBIs as the Pirates were swept in the 1974 and 1975 National League Championship Series by the Los Angeles Dodgers and Cincinnati Reds, respectively. Following the 1976 season, the Pirates traded Zisk along with Silvio Martinez to the Chicago White Sox for Terry Forster and Rich Gossage.

It's a really cute idea but the way they've done the randomization makes it so hard to have fun playing.
The puzzles are the biggest thing to the game, but they are completely randomized. The screenshots of the game are totally false, the puzzles they show you are not what the actual puzzles are. The puzzles they show are rare special rooms players can encounter; but the regular puzzles are nothing like those.
The regular puzzles are literally just an array of random objects and creatures, dumped into a cluttered room. The puzzle solving element is players loosely trying to figure out how to get one thing to another thing, or get through a cluster of things, or transport one thing to another thing. It is completely unstructured, there is no logic or thought to solving the problem it's just about figuring out the loose way to navigate through the problem by moving things around. It feels totally empty of satisfaction or even stimulation to play because the puzzles are just a jumbled mess of items which are solved by just moving them around until they align in your favour. There's no overarching solution or method, it's just the player moving randomly placed junk around until they force it into the solution they need to pass.
Beyond that there's lots of frustrating elements to the puzzles. Some enemies randomly teleport around the map and serve as blockages, they randomly block certain ways everytime you move; how do you get them to stop blocking you, you move around until they teleport to a place that isn't in your way. Pointless, arbitrary design. There's lot of enemies that are borderline impossible to avoid because they instantly hit you if you get remotely close, or they attack inconsistently so sometimes you can pass sometimes you can't. Some enemies blatantly game over you because they instantly teleport you out of the map if they hit you; yet the game can spawn them right ontop of the entrance or near a significant area you need to reach. It's possible for the player to get straight up trapped among objects they can't move, it's possible for objects to randomly not me moveable even though you need to move them to progress, it's possible for random objects to not trigger their primary function which you also need to progress. There are many ways that the game can straight up screw the player over, all because it's randomly generated in such an obnoxious and unstructured way.
Puzzles are about finding solutions, randomly generated puzzles like these completely defeat the purpose of this because the solution isn't logical or satisfying to achieve because it's just a loose brute force method found amongst the random.
The art and world design, everything thematic feels very nice. The game makes it seem like a side-feature is the ability to talk and bond with the characters around town with this whole; play as an anonymous stranger who is nice to everybody and friendship is spread all around kind of theme.
That's what it really seems like, which was sweet, until it suddenly shows that it isn't like that. Certain characters will actually judge and get upset with you if you befriend other characters. So you're running around being nice to every body, having a lovely time then you get told "Oh, you like THAT person. They aren't one of us, and honestly, I like you less because you are nice to them. We can't be friends anymore.". And suddenly, you're hit with a dose of reality that some humans just suck; in a game that looked like it was about being nice to every body and having fun. So now you feel weird because you just literally were socially judged in a video game, and now you have one less of the few characters to talk to because that one sucks so why would you want to talk to them anymore. They don't want to be your friend anyways apparently. The game deceptively makes it look like it's supposed to be a pseudo-reality where every body is nice and it's all about friendship, then it suddenly brings in reality and ruins the precedent it set. While making it so you have less characters you can bond with now then before.
The game also acts like the anonymity of the protagonist is another key feature. Which it completely looks like it is. Then suddenly, you are given the option to remove your hood to show a character what you look like. If you choose to not do this, you cannot increase your relationship with them or any other character until you do. When you do, it destroys the anonymity of the protagonist and their entire atmosphere in the world; and you can't even put your hood back on. Perhaps this is meant to be the protagonist opening up to the townsfolk by showing who they are, but when you actually do it in practice it doesn't feel like that at all; it's just this sudden dialogue option which gates future dialogue options unless you ruin one of the most base themes of the game. So basically, the developers make you sacrifice one of the biggest thematic elements of the game, for a special moment which doesn't actually work in practice, just so you can talk more to the townsfolk.
And if you die without activating any of the revival lights beforehand, which the game does not explain, it will flat reset potentially a third or more of your progress towards beating the game. It's not that the game doesn't save unless you use the lights, it's literally just programmed to remove massive amounts of your progress as punishment for dying at all unless you activate that arbitrary and unexplained game mechanic.
It seemed like a really great time but once again developers choose contradicting game mechanics. Game includes friendly social interactions, game scorns player for being friendly; protagonist is mysterious and interesting, content is gated until you reveal their appearance; game is about puzzles, puzzles are random jibberish.
It only took around an hour to beat half the game roughly, before death reset almost all that progress. So, the unsatisfying and socially upsetting design of the game aside; it's really not even big enough to remotely justify its price.

Though I've played a lot o roguelikes, this is my first experience with a RL puzzler, and I found a lot to like.  Starting with the gameplay, the simple starting point of throwing objects around to clear paths and make groups quickly grows increasingly complicated due to the large number of possible item interactions.  However, this is introduced sufficiently gradually that you don't feel swamped by knowledge.  The difficulty curves up well, with early years generally quite simple but the end of the game presenting a genuine challenge.  The fact that you don't need to save every child means that, if you get a really bad map, your game isn't ended.  Finally, breaking the action into 15 years makes this game ideal for short, coffee-break sessions.
The story and setting are given much less emphasis, but if you pay attention you to these details you'll be rewarded.  There's a darkness to the game's setting hidden behind the bright visuals.  The game's overall message is also far from cheerful.
My biggest gripe was that the controls were sometimes a bit sluggish, which shouldn't be an issue in a turn-based game but occaisionally led to my making unintended moves.  I also found the relationship mechanics a bit tacked-on.
In general, though, I'm glad I picked this up.  I wouldn't class it as something you have to experience, but would definitely recommend it.

This was a super adorable roguelike/platformer combo that’s a great timekilling game. It has wonderful art. I wish there were stuffed animals of the people, they’re so damned cute. Its biggest sin is that it can feel reptitive, but I had a blast playing it in short spurts.
You play as the Ranger, who comes to a small town to help rescue children during their harsh winters. Over the course of 15 years, you can build relationships, rescue kids, and explore the dangerous wintry forest surrounding the town.
The game is a roguelike both in the procedurally-generated forest-dungeon and the fact that if you die, you have to restart from the beginning. Other than that, it’s primarily a puzzle game, where you match and combine objects, conserve your Energy (ie, HP) and attempt to rescue all of the children each year — or at least enough to justify your continued employment. As you build relationships with the townspeople, you’re gifted special items that buff you, sometimes at a price.
One of my favorite things about the game was that the NPCs and the Ranger themselves are also generated differently each time you play. Each NPC has a variety of skin- and hair-color options, as well as different names, that make the town seem vibrant and inclusive. The Ranger’s appearance and gender are determined by how you play and the way you interact with the townspeople; I had fun creating all different looks. It’s also the complete and utter opposite of this, which is amazing.
The writing itself was whimsical and sad, with a good sense of humor and was generally atmospheric and enjoyable.
I initially started trying to save every child in the forest, but after only getting as far as year 7 after a ton of playthroughs I finally decided to play through til the end (and in terminal years, it’s possible for the kids to die while you’re out there, so doing a full playthrough where you save everyone must be ridiculously difficult). Once I decided to let children suffer for my benefit, it only took me two tries to get the full fifteen years.
As I said, the game can get repetitive. If you’re the kind of person who likes to sit down for marathon gaming sessions like I do, this isn’t really suited for that. But what it was great for was when I had 30 or 45 minutes at a time to kill. I’d play right before bedtime and then by the next night I’d be like, “Alright, time to save some kids, let’s do this.” Which is all you could really ask for from a game like this, I think.
Oh — and I actually played this with the sound on! I thought the music and effects were nice and contributed to the atmosphere as well.
All of that said, the full retail price of $15.00 is insane. I got it for $5 during the Steam summer sales and that was an entirely fair price. I might even pay $9.99 for it, but $15 is ridiculous for the 11 hours of gameplay I got out of it.
I also thought it was odd how long some of the loading screens were, especially in the town. I could see a long delay while it was loading the level, but I’m not sure why simply going in and out of my house took as long as it did.
Finally, I was a little disappointed we didn’t get more worldbuilding. I specifically wanted to know more about the Ranger — why were they a Ranger? Why did they only have 15 years to live? — but more about the town would have been nice, too. I felt like the game teased a bigger world and then never followed up on the promise. The title juxtaposed with the Ranger’s mysteriousness in particular implies that they’re doing something extraordinary, but we never find out the details of it. I didn’t want a novel, but some in-dialogue revelations would have been nice.
Overall, though, this was a really nice game. Next time it goes on sale, definitely pick it up.

Right. So. I've had a while to simmer down, and 2K, (tyvm) listened to the angry mob and patched things up a bit. So, I've changed from NOT recommend to recommend.

Pros: Yeah, they fixed most of the glitches, though they do still occur, but it's so rare now that I don't really mind anymore. They fixed the "We Don't Care parts" of MyCareer Postgame Show, although for some reason Earnie seems to be the only one ever saying a name/nickname.

Really fun! I bought this during the last chirstmas sale partly because it was cheaper than chips ($0.49!) and partly because of the critical acclaim it received. Originally I played about half an hour of it right after the purchase and I didn't really dig it. I'm not sure why but it didn't quite click with me. This may have had something to do with the fact that I rarely play rogue-like's before (I'm generally prefer the more orthodox action/platformer/driving games).
I recently restarted playing it again out of curiosity, thinking I didn't give it a fair chance and boy was I right about that! I'm about 9 hours in and I'm loving it. All the different stacking abilities and items make it incredibly diverse and super addicting. This is also helped by the range of procedurally generated map layouts (although this is starting to repeat a bit but since it's contantly varied and random, it keeps things fresh).
I'm a sucker for finding hidden areas and items and Isaac does a fantastic job of encouraging me to continue finding them because the payoff is always worth it.
I also like the story, playing off the biblical tale, which, alongside the killer aesthetic, gives an amazingly creepy vibe which remains consistent with every new part of the story you uncover and every new and weird item/power up you find.
If I had anything bad to say it would be the 30FPS lock, the 4:3 aspect ratio, and the weird frame drops I seem to get in crowded dungeons (although I'm told that some of these issues are tied to the Flash engine).
Overall I say pick it up if you haven't. It's a lot of fun and I can't recommend it more.

I just finished "Of Orcs and Men." I really enjoyed this console ARPG in its PC form with a gamepad. It has nice visuals, sound and music as well as a very good story with likable dual protagonists, both of whom you control throughout the adventure. The combat system which goes into slow motion when you hit a button to begin selecting up to 4 attacks or abilities and returns to normal speed when you are done is fluid, involving and fun. Switching between the characters in combat is a breeze. The streamlined UI is a pleasure to use with a gamepad. The game is very light on loot but your characters are always progressing via level ups with new skills and abilities as well as loot you acquire from chests and defeated enemies. You sometimes also get loot from merchants who can (and you'll always want to do this) upgrade your armor and weapons. The game is not about constant looting of stuff though. It is about two great characters on a quest with a good story with fun combat along the way. The Orc Arkail, is a warrior and the Goblin, Styx is a rogue who is a lot of fun to use for his stealth abilities at times. I found it best to develop Arkail as a tank and Styx as melee DPS but you can give focus to DPS on Arkail and ranged DPS on Styx if you prefer. I give it a 8 out of 10 and feel the game was underrated by professional reviews and some PC gamers alike who I think didn't give it a fair chance based on it not being a "PC game" but rather a console game ported to PC. It is a good solid port. I experienced no problems with it. Steam tells me I played it for 29 hours but subtracting out snacks, etc. I think it was probably more like 25 or 26 hours roughly and I took all side quests and checked everywhere for chests as I went along.

There are many mechanics that are left to be desired and there are several situations in the story line that make you wonder why the devs didn't make it a playable part of the game. That said though this game is a lot better than it gets credit for.
Voice acting isn't the best ever but it's certainly passable. The main characters seem to actually have a team style relationship, which is good since you play both characters throughout the story. Level design isn't amazing, there are a lot of nooks and areas that look like they should be 100% accessible but aren't. But it's also not the worst I've seen.
The game employs a stealth mechanic but there's not a way to stealth through an entire area as you play both characters at once and only one character can stealth. That doesn't mean it doesn't have it's place, it's still very useful.
Overall the RPG mechanics are pretty solid. Both characters get attribute points when they level up as well as a new skill to learn or upgrade. And both characters skills play off eachothers strengths and weknesses quite well. You'll obtain gear from a few chests and sacks or at a vendor, not from combat. Items are upgradeable, but only once and have different attributes that fit a few different play styles.
Combat itself is probably the most dissapointing. You'll have to que up attacks thru a combat menu for each character and watch it take place rather than have direct control yourself. But really as the game progresses the combat mechanics have a more tactical feeling and it starts to become more natural.
You'll get some choices to pick through in dialogue menus, but there's only a couple that actually have any real affect in the game.
I liked my playthrough of this game. The story is kind of fresh feeling, if a bit predictable at times. Gives a feeling of many intelligent species and races, rather than the typical feeling of orcs and goblins being mindless violent beings.
This game is worth playing, I may even play through again some time.

As a veteran fighting game player, I can honestly say this is one of the most refreshing, enjoyable fighters in recent years. Not only does it sport a lovely art style, soundtrack and character styles, but it has a very down to earth system that both new and old players alike can enjoy.
The common complaint I hear about fighting games aray in all shapes and sizes, but the one that honestly strikes me the most is how complicated it is to control and the overwhelming amount of information spewed at the player when getting into the genre. The beauty of Under Night is within its simplicity and overall capacity to handle even the newest of newcomers and the most hardcore of masters. Its control scheme is easy to pick up and begin making your own cool looking combos with ease, but it also allows those who are willing to put in the practice pull off long winded, high damaging strings.
Honestly, if you're looking for a game to get into that maybe you haven't seen before, this is perfect for you. With a large emphasis on area control (every move in the game boasts huge range) and high octane, aggressive play, you are guaranteed to get those crisp, meaty impacts in fighting games you've always been looking for.
One of the biggest perks for me was its accessability. Save for one character consisting of charge attacks, most of the lineup sports nearly identical stylings in attack performance and joystick motions. I've heard complaints about the simplified control mechanics, but I think it's personally a great gateway into playing new characters and understand fighting game functions fast. Plus, aside from every one of them having similar controls, they all feel incredibly different in style.
I would almost say this game is like a celebration of fighting games in general. The movement is fairly heavy and strategized (like Street Fighter) while also being flashy and combo heavy (like Guilty Gear). In fact, every character is almost like having another game's character in the fray with that special Under Night twist. Wanna play a Ryu-like Shoto Ken with a sword? You have Hyde. Wanna play a Persona 4 Arena styled character with interlacing combos? You have Orie. Wanna play practically a ninja Taokaka from Blazblue with more setups and projectiles? you have Seth. Almost every character is like this, there is something for everybody to enjoy here.
While one thing I need to point out is balancing is a little on the High-Middle-Bottom spectrum (there are three God characters, most of the rest are even, and the bottom three are difficult to win with) and these are getting fixes in an upcoming update. It is possible to be good and win a tourney with any of the available characters, some can do it with much more ease and others will have a much more difficult time.
If you are worried about how the PC port will run in conjuction to the PS3 port, I can most definitely say this game is worth your buck. I've ran into a couple of problems with getting my 8arc fightstick to run properly in-game, and pad support seems to be an issue im hearing a bit. With a little tweaking it will work for you, you just have to be patient with it. Netplay overall feels better than the PS3 for me, possibly because my PC can just run it better. Load times are non-existant and the game feels incredibly fresh on PC.
Right now there seems to be common issues with getting in ranked matches, so hopefully this will be fixed, and jumping into lobbies can be a hassle. These are problems that need to be addressed, but I would be lying if I said the netcode was bad. Once I did get into some games with some anonymous opponents, I found it nearly lagless and I was able to pull off my usual combos seamlessely, save for matches with opponents who had awful connections. I'd say jump into this at your own risk, I can't guarantee lagless, perfect matches, but I have had fairly good experiences with the network, so I wish the best for you too!
I have a hard time not recommending this to anybody wanting to get into a fighting game. There are plenty of guides out there and a very dedicated community of players who are usually willing to help you get better at the game. If you want something fast paced, strategic, flashy and overall fresh, I'd say buy this game now.

Perhaps what should be noted first is the most apparent flaw of this title and it's not the game itself but the pc port. As you would be able to see in several reviews the game doesn't run properly in some people's systems and doesn't run outright at all in others. So for most of the pc community you pretty much need a 3rd party program in order to run this game properly, if at all.
This is in very poor form on Square Enix and Platinum Games's part. Triple A devs shouldn't marginilize proper support from a sizeable chunk of its demographic... but really, come on now, what else is new?
We're pc gamers, however we may feel crappy that we're always treated the least after consoles, however we may cry injustice we always find ways to do the stuff we want ourselves. And if it wasn't for the smart people who mod games we wouldn't have known about the crap that we thought we didn't need in the first place. So it's up to you protest and not touch the game at all because of principles, or begrudgingly download a miniscule program that's not hard to use and experience one the best games released to date.

And surprisingly enough I can't recall encountering any bugs in my entire play through.
I can definitely say that this was the best game I've played in a while, and it makes me very glad I waited for it, so absolutely recommended. The pro's outweigh the con's in my opinion. Go download Windowed Borderless Gaming or the FAR mod because they're essential, any one will do.

Oh, man. . . . Wurm Unlimited. Where the heck do I start?
So here are the pros/cons of Wurm Online, then I'll do pros/cons of Wurm Unlimited.
Wurm Online:
Pros
1) The game is more realistic in terms of crafting, skilling, etc. than any game I've ever come across.
2) A sense of accomplishment is just around the corner as you build up your character, your deed, or just run off exploring all over the beautiful landscape.
3) Many will disagree with this, but I think the graphics are a 'pro' for me. I really enjoy the graphics. It's not crazy, but they aren't Minecraft. It is a gorgeous game, in my opinion.
4) The freedom you get in the game is astonishing and absolutely mind-boggling.
5) Just one more plank.
6) Okay, okay, just one more.
7) Ya' know what, I'll just finish this wall.
Cons
1) For most people, the menus/submenus will be a red 'x' against the game. But honestly, most things are intuitive (use a saw on a log and you'll make things that you would if you were using a saw on a log in RL).
2) HUGE learning curve (although once you learn how to play, you're like 'duh..that makes sense').
3) Fighting anything, especially early on in your Wurm life, can take for-EVER!!! This has always been a detractor for me in the game. That said, I must also note that once you obtain a decent QL (quality) weapon with some nice enchants, the battles are pretty quick, but getting the silver to buy such weapons will take a lot of work!
4) Just one more plank.
5) Okay, okay, just one more!
6) Ya' know what? I'll just finish this house.
Wurm Unlimited
Pros
1) It's friggin' singleplayer if you want! Take all of the pros from above and plop them down into a singleplayer mode where you can be a GM and fart around on a server! For a lot of players, this is just what they were looking for!
2) No subscription needed and there are tons of servers available - including my own -- Taking Without Constent Dedicated 24/7 -- no subscription needed with the same awesome community-driven action!
3) The GMs of the online servers for Wurm Unlimited are going to be able to help you much more than they ever would on Wurm Online! Your experience could be free from some of the most frustrating aspects of the game if you choose the right server to play on!
Cons
1) They changed the way skills are gained and it was a pretty gnarly overhaul. Funny because I didn't think it could be as big of a change, but after playing for 100+ hours, it was a big change. The only con here, however, is the fact that the GM has to constantly tweak the settings to get it close to being realistic, but not annoying (especially the farming).
2) The rest are just the same as for Wurm Online.
Overall, this game is simply amazing. When I get on, I get lost in the Wurm world. I'm a GM now and am hosting my server through Citadel, and I must say, it's awesome to have an investment into the game like I have now. And if you're looking for a great server that will be focused on community, and alleviating a lot of annoyances in the game, look no further than TWOC - Taking Without Consent.

Definately not a game you want to pick up casually if you've never played the MMO. Its my honest reccomendation if your considering this game, to do some research. Definately watch some videos of gameplay other than the ones listed on Steam.
There's a real steep learning curve for this game that's pretty frustrating if your not playing on a server, or the MMO. You don't have the opportunity to ask 'Noob' questions via chat like more experienced players have been able to before.
There's also not a wiki support for the game like will find with other sandbox games (like Minecraft) that detail how to craft items, or what the prerequisite to obtaining the are. As others have commented below, it is possible to find the information you need to get started; but you'd better be ready to spend a heafty amount of time watching Youtube Videos, and browsing forums before you'll be able to actually play the game.
For example: the developers do a poor job of setting expectations for how long it will take to build your empire. In the video, building  speed is obviously sped up - but  if your expecting to get even a wall built within your first 5 hours of gameplay you're in for a surprise. To build a wall requires wood, and nails. Wood is pretty easy to obtain. Chop down a tree, cord it up, and then saw up some boards. However, to get the nails is an entirely different story...
To tunnlel out a mine takes 'actions' and the default action for mining is roughly 9~ seconds. It takes between 30 to 50 'actions' to move one block in. That's Roughtly 4 ~7 minutes to mine ONE 'block' in. Now imagine you have to find the iron 5 blocks deep that it takes to make the nails, to build your first wall.
I'm not saying this game doesn't have the potential to be fun, but if you're looking for a sandbox you can pick up and run with in an afternoon, I'd suggest watching some Lets Play videos first to get your feet wet.

Revelations is filled with old school Resident Evil horror which reminds me of the original games that started the series off. Before starting the game, I didn’t expect much seeing as it was originally a 3DS only title. But I was really impressed with the PC version!
The story is decent. It was well thought out, filled with twists and turns, and unexpected.  The characters were well established (although I wasn’t a fan of Jill’s voice actor). There are all sorts of themes I could mention, but like all my reviews I’d prefer to keep this spoiler free!
The gameplay is pretty much the same as Resident Evil 5 and 6, simple yet satisfying. There are various enemy types with different weaknesses and numerous boss fights. The amount of different weapons is good, and the ability to upgrade them keeps things fresh.
The graphics are clearly dated by comparison to Resident Evil 6 (released some months before as a major released on consoles and PC). But they still look good and have definitely been re-vamped for the PC. The swimming sections are particularly pretty, even though there are so few of those moments :(
I’ll also mention that in almost every respect, the overall game is significantly better than Resident Evil 6. No more mindless campaigns with a chopped up storyline. No more glitchy graphics. No more sub standard plot. As a fan of the Resident Evil, Revelations managed to pull off a good balance of nostalgia with next gen controls. It felt like one of the original games but with modern elements. I was really happy with that ^^
Overall, Revelations is a very good game and any fan of the original series should get playing! If you played Resident Evil 6 and enjoyed that game, this one might be a bit too different for you.

Resident Evil Revelations unlike the more recent releases of the Resident Evil series comes somewhat back to the series' roots of hunting around mansions, finding keys, and shooting big monsters at the end with rocket launchers. Read full review here -

Jill Sandwich returns in the best Resident Evil title in years.
This DS port surpasses both the lacklustre RE5 and the wankfest RE6, and whilst the levels are not too ambitious, this title has far better pacing than any RE game since 4. The new limited ammo and new upgrade system help stop the game from becoming the gunfest of the previous titles, but what I felt hurt the game was the removal of the context sensitive melee attacks for head and knee shots, which in previous titles made combat feel far more fluid. Instead, Revelations arms the player with a one-button knife attack, which allows for some cheap kills.
The excellent new Raid mode is the replacement to previous title's Mercenary mode. Gone is the time limit that crippled the previous version; instead we get to maintain a constant inventory and level up. It feels like everything The Mercenaries always should have been.
The Real Resident Evil 6 out of Ten

Let me make it very clear from the beginning why I'm recommending Resident Evil Revelations at all - Raid Mode. This minigame is what will sap up most of your time, and can take anywhere from 70 to over 100 hours for you to unlock characters and bonuses, find rare weapons and achieve S ranks.
On to the campaign.
Resident Evil Revelations plops RE mainstays Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine into a 'web of intrigue and conspiracy' (inverted commas because....) with new partners, Parker Luciani and Jessica Sherawat. After Chris and Jessica drop off the grid while investigating a possible terrorist group's revival, Jill and Parker and sent to check on them. Parker and Jill end up at an abandoned ship, the Queen Zenobia, which is where most of the Campaign happens. The plot of Revelations is the cheesiest, lamest, cheapest, worst pulp fiction plot I have ever come across. There is no criminal mastermind in this game, the game IS the criminal mastermind for coming across as utterly cheap and unconvincing.
Through the campaign, certain parts and boss fights just drag on and on. Instead of creating tension, you start hoping for the game to just be over and done with. The unconvincing, cheap plot makes this worse because you often just feel like a fool wandering the corridors in search of keys and key items to unlock this and that - but for what? Everything feels like a wild goose chase - and players who have finished this game will know what I mean.
The controls are a step up from the uncomfortable, inconvenient 3DS ones. The ability to map your subweapons to specific keys will allow you to toss subweapons (grenades, decoys) quickly, saving your skin in precarious Raid Mode situations. Where the triggers on the 3DS were cramped and caused hand fatigue, you'll of course find no such problem on the PC. The half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥dodging is still here, however. There is no laser sight in this game. Be sure to turn off Acceleration/Auto-Aim and other options in the game's menu, because your crosshairs are going to be 'sticky' otherwise, making it harder to aim.
For Mercenaries veterans, Raid Mode is definitely a different flavour. Instead of building combos and adding time, the game offers 20 stages, all mini-maps taken from the main Campaign. In each, your objective is to get to the end point. To get there, you have to make your way through the map, kill enemies for keys, etc. To make Raid Mode challenging for trophy hunters, Trinity Bonuses (achieve No Damage, kill all enemies, play at lower level than recommended) have been added, and will often require a good co-op partner for you to get them all.
You choose from a variety of characters, each with different weapon perks, pick 3 weapons from your inventory and then enter the stage. Generally, there are characters for different playing styles. E.g. Morgan Lansdale, with his Rifle and Magnum perk, will be popular with people who like the powerful but slow-reloading weapons.
Co-Op has a number of known issues as well, such as horrible lag and failure to find matches. The lag affects gameplay badly, since enemies will regenerate health, enemies might continue walking around despite having 0 HP, enemies (and your partner) 'teleport' across the map, etc.
Revelations is a rather weak game. It hasn't got an amazing combat system, it hasn't fully retained the flavour of older RE games, it gets utterly boring at points, the enemies are rehashed zombies, it's not an immersive or convincing game world, etc. But I still recommend it for the co-op experience of bonus-hunting with a partner. Raid Mode is a content-heavy section that stands well on its own and has high replayability. For players who lament that this game is a 'disappointment' and a 'disaster', my reply is to simply play through the game to get your money's worth, then uninstall it from your system and be done with it. This is the new direction the games are taking, and you of course, as a consumer, have the choice not to part with your money and time.
Revelations gets a 7/10 from me.

Wildstar is an amazing game, with an amazing story, and one of the most interesting universes I've seen in a video game. I love this game, the feel, the sense of humor, and the soundtrack. It is feature-filled and in a market cluttered with a lot of the same ideas, it managed to be very unique. The housing system is second-to-none. The soundtrack is far above the average game soundtrack. The dungeons and raids (from what I've seen) are quite unique and well-designed.
Wildstar is plagued by the fact that it is an MMO, and thus depends on outside players.
The biggest flaw of Wildstar is that it's not a particularly well-populated game. NCSoft and Carbine had a few opportunities to relaunch the game, to revitalize the image, to prove that they were going to keep regular updates coming and to support the game. Instead, with the relaunch, nothing about it really changed enough to give it that jolt of energy it needed. The damage inflicted by a rushed launch was too much to heal over by a new trailer and a few days' worth of content.
It's a very low population game that will remain low population because of a refusal to do what it would take to revitalize it.
It's unfortunate. With funding and time and a real revamp, this could be the head of the market, I have no doubt.
All that being said, I still recommend it, highly. It's still a fun game, the lore and soundtrack and world are well-worth exploring. I hope that it eventually gets recognized for how strong it truly is.
My greatest hope is for an expansion that seeks to paint a new picture. A clear cut from where we are now and a new vision for the future. I'd gladly pay for it.
If absolutely nothing else, I hope that the Wildstar universe lives on in some way. If not through this game, as an MMO, then I hope they make a single player game set in the same universe.
PS: I've played a lot more than the timer says, I played it long before the Steam release.

This popped up once as a Steam recommendation for me and I wasn't sure I would like this game as I have played others along the same lines. At first glance, there were some things that bothered me, such as the flawed chat censoring that borders on funny with what it does/doesn't filter.
However, the more I have played, the deeper I have been pulled into the game. I hear complaints all the time about how this or that is unbalanced, but generally I have found it is the person and not the game that is unbalanced. Some complain about subs or carriers being too weak, but played well they can be the terrors in a fight. Part of this is also that some classes of ship get better at higher tiers (i.e. levels).
The game is actually very complex and part of the problem is many players don't learn the role of their ship well. For instance, spotting is based on a wide variety of factors (capability of the ship, upgrades, commanders, equipment, speed, etc) and destoyers are the primary spotters for their side. However many players will charge in with their destroyer to attempt close range torpedo runs (which can be deadly) and die quickly due to their low armor. Battleships without something to spot for them are considerably more disadvantaged despite all the firepower at their disposal.
Another example is that the part of the ship you hit also has a significant impact on the amount of damage you do and the parts of the ship that you can damage destroy. This is something you start to learn and try to take advantage of as you play. Beyond that, your choice of commanders can make a significant difference in many ways: do you want to be more accurate, do more damage when you hit, see further, reload faster, etc.
Sure, there are paid options that can help give a player some advantages (true in any type of game like this), but they aren't absolute trump cards like some games. Sure,  you can buy "gold" ammo/torpedoes, but they still have to hit you with them to make them count. There are "gold" ships, but typically they aren't any better than a fully upgraded ship of the same tier (i.e. level). You can spend gold to get more commanders, but there are options to get commanders without gold as well, it just takes more time.
All in all a good game that I enjoy to play. I only wish there were more players to make matchmaking take place more quickly. Sometimes you have to guage at which tier and which class of ship will give you the bast chance of getting a match quickly, and that is another skill you need to learn in the game.

This is one of those games that have been sitting in my wishlist for some time. I really wasn't sure if I'd enjoy the gameplay, as I couldn't really get the feeling from the trailer and screenshots (no doubt a game that would have benefited with a demo). I decided to finally give Road Not Taken a try and absolutely loved it!
The art style, characters and dialogues are just adorable (seriously, the little descriptions and dialogues when you talk to the NPC's or give them gifts will give you a warm, fuzzy feeling in your belly). The story is simple, yet nice and poetic (leaving much to be interpreted by the player, which I personally love) and the gameplay is indeed quite interesting. I can't think of another game with a gameplay like this. Sure there are games where you combine items to form new items, but the strategies you need to come up with to move around and not waste energy are something a bit different. Also all the interactions and having to move or run after (or away from!) some of the creatures are an extra challenge. It's fun to learn over time how to combine different items and how they act and react to each other, figuring out cool new strategies. Oh, at first the ending felt a bit underwhelming, but there is more to the game, a more complete ending. Though it's maybe not that special, I felt it was a nice little reward for the effort.
Definitely a great game, though I'm sure it's not for everyone.

As an avid Warmachine player this game is a massive disappointment. While the designers attempts to capture the feel of Warmachine are admirable they fall short. Some abilities had to be changed or altered and this is understandable. Feora's feat doesn't function correctly at all. The changes to make infantry are interesting however the execution fails especially with weapon master models. The scenario modes all lack kill box which is a pain when you are already playing with a shortened unit list. I had one game where a Knight Errant walked up and hit The Avatar for 18 damage with a critical. Speaking of which the randomization doesn't seem random. There are streaks where you will miss frequently and then only get critical hits after that. My dice are more average then the random number generator and I rolled 7 sets of snake eyes in a single 50 point game at Lock&Load this year. The maps lack terrain and you don't get to see your opponents deployment if you are player 2.
Negatives
- Warjacks don't have systems
- Weapon ranges are messed up
- No counter deploy
- Lack of terrain
- No kill box (screw you Severius)
- Feora's feat doesn't function correctly (I'm sure there are other issues but really?)
- 3 Weapon Master Infantry will drop Avatar with criticals
- When you boost a spray all to hit rolls seem to be boosted with a single focus
- Limited by using a grid system (you lose so much finesse with the placement of things)
- You can't cast a spell then fail a charge for extra movement
- Star system is janky as hell, opaque, and demonstrates a failure to understand Warmachine.
--Using the numbers from Warmachine would at least make sense as it is math. The star system isn't consistent as it bins certain numbers together. i.e. def 16-18 may all be 4 stars
-Criticals in general, everything can critical
-The FAQ and manual are useless, go lose some quick match games and you can slowly figure out how things work by losing
- In general I feel like the designers took Warmachine and tried to make it their own version while tossing away an already solid system for something they came up with while drinking one night. People have spoken with them at conventions and during early access about the star system and other things. The designers answer was a fairly condescending "Trust us, we are game designers." You should just code the existing game, not hack it to pieces.
-Pros
-Nice idea to change infantry over (I still feel it was unnecessary to alter the game this much)
-Animated warcasters! Seriously this is probably the second best thing
- Best thing is you get to play a story in the Warmachine universe
TL;DR Can't recommend, Won't recommend, Disappointed Kickstarter as we were promised warmachine on the computer and we got poop.

As  a Tabletop/War Gamer in general and especially a Warmachine/Hordes player, someone who followed WMD when it first announced a Warmachine game and a backer of the later Kickstarter-Project I truly hate to say that I can't recommend this game. The developers had enought time to fix some major bugs or design flaws, but they didn't. Performance issues are still at hand: if your game kept running  for a respectable amount of time without a crash, than that just means a crash is a soon-to-be occasion. Not a "possible" occasion, a crash -will- occure. The UI is quite obnoxious, but usable, and keeps looking like a developing kit.
For Lover's of the tabletop: Yes, it is nice to see some of your beloved units, 'jacks and 'casters moving, but that depends on the FPS rate at which you stop talking about movement. Same goes for the cutscenes betwen the missions of the No Mans Land campaign: they are more like the stills with subtitles on a classic Nintendo game, but with sound/voiceacting. The Nintendo would've had sound, if the system could've done it. The PC/Mac System could handle motion...
But back to the issue for people coming from the Tabletop: Its not a good representation of the game you know. It has a good number of similarities, yes, but sadly just enough to make you wonder (or in case of a backer: shake your head out of utter lack of understanding) why they didn't designed the game as closeley as possible to it. From a lackluster point system to represent the ability scores of your army to a just as bad changed scale of for the hitpoints.
Never dream of seeing a Trencher act in a concert with 5-9 fellow unit members. He's just a solo with massivly boosted hitpoints, to keep large numbers of grunts out of the game, because "the engine could not handle that". That leads to things like AoE's being of more than questionable value against, well, anything, because they were designed to benefit from the existence of single-wound infantry or low HP medium Infanty. Quite easy to see the error here. Well, wrong engine then, I would say...
Keep in mind how the game is named: WARMACHINE: Tactics. Warmachines. That are, to my understanding, the Warjacks, the defining feature and a great bit of the appeal the whole system has to most of its fans. It's steam-powerd fantasy. The Trencher is not steampowerd, the Ironclad is. And the Warjack didn't get the same treatment of powerscale adjustment the units got, which lead to funny things like 3-4 mechanithralls ruining a warjacks day.
To my dispair, as much as I like Kickstarter and as much as i cheered for WMD to take the challenge of creating a video game adaption for warmachine, I think Kickstarter allowed WMD to get through with what they tried the first time they started developing for Warmachine: taking a bite way to big for their mouth, trying to design something that's way too large for them, playing in the big league while not able to hold the bat straight.
W:T has potential, much of it, but I can't quite see the nurturing enviroment developing it needs to flourish.

Borderlands: TPS is not a game about you. It's a game about the villain.
This is what I absolutely loved about this game. Sure you may be the player; sure the NPC's acknowledge your presence; but in the end, this is Handsome Jack's game.
Ever read one of those "Top 10 video game villains" on the good old internets? Ever had that feeling of disdain while reckoning that Bowser's in there? Well my friend, if you did you probably want something more from an evil character than just an "Evil" label. And my god, does Borderlands: TPS deliver.
I can't tell you much about Jack without spoiling really crucial stuff, but know that he's something quite unique. More than once, you'll find yourself thinking that, heh, maybe he's not wrong. Hell maybe he's right. He's a brutal individual, with a peculiar sense of humor and a "Greater good" attitude that drives him to commit atrocities. He's made to be absolutely despised. But he also wants to be a hero. He also has a picture of his daughter on his desk.
This should give you a general idea about the kind of engaging plot you're gonna live through Borderlands: TPS.
The gameplay's Borderlands 2. Nothing new, nothing different, if you enjoyed that one you'll like this. Be warned tho, it's VERY glitchy. Items clipping through the floor, AI freezing the enemies, and the list goes on.
Still, I strongly recommend you play this. Yes, even if you hate the gameplay, the story's SO WORTH.

DISCLAIMER: This game was made on flash, and it often pushes it to its very limits. Even on pretty good gaming PCs, this game suffers frequent slow downs and stuttering, thanks to this. If you wanna play this awesome game without all of those issues, I'd recommend purchasing The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth. It's more expensive, but there's also loads of new content, and it's overall an improved experience.
The Binding of Isaac is a retro style rogue like game. At first it might not look that impressive, but let me tell you, this game is quite addictive. It's unforgiving when it comes to difficulty, mostly because, just like any roguelike, death is permanent, and each time you start a new game, the map, the enmies, the bosses, the items, and other stuff are randomly generated.
That means, sometimes you'll have excellent runs, where the game loves you, gives you the best items (There are TONS to collect), and isn't that merciless with it's enemy placement. But sometimes, it's quite the opposite. The game HATES you, and will do anything to ♥♥♥♥ you up before you reach the end. Few health pickups, tons of hard enemies in cramped rooms, no good items, so on, so on.
But even if this game trolls you, and screws you up really hard....For some reason, you'll probably get hooked to it. You will die, and die, and die, and die. But you'll want to try it over and over again. I can't explain this feeling.
The music is simple and effective, and it doesn't really get old, some tracks are pretty amazing, too. The artstyle and graphics are well, 16 bit era stuff. Pretty good. The game seems to lag at times when there are lots of things on the screen, though. I usually play on low graphical settings to avoid that.
It's full of references to other kinds of media, biblical themes, and all in all, it's pretty good at what it does. Also, it's cheap.
I would definitely recommend this game, if you like getting kicked in the♥♥♥♥♥before you ask for more. If you don't like hard games that tap on your Luck stat, then, well, stay away.

The Binding of Isaac is a Flash-based roguelike dungeon crawler reminiscent of early Legend of Zelda games developed by Edmund McMillen and Florian Himsl. Inspired heavily from the Biblical story, the game follows Isaac (and a variety of unlockable characters) escaping from his Christian fundamentalist Mother, to whom a voice of God commands to sacrifice Isaac.
* Gameplay
After escaping from his Mother’s wrath, Isaac finds himself in a basement filled with monsters. Each floor contains a set amount of rooms culminating with a boss fight that must be cleared in order to advance to the next floor. Along the way Isaac can collect pennies (nickels and dimes as variants) to spend in a Shop or an Arcade, bombs to blow up obstacles or enemies and keys to unlock chests and Treasure rooms. The items found in Treasure rooms, after completing a boss fight and other ways are the core to improving Isaac’s tears (bullets) and fighting abilities. For example, an item can make tears homing, poisonous, increase damage and so on. My favourite is the Ipecac item, which makes your tears explosive and always poisonous. If requirements are fulfilled, Isaac can after a boss fight trade his heart containers to the Devil in exchange for powerful items, or alternatively, avoid taking deals with the Devil to acquire a chance for an Offering from an Angel (Wrath of the Lamb DLC required) which can be useful as well.  The game at first seems very difficult, but as it is completed more and more times, new items, characters, alternate bosses and floors can be unlocked, ensuring there will always be a reason to explore. The game also features many references to McMillen’s other games, such as Super Meat Boy and Time ♥♥♥♥, as well as popular games such as Super Mario, Legend of Zelda and others.
* Expansions and the community
While the base game is fairly extensive, I heavily recommend obtaining Wrath of the Lamb DLC, which adds 98 new items, a new character, new floors and many other content that improve the experience. Owning said DLC is a prerequisite for the Eternal Update, a free addon developed by Florian Himsl that adds Hard mode, which offers a brutal experience for those feeling the base game was too easy. The Binding of Isaac is very popular and well known, as a result from famous Youtube Let’s Players such as Northernlion and Bisnap. Their unique ways of playing the game have inspired many more to try the game themselves.
* Closing comments
The Binding of Isaac is a very charming (although rather macabre as well) game which is a must have for anyone interested in roguelikes. It can be obtained for 99 cents from Humble Bundles or Steam sales, DLC and awesome soundtrack included. A worthwhile play even after the release of Rebirth.

First off, this thumbs down does NOT mean that Stellaris is a bad game or that I haven't had fun playing it.
It can actually be a lot of fun to play, and the extensive selection of mods only makes it better.
However, this game has been out for over a year now and many core mechanics are still fundamentally broken. The AI is still idiotic most of the time, relying on cheating (massive production, resource  and research bonuses) to even be remotely competitive.
Fleet mechanics also still need a major rework, as the higher tier components actually have an increasingly worse price/performance ratio and are generally a waste of time to research. Armor mechanics, strike craft, and missiles are broken in a way that makes them useless in a fight with how easily they are countered.
There are also some strange decisions regarding other game mechanics. The colonization mechanics don't really make sense. Why can my race, which is from a continental world with a wide variety of climates, not colonize a desert world or an alpine world without researching a bunch of advanced technologies or terraforming?
When an AI decides to close borders to you, there's nothing you can do about it except declare war on them. No diplomatic options exist to even send a science ship into their territory to research the next thing for your questline, or put a cloaking device on it to sneak it in anyways.
War demands are equally silly. Regardless of my military might, I can only actually claim worlds that I demanded at the start of a fight and have to give the rest back, and the amount I can claim is dependent on statecraft research. It doesn't make sense and is quite annoying. I can see a reputation penalty for aggressively conquering worlds, but to arbitrarily say that a militaristic empire that doesn't care about what the rest of the galaxy thinks has to return a world they've conquered because "reasons" doesn't really make sense.
Espionage is entirely MIA, there's no game features or mechanics for this at all. Seems like a strange oversight and severely limits the capabilities of non-militaristic empires. Everything is about fleet strength, nothing else really matters.
Then there's the victory conditions. The only way to really win the game is via military supremacy. There's no science/spritual/peaceful victory of any kind (other than maybe uniting the galaxy under a federation, good luck with that given the AI stupidity).
Overall, this game has a lot of potential, but here we are a year after release and it's still a beta product being sold at full price, with relatively expensive DLC to boot. The game is still under active development and is continuously being tweaked/improved so hopefully someday it will live up to its potential, but right now there's still a lot of broken aspects to this game that don't show any signs of being fixed right away.
If you're a fan of 4X games and can get this at a good price (Humble Monthly for example), there's enough hours of fun to be worth it, but I can't recommend it at full price given the number of fundamental issues still present a full year after release.
Edit: Didn't expect my review to be the top rated review on Steam for Stellaris.
My initial review was primarily pointing out issues I had with the game, so it's only fair that I also point out some things I liked about it.
The early game exploration and science quests are a great mechanic and I really enjoyed it. Unfortunately, this fun only lasts until the mid-game once all the planets have been surveyed (or your stupid AI neighbors have closed their borders). Since this was the part of the game I enjoyed the most, it's sad to see it fizzle out so early.
Meaningful leaders are also a great thing in this game. Aside from your empire's supreme leader, lesser leaders can be recruited as admirals, generals, governors, and scientists. Leaders gain experience over time and level up to become more effective. This mechanic is powerful enough that I've seen very effective empire builds that just focused on maximizing leadership, and I thought that was a neat mechanic.

This game is lots of fun when it works, and for singleplayer it works perfectly! There's a nice curve in difficulty - players learn how to avoid basic enemy movement patterns and adopts strategies for attack in the first few levels. In later levels enemies perform new patterns that the player must adapt to or suffer greater penalties to health than before. I revel in the challenges the game presents, and the way it rewards skillful movement and planning. Each town is a welcomed rest and keeps the action engaging rather than exhausting.
Multiplayer should be an even greater joy, it's great fun coordinating with a friend and reaping the efficiency of two players dividing duties and actively harvesting resources. however multiplayer has always ended in a mess for me and my friend. I'm unsure if it is due to poor connection because the initial levels work without a hitch. Once we'd reach level 10 and on though everything starts to go to hell. Enemies lag out of place, projectiles spawn unattached to a source, flickering phantoms of beasts would hover in place after death. Occasionally the ground wouldn't load and I'd fall into an inky abyss. It's worse that the multiplayer functions at all because it's only after great progress has been made that everything goes wrong. In one round I even lagged a full level behind. My friend would enter a door, and I'd enter the (unplayable)level he'd just been through.
I understand that with a rogue like game you can't just have a player joining part way through, so allowing a disconnected player to reconnect might not be the best solution. But most games with multiplayer I've played will at least give you an indication that the connection is unstable. It'd be nice if the game recognised a poor connection, and stalled or paused players to try and reconnect/ stabilize. I admit I have no idea what is necessary to actually maintain a multiplayer session, but my experiece so far with it has always ended poorly, and that experience is all I can contribute. If the connection issues could be fixed up I'd happily buy copies just to distribute them to friends and spread the joy, but for now I Guess I'll wait til my friend and I can get a better connection :/

There is a short list of developers that have a "house style" and Spry Fox is definitely one of them. So if their style is to your liking, then you should definitely enjoy Road Not Taken. The whimsical Spry Fox art is on full display, and there are plenty of bears! Seriously, the art is just great. Cartoony paintings of wildlife and other bizarre creatures in a wintery wonderland. (A wintery wonderland that will kill you. Many, many times.) One of the many nice things about this game is that it is pretty much unlike anything you have played before. In a nutshell it is what you might call a dungeon crawl/turn-based puzzle hybrid. There is very little hand-holding and a lot to figure out on your own. When it comes to combining objects into more useful objects, a little bit of memorization is required. Actually, one of my gripes about the game is the illogical nature of many of the combinations. Feels totally random at times, which is frustrating. And the difficulty level really spikes towards the end. But each run will be slightly different than the next, and that makes for lots of strategy building and replayability. Road Not Taken gets an A+ for presentation and originality, but maybe a B+ for game balance and logic. Hopefully the game did well enough to merit a sequel. Check it out if you want to try something a little bit different!

The Binding of Isaac is a Flash-based roguelike dungeon crawler reminiscent of early Legend of Zelda games developed by Edmund McMillen and Florian Himsl. Inspired heavily from the Biblical story, the game follows Isaac (and a variety of unlockable characters) escaping from his Christian fundamentalist Mother, to whom a voice of God commands to sacrifice Isaac.
* Gameplay
After escaping from his Mother’s wrath, Isaac finds himself in a basement filled with monsters. Each floor contains a set amount of rooms culminating with a boss fight that must be cleared in order to advance to the next floor. Along the way Isaac can collect pennies (nickels and dimes as variants) to spend in a Shop or an Arcade, bombs to blow up obstacles or enemies and keys to unlock chests and Treasure rooms. The items found in Treasure rooms, after completing a boss fight and other ways are the core to improving Isaac’s tears (bullets) and fighting abilities. For example, an item can make tears homing, poisonous, increase damage and so on. My favourite is the Ipecac item, which makes your tears explosive and always poisonous. If requirements are fulfilled, Isaac can after a boss fight trade his heart containers to the Devil in exchange for powerful items, or alternatively, avoid taking deals with the Devil to acquire a chance for an Offering from an Angel (Wrath of the Lamb DLC required) which can be useful as well.  The game at first seems very difficult, but as it is completed more and more times, new items, characters, alternate bosses and floors can be unlocked, ensuring there will always be a reason to explore. The game also features many references to McMillen’s other games, such as Super Meat Boy and Time ♥♥♥♥, as well as popular games such as Super Mario, Legend of Zelda and others.
* Expansions and the community
While the base game is fairly extensive, I heavily recommend obtaining Wrath of the Lamb DLC, which adds 98 new items, a new character, new floors and many other content that improve the experience. Owning said DLC is a prerequisite for the Eternal Update, a free addon developed by Florian Himsl that adds Hard mode, which offers a brutal experience for those feeling the base game was too easy. The Binding of Isaac is very popular and well known, as a result from famous Youtube Let’s Players such as Northernlion and Bisnap. Their unique ways of playing the game have inspired many more to try the game themselves.
* Closing comments
The Binding of Isaac is a very charming (although rather macabre as well) game which is a must have for anyone interested in roguelikes. It can be obtained for 99 cents from Humble Bundles or Steam sales, DLC and awesome soundtrack included. A worthwhile play even after the release of Rebirth.
