Having run through it again; my thoughts changed but my overall basis has not.
having now played through Rougelikes of many different types and forms after beginning to enjoy them, and then being yelled at in a previous review for faulting the game for my own faults, I return to the basement with a different point of view, and a new 'meh' for you.
Granted, I made that review quite some time ago so its likely I actually did fault the game for me being bad. Who knows.
Whenever I play it, I can't get into it like I could with say, my current favorite RL; Enter the Gungeon.
Couldn't tell you why but killing Pin was more of a chore than it was exciting. When I lost it wasn't a big shocker, but it did make it harder to click the replay button.
Monstro again.
He's mega easy and provides no challenge in my opinion, so I lost that one based off of my own mistakes. That's all well and good.
But here is the weird thing;
I loved Enter the Gungeon. Its RNG either made games easier (subjectively, mind you) or harder just like Issac.
I love Issacs music and I also enjoy its gameplay to a level.
All the dudes you fight are neat and keep to the same level of creepiness as anything else.
So lets take a second and talk about RNG.
Gunegons RNG typically gives you anything that could be, and usually is, a major positive; a new gun, more weapons, hilarious weapons, items, the like.
Usually you gauged positives and negatives based off of whatever you got, or if you died to it because it was a mimic, but you only die to mimics once.
Issac gives you items, mushrooms that either provide a help, or a hurt, depending, Same with pills. This keeps it interesting and keeps you on your toes but I can't help but ask why we get punished for playing the game.
Stick with me here. Why is it that when I eat a pill the game goes "oh no" and suddenly I am dropping bombs everywhere. Its not about fairness. Its not about 'game flow' or more specific things. I don't care if the game enjoys keeping me on my toes, but it just feels so uneeded. Its not dissimilar to that Lava segment in Rive that could've been removed totally and have nothing change. It really didn't improve the game at all, and merely made it difficult because, well, they could, rather than just throwing some things in there for me to shoot, because at least then, its not an instant death.
This is just one instance, mind you, but I can imagine it applies elsewhere.
I just think its dumb to throw that in needlessly. At least in the tutorial level of Dark Souls, you're warned about the boulder coming down the stairs so if you get smacked by it, its your fault.
Am I seriously to be the one to blame for picking up a mushroom? You can even reason that "oh it can either help or hurt and you get either rewarded or punished based on that risk you took just like actual mushrooms", and that would be reasonable
But it doesn't make it the game more fun or serve to change my opinion.
This one time, I got a powerup that make issac look cool. I thought that was all it was; added flair. Admittedly, cool added flair, but no, it also made him incorporeal and allowed me to travel through rocks. Thats an amazing little thing to just hand us, and an aspect of the game I never thought of.
These two little stories go to show just how wild the RNG can be, but there is a fun middle-ground, where sometimes you'll get things that just seem to have no purpose at all, and merely exist.
Chocolate Milk is likely my favorite 'arrow' that I got during my plays.
I still didn't enjoy it, but you still might / 10

Loadout is a free to play game that takes the term and sets the standard of what that term should mean. You cannot "pay to win" in any way, shape or form. When it comes to transactions, the game will only let you choose what your character looks like as well as what they wear. In fact, you can choose to not wear anything AT ALL and taunt your enemies when they die, but just for a price. If that's something you might find to be too offensive, then that's OK as you can turn nudity off.
With Loadout, weapon customization is literally the name of the game. Want a rocket launcher that explodes into sticky mines that heal people? Done. Want a sniper rifle that sets the target on fire? Done. How about a spooling, gattling gun laser rifle that chains lightning to nearby enemies? Done. With the system of Loadout you can take any combo of their creative options to wild, comical, yet practical weapon configurations.
The game itself plays out at a medium-fast pace where you don't find yourself in "instant death" type of scenarios like in AAA shooters, but rather you can react and dodge their shots in an Unreal Tournament-style and come out on top even when they're the one with the drop on you. Of course, much like Unreal Tournament, this is a very "jumpy" game where moving in 2 dimensions is probably going to get you killed. This may sound bad, but it introduces a little more skill to the game as highly accurate players will have no issue combatting opponents who think that their dodging and jumping will save them.
There are a lot of seemingly minor mechanics that mean a whole lot to how the game plays out, such as a CTF that replaces the flag with a huge hammer that you can slam-kill foolish opponents with for more flag capture points, or how you will find yourself on the enemies radar if you sprint or fire, but you won't be on there if you don't do either.
Overall this game comes across as very silly and that may put some serious players off, but honestly it is a free to play game that has a rather small download and runs at max FPS all the time, so there isn't exactly any risk in giving it a whirl for a few hours.

Loadout is throwaway, silly entertainment. It gets you into a game, raises a smile, and spits you back out again. It’s scrappy, with a few rough edges in the level design and art. But it’s endearingly dumb, and I really think you should, at least, have a try.

I was pretty on the fence about this game as I have been looking for a game to finally be a good follow-up to Master Of Orion 2 and in the last 20 years I have bought quite a few. This is the first 4x space game since Moo2 I have actually thoroughly enjoyed playing.

good game. solid mechanics. its a good 4x type game for stratagy players... i have spent about 11 or so hours in one game so far and i am going to base my review off that 11 hour game so far.
good early game. there is lots to do in the early game. managing your income and resources is critical. finding a way to get what you dont have is a good chalange. for example, getting more influence to get more learders. really like the early game of this game.
mid game is still pretty good. as you expand you start to find other races. it becomes a game of picking your boarders and making sure you have the best possible posision for the late game. start to min max things here. building army's.
however i wish the late game is where the game falls apart... I wish there was more in depth mechanics. for example, defence in the late game becomes a joke really. AI fleets always travle in a blob, so you will have to have a blob bigger then them to beat your AI at war. There are no good defence structers in the game. Star ports and space stations will die instantly in the late game because the fleets are just so powerfull by then.
there is no point to having a war in the late game unless you have a massive fleet that is bigger then your AI counterparts fleet. there is no stratigic possioning or tatics. with the star systems so close to gether it becomes a game of cat and mouse to defend star systems... its stupid honestly.
there needs to be tech for structures that can match fleet power, or tech that can restrict fleet movement. something so that its not just, warp in, shoot the AI fleet, Warp out. wait for the fleet to show up again. warp in, shoot the fleet, warp out.
combat is automated. there is no controle other then telling them where to go.
and the most annoying thing is that there is no other means of attacking the AI with out war. no spies. no electronic warfare. no culture or anything. no other means of defeating an AI without actual fleet power.
just wish there was a way the game could be better in the late game.
other then that its a good game. after 11 hours in one game, i think i have experianced all there is to the game. good thing the game has such a good character/race customazion. you can always start another game and try out a new type of playstyle.

This one is... Interesting.
I definitely recommend it, it's good. But, I do have a lot of gripes.
I'd say try it, but wait till it goes on sale. I got all the DLCs as well as the game for 50$, and i'd say that's worth it. Maybe a wee bit overpriced, but considering I could have bought something completely crappy like Battlefront, I won't complain.
Gripes-
Diplomacy is, well, quite frankly,
Trade is a background feature, and diplomacy definitely isn't up there. In the end, in order for the game to remain fun, you need to take over other empires by force. You can join a federation, but if you do you might as well just start over. Cause in a federation... Nothing changes. You, and all the other empires in the federation, stay as separate empires. No more expansion. And when the game is pretty much based on expansion... Yeah. If there was an endgame thing where your federation would blend into one empire you could control, i'd feel very differently. But i'm someone who doesn't feel satisfied playing in a federation. 'Banding together with other empires to fight enemies' sounds cool as hell to me on paper, but what ends up happening is, the galaxy quickly fills up (you'd be amazed how fast a 1000 star galaxy, which is the max, runs out of free systems to own. At that point everything stops, unless you start attacking eachother) and you're stuck next to them. Diplomacy, as I already said, is very underdeveloped. Therefore, the only people you will be able to get to join your little federation is pacifists. Nobody else is willing to join you, most of the time, and there are very few ways to raise their opinion of you enough to convince them, if you can raise it at all. So you, and your pacifist federation, are stuck. The pacifists wont fight anyone, so it's up to you. I suppose you could convince the federation to attack other empires when you become leader, but i'm not sure if you can actively assimilate them into your empire. I played in a federation once, quite some time ago, so the details are fuzzy. But what I do remember was that it was unfulfilling.
Getting off of the federations topic, there's not really much else to do. You can form a defensive pact, a non agression pact, and you can vouch for the sovereignty of an empire (so if anyone attacks them, you automatically enter the war), but that's pretty much it. Not very fun.
The government and ethics system is honestly kind of generic. You get a tree for ethics, going around, militarist, spiritualist, pacifist, materialist, etc. They don't do a whole lot other than effect other empires' view of you slightly (spiritualists will like spiritualists) change the outcome of some anomalies (materialists may try and find a rational explanation for something, while spiritualists will just attribute it to divine providence, sometimes having different outcomes depending on your ethics) and adding small buffs to your pops. But really, your starting choices in ethics matter little, as factions are a thing.
Speaking of factions, I hate them. Basically, it means if you are a militarist nation, at some point pacifism will become a thing, starting it's own faction. There are things you can do you influence faction happiness, but generally you have to favor one over another. Unhappy factions, unhappy pops. So now, every pacifist in your empire has a base happiness of 20% because their faction is upset that you're at war with someone. Pretty much the only thing you can do about this is to purge all your pacifist pops, which is annoying. There's no real low-key way to remove it.
Space combat is also pretty generic. There are a lot of options for customizing your ships, but at the end of the day, max shields, plasma cannons and neutron torpedo ships are *vastly* better than anything else. There are few ways to specialize your fleets and generally, this is a bad idea.
Multiplayer, is... Completely broken. I've tried several times to play with my friends. Usually, even if joining his game through
, it just comes up with 'game not found'. If we do manage to join up and get together, desync occurs almost immediately. Apparently it has plagued paradox games for all time. And once you desync, the game completely breaks forever. The only fix for this is 'god-like connection and a beast PC', which isn't really a fix, more like a 'it might work'. And of which I have neither. So singleplayer is what you'll really be doing.
Good things-
Exploring is pretty fun, as are anomalies.
Spreading your empire is very satisfying, at least in the early game.
The traditions and ascension perks are all pretty cool.
Researching all the technologies is very fun.
Upgrading your fleets with better and better stuff is fun, but as stated by the end game plasma neutron ships are basically the only thing you want.
You can build a dyson sphere. How cool is that?
I might sound like I don't like the game, I do, but quite frankly, it's overpriced. It's got a AAA pricetag and DLCs to boot, but feels like a very simple game, for a strategy game. People expect a generic campaign they'll finish in an afternoon from CoD, as they play mostly for the multiplayer. But the game itself feels underdeveloped, and the multiplayer is broken, so what's a guy to do?

First off: Yes the game has flaws and is old, but it's still not bad. This is also not a pro-con-post.

I think I made the right decision when I joined one of the bigger servers after a friend recommended it and had really no issue with the people on it. Yes there can be idiots, but you find them in all survival-ish and sandboxy games with community driven servers.
Overall the community is nice, some are elitists but that's the minority.
Now to the game: Since I knew WO, I knew how the interface is a bit clunky and can be overwhelming, but after taking some time it really is nice. Yes, you interact less with the world due to the submenus and stuff, but overall you get more out of it.
What I see in most negative reviews is "I die to XY, it's a joke". Well yes and no. If you start out, your skill barely shows you where to hold the sword and not just grab it on it's blade. It takes practice to actually get used to it (as in real life, not as hard as in-game but it does). Best thing to do: Hit some trees to get the skill up and it will be easier.
Combat isn't the strength of the game, and I never really saw it as main selling point - It is fun to go out there and kill stuff, but only with a few others or if you have the actual skill and high quality items to do so.
The main selling point is the sandbox. And I love it. You can terraform the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game (if you have the skill to do so), you can basically build your dream house, castle, town, whatever if you invest some time into skilling up the specific skills, which should be possible by creating the actual needed resources.
Right now, we maintain a rather big town and there is always something to build or to help out.
The only downside is the advertised single-player. You can do it and it might be fun if you change the rates high enough, but overall it is not meant for single-player.
Also for the needed server: All claim they are having issues with it and I have no clue what they do. I went through the settings without any guide and just started it. Could connect without issues and it was only showing up on LAN.
Multiplayer is as fun as it was in WO: Work together and not against each other, unless you are on a PVP server. But there are also Kingdoms.
TL;DR: If you like a sandbox, that is not focussed around pve-combat and want to play with others and get over window management and older graphics, then this is the way to go.
For anyone eager to just try it, don't buy it. Go to Wurm Online, play there for a bit until you get some skills to the F2P level 20 skillcap and see for yourself. If you survive as long as that and you enjoy it, then get WU and play on the bigger servers.

Wurm Unlimited is a sandbox game where you can do almost anything you can imagine, IF you are willing to put the time into it.
The learning curve is steep, the Wurmpedia is super helpful and has lots of information available. If your able to play for more then the first few hours you will probably enjoy the game alot.

Resident evil: Jill's fine butt returns.
First of all pre-warnings:
Just fair reminder that there is NO SINGLEPLAYER CO-OP, it only has "raid mode" co-op which is your standard mercaneries but with set levels and enemies. No waves. Just "go from A to B while killing 15 enemies".  Which is surprising because you effectively have partner with you all the game.
Co-op mod is being devoloped by fans but it has lot of problems to hurdle first.
Dialogue, story and voice acting is pretty horrible and you should NOT buy this "for the story".
Not even "capcom horrible", they are just plain bad facepalm level. Its super awkward B-movie quality.
At first you dont notice it because its your typical Resident Evil one liners of "we need to help CHRIIIS" "OKAY lets GO".
Later on it you will just think "who intern made this up" and towards end I just couldnt bare the horrid non-surprising story and writing. The low budget and dismissive attidute towards story "because its portable game" shows on this side.
Gameplay:
Kinda fun at start if you liked RE5 with mix of RE6 (you can move while aimin but its RE5 styled over the shoulder).
However, it gets REALLY repetive and enemies can get bullet spongy later on. The gameplay is effectively POINT GUN AT ZOMBIE, SHOOT TILL DEAD with very rare QTE "get out when being grabbed". The scanning element is cool addition but you either end up waving that device around most of the game which is distracting or just forget it unless you are out of ammo.
Around middle you will get the classical "we have to go back to the start of the game because reasons" level re-use, gladly thats fast because you dont have to unlock all doors.. but kinda waste of time.
Graphically:
Shows sings of 3DS port and the animations really show it - your character slides side to side with minimal animations when running around, shadows are blocky and some textures are blurry and not really worthy of "HD".
Would not recommend for full price unless you are diehard RE-fan. Get it cheap.
If you are looking for good 3rd person shooter / horror this aint it. Get RE5 or new RE4 HD instead.
If you are lookin for cheesy b-movie resident evil  which makes you facepalm and trigger finger numb, this is it.

I've played this game a few times, and I have a few problems with this game that I think need to be addressed before I'll think about playing it any further.
1: Infantry. Those of us who play the actual game know that infantry come in the Unit variety and Solo variety, and that warcasters have spells that are designed for units of infantry such as Arcane Shield or Iron Flesh. In this game though, each infantry model is treated as a solo, which is a huge problem for casters like Stryker1 who depends on Arcane Shield to gain advantage.
2: Clumsy UI. This is an issue that I suppose will be fixed over the course of development because it's a vital and integral part of the game, but it has definitely screwed with me doing exactly what I want to do with my 'jacks and infantry. It hasn't even really been improved over the course of the beta, so I'm not sure what to expect from the final version.
3: Shrouded game mechanics. WM is an easy to understand game on the tabletop with concrete stats and open game mechanics. This game for some reason decides to change the core concepts of the tabletop game into some hazy system of unexplained stats and not quite clear method of RNG. This combined with the change to Infantry (5 damage boxes instead of 1 damage box) brings on a noticable balance change that I'm not on board with because the spells remain largely unchanged from the tabletop version (arguably balanced for that format and not this one). I have no idea why it was decided that the game would change the core mechanics of the game so drastically when they were entirely functional and successful in the tabletop version.
Unless the game is changed back to a totally faithful reproduction of the TT version, I'm not coming back to this game because that's what I wanted out of this game. For those of you who aren't TT players, the game might be better for you, but I as a TT player am definitely not on board.

This game is very well made.  Its primary method of play is strategy of combat.  You are provided with two protagonists, an Orc and a Goblin.  Most obviously, one is a brutish tank capable of dealing extreme damage and taking punishment, and the other is stealthy assassin capable of fighting both in melee and range, and is better suited to the delicate tasks.  That said, the impressive thing is how well the two characters pair in order to provide an excellent play experience.
The story behind the game is well written, and the voice acting for the characters is rather excellent.  The protagonists being an orc and a goblin is exciting, even if some of the storyline elements can be viewed as cliche.  In fact, the voice acting and writing is so well done it makes it obvious that the 'conversation' animations are limited.  That said, the limited animations feel 'right' to both the dialog and the gameplay.
Of Orcs and Men is a game that focuses on the well defined and executed gameplay, rather than the shiny baubles most companies seem to focus their efforts on in order to distract the player from poor gameplay.  The pairing of the characters, and the inner dichotomies of their skill wheels provides rich gameplay for the mostly well designed battles and encounters.  Perhaps the most frustrating of encounters are the boss battles, because your have less time and space to plan and execute battle strategy, but it's just one more layer to an interesting game and story.

Sadly it would appear this game is an unplayed/underrated gem. I myself only picked it up during the recent winter sale & there is little about it on the web, especially positive. I was surprised by how much I enjoyed this game given how much negativity there is surrounding it.
I am a fantasy lover & playing as something other than yet another human or elf was a welcome change.
The twist is that the orcs & goblins are the oppressed race who are  brutally murdered, tortured & turned into slaves & pets by the evil human race.
Of course not all orcs are pleasant & not all humans are power hungry racist zealots.
The music was a character itself, it has been a while since I really got into the music in a game & have found myself humming various songs.
The combat is rather like that of Dragon Age, during battle you can hold space to slow down the action to a crawl giving you time to select what skills you want the characters to use; doing so is advisable as you won't win many battles spamming the auto attack. Although I found for the tougher bosses spamming the stun punch is pretty much the only way you can win. The game has it's faults, auto saves can be annoying, the last fight in particular, some parts of the cutscenes cannot be skipped, you will often get stuck in endless revives meaning just as you revive one character the one doing the reviving will die & this can go on & on & on dragging out fights. Much like The Walking Dead this game is a one time ride, it's linier & everything is a corridor so unless you care about achievements enough to go through a second time I doubt you'll play more than once. I personally found the use of the word ♥♥♥♥ & it's variations distracting, not that I'm offended by swearing I just thought it was used way too much & isn't really a curse word that fits the setting; I prefer it when fantasy games make up their own curse words.
All in all I had fun with this game, certainly enough to recommend it though not at full price given it's issues & short length.

We live in a world where MKX is actively giving the finger to PC players by restricting content to console ports, and SFV is a full gaming package the same way a chicken bone and warm beer is a good lunch. As someone who's been thirsty for a good PC anime fighter since Touhou 12.3, I'm thrilled to see Under Night get ported onto Steam in good condition. Could use some mouse-driven menus and less wonky keyboard controls for said menus (this game works best with a controller, if it needs to be said). Other than that, it's a solid PC port running at 60 FPS at 1080p. You'd be hard pressed to find a machine it
run well on.
For the uninitiated, this is a 2D fighter featuring 16 different characters, half of whom are in high school as per anime fighter tradition. Don't bother with the story; you don't need to know it. You just want to see gigantic lizards being summoned out of books by a glasses-wearing hipster, whirling blood scythes of doom controlled by a maniac who forgot to take out his Tokyo Ghoul contacts, and of course, very large swords being wielded by very pretty ladies with very large...erm...assets. Controls are tight and responsive for the most part (although F,D,DF is not an easy input for anybody), combat is satisfying and tense, and so far I've had a blast playing this game.
If you have a thing for flashy and engaging combat, but also don't want to put up with any of the recent AAA fighters' shenanigans, give this game a bash. If you are an MKX or SFV fan, pick this up anyways. A very solid investment at $30

One of the most underrated fighting games in my opinion. Nothing is really outstandingly different from other fighters, but everything feels good and is overall well balanced for low to mid level play (not sure about high level). If anything, this lack of bells and whistles is really what makes this game function so well and creates an easy to learn, difficult to master scenario. Works well with a controller or stick, haven't tried keyboard but I'd assume it works well enough there as well. The characters are all super fun to use and it's hard to pick a main, and even when I lose I still want to keep playing. My hours on here don't reflect my overall play as I've played quite a bit at a friends house on the ps3 version.
All in all, if you're interested in a solid fighter that's fun to play, this is a great choice.

Better than I remember it on PS3. Before I lost my game disc, that is.
Fighting is extremely fluid. The game is easy to learn, but hard to master. Complex system mechanics and lots of meter management await for those who want to dive deep.
The cast is varied. No two characters play alike. Or look alike. No clones in this fighting game.
The game is easy on the eyes. Buttery-smooth 60FPS spritework, hand-drawn goodness. Of course, that comes with a downside. Anything above 1080p is scaled; nobody is going to re-draw complex sprite-based animations for every resolution under the sun.
Colors and effects are nice and popping, interface is pretty clean, and the game lets you know if you performed a combo that isn't a true combo - great for newbies to know what's techable and what could potentially be punished if their opponent catches on.
If this is your first fighting game, it's not a bad choice, but the games Arc System Works actually developed (not just published like this one) and Skullgirls all have very in-depth tutorials for complete fighting game newbies to learn basics that are not only useful in the game they're in, but in every fighting game.
Finally, if you want a community, check out the discord chat.

Under Night In-Birth ported to Steam?! 2 year old game (4 if you want to count arcades) that was ported to PC by ArcSys. This beautifully anime pixel artstyle fighting game made it's way across Steam/Pc for others to be played. The visuals and colorful aspects of the game would appeal anyone who enjoys good, vibrant art style along with flashy effects. The OST is the best in the fighting game genre with it's variety of character's. Different characters to choose from, different stages and modes to play through. You can enjoy various gameplay mode's such as Arcade, Survival, Time Attack, Training and Network! You can also customize your characters by puchasing colors set to your profile, as well as your online Avatar, Title plate, and title! Play in VS, Arcade, or Network to rake IP points to buy all colors! *10 additional colors for every character to purchase in the store*.
Under Night in-Birth is my favorite fighting game, however, it is being proclaimed dead by the FGC. It my favorite fighting game, I will give it my honest review for anyone than being biased about their traits.
Gameplay (8/10): For those who enjoy fast, chain-combo'ing fighting games, this one's for you! If you've enjoyed Blazblue or any of it's iterations, give this one a shot! Flashy vibrant colors, awesome sound effects, and an enjoyable soundtrack to go through makes this the perfect anime fighting game. Different variety of characters to choose from, all being very distinct to their character and not being copy/pasted. Modes ranging from Arcade, Time attack, Survival, and Network, you can choose to play different types for maximum playthrough.
Netcode/Online (8/10): Having played Network as soon as the release, based off the initial Netcode, it is most like the PS3 version of  the game. Rarely any lag spikes, and smooth sailing for your combos.
Artstyle (10/10): The game's beautiful!! For being an anime pixel game, you can expect non-boring colors while playing Under Night.
Sound/BGM (10/10): Best background music and sound effects in the game. You can expect different style music, and very fitting and distint to one character's personality. Hard to get tired of listening to any of these OST.
Offline 1v1 (X/X): Being a port from the PS3, you can safely assume that offline is much better than online. I haven't tried this offline yet, but basing off online you can expect it to be just fine.

So full disclosure off the top, I was actually lucky enough to work with one of the creators of this game at a previous job before she left to pursue her dream to make it.  She was one of the most talented artists at said ad agency, so I knew she was going to put together something special when she told me her plan.  Biased?  Probably, but given the other great reviews on Steam, I don't think I'm talking out of place.
When I first saw the teaser and images from Planet of the Eyes I immediately thought of a sci fi game from my childhood that I absolutely loved for its groundbreaking gameplay and art direction, Another World (google it if you haven't heard of it).  I'm not sure if they drew some inspiration from that title, but after playing the game I can safely say Planet of the Eyes carries itself as its own beautifully executed independent work of art.  It's simply a fun game with a classic science fiction atmosphere, great voice acting, spot on physics, and clever animations.  I'm only 30 minutes in, but I haven't encountered a single point of repetition, and I'm having fun discovering the new monsters and obsticles around each corner.  I've even been screwing up on purpose just to see what happens.  Nothing feels out of place, and the game transitions from environment to environment seamlessly.
All that said, and not to sound overly dramatic, I think what I love most about this game is the fact that it was made by people who took risks to follow their passion and it paid off.
And now that I got that out of my system it's back to the next puzzle.  Congrats you two, you should be proud!

Revelations feels like a big step in the right direction for the RE franchise. I certainly enjoyed it far more than RE5&6. I still wouldn't call this horror, because the AI partner negates the possibility of a tense atmosphere. But at least the gameplay feels more like survival than action. Combat is slow paced and enemy numbers are low, but even with superior mouse aim, ammo was a little scarce. I needed to explore a little to find hidden supplies. Thankfully none of the more frustrating sequences from RE6 are included in Revelations. There are only a couple of short turret sections and even the QTEs feel natural (just shake mouse when something grabs you). The story is the usual RE (terrorists release a virus, stop them!) and lasts around 8 hours. Its very stable and plays great with KB and mouse. The graphics are basic, clearly showing the game's handheld origins, but it doesn't harm the experience too much. Definitely worth playing.

You should play this game for it's
. You cannot hold a conversation of any length without it triggering at some point. Complaining about someone suiciding on your team? Can't. Suicide is a bad word. Want to complain about passive-aggressive behavior? Good luck: Passive is a bad word... because it contains ♥♥♥♥♥. Absurdity reaches a pitched fever when you try to describe a map in a
game and it pukes on you for using the word 'canal'. Not that this is any of a surprise... China is good at exactly two things: Censoring the **** out of everything and producing lead-infused childrens' toys.
Which leads me to the game itself:
. The map selection is small. Submarines and carriers are severely underpowered, and battleships can be easily sunk by one or two torpedoes... as long as you spend money to get the gold-plated versions. Regular versions require about 4 torpedoes to sink one. And destroyers and cruisers can launch 4-8 of these, so you're still pretty screwed even without the Credit Card Ultimate Upgrade(tm).
The carriers are cursed with planes that are easily shot down, can be seen at over three times the distance they can spot at, and as a courtesy, fly low, slow, and in straight lines or hopelessly long and predictable semi-circles. And the torpedo-dropping ones even helpfully do a full circle about the release point before dropping most of the time. Basically, you have to be asleep at the keyboard to be damaged by a plane, and this assumes you didn't faceplant onto the "W" key and aren't completely stationary. Even at that, you can expect to only have your planes hit the target about half the time.  Unless you spend money, in which case all of these problems go away and you're gifted with planes that fly fast, have 21st century stealth technology, and shoot lasers. Okay, I'm lying about the lasers... but the damage they put out makes you wish it did... a single gold-plated torpedo could probably take out a small island.
I could go on, but I think you get the point: It suffers from terrible balance issues, and feels like a cheap knock-off of world of tanks, but with ships. Which, well, you know...
. Even assuming you like the game, you're going to be in a league of your own: There's only about 300 or so people on the server in the evenings, so if you advance far enough in the game to have decent ships, you'll be staring at a loading screen forever. And, if you don't advance far enough, you'll die to some guy with money to burn who will sink you with his credit card, because at the lower tiers, skill is pretty irrelevant. But, if you do decide to play the game, do yourself a favor: Don't ever type anything in the game. Because sooner or later, the filter will trip, and if you spend any time at all chatting, you'll probably get a moderator (or a script; I'm not sure how it happens, I just see a lot of complaints outside of the game) to mute you. I have played both Steel Ocean and World of Warships (WoWs). Both games have their appeal and niche.
If you prefer a bit more depth to your ship combat, especially when it comes to your ship's equipment and crew, then give Steel Ocean a try. Its equipment and tech tree are actually more reminiscient of World of Tanks (WoT) - you research upgraded weapons, radar, sonar, engines, etc. You assign officers to the captain, gunner, radio and similar crew slots.
I will say the farthest I've gotten in Steel Ocean is Tier 3, while I've gotten to Tier 8 in WoWs. (I've also played a lot more WoWs than Steel Ocean.) Battleship combat feels a lot more interesting in Steel Ocean, where you get to fire your main batteries in artillery mode, and actually control your secondaries.
Also unlike WoWs, Steel Ocean implements submarines in a manner that seems to have found a balance. While on the surface, you are vulnerable to cannon and torpedo attacks, but you move at your fastest speed and needn't worry about air. If you submerge to just beneath the surface, cannon can no longer attack you, but you are now able to be damage by depth charges. You also have a time limit (3 minutes, if I recall) of air. If you go to the next, deepest, level, you can only be hit by depth charges, but your air is used much quicker. You're also slower in both submerged depths.

The camps you visit will act as a hub for your quests.

This is an excellent entry in the Total War series, better than its predecessor (Rome) and its next 2 successors (Empire and Napolean). The time period allows for exciting gameplay and lots of variety. The campaign mode fixed a lot of the problems from Rome (late game issues like being unable to deal with large cities and distance from capital). This game also introduced randomization of soldiers, so they all look different instead of being an army of clones. This game has one of the best experiences of building a globe spanning kingdom from 1 or 2 settlements. AI isn't amazing, but smart enough to put you in some tough situations now and again, especially on higher difficulty settings.
DLC campaigns are fun and add interesting scenarios.
All in all, lots of fun, tons of nations to play with, meaningful differences in unit types, and challenging strategy.

UNIEL is a very solid fighting game, developed by French Bread. You might be more familiar with their work on Melty Blood, and if you are then you should certainly already know the quality of the game. The roster in UNIEL is amazingly varied, with everything from your robotic lolita girl, to a creature that looks like he came straight out of EVA. Gameplay-wise, the roster is balanced as well, with the top-tiers not being as dominating as one would usually think they are in an anime fighting game.
One thing that might shy people away from the game is their previous experience with anime fighters, the overly fast pace and intense combo game in particular. While there is potential for long, execution-heavy combos, they are not mandatory to learn the game, which is going to come as a relief to many. Your bread and butter can be found online without much difficulty, and the community tends to be very welcoming towards newcomers.
With it previously having been a PS3 exclusive, the PC playerbase have previously not had access to the game. Fighting games have a terrible tendency of getting the previous iteration released on PC just when the new one is coming out, but that's not the case this time around, as the sequel titled UNIst, is still not out on console. UNIEL is the latest iteration on the franchise both on PC and console, so don't worry about making a poor business decision in that sense.
I hope you all have as much fun with this game as I have. If there's ever any questions you might have over the game, feel free to message me and I'll be glad to help. Happy playing!

Ah, Stellaris.
A unique sort of 4X / RTS hybrid, although the RTS aspect isn't based on APM.
Pros:
-This game lets you design your own race and empire, from appearance to traits to government type, which is great - especially if you like roleplaying.
-Exploration is fun, with a ton of events to discover, all with varying effects on your empire, the planets you inhabit and even the universe itself.
-Tons of content and ways to play the game.
-Great soundtrack.
-No two games are the same
-Early / mid game is amazing and dynamic.
-The large scale of the game means that you won't be steamrolling from the very moment your empire even spawns
Cons:
-Combat needs to be reworked, as the current meta revolves around stacking the most basic unit to overwhelm other fleets with sheer numbers.
-This being the first paradox game that I actually bought DLC for, I find the biggest DLC (Utopia) somewhat lacking.
-Rather buggy at the moment (Running out of food doesn't actually do anything at this point, certain event chains can't be finished, ethic attraction doesn't do anything etc)
-Late game can be a bit of a drag (However, this game IS more of a sandbox than an actual conquer-the-universe type of game)
Despite these flaws, I've had a ton of fun with this game and I'll continue having a lot of fun with it.
Definitely worth a purchase.

I'm having a hard time deciding whether or not I can recommend this game.
I used to enjoy playing Civilization, so it's not like I've never played an RTS before. Stellaris is very pretty, but you spend so much time managing the game at the Galaxy map that you never get to really appreciate how pretty the animations are. You're mostly just doing administrative stuff.
The first time I played, I was hopelessly lost. The tutorial mode is almost nonexistent-- there are commands that took me 15 hours to discover. Tweaks and ways to adjust things that never occurred to me. And the submenus are pretty poorly laid out-- there's not a lot of intuitive aspects to managing your game, you just kludge through the menus until you stumble on what you're looking for.
The AI is incredibly frustrating. Diplomacy feels very broken-- it's difficult to tell what'll anger them, what makes them happy, or to find ways to allay things. Once they're Hostile to you, you're basically hosed, because the AI will send a massive fleet directly for your least defended system and they'll run through your Empire until you have to surrender to them. It's impossible to defend against blitzkrieg tactics unless you keep your empire very tiny and very defensive focused. There are zero diplomatic options once your enemy hits Hostile, at least none that I've found.
That said, I'm 20 hours of playtime into Stellaris and I keep wanting to come back to it. It's very engaging and requires a dextrous amount of multitasking. But at the moment, I've started and lost two games, and I'm not sure I want to jump back in yet.

It is a common joke among Paradox Interactive fans that Paradox games are like a fine wine. They get better as they age and it is often unwise to partake of them too early. For better or for worse, Stellaris fits this mould. Much has changed in the game mechanics and meta since its release. Largely for the better. One year on is often quoted as the best time to pass judgement on Paradox games. So how does Stellaris stack up?
Pretty well actually, it is deep and engaging while remaining more accessible than the average Paradox Interactive game. Of course that is not unlike saying that the Pacific Continental Shelf is less deep than Marianas Trench. There is a lot to learn in Stellaris and plenty of things that you would need to intuit or more likely read up for yourself. Overall the game nails solidly the sense of exploration and wonder that a space based 4X should have.
It is not all a bed of roses though. Space combat, which is to say practically all of the combat in the game, is still under the control of a lobotomised AI. You cannot even tell your ships which target to pick, you can only tell them to attack or run away and let the AI decide which vessel it strikes first.
The AI also has the annoying tendency to form mutual defense pacts to the point where it makes pre-Great War European politics look tame by comparison. If you are of a particularly bloodthirsty bent, you will find that you are often constrained by the alliances between several lesser powers keeping your ravening horde of alien locusts from devouring an entire species whole. As you know, you would be in real life. Having a soft limit on your controlled worlds also puts a damper on expansionists unless they are willing to trust many worlds to the sector management AI. Keeping players from running roughshod is one thing, always feeling like the game mechanics are trying to stop me from doing what I am supposed to be doing is quite another.
The kind of actions that you can perform in this game can truly plumb the depth of sapient depravity up to and including the ability to use advanced genetics to modify a slave race to become especially succulent treats for your core population. Somewhere out there I am sure that some race's version of Thanksgiving is intermingled with the mass culling and genocide of another species.
Overall this game is still very much  Paradox game down to the ground. Obtuse, difficult and immensely engaging. If you ever need to hook one of your friends into Paradox's orbit, presumably because you are a masochist who believes in sharing the fun, this would not be a bad game to start with. It avoids some of the pitfalls of earlier games but has a better degree of accessbility.
Also making a race of carnivorous penguins to devour the entire galaxy never gets old.

First I'd like to say I really enjoy playing this game. While it is a free download I'd recommend getting the premium membership. Which you can buy the premium time in any increments you want. I believe $5.00 gets you 3 days. You earn money and experience much faster with a premium account. Which allows you to purchase upgrades for your ships quicker. Destroyers, Light Cruisers, Heavy Cruisers, Battleships, AirCraft Carrriers, and Submarines are the ship classes. The Destoyers, Light Cruisers and Heavy Crusiers have a farely straightforward learning curve, scouting than running and gunning. The battleships take some getting use to, think of them as artillary that hangs in the back early game than move in close range late game. The Submarines will take some time to learn how to use them effectively. They can be a real pain to kill and if left unchecked can be devestating. The Aircraft Carriers have by far the hardest learning curve. They only start at tier 3 which when put up against  tier 3s and tier 4s of the other ship classes the first time you play a carrier can be frustrating. During a battle each ship has a particular job to fill for the team. While ultimately the goal is to sink the enemy fleet, you can also capture their base for a win. There are plenty of maps and game modes to play and for me it doesn't seem repetitive.   Also, each ship can hold 3 pieces of equipment that will boost a particular parameter. This costs coins (in game money) to purchase and the bigger the benefit the more costly a particular piece of equipment can be. The developers are always running some kind of event that boosts experiance earned and/or credits earned. Big plus is free premium ships! Once you have logged in 15 days you get a free tier 2 Light Cruiser, after 30 days a free tier 4 Light Cruiser. What this game needs is more players, it can have a max of 15 players on each team in a match. More times than not it's usually 8-10. Que times can be long if you are trying to play a particular tier and not many people are playing it. All in all its a free download, try it out if you don't like it uninstall, nothing lost.

This is a fun, thematic puzzle game with a pretty solid challenge level. You are a ranger responsible for rescuing children lost in the woods, amongst strange items and dangerous creatures. The theme is rather dark, even depressing, but it holds together well.
The puzzle aspect is basically moving stuff around to get past obstacles. Some objects/creatures just sit there, others move around or actively pursue (or avoid) you, and many objects transform when they hit each other. Figuring out these "recipes" is a big part of the game, which is usually fun, but occasionally you'll forget and have an item you need get combined into something else! You have an in-game log of items and recipes found, but you really need to remember them as you play.
You have a limited amount of energy (hit points) each year (level), and if you run out, you die. Moving things in unlit rooms costs energy, and some things/creatures will damage you for varying amounts of energy. In addition to finding the children, you will need to find or make food to raise your energy—this is a critical part of succeeding! You also want to make fires to light up each part of the forest so that moving things doesn't cost energy. Figuring out how to do both is a big part of gameplay.
During play you can form relationships with certain characters in town and in the forest, gaining charms that give you bennies, and eventually marrying them if you get really close to them. You can marry all the NPCs, male and female, if you want. But you are not guaranteed a long life with them....
Replay value is pretty good as each year of your career the forest and its denizens change, and the charms are given to you in different order. It's never the same game twice, although there are a few set pieces that are always the same.

This game...wow. So much can be said about this game. I can't get enough of it! Here are a few main categories to sum up just some of the many amazing things about this spectacular game:
The Gameplay:  The dungeon randomization makes every year and every life unique, and it is up to your wit and problem solving to decide how to best craft and cluster the right items in order to get to the children. Sometimes the game can be UNBEARABLY HARD, but you still push on 'til you die or have to return to town without having saved all the children. Many of the negative reviews I see have to do with the difficulty of some of the dungeon generations, and yes, it CAN get infuriating! But there's nothing wrong with just starting a new life -I did it several times and got amazing careers afterward.
Energy preservation is key -a simple step in the wrong direction can take your life, or make your journey incredibly more difficult, so it is best to evaluate every room before taking action. You also do countless backtracking trips as you need to craft and arrange items with just the right amount of items, so your adjacent rooms are your friends. Low on health? Have an axe in one room and a ninja bear in the other one? Just throw it over and kill the bear for your apple. Need to get rid of a dark spirit AND acquire health? Take the blue fire from one room and throw it at the spirit in the other room to get a very helpful stew.
I LOVE how creativity is emphasized -there are numerous ways to create the same item, and this mechanic can be both beneficial (multiple ways to make food) or detrimental (multiple ways to create daemon bunnies or dark spirits). The "teleport to mayor" mechanic can save your life in very many instances, or help you get to a room from one entrance if the other entrance is blocked or dangerous.
Because this game uses permadeath, you should always find ways to acquire money, rice, or berries, because the game is graceful in providing you a shrine to offer to and ensure that you will respawn. However, you lose very important charms upon death, so sometimes leaving some children behind when in a rut is a better choice than dying and letting your character respawn with next to nothing.
The Art:  The art is beautiful, charming, and deceptive- very gruesome and dark themes can be overlooked because of how cutesy the art style is. The atmosphere is remarkable -the sounds, surroundings, and music totally and completely immerse you, making you easily waste hours upon hours on this game.
The Characters: The customization in how you build your relationships -friendships and romantic- with differently generated characters every life gives you the desire to do better in the dungeons, and thus, receive more rewards to use as gifts to give to villagers. The dialogue is hilarious, sad, moving, touching, and sweet -the writers of this game put great thought and work into the dialogue. It makes the game that much more alive and real to you, and in combination with how you've built your relationships with the other characters, it can get you emotionally invested. I felt happy when a character would do kind gestures, return romantic feelings, and became unreasonably upset and sad when they would cheat on me (in romantic relationships) or simply decide they didn't like me anymore. I had to take a step back once in a while to remind myself that THIS IS A GAME! XD
This game holds a dear place in my heart, because you can see all the heart and soul the development team poured into it, and it offers infinite playtime that can always feel fresh and enjoyable. Because of this game, I have become a loyal follower of the small game developer team -SpryFox. There is something incredible about a small indie game developer doing so well with their games and it's encouraging for all other small groups of developers and artists that want to make their dream games become reality.

If you enjoy the Diablo or Torchlight series (or PoE), you will enjoy this game.  I've logged literally tens of thousands of hours on those series, and Chronicon stacks up very well against them. It incorporates much of what works in those games (procedurally generated loot,  an "enchanter" NPC, complex skill trees, powerful legendary items and sets, etc) and puts its own spin on things.
It has more content than many finished games. Getting through the portion of the main story that's already released took me ~20 hours (4 out of 5 acts at this time), and I've spent over 100 additional hours mastering endgame content with no end in sight.
The primary developer is very active on the discussion boards, responding to bug reports and suggestions frequently. He's fixed the majority of bugs reported, and he's implemented hundreds (thousands?) of player suggestions. Also, the game is updated regularly, with both major and minor updates.
All-in-all, I've gotten ridiculous value out of this game.

Short version: Don't believe reviews older than March 2015. The game is better, prettier, and more stable than ever before. It still might not be for everybody, but it's worth a look.
UPDATE: August 2016 - Updated spell effects, all new UI, somewhat improved AI, and generally very attractive and stable performance. This is how the game should have released, and more updates are on the way. I can recommend it still.
Long version:
I've been playing since Early Access, but wanted to wait until the last of the Kickstarter DLC was released before writing a review. In the meantime, I've watched a nearly unplayably buggy game get lots of fixes and polish from the developers, and now I feel like it would be fair to give it a balanced review. APRIL 25, 2015
PROS:
+Excellent character models and animations fully capture the look and feel of the Iron Kingdoms setting.
+Very deep core gameplay draws many concepts faithfully from its table top origins.
+Single player story is decent, written by game creator Matt Wilson, and has some fun missions.
+Each faction is very distinct, and has a good (not great) variety of models.
+Multiplayer is fun and intense. I've only dabbled, but I could get hooked.
+SP Skirmish mode is okay for testing teams or admiring art assets.
+Highly active and invovled development team communicates regularly with players.
Minor Drawbacks:
* Some spell and engine effects are too shiny/intense for my taste.
* The balance between troops and warjacks has shifted quite a bit in favour of the former. Feels different from tabletop.
* No Man's Land single-player campaign leaves out two of the factions almost completely (3 if you count Mercs).
* Limited unit selection in early matches means not as much replay value for single player campaign.
* The user interface has been improving, but it takes up a lot of screen, and isn't the prettiest.
* Some of my favourite units aren't out yet, and I know I'll have to pay for them as DLC someday.
* Controls and camera are better than ever, but still take getting used to.
* There isn't a large enough player base to guarantee fast MP matchmaking yet.
Major CONS:
- Core game features are not yet implemented
(no Hotseat, no Asynchronous MP, no painter, and only stupid-easy Skirmish difficulty)
- Single-player campaign has bad AI, and compensates with waves of suicidal dummies.
- Certain graphics configurations caused the game to crash frequently. I'm good now, but it was unplayable at times.
I recommend this game more than I ever could have before, especially to people who tried an early build and gave up because of the bugs and lack of polish. It is very playable, very fun, and worth coming back to.  For new players, I would recommend it if you are a fan of the Warmachine universe, or if you like skirmish tactics games. Just be aware that there's a long road ahead for continuing development.

Only played the demo, mind you, but I found the game to be enjoyable and playable, but not without it's faults.
Been a while since I've played the table top version, but from everything I see, it seems to stay very true to the source material, and I feel that it captures the feel of the game well. The Warmachines feel satisfactorially weighty, and there is some satisfying moments when they smash infantry units into the next postal code.
There are some problems, however, at least in the demo.  The biggest fault is the interface, which is a trainwreck. I had trouble controlling the camera, and sometimes even knowing what I was doing. Occasionally I would know what I was trying to do, but I couldn't seem to get it to function quite the way I expected, or I wouldn't be able to perform an attack with no clear indicator as to why not. Again, this is just my experience with the demo, which may not reflect on the full game.
Another example of interface hijinx, is the camera positioning itself behind buildings when playing on urban levels. This happened mostly with the "action" shots of my figures doing things, so it was nothing I needed to see, but it was irritating.  Poor, shy camera.
The AI also is nothing to write home about. They seem mostly interested in getting as close as possible, and don't often surprise you.
If you enjoy Warmachines on the tabletop, I feel like this is worth a look. I don't feel like this game will knock anyone's socks off (again, based on my experience with the demo), but it is enjoyable to play, and the story seems interesting if not necessarily rivoting.
Overall, I recommend this game, although I feel like the price is a little high, and will probably wait for it to go on sale before I purcahse it myself.
As a final note, I really had no luck using a controller in any meaningful way. I know it says "partial controller support" but and it's true that it recognized and responded to the controller, but since it is not playable with one, it kinda defeats the point.

-Exploration is fun, with a ton of events to discover, all with varying effects on your empire, the planets you inhabit and even the universe itself.
-Tons of content and ways to play the game.
-Great soundtrack.
-No two games are the same
-Early / mid game is amazing and dynamic.
-The large scale of the game means that you won't be steamrolling from the very moment your empire even spawns
Cons:
-Combat needs to be reworked, as the current meta revolves around stacking the most basic unit to overwhelm other fleets with sheer numbers.
-This being the first paradox game that I actually bought DLC for, I find the biggest DLC (Utopia) somewhat lacking.
-Rather buggy at the moment (Running out of food doesn't actually do anything at this point, certain event chains can't be finished, ethic attraction doesn't do anything etc)
-Late game can be a bit of a drag (However, this game IS more of a sandbox than an actual conquer-the-universe type of game)
Despite these flaws, I've had a ton of fun with this game and I'll continue having a lot of fun with it.
Definitely worth a purchase.

After almost 100 hours spent in XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within i was desperate for another squad oriented - turnbased strategy game, and suddenly there was WARMACHINE: Tactics.
Within the first two missions, fatal problems with the game become rather obvious, making it a real act of patiens to play the game.
The game just suddenly freezes sometimes, it seems like some animations or certain hit-FX are just badly coded and making your PC randomly freeze on certain actions. Which is odd because the game runs perfectly fine else. The motion blur is sickening, but can be disabled.
The camera is a absolute mess, on 50% of the actions it clips through walls or buildings, and it randomly jumps between your previous location and the current action of your enemy. Instead the camera should stay on the enemy, if its the enemies turn.
Hotkeys for ability seleciton and general UI seem unfinished. As an example: sometimes you can boost the attack (aka chance to hit) or the power (dmg) of a selected skill, sometimes boosting attack does both, but the UI shows a total useless "power" button too, instead of having a third kind of button "attack + power".
Unit selection progress is a mess, and the game doenst communicate basic rulesets to you, for example choosing combined range attacks on normal soldiers will only allow you to move and attack with normal soldiers, until the attack is finally executed. Another example would be out of turn actions. In general you are never sure in which "phase" of a turn you are in, or which units actually still have moves/actions left to perform, and why.
Another problem, in direct comparision to XCOM:EW, you cant move units while others are still in their movement, even worse, the game forces you to watch a action cam of every unimportant action you take with any unit (third person camera follows basic foot soldier on a simple move command). A game like this should only highlight important actions or at least give you a option for it in the menu, thats pretty much standard. Instead it unnecessarily makes the game slow, and you are often just waiting for your own units to peform ,rather then thinking about what to do.
Its a shame that there is so much negative to say about the game as the basic idea is actually pretty good. You can only use your mechs when your hero is in range of them, making it vital where you position your character. Normal food soldiers are uterly useless if not used in the correct way. Further you have to think ahead and decide if you want to do more with your hero or your mechs, as you have to divide focus points between all of them at the beginning of your turn, which are a vital resource for power attacks, spells and boosting chance or damage of your attacks for either of the units.
So my final verdict of the game is the following, it has a really good base concept under the hood, but the lackluster UI, the very limited camera, and the forced action cam, as well as unclear mechanics make it to much of a hassle. The game simply feels unpolished and unloved on everything it does. I'ld love to, but i cant recommend it.
'nuff said.

Cons( These are the reasons why I eventually stopped playing)

-Gearing for harder content is difficult as you need to do hard content for the gear and groups just disband if you underperform
-Found the guild system to be stale as it doesn't promote any teamwork except for buffs that need a different currency to buy

-Story progression at max is impossible unless you're insanely geared or have a group doing it(good luck)

-There are still issues I see that haven't been fixed.

Pro's
- good graphics

(with some shooter elments ), a bullethell like experience, a 2d platformer and some other elements (i dont want
to spoil for you)
- you have a great choice of "plugin chips" that act as a skilltree or something like that... you have a set capacity,
with each ship taking up a set amount of space, the better the chip, the more space it takes
there are different kinds of chips, defense, attack, support, main and hacking (wich comes later into the game)

toped my favoriet game i had for 10 years (since my early days of gaming)
now to the con's, or more the con, cause i only see one bad thing
- this game as a problem with the developers fixing one bug thats is here since this game released, this game has
a resolution problem that CAN reduce your game experience (but there is a good mod named "FAR" that fixes

So this game is easily one of the best indie games I've played in a LONG time. I bought it way back when it was in early access, not knowing anything about it and was really surprised. It took everything that is good about crafting games (using tools and weapons to get better tools and weapons without the mindless grinding for materials and base building) and combined it with the best parts of a rogue-like (fast paced gameplay with high-risk-high-reward elements). I easily have put 25-30ish hours into this game single player.
The multiplayer is where the game is at its best. Because there are so many classes, races, accessories, etc., the game has some great depth and allows multiple players to combine different and unique characters to create an unstoppable team. The combinations are seemingly endless and creates one of the most unique multiplayer experiences I have played in a long time.
I 100% recommend this game. It isn't just an indie game that you buy and play for a few hours. It's a game that I feel really stands up to the competition that is modern indie games. There aren't that many games out there that provide both a single and multiplayer experience like this one does, and both are musts to get the absolute best experience from the game. Plus, you just can't beat that price for how much game there is.

This game has many excellent qualities, such as the charming and immediately-approachable art direction.  However, I cannot recommend this game due to its solid yet shallow gameplay that fails to cohere with the superb presentation.
The core mechanic can be described as combining items to create a new item.  Good games are often based around simple mechanics.  But in the case of Road Not Taken, this simple mechanic does not combine with other mechanics in interesting ways.  Sure, there's a creature that knocks other items around, ice that switch places with another item, etc., but such additional rules do not combine with the core mechanic to create a new space or domain.  In other words, the item-combination is vast, but the rule-combination is shallow.
This problem could be avoided, I think, with better interface.  I am a fan of some wide-but-shallow games, e.g. Dota 2, that presents that user with contextually needed information such that the wideness of the game world isn't an incumberance for the player.  Something as simple as, let's say, filtering out the alchemy list based on the items available on the current screen would have made this vastness a lot more approachable.
The art, as charming as it is, could have been tailored to fence-in the player from getting lost in the vastness of the game as well.  For instance, angry animals seem to attack the players seemingly randomly, as there is not visual indication of which direction they will attack (or maybe i'm should be more observant?).
On the plus side, this game touches on many themes that most games do not explore and evokes grief, sense of loss, and the sort of sad beauty that is hard to evoke in any medium.  For that, the developers should be lauded.  However, in the final analysis, I cannot recommend this game as a game, though I would recommend a short playthrough (at a friend's house? or if it's on sale?) as an experience.

The gameplay videos don't do the game justice. What is Chronicon? It's a top-down action RPG which borrows from many other popular games in the genre (primarily Diablo II & III), while offering a very laid-back experience which you can enjoy at your own pace.
The game currently offers 4 classes, and 5 difficulty settings. The primary archetypes are covered, don't worry.
The difficulty settings aren't just for fluff, they increase drop-rate bonuses at the risk of harder enemies as well as reduced player resistances. As an added perk, the best gear can only be obtained from the highest difficulty setting. (Also, the best items cannot be gambled)
While the game does borrow from others in its genre, it manages to bring those elements into a very playable and addictive package.
So, you might be asking yourself, SELF! I've already played the 'greats' of the genre, is this game still worth it?
Yes, absolutely. The game is a steal at its price.
In conclusion, the title builds upon a very solid foundation of Quality-of-Life elements aRPG fans expect, while adding in some new surprises as well.
I'd highly recommend this to anyone, fans of the genre or not.

With patience and a few well searched how to video's, I believe you will enjoy the slower paced version of this wonderfully simple and yet extremely complex work of art. I most certainly do and look forward to what more they will add into it... Hedges? Bridge ramps? A way to edit storgae capacities a bit easier? (hint, hint, nudge, nudge)

A true sandbox experience, with nothing to stop the player from creating whatever they choose. It can be sometimes annoying to learn the ins and outs if you are playing solo or with a few newbie friends since you cannot just ask your question into chat, so be prepared for possible growing pains early in the learning curve. The Steam forums will provide the answers you need if you become confused about how to proceed or what to do. If you enjoy building / crafting games in general, this is likely to be a good title for you. It seems well-optimized and does not require a top of the line computer to max out the graphics settings, allowing you to play in a visually satisfying world.
The game ships with 2 separate modes, creative and adventure. Creative is a blank canvas of a world, and Adventure has a storyline with Kingdoms and NPCs established around you. You can create your own server and password protect it so that only your invited friends can play with you, or you can join another player's server if you prefer. You have full control over the settings that determine the percentage of aggresive creatures in your world, or the timer for how long your crops take to mature, as well as GM abilities to modify or create objects.
Unlike the online version with its monthly fee, it is a good title for those who have demanding schedules or varied interests, since you own the product and can return to it at will. It is said that the further development of the game will follow the development of the online version, so that updates and patches will become available.
Building / crafting games are, by their very definition, a lot of work to make all the creations that you want. If you understand that at the start, then this is a rewarding title with much satisfaction to be gained from it.

This game has a number of obvious issues, the most damning is the horrible camera which every other review has already covered.  The gameplay itself is mediocre; activating units is clunky and the selection of units is unintuitive even after the (poor) tutorial at the beginning.  After 5 missions, I finally realized I could just click on a portrait to activate a unit.
The objectives aren't always clearly defined as far as exactly what you need to do to complete them.  The worst part of the missions is that the camera will instantly cut to an objective and then instantly back to a unit, leaving you no idea where the objective was on the map.  Panning the camera there and back would be a huge improvement to give a sense of direction.
A few of the levels have impossible terrain to see what the hell is going on as far as the lines drawn on the ground for movement/spells/etc because the light blue or yellow lines aren't visible whatsoever upon the white snowcovered ground.  Also, it's hard to tell where the mission is trying to have you escape to at times because there's nothing differentiating the escape point from any other hard edge of the map.  Beacons would go a long ways in a few of the maps.
It's also super frustrating when you go 98% through an hour long mission just to have one of the characters die at the end to cause mission failure and require you to play through the whole thing again (and again, and again, and again) because they don't allow saves in the middle of missions.  It makes gameplay feel like a torturuous chore and that they're punishing you for trying.
If you're a fan of the tabletop game (like myself) and you want to know the fluff behind Jakes then you have to suffer through this game.  I've heard it's making strides in the right directions and I honestly think there's potential here but it's not polished enough yet to recommend and unless you love the backstory of the Iron Kingdoms I would wait for this game to get another 6-8 months of patches and fixes in before you play it because it's going to leave a bad taste in your mouth.

Oh, I SO want to like this game. The characters are fine, the setting awesome, but there are just Too many noob mistakes and game breaking bugs to recommend it to anyone but the most avid fan of the Warmachine miniatures game.
Much of the time it feels like you're trying to force the game to behave more than thinking tactically. This is due to a series of major annoyances:
- The 3d engine cannot seem to understand which square you're pointing at, making you constantly 'misclick' and have your troops move to a wrong square, which can cost you the game if someone you need buys it to a free strike
- Free strikes, while we're on it, do not seem to follow the same rules for the player and the ai.
- When moving, the trooper will often turn to a random facing after finishing the move, which looks hilarious at first - the tropper dashes over barrels and walls, then turns around as if pleased with his little hurdles run, but is soon annoying as hell when you have to spend time turning all your troopers back to face the enemy after moving.
- The game rules are explained only in a rudimentory sense, making it near impossible for a person who hasn't played the miniatures game to understand, and is then changed in arbitrary ways. Since when does a Bastion have a charge move longer than the range of a Trencher's rifle? Why no hit locations, systems to disable on jacks? And infantry have Lots of boxes, while jacks have not been significantly boosted.
- Line of sight does not take object height into account; a jack cannot shoot over the heads of infantry. And it seems that if any los possible crosses a square with a friendly trooper, there's no los.
- Scenarios feel forced; there seems to be little to no room to actually Play here; you pretty much have to solve the problem the developers want you to, or fail, to the point where overwhelming forces are put in to push you as fast as possible this way or that. And not reading the mind of the developers correctly the very first time Will cost you the fight.
- No save. Which makes the next problem even worse:
- The games take a Long time; a fight often takes over an hour even if you fail pretty fast, and I've yet to play one that could be completed in under 1½. This is Way Too Much Time, and feels very unnecesary.
All in all, I am sorely disappointed. There is still hope, but this one needs Major fixes.
