I used to love this game, but the last big patch has ruined it.
1. For starters, the default game settings are now set to "Miserable Experience". You won't be able to create an empire due to how scattered it makes all the habitable planets in the galaxy. But while your tiny, far flung scrappy little population will be slap-fighting other empires with similar problems, the end-game crisises have no such issues. So expect to lose the game when they show up. So, new players beware! Set inhabitable worlds to 4x at least for a real game.
2. Fallen Empires. Beyond end-game powerful, these menances can and will suddenly decide to ruin your empire. You can just bumble into them on accident and start a war with an enemy 1000x your strength. Sure they may not take much of your empire, but that won't matter because you are weakened and all the other sharks in the pond will come after you. You're basically crippled for the rest of the doomed game. Even if you don't have this happen, you'll have to tip toe around the pushy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s all game. It sucks.
Should an empire awaken, well, prepare for the most unfair fight to lose your game ever. You can control the galaxy and one of these things will still wreck everything you have. Were you winning? SORRY, Stellaris decides that YOU LOSE.
3. New players are screwed without knowing how to control the difficulty of starting games. No matter how much they try to make this game about the story of your empire. It's still a 4x. Grow faster and stronger than everyone around you OR ELSE. This is made unfairly hard by the sheer number of random things that can utterly blindside you and make you lose the game. If you're starting out, make sure to turn off Advanced AI starts and fallen empires.
To put the cruel, no warnings nature of the current Stellaris into perspective. I've played since launch and beaten it many many times (Fallen Empire and Crisises included) before the big patch that ruined everything. I lost the first 5 campaigns I started post-patch due to things that were completely outside of my control. It's HARD. But that's not bad. What's bad is that it's UNFAIR. You can't see the middle finger coming most of the time and when you do it's way too late. Time to reset.
(For example: Settling on a new world, only to surprise discover a nearby alien empire. Only to have them declare war on me b/c I settled to close to them. No chance to avoid the war at all. New colony gets burned to ash before my fleet can arrive. Oh, and this is at the very beginning of the game. Fleet gets pwned, neighbor empire senses weakness and also declares war. Game over. This sounds ludicrously unlucky, but its par for the course in my experience.)
So yeah, I can't recommend this game anymore. It's not friendly to new players at all. You will have to read a lot of guides and sink a lot of hours in just to successfully get out of the beginning. Even then, if you don't like losing 20 hour campaigns to unfair, unavoidable, unfightable bull, then you'll need to be a very elaborate save-scummer.

Stellaris is Paradox through and through. It's somewhat comparable to Crusader Kings in terms of how it feels and plays while still being a unique game on its own. It looks good, gives you the possibility to either control much of your empire on your own or automate most of it and concentrate on other things like ship building. Here you research a ship hull and then fill it with subsystems. You don't get to choose what it looks like but you can define what role it will have in your fleet.
Because of the great modding community (I especially enjoy the Star Trek Mod called New Horizons) I can recommend Stellaris without a doubt. However, two things need to be said so that you know what you get here:
- The bigger your empire gets the more you HAVE to automate. You will need to create sectors which are governed by your AI and add planets to them since you as the leader can only govern a limited amount of planets. This number differs between species and leaders but it will become a factor pretty soon. You never loose all control as you can set a development focus for sectors and supply them with ressources but some of the hardcore hunters for efficiency might find it disturbing to give so much control over your empire to the AI
- The game has a huge focus on diplomacy. War is expensive and while being a valid option to solve disputes, it also has a serious limit: The Warscore. At the beginning of a war you choose what you want to achieve with this war. War goals are limited by species with the more peaceful ones never being able to add the more brutal goals like destroying a species' presence on a planet. The real deal, however, is that every goal costs points and one can only add up to 100 points. If you go for the most useless and undereveloped planets, you can maybe add up to six of them. If the war is won only these six will go to your empire. Even if you crushed the enemy and invaded every planet he had, you will only get the six you added to your war goals while the other ones will remain in your enemies hands. Once peace is made you are restricted from declaring war for the next 10 ingame years. People who want to take the galaxy by force will find their game seriously limited by the Warscore and war goals.
Still, if these two points don't bother you then Stellaris is surely worth a try.

I do not know what to say other than what has already been said. This game is astounding and, hopefully, when you buy the game you will go into this purchase as one of the most fruitful investment towards your entertainment. I say that because exploring, advancing, and learning is the holy grail of this game. The creators did not create this game for you to spend your money and then end, rather, to continually be delighted within your discoveries in each new game you create. As you collect the DLC's this game only gets better. If you purchase this game and you keep an open mind, understanding that there will be countless of possibilities, than you will be satisfied. :) Hard for me to usually say as many material goods do not "satify" me.
In the beginning, I almost asked for a refund, because it was complicated, but hey! After you understand what is going on, this game is awesome!

Preface: I bought this along with all (7 in total) DLC currently available, including the "Utopia" expansion, as of this writing. I am writing this review with all current DLC and the "Utopia" expansion in mind, as a "complete" game. I MAY edit this when additional DLC arrives.
PROS: This game appears to have taken influence from a little bit of everything, such as Stronghold, Age of Empires, Total War, Mass Effect, Star Wars, Star Trek and even a bit of Farscape. The music is top notch and the in-game music player is a GREAT idea. Resource and Technology managment is well put together. UI scaling is a useful setting many RTS games fail to implement and it is much needed, not just in this game but 100% of all RTS games. The game looks fantastic graphically, and the mechanics are also pretty well implemented. The idea of running a government, picking your ethics and such is absolutely brilliant as a mechanic, love it. The needed and much advised tutorial (more on that later) is well done and utilized in such a way that it feels less like a tutorial and more like just part of galatic life. Just all the options in this game really adds to replayability and the overall feel, the game just feels beefy and huge, as it should. All the different species are always interesting (though funny at times) and really seem to differ with little repetition. This game, if you are a fan of RTS, is quite immersive and my first playthrough was 10 hours straight before ultimately failing miserably. I found myself addicted to this game on several occasions.
CONS: Of course, everything has its faults and this game is no exception. It has a hefty learning curve, took about 2-3 hours just to get comfortable with all the mechanics and UI features, even with the tutorial. I found that, either I am slow (quite possible) with advancement, or all the other empires seem to grow and advance quite too quickly. I have played 3 playthroughs (on my 4th) and two of those resulted in a loss with no clear reasoning as to why and was NOT invaded. The tutorial actually saying "pops" in place of saying "Population" is a personal pet-peeve of mine, it feels lazy and not empire-like. Indoctrination of lesser races seems to take way too long for such an awesome game mechanic.
Conclusion: This game may have been better served as an "Early Access" release because aspects of it DO seem to lead to the conclusion that it is unfinished, even with all the current DLC. This is not to suggest that the game is unplayable or not woth buying, it still remains a fun game to play. Given that this game is from the developers of "Crusader Kings 2," expect lots of DLC in the future, after which this game may feel more complete.
RATING: 7/10

I want to like this game, and I did get some enjoyment out of it, but it has some very serious problems that never get properly addressed. I think the devs are trying, but something is getting lost in translation somewhere in the process. I can see a great idea here, but the execution falls *just* short.
After 450 hours I have yet to actually beat the game, not because it's that long, but because every single playthrough I attempted hit some fun-ending bug/issue that caused me to quit it. A couple of my longer attempts managed to end *mostly* because I was bored and finishing the job was a mere formality.
A few issues that caused me to abandon playthroughs:
* Achievements broken and will not unlock, and won't unlock after path either (have to start over). This happened on two separate major updates.
* An fallen empire that I had never met declared war on me out of the blue from across the galaxy over colonizing a tomb world, which had no markers that they considered it special (which is a thing that can happen, this planet simply lacked the markers). This was during two other simultaneous wars and I got crushed as a result.
* FINALLY got the broken and buggy precursor civilization event chain to work, only to hit the "achievements are broken lel" issue, so I rage-quit.
* My empire was being hit hard by others half my size. I examine my planets to find that the sector AI has not been developing them at all. Literally 70% of my population was essentially unemployed. And I can override them without influence, which is the hardest resource to get in the game, so I was basically just stuck either restarting or slogging, so I quit.
* The sector AI has actually caused me to quit on at least 3 games. Each major patch they claim to have fixed it, only to have it hit other fundamental issues.
* Spawned inside the borders of a civilization with end-game tech that proceeded to declare war on me with the goal being to purge that colony entirely. My only colony. They succeeded. (Admittedly, this is largely just bad luck.)
* I wanted to expand militarily, but literally everyone around me was in a defensive pact, which by the game's rules should drain their influence to 0 and bankrupt their entire culture. But it doesn't. So instead I was simply stuck 'cause I couldn't fight the entire galaxy at once.
* I wanted to expand militarily, but when I declared war I found out that my only weak neighbor was in a defensive pact with someone on the other side of the galaxy. Who I could beat.. but not reach. I occupied every planet from the weak neighbor but couldn't reach the other guy and was forced to earn "warscore" from killing the fleets that found their way to my area more than 20 years later. An entire game is decided within about 200 and is in "end-game" mode in 100. I can occupy their planets unchallenged for 20 years and not be allowed to simply call them mine.
* I wanted to expand militarily, but I was only allowed to take like 2 systems from the opponent every 10 years.. on a map with 1500 systems. And due to defensive pacts, that locked me out of taking from anyone else nearby either. (This one has been fixed, thankfully).
* I wanted to play a non-military game- just kidding, those don't exist here.
Aside from that, the mechanics are simple despite themselves. They try to be complex and interesting, but it all comes down to one thing: Economy. Develop economy so you can field a large fleet of ships so you can crush your enemies. It's a game that wants to be an RP-focused endeavor but ends up an RTS in space.

has loads of charm. Its characters with their childlike proportions, animations showing exaggerated emotions from tears to joy, and even its core mission of returning lost children to their parents all achieve a heartwarming feel. The gameplay is tricky without being rage-inducing, and procedurally generated such that the solutions to the obstacles it throws your way never become rote.
The game also does an examplary job on the diversity front. Most characters (the protagonist and about two-thirds of the townsfolk) have their appearances randomized from one game to the next, most noticeably in skin tones that range through much of the human spectrum. You choose the main character's gender through a subtle dialogue choice, or can choose not to reveal it at all; whatever you pick, you're free to romance any of the six eligible objects of affection. It's successful and understated, a perfect example for what baseline assumptions of such things
be--in stark contrast to the usual default of "straight dude protag woos straight lady NPC in a fantasy world full of white people."
Some past reviews complain about the game's difficulty. I suspect those reviewers played before the recent rebalancing that made a big chunk of the difficulty opt-in. If you stick to the "normal" difficulty path and hold on to a paltry bit of resources to spend on checkpoints, reaching the end of a full playthrough (called a "career," fifteen levels' worth) will only take you a few hours. If you don't have a head for turn-based maneuvering puzzles (think Sokoban, Adventures of Lolo, any Roguelike, etc.) at all, then I could definitely understand steering clear, but for the average gamer difficulty is not a concern.
My only complaint about
comes on the technical level: for some reason, this very unassuming game grinds along like it's a boundary-pushing video resource hog. Expect to stare at the initial loading bar for half a minute or so each time you play, and stutter for a couple of seconds on scene transitions. Perhaps installing to an SSD might help.
Highly recommended for anyone who appreciates the occasional break from washed-out grimdarkness and ultraviolence!

Do you love Diablo 2, Path of Exile, Grim Dawn, or Torchlight? If the answer is yes then you've struck pixelated gold.  Chronicon was certainly inspired by some of these titles, most definitely Diablo 2.  Considering it's in early access right now, it really does not get much more polished than this. I have encountered perhaps one or two minor bugs.  The developer frequently communicates with players on the forums, listens to feedback and is incredibly receptive to it good and bad, no matter how critical.  He responds to you, questions your feedback and whether it would be included in the game, and works on reported bugs almost immediately.  You don't see this kind of interaction and dedication often anymore.  This guy is passionate about making his game into something spectacular.  This alone is a reason to buy the game; it feels good to support dedicated and hard working developers.
Back to the point though,  I've put in about 30 hours of play time and I've only made 1 character.  In fact, it took me about this much time to reach 100, the max level at the moment.  There are 3 other classes to experiment with, so the replayability is there in that regard.
However, Chronicon suffers from a few issues that did not take long to realize.  The only big one seriously worth mentioning that may or may not ruin the experience for some  is the loot.  The worst part about the loot is that it becomes VERY redundant VERY quickly.  What does this mean? Well, you can come across the exact same unique type item 5 or more times in a two hour session.   You will hear a loud THUD in game notifying you that a unique or legendary item has dropped, then when you pick it up and find out it's basically the same thing from before... it's kind of disappointing and makes looking or grinding for loot meaningless and just not something you look forward to at all.
When you do happen to find a moderately good item it will be MARGINALLY better than your currently equipped one, even if your old item is 20-30 levels lower than your new item, the new item will hardly be an upgrade.  To make the new item worth equipping you will need to enchant it, modify the kind of sockets it has, reroll the attributes, and essentially fine tune the item at a vendor to your exact liking... this is a great feature but it's time consuming and feels like a cheap attempt at simply avoiding designing BETTER gear.  Also, there is no way to take gems out of equipment.  You can only destroy the gems and keep the item.  Why? This seems so backwards to me.  The polished variety of gems (the third tier and best gems you can acquire) must be crafted using lower tier gems and can be really costly/time consuming, because you have to farm for lower tier gems  before you can upgrade them.
I don't mean to sound overly critical here at all but this glaring issue with loot is noticeable fairly early on and gets progressively worse the closer you are to max level.  You would think different and considerably better loot is obtainable the higher level you are but in the grand scheme of things, it feels like the opposite.
One more small issue I have is the minimap.  You can shift between different sizes and where the minimap is placed in game.  The problem is when you want it to take up most of your screen, it is difficult to see particularly in certain environments while you're playing.  It could use a little enhancement I suppose because I've had to really focus on the minimap at points just to figure out where I'm going.  I realize it's not meant to be very bold or anything because it would get in the way of the game, however, there should be a balance between not being a distraction and visibility.
Despite some of its flaws, which I'm sure will be worked on prior to official launch day, Chronicon is a lot of fun and can scratch that itch you've been feeling for a solid hack n slash experience. It's definitely a good time, easy to learn, has 5 difficulties and isn't complex or intricate like Path of Exile which to some may be a plus or a negative depending on what you're after.  Ultimately It's worth the asking price in my opinion.

A cute puzzle game. It's hard to describe.
Your goal: To save all the lost children in the woods and reunite them with their parents.
Your energy free controls are to move up/downleft/right, to pick up everything around you in the four directions, and to throw them all at once. If you move while holding something it will take precious energy. You can match several of similar items, or different items, depending on "secrets" (crafting recipe?) that you learn through play or from villagers. Like throwing the axe at a tree makes a log, and throwing two logs next to each-other makes a campfire which reduces the cost of carrying things on that screen, or putting three beehives together makes a jar of honey which gives you a little bit of energy.
Sounds simple, but while the controls are simple, the puzzle nature of trying to get to the kids, get them to their parents (or vice versa), get the kids to the starting area, or open pathways to another part of the forest can be complex. Sometimes it's downright frustrating but not in a bad game design way, just a yell obsceneties at the angry racoons who claw you if get next to them, or ninja bears who might block your path randomly way.
Don't let the art style fool you, this game starts off fairly easy, but difficulty can spike. You won't always save all the kids, but that's okay. You can quit trying to help them at any time, but saving half or more of the kids is the minimum to make the mayor okay with your work. (Edit: Apparently failing to save half the kids 2x in a row kills you causing the revive mechanics to fire where you lose some of your items.)
There's an aspect of the game of getting to know the villagers that essentially breaks down to giving them the right gifts to raise your friendship bar. I got married to one just before the end of my first game! I'll definitely be playing at least one more full game of this title because the levels are somewhat randomly generated so it has replayability.
One full game took me between 5-6 hours.

a somewhat fun little arpg if you like to feel overpowered as you plough through fairly shallow content. it is proably only really worth it if you catch it on sale and need to scratch that arpg itch but have already beaten everything else.
pros:
- responsive input, no lag, well-optimized. feels very "snappy"
- fast paced once you've got some +movement speed and a mobility skill
- tons of useful user interface options
- cute sprite pixel art
- funny boss voice lines and characterful npc dialogues
- wide variety of skills, effects and elemental damage types
- multiple difficulty options
- very few, very minor bugs
huge detailed list of cons/flaws:
- there is almost zero story / plot / lore / worldbuilding / character development
- suffers from extreme screen clutter. you can often barely see what's happening amidst all of the spell effects
- the mechanic of slowing your character's movement speed by half when walking over obstacles (pots, foliage etc, which ther are thousands of, everywhere, always) is completely unnecessary and irritating
- the map is very hard to read, especially in dark or grey areas, which there are a lot of. it can't be scrolled, it has no background opacity option, the player icon is brown on brown/grey, and it can't be zoomed out or scaled down below 100%. you also have to press tab four times to toggle it
- lots of enemy types that manage to be irritating without being difficult, especially for shorter range builds (enemies that burrow, become invisible, leap around rapidly)
- lending to that, there are not enough "pull" skills to draw mobs in (barbarian only i think)
- mysterious crystal chest puzzles are repetitive
- killstreaks are fun to try for but are often interrupted in dumb ways, eg by packs of mobs that slowly emerge from the ground and can't be attacked until after a lengthy animation
- powerful unique and legendary gear is honestly just far too common, with 0% magic find
- even a fully expanded inventory is still too limited in size for the amount of loot that drops
- game seems too easy on the second-highest difficulty setting, but too difficult on the highest
- incoming damage feels very spiky; it's either so negligible as to be pointless, or you die instantly without being able to react. no in between. tanky builds are not viable
- shrines are common and very strong in a game where you are already overpowered. but one in ten shrines instant-kills you for no reason?
- the semi-common "elixir of flames" consumable gives a 3800% damage burn, which allows you to kill all bosses in like 4 seconds. what's the point?
- if there are any cool secret areas, they are a little too well-hidden, because i never found any
- no character appearance options and gear isn't represented visually
- bosses all have boring vanilla mechanics until the 4th act. they just stand or slowly move around and cast aoe spells
- every effective build type with every character feels very same-ish. you spam one single powerful aoe ability that you pump up with tons of passives.
- gemming and enchanting offer too little of a return on investment to be worthwhile pre-endgame, especially with how frequently you are replacing your gear
- lots of pointless/useless resources, stats and bonuses like mana, rage, souls, thorns, light radius, orbitals, minions, health and mana globe pickups. things that are there but aren't worth investing in or just kind of get managed automatically without changing how you play or equip yourself in any meaningful way
- lots of the sound effects are pretty grating
- tilesets become repetitive. there are tons of caves that all look the same. every "mysterious portal" map uses the same tileset.
- some story maps are unnecessarily huge
- high-tier class armor sets provide no interesting bonuses or skill modifications. just % increase to damage type, % increase to passive proc chance
- the tooltip descriptions for certain stats and effects is obscure and unclear
4/10

If I had to pick my second favorite Total War game it would probably be this one.
You play as ruler of a nation during the feudal era of Europe and parts of Western and Central Asia. As this ruler it is your job to spread the dominance of your culture and religion across the old world while trading, bartering, negotiating, and fighting with other nations who are more than likely just going to be more heads on the pikes at the end of your campaign.
It is a time of great uncertainty. The powers of the world won't stop calling one another mean names and every now and then you have to send a priest out to deal with a heretic in what is essentially a bible fight.
Like Rome, Shogun, Medieval I, and the games after it, Medieval II is split between a campaign map and a battle map that changes depending on what location on the campaign map the battle takes place in.
You still have the usual things, you build your cities, do diplomacy, move your armies around on the map, command huge armies in battle, things like that. So lets talk about all the neat little things Medieval II adds to the formula.
One, there's an obvious graphical improvement. Medieval II looks miles better than Rome, and adds other improvements such as a change in unit models depending on their weapon and armor levels. If your peasant spearmen are equipped with chainmail then the chainmail will actually show on their models instead of it just being implied to be there.
Second, the addition of religion and mercantilism adds another level of roleplaying to your campaign as you attempt to convert peoples of other faith or do battle with other merchants for economic resources and business rights.
Third, new animations and battle damage are added to your armies. So sometimes you get to see a cool little animation where a soldier will beat up an an enemy and call him mean names. There's also blood, while not as gory as later Total War games, your units will get drenched in blood the longer they fight, indicating how long that individual  soldier has before biting it.
And fourth, the soundtrack is probably the best Total War soundtrack to date. My personal opinion, but my opinion is great.
There have been also a few events added to the campaign mode. Things such as the Mongol invasion, the black plague, discovering the new world, Crusades, Jihads, the Pope excommunicating you because you're too radical and he's tired of your skateboard phase. etc.
Wow, all these cool things! So what's wrong?
A few things.
First, the AI once again doesn't like to cooperate. They're ask for trade rights, map information, and an alliance one turn and then attack you the next. Broken armies of 50 or so people will gladly die to your thousands rather than end the war, and the Pope always seems to demand that you stop a war you're winning even though more than not you didn't start it. He's that kind of school principle.
When it comes to the mid 2000 Total War games I feel like it comes down to preference. Do you prefer antiquity to feudalism? Or do you like Knights over Legionarries and Hoplites? Either or you can't go wrong with Medieval II.
The additions to campaign mode are welcomed and there's plenty of meat there if you treat the Total War games more like a roleplaying game than a strategy game. I have about as much time on the physical copy of this one as I do in Rome: total War.
And if you want, you can still technically play as the Roman Empire in the form of the Byzantines. It's not really the same thing, but hey, they're there.
Also, the modding scene is friggin astounding. Everything from gameplay tweaks to full out new games.
Two that stand out to me are "Thera: Legacy of The Great Torment" and "Third Age: Total War", the latter being a Lord of the Rings total conversion of the Kingdoms expansion pack.
Medieval II: Total War gets a big number out of a big number.
Odontophobia is the fear of teeth.
The Curator:
10/10. My favorite total war game ever. Countless mods, limitless enjoyment, and plenty of gameplay, for just 10 dollars. Recommended to ALL strategy game fans.

The Binding of Isaac is a twin stick shooter roguelike. You play as Isaac, a little boy trying to escape his ridiculously religious mother that believes god wants her to kill her son. So he runs into the basement, going deeper and deeper, to escape her. You can move in eight directions and fire in four directions. You go through a series of square rooms similar in style to that of a Zelda dungeon from NES. You fight enemies in the rooms and get rewards for doing so. You might find keys for opening doors and chests. You might find bombs for blowing up rocks, walls, or enemies. You might find coins to spend in shops. And you might find shops, treasure rooms, or treasure chests filled with secondary items, powerups, or just some more health. There are a few unique rooms like challenge rooms where you get treasure for fighting some waves of enemies. Some rooms let you sacrifice a random amount of health for a power up. Some rooms even let you trade your total permanent hearts for powerups. These powerups are the main draw of the game, as they can change your stats and give you any number of strange powers or passives. It's tough and you're going to die, but death just means you get to start fresh and see what kind of new things await you in the randomly generated game. There are even a few characters to pick from and a series of challenges you can try out. PLUS a big batch of DLC in one great package to add even MORE things into the random mix of fun.
This game suffers from its randomness. It's certainly the appeal, but if you get dealt a bad hand of powerups then you just have to deal with it. Lots of skill can make up for it, but sometimes it feels very unfair because it's random. It's troublesome to go grab for a powerup only to have it actually power you DOWN instead. Also, the tears you shoot can be hard to aim because they have a bit of an arc to when they are in the air and when they land, which isn't the easiest thing to gauge in a top down 2D environment. Hitboxes can also be a bit hard to tell sometimes due to the rounded, somewhat squishy style of the characters. Also... while the game does direct you to the program suggested for making controller support, there's not controller support in the game itself. Why not just add in controller support in a later patch? That's a minor annoyance but... it's annoying.
The thing that makes this game so great is that you can play it over and over and over again and it's different every time. There's so much content here for the price of 5 bucks it's insane. It's an amazing buy for one of your first Steam games, especially on a budget because there's lots here. And the DLC is reasonable if you want even more content. The challenges and characters and item combinations all make for endless possibilities. Your run can take five minutes or two hours. There are multiple endings too so the replay value is through the roof. I can't recommend it enough. The Binding of Isaac gets an 8 out of 10. I hear Rebirth is good... maybe I'll be able to play it someday.

A gleefully stupid game, Loadout is the sort of game that kids would imagine a "mature" shooter to be. Crude and offensive but never overtly so, the game flows well in both combat and introducing gamemodes. It borrows a lot from Team Fortress 2, from art style to map design, but the game is different enough that it doesn't feel like a ripoff. It's also a Free to Play game with all the cash shop items being purely cosmetic and having no in-game value, other than it makes you a little bit easier to spot and shoot. The unlock system evokes memories of Blacklight: Retribution, without having a cyclical "rentind" system or taking forever to grind out. On the downside, the maximum player size of a game seems to be eight, with four on each side. All in all, I'd say this game is worth picking up to try if you're not easily offended and should be around for some time to come, as long as the developers continue to add to it.

More FPS than Simulation.
The ships drive like go-carts.  Part of the intensity of naval combat is waiting for your guns to come to bear.  Ships that steer quickly negate the delay in placing the guns on target.
The aiming system treats the gun accuracy as if this is an FPS.  Holding aim longer improves the accuracy.  This introduces a level of intensity in taking a shot.  However, this method does not hold up well as a simulation.
The ship spotting system is a novel approach.  Ship positioning becomes a tactic in determining enemy disposition.
I must admit.  I only played for just over half an hour.  However, the first mission felt like a shooter game with waves of enemy coming at me.
Overall, I prefer a simulation which is less FPS and more about planning and tactics.

As strategy games go, this game still needs a lot of work, in my opinion.  The control interface is clunky and unresponsive, it's too easy to give the wrong command to your units without any way to undo them, actually activating your units gets exponentially more tedious the more units you have under your control, the maps are difficult to read in terms of where you can and can't go, even the distances your units can move becomes impossible to determine on certain maps because of the color schemes, the minimap is almost unusable because of how little information it gives you and how difficult it is to navigate around, mission objectives are revealed to you either very obviously or way too obscurely (there is no middle ground), and for some reason shields seem to be more effective weapons than spears, swords, and guns.
All that said, it's a decent adaptation of the miniatures game, but unfortunately the mechanics slow the game down, rather than enhance it.  Smaller games are the most fun, which is really unfortunate given that they keep adding more and more options for you to use, with the end result I imagine being that one would be able to pit sizeable armies against one another. This game has some potential. I did not play it PvP or with others and I think if there's any real fun to be had with this game it would be with that.
The primary problem I had with this game is a lack of NPCs. It has as amazing crafting system, but to build a lot of things you have to be a jack of all trades mining, smithing, sewing, cooking, and so forth. For example, you can be a great wood worker, but that doesn't help you make metal arrow heads which are required to make arrows. There probably should have been some more primitive options like flint arrow heads or something.
Anyway, you would think you would go to a town and trade for the items you are not prepared to make yourself. But when I finally found my way to Hearth (a city in the game), There was only one NPC that would talk to me who was obviously there to guide new players on what to do (although by the time I found him I had been playing for an entire day already and knew how to do pretty much everything he taught). He eventually directed me to an NPC that did nothing but stand there who was, I suspect, probably the guy you are supposed to trade with. Basically, there was nothing in the city to interact with which largely made the city pointless.
And that really gets to the point of "Why are you crafting all this stuff?" I suppose there's something sort of "Mine Craft" about this game. But we've had an over abundance of "You're alone in the world - go build some stuff" games.
This is really the MMORPG handed over to you. You have to setup your own server to play alone.
But this also means that if you had a group of friends, you could maybe all play on your server and each could take on different roles as you work together to build a city and such. That might make up for the lack of NPCs.
Some people seem to like it for PvP, although I personally don't think a crafting game is ideal for PvP. I personally don't think you should have skills and levels for PvP as everyone should basically be on the same level and it should more rely on the player than how much grinding they've done. A level 20 is always going to beat a level 3, so what's the point? Get everyone on the same level and then it becomes about the players rather than their characters. But some people are enjoying it for PvP; so more power to them.
Overall, I felt it was mostly a waste of money. There was a lot to like about the crafting system and survival system, but overall I just didn't feel like it delivered.

*Update*

Due to my stubborness and the money I spent on this game, I have persisted in trying to open this game up to see if it got better with a little more understanding.  I have found it is in fact a very deep and amazing game along the lines of Minecraft (I say that loosely due to the fact that it is much more in depth than Minecraft).  As you can see, I have sunk 90+ hours into this game, 70 of which was with my wife who also bought the game to give it a try.  About 15 of those hours was dedicated to leveling a 12x13 patch of land between a bay and a small lake to build a castle and courtyard.  While I know it is a big job to build such an abode, we find that it is entirely too time consuming.  90% of the time you are waiting for action bars ~2-5 seconds each, but we are talking thousands of times.  To level the land we have scalped and gutted a hill behind where the castle sits for the dirt and stone with the intentions of leveling the hill itself when finished.  This hill is almost completely gutted now, and I have found absolutely no information either on forums, wurmpedia or youtube on how to actually demolish the carcass of it.  It wont let us mine the outer walls, so now we are left with the eyesore blocking our view to the bay.  With all that work and all those hours and all that material, we have only finished the shell of the first floor and half of the second.
Now, having said all that, this is my point.  I play video games a lot.  I almost eat, sleep and breath them.  It blows me away that it is such a large game that has been around for about ten years and it still has actions, items and other good to know things that either has no description or explanation that is plainly worded and easy to understand.  Or if there is it is so hard to find.  It took me several attempts to find an explanation on how to expose a rock face to make a tunnel I don't have to climb to (you have to dig all four corners of a tile until you hit rock).  Why was something so simple yet so necessary wrapped up in a 20 minute video on youtube instead of being the first thing stated on the ingame wiki?  Why is there no back button on the crafting guide menu?   I stand by my initial review.  This game is definitely for people who love Minecraft but want better asthetical creations and not only have the time to devote to the creation but also the patience.  Either that or many, many friends that will play as well to help with the man hours needed to complete projects.On the server list you'll see tons of servers, but most are empty and locked or they have 1 to 2 players on it.  That is the player base and it is remarkably small.
Update, Mar 2, 2016:
I admit, my initial opinion of this game was a little harsh.  190hrs+ in the game and I still have much I don't know in regards to certain aspects of the game, such as religion, magic, etc.  That being said  I have changed my mind about the monotony of the game, but it comes at a serious learning curve.  Navigation in the world sucks in my opinion.  It's easy as hell to get lost if you dare to explore, especially in dense forests.  It does have a remarkably indescript map and it leaves you wondering which hill you are standing on or which channel of the sea you are looking at since you don't have a character marker on the map.  As of the latest patch farms are now useless because crops timers aren't working so they will only grow with GM powers.  Here's hoping they hotfix it soon.    Aside from navigation and the complexity (including server management) the game is pretty good.  Incredibly in depth, and like I said before, minecraft for adults.

Good sandbox/rts/godgame/rpg/citybuilder.  It's pretty basic, you choose from a couple dozen maps to play out a skirmish with a few other factions (You can set handicaps and a surprising number of options with their potency.  In other words, if the AI is too easy, you can have them cheat.)  Then there's the survival, which allows you to set waves of enemies invading your village to a certain amount after a set time has past, or you could just set the waves to 0 for unlimited invasions whenever you want.  Just push the invasion button.
Pixel-customization is there, but low at the moment.  I really wish there was more options with regards to what you can do with your characters.  I hear it all can be modded easily by those who have the ability to create assets.
I should mention that you are in charge of one character (More if you choose companions from your roster of created characters.), and the villagers pretty much just hoard their own resources and pull from those themselves.  I'm not sure if their AI is set to take advantage of all the mechanics, the buy/sell mechanic from the market in particular and recruitment from the barracks.  The most I can say there is that I hope the developer will get to it, as this game is still in early access.
I love grindy games, and this is a very grindy game.  I believe you can grind to very high levels both character level and skill levels.  You cannot take the equipment you make from one match to another new one, which kinda made me whine but I could understand there needs to be at least some balancing between games.  You're basically starting from scratch every match, with the exception of your characters level/perk/skill levels.
You can set the starting age and ending age.  You can customize the AI of your companions and main character, and even automate them so they carry out the AI priorities.
It's great fun for pixel-junkies like me who like to create their own narratives in games.

I bought this game yesterday for the $7.00 sale and have 31 hours as of posting this. Certainly feel I've already gotten my moneys worth and really hope this game continues to grow in content and perhaps have a sequel one day.
PROS:
~Almost everything you do lvls up a skill; farming, woodcutting, everything... character creation gives you a bonus in certain things but even a dwarven tank with armor making occupation can master magic, farming, or w/e just depends on how much you use it.
~The sheer amount of skills is staggering.
~Building and crafting: there is so much!
~You can recruit an army, yes an army of NPCs you pay for by selling resources, just awesome haven't seen that in a game before.
~Graphics: It's defidently oldschool as am I, reminds me of suikoden.
~Customization: Below I explain cons, the AI customizations allow you to try and balance the fights better. From age progress speed to population amount you can customise alot.
~LAN multiplayer: Been playing with wife and we both enjoy the game together, not sure(but hope) we can be against each other but she likes the team play better anyway.
CONS:
~AI is dumb; ally and enemy AI alike will sometimes attack towers with no hope of destroying it and be killed in the process, if it's the ally you're forced to keep making resurrection totems to revive them so they'll do it again over and over or just let them stay dead.
~Ranged attacks way too OP for dumb AI; Ranged missiles(darts, arrows, etc.) move very slow, this allows you to literally dodge enemy missile attacks, but land your shots everytime becouse AI don't dodge. As for melee they're usually slower and you can kite them, run shoot run shoot until they flee or die.
~Difficult to make challenging: Me and my wife by ourselves(no npc allies) at 10% age increase speed against 4 opponents with 6 population each at 25% age increase speed, and +10% power offered no challenge. Basically 2 vs 24, they have increase dmg and unlock new tech way faster and we stomped them. Huge part of this is how easily a bunch of defence towers make enemies just melt as you go about working on w/e.
~Tutorial is too fast paced: You're basically thrust into missions that slowly progress through the ages, which allow you to build new things as you go. Sadly you have up to 5 minutes to prepare each lvl which is barely enough time to harvest some resources and make a little gear before the attack, let alone time to explore the new buildings, and things you can craft. Don't be too discouraged by this, the other game options such as skirmish will provide you ample time to learn all aspects of the game.
Conclusion:
I really enjoy this game and recommend it to anyone that likes crafting/building games ESPECIALLY if you have a friend you can play LAN with. I really hope the dev can make the AI more challenging becouse right now it's so easy to exploit there weakness which is inabiliy to dodge missiles while I can. Hope this helps you potential buyers.

This is a tower defense inspired game where you play as a single hero in a town of heroes. It's a bit like Majesty, except you also control a hero. The other heroes run around, build things, fight, etc. The AI is not very good, but it's way better than having to control everyone manually.
Buildings that craft things wear out...and rather quickly. So a big part of this game is actually upkeep. Your three stats (health, stamina and mana) all regenerate very slowly, so you need consumables to keep them up.
You need to gather some raw resources, process them into refined resources, and then combine them in some other building to make the final product. Meanwhile, waves of enemies attack you.
There are about 8 (?) technological levels that you progress through. During the campaign, it's after certain missions. But the campaign is a poorly written (many many many spelling and grammatical errors), kind of stupid, and for all intents and purposes it's just a tutorial to introduce you to the buildings/items step by step. Which is fine...you'll finish the campaign in an hour or two.
What is nice is that your hero levels up every time you play it...whether it's in a skirmish map or during the campaign. As you level up you gather faster, hit harder, etc. There isn't a level requirement for any equipment though and the levels, while helping, aren't overpowered. Probably minimum to maximum level is double to quadruple efficiency. It's nice but...takes a long time to get there.
The game is kind of fun to watch and play. You can set it up to be pretty easy, or very difficult depending on how many enemies you spawn and how many townspeople you start with. By adjusting those levels you could probably find a survival mode that suits you.
But it doesn't take long to 'see everything'. And although there are different types of weapons and spell classes and so on...everything is more or less the same.
The format of the game feels like it would do well with more creativity in weapon/enemy choice...the type of game is pretty cool. Unfortunately, it doesn't seem like it's going to get much better than this.
tl;dr: it's a cool sandbox survival game but the developers have made it pretty shallow. Play it for a weekend and then probably never play it again.

Best Resident Evil since RE4 in my opinion.
It manages to refine the system and mechanics of RE4 with out going all Bro-ops Dewrito mode that RE6 did. As long as you're playing on normal difficulty or higher, it's a pretty intense ride.
Set between Resident Evil 4 and 5, Revelations details Jill and Chris' early days in the BSAA, with the plot switching back and forth between locations, characters, and time. While nothing significant happens here that affects the series' cannon, it does a decent job of telling it's own self-contained chapter of the RE Universe.
Raid mode takes the place of Mercenaries this time around, and is best described as a Resident Evil/Borderlands hybrid. You run through levels from the main game (solo or in co-op) to earn new weapons, upgrades, and to level up your characters. Its a fun distraction to the main campaign, and if it hooks you, you'll sink a good 10+ hours into it.
There are a few downsides:
-While RE has always had a thing for bad dialog, this installment has some of the biggest cringers in the series.
-If you already own it on 3DS, there isn't really anything new (aside from improved visuals and an improved control layout) to make you come back for a second round.
Overall however, Revelations is a great direction for Resident Evil to go in. Even with the flaws, none of them are dealbreakers, and if you liked Resident Evil 4 or 5, you really should give this a try.

While RE6 was a guilty pleasure, I can safely say this is a genuinely good Resident Evil game. There are a number of artifacts that remind you of this being a handheld port -- the episodic format mainly, but poor textures as well -- but this a step back towards RE4; less action, more survival horror.  Well, maybe not horror.  Nothing in this is scary, per se.  The weapon customization is excellent, and this game's arcade/mercenaries mode (called raid mode) is suprisingly good, being what I can only describe as a mini-campaign.  Raid mode is multiplayer if you want, the campaign is single player with an AI partner you'll barely notice because he does nothing and I'm pretty sure can't die at all.  The story is awful, but that's Resident Evil for you.  If you can get it on sale and liked RE4, you literally can't go wrong with this.

This is probably the "best" Resident Evil (on the PC at least) so far. It takes all the strenghtes in atmosphere and storytelling of the first three entries and combines it with a control scheme that acutally makes sense. This game is a great throwback to the original RE 1. Despite the many differences and improvements, it still has countless stylistic references to the original and it "feels" a lot more like RE 1 than RE 4 - 6 did. Gameplay is very solid (with a controller), difficulty is challenging but not too stressfull and the pacing is very well done.
On top of that, a very nice action mode is added for short burst of monster hunting.
Having played all PSX and PC RE games, I never really liked the first three REs due to the completely unusable controls. RE:R fixes those. I also liked the "actionized" RE sequels (including 6, which is nice, but only for fans willing to accept change). Effectively, RE:R combines the controls of RE 5 with the strength of the RE 1 - 3 story and atmosphere. All in all, you can see that a lot of very smart design choices have been made in regards of the game, keeping frustration to a minimum.
But, all said and done. This is still a Resident Evil game. That means a a completely bonkers (but not bad) plot, a lot of narm and very unique character design. You either like it or not. If you can live with that, RE:R is a great entry into the series for players who haven't played any RE yet. For fans of the series it is a must play.

There's a myriad of sources out there that can cover the intricacies of gameplay far better than I could, so I'll try not to waste your time reading my review, when you could be in Medieval II fighting off 8 invading factions simultaneously, and outsmarting every enemy general on the battlefield.
Outmaneuver enemy armies of better equipped knights and professional crossbowmen and win by epic, narrow margins with your  town militia and peasant archers in the early game, then laugh when you yourself raise armies of knights, and crush peasant armies with K/D ratios of 1:100 in the late game when you have so much excessive gold, you find yourself building Huge Cathedrals and Brothels in every corner of your empire just to drain your bloated treasury.
There is no better feeling than when you've crushed all other factions except Denmark, Russia, Turkey, and Egypt, who then decide to form a super-alliance to prevent you from conquering the 20 remaining territories on the map, which you then do anyway.
Unrest growing in a city? Raise taxes to Very High, move your entire garrison outside the city, and then wait. When the city rebels in 3-5 turns, besiege the city, kill the rebel soldiers, and then exterminate the populace to reestablish peace in your empire.
Tired of using battering rams? Send 5 spies into an enemy castle for guaranteed access to Didney Worl! Laugh as the gates open as your troops surge through, and kill the French King to punish them for their crime of daring to proclaim French cuisine as superior to Italian.
Artillery Elephants.
When your general kills enough prisoners of war and exterminates the populations of enough cities, he can earn the epithet, "The Butcher". With 10 stars of command and 10 skulls of dread, Bindello the Butcher held off the Mongol invaders with little more than armies of Spear Militia and Peasant Crossbowmen. Unfortunately for him, Bindello the Butcher eventually died in an earthquake when I sent him to retire on the Iberian Peninsula.
Vanilla AI sometimes fails to attack you with large enough armies.
Vanilla AI sometimes lets you siege their capital for several turns, even though they have a full army nearby that could attack your besieging army, and break the siege.
Executing Prisoners makes your faction "Untrustworthy". Why should enforcing capital punishment have any effect on trust?
Vanilla AI will break a 50+ year old alliance to attack one of your lowest income villages, even though your army, wealth, and territories outnumber theirs by a ratio of 6:1.
Vanilla AI will declare war by blockading one of your ports, and then failing to attack or do anything else for the next 80 years.
Although Battle AI is mostly competent, if not brilliant, there have been a few scenarios in which opposing generals appear brain dead. If you siege a castle, and the AI has external reinforcements, the reinforcements have a decent chance of just camping outside the castle, and letting you slaughter its defenders without trying to aid their own faction.
Online experiences are limited to battles in the base game, although it appears you can run hotseat campaigns in the expansions. My experience with online multiplayer as been extremely limited, as my first online match was this year, more than a decade after this game was released. Nevertheless, I have been extremely satisfied with the handful of matches that I have had. Be warned though; in 2017 and beyond, it will be hard, if not impossible, to join an open match. Join some Medieval II groups, or tell your friends to buy this game if you want the most out of the online battles.

The Binding of Isaac is a twin stick shooter roguelike. You play as Isaac, a little boy trying to escape his ridiculously religious mother that believes god wants her to kill her son. So he runs into the basement, going deeper and deeper, to escape her. You can move in eight directions and fire in four directions. You go through a series of square rooms similar in style to that of a Zelda dungeon from NES. You fight enemies in the rooms and get rewards for doing so. You might find keys for opening doors and chests. You might find bombs for blowing up rocks, walls, or enemies. You might find coins to spend in shops. And you might find shops, treasure rooms, or treasure chests filled with secondary items, powerups, or just some more health. There are a few unique rooms like challenge rooms where you get treasure for fighting some waves of enemies. Some rooms let you sacrifice a random amount of health for a power up. Some rooms even let you trade your total permanent hearts for powerups. These powerups are the main draw of the game, as they can change your stats and give you any number of strange powers or passives. It's tough and you're going to die, but death just means you get to start fresh and see what kind of new things await you in the randomly generated game. There are even a few characters to pick from and a series of challenges you can try out. PLUS a big batch of DLC in one great package to add even MORE things into the random mix of fun.
This game suffers from its randomness. It's certainly the appeal, but if you get dealt a bad hand of powerups then you just have to deal with it. Lots of skill can make up for it, but sometimes it feels very unfair because it's random. It's troublesome to go grab for a powerup only to have it actually power you DOWN instead. Also, the tears you shoot can be hard to aim because they have a bit of an arc to when they are in the air and when they land, which isn't the easiest thing to gauge in a top down 2D environment. Hitboxes can also be a bit hard to tell sometimes due to the rounded, somewhat squishy style of the characters. Also... while the game does direct you to the program suggested for making controller support, there's not controller support in the game itself. Why not just add in controller support in a later patch? That's a minor annoyance but... it's annoying.
The thing that makes this game so great is that you can play it over and over and over again and it's different every time. There's so much content here for the price of 5 bucks it's insane. It's an amazing buy for one of your first Steam games, especially on a budget because there's lots here. And the DLC is reasonable if you want even more content. The challenges and characters and item combinations all make for endless possibilities. Your run can take five minutes or two hours. There are multiple endings too so the replay value is through the roof. I can't recommend it enough. The Binding of Isaac gets an 8 out of 10. I hear Rebirth is good... maybe I'll be able to play it someday.

What's more is some of the "upgrades" can make your life harder in the game, such as the boomerang tears and the laser tears. Because every single enemy in this game is fought by simply kiting, the implementation of upgrades that are more shooter/defensive on your only offensive source seem very odd.
All in all, this game is a mess. If you want a game similar to this, but actually made well and with sensible game mechanics, pick up Castle Crashers. Don't waste your money on this piece of trash. Preface: I bought this along with all (7 in total) DLC currently available, including the "Utopia" expansion, as of this writing. I am writing this review with all current DLC and the "Utopia" expansion in mind, as a "complete" game. I MAY edit this when additional DLC arrives.
PROS: This game appears to have taken influence from a little bit of everything, such as Stronghold, Age of Empires, Total War, Mass Effect, Star Wars, Star Trek and even a bit of Farscape. The music is top notch and the in-game music player is a GREAT idea. Resource and Technology managment is well put together. UI scaling is a useful setting many RTS games fail to implement and it is much needed, not just in this game but 100% of all RTS games. The game looks fantastic graphically, and the mechanics are also pretty well implemented. The idea of running a government, picking your ethics and such is absolutely brilliant as a mechanic, love it. The needed and much advised tutorial (more on that later) is well done and utilized in such a way that it feels less like a tutorial and more like just part of galatic life. Just all the options in this game really adds to replayability and the overall feel, the game just feels beefy and huge, as it should. All the different species are always interesting (though funny at times) and really seem to differ with little repetition. This game, if you are a fan of RTS, is quite immersive and my first playthrough was 10 hours straight before ultimately failing miserably. I found myself addicted to this game on several occasions.
CONS: Of course, everything has its faults and this game is no exception. It has a hefty learning curve, took about 2-3 hours just to get comfortable with all the mechanics and UI features, even with the tutorial. I found that, either I am slow (quite possible) with advancement, or all the other empires seem to grow and advance quite too quickly. I have played 3 playthroughs (on my 4th) and two of those resulted in a loss with no clear reasoning as to why and was NOT invaded. The tutorial actually saying "pops" in place of saying "Population" is a personal pet-peeve of mine, it feels lazy and not empire-like. Indoctrination of lesser races seems to take way too long for such an awesome game mechanic.
Conclusion: This game may have been better served as an "Early Access" release because aspects of it DO seem to lead to the conclusion that it is unfinished, even with all the current DLC. This is not to suggest that the game is unplayable or not woth buying, it still remains a fun game to play. Given that this game is from the developers of "Crusader Kings 2," expect lots of DLC in the future, after which this game may feel more complete.
RATING: 7/10

I want to like this game, and I did get some enjoyment out of it, but it has some very serious problems that never get properly addressed. I think the devs are trying, but something is getting lost in translation somewhere in the process. I can see a great idea here, but the execution falls *just* short.
After 450 hours I have yet to actually beat the game, not because it's that long, but because every single playthrough I attempted hit some fun-ending bug/issue that caused me to quit it. A couple of my longer attempts managed to end *mostly* because I was bored and finishing the job was a mere formality.
A few issues that caused me to abandon playthroughs:
* Achievements broken and will not unlock, and won't unlock after path either (have to start over). This happened on two separate major updates.
* An fallen empire that I had never met declared war on me out of the blue from across the galaxy over colonizing a tomb world, which had no markers that they considered it special (which is a thing that can happen, this planet simply lacked the markers). This was during two other simultaneous wars and I got crushed as a result.
* FINALLY got the broken and buggy precursor civilization event chain to work, only to hit the "achievements are broken lel" issue, so I rage-quit.
* My empire was being hit hard by others half my size. I examine my planets to find that the sector AI has not been developing them at all. Literally 70% of my population was essentially unemployed. And I can override them without influence, which is the hardest resource to get in the game, so I was basically just stuck either restarting or slogging, so I quit.
* The sector AI has actually caused me to quit on at least 3 games. Each major patch they claim to have fixed it, only to have it hit other fundamental issues.
* Spawned inside the borders of a civilization with end-game tech that proceeded to declare war on me with the goal being to purge that colony entirely. My only colony. They succeeded. (Admittedly, this is largely just bad luck.)
* I wanted to expand militarily, but literally everyone around me was in a defensive pact, which by the game's rules should drain their influence to 0 and bankrupt their entire culture. But it doesn't. So instead I was simply stuck 'cause I couldn't fight the entire galaxy at once.
* I wanted to expand militarily, but when I declared war I found out that my only weak neighbor was in a defensive pact with someone on the other side of the galaxy. Who I could beat.. but not reach. I occupied every planet from the weak neighbor but couldn't reach the other guy and was forced to earn "warscore" from killing the fleets that found their way to my area more than 20 years later. An entire game is decided within about 200 and is in "end-game" mode in 100. I can occupy their planets unchallenged for 20 years and not be allowed to simply call them mine.
* I wanted to expand militarily, but I was only allowed to take like 2 systems from the opponent every 10 years.. on a map with 1500 systems. And due to defensive pacts, that locked me out of taking from anyone else nearby either. (This one has been fixed, thankfully).
* I wanted to play a non-military game- just kidding, those don't exist here.
Aside from that, the mechanics are simple despite themselves. They try to be complex and interesting, but it all comes down to one thing: Economy. Develop economy so you can field a large fleet of ships so you can crush your enemies. It's a game that wants to be an RP-focused endeavor but ends up an RTS in space.

Update: after some time (and 74 hours of playing Road Not Taken) I decided to change this review to positive. I still think the game has all failures that I was talking about, but it also has some marvelous merits. Road Not Taken certainly isn’t for everyone but it deserves a try.
If you don’t know this already, Road Not Taken is a quite hard puzzle-rougelike game, where you take the role of a ranger, who helps to rescue children. At first your character wear a hooded cloak and you don’t even know how he or she look, but if you start friendship with some villagers (and you better start it, believe me), your character remove a hood and… their look and gender depends of the character who you first become friends with. Like, if you start friendship with the girl in an animal’s hut, you will be girl in an animal hut with random hair and skin color and so on. It doesn’t influence anything in a gameplay, but still it’s a fun feature.
Game mechanic is explained in a game itself, so I just go for pros list.
Road Not Taken has three aspects that are made it so unique and wonderful: very cute graphic style, characters with their own past, personalities and views of life and the most important – many philosophical aspects and dialogs through the game. Never ever you’ll see such sad, touching and thoughtful dialogs about rice or bunnies, trust me.
And now: why I still think that the game isn’t for everyone and you should think twice or thrice before try it. The answer is a quite simple really – Road Not Taken is a hard as hell. There isn’t any “undo” or “replay level” button – if you made a mistake (and you WILL make it a lot, especially in the beginning), than you made a mistake and there is no way to step back. First few levels will be merciful for you and you still can progress even if you made some wrong steps, but the game become more and more hard with each passing level and eventually you get the situation where you grab a wrong item, throw it away and screw it all with a big “BAM!” with a cherry on the top. And now you have to start all over again. At the best case (if you have a backup way with a shrine) you’ll just lost your entire inventory and half of the trophies and start the level once more. At the worst – you have to play all over again with the new character.
So in the end I suggest you – don’t look on the cute and marvelous sides, think it over! If you are fan of hard puzzle games and rougelikes – maybe it’s really your wonderful choice, consider to buy it. But if you are the casual gamer and don’t like frustrating experience and whole “screw it all in few seconds with a simple wrong move and start all over again” thing – think again, maybe this game just isn’t for you. I still love and hate it in equal parts even after so much time, that I spent playing it and after completing it three times in row.

Road Not Taken is a simplistic and cute puzzle-roguelike taking place in a winter village where children frequently get lost in the woods. You play a ranger mysteriously tasked with finding the children and returning them to the village. Each level consists of a randomly generated 3x3 grid of rooms with 8x6 tiles each and you can move horizontally or vertically through them. Of course, there are many obstacles in the way and you have to use your magic powers to lift and throw them. The game uses an energy mechanic which is drained whenever you carry an item a space or take damage. When you reach zero energy, that’s game over and you can also lose by failing to rescue at least half the children per level too many times. There is also a recipe mechanic where certain items or monsters can be combined with other things to create new items (or monsters!)
As far as I can tell the game doesn’t have a whole lot of replayability besides unlocking creatures to ban from the forest and learning recipes, so I don’t think it’s worth the full price of $14. That being said, it’s still a good pickup if you’re into puzzle games with a cutesy look and feel.

At it's core, this is a tile matching puzzle game. Some of the tiles have different properties, but at its heart you are moving and matching tiles to solve puzzles and open up new areas. You have a limited number of moves to use and unused moves carry over to the next map, forcing you to make choices for whether you want to fully complete one puzzle, or save those moves for the next, harder puzzles.
It is procedurally generated and there is permadeath, but you don't really become all that much more powerful over time, nor do you really acquire new abilities. For the most part, the puzzles just get harder (and some of the late puzzles are butally hard) and the perks you acquire often aren't that helpful. It's mostly just hard. This isn't inherently bad, it's just not for people who want a short, easy puzzle game.
There is also a romance plot that is driven by one major player choice (who to befriend). You can romance a wide number of characters and learn more about them, mostly by bribing them with food. I have yet to complete a full playthrough, so I haven't seen a resolution of a romance plot yet, but it's an interesting little take on choice, consequence, and circumstance that could probably be a game all its own. There is also some interesting backstory discovered in pieces at random throughout the game, but I'll leave that for others to discover themselves.
Overall, this is a fun game. It has its flaws, and the difficulty curve is a difficulty wall at times, but for a game that calls itself a roguelike I honestly can't be too surprised. It's still fun, and the backstory is interesting. Worth a shot.

Before I get started, a lot of the negativity comes from my personal opinions.
This game is fun and it is like a mix between Battlestations Pacific and World of Warships. If you are familiar with Wargaming games then you'll understand how the progression system works. The graphics are decent and you are able to manually control AA guns and secondary guns.
I do not know how to feel about submarines, but they do provide a distraction for destroyers so battleships can deal damage. If you played WOWS, you know what I mean.
Gameplay is like anything other online game. You would get people going off to do their own thing and there is rarely any teamwork. But on the rare occasion that there is, it is awesome and can be quite cinematic.
One game that I remember in particular is when I was gunning down a destroyer and after it sunk, I lost most of my health from torpedoes. The torpedoes came from a submarine and the last destroyer on my team sailed back and forth screening me from torpedoes and dropped depth charges. I spent the rest of the game dodging torpedoes and the destroyer continued dropping charges until he sunk the submarine.
It might not sound too great, but it was definitely a heart racing moment to see who would win as submarines are sneaky little buggers.
Now onto what I personally don't like about this game.
The ships do not handle like ships. They do not feel like they have any weight to them. It doesn't matter what class of ship it is, they all start and stop on a dime.
The HUD can also be very confusing. There is a lot of information, but it is not marked very clearly and it is easy to mistake one indicator for something else. For those who have seen TheRussianBadger's BF4 video when he shows a satirical example of cluttered HUD, this game's HUD felt something like that.
Also, I was not able to remap my keys to exactly how I wanted them. I played many hours of WOWS and I tried to remap my keys to be similar but there were not enough options to do so.
There are also plenty of ships to choose from, but there are also a lot of ships that do not exist in this game. Such as the German H-class, Japanese A-150 class, and American Montana-class, as well as most Russian ships. I personally do not like 'paper ships' so that is a negative for me. And yes, I know WOWS is no different.
Like I said, a lot of my dislikes are my own personal opinions. Other than that, this game is not bad. If you like World War II era warships, give this game a whirl and see what you think of it.

I bought Magicite on sale, and left it in my library for a little while. Once I finally got around to it, I jumped in. Honestly, I expected very little from this game, I don't think I paid any more than five dollars for it, and set my expectations accordingly. Needless to say, I got the amount of enjoyment and satisfaction I expected tenfold. Magicite is a game in which you choose a race, a stat-boosting (or ability granting) hat, a set of traits, and stats and are thrown into a dangerous, procedurally generated world full of monsters and resources for you to collect and craft with along the way. Magicite's crafting system is basic, and short, but not disappointing. I recomend figuring out all the crafting recipes yourself without the use of a guide until you're truly out of ideas in order to keep things interesting. Trust me, discovering new crafting recipes by experiment is immensely more satisfying than 'discovering' them on the Internet. My first adventure was short lived, I quickly discovered that Magicite was a pleasantly difficult game to play by oneself. But the difficulty didn't aggregate me, instead it interested me. I was hooked, they had me. I played my evening and night away. Magicite is also great fun co-op. After I learned a lot more crafting recipes, I told a friend about it. He bought it, and we gave it a whirl. Honestly, I think this game was meant to be played in this way. We switched roles between resource collector and offence, and it worked out so well. We would blow past levels and get farther and farther. Until just recently we made it to the end, and beat the game. I've never paid so little for a game that gave me so much satisfaction, and it's not done. Once you beat the game, you notice that there are many hats, races and companions to be unlocked if you complete certain acchievements, such as "beat the game without chopping a single tree" or "beat the game without killing any monsters" for a budget-priced game, it's got some good replayablility value. Magicite will keep you interested, and having fun, and you'll always feel good about paying so little for it.

This Game does NOT play like the tabletop at all, DO NOT BUY IF YOU ARE LOOKING FOR A REMAKE OF THE TABLETOP:
- They have removed STR and POW and replaced with DMG (same for melee and ranged)
- There is a MAG stat (I have no idea what this does, probably same as MAT or RAT for magic)
- Infantry (not solos) do not behave as units and instead play like solos (and even have health)
- There is a box grid for movement and range checks that allows for full pre-measuring
- No damage grid for Warjacks, just health
- Warcasters "Level Up" apparentley
- The base stat values have been changed, e.g. 2 - 5 ARM base
- There is no "dice rolling" everything is just straight up decided by a % chance, this changes how boosting works as well as removes critical misses (rolling all ones) and perfect hits (rolling all sixes)
- Criticals have been changed and now just deal extra damage instead of applying critical effects
I'm sure that there are more problems to be discovered, if you want to see for yourself download the demo. DO NOT BUY THIS GAME IT'S TERRIBLE. If you like the warmachine universe go and buy a battle box, some glue and paint then go to your nearest wargaming store and have fun there, it will be much more worth your time and effort.
