Keep in mind this game isnt finished.  Id only buy it if you want to help beta test and support the developer financially.  If you have read the negative reviews thus far, you will have found out that none of them even played beyond the tutorial campaign. (Which will be overhauled in the future) Even in its current state the game is still surprisingly quite fun and addictive, if you can tolerate dealing with the occasional glitch or freeze up or crash.
EDIT: After much testing it seems that the game cant handle higher FPS settings more than 24 FPS without freezing up or crashing. 24 FPS is enough to play on high textures with minimal or no screen tearing.  Although you can set the game to use 60 FPS, the game will likely freeze within an hour or 2 of play if you do.
The real meat of this game is custom survival games and skirmish games(vs other villages), either against the AI or with/against friends in multiplayer.  The multiplayer part so far appears to be LAN only.  But the dev plans to make it full multiplayer.
Custom survival is that.  Custom.  You can create your own entire village of characters, though you can only control one at a time, but they will all be what you want, and all have whatever names you give them.   You set timers for events and how hard you want it to be.  The maximum time so far is up to aprox 16.5 hours with 99 waves of enemies.  Starts out rather easy but after a dozen waves or so you will be screaming for mercy as the types of enemies you face get stronger and stronger, possibly more numerous, depending on the settings you choose.   And then you will scream even louder if your game freezes up or crashes.  But crash or not, your characters progress is still retained, regardless if you have made a save game.  So thats still a reason to keep playing, anyway...
Apparently the game is recording every change to characters in real time.  Every skill, every level up is saved as it happens. Your created villagers never stop gaining experience and levels.  They retain all their gained skill levels forever and have them in every game you play.  One of the achievments you can get is to have a character at or over level 1000.
Skirmish mode is also totally customizable.  You can create a custom village just like with custom mode.  You can play with up to 8 villages on a map(or monster dungeons), but you can only control one villager at a time, always.  You are, however, able to group up and give commands to hired mercenaries and constructed golems and battle machines in order to conduct organized attacks/defenses.  If you do not control them, the AI simply has them do whatever it wants. There is no diplomacy.  Everything is out to get you and each other.
The AI isnt that great right now.   The Developer is currently working on improving the AI.
Despite the game being unfinished and with issues, it is still incredibly fun and engaging.  The tutorial is not however.  If all you play is the tutorial campaign and you think that is the game, then you would be mistaken and go to write yet another ill informed negative review.
There is only 1 person developing this game, so progress is quite slow.  You can quickly tell from the game dialogues that this guy doesnt speak english as his first language.  Its up to you if you want to get it now.  But if not, I suggest following it and adding it to your wishlist.  This game has great potential.  I still enjoy it despite the freezes, crashes and bugs.  I believe the game will be well worth playing and very popular once the bugs are hammered out.
Only buy this game if you want to help out with development, giving feedback, bug reports and ideas.  Its gonna be a long slog until this game is ready for release.

Unfortunately the game is let down by it's flamboyancy in places and some of the newer characters (Jessica in particular) are just downright annoying and don't fit the vibe at all. However if you see this game on sale in any of the Steam Sales definitely pick it up - it's much better than the likes of RE6 and RE: Operation Raccoon City and pretty much feels quintessentially Resident Evil.

Looking for a free-to-play sci-fi MMO that you can relax in, have fun, and laugh a bit too? WildStar's for you then.
Seriously, this game is whimsical at its best. The story takes a satirical comedic nature and twists it with elements from a lot of your popular sci-fi franchises. On the Dominion, the "evil" side, you have a race that is entirely robotic, like the Cylon, as one example. The story is halarious as is the game's VO for things that normally wouldn't have one, like leveling up. When you level up, the game says, "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ you leveled up! Good job, cupcake!" It's funny and the art style is in the vein of Star Wars Rebels.
So you might be asking, "Huh. Sounds like a game that doesn't take itself seriously, instead opting for a laughfest. I'll pass." I'll encourage you to hold the phone right there, becuase you're wrong. Sure, it does have comedic aspects to the story, sure, the art style may be silly, and sure the voiceovers in the game may be off-the-wall, but the gameplay itself is refined, simple to hop into, and straightforward to use. This isn't a type of game where they focused on making the game as off the wall with the story as they could and forgot about the way it actually plays. It's efficent, easy to hop right in and play, and does a very good job of explaining how the game works WHILE having a story that is funny and fun to play.
Overall, I can't recommend an MMO more than WildStar. I'm still in the tutorial in this game, but I'm already enjoying it very much and laughed so hard in said tutorial I almost dropped my laptop. I'm very much enjoying myself in this one, and as such, I have no other choice but to recommend you download this one, cupcake!

Pros:

- Don't have to run between npcs to report on quests
- Fun combat, way more active and involved than some other mmos I've played

Cons:
- Lots of "deadgaem" comments in chat basically all the time (though finding groups for raids and dungs is ridiculously easy)
- PVP pops like once every three billion years
- UI can be kind of awkward at first
- Storyline isn't particularly noteworthy or inspired
- Lots of generic "kill ___ number of ___" sidequests
TL;DR: If you're looking for a fun, visually appealing game with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of dynamism, play Wildstar. If you're looking for something with serious PVP or a deep story, look elsewhere. Imho it's kind of a "love it or hate it" game-- there's not much room for "meh". (Also, this is straight up one of my favorite games, so I'm sure I'm biased!) A little ARPG with a lot of fun!
Positive:
- Nice art style (not for everyone, but I like it)
- Four classes with different playstyles
- Five difficulties, can be changed before loading the character
- Four skill trees for every character
- Multiple skills to choose from for different skill slots (for example three different heal skills with different healing mechanics to choose from for the Templar)
- Additional Mastery tree, with capped bonuses and a few which allow to spent unlimited points into it (like flat damage for example)
- Easy to access respec potions, they allow to try out all the possibilites the skill trees offer
- A lot of gems and an enchanting system allow for customization of items
- Main story with currently four acts (a fifth is in development) with different themes
- Endgame anomalies: Randomized areas with growing difficulty for every higher level
- A lot of options to adjust UI parts
- Very good performance even in high dense areas with a lot of stuff going on
- Low price of $9.99 for a lot of possible hours of playtime
Negative:
- Not as much depth as similar games like Grim Dawn (especially item affixes)
- The controls are a bit different then other ARPGs. I prefer the WASD movement here, although I always play ARPGs with click to move (which is possible to choose in Chronicon, but the targeting feels weird).
- The music/soundtrack can be a bit of repetitive after some time
- Shrines have a low chance to kill you, which can be annoying

Patch 1.6.1, May 2017, 100+ hours played.
Game: I really like it. I still play it alot.
Product: Way too buggy for the price.
Thoughts: Civ V (1'500+ h played) was also an abysmal train wreck for a long time after release, but now it's pretty great. Buy early, if you believe that game will eventually reach maturity. If in doubt, wait and see. Paradox has very good credibility in my eyes for eventually reaching the goal (more or less ready product).
I have since discovered that when you start your game, there is a setting "End Game Crisis" which you can set to OFF. Should I change my recommendation? ...not quite yet. Product still has bewildering number of issues, some of them such that I cannot believe they were not immediately discovered at testing. I will still go with: "Wait and see" or at least "Make an informed decision to purchase" (but not caveat emptor, since you are smart enough to read these reviews).
The game. As some have put it, Stellaris is Europa Universalis in Space and that certainly rings true, as much of the game feels familiar if you have player EU, HOI or other Paradox games. Stellaris also shares some of the issues from others in that when the game is very complex, at times it is difficult to locate the controls for what you need (but you will become familiar with the UI, trust me - these games take time). UI design would benefit from some love, if nothing else, there are hundreds of obvious places where notifications should offer links/controls to the related dialog window (heck, the key words are already bolded and colored - now just make 'em into links and save me a bag full of unnecessary clicks, please). Aesthetically the game is very pleasing and easy on the eye. I consider myself spoilt rotten with visual candy when I saw planetary bombartment in zoom. Some minor issues still linger, such as at times weapons fire does not receive connecting coordinates and you are likely to see occasional group salvos, generally towards the star, instead of the foe. But I think you will also enjoy very large fleet battles like me, zoming about and forgetting that I have an empire to run.
Stellaris has some really clever game design features that set it apart from all the others that I have played. It has depth and content - and humor (just here and there, with tastefully small quantities not to affect the general mood). ...but some aspects seem as if they're still under development. Such as, something as central as, ships and their design. There is nothing inherently broken or wrong per se, in the current implementation, but it is lacking in many aspects. Most notably, each design quite obviously needs to have a preferred range setting. Now your weapons layout produces some kind of a decision for you - and in my case, mostly the wrong one. Admittably, no matter what you are flying, it seems your fleet will always close in for a knife fight, even if it is kitted with poorly tracking extremely long range weaponry. Time to sack the admiral again.... if that only helped.
Even at patch 1.6.1, the game is riddled with bugs. The game hasn't crashed and I think it is mostly the game designers and developers with scripting related issues that earn my disapproval. And testers too.
One such poorly tested issue consistently prevented me from completing a game. It was an end game crisis, the Galactic Scourge (75% chance of occuring). It seems to have been "boosted", perhaps too much (apparently this will be either easy or deadly, depending on your galaxy size...) - but you CAN disable it by switching end game crisis off when you create your game. What especially bothers me with Prethoryn (The Scourge race) is that they ignore all game economics and play by different rules. You cannot use attrition as they magically gain replacement fleet for every one you destroy, but you may not realize this before it has frustrated you to no end. Google-fu and posts by other players may be needed to get you (like me) into speed. But, indeed - I have been defeated by this even and lost the game consistently for four times now... even with new understanding about Prethoryns unfair reinforcements.
In smaller scale, issues are numerous and varied. For example related to the above Scourge, when you rush to the rescue taking control of a planet where Prethoryn are exterminating locals, it won't stop! Finally the planet is empty of inhabitants (which I might accept if the game explained the unstoppable process with virus/something else)... but that YOU now get get a diplomatic penalties for genocide .. and possibly multiple war declarations to boot from the angry other civilizations. Races that forgive easy, will forget it in about 100 years... others take much longer. Thank's! I'm sure to help again!
At any rate... Bottom line is that during my yet modest time with the game, I have already encountered alarming number of bugs, many of them the kind that seem to hint towards half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥testing practises (ie. dumb and/or obvious mistakes). I feel that this should not be, not in a product of this price range.
Bottom line: Some issues are likely to induce frustrations, even anger. But it is beautifull, intriquing, engaging, surprising, daunting, rewarding and it is going to ruin your studies/social life/marriage. I am not recommending at this time because I feel that the product is just not ready yet - meaning that if I would have fully understood the current state, I would have post poned my purchase. But I would recommend you to follow this closely and try to figure out when this might be ready-enough for you!

So I am an old strategy game player, I grew up on Final Fantasy Tactics (PS1 and on) as well as more modern ones like X-Com (new version).  Ive also played the tabletop version and the Iron Kingdoms RPG.  So how does this game stack up?
At this point not very well.
Graphics are alright, with Warjacks looking nice and they have the feel of the clanking powerhouses they should.
However controlling things is a little frustrating, and I had several instances where units had no line of sight to units directly in front facing.  Camera issues, as mentioned in nearly every review, are a constant issue.  Game preformance chugged once in a while and I had an odd issue where once in a while when selecting units, that their movement grid did not show up, or in one case showed the movement grid of a different unit.
The cutscenes are decently voice acted....but the models are not animated, which is made obvious when the game zooms into their statue-like faces, talking without so much as lip flap.
There is potential here, but this is still early access, even if the label is gone.  For the price, even at 40% off, not worth it based on the demo.  Warhammer 40k Dawn of War or X-Com are far more polished.
Maybe after 4-6 months I will revisit this game, or if a more significant sale happens.

This game is interesting and good for a few hours diversion at this point. I like the idea behind it, kind of an RTS/Simulation hybrid where you are only in control of yourself--the other villagers do their own thing. Your main goal in each stage is to survive against an onslaught of monsters or wipe out the enemy village and its soulless, nameless automatons of evil before they do the same to you. I like the fact your main character's stats are persistent across all the stages, and even free mode, so you can constantly grind up your skills to make yourself the Lu Bu of your tribe.
It is impossible to really describe in terms of other games as I have never played anything quite like it, but it works pretty well and leaves me eager to see how it turns out if the developer keeps at it, which so far he has.
Make no mistake, there are a lot of *cons*--the AI needs work, the scenarios need fleshed out, and the English translation needs attention from an expert (i.e., a native speaker)--to name a few. Still, on the whole they are off to a good start.
$10 seems a little steep for what you get at this point considering you can get Skyrim on sale for $5, but it is obviously developed by a very small team experimenting with things that have never been tried before--and they have been updating it--so I don't feel bad paying it.
I recommend this if you like RTSs and simulations and don't have anything against quirky indie games, or are on the lookout for something completely different.

Aurora Dusk: Steam Age is a fun game. The mechanics are interesting. I see it as a mix between majesty, spellforce and settlers. You control your avatar but you're not the hero like in most games, instead you work together with the other AI to get things done. You can play a big role however by planting enough resources, starting buildings (so the AI finishes them for you), and gear up so you can defend/attack with your hero and golems, mercenaries you can recruit. The AI do as they please, sometimes very helpfull by setting up defense towers/ golem defense and attacking your enemy. Sometimes not so helpfull by building a bunch of buildings you don't need, gathering recources for the hell of it. They never seem to build a market though, unless you start it yourself. The campaign has 20 maps and takes about 7 hours on normal difficulty. There are 6 difficulty's so you know what to do. Survival and Skirmish Mode.
I would like to see the option to hand out roles to some people. Make one person a landscaper going around planting resources. A builder focusing on setting up every building (and not 3 baracks for one town). This would allow the player to focus on more specific roles as well. One skirmish game I decided to be mercifull and keep one enemy peasant (I called him Bob) alive. While I build my artilly weapon Bob managed to revive his fellow peasants and they rebuild their town. The AI is pretty good, just needs a bit tuning.
TLDR: Great game made by one developer, that continues on improving this game. If you are into this kind of games, the price is worth it.

Let me start off by making it clear that this section of this review is solely on the game and not the technical part of it. To start this review, let me just say that this is one of the most unique game that I have ever played. It is a typical hack and slash game with some RPG elements baked in it, but what sets this game apart from the rest is its way of delivering its story. Match it with the albeit empty but atmospheric world and the game's on point OST (definitely a masterpiece btw), what you get is a refreshing and unique game which hits you right in the feels in the end. Definitely a recommended piece of art.
Now for the technical side of things, it's a below average PC port (I have seen worse). You have the famous resolution problem and white screen problems, though I have not encountered any of these problems (before applying the MOD, mind you). The only problem which I seem to face is that my PC seemingly freezes randomly throughout the game. But luckily applying the MOD fixes it too. The GTX980 recommended specs seem absurd for a game which looks like a PS3 game graphically.
In the end, it's up to you if you decide to purchase and support this game or not. It's definitely unjustifiable for a game of this price to not receive any fixes after almost 2 months (as of time of writing) and instead what we get is a paid DLC. But on the other hand, if you can accept a MOD as a "alternative" fix for all the performance issues, then it's definitely worth giving this game a try.

I have played and loved Wurm Online for over three years, but always wished I could have more freedom to do what I want in the game. I always felt my creativity was limited by the need to gather resources and put more time into making it real than I could give.
Wurm Unlimited has changed that for me, and yet still offers so much more. Not only can I use a GM-level character to build anything I desire, but I can run a server and share it with my friends. The community has already created some wonderful tools that allow you to make custom maps, and the modding community is just getting started.
The game is rather easy to launch and manage for most people. Each "server" is in it's own folder, so I can easily make copies, zip up the good ones and store them for later, or switch between if I goof up too badly. There's a Linux-based dedicated server for cheap, cost-effective hosting.  (Server going on a $20/mo Linux VPS)
That doesn't even touch the Adventure mode, which allows a player who has never played Wurm get a real feel for some of the aspects that even MMO players never really experience. You get to work on ascending to godhood, to gain powerful sorcery items, or do what ever! Totally up to you. It's what I'd like to call "rails-optional"
I know some folks have had a hard time running the game, but those issues seem to be more related to hardware and software set up than anything else. Windows 10 64-bit, with the latest Java installed, nVidia GTX 960, 16GB of RAM running on my old Athlon FX chip and the game and server both run flawlessly. (I even play Wurm Online AND Wurm Unlimited at the same time usually.)
If there's any downside I can think of, it's that this isn't the type of game for everyone, though Wurm Unlimited does allow you to tailor it more to your play style. There's a learning curve, but sites like
are there to help get past that.
All in all, I'd buy it again (right after I re-up the subscriptions on my four accounts on Wurm Online)

Simply chaotic. Shortly, Lonney Toons for the easily bored. The pacing is spot-on, with respawn times just long enough to admire the stupidity of the weapon someone just killed you with, but short enough to get back into the action without delay. The weaponcrafting is incredible, with a nicely integrated Tech Tree. Let me elaborate. When you finish a round, you gain three things: Blutes, XP, and Spacebux.
Blutes: Used to unlock weapon parts in the Tech Tree. You gain about a score (twenty) Blutes when you lose a round, 100-200 when you win, and about 2,000 when you level up.
XP: Gained after finishing a round. Advanced you XP bar, which gauges how far along you are in your advancement of levels. (As far as I know, there is no level cap.)
Spacebux: Used for buying cosmetics, which you can unlock through leveling. You CAN buy them for real money, but it is entirely optional, as you gain approx. 130 per round win.
Sadly, that is all I can tell you without spoilage. The less you know, the better.

First Impression:  I really want to like this game, I really do.  It has a lot of the things I really enjoy like exploring, crafting, trading etc. However if you're the independent type like me and want to do it yourself with as little help as possible then this game probably isn't for you. So after 12 hours of play, I've had it.
As a newb, you start with a variety of things you need to make your way in the world, e.g. a carving knife, tent,  rope,shovel, pick axe, saw etc. The crafting system is fantastic. Everything works well until you try to take on your first animal/monster that has more strength than a rooster, a dog for instance.  Your death is all but guaranteed which results in everything you collected and made dropping on the ground and availble to anyone who decides they want it.  Ok not so bad, just don't pick on things above the level of a rooster like dogs, or sheep, or cows or seals etc.  Leave them alone and they leave you alone.
Unfortunately many critters are aggressive, and appear virutally everywhere in the game, wolves for instance. As a newb even these lower level critters are impossible to defeat.  This has the effect of restricting your ability to build things because if you die in the wilderness you spawn someplace else and likely far away. And good luck trying to find your corpse to recover your stuff inasmuch as there is no way of identifying where you were other than guesstimating using the game map.
With a better combat system and more low level stuff to kill that would allow you to level you combat skills faster this game would be almost perfect. Unfortunately killing roosters, WHEN you can find them, gets old fast.

As low as you dont demand high res texture packs and have half a brain you will probably like this game.
As a side note the modding community on this is moving as a lightning pace.

How do you manage to make a game so horrendously broken? Unnecessarily long loading times aside (Especially for a trashy looking 2d game), I booted it up and I have to say, at least it managed to detect my screen resolution correctly. It went downhill from there.
First off, the game's locked to 30fps, which is a nightmare. I alt-tabbed out to confirm this with FRAPS, and upon alt-tabbing back in, all of the art assets had been stolen, just like my money when I bought this trash. I was presented with a black screen with just the text overlaid on it.
I rebooted it (I have no idea why, I should have just quit there and then), got past the introduction cutscene and mission for a second time, and decided I wanted to turn down the repetitive, irritating soundtrack and noises. Nope. I had two options: On or off. I mean, sure, I could go to the Windows Sound Mixer and turn down the program's sound, but that would mean alt-tabbing out, a "feature" this game doesn't support. Shame. I decided to opt with keeping the sound on and just switching from headphones to speakers so I could control the sound there, but I digress.
I continued on with my "quest" (Can you call it that? I don't think many self-respecting "quests" would consist of overcoming a series of mild annoyances), and wanted to see if I could switch from full screen to windowed in the hope that that would let me alt-tab out. Nope. If you want to change between the two you have to reboot the game, something I'd done twice at this point. It might not be a problem, but the game doesn't actually seem to have any clear way of how to save your progress.
I carried on, ignoring the plethora of bugs and missing features I'd encountered, into the third room. There are two NPCs in there that you can talk to. I spoke to both of them, listening to their unimportant small-talk (Why did they even include this in the game? It doesn't add anything and it's just infuriating to have to click through). After going through the boring dialogue, I saw something. Huh, there are three badly drawn boys (Hue) on a stage with musical instruments. This looks interesting (Funnily enough this was the first time I'd said this in my half an hour of working through the bugs). I interacted with them and the credits played. I felt a sigh of relief, thinking I'd completed the game and wouldn't have to play any more. Alas, after finishing the credits I just spawned back in the room I was in. Great, I had to play yet more of this. What's that? There's an exclamation mark above the heads of the two NPCs I spoke with before, indicating they have new dialogue. Oh, how exciting! I couldn't wait to hear what they had to say, especially after the thrilling heart-to-heart I'd had with them just minutes beforehand. What *could* have transpired in the time that I was gone?. Oh... It was the same dialogue they'd said before. Either they have Alzheimer's or the game forgot to save my progress before I watched the credits that for whatever reason, the boy band up on stage had access to.
Carrying on, I moved onto the next area and finally got presented with a puzzle. I completed the puzzle and teleported back to the town, at which point I was presented with a console, a pause menu, and a "which mod would you like to play?" menu. I closed all of the boxes as I didn't recall asking for any of them (Unless Alzheimer's is now contagious, in which case I may have contracted it from the boy band). I tried to move. Nope. I tried to hit escape in order to leave this hellhole. Nope. Nothing was responding and yet again, half the "art" assets hadn't even loaded. It was at this point that I hit alt+f4 and decided to remove this broken mess from my hard drive.
Oh, did I mention this isn't even a roguelike, in any sense of the word?
Honestly, just avoid this. I'd recommend playing anything else instead. Bad Rats or Infestation would be a better choice.

A little rough around the edges, but quite fun. Especially fun with some extra players.
When Magicite was recommended to me, it was pitched as being like Spelunky with a little crafting peppered in. Obviously, this pitch was made by a friend who knows how much I'd played Spelunky when it was still in beta. It's not far off, though. The game is about tearing through randomly generate levels to progressivly harder sets of stages, collecting treasures and upgrades to help you make it to the end of the game, all with a very small health pool and extremely limited forms of recovery. And, yes, it is fun!
However, Magicite is far from a polished experience. First of all, I think it grasps the wrong end of the roguelike stick entirely. A big part of what makes roguelikes fun is the randomness; you never know if you're going to get a great set of equipment and throw it all away in hubris or struggle to keep alive at the razors edge of your wits because the game dealt you an awful hand for your class of choice. Add crafting immediately cuts down on this immensely; because crafting lets you design the direction your build will go. You know you're going to get a usable setup, at least, because you created it. Other than that, there are bugs-a-plenty, especially in multiplayer, and a lot of what makes you keep trying, the different classes, hats, and companions you get as rewards from different kinds of runs, range from irrelevent to horribly game-breaking. For example, the companion you get from beating the game once spits out random items from time to time, but it seems to choose from every item the game has and with equal weight. We found it would often barf up end-game equipment in the very first level. Amusing, but not exactly well-balanced.
I would recommend this game to people who like challenging games, but find the randomness of true roguelikes frustrating, and have at least one friend to play with (and a decent understanding of Hamachi). It is fun if you can find it in yourself to overlook the roughness in its design.

Admittedly it is clearly a work in progress, but I would call the base game a decently completed product. The optimization is lacking a bit as the frame rates will be surprisingly low on high settings for rather powerful computers. That being said, the system flows very well, it is very pretty for a turn based strategy game, and if you enjoy the Iron Kingdoms lore, it is very hard not to enjoy the game. Haven't suffered a single crash to desktop, did once get a freeze, but considering the state my OS is in, that's generally fine :P at least it wasn't a CtD or a blue screen.
Gameplay is fun, although some of the scenarios can be kinda brutal. I wouldn't say the AI is smart or dumb, but it's generally competent. Occasionally I saw it miss out on a prime charge opportunity but I think that's a part of the way their priorities are weighted - typically the AI will try and kill your warcaster rabidly and sometimes it can be a little less than defensive if you take advantage of that behaviour.
BGM is majestic but unobtrusive. It's appropriate without being distracting. Ingame graphics are decent, so far no animations for cutscenes, which is a shame but I can live without. I generally enjoy the voice acting, occasional incidents of "nope, try again" but generally good and excels in some places. Not a game where I would go "THIS VA IS AMAZING" but not also one where I'd be like "CANNOT PLAY BECAUSE OF THE VA".
Occasional problems with the interface. Sometimes I'll attack the wrong thing because it's tricky to line up the target, but not that often, frankly. Still could use a little work. Don't seem to have had a problem with the camera as other people do. But yeah, definitely a game I can recommend for people who don't mind an indie title. I don't play for just the graphics so I'm willing to overlook them for the sake of fun, and I have had fun, that's all she wrote!

I am really pleased with this game.  I am a longtime World of Tanks (WoT) player, and played about 1000 games in World of Warships (WoWS) since last fall.  I really love naval history, and tried my absolute best to enjoy World of Warships.  But then I found Steel Ocean...
I uninstalled and reinstalled WoWS about 8 times over the last 6 months.  Why?  Becuase as much as I loved the concept, I felt that Wargaming (WG) just could not fix fun-killing aspects in gameplay.  Additionally, there was a critical lack of content: WoWS has been out just a couple months longer than Steel Ocean, yet there is still no Royal Navy tech tree, and no German battleships.
Steel Ocean solved both problems for me: The gameplay is faster and more dynamic, the matches are more fast-paced and stress-free, and there is a wealth of content that bodes well for the future.
Let's talk about the gameplay first, and how it is better than WoWS.
For me, WoWS really dropped the ball on aiming.  In that game, you can learn how to lead targets and know exactly where to hit a ship (ie, the citadel), but then RNG takes over and sends your shells into the water around the target.  It is incredibly frustrating and depressing.  Steel Ocean, by contrast, uses the World of Tanks-style aiming circle, which allows you to use your skill much more in aiming: Take the time to aim properly, and you will hit hard.  That is a much better system in my opinion than aiming correctly and saying a prayer to the RNG gods before you click.
Steel Ocean also features faster games.  One of my constant gripes about WoWS was that it took forever for matches to unfold.  It was not unusual to spend 5 minutes sailing into position before firing a shot.  Furthermore, it was not unusual for matches to run the full 20 minutes.  And if you lost, you felt like you wasted a good chunk of time.
Not so in Steel Ocean: It's more of an arcade experience, and that means you get into action fast, and the action is fast once you get in it. Matches don't run more than 8-10 minutes usually, and if you lose, no big deal.  Just play another fast, action-packed match.  I find this a lot better psychologically, and I feel less pressure.
Steel Ocean has a better spotting system and it rewards spotting damage.  This allows destroyers to play their role as scouts.  In WoWS, destroyers are an utterly broken class that can see everyone while remaining invisible, then launch devastating spreads of up to 15 torpedoes at unsuspecting targets.  They spot targets for larger ships, too, but they are not rewarded for the damage these larger ships do to the spotted targets.
Steel Ocean destroyers are not the all-destroying plague that they are in WoWS.  Rather, they are part of the team, providing the spotting that the bigger ships need.  Sure, they can use torpedoes at close range.  And here is another thing that Steel Ocean does better than WoWS: You can only fire one torpedo at a time, and you have to aim them yourself.  There is no lame "aim assist" for torpedoes.  Only your skill and positioning will determine if you hit.
Another problem with destroyers in WoWS was that they exploited a poor armor penetration system.  In WoWS, enormous battleship guns could "overpenetrate" small targets and cause minimal damage.  This led to the ridiculous situation in which destroyers could charge battleships, take a few hits from their enormous guns, and get away with it.  Worse, WoWS never even published the penetration numbers for all the guns in the game.  Steel Ocean, by contrast, tells you exactly how much armor a shell can penetrate, and it performs accordingly.
WoWS' odd armor penetration mechanics also led to the bizarre situation in which attacking a ship bow-on was preferable to fighting broadside.  In other words, crossing the "T" was actually a poor tactical choice in WoWS, despite naval history to the contrary.  In Steel Ocean, by contrast, if you bring all your guns broadside and land a solid volley on a bow-on target, he will have a very, very bad day.  And this is only logical.
Steel Ocean also features subs, which are something people in WoWS have wanted and never gotten.  Wargaming always said they would be impossible to balance, but Steel Ocean has proven that claim wrong, too.  Steel Ocean balances subs by limiting the amount of time they can spend submerged, and by forcing players to manually aim their torpedoes.  Furthermore, every ship in Steel Ocean has sonar, which can locate a sub in time to take precautions.  Additionally, Steel Ocean provides a hard counter to subs in the form of destroyers and cruisers, which are not only hard to torpedo, but can both permanently keep eyes on subs and destroy them with depth charges.
Although I am not a sub player, I do not find subs game-breaking at all.  They are part of the team, and in my opinion they add to the overall wealth of content that is lacking in WoWS.
Unlike WoWS, Steel Ocean also lets you manually control all your weapons systems.  As a battleship, for instance, you not only get to control your main guns, but your secondary battery, too.  And you get to shoot your AA guns when planes appear.  This adds another level of immersion and skill, not to mention fun.  In WoWS, both AA and secondaries were controlled by AI.  The secondaries could not hit a thing, and it was super frustrating.  So seeing the manual weapons control feature in Steel Ocean was like a breath of fresh air.
Concerning content, the edge once again goes to Steel Ocean.  Unlike WoWS, Steel Ocean has full tech trees for Great Britain and Germany.  WoWS focuses primarly on the US and Japan, for which Steel Ocean has even more ships (and subs).   It also has way more premium ships of all types.
I got sick of waiting for WoWS to release the British fleet.  A naval warfare game without the British is like plum pudding without the pudding.  Additionally, I was dying to play German battleships.  Steel Ocean has a full line of them.
WoWS has wasted its time with fictitious Russian ships.  Russia was not exactly known as a pre-eminent naval power at this time in history.
Now, are there flaws with Steel Ocean?  Certainly.  First off, there is a relatively small player base.  This makes for longish queue times and small matches.  Hopefully word of mouth and time will increase this number.
Second, the graphics and modeling are not as impressive as WoWS.  But to be honest, when I play a game I want to have fun.  If a game looks nice but isn't fun, who cares?  For me, the graphics are good enough; the gameplay makes them more than tolerable.
Third, gold prices for premium ships are high.  But this is a bit misleading, because Steel Ocean provides numerous bonuses for gold purchases.  Unlike WG, which never offered bonus gold, Steel Ocean gives you double gold when you buy certain bundles.  So if you buy 25000 gold for $50, you actually get 50000.  This seems like a very reasonable deal to me, and far better than anything WG ever offered.
Steel Ocean also allows you to "invest" your gold into a "growth plan."  When you research ships of each progressive tier (up to tier 8), you get a portion of your gold back, with interest.  By the time you research the Tier 8, you make DOUBLE the gold back you put in.  You also get a boatload (no pun intended) of free XP to help you buy necessary modules when you research each new tier.  When was WG ever so generous? (Answer: never).
Fourth, critics complain that the game is too twitchy, too fast.  They say the ships are too maneuverable and that they move unrealisitcally.  But I actually like this part of the game.  Unlike WoWS, you actually can dynamically dodge torpedoes and incoming fire, even as a battleship.  What makes this game fun is that it moves quickly.  Faster moving/turning ships are part of that experience.
In sum, Steel Ocean has its flaws.  But if you want a genuinely fun naval shooter, this is it.

This game is the only real competition to WoWS on the market...and in many ways, it is the superior game.
First, we'll start with what areas WoWS beats SO:  WoWS is prettier.  WoWS has a better grasp of the ranges involved in Naval Combat, and is slow paced enough that it feels more what you'd expect from a simulator.
Now, we'll do how SO beats WoWS:
-Less RNG dependant:  Big guns get calibrated by their crews between shots.  SO has a mechanic for this, WoWS does not.
-The gold system is better...not only can you buy packages (which, the first time you buy them, you get double the gold), but you can buy into a growth plan that has additional benefits as you level, as well as giving you back more gold than you put in over time.
-Premium time can be bought on the standard daily countdown method, or a per-battle method...meaning that if you don't have time to go into the game often, you can use the per-battle method of premium time and not feel pressured to play because your prem time is running out...meaning this game is much more accessible for casual players.
-Battle scarring is much better in SO than WoWS.
-You can fly any country's flag over any ship...you can have a Fubuki-class destroyer flying British flags, or you can have a South Carolina-class battleship flying Japanese colours, if you so desire.
-Ships, ships, and more ships.  This game has way more ships in it than WoWS.
-Fire, the eternal bane of BB's in WoWS is still in SO...but done much more realistically.  If your deck is on fire, it doesn't eat away at your survivability...the only time fire does that is if it's in something important.
-Control every major weapon on your ship.  Your main guns, your secondaries, your heaviest AA guns, torpedo launchers, and depth charge launchers.
-Subs.  This game proves that subs can work in this genre, and they work well.
-The game doesn't baby its players with a lead-indicator for torpedoes...it respects its players intellengence, assuming that people will be able to figure out how to lead enemy ships and develop torpedo strategies on their own.
-Carriers have more options to choose from for their planes, and aren't locked in with pre-set squadron arrangements.  If you want to use nothing but torpedo bombers, go ahead!  You might regret it, but you can do it.
-Unique ships, like the Ise BBV (part carrier, part battleship) and the French sub with the big cruiser guns...yes, these ships actually existed.
-Every ship can launch smoke bombs, as long as you buy the consumeable.
-Night battles, complete with flares and searchlights to seek out and illuminate your enemy.
-Maps that have vision-obscuring fog patches around Islands.
-Components to tailor your ship more towards your playstyle without sacrificing the feel of what that ship is really all about, or making it over powered.
This game has its competition beat, hands down.  While it is a faster paced game covering a smaller area when it comes to distances, it isn't overly crammed so you lose the immersion...it balances the need for direct player interaction without sacrificing too much towards the 'arcady' spectrum.
Trying to go back to WoWS after playing this feature-rich game is nearly impossible.  Being subjected to massive RNG again is intolerable.  Watching planes enter your AA field and linger for long periods of time before bombing you at their leisure is annoying.
Steel Ocean is my game of choice, and I make no bones about it.

So I was pretty bored one afternoon browsing through the steam game list, looking for something decent and RPGish... and then I found this diamond, concealed among hordes of other games.
So the game had me create a character to play with, I created a cute catgirl hunter. Thinking, I am going to go to the woods and hunt wild animals and... do whatever I should do in this game to earn a living. And I ended up playing as a wheat farmer, with a windmill and a bakery, swimming in money and hiring mercenaries to take out adjacent villages, as close to a king as it gets.
That being said, the game is very interesting. It consists of playing a character among many other computer controlled equals. So it is to be expected that the beauty of this game is it's great AI, which really gives the world a life of its own.
What surprised me the most is that the AI characters are extremely clever. The game world is chaotic, with barren lands, having to work the land with magic to get raw resources, having to process those very resources to come with something useful all of this while having to defend against monsters and other villages and even making sure that they have sufficient resurrection spots to come back to life if they are killed. Most other game AIs would be a little dumb for such a challenge, but this game has the Albert Einsteins of game AI, they are surprisingly capable of coping and indeed thriving in their chaotic virtual world, and remarkably, build a thriving town given enough time.
And funnily enough, as so often happens with something that appears highly intelligent (thinking of dolphins here), a strange bond starts to develop with these simulated characters. I was distressed when an enemy villager in horseback was picking off some of my village's weakest and poorest members (without horses or armor).
The villagers are very helpful, defending when under attack, or even raiding the foreign village when they are well armed. Most of the time though, they go about their lives: farming, building their houses, building furnaces, generally speaking teching up their village and living within it, doing whatever they think is best for them and the village. I was building a tower to protect my windmill and left some stone lying about for that end, all of a sudden I had some 3 villagers helping me finish it, it was heart warmingly funny and awesome, then it was hillarious when an army of undead monsters died for good trying to invade my farm.
It kind of takes me back to my early MMO playing days, harvesting, smithing and going out for some PVP kills. Except these are all AIs, and it is very satisfying to live and act in a world populated by these remarkable AIs, basically it offers near infinite game content with intelligent opponents.
Goodness, I truly loved it, and it is not every day that I find a game worth reviewing. I love playing among AI characters, and the smarter they are, the better I find these AI sandbox games to be. It's like creating your own world where you can do whatever you like.

I don't envy any professional reviewer who had to write something about
Because while it is quite brilliant, it's also a very complicated and deeply peculiar game.
It's a fighting game obsessed with one central question: Why do we fight?
It's a game with an unpredictable structure and an even less predictable plot, going this way and that and then back again before looping on itself.
It's a game that's very cheerful and silly but then it's not.
It's a game of endless surprises big and small.
It's not a game with shocking plot twists that turn everything upside down. It's a game full of small nagging suspicions adding up to a slow-burning realisation. And it's a game about seeing the characters inevitably arrive at the same conclusions. And struggle.
It's a third-person fighting game that's also a twin-stick shooter and occasionally other things as well, depending on its current mood.
It's a game where when you watch the end credits roll for the first time, you haven't understood anything yet and seen barely half of it.
It's a game whose weapon descriptions alone are masterpieces of small-scale writing, and I'm not even joking here.
It's a game whose DLC includes the line "Before you enter, we'll have to save your game due to reasons. Will that be okay?"
It's a game whose DLC is just a very straightforward series of arena battles but then it's not.
It's a game with a brilliant soundtrack, deftly adding and removing layers from its tracks in response to what is currently happening.
It's a game so sad that it's happy.
It's a game so happy that it's sad.
It's a game that keeps the slightly obnoxious Japanese habit of ending games with an incongruous pop song that only seems to shatter the mood, but then it turns everything around, pulling the rug from under your legs one last time.
Or was it the last time?
It's a game that you think you understand but then you don't.
It's an excellent fighting game.
It's a great story.
It's a rabbit hole that has no end.
It's a wonderful and smart videogame.
I love it.

If you have any interest in game design or gaming as a medium of art, play this game. NieR:Automata is many things from being an existential horror to the combat being equated to sexual pleasure. It blends together visual, audio, gameplay, and interface not to enhance but to be the foundation of the narrative. This narrative plays into the overarching themes and motifs while rewarding those who pay attention to the neatly layered story only a game can convey.
NieR:Automata takes place in an open world setting split into about 5 major zones with decent density of side narratives. While these side quests can be tedious, they have tangential payoffs that are both self contained and to the main narrative.
This game does not try to push the graphical boundries but is still aesthetically pleasing and consistent with the world's atmosphere. The rich dynamic musical score is integeral in building the atmposhere for the world and its scenes. On average there is about 4 versions of each musical score that is evoked dynamically based on player action and scene context.
The gameplay loop is a highly serviceable hack and slash with bullet hell by Platinum Games. While the core mechanics are not as in-depth as other Platinum Games, the highly customizable weapon sets, special abilities, and passives keeps things fresh for those who experiment. The difficulty is largely hit or miss depending on a player's progression. Majority of the boss fights could have been a little more engaging mechanically for higher difficulties. Most of the time, the strategy was too simple vs the amount of options available. The way easy mode setup is a nice addition as it lowers the barriers to entry. There is no shame in using this mode and it is even useful to lure in less savvy gamers.
At times, NieR:Automata sacrifices gameplay enjoyment just to fulfill its narrative in true Yoko Taro fashion. Consider,
Route B's significance is the very reason the majority of players dislike this route. This route contextualizes the two motifs of repetition and combat. Authorial intent is if it makes the player feel something the gameplay will take that negative hit. The obvious downside is the average player enjoyment will decrease due to this sacrifice. As game design, it truly evokes an intentional feeling of dislike that only a game can.

To me, this game is the physical incarnation of frustration and therefore I can't recommend it to anyone; in my opinion games are supposed to be fun and I didn't have any playing this Flash game. The only features I like are the character designs, the music and the contrast between gore and deformed enemies on the one hand and the fact that everything is drawn in a cute, thick lined stile on the other. And that's about it.
In my opinion, the main issue in this game is balancing and how heavily it leans on sheer luck. Before you've unlocked any other characters, you will play as Isaac, who has three hearts for health. Most things that hurt you (such as touching a fly or getting hit by a blood drop) will take away half a heart, while some others (such as explosions from bombs) will take away an entire one. Initially, the only weapons against your enemies are your tear drop shooting eyes, which only shoot in four different directions, one direction at once. Many enemies will be capable at shooting blood drops in either more directions or multiple directions at once, will suddenly charge you, will be capable of jumping or flying over obstacles you have to walk around or a combination of these abilities. While shooting in four directions, you will find yourself more than once being unavoidably driven into a corner shooting enemies while in the end getting hit by something anyway. This is most prevalent in boss levels; many bosses spawn smaller enemies, giving you the choice to either kill the boss first so he will stop spawning more enemies that will trap you, or to kill the enemies so they can't trap you while the boss just keeps spawning more enemies. And just try to dodge enemies when you always slide a bit.
Since everything tries to kill you, you'll heavily depend on the pick ups you can get and rooms you'll venture into (levels are randomly generated). And that's where bad luck will get you. Such as having keys but nothing unlockable to use them for, or having lots of locked items around but no keys to unlock them with. Or a huge amount of enemies and no hearts spawning to heal you. There are also numerous pick ups with no description whatsoever that can either increase or decrease your health and your abilities and rooms that will pain you upon entering and leaving with no guarantee there will be something good in them.
TL;DR: Everything tries to kill you and only if you're very lucky, the game will grant you something to either fight your enemies or improve your health, all while being limited to shooting in four directions.

Overwatch comparisons;
Yes the 2 games have a pretty blatantly similar style. Characters, abilities, game modes, etc etc.
Honestly who cares? If Dota and LoL can coexist,so should these.
What's different in paladins?
- combat feel and ttk. Paladins is a much more satisfying "shooter" than overwarch. Overwatch focus mainly on paper rock scissors rpg-esque combat where as paladins has more focus on actual shooting. There are all the classes present including tanks and healers but they don't feel so rigidly forced to only do that one thing. Shooting is still the focus. Time to kill is much faster than overwatch as well. This allows tanks and healers to contribute to combat in a more meaningful way than overwatch.
- builds. In paladins you customize your load outs using various cards which drastically alter how each hero plays. Where as overwatch you're stuck with a vanilla hero. Similar to talent points in mmos.
- items. Much like a moba you buy items in your spawn. Don't worry though it's streamlined into 4 easy categories and you will grasp it quickly.
Yet another layer of customization to suit playstyle and team compositions.
Stuff I dislike;
- network performance is pretty terrible. Expect lag, freezes, and entirely dropping games. They can only ride the "open beta" train for so long, it's not acceptable in 2017, nor is it acceptable for a game actively making money from their beta.
- queue system. It's exactly like a moba. Which is why I hate it. Overwatch wins in this department with ease.
- character select phase is way too long and they add a customize phase so people can play dress up on MY time. Wrong. That needs to go. Unnecessary waste of everyone's time.
- convoluted f2p currency system. If you've played smite you know the drill. It almost feels worse here.
I personally don't care about skins and cosmetics but I DO care about game balance.
There is a currency called essence which is then used to unlock various cards for each heroes template. Problem is the default cards and templates are garbage and not viable so you can't just up and play any hero you want. Even if you buy the reasonably priced (imo) founders pack. You will be gimped until you grind enough to buy cards you need. Not sure what the reasoning is here but seems like a gate which only ruins the otherwise fun experience
Overall a fun addition to the hero shooter family and hopefully they can clean up some issues before leaving what seems like a 3 years beta.

A total steal for the money spend. It's a diablo style dungeon crawler with pretty much everything you would expect. Loot, Gems, Entchanting, Skill trees etc.  It's pretty impressive what the dev have done here, this game feels like diablo 2 and in some aspects even better.
Chronicon has 4 classes, all of them have a different source of energy for their abilities.
The appearance of the class depends on the number of skill points used in a specific skill tree.
Every class has class specific Items and Item sets.
Berserker (your typical high dps melee brawler guy)
Warden (a Hunter/ Ranger with some magic skills as well)
Templer (your typical Tank/Dps/Heal hybrid)
Warlock (Mage - the caster dude, any game needs one tho)
Items in Chronicon have 6 different tiers: Ordinary, Common, Enchanted, Rare, Unique and Legendary. There is also a tier called True Legendary, which are items that can only drop when you have a character level of 100 and are playing on Legendary difficulty.
You will be extremely surprised how good this game is (if you like the artstyle of course !)

Early Access Watcher Reviews Aurora Dawn: Steam Age
Update Version: v1.2.2

Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the review.
It has taken me awhile to figure out the best way to come across this game. The major issue is not with a technical problem or a gameplay issue, but with the free version offered by the developer. The two versions are different in regard to content (the Steam Age along with all the items, buildings, materials, equipment and enemies along with it) are exclusively to the paid version. It is not much of a difference and the real conflict is with whether it is worth the price to pick up the paid version. I will go ahead and say get the free version to determine if you like this game; I am not leaving it at that though.
The main objective of the game is to survive the increasingly difficult assaults of Dusk monstrosities. You create a character and journey to Aurora in the hopes of saving it from the Dusk while building your skills by participating in the activity each skill represents. Mine to increase miner, leatherwork to increase tanner, get hit to increase shields and build to increase builder. By increasing your skill levels you also increase your main level and perform tasks faster. There is a mana system for spells and spawning resource nodes, energy for completing tasks, and hunger that affects energy restoration. While you are accompanied by AI companions, you can also hire mercenaries to fight under your control. This makes combat a little easier since the enemy tends to split apart to strike multiple enemies, which is a plus given how some games just send enemies toward the player in a mindless rage.
The game bolsters three game modes: story missions, wave survival and team deathmatch. During each story mission (which moonlight as the game's tutorial), you are given time to build and equip along side your companions until the waves of Dusk monsters strike. Wave survival is the same, but you are able to customize the number of waves, number of enemies per wave, difficulty of the wave and frequency of each wave. Team deathmatch is similar to a RTS style team fight with up to eight players. Depending on the difficulty setting, you could get through the story missions in three to four hours.
What could make or break this game for someone is the focus on a passive community. You can either focus on assisting the AI controlled companions or focus mainly on yourself while they go about their own business. The contributions you make during each mission feels minuscule and it usually falls back to self-improvement to ensure you are as battle ready as possible. You can place defensive structures and buildings hoping your companions will build it, but a lot of times they decide to focus on their own agendas. It is quite possible to complete each mission by handing over your character to the AI as well. This kind of defeats the purpose though and turns the game into a visual simulation.
The Dusk is not the only trouble affecting Aurora; crashes and select audio issues were present. These issues were present in the demo version and the current build of the paid version. Each mode is at risk of being hit by a random crash while I only noticed the audio cut outs happening in the campaign. Crashes occurred about a third of the time in the team deathmatch game mode making often saving a requirement.
This game was rather difficult to properly judge. I have not seen a case were a developer was willing to release a demo version this similar to the paid version. The passive community brought an interesting twist to the table, but in doing so isolates the player in terms of personal growth. This could be why it was implemented; not knowing what the end goals of the AI can lead to an underwhelming force to combat the Dusk though. I will recommend this game, but I cannot stress enough how important it is to try the demo version before purchasing this game. It is the rare case you have a clear view of what to expect in a early access title.
Pro
- Robust demo (play it before buying)
- Distinct art style for sprites and characters
- Unique AI system
Cons
- Crashes
- Audio errors
- Passive community can be a deal breaker for some
Special note: I also noticed several grammar and text issues during the course of the campaign. I did not use it in consideration of this review and honestly have no right to question considering my own faulty grammar.

Resident Evil Revelations was an exclusive game for the 3DS was released in 2012
Capcom decides to Share Their Sweet Baby with us on Consoles/PC. for those like me who played this game on the 3DS you know that this baby is a must play on PC.
Resident Evil Revelations is the most fun RE game I've played since RE4 and is much better than the disappointed Resident Evil Games that was released nowadays. Resident Evil Revelations takes place in between the events of RE4 and RE5.Familiar faces Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine will be in the story plus new characters such as the charming Italian male named Parker,the flirtatious Jessica,specialist operatives named Keith and Quint whom are military style units and Quint is a specialist with tech stuff,commander O Brian who works for the organization named BSAA that Chris and Jill helped create to stop bioterrorists and the red-haired Raymond who is an agent from another organisation who has a mysterious aura to him and you aren't sure to trust him or not
The story shows the events that happened to a once beautiful city named Terragrigia which was built on an artificial island (you'll see how it's surrounded by beautiful ocean scenery) and the city was high tech,used clean energy but a series of disasters happened to the city .The story takes you to before and after Terragrigia was destroyed.All I will say is a bioterrorist organisation named II Veltro whom are against government control come into the story and the BSAA are a group whom were created specifically to combat bioterrorism and the group was founded with the help of known RE characters Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine.Jill and her partner Parker go on an infiltration style mission to spy on or stop II Veltro but they go missing and Chris and his partner Jessica go searching for Jill and Parker and you'll also control Keith and Quint.The individuals in the pairing of characters can change too.I like how the story shifts it's focus on different pairs of characters because it makes the story feel more thrilling by making you wonder will they be able to find each other or not or will they survive
The story does a good job to fill you in one what happened to Terragrigia and explains about Terragrigia in detail with some beautiful cinematics and it makes an attempt to fill you in on story elements that happened in past RE games
The story also has a bit of character flirting and romantic interests mixed with a lot of seriousness and personally I like how the story is that way because the story is still disturbing and very serious and can be emotional but the romantic interest/flirting stuff and humor give the characters/story a nice break from some of the intensity at times
The gameplay in RE Rev is a great mix of classic survival horror and action gameplay.For much of the game you'll need to be conservative with ammo because ammo isn't plentiful like it is in RE4/RE5/RE6 which means you'll need to make headshots or cannot miss too often when you shoot(this adds more intensity to the gameplay as you'll try to make your last few remaining bullets count and was something that was missing in RE4/RE5/RE6.
Overall: Probably the best original release title so far and it brings back the survival horror elements that classic style RE fans miss but uses the mechanics introduced in RE4 very well. so Add the creepy atmosphere, great graphics/beautiful cinematics, nd story/characters and you might care about make this game great/Superb

Patch 1.6.1, May 2017, 100+ hours played.
Game: I really like it. I still play it alot.
Product: Way too buggy for the price.
Thoughts: Civ V (1'500+ h played) was also an abysmal train wreck for a long time after release, but now it's pretty great. Buy early, if you believe that game will eventually reach maturity. If in doubt, wait and see. Paradox has very good credibility in my eyes for eventually reaching the goal (more or less ready product).
I have since discovered that when you start your game, there is a setting "End Game Crisis" which you can set to OFF. Should I change my recommendation? ...not quite yet. Product still has bewildering number of issues, some of them such that I cannot believe they were not immediately discovered at testing. I will still go with: "Wait and see" or at least "Make an informed decision to purchase" (but not caveat emptor, since you are smart enough to read these reviews).
The game. As some have put it, Stellaris is Europa Universalis in Space and that certainly rings true, as much of the game feels familiar if you have player EU, HOI or other Paradox games. Stellaris also shares some of the issues from others in that when the game is very complex, at times it is difficult to locate the controls for what you need (but you will become familiar with the UI, trust me - these games take time). UI design would benefit from some love, if nothing else, there are hundreds of obvious places where notifications should offer links/controls to the related dialog window (heck, the key words are already bolded and colored - now just make 'em into links and save me a bag full of unnecessary clicks, please). Aesthetically the game is very pleasing and easy on the eye. I consider myself spoilt rotten with visual candy when I saw planetary bombartment in zoom. Some minor issues still linger, such as at times weapons fire does not receive connecting coordinates and you are likely to see occasional group salvos, generally towards the star, instead of the foe. But I think you will also enjoy very large fleet battles like me, zoming about and forgetting that I have an empire to run.
Stellaris has some really clever game design features that set it apart from all the others that I have played. It has depth and content - and humor (just here and there, with tastefully small quantities not to affect the general mood). ...but some aspects seem as if they're still under development. Such as, something as central as, ships and their design. There is nothing inherently broken or wrong per se, in the current implementation, but it is lacking in many aspects. Most notably, each design quite obviously needs to have a preferred range setting. Now your weapons layout produces some kind of a decision for you - and in my case, mostly the wrong one. Admittably, no matter what you are flying, it seems your fleet will always close in for a knife fight, even if it is kitted with poorly tracking extremely long range weaponry. Time to sack the admiral again.... if that only helped.
Even at patch 1.6.1, the game is riddled with bugs. The game hasn't crashed and I think it is mostly the game designers and developers with scripting related issues that earn my disapproval. And testers too.
One such poorly tested issue consistently prevented me from completing a game. It was an end game crisis, the Galactic Scourge (75% chance of occuring). It seems to have been "boosted", perhaps too much (apparently this will be either easy or deadly, depending on your galaxy size...) - but you CAN disable it by switching end game crisis off when you create your game. What especially bothers me with Prethoryn (The Scourge race) is that they ignore all game economics and play by different rules. You cannot use attrition as they magically gain replacement fleet for every one you destroy, but you may not realize this before it has frustrated you to no end. Google-fu and posts by other players may be needed to get you (like me) into speed. But, indeed - I have been defeated by this even and lost the game consistently for four times now... even with new understanding about Prethoryns unfair reinforcements.
In smaller scale, issues are numerous and varied. For example related to the above Scourge, when you rush to the rescue taking control of a planet where Prethoryn are exterminating locals, it won't stop! Finally the planet is empty of inhabitants (which I might accept if the game explained the unstoppable process with virus/something else)... but that YOU now get get a diplomatic penalties for genocide .. and possibly multiple war declarations to boot from the angry other civilizations. Races that forgive easy, will forget it in about 100 years... others take much longer. Thank's! I'm sure to help again!
At any rate... Bottom line is that during my yet modest time with the game, I have already encountered alarming number of bugs, many of them the kind that seem to hint towards half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥testing practises (ie. dumb and/or obvious mistakes). I feel that this should not be, not in a product of this price range.
Bottom line: Some issues are likely to induce frustrations, even anger. But it is beautifull, intriquing, engaging, surprising, daunting, rewarding and it is going to ruin your studies/social life/marriage. I am not recommending at this time because I feel that the product is just not ready yet - meaning that if I would have fully understood the current state, I would have post poned my purchase. But I would recommend you to follow this closely and try to figure out when this might be ready-enough for you!

WildStar’s eight playable races are divvied up comfortably between two factions both fighting for control of Nexus, the forgotten homeworld of the Eldan. Hyper-advanced race, which neatly sets the tone for a familiar two sided confrontation. But even with the Dominion-Exile conflict now raging across the planet’s surface, your adventurer is the least interesting parts of this saga. Much of WildStar’s real story is locked away in voiced data recordings, welcome yet sporadic cinematics, and an in-game encyclopedia.
World comprised of over a dozen independent zones across three continents and an orbiting celestial body. But Nexus instills a pervasive feeling of insignificance when facing the antiquated relics and natural wonders towering overhead, and it’s often stunning to behold from the tops of those vantages, overlooking its motley biomes and colossal setpieces.
It’s clear that mobility is a core tenet of WildStar, with so much emphasis on fast, fluid motions. Double-jumping and sprinting add interactive elements to movement, the benefits of which are exponentially noticeable atop a mount or hoverboard. Combat is similarly transformed into an action-oriented dance of precision target painting and chaotic dodges.
Each of the six classes feel mechanically unique and handle differently, though all are capable of holding their own when it comes to dishing out damage, as well as supporting a party in a healer or tank role. The secret is WildStar’s devious Limited Action Set system, which restricts your action bar to eight skills at any one time, forcing tough decisions tailored to each new fight revolving around how you’ll allocate points that increase those abilities potency and add new effects.
Player housing in particular brilliantly combines open construction and aesthetic freedom with tangible benefits. To me, this game is the physical incarnation of frustration and therefore I can't recommend it to anyone; in my opinion games are supposed to be fun and I didn't have any playing this Flash game. The only features I like are the character designs, the music and the contrast between gore and deformed enemies on the one hand and the fact that everything is drawn in a cute, thick lined stile on the other. And that's about it.
In my opinion, the main issue in this game is balancing and how heavily it leans on sheer luck. Before you've unlocked any other characters, you will play as Isaac, who has three hearts for health. Most things that hurt you (such as touching a fly or getting hit by a blood drop) will take away half a heart, while some others (such as explosions from bombs) will take away an entire one. Initially, the only weapons against your enemies are your tear drop shooting eyes, which only shoot in four different directions, one direction at once. Many enemies will be capable at shooting blood drops in either more directions or multiple directions at once, will suddenly charge you, will be capable of jumping or flying over obstacles you have to walk around or a combination of these abilities. While shooting in four directions, you will find yourself more than once being unavoidably driven into a corner shooting enemies while in the end getting hit by something anyway. This is most prevalent in boss levels; many bosses spawn smaller enemies, giving you the choice to either kill the boss first so he will stop spawning more enemies that will trap you, or to kill the enemies so they can't trap you while the boss just keeps spawning more enemies. And just try to dodge enemies when you always slide a bit.
Since everything tries to kill you, you'll heavily depend on the pick ups you can get and rooms you'll venture into (levels are randomly generated). And that's where bad luck will get you. Such as having keys but nothing unlockable to use them for, or having lots of locked items around but no keys to unlock them with. Or a huge amount of enemies and no hearts spawning to heal you. There are also numerous pick ups with no description whatsoever that can either increase or decrease your health and your abilities and rooms that will pain you upon entering and leaving with no guarantee there will be something good in them.
TL;DR: Everything tries to kill you and only if you're very lucky, the game will grant you something to either fight your enemies or improve your health, all while being limited to shooting in four directions.
If you're no masochist, please don't be misled by the fact that the user reviews are "overwhelmingly positive".

Overwatch comparisons;
Yes the 2 games have a pretty blatantly similar style. Characters, abilities, game modes, etc etc.
Honestly who cares? If Dota and LoL can coexist,so should these.
What's different in paladins?
- combat feel and ttk. Paladins is a much more satisfying "shooter" than overwarch. Overwatch focus mainly on paper rock scissors rpg-esque combat where as paladins has more focus on actual shooting. There are all the classes present including tanks and healers but they don't feel so rigidly forced to only do that one thing. Shooting is still the focus. Time to kill is much faster than overwatch as well. This allows tanks and healers to contribute to combat in a more meaningful way than overwatch.
- builds. In paladins you customize your load outs using various cards which drastically alter how each hero plays. Where as overwatch you're stuck with a vanilla hero. Similar to talent points in mmos.
- items. Much like a moba you buy items in your spawn. Don't worry though it's streamlined into 4 easy categories and you will grasp it quickly.
Yet another layer of customization to suit playstyle and team compositions.
Stuff I dislike;
- network performance is pretty terrible. Expect lag, freezes, and entirely dropping games. They can only ride the "open beta" train for so long, it's not acceptable in 2017, nor is it acceptable for a game actively making money from their beta.
- queue system. It's exactly like a moba. Which is why I hate it. Overwatch wins in this department with ease.
- character select phase is way too long and they add a customize phase so people can play dress up on MY time. Wrong. That needs to go. Unnecessary waste of everyone's time.
- convoluted f2p currency system. If you've played smite you know the drill. It almost feels worse here.
I personally don't care about skins and cosmetics but I DO care about game balance.
There is a currency called essence which is then used to unlock various cards for each heroes template. Problem is the default cards and templates are garbage and not viable so you can't just up and play any hero you want. Even if you buy the reasonably priced (imo) founders pack. You will be gimped until you grind enough to buy cards you need. Not sure what the reasoning is here but seems like a gate which only ruins the otherwise fun experience
Overall a fun addition to the hero shooter family and hopefully they can clean up some issues before leaving what seems like a 3 years beta.
