Addressing the many negative comments I've seen posted as reviews about this game:
The game is not pay to win - there is definitely one significant ship which you can only buy which outclasses it's peers, but it is not a game breaker - not when weighed against the 100+ ships thoughout the game.
The game is under-populated still but the community is active and we have some good and some bad people like any game. On balance I think there's probably more good people .. but equally there's a fair bit of frustration as people don't understand some of the gaming mechanics. I'll give you an example so you can see why people can and do rage:
All ships have a built in scouting range, but equally all ships have a built in level of disguise - and this disguise level lowers the effective scouting range of the opponent. The disguise becomes more effective the slower you sail. The disguise is also much better on small ships (they are of course easier to hide) and smaller ships typically have better scouting range.
What happens then is destroyer captains with skill slowly sneak their ship towards the enemy and their battleship team mates use their vision to shoot from out of sight.
If the destroyer captain fires his disguise is cancelled immediately (the disguise penalty lasts for a short period like 15 seconds), so a good captain doesn't fire - he simply spots for the big naval guns on his team and they do the killing. The net result is new players being very upset that they have been "magically killed" by "invisible" opponents.
Some people will explain what has happened, some will stay silent to retain their advantage.
What is at fault within Steel Ocean is the chat system is very limted - you get to type a line at most and five lines in reasonable succession is deemed spam. Communication in the common area is quite limited. This really doesn't help of course.
There were issues early game where it was believed some teams were cheating by calling locations if they had members on both sides. I have no direct experience of this, but I can say it appears to be a dead issue now. The real issue is very skilled players sailing low tier ships which are the battles in which new players congregate - it's not a problem which will go away soon because some players will swap to the low levels if they are more heavily populated in order to get a game. Equally if I were to want to develop a new ship I would have to start low and build up, so as a longer term player i'm forced to join the new guys.
My solution is to tell people some tips in general chat so they at least learn something during the game - of course not everyone does this.
Note: long-term players do have an advantage as their officers give tangible benefits making their ships better pound for pound. Equally as in Smite or DOTA etc, game experience is a real factor too - this is compounded if experienced friends team up vs a random pick up group. Having said that, I have been on the winning side as a pick up group vs a "pre-made" and equally have lost as part of a "pre-made".
I've kept my original review below, but felt it needed updating, given some community issues now seemed to be solved and the general level of connectivity has vastly improved too (I used to get significant lag and random disconnects, which now simply don't happen).
My understanding is that as a Chinese developed game, the developing company is somewhat restricted in the advertising it can do to promote the game (apparently there are domestic restrictions). So I would repeat my advice from my original review:
The game is good and free, so if you like the idea of a WW2 naval game which rewards thinking but isn't dependant on reflexes - try it.
******* Original Review ********
A brilliant game marred by a lack of promotional effort to increase the player base. There's a lot to love and for the most part it is done very well - my single biggest gripe is connection issues, but these would be resolved if more people signed up to try - as the population expands it's worth the development team adding more server facility. Of course this is an assumption, but it's a reasonable one.
Primarily the game is PVP, but there are reasonable PVE tutorials with friends, to allow you to try the mechanics for yourself.
Given it's free, if you like WWII ship combat, you want to actually sail and aim (nothing overwhelmingly complex, but also a requirement for skill and intelligence) and you like having a variety of ship choices and some degree of customisation, plus the choice of ship size .. sub, destroyer, light and heavy cruisers, battleships and carriers .. I'd suggest you try it and see what you think.

10/10/17 update: I've made some minor additions to my review to account for new features of the game.
I love this game.  That said, there are some things you should know before you buy it, or else you set yourself up for disappointment.  Most of the negative reviews are from people who didn't know these things before they purchased the game.  That just means the game wasn't meant for them, not that there's anything wrong with the game.
First, and most importantly, this game does not hold your hand and guide you through how to play.  Exploration and discovery are part of the game by design.  You get a few popup messages explaining some basic concepts, but then you're on your own.  Plan on spending a healthy amount of time on the Wurmpedia looking up how things work, or you will find yourself disappointed and frustrated.  Alternatively, if you like a challenge, it's possible to discover how things work on your own by trial and error, but not many people can do that.  (10/10/17 Update: This also adds to the feeling of accomplishment when you finally build up your settlement as you want it.)
Second, the graphics are not visually impressive.  Some of the graphics are from as long ago as 2006.  They serve a function, and that's it.  If you buy this game expecting AAA modern graphics, you will be disappointed.  Don't expect much from the graphics.  (10/10/17 Update: There has been a graphical upgrade recently, but it's still far from AAA graphics.)
Third, this game is *deep* and can be overwhelming for some.  If you get the chance, take a look at the Skills window and browse through the list.  (10/10/17 Update: There are over one hundred of them.)  Every one of those skills is implemented into the game and affects what you can do in it.  There are also a few actions that don't have an associated skill.  If I haven't convinced you to devote time to browsing the Wurmpedia already, this is a very good reason to do that.
Finally, this game is about survival in a medieval fantasy setting, not about action.  Don't expect much from combat.  Combat is pretty much just targeting something and just making sure you're the right distance from the target to effectively fight.  Instead, enter the game with the expectation that you'll have to "work" towards building your home and training hard enough to put up a fight against hungry spiders, and that the game will reward you by allowing you to make your permanent mark on the game world.
Your actions have lasting impact in Wurm.  Long after you stop playing on a public server and the buildings you constructed start to crumble, other players will be able to explore the ruins of your settlement and discover what you did there.  If you play on a server that has been around long enough, you can do the same, and it's pretty fun.  (10/10/17 Update: The upcoming Archaeology and Restoration skills will enhance this feature once they make it into the game.)
If you're still wondering whether this is the game for you, just try out the MMO version of this game, Wurm Online.  It's free to play, if you don't mind the level 20 skill cap, or you can pay to go premium, which unlocks higher skill levels.  Wurm Unlimited is essentially an official private server for Wurm Online, so if you find that you like Wurm Online, but either can't afford to spend money each month on premium and deed upkeep, or don't have the time to invest regularly into it, then Wurm Unlimited was made for you.

First off, I will say that this game is not for everyone, and If you have never played Wurm Online, then I'd recommend to try it before you think about buying Wurm Unlimited.
I started playing Wurm Online sometime in late 2009/early 2010, and I loved it. However, I did think the grind was a bit too harsh, and eventually I couldn't afford to pay for premium anymore, so I quit playing. I moved on to other games, the most similar being minecraft, but nothing ever came close to Wurm for me, so I ended up logging back in every few months/years to see what's changed, but never sticking around for long because I couldn't get premium.
Now they have released Wurm Unlimited, a stand-alone, one-time payment version of the MMO, and needless to say, I was really looking forward to getting it. It's basically what I've always wanted Wurm to be, a one-time payment version that lets you do everything the game has to offer without limitation, and even lets you play on other people's servers, or even your own.
Now I guess I'll put a list of Pros/Cons.
Pros:
1. A true Sandbox game that lets you do whatever you want, wherever you want, now at your own pace since you can modify the speed at which you do things and gain skill levels.
2. Everything is made by the players.
3. Hundreds of different skills and thousands of items you can craft.
4. Maps can be gigantic, don't expect to see many people come to visit you if you manage to build somewhere on the other side of the map :P.
Cons:
1. Very large learning curve, this game is NOT noob friendly, this may be a pro to some, but if you expect to have you hand held, you will be dissapointed (unless you get into a nice village that will help you out).
2. Graphics are pretty dated, though you can still find some places with beautiful views.
3. Still has a few bugs, I haven't run across anything game breaking though, mostly just stuff to do with animations and stuff.
4. Not sure if a bug or not, but as of the time of this review, you can't play without internet access. It isn't a big deal for most, but some people may be thinking of buying this so they can play when they are without an internet connection. As of right now, you cannot.
So, if you tried Wurm Online and liked it, but thought the grind was too painful, don't want/can't pay for premium, or you just don't like MMO's and jsut want to play by yourself or with close friends, then you will most likely enjoy Wurm Unlimited. If you have NOT played Wurm Online, and Wurm Unlimited sounds interesting to you, please try Wurm Online first, it's free to try out. Don't complain in the forums or something about it cause you bought the game without researching it.

I am a huge fan of both RTS and Warmachine, but this game fails on both accounts. The game itself is very poorly implemented, with a clunky and primitive grid system rather than the more typical "stand where you want to" that is the industry standard for RTS games. Use of a hex system would have been better if the devs were unable to manage a non-grid. The display starts out fine, but every corpse, ability, spell and so on adds to the clutter and general poor presentation; this is amplified is the grid display is turned on (to allow counting of ranges etc), rapidly becoming a tangled mess. If there's a control-area spell or feat in operation the display is utterly useless, as it colour-fills every square the spell or feat is effecting. It gets to the point that the player cannot see where the various units are or even which ones are still alive.
This game is missing basic functionality. The game only saves between missions - there is no option for saving mid-level, even in the single player campaign. This means that the player has to dedicate around an hour minimum, solidly, to each level. Need to go out in 45 minutes? Have something else you need to get done? Your wife/child/pet etc need you for something? In that case, you're either unable to start the level or, if mid-way, have the choice between ignoring the thing you need to do or loosing all the level and re-starting later. Very poor.
The control system is clunky and can lead to gameplay problems. Changing the direction a unit is facing often snaps to the wrong direction (ie not the direction you clicked on), leaving problems such as being unable to shoot, presenting your back to the enemy or being unable to charge next turn. Lines of sight seem rather arbitrary, leaving the player guessing at who can see whom and from where.
The AI is frankly laughable. Enemy units will sit where they started unless you get close to them or shoot them, meaning most levels are simply a case of nibbling away until the enemy are all dead. There's rarely any challenge. The level design tries to compensate for this by spawning more and more enemies, including heavy warjacks, but this leads to a very unsatisfying experience.
As a port of Warmachine to the computer, the game also fails. For some reason, they've fundamentally altered most of the rules (eg Def and Arm, RAT/MAT and so on being 1-4), the feel of the game (infantry are unreasonably tough), the scale of the game (you'll have a handful of infantry and a couple of 'jacks - maybe 20 points on the tabletop) and the abilities of almost all the units. All infantry operates independently, with no units.
Overall, I would call this game a failure, and give it 3/10. Do not buy.

Spells before movement: I can see why they removed this, they probably didn't have the techno know how to prevent a "move, spell, moveback" tactic. Instead they count spells as an action.
DEF and ARM: there was moments when I thought "how would that guy hit/damage him!?" Like the normally POW11 Trencher rifles doing 5 damage to a Juggernaught.
But, I do have to commend the designers, it certainly has alot to offer, but I don't think they have the know how to polish the final game.
Pro's
Graphics are amazing, and bring the universe to light (it would be nice to have an army painter though, I did play a field grey (AKA green) Khadoran force)
True to tabletop gameplay
Con's
very clumsy camera tracking: I had my units go round a corner, not knowing their was the enemy mere squares away. Camera's getting blocked by scenary. Even at one put the same buildings took away all the scenery and units, but leaving the HUD and overlay, however the game returned to normal quickly.
In all, a very good game, but does need a final polish for it to become an awesome game!

I just don't know. I seem to have the free demo of the game. I've played the tutorial and the first actual mission. This is where I stand:
- No idea what the story behind Warmachine is. I have heard about the game, but that's it. The campaign starts of weirdly and the dialogue is infurating in my opinion. That the characters are not animated when talking doesn't help either. It's been 10 years or so since I last saw 3D rendered characters who couldn't move their mouths. If you don't want to animate that, fine, it's a strategy game, I get that, but zooming into their faces during every cutscene is a moronic idea then. Also the campaign is extremely boring so far. The dialogue, the characters, the "humour". It just feels off and not interesting at all.
- The gameplay. It seems to have depth, I'll give them that. Your units are different enough at the start at least. Warjacks look awesome and have a ridiculous miss rate of 40% in melee vs basic infantry. Seriously? I was a bit underwhelmed. The pacing is wrong here. After introducing the warcaster as your hero unit and then almost immediately afterwards giving you your first warjack I've gotta say that that thing is just a big bullet sponge right now...kinda sad. Navigating the attacks and spells etc. is more or less intuitive. They have included tooltips why an action is not possible, which is cool. Unfortunately those tooltips are only available for some actions. Why? God only knows.
- The controls. They are not that great. The whole game feels sluggish and partially unresponsive. At times you don't know why you can't commit an action...example in mission 1: You need to shoot at barrels with your warcaster. Well, ok. You select that woman, move her into position, click on the ranged attack button and the attack automatically lights up. Cool, works. You can also click on the barrels to shoot them just like with any other enemy - in theory. In reality when I got to the second set of barrels I could not ♥♥♥♥ing select to shoot them. I had free LoS, no enemies near me, yet I could not select to shoot the barrels. I realized a turn later that there are small next/previous buttons for enemy selection as well. Cycling through those I eventually got the barrels selected as my target. But why? Why make this such an effort?
I think you can get used to that, though.
- The camera. Oh my god the camera. People were, unfortunately, right about that ♥♥♥♥ing camera. I messed around a bit with the camera options, but none of the settings are satisfactory. Moving the camera is sluggish as hell (thank god I disabled motion blur...yes this game has motion blur, for whatever reason) and unprecise. You can move, rotate, zoom...blabla, but it doesn't feel natural, especially in free camera mode. Since it is a turn based game I can also kind of live with that. What I can't live with is the combat camera. I have disabled action camera, but as soon as the AI makes their move, the camera goes bonkers. Example: An enemy unit is selected, the camera jumps to that unit, the unit movies, the unit stops. The camera jumps BACK to your previously selected unit, then back again to the enemy unit as it makes its attack. It does this all the time. It literally makes me feel sick. Sometimes the camera just doesn't scrolls to the edge of the screen during such a move and then back again. Why? Why can't you just focus the camera on the unit that moves, but not actually follow the unit, but just show the area in which the move is being executed? The simple following every unit at closest zoom (yes it does that as well, zooming ♥♥♥♥ing in every time) makes my head spin...again. The camera is a mess.
- The graphics. They're serviceable. They look good, but something feels off. It's all too blurry somehow. Even the written dialogue text is blurry. It looks cheap. The actual assets look good, but as a whole it's not quite there. Landscapes are ok, but they also could have done a better job with the UI highlighting actual units - friendly and enemy. At times they just meld with the landscape...pretty annoying.
- Price: A 30 euro price tag for a kickstarter funded game is quite a lot. I'm not sure how much you get for that. I think 4 factions in MP and the campaign, the boring campaign with 20 missions. You will, however, only play the annoying red head afaik...boring, boring, boring. I guess they may do other campaigns for other factions, but at this point I'm not even sure they should. Additionally they want to charge you for upcoming content as well, of course. DLC, yay. Right now that is the "Retribution" faction bundle for skirmish and MP for whopping 15 euros and the "mercenaries faction". I think they are a faction, sold either as individual units or via 3 bundles for a total or 20 euros! I think you can use them to supplement any army...being mercenaries and all. I get it: You want to make money
BUT! If you fund your game through kickstarter for almost 600,000 dollars (+ whatever additional funds you received), then proceed to sell the base game for 30 dollars with only 4 of the 6 (or 7) factions of the actual tabletop game, and THEN proceed to sell those same factions for another 35 dollars, while at the same time your game is full of bugs and needs to be improved in almost every aspect, I think you don't deserve my money at all. That is the deciding factor why I choose to rate this game negatively. A lot of things can be fixed or improved, but the pricing is a hit in your face. Not to mention that there will most likely either be more DLC or that's it...it's not worth it imho. If you're a Warmachine fan, chances are you're gonna play the tabletop anyway.

I've played Aurora Dusk throughout its pre-Steam development and as a fan of games with interesting, dynamic AI, can recommend it to those interested in the same mechanics.  The graphics and animations leave a bit to be desired, and the UI is clean but fairly bland.  In spite of these issues, the gameplay itself reminds me of a combination of a use-skill-to-improve RPG (think something like Ultima Online in a microcosm) and The Settlers, where you build up a town with a supply chain (e.g., logs must be cut into boards to be made into some final product at another facility).  It’s an interesting hybrid-genre game, and its major strength is its insistence on making the player’s character a small cog in a larger, dynamically functioning economy driven by the AI.  It isn’t my strongest recommendation ever, but given its unique focus, I endorse it.

Let me start off by making it clear that this section of this review is solely on the game and not the technical part of it. To start this review, let me just say that this is one of the most unique game that I have ever played. It is a typical hack and slash game with some RPG elements baked in it, but what sets this game apart from the rest is its way of delivering its story. Match it with the albeit empty but atmospheric world and the game's on point OST (definitely a masterpiece btw), what you get is a refreshing and unique game which hits you right in the feels in the end. Definitely a recommended piece of art.
Now for the technical side of things, it's a below average PC port (I have seen worse). You have the famous resolution problem and white screen problems, though I have not encountered any of these problems (before applying the MOD, mind you). The only problem which I seem to face is that my PC seemingly freezes randomly throughout the game. But luckily applying the MOD fixes it too. The GTX980 recommended specs seem absurd for a game which looks like a PS3 game graphically.
In the end, it's up to you if you decide to purchase and support this game or not. It's definitely unjustifiable for a game of this price to not receive any fixes after almost 2 months (as of time of writing) and instead what we get is a paid DLC. But on the other hand, if you can accept a MOD as a "alternative" fix for all the performance issues, then it's definitely worth giving this game a try.

Road Not Taken is a roguelike game developed by Spry Fox, and it has made me childishly addicted. You are a ranger whose job is to save children who have gotten lost in a cold winter forest. Every year the children are sent in to pick special berries with rejuvenating properties, and every year some children are lost in the process...
The puzzle mechanics is easy to understand but more difficult to master. To get to the children you have to go through a number of rooms. The rooms are closed down, but can be opened by matching objects in the room; Three stones, five deer, two trees etcetera. You can either lift the objects or throw them in a straight line. And, of course, the different objects behave differently which means you have to have different tactics depending on what the rooms look like.
Every time you move something it costs you energy and this is the key part: Rearrange the objects where you want them, but do it in the most energy-efficient way. Lose you evergy and you have to start over. (All over, from the very start! Roguelike, remember?)
Some objects can also merge and turn into completely different things. If you are not careful, you will get chased by angry spirits or become stuck behind an immovable rock.
After every finished forest level you return to the city where you meet the citizens. If you bring them gifts they help you by giving useful information or equipment that gives you an advantage in the forest.
Baked into this charmingly simple (and yet deviously difficult) game is a very serious undertone. Not coincidentally, the game shares title with a poem by Robert Frost about the roads we don't take in life. This is very subtly done but it makes the game so much more beautiful. It actually relieved my own midlife crisis but for some if may be a cause one... Either way it gives a nice depth to the game beyond just the brainteasing puzzles.
The game has, as mentioned, become an addiction for me. It has almost everything you could possibly want: Frustrating but rewarding gameplay, cute graphics, atmospheric soundtrack, and a layer of deep existensialism. There are some smaller bugs and I have run into a few rooms that are literally insolvable, but beyond that I haven't found anything that I don't like.
Also: It is free if you have PS+, so there are no excuses not to try it!

CLUNKIEST GAME INTERFACE SINCE GAMES WERE PLAYED ON STONE TABLETS!
Seriously this is almost unplayable! Whever play tested this for the developers must have had some kind of deal with a rival firm because there is no way this should have passed testing. It's not the size of the UI or the fact that the units move on a square grid (these are pretty much the same as XCOM and that gameplay is excellent) it's just the fact that it will often not register what the player is doing. Trying to change the facing of your units is best guess because often the arrow pointer just wont follow the mouse direction so you just press excecute hoping that the 25% chance you have of getting the orientation you want will come out. Also whilst the units move on a grid the curser option does not and so it is often pot luck which of the available squares your unit will move to. This could all be fixed witha  decent patch but it needs to happen before the game can be played.
On another topic buildings block the camera and so unless you are playing on an empty map you can't get the camera into a position where you can accurately see what is going on. The entire second campaign mission is played through narrow streets and no matter where you place the camera it is trying to look over a wall. This can make the UI even more infuriating as you try to wrestle with the camera to get it to look at the squares you want only to find that the UI has frozen your unit so it can only move in the opposite direction!
The other thing I noticed is that the game can be very tight lipped sometimes about which unit you should be using. If you have a unit that hasn't completed it's action you can't select the next unit even if all you can do with the previous one is end it's action but it often won't tell you which unit you should be selecting. This is likely something that will come with practice and as I said I only played the demo so maybe it is something I will get used to in time.
As I said at the beginning I did enjoy the missions I played of this and I am going to keep it in my wishlist but until they patch the UI and camera I certainly won't be spending any money on this and I suggest you don't either.

Pre-dating Minecraft and most other sandbox games, Wurm is a remarkably deep and broad sandbox game that does not treat the fast-food game-play entertainment market kindly at all.
Every element of this sandbox is not only challenging, but provides a real sense of accomplishment to those that are looking for a long-term sandbox game; not a fleeting experience.
The survival system is complex and very reasonable, the crafting system is deep and complex enough to keep a sandbox enthusiast very engaged and interested.  You can claim property, tame wild-life, farm, and build a village to a city with impunity; anything from boats, ships, transportation carts, pavement, defenses, tools, weapons, armor, houses, etc.
One might be initially mentally blocked due the graphics, but if you put deep and rich game-play and game-play mechanics ahead of that, then this is worth the look.
Many very dedicated private server owners are ex-Wurm Online players, and they are there for the long-term.

Do not pay for this game.
The server that runs in the background has serious memory leaks and writes constantly to the servers drives rather than using the standard practice of batch writes.  Running this on any server is going to be a huge resource hog.  If you thought you would run this on a local machine and connect locally you will wear out your machine very quickly.  I am sorely upset that it took me over the two hours playtime to discover these issues and so cannot get a refund from steam.
This server cannot run in offline mode and the client is useless unless there is an internet connection as a result.  Even on a local lan the server requires authentication through steam.
Steams refund policy for server based products needs to be examined.  2 hours is not enough time to examine a server based product.  You have to run a server for 10-12 hours to get matrix on performance.
At any rate there are so many pitfalls in this offering that its wasted money.  Very disappoited.
Was really hyped to play this, but it would never connect to a server without crashing, had to get it refunded. I will gladly purchase again and rewrite a review if this problem is resolved.

An incredibly deep pioneering sandbox truly gives you a vast multitude of choices. The crafting system is very complex, and the number of things you can build (from ships, to carts, to houses, to forges, to blacksmithing tools, to woodcutting tools, to looms, to horse equipment, to bows, etc.) give you absolute freedom over what you want your character to specialize in. Because of how complex it is to make a "simple" item, such as a crate, everything you accomplish truly feels like an accomplishment, and the objects that you create have a great deal of permanence and pride associated with them.
On many servers, there are no pre-set "quests" to go out and do. Your level of enjoyment is purely dictated by goals that you set for YOURSELF, not goals set by NPCs.
In addition to this, there is a solid system set in place to start a village with your friends, and on certain servers, expand that to a kingdom if you have enough followers. Because of the length of time it takes to accomplish certain tasks alone, it is an enormous advantage to team up with people, and cooperate to achieve a greater, overarching goal.
It's impossible for me to give a comprehensive overview of the game, since I have only played around 30 hours at the time of writing this, but from what I've read, my small party has not even scratched the surface of what's possible in this game.

Wurm is one of those rare games that makes memories.
I can think back to group activities that took part in from years ago.
In Wurm you really have to really plan every outing.
Who's got the healing covers? ...Who's bringing food and water? ...Which set of armor are you going to wear? ...Are we bringing a wagon?...Does anyone know the way there?
Landscaping and building takes real planning and resource management (not to mention time) but you are rewarded with the ability to make a truly unique (and sometimes beautiful) mark on the land that will stand for ages with upkeep (or slowly fall into ruin with abandonment).
Every aspect of structure and item creation is covered. Make a chest out of pine?  Meh. Make it out of cherry or apple? How nice!
You'll find yourself saving high quality cuts of different woods for specific purposes as you travel through the forest, or snipping sprigs from plants for planting back at home later. Don't get too comfy while you're out there raking your garden though. A young troll might wander out of the woods and turn you into dinner.
Adventuring is really an adventure. Take a wrong turn and you can become fantastically lost.
Wurm is an epic game and the amount of detail is staggering. In my opinion it's second only to Dwarf Fortress in detail.
Since Unlimited relies on private servers, I would stress that one carefully vet a server before committing to play there as weeks of work you put into your home could be undone in seconds by an immature admin. Hope this helps!

After playing Wurm Online for 3 years on the Epic PvP cluster, being an Emperor on one of the main servers and being actively involved in PvP during that time this release came as quite a shock, after paying monthly subscription fees that were up and down in cost personally I felt a bit cheated of my money - until i realised, what is the point in paying a monthly subscription when you are given access to the entirety of Wurms code, free to edit (but not redistribute) and access to play how you want, with easy server setup and lots of customization, why keep paying monthly to play something when you can play it FOR ONE PAYMENT!!
The learning curve is steep for this game however, if you are playing with the normal 1x skillgain modifier it will take years to actually achieve something (similar to WO's freedom cluster) or 2x which is somewhat bearable (Also comparative to the Epic cluster.) And knowing all the tips and tricks for grinding is something that takes time to learn in this game, however there are plenty of guides springing up right now, or you could just make an account on the wurm online forum and post any queries you may have there.
PvP is a little strange in this game for those who are wondering what it is like, the combat is purely RNG based with a little bit of button mashing / changing fighting stances and doing shieldbashes or special moves, and it has been argued for a long time that this is quite a unique system, that has existed for god knows how long now.
and if you are wondering why i would waste over 130 days worth of ingame play-time, the one incentive that has kept me playing all of this time is the huge fights, the biggest that I have experienced was a 25v25 with over 100 horses dead (all fully geared and enchanted) that gear alone takes much time to create (as it was on epic) and then you have player gear like plate armor, moon metal armor (with various advantages) and weapons of all different kinds and types. You get adrenaline rushes when people rush at eachother fully mounted and geared, with combat priests etc. Looting the corpses of your enemies is extremely rewarding - and you do not need to take long to regear now due to server customization (action timers have now been made customizable).
there is a rare item system in this game, it's very simple, and goes worst to best
Common, Rare, Supreme and Fantastic.
Getting rares is the most common, supremes quite a bit less and fantastic items are basically ridiculously hard to get, and usually are something useless like dirt lol.  Each stage of rarity colours the item differently. Rare is blue, Supreme is Green, and fantastic is a harsh pink.
You can also ascend to be a god/demigod by winning a valrei items (valrei being the moon the gods live on) or tomes that boost your players resistances/debuffs and giving special karma spells that you can utilize for a variety of tasks (this is considered one of the few endgame features.)
And honestly I could type away all day about things in this game, but there is just too much content - if you want to understand this game best you really will need to play it properly - and you will get frustrated and annoyed along the way. But that is the fun of Wurm.
8/10  - Some silly features with flawed logic, and questionable systems (valrei is coded very weirdly and can be really buggy) but has immense replayability and lots to do and explore at your own pace, grab some friends and you will not stop playing guaranteed.
I would reccomend this game!

Look. I'm not going to say that this is the best Naval Warfare game out there. Nor am I going to say it's better than World of Warships, because I've never played it. But what I can tell you for certain is, that like all Free-To-Play games, there will be grinding, anger, censoring, tears, happiness and satisfaction.  As a new player, you'll launch the game for the first time, login and then sit on the port screen. You've got the 4 factions most games based on WW2 have; Britain, Germany, Japan and America. Along with two more possibly to be factions- France and China.
You'll go into your first game as a tier one, do a few matches and get to tier two. This is where things start to define who you are and what you want to be in this game.
For Japan and America you can choose to go down all lines - Cruiser, Battleship, Aircraft Carrier, Submarine or Destroyer. For UK - Destoryer, Battleship and Aircraft carrier.
For Germany - Crusier, Submarine and Battleship.
Choosing what to do here will determine what you do for quite some time or to the tier you want to get to. Playing this with friends is definelty a must have, however "thanks" to the devs, the party size is now a maximum of 3 - used to be 5. But you can still have more than enough fun with 2 of your mates.
As there is with all F2P games, there is a premium currency. Gold. Gold can be gained several ways, ranging from winning 5v5 battles and being on the leaderboard to buying it. So it isn't just money used to get it. Along with that, the game gives users V.I.P battles, which gains bonus XP (Both Global and ship based) and Silver (Ingame currency).
Each faction has their own strengths and weaknesses. Germans have good accuracy while dealing lower damage. Japan are the tanks of the ocean while America is the all-rounder. Britain has the best sonar and great AA defence.
After a while, you'll notice that the game isn't perfect however. There are bugs here and there. Matchmaking issues in higher tiers where few dare to venture. Then you have the censorship which censors words like system. Although some sound game breaking, they really aren't. When players get to higher tiers, there goes the problem of bad balance in late tier games. Every game has their problems and none are perfect. And this game isn't an exception.
A very good sign of a game like this is, although 1 year old in the Chinese market, the developers are active and from what has been said in many of the disucssion threads has been carefully and sufficiently thought out and replied to via their community officials.
The game itself rewards players who are loyal -with regular login rewards- and those who play a battle correctly. It punishes those who make the wrong decision, however there are tutorials to start new players off.
Finally the graphics of the game; they're not what you'd call amazing but they run well and the gameplay is more than worth having a slightly less 'pretty' game.
TL:DR;
WW2 factions, which are good at things and have boats. Team up with 3 people and wreck stuff! F2P game, so expect there to be premium vehicles such as the Tirpitz (Worth around $70). Game isn't perfect but hey, who/what is? Has active devs who care about the game but don't know how to promote the product so low playerbase... Rewarding game for players and harsh for stupidity. Ok graphics. Not the best but it runs.

I'd like to write an indepth review, but I won't.
I am a massive MMO enthusiast, I've got 8 years of WoW under my belt, and have played everything from Archeage to SWTOR, Guild Wars to Firefall, just a brief few, whether they were good or bad.
I heard of Wildstar when it was released, and at the time was too engaged in WoW to give it any attention, I didn't think much of it at the time of hearing of it, however a few of my guild members were actively talking about it, meaning I had to take some notice.
It's now 3 years on since it's release, and I've gotten round to giving it a chance.
Some Pro's and Con's
Pros:
-UI and general HUD layout are very similar to other MMOs, I see this as a pro because it's not confusing. It's easy to work out where everything is. Your action bar(s) are right where they should be, inventory and menu bar are to the sides. It's simplistic and that's great.
-The Map is beautiful, it's just perfect, I wish other games had a map like WS.
-Character customization is on point, its a judging point. If I'm going to put several hours, days, weeks etc into my playtime of a game, I want to be able to customize to a point that I have created something unique that I am happy with, WS has that, with movement of: Eye Width, Chin Height, Cheek Width etc. It has all the sliders and the presets, loads of hairstyles and eye colours.
-Lore is aplenty, there is so much, I keep collecting books everywhere and each one pops up with a new lore point or interesting story. You get lore when choosing your faction. It's great for RPer's (Not that I am one, but it's a bonus).
-Skills, so glad there is Tradeskills/Professions, most MMOs have them, but it always makes me happy to see them added.
Cons:
-Excitement: This is a personal issue, and not something that everyone will have, but still including it. I just don't feel that flair of excitement when I jump into a new (another) MMO, I had it when I started MMO all those years ago, and I had it with Guild Wars, but when I try new MMOs now, it's like, "Oh, another game, well, lets have a look." - There's no excitement to get home and continue my adventure. Excitement to see new places, just isn't there.
-Clutter is a big one with WildStar. I'm far from new to MMOs, but I am so bloody confused by this game, going to contradict my statement on the UI here, but everything is so messy. I just can't... it makes the game hard to play, but not in a challenging way. In a, I can't find my way, but this game is a mess.
All in all, I wish I'd given WildStar a go back in 2014 when it launched. But I can understand why the game is quiet. You go online and it feels very empty, void of players.
I would recommend WildStar, but not to a new player of MMOs, I feel you need to have a backbone to this genre and start off with something else, because it's just not easy to get into. Saying that, it does have a very nice tutorial, but I skipped through.

Miss Shapella never married. Road Not Taken is Miss Shapella.
She was married to her job: teaching know-nothings like Ninth-Grade Joshua (me). She gave it everything she had, calling us to an intellectual maturity beyond our years. Many remembered Miss Shapella for her impassioned engagement with us, trying to instill the difference between meiosis and mitosis. Though for me, very little of it stuck, due to sickness keeping me from regular attendance. But she had mercy on me for being sick, still challenging me to excel beyond my expectations of myself. Other teachers failed me outright when I couldn't answer the questions on finals. Miss Shapella gave me a passing M (for Medical) when I failed her final test, believing in my potential to have passed if I had simply been there more often.
Like Miss Shapella, Road Not Taken calls me to an understanding that goes beyond what my brain seems capable of.
Taken from:

It could have come from @GameIdeaMachine.
"A cross between Triple Town and Sokoban, except a roguelike, set in a town with a dark secret, with a philosophical message."
To be honest, while Road Not Taken is a decent work of procedural puzzle generation, it's not quite a 'roguelike'. Despite the emphasis on 'choices', there is very little you can do to ensure you'll do better in your next year, or as the next poor fool in a 15-year quest to save the children of the town. You can ban a couple of items, choose from mostly identical equipment, and pick between easy or hard missions.
The easy missions tend to be randomly too easy: the hard missions tend to randomly be piles of objects you have to muddle through. The "recipes" you learn as you go are by and large useless, except for the two or three you'll keep to heart and use every time.
It's still a pretty good puzzle game when it works, though. The framing story is also quite unique: it's delivered in the smallest pieces that need to be recalled and put together, and every nitpick you might have about the plot is eventually answered.
The framing 'town' parts are purposefully random. Spend your resources wooing a townie, level them all the way up to True Love Forever, and they might still decide to ditch you for someone else at Year 15. Unlike the carefully exacting main game, the town section is one gamble on the future after the other and proud of it.
"There are no stories here, just circumstances", one of the townies says. Yep. No comforting answers to hard questions like "am i doing the right thing", here. After some time you might wonder whether you should not only stop rescuing the children but actually set the entire town on fire; yet there are only so many options to you. Marry or stay single. Have children or not. Easy Mode or Hard Mode. Die in a struggle to get the last child out of the storm, or carefully pace yourself to your retirement.
In short, it's a game about choices more than it is about the consequences of those choices. Take it, or leave it.

Orignal review from 2015:
This game was released too early - this is the charge that most people level against this game, and they are right, I don't think anyone would really disagree. It was incomplete, buggy and not very well optimised. The majority of the negative reviews seem to focus on this.
However - I would say it has come on in leaps and bounds since then.
I backed the Kickstarter though I hadn't heard of Warmachine, let alone played the table top game, I like turn-based games and liked the sound of the theme.  When I first got access to it, all the points I touched on in my first paragraph left me frustrated, So I stopped playing it for a while, now though coming back to it, I've found it so much more enjoyable.
WhiteMoonDreams have added a ton of content and have been releasing fixes and updates on a regular basis.
The focus of the game, and subsequently the development, is on the Multiplayer which means that the Campaign is still lacking -The AI is basic and doesn't offer much of a challenge (this is slated for improvement in the future). The same can be said for Skirmish - however it's a good place to test out a list or a new tactic, albeit whihtout a sensible response from the opponent, before trying it in Multiplayer. My point here is that if you are more interested in the Campaign than the Multiplayer, you'll be disappointed.
A Multiplayer (with limited unit selection) demo has just been released - it allows play against existing players as well as other demo users. I'd suggest giving it a try.
The next feature that I am most waiting for is asynchronous play - being able to take a turn at a time when I can fit in 10 minutes without necessarily having to be online at the same time as my opponent will be great for me. By that time I also expect lots more fixes and improvements. I'll probably come back to this review at that point and give some more thoughts.

To preface this review, I was a part of the Early Access and have been periodically checking in on this game since then. I also play the tabletop.
Warmachine Tactics is yet another multiplayer-centric game that wants to charge you a box price and then additional expensive DLC bundles just for new multiplayer units. The problem with this is that their multiplayer mode isn't robust at all. It's like having a dedicated online FPS with only one match size (6v6, for example), one game mode (deathmatch), and a few maps.
An expensive box price or expensive multiplayer DLC bundles. Pick one. $15-20 for faction bundles is is silly on top of a $40 box price. I might as well purchase models for my actual Warmachine army instead.
It's important to note that if you have no previous experience with Warmachine, this game is not a very helpful place to start, as almost nothing is explained and what tooltips there are, are not useful. This is doubly true in multiplayer, where only previous Warmachine experience will make sense of the squad building menus.
I really want to like this game, but they translated a lot of tabletop mechanics poorly, the controls are finnicky and punish people who don't play the tabletop, and the campaign is painful. Very little documentation in-game about what stats mean and what the various units are does not help this situation. It tries to be an 'almost Warmachine but not quite', and succeeds at being different. Different, however, is not better.
The graphics are really nice, the game just suffers from being very time-consuming in unnecessary ways. The primary draw of Warmahordes is objective-based gameplay, territory control, and good scaling of game mechanics from small skirmishes to large battles. There's only one mode (kill the enemy warcaster) in Tactics, one battle size (50 points), and only a few maps. Because all matches are 50 points, there's no such thing as a 'quick game'. All matches will typically take an hour or more to conclude, and that's a large problem for casual play.
I wanted this game to be a gateway drug to Warmachine's tabletop, but only people who already enjoy the tabletop will be very interested in playing this, or paying for DLC expansions for their favorite factions. It lacks the strategic depth and breadth that makes the wargame so interesting, and that's a shame, because with more game modes, variable match sizes, and maps balanced for objective-based play, this game could be something great.
Instead, they're developing expensive DLC faction add-ons for an anemic multiplayer experience that desperately needs more features, such as hotseat play. The ability to speed up or disable animations would also be nice, when you consider overall game length and how much of that is spent watching units take actions.

Fun game, think Battlestations Midway with more detailed ships and no direct control of aircraft; instead you manually line up attack runs which requires a bit of skill. Instead of merely having main calibre and AA, often ships have sub calibre as well as torpedoes and depth charges.
The game has a very arcady phisics engine compared to real life. That being said, I would not play a fully realistic naval simulator online because I don't have the literal ALL DAY it would take for a single match. You want this level of arcady because otherwise there would be very little to do. People complaining about the physics engine are fools, in real life it would take battleships miles and quite a few minutes to turn around completely. Does spending the first ten minutes of a match turning sound fun? I didn't think so.
Combat is about trying to predict where your opponent will be, and destroyers are nimble enough to dodge large calibres at long range. This creates a dynamic where submarines are excellent at hunting battleships and carriers, which have a range and firepower advantage against cruisers but whose weapons have difficulty hitting destroyers. Cruisers, however, are potent destroyer hunters because of their many accurate guns that have a range advantage. Finally you have destroyers (and light cruisers, to a lesser degree) who excel at submarine hunting, but whose main calibres are typically unable to damage ships classed cruiser and above. Destroyers have torpedoes, however, which can hit subs at shallow depth, and decimate any ship, as well as depth charges for antisubmarine duty.
This creates an interesting interdependence where destroyers and light cruisers act as scouts and spotters for battleships, and matches typically have these close range battles surrounded by long range skirmishers like battleships and carriers, who try and get hits in against the lighter ships. Once this phase ends, the side with scouts hunts down the remaining enemies. e.g. Typically a lone battleship will have a great difficulty against several destroyers, however victory is still possible with a cool head and good positioning. It would be a much different story, however, if it was a lone destroyer against two or three battleships. The balance in the game reflects reality without sacrificing fun simply by limiting the amount of larger ships on either side - you wont see 10 BB and 2 DD on a team, for example. Every ship has a role and straying too far from your duties is a detriment to the team. If the battleships on one side rush its GG for them unless the other team makes some fatal mistakes as well.
Individual skill plays a major role and is well depicted in the battles within your range bracket. In a fight between destroyers, the better captain can win by quite a margin in most cases, so you never feel like you're simply giving and recieving damage at predetermined rates merely waiting for one side to die after doing a certain amount of damage in return. There is no RNG either as all shots, even the dropped bombs and torpedoes from aircraft, are manually aimed. The only things that aren't are the machine guns on the ships and fighters who have AI to kill bombers and scouts. You even get manually controlled flak cannons on your ships, and if you dont use them because you have tunnlevision on the target and didn't notice the bombers coming in then you're going to end up spectating for the rest of the match. There is a real sense of danger during battle, as the slightest mistake can have serious consequences, and no ship is more than one solid volley from a battlship or one spread of torpedoes away from going down.
Overall this game has been quite enjoyable so far and for the low price of free, if you haven't downloaded it already you may be showing early signs of a rare form of alzheimer's that causes you to forget how awesome WW2 naval battles are. If so, download this game and go to a doctor.

TL;DR = Addictive hack n slash, crazy amount of customization, loot, and options.  Will only get better.

I like the art design for certain things, but wish there was more animations, and also wish gear showed up when equipped.  As is, levels and monsters feel very static and lifeless, but it's still fun to try to run through slaughtering everything and gaining bigger killstreaks.

Chronicon is a ARPG with lots of loot and tons of different ways to play.
Almost all maps are randomly generated.
You can compare the skill tree to Grim Dawn, but with choice from all trees instead of just 2.
There are allot of effects your attacks make, but because of the pixel style it can be cluttered at times.
Overall it's a really fun game, I like loot games like this.
Keep in mind that it's not a complete game. Here are issues I have with it when writing this review:
- The start of the game gets easy fast, however suddenly the game ramps up and you'll die quite allot.
But if you keep going you'll get good loot and it becomes easy again. I am playing on the second highest difficulty and the only thing stopping me from playing max difficulty is that bosses take FOREVER to kill. The game needs a bit more balancing.
- The font can be wonky sometimes because of the filtering. The bigger text has a strange font that seems a bit out of place, to me it doesn't really matter.
- You can filter out equipment depending on rarity, but potions, scrolls and chest keys will always be highlighted. I wish health potions, mana potions, keys and scrolls of return where automatically picked up. That would make looting a bit less tedious.
- There are no dedicated slots for items you always carry like health and mana potions.
- Story text scrolls down far too slowly, making me skip all dialogs because my patience runs out.
- The minimap shows too little and I end up having the big map overlay on at all times. It kinda gets in the way. A zoom slider and size for the map would really help.
- The thick pixelated effects can really clutter up your screen, I wouldn't mind if they where the only thing not pixelated.
- All other stat-changing potions have to be used manually. I'd rather have them used automatically.
There are things it does really well too:
- Variety in color schemes of enemies depending on their elements.
- Thick hordes of many, many enemies.
- Lots of elements.
- Three types of gems of ALL elements you can fit in 3 different types of socket. All gems also have 3 levels. Finally, you can put sockets on items whenever you want, irregardless of level.
- You can make complex synergies with your attacks and set bonusses on your equipment.
- You can upgrade, reroll and reroll the numbers of all secondary stats without being locked to 1 afterwards.
- Endgame levels that get progressively more difficult. When you get stuck, you can lower the level of those levels with a scroll.
- I love the music, the forest has my favorite soundtrack of the game.
- Cool sound effects.
- You get a satisfying explosion when you get a killstreak, it would be cool if there were more tiers though.
- NO MOVEMENT SPEED CAP! YEAH FAST! CHILIDAWGS!

I recently discovered Magicite, a cool horizontal scrolling platform game blending some RPG and crafting elements, with combat and magic. I’ve always been a fan of the ‘sideways scroller’, from Super Mario Bros. to R-Type (I would add Jet Set Willy here but it’s room-based and not strictly a scrolling landscape…) and the simple mechanics of running, jumping and picking stuff up is forever engraved on the fabric of the gaming universe. The beauty here is the Magicite world is procedurally generated – not a new concept in games but it creates a wonderfully unique environment each time, albeit a very familiar one, with platforms, monsters, chests, trees and other resources with which to interact. Oh and Magicite is a Rogue-like game. So when you dead… you dead.
Each level in Magicite is one of a limited set of ‘biomes’ – forest, swamp, fire-land etc., each with different creatures and hazards. In single player, it can be fiendishly difficult particularly if you get a bad level generation (lots of monsters and not much space to manoeuvre) but once you get started and build up a stash of items, weapons and armour, you’re on your way. You can chop trees to collect wood and sticks, turn the wood into planks and the sticks into handles, turn the planks into blades and make tools and weapons: axes, picks and swords. Then you can mine stone, and iron, gold and diamond to make better tools and weapons… and armour. The better the tools, the more resources you get. The better the armour, the more likely you are to survive. And creatures can drop hide and pelt, food to eat and other useful things. Your character needs to eat regularly as well as keep their health topped up with potions.
At the end of each level is a choice of three doorways. The doorway you choose decides the next level so it’s best to stick to forests or swamps for the first few so you can build up resources and items, and have a fighting chance of making it to the end. In between levels are ‘towns’; safe (ish) areas for buying and selling, crafting metal bars and making armour and clothing. It is probably important to say at this point that Magicite has some vague archetypes for developing characters. You can focus on melee combat and make metal armour (fighter), or make bows and arrows and hide armour (ranger), or make wands and cloth armour (wizard); all these things can affect your stats, how much damage you inflict, and can take, how fast you move and your magical ability. Progression through levels also increases these things depending on your race and other abilities. To start with, you are limited to one race but a neat achievement system unlocks different races, variants, hats (oh yes) and companions which become available for your next run.
Another feature, one that is intensely annoying to start with, is the Scourge. If you spend too long on a level, a nasty monster turns up and beats the crap out of you – unless you get to one of the doorways. This gives a sense of urgency and propels you through the levels, creating a fast and often chaotic game. It has a multi-player mode which is when the game comes alive. Even playing with one other person improves the game considerably. One of you can focus on wood while the other is the miner, one can be melee while the other is ranged. The magic side is probably the most difficult to master but very powerful. You have to collect bugs (using nets made from sticks and spider webs) to make gems with which to craft wands. Some things need NPCs (metal bars, cloth) but most things can be combined by hand and on-the-fly as you fight through levels.
There are a few ‘bosses’ in Magicite. Destroying spider nests will inevitably spawn a brood mother – this is pain at the start but soon you will be destroying every nest you can find to increase your loot, and a final boss can be found on the last level. I’ve been lucky enough to complete Magicite a few times in multi-player (with a lot of help!) and this will unlock some of the powerful achievements. It would be great to see Magicite expand into a more complex game, especially the crafting which is very limited, while retaining its simple concept. More variety and unique items would be great, like the wand that generates zombies, as well as more weapons and armour. The game could also use a few new biomes with more variety but overall it’s a great concept, fun to play and challenging.

Beautiful and intriguing little puzzle game. Move and combine elements to rescue children that are lost in a snowy forest, full of strange and spooky characters. The art style is lovely and the music suits it perfectly, it feels a lot like a folk fairy tale. There are rogue-like elements so expect to die repeatedly and learn new recipes and secrets as you go - there's a lot of hidden depth to what you can discover.
The difficulty can be a little harsh at times, many of the rooms are dynamically generated, occasionally leaving you with unsolveable puzzles. The developers are addressing this by adding a 'normal' mode to make things a little easier. I've been playing on what will ultimately be 'hard' and would suggest sticking with that unless you really find you can't make progress.

This is a reasonably straightforward puzzle mechanic conveying some very complex and often dark concepts. The art style may be cute but the world is unforgiving - it is very possible to irretrievably trap a child you're trying to rescue, or fail to get to her before a hungry witch or spider does. This is part of the appeal, I think, and also part of the game's theme. Life is hard, and you can't always save everyone. You can't always achieve the things you think you're meant to. I think this is beautiful, but I also understand why they're implementing an easier difficulty level in a future update. The wall most players run into at Year 5 can be very frustrating.
The art and music provided by Brent Kobayashi and Daniel Simmons is deeply nostalgic for players of the late MMO Glitch.
This is definitely worth playing, though I must confess that before I started playing I had been prone to some gloomy moods already. Occasionally you run into some enemy creatures that whisper things echoing what might already be in your dark thoughts. I think this could go either way for different players - it can be helpful to work through those feelings with the game, or it might amplify them and make you feel a bit worse.

There are many things that we take for granted. Unless we are faced with an unpredictable event, we almost never have to worry about food or water not being available. Even if at that time, it isn’t quite affordable. What Ayo: A Rain Tale touches on is water. The one thing that we can buy bottled at the store and leave running in out sinks. Our young protagonist, Ayo, sets out to find water for her family. Sadly, the treacherous trail to water is more dangerous than it first seemed. Though, with encouragement from her family, Ayo can certainly do it.
With only her clothes and a water container on her back, our wits and the help of a few spirits will help you in the journey. Throughout your journey to get water, you will face many dangers. From thorns to wolves that only manifest based on what color is activated. With two traditional bosses that you have to face before you get to water. Luckily, there are two spirit twins on your side that will periodically grant to powers, such as the strength of a boar. The rest is mostly just platforming, which is sadly your enemy as well.
With platforming being the main aspect of the game, it is not as good as it should be. If the game is meant to be difficult, it is best to make the mistakes the player’s fault rather than the game’s. Such as with rogue-lites, you can’t make deaths in say The Binding of Isaac be because an undodgeable attack. Rather you will die because you didn’t dodge an attack fast enough or an item you picked up is working against you. While the platforming in A Rain Tale is not difficult, you will constantly be faced with Ayo having to grab onto ledges to pull herself up. There will be times where you know you can make a jump but Ayo decides to not grab onto the platform or Ayo can grab onto a platform that looks like she probably shouldn’t be able to. Either that, or a jump looks possible but is actually not. Perhaps some adjustments with the distances could’ve made it more believable throughout and to make sure Ayo can consistently grab onto ledges.
There are some puzzle aspects, mainly having to do with platforms that Ayo will only be able to stand on depend on the color activated. It’s not too difficult, with only the question on if you can platform through it kept on the mind. There are some complicated moves, such as having to switch colors midair, but it does it easy with practice. It is highly likely that you will be able to make it the first try, but mistakes from the game and you might still happen in late game.
Another aspect that can be improved on is the zooming in and out. Based on how big or tight a space is, the camera might pan in really close than pan out once you get to a more open area. There are some areas where this is no problem, however there are areas will cause the camera to be in a constant change of zoom. Making you wait a while before you can see what you are supposed to jump on next. Ultimately becoming annoying since it could have easily kept the same to avoid this. This also causes some inconsistencies with deaths. If you fall down a certain height, without the ground being viewable you will die, but at the same time if it is, you will live. If it even more annoying when you know it is there but you die where you shouldn’t.
I would be lying if I didn’t say that I quit the game for a while. In the first area, the caves you end up in right after falling in a well, there was this one jump that I just could not do despite it looking like Ayo could make it. I remember a collectable teasing me, but I kept missing it and sliding down to what is essentially the starting area. What made it worse was that some jumps that I made before, Ayo would suddenly not want to grab onto a ledge also causing my death. If I didn’t return, I would not have been to the more enjoyable parts, which does better with keeping otherwise frustrating jumps more on the player than the game. If you can get past the beginning, you will definitely want to be in it for the long haul.
One of the most puzzling thing about this game is the music, or the lack thereof. Music is present on the menu, but it stops once you get control and only returns for certain parts of the game. Relying on ambience is good, though hearing the same sound effects can be a little grating at times. When the music is present though, it does have charm. With the art, it looks nice. Being colorful, but at the same time believable that you are in whatever setting you are in. Adding little touches, just as Ayo’s clothes corresponding the color that is activated. The only thing that does not stand up to it is the backgrounds, which can be a little dull. Though with what seems to be a trend, it does get better towards the end.
Ayo: A Rain Tale certainly tries hard to bring that women and girls in Sub-Saharan Africa are sent to fetch water, having to carry a 40 pound container back, due to no access to clean water to light. In Sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia, many communities have no access to clean water. Travelling miles each day to find collect water and lug it back home is a task that falls overwhelmingly on women, taking away from time they could spend learning and helping their families. The UN estimates that women and girls across the world collectively spend 200 million hours each day collecting water—”a colossal waste of their valuable time.”
Ayo: A Rain Tale is a beautiful interactive metaphor that sheds light on this issue. You play as Ayo, a young girl from an unspecified African village on her daily commute for clean water. With an empty cannister on her back and the scorching sun overhead, she sets out across the savanna.
Despite a painterly art style, the first level is entrenched in realism: Ayo can jump only so far, and sun-baked rocks and trees form simple platforming puzzles, set against a backdrop that looks like a still-life painting of an African landscape. That starts to change when a dust storm whips up, a vision of a stampeding buffalo caught up in the swirls and waves, and Ayo falls into an underground network of caves.
As she looks for a way out, Ayo stumbles upon a pair of masked twins who offer words of encouragement. They also gift Ayo the power the mouse, allowing her to crawl through narrow spaces, and with that power, she’s able to continue working her way through the caves until eventually she gets out.
The rest of the game sees our hero travelling across increasingly fantastical environments, from a mystical veldt to a lava-filled subterrane to the very clouds themselves. She frequently runs into the twins, who have a new proverb and a new animal power for her each time: the rhino gives Ayo the strength to push boulders around; the antelope grants her a double jump; and the owl gives her the ability to change the colour of her shawl, in turn influencing the presence (or lack thereof) of blue and yellow platforms throughout each level.
On a purely mechanical level, this makes for a solid but not groundbreaking puzzle platformer. Ayo: A Rain Tale has you moving blocks around to open paths or neutralize hazards, jumping between platforms that crack and disappear if you stand on them too long, and alternating the existence of coloured platforms and walls that block your path. Collectibles take the form of droplets of water, some easily found along the way, and others that require bit more work. Stripped of context, it’s typical platformer stuff.
But you can’t strip the context from a game like Ayo: A Rain Tale, because it’s the context that gives weight and meaning to every action. This isn’t a fun, lighthearted platformer even though it plays similarly; this is a story of one girl’s struggle, and a metaphor for the real struggle that millions of real girls go through on a daily basis. Every hazard is representative of the real dangers faced by Africa’s water carriers, be it the heat, the dangerous wildlife, mosquitoes, windstorms, or precarious terrain.
Even rain—such a rare and precious commodity—can be a threat. In the last couple of levels, Ayo literally ventures into the clouds, where torrential rain and lightning get in her way. The final boss is the full force of stormy weather, brought to life as a buffalo spirit, that Ayo has to flee from. Even in its most fantastical moments, the game’s connections to the real word and the message it wants to tell are laid bare.
Likewise, the “powers” that Ayo gathers on her journey are symbolic of the perseverance and resilience of the water carriers. Each new ability is accompanied by the sharing of a proverb, acting as both a lesson in life and encouragement in the face of Ayo’s challenge—”Do not let what you cannot do tear your hands from what you can.” The thing that carries these women and girls through their journey is their strength, their grace, their intelligence, and their wisdom.
But the most potent and powerful moment in Ayo: The Rain Tale comes right at the end. You might consider this a spoiler, so skip a few paragraphs if you’re particularly concerned about such things. I think the power of this moment comes in experiencing it for yourself, not in it being a surprise, and it needs to be talked about to convey the full weight of the game.
Having fled the final boss—crucially, you don’t get to kill it, because you can’t stop a storm—Ayo begins her trek back to her village. At the start of the final level, the game suddenly pulls back to reality, and all the fantasy elements that had been slowly building up over the course of its run gone. Tired and now carrying a full canister of water, Ayo’s even less able to jump than before, and she walks with a pained sluggishness. She no longer has any of her powers. The fierce afternoon sun beats down, and spending too long in its gaze causes Ayo to faint, sending you back to the last checkpoint.
The last level is a lethargic, tedious trek from one piece of life-giving shadow to the next, and I say that with the highest praise. It’s lethargic and tedious (though not difficult or frustrating) because it needs to be to really drive home the point that the game is making. As beautiful as the fantasy metaphor spanning the rest of the game is, it’s when you suddenly lose all the things you’d gained and are thrown back into reality that Ayo: A Rain Tale has its strongest impact.
For anyone who sees games as more than just “mindless” entertainment, but as an art form with the power to change the world, Ayo: A Rain Tale is a game you don’t want to miss.

Let me start off by saying I stumbled across this game in the Steam store in my never-ending search for good loot-grinding games/ARPGs.  And this one is really fun and satisfying.
You pick between four classes: Berserker (melee fist-fighter), Warden (an archer, basically), Templar, and Warlock (combination of a mage and necromancer).  Each class has multiple talent trees you can invest points in that result in different active and passive skills and damage types.  I'd recommend trying them all; I typically dont like melee classes but I'm loving my Templar.
You start off in a building called the Chronicon, with a merchant and several other NPCs that offer services you can unlock as you progress.  You grab the first couple quests, and off to the dungeons you go.
Dungeons are filled with enemies (duh), loot from said enemies and chests (double-duh), traps, and mini-dungeon rooms.  Enemies can have different buffs applied to them or be a rarer quality which makes them give better loot or have different fighting mechanics; for example, one buff might make the monster explode after you kill it.
Loot is broken down into tiers: Ordinary (white), Enchanted (blue), Rare (Purple), Unique (Pink), and Legendary (Red).  As with any other game, higher tier loot offers better stats and sometimes interesting passives, such as a pet, or a floating orb that does damage to targets near you.  Loot also consists of Crystals (currency), multiple tiers of multiple colors of gems, and some other weird crystal currencies I haven't found a use for yet.
The game offers 5 (I think?) difficulties, and I've been played on the third/fourth highest right from the start and the game feels balanced enough.  Rare monsters and boss fights will have you chugging hp/mana pots like no other, so make sure you buy lots from the merchant NPC.  Boss fights actually start to have mechanics once you get past the first one, so be aware of their abilities, how the combo them, when they're going to use them, etc.
Local multiplayer is REALLY fun if you have a friend to speed-run through the dungeons with and build up monster-gibbing exp combos.
Overall this game is really fun, the pixel art is nice, and there are LOADS of puns and humor to appreciate (for example, a miniboss that's a Bat named Outahel.  Get it?  Or a treasure-hoarding goblin that drops a Unique ring, named Mollug (LOTR fans, anyone?).  The game is really charming, the music is relaxing and catchy, and the combat gets really fun.
That being said, here are my suggestions/cons:
-Early game combat is REALLY dull.  The first 10 levels or so on a Berserker and Templar are especially boring.  You do very little damage, the only attack skill you have sucks, and drains mana like no other.  They really need to do something about the early-game.  The game should be fun right from the beginning, not 10 levels in; and some of the people in the reviews have mentioned this as well.  However as soon as you get your 2nd/3rd skills, fights get really fun.
-The loot filter could use some work, and its buggy when you play local multiplayer.  When I use a keyboard and my gf uses a controller, after you defeat the first boss in the secondary zones I cant click the names of the loot to pick them up like 60-70% of the time like I usually can.
-More classes would be nice.  Even if you had to split the Warlock into a Wizard and Necromancer and give them each different skill trees, or add some kind of spear-wielding mid-range class, or maybe some kind of assassin.
-I'm not sure if it happens later on, but more loot that gives pets or active skills would be cool.
I really love what you guys have done with this game so far.  Excellent work!
OVERALL RATING: 9/10
