you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Imagine if the devs who made that infuriating puzzle game Triple Town turned it into an infuriating roguelike with match-three elements, permadeath, and randomly generated dungeons.  Because that's exactly what happened.  10/10 would scream at my monitor and throw my mouse across the room again.

is described as a Roguelike Puzzle game, in which you throw and move objects around with your magic staff to rescue children trapped in the Forest. Some puzzles are hand-crafted, but the majority are procedurally generated.
The Art and Music are great! Wonderful Art Style and the music is a nice addition to the levels.
Procedural generation is a double-edged sword. Yes, you're going to get rooms in which things are laid out in an easily-solvable manner, but you're also going to get rooms that are basically broken (or quickly made so by a bad move). For example, Bear Statues "stick" to nearby objects, so if you get an object in a corner behind a Bear Statue, you are pretty much out of luck. Good luck corraling six Deer or other animals (which move around on their own) to unlock a door. A single novice move can render entire areas of the map inaccessible.
The difficulty curve is brutal, and saps fun out of the game. Year 4 (of 15) seemed to be my Year of Death for a while, but with practice I've made it all the way to Year 8. Of course, Roguelikes have death, but after you die you should have some incentive to want to play again. In RNT, Death only occurs after several frustrating rounds of losing life/energy, and then when you are at your weakest, the Doom Spirits hunt you down and kill you. Where is the fun in that!?
The Save/Checkpoint system actively discourages you from using it - what is up with that?
I know people will argue that the game is about hard choices and you aren't intended to save every single child in each individual year - but that makes me wonder about the narcissistic sociopaths who lack empathy for children freezing to death in the Forest.
In summary,
. There’s potential here, but in Road Not Taken’s current state, I cannot recommend it.

It initially reminded me of long lost point and click adventure games when I first viewed the trailer videos. However, it quickly becomes apparent that with no clear direction or reliable strategy involved, it simply becomes a matter of randomly flinging groups of items together until you get a favorable reaction. These are then noted in an in-game journal, and you spend the rest of the game desperately flipping through its pages looking for some sort of advantage to be culled from the horrific assortment of hazzards and obstacles that work to make your gaming experience both futile and frustrating.
NOT ONLY are some levels seemingly impossible to pass, but "saving your progress at shrines" only means you respawn at the beginning of the current level... with NONE of your items or relationships SAVED!! Rogue-like indeed!
The designers do win points for a creative new type of game, great art, music and cut scenes.

When i first bought this game, i could not find the click to move option . The controls felt cumbersome. The developer advised me where the click to move option is. The game controls feel pretty good with the click to move option (like diablo). This game reminds me a lot of diablo 1. There is more skills for your player to use than in diablo 1 which I like. The game has a cool zombie undead theme for the enemies.

All the classes are unique and each have a VERY expansive skill tree as well as a talent tree, allowing you to customize each class and each character to play vastly different than the others. There are also multiple 'builds' that you can do with each character... do you want to be an AoE-mage that spews flames everywhere and turns the entire screen into a fiery-hell? Or do you want to be a single-target glass-cannon that can kill bosses in a few seconds with icicle shards? This game comes pretty close to having as much character-customization options as Path of Exile does... and that's saying a massive amount, since Path of Exile is the king in that department. There's honestly nothing negative to say about this game... you'll get WEEKS of gameplay out of it... the combat is very fast-paced and smooth as butter... the music is nice and relaxing... there's a very large range of different enemies to slaughter (including many level-bosses)... and there's more loot than you'll know what to do with. And all that for $10! You can't get better value... if the gameplay and aesthetic looks interesting to you, then don't wait... BUY THE GAME!

A strong entry into the ARPG LootGrinder genre. I've put hundreds of hours into Diablo III, I've played TorchLight 2 through two times and I've dabbled around in Path of Exile.
This game is honestly my favorite of them all. I held off on it for the longest time due to how "janky" it looked in the trailers and it's true, even diving in and playing, the visuals are nothing amazing.
But the gameplay soon swept me up. It was slow in the beginning but I told myself, all ARPGs are slow in the start, because they are. Once my character got solidly rolling along, I was having alot of fun with it and I still am. I'm gonna be putting many, many, many hours into this game for absolute sure. I'll go ahead and wager 100+ at the minimum.
The high point of this game to me is the loot. Loot rains from the sky in this game, you find tons of items everywhere, and while leveling I was always finding not just *better* items but items that felt exciting and like major upgrades. This guy gets it. The CORE of this genre is finding exciting loot and atleast in my opinion, this game answers that call beautifully.
I kept finding items that I'd stop and go:  "Oh wow, look at this one."
That is what makes this game shine.
The controls are good. Again, the visuals are not that great, this includes many of the abilities but there is no doubt the abilities respond and fulfill their functions as expected. Over all, this game is in a very solid state, atleast in my experience.
The dev is also all over the forums, he's been engaging with this community, honest, forthcoming and responsive to his playerbase's concerns, questions and problems. He is clearly invested in working hard on this game. He is one of those devs that is demonstrating how you handle this gig. He is doing a brilliant job.
The only thing that may be a turn off for some people is the dev has done alot of thinking about it and confirmed there will be *NO* Multiplayer. He did not plan for it in the start and that it is beyond his skills at the moment and beyond his time table to go back and try to accomplish it now. He has said if there is a Chronicon 2 to follow, it will come with online multiplayer right from the start but that  this one will not have it.
Beyond that, this is an absolutely great game once you look past it's graphics. You can't judge a book by it's cover, as they say, and this game is yet another reason you should never judge a game on it's initial looks. This is a real gem.

I'm writing this review based on two things:
- My 4+ years of playing Wurm Online
- The 16 hours I have played Wurm Unlimited
To start, Wurm is one of the best games I have ever played. The community in Wurm Online was always great, minus a few griefers here and there. It has one of the most in-depth crafting systems I have ever seen. And what makes it even better is that you can do anything you want to the world. Want to flatten that mountain or hill over there? Do it! (Although it might take you a while). Want to build a large canal connecting two bodies of water? You can do that! Want to convert a scorpion covered desert into a lush green forest? That can be done. This is probably the single most important reason I stuck with Wurm Online for so long.
Another thing I like about Wurm is the graphics. Yes, I know some of you are thinking "How can you like the graphics?".. But it's not so much about comparing it to current game graphics, obviously current graphics are superior. But that is something that gives this game character.
The next thing I want to talk about is the UI and controls. I've noticed a lot of people complaining about these, and I don't understand why it is such a bad thing. Yes, the UI might take a while to get used to, but once you get used to it, it isn't bad at all. Same goes for having to click and drag to look around. I understand most first person games do not do this. But once you get used to it, it isn't bad.
Last thing I want to address is the learning curve. I will admit, it is very steep. But it can help a lot if you play with someone who knows how to play. When I first started Wurm Online, I think it took me over a week of playing to finally grasp most of the basic concepts. But I am glad I didn't give up, because it is one of the most fun and relaxing games to play in my opinion. So my advice to all noobs out there, don't give up just because it's hard. If you work hard and learn, it will be very rewarding.
My summary of Wurm Unlimited:
Pros:
- Very relaxing.
- In-depth crafting system.
- Worlds are plenty large enough for a good amount of people.
- You can host your own servers for solo/playing with friends.
- You no longer need to pay for premium like in Wurm Online.
- You can have full control over the server settings, such as no upkeep, skill gain, etc...
Cons:
- For noobs, there is a steep learning curve.
- There are some bugs that I have ran into, such as mounting/dismounting horses crashing my game.
All in all, this is a good game for those who are willing to spend some time working in the game. For those who aren't, you can join a server with higher skill gain. Hope this review helps! Have fun and see you in Wurm!

Warmachine Tactics is a thrown together mess. If you plan to buy it, wait for it to be on sale. The campaign is hardly worth the effort as it is broken rather than genuinely difficult. The skirmish matches are OK, but the enemy AI leaves much to be desired. Think of this game as a multiplayer only rather than any kind of fulfilling single-player experience.
STORY:
The campaign is arduous and the difficulty mainly comes from the game being broken rather than genuinely hard. The campaign flip flops on which characters are critical to your success and nothing is more frustrating than seeing "Keep Jakes, Sarge, Rourke, and your Warjacks alive." However, several missions throughout the game only have "Keep Jakes alive." as your main objective. It gets incredibly frustrating when you have taken the enemy units apart and their one remaining unit runs past all our others to critically strike one your five or more essential characters, causing you to instantly lose the game after you may have put an hour or more into it. Though the campaign claims to sport an "extensive, story-driven experience"; I felt that it was sloppy and the story is one-dimensional and dull. Your character, Lt. Allison Jakes, proves her worth as she makes the worst tactical decisions possible and costs countless lives of her loyal men as they die for her petty revenge quest and foolish mistakes. Multiple times in the story, she defeats an enemy warcaster who then begs for their life causing her to stay her hand, only so that they can attack her while her men stand idly by. So many of the "story moments" in the game involve Lt. Jakes forcing her men to charge into completely avoidable conflicts causing them to die in droves as she celebrates her tactical genius. I hated Jakes by end of the campaign. But worry not all you fanboys, all of the other characters will constantly yammer on and on about how amazing and brilliant she is.
PRESENTATION:
The game has nice animations and I really enjoyed the look of each unit. However, glitches abound and many times the enemy characters can run straight through walls to attack you when you thought you were safe. During the enemy turn, the camera bugs out like mad, crudely snapping back to an overhead view of your troops before being wrestled away from you to watch an enemy character stroll towards you and snapping back into overhead again. The process can be nauseating and since you will usually be hilariously outnumbered (in the campaign), prepare to watch the sickening camera jolts for a good 3-5 minutes each enemy turn.
All who have played Warmachine know the importance of unit facing. If you haven't, then basically you get a higher chance of damage by hitting units in the back; also, you need to actually be facing a unit in order to attack it. Warmachine Tactics seems to think that it knows where your units should be facing better than you do; often crudely spinning your units to face a random direction after a completed movement. This forces you to micro-manage your units' facing after every single move.
Sometimes the textures and colors of the terrain completely blot out your unit movement graphics (the little colored halo on the ground that indicates where you want them to move to). This makes viewing countdown timers, movement grids, facing arrows, and many other essential graphical cues, nearly impossible in some levels.
The game also feels the need to prevent you from pausing it, ever. You can bring up a pause menu, but the game continues to run in the background. This can be very annoying even though with a turn-based game you don't need to worry about being attacked during your turn.
SUMMARY:
There is a lot more I could say about this game, but in the interest of brevity I will hold off for now. Just know that for $39.99, you will be getting little better than a late Alpha or early Beta stage game that is riddled with issues. Yes, the units look pretty and there are plenty of different units to choose from (go Stormblades). Unfortunately, this game shames its table-top counterpart by being sloppy and bug infested. I do enjoy playing the Skirmishes and the multiplayer is not bad. If you really love Warmachine, pick this up, but only when it's on sale.

I really want to like this game. I loved the tabletop wargame and was looking forward to this like you wouldn't believe. And as far as a port of the tabletop game...it works. Visually it may not be stunning, but it's faithful to it's source...the control system is easy to use and manages to reflect the tactical side of the tabletop game...so if you are playing against a human opponent, this does what it set out to do.
The campaign doesn't.
The campaign has a horrible habit of spawning opponents with no warning or indication, even repeat spawning, so the tactical side of each mission goes to the wayside. I think the mark of a good strategy game should be the ability to complete each map by being good at marshalling your forces and being a good commander...not by having played each map to the point that you know where all the spawns are and how long to hang around in one place. But repeat plays are the order of the day, here. You play the maps, get your butt handed to you by the enemy forces...not because they were better, but because they got a spawn...and then once you learn all the stuff that happens you play through and win. Your strategy is dictated by the timed events in each map, which leaves you with little actual room for innovative tactics.
The map that drove this home is one where your force is breaking through a gate, while being attacked by pursuing forces. Those forces are represented by increasingly tougher waves of spawned enemies, that will just continue to spawn until you move through the gate...so setting up a defensive line and weathering the storm is not an option...you're forced into a survive then run tactic.
And thats the problem. For a tactical game...the campaign wants you to do what IT considers the best tactic. Railroading is not fun in these kinds of game. So until that improves, I can't recommend it.

I was hopeful for this game, but they strayed too far from the original mechanics, devoted a larger percentage of their time to modeling than they probably should have while under optimizing it, and even cut core concepts.
I have not yet finished the campaign, but so far it feels far too much on rails and forced, what they want to happen will happen regardless of what you try to do to stop it (for story reasons). You get the units they give you, and must play according to what you are given to succeed. They don't explain things you are shown until they feel you need to know, in an early mission you are shown in-game cut-scenes of someone running around at least 2-3 times before they tell you anything about what you are seeing and why it is relevant and potentially too late for you to react. It feels like all of the events that occur are just sitting waiting for a certain turn number before it tells you about it, I was stuck on one mission waiting for a thing to occur because I'd done too well the turns before. The leveling mechanic was a great idea, but also felt very generic. I would have enjoyed earning experience on unit types and being able to customize my forces.
Overall, it feels like this was wasted potential. Stopping all bandwidth usage doesn't seem to help fix the server so you need to start again.... This happened a few times to use which ruined the run but we managed to finish the game on a run with no lag so this is also something to just be aware of on your end.

Turn Around is a game about a guy who has spent the last 20 years of his life living in the forest. One day, when coming home from his most recent hunt, the guy finds a note in his house that says "turn around". That's the entire plot behind Turn Around, and it's only from reading the description on the store page that this much is known. There's no dialogue, written or spoken, actually within the game, and the entire experience lasts 10, maybe 20 minutes if you're slow, at best.
The first couple of minutes is spent following a linear path to the house in the woods, but thereafter everything turns dark and you're tasked with finding 13 items scattered around a rather large map; once you've found all of the items, it's game over. There are no jumpscares, or any scary elements at all really, save for the two appearances of a rather cute looking monster; you don't get chased, you don't get scared, you can't die. The store page promises a "scary atmosphere", which is untrue, "high complexity for fans of hardcore" which is also untrue unless you think that finding 13 items is difficult, "good soundtracks" when the entire soundtrack is missing, and "nice graphics" when the bright graphics are blurry and the rest of the game is almost pitch black.
Given that the tagline for Turn Around is "survive at any cost", one would think that there would be some type of survival element to the title. Alas, that is not the case, and the graphics look a lot different in the actual game than how they appear in the screenshots on the storepage. This game is definitely not worth the $2.19 CAD when not on sale, nor the $1.09 I paid for it at a half-off discount. There's one comment from the developer in the forums stating that this title is for "high-end PCs", other than that they have gone silent; even in regard to the multiple people who were promised free keys. Another game by another scummy developer, shamelessly shoveling garbage onto Steam with no intent on bettering their skills.

Let me start off by saying this:
I consider the NBA2k series as one of the greatest gaming sports series of all time, and as a sidenote - I still consider NFL2k5 as a far better alternative to the modern EA equivalent. This should let you know that this review will be at least somewhat subjective, then again what review isn't?
NBA2k17 has many flaws such as:
- Vague (at times utterly game-changing) patch/hotfix notes. The vagueness actually goes as far as 2K implementing changes, without any notice whatsoever.
- An outdated engine. The game looks gorgeous in some areas, don't get me wrong, but it's rather evident that there's an older, somewhat polished engine in place, as opposed to a state of the art one.
- Incredible bad matchmaking for a game that was meant to be an entry to the e-sports scene. In a handful of modes, namely Pro Am (5v5s with the NBA ruleset in place) and My Park (a more arcade-like mode including 1v1v1, 2v2s, 3v3s and 4v4s) you're merely dumped in an instance/lobby, with outdated and time-consuming methods of matching up with people.
It's incredibly difficult, arguably impossible to match up against friends in the former game mode (Pro Am), as well as play against other teams on a schedule. A real headscratcher for any competitive online experience.
- A steady flow of game-breaking gllitches like getting kicked out of lobbies, mid-game even. I don't have to explain why the latter is infuriating especially.
- The obvious intent of baiting people into buying virtual currency to quick-level their characters. There's a definite increase in their willingness to go the extra mile for that purpose as well. More animations are VC locked, as well as a plethora of other game altering mechanics. Not to mention that all of the above got more expensive in the process. Make no mistake, this game is a real grind. A fun one, nontheless.
- Last but not least, there's a good number of cheaters on PC. It's difficult to be exact with the numbers, but with the introduction of 2K's archetype system, it became a little easier to tell who's who. It gets really obvious when builds pull off things they technically shouldn't be able to, or pull through on terrible plays with a consistency that's unheard of. Not to jump the gun on this subject though, this happens occasionally. Different story when it becomes the standard with some characters.
There's little to no intervention or support from 2K on this matter, either. If you can't deal with cheaters and modders whatsoever, do not purchase this game.
Onward to the mechanics:
- The archetype system.
I'm torn on this. I can see where they meant to go with it, with the introduction of the e-sports aspect and all, but seeing so many things about the game don't click with that notion as of yet, it all kind of falls apart.
You're basically a glorified roleplayer, depending on what difficulty you play at naturally.
(To give some perspective on the impact of the difficulty setting;
Rookie - you hit everything, you can do everything, attributes and badges aside. You're a god. Your teammates are the extention of you, and they'll become 70% shooters from everywhere on the field.
On the other hand, your opponents cannot do ♥♥♥♥ all. They'll miss open middies, open 3s (at max ratings), they'll fumble the ball at every turn.
You can't lose, even if you tried deliberately you would have to throw the ball away at every possession.
Pro - Same as the above, FG% are a little lower on your side and a little higher on the opponents side, they also become more aggressive and they're not as turnover prone anymore.
Allstar - Pretty balanced, we're getting closer to a simulation now. You still hit shots at a higher rate than you should, as well as your teammates, the opponents aren't as much of a no-show and play more according to their stats. However, if you're proificient at the game already, this difficulty will lead to a blow-out every time.
This difficulty is also where a few headscratcher misses on your behalf creep in. No biggie. Yet.
Superstar - Many would argue that this is the most balanced difficulty of them all, and I would have to agree. 2K equalizers and sliders kick in as to hold you and your team below a superhuman FG%, the opponents are better at locking your attempts down, and score at a good pace in turn.
HOF - A very frustrating difficulty in my eyes. Not because I can't win. A majority of good players will still go out as NBA champions at the end of the day. Fact of the matter is however, that it becomes overly obvious that the odds are stacked highly against you.
Throw a pass into the post? Your big's matchup will slide around and snatch that♥♥♥♥♥♥mid-air. The passing lanes get clogged up real quick, inhuman reflexes force TOs on many occasions.
An opponent gets the ball somewhere near the post? Automatic freethrows, if not and1s en masse.
Open 3pter? Better be rated at 94 for that shot.
And so forth.)
Getting back on subject with the archetype system. It's lost its identity online, because at this particular point, every build is capable of doing everything. Perhaps not JUST as well the specialized counterparts, but let me put it this way:
if a max sized point playmaker is better at slashing due to on-the-ball speed and handling than a slasher
if all archetype can hit 3s from corners with mindboggling success (think 50% and upwards), despite a 30 rated 3pt shot
...something's amiss.
The real problem with that is that everything sort of...becomes the same in terms of gameplay. Can't gamble on non-shooter archetypes, because everyone can shoot. So if you defend every build the same, as in can't give space because of the threat of a jumpshot, can't guard up too close because they'll blow past, it kind of defeats the entire idea of the archetype system.
- Height playing a HUGE role.
Listen to me, if you are undersized, don't even TRY and drive if the lane isn't 100% clear.♥♥♥♥♥♥ even if that's the case, chances are you'll get chase-down blocked or swiped from a big.
It's like finishing around the rim stats don't even matter on drives. Are you big, are you fast? Go ahead and drive even through contact. Are you small(er)? Don't, even if you're rated 40 points above the former in the respective attribute.
Onto the good points;
Nothing comes close to this game in terms of simulation and gameplay value. The controls feel responsive and fun, shooting mechanics are enjoyable and intuitive. Everything comes together well, and when you play career games, on the right difficulty...there's just no game that comes close to that feeling of being a part of a bigger simulation.
Presentation is fantastic, maybe a bit repetitive if you've played the predecessors like I have, but they're still very informative and immersive.
So despite all of 2k17's flaws, if you love basketball, if you love good sports games, enjoy simulation or perhaps a well tuned presentation, this game is for you. Especially when it comes at a discount ;).

First off, DO NOT pay $40 for this game. Given its current state, it still feels like a Beta version.
That said, the gameplay is actually fun, and the story is pretty good. It's a decent digital version of the tabletop game. It's not an exact port, but the changes work quite well for a video game format.
The major problems with the game are technical, and those can (hopefully) be fixed. The UI is clunky and unforgiving. It's not terrible, but there are certainly times you find yourself cursing the game because you committed to an action, only to find that you what you did isn't what you really wanted to do. In a game with no mid-game saves, those mistakes can be lethal. (Note, I'm not talking about tactical errors, but those times where the UI gives you a false perspective of what will happen.)
The graphics can be a problem, especially on snowy maps, where you can't even see where your units can move. You spend a lot of time squinting at the screen, moving the camera for better angles, and ultimately guessing that where you click will actually work as you intend (even with the grid on).
It's also sub-optimized, so the game takes up way more space and memory than I think it should, compared to similar games. This is another reason why I avoid kickstarter or early access for video games. When the money is collected before the product is finished, there's less emphasis on creating a fantastic game and then putting it to market, but rather trying to release an acceptable product and pocketing whatever's left over.
Overall, though, I'm enjoying the game. The developers are still working on it, too. Hopefully they'll finish cleaning up the bugs, graphics, and UI problems before they decide it's not worth the added expense. In the meantime, though, don't pay full price; its just not worth it right now.

This game is probably one of the most fun games I have ever touched.
In general, you start out with 1 race, and a set of skills. You spawn in a forest where you have to get resources to survive and not die. Later on you unlock more races, hats, variants and things as such that give you stat boosts or special perks.

There is difficulty to this game, as not only are the enemies hard but there is also permadeath. Permadeath would pretty much be the only thing I don't like about the game, but thats more of an opinion, as permadeath in a game is not wrong its just some people like it and some don't. But having permadeath actually makes you want to play the game more and more to get further than where you were before.
If I were to compare this game, I'd say it would be very close to something like terraria, but I don't usually like comparing games. Why? Because games like this are unique. This game is its own thing, nothing like I have ever played before. It showed me a whole new type of platformer and I am just so happy this game fell into my steam library.
So, would I recommend this game? Certainly. Definitely worth the price!

NieR:Automata is an action role-playing video game as stated by wikipedia. Switch to my personal opinion regarding this game, as for me PlatinumGames did very good job on mixing Hack n' Slash genre with A-RPG elements on it.
Gameplay
NieR:Automata delivering top notch fast pace combat quality that testing both reflex and speed of the eyes to the player. HUD menu can be accessible conveniently on real time while on Combat, provided with upgradable skills, perks, and Pod as companion while combat. Combat system is something that i can safely said overshadow combat system in FFXV, mind you i played both game btw, but only nearly 50 Hours on FF XV, and NieR only around 14 Hours and not discovering all weapon and style yet in game. Combat feels just feel great with soundtrack playing on background to keep it more dope. Aside from greatness of combat system there is also minor weakness for me, Camera system. Camera view system can be bad sometime, majority in-game exploration camera center you as 3rd Person View, on Narrow path camera will switch as Side scroller and not centering your movement as long as you don't reach end of screen, combat while on side scrolling view can be pain sometime. With Speed of combat while side-scroller view mode giving you hard time to track protagonist movement on screen, plus character looks smaller on side-scroller view, but it making player easier to navigate and not deviate on mission from the path.
9.5/10
Soundtrack
This is the best part of this game, the Soundtrack i meant. Soundtrack just accurately played on each situation, Calming & relaxing music on base camp/bunker, Soundtrack while exploring City Ruins just beautiful and mesmerizing, then come to Soundtrack themes with each bossfight it just purely amazing. Every soundtrack played on Bossfight, really pumped the player  on action while combating. But most of time, sad emotion driving soundtrack played in-game.
10/10

So I spent probably 8 hours playing with a friend today (the 2nd or 3rd day I've owned the game) since we were both off of work and I gotta say I have mixed emotions about this game. It was hyped up to be amazing and I don't see what all the hype is about.
First of all, unless you play on the fastest speed setting, it is PAINFULLY slow and boring. It's even kinda boring with the speed all the way up.
You don't really have any control over battles whatsoever, your production of certain things inexplicably dips down into the negative for no apparent reason all of the time, there's never enough energy / minerals to do anything, the research available seems completely random, which means you can easily get screwed, and on top of all of that, by the later part of the game some race from outside of the galaxy came in and started dominating everyone. I thought I was pretty secure with a fleet at around 30k power and this race of creatures had multiple fleets at ~60k... there's no possible way to defend against that.
For most of the time you're just sitting there all bored waiting for things to be built and for time to pass. The graphics are 'meh' at best, the music is 'meh' at best (and very repetitive as this game is usually played for long periods of time), and there's a lot of gameplay mechanics that either don't make sense or are hidden away and even with the full tutorial on, you never get an explanation as to how and why many things work they way they do.
I'm super glad I got this in the Humblebundle monthly deal because if I had spent full price on this I would be asking for a refund in a heartbeat. It's not 'bad' per se - I just don't get the appeal. Who wants to sit for hours and hours slowly building up a civilization, just to get r@ped by impossibly strong invaders near the end? Game last forever, even on the smallest map size, and generally speaking the entire experience is a bore.
I am sure that for people who actually enjoy this type of game, it's great... but holy cow is this a tedious and boring experience for me... and this is coming from someone who actually likes many types of games that most people consider boring. If you are thinking about buying this game and you have no experience whatsoever with this type of game, let me break it down for you in a nutshell:
For the first SEVERAL hours you will be learning how to play the game as it is very complex, and even when the tutorial hints are over there are many things that are not made clear, things don't make sense at all sometimes. The gameplay is painfully slow and combat comes down to having the larger fleet / superior technology. There's no skill involved in terms of the battles... it's just a pure numbers game. I think that if you're a fan of really LONG games like Risk and want to play this against friends with no AI or fallen empires, you'd probably like it, but personally I feel like I just wasted 18 hours of my life in the hopes that the game would eventually get good. It didn't.

About halfway through was when I noticed I was having fun. My bad mood started not right away, but maybe somewhere in the first couple hours. I'd just come off a long stint of BL2, where the jokes still make me chuckle after the 8th+ time. I could write this whole thing comparing the two, and that's been done already, so you'd just be hearing that crap with my own spin.
The Borderlands series has my heart in a deep way. It's the game that brought my wife and I closer through Coop LAN gameplay, online with old friends who live too far for us to hang IRL. My bad mood wasn't bad because I was surprised by what I was experiencing. I'd read a few grumpy reviews and I always listen closely to the hurtful words people use about these controversial titles that maybe thousands of people pour their efforts into bringing alive.  The extreme words spewed by folks who probably don't understand the trials of assembling AAA titles that carry loads of community pressure. When people use extreme words about something they themselves did not create, then, huzzah.
I want to say a lot. I want to praise it for the mood change it gave me. It made me realize that I was expecting it to entertain me in a similar way as the previous titles. It's a little bit like the difference between Weezer's Blue album and Pinkerton. Pinkerton sort of dissappointed me when I first heard it. It didn't have an 8minute track that I'd fallen asleep to in a dental office and had a short fantasy about skateboarding away from a pack of storm troopers.
Pinkerton introduced a tone shift, key elements that opened me to the voice and mind of Rivers Coumo. Took me away from the mostly joyful sounds put to, often easily overlooked, actually saddening words. It was a positive sound to some heavy language. Like someone getting the shirt torn off their back on the first day of school, but they still show up and smile for the class photo. That's Borderlands 2.
The Pre-Sequel, like Pinkerton, isn't trying to fake it anymore. It's still charming, beautiful, seemingly unpolished, and maybe so. The darkness amidst that charm is a real feeling, it sings to an aspect I wasn't anticipating.

I watched the steady stream of negativity that seems to follow this game. I've been an intermediate players of warmachine, and really love the world/theme that the Iron Kingdoms titles have to offer. When the game came on sale, I decided to give it a try (despite the enless pages of negative reviews). I gave myself two days to try the game before writing the review. I really wanted to see how the game took me, and not just offer my initial feelings. So... the pros.
Pro's:
-(Gameplay) The game is a great computer adaptation to the warmachine franchise. It gives you a real sense of strategy and tactical requirement to play.
-(Gameplay) The units are very well modeled and armed after the tabletop. This allows a player who is familiar with the game world to get an immediate feel for how the units are supposed to play.
-(Gameplay) Above all else, once you learn the UI, this game is FUN. That's right, FUN to play. This isn't a CoD style action game, but more a kin to UFO style combat. Your decisions and dice rolls will have immediate consequences in your battles.
-(Campaign) The landscapes of the game are fantastic. It's crowded and but believably built.
-(Campaign) The characters of the campaign are diverse, offering a variety of witty, funny, and serious moments to the game.
-(Multiplayer) I really wish the game had co-op featuers. If not for the campaign, perhaps for larger multiplayer matches.
-(Multiplayer) I played a single match between kador and cignar. The match was very pitched and until the end, we weren't sure who was going to win.  Ultimately, an assassination run by my charger clinched the victory (combined with a disruption pistol on my opponents dreadnaught).
-(Multiplayer) The range of units and unit synergy are fantastic. And they keep releasing new units, which will further change the dynamics of the matches. From disruption bolts, head-butts, and stunning lightning bolts, there's seemingly dozens of combinations to change a dire situation into a chance!
Cons-
O.K... There are a lot of cons. As I'm sure you've all read. But the one things that I'd like to point out. These Cons can be FIXED. This game feels EARLY, like a beta. Hopefully, the developers will continue to smooth out the engine.
-(Gameplay) I really wish that you could CHOOSE the upgrades your units/warcasters get at the end of the mission. It would be a nice way of customizing the hero to your own preferences.
-(Camera) The camera is terrible. You frequently find yourself needing to change your angle and rotation to get a good view of whats going on. Sometimes, things are going on that are obscured by terrain when your opponent is moving. I found the arrow keys better for moving around the battlefield than the mouse commands
--Objects(Like buildings) can get in the way of your issueing move orders, even if you do not SEE a structure in your way. It's due to poor clipping during object creation. Measure twice, move once. You may need to change your angle before continueing your move.
--WHY does the camera rotate around beneath your god-view feet, and not rotate around where your focused? Developers, please fix this...
-(UI) The UI is also... horrible. It's takes a while to get used to, and offers little to no explaination as to why things can't happen.
--There is no seamless change from your turns movement to out of turn movement (energize or quick work).
--There is no explaination to which unit you are currently "stuck" on (untill you've ended ALL it's phases/turns). There may be a slight hue to the circle below it, but that's not much to go on.
--The UI takes up too much of the game screen. It may have pertinent information (it usually does), but it also impedes the atmosphere of the game.
-(Grapics) I realize you saved a ton of money by using still art for the cut-scenes... but really... you think it would kill you to have moving mouths and a believable conversation going on?
-(BUGS) The game is very buggy...
--Units sometimes graphically face the wrong way.
--The game will crash if you complete conversations or objectives in the wrong order (In your very first mission, I crashed my game when I ran to activate Bandit with my warcaster earlier than the game wanted me to (Since I know in game that warcasters can activate jacks). I bypassed the first conversation (about being attacked) by fleeing straight to bandit (where is bandit conversation) and when the first conversation finally happenned, it crashed the game. So please, treat this game like a story, and follow the flow of the game.
Conclusion: I'm recommending this game. It's a diamond in the rough. Some very... rough... rough. The problems that exist in the game are superficial and can easily be learned and avoided. The core mechanics of the game are still very fun, and if you're into this style of tabletop emulation, I highly suggest trying it. It's all the better with friends. And please, wait a day or two before writing a review out of anxiety. The UI isn't impossible, it's just not intuitive.

TLDR: Awesome game! Free to Play! Needs more players...It's only a "dead game" if you don't play it.
The Good:
The artstyle is gorgeous, the spell effects are visually stimulating, the character combat animation is smooth (right up there with WoW and GW2), it's free form combat system and combat telegraph (with the option to auto-target/ tab target) is a breath of fresh air from playing so many tab targetting MMORPGs; the lore is familiar (coming from  playing WoW for so long) but the execution is interesting.
Wildstar has Expeditions, which are like solo-able dungeons, with their own intro/outro cinematic that has a nice black and white TV sci-fi feel to it. There's actual 5-man Dungeons that require the usual tank, healer and 3 DPS; and then there are 25-man Raids which is beyond my skill level right now.
The Free To Play version of the game is it's base verson of the game the way it was meant to be played, with the subscription version giving you more rewards and XP but absolutely no gameplay advantage over the Free to Play player.
Wildstar has one of he best In Game Stores I've seen in MMO's, which focus mostly on cosmetics, vanity items (armor dyes, pets, mounts, decorations for your house...), and also XP and reward boosts, but no pay to win items what so ever.
You have a player house, A.K.A, Sky Plot, because it's literally a plot of land floating in the sky that you can build on, and it's given to you for FREE at level 15 (or you can buy it and have one at level one, it's all preferense) which is, as far as I know, the only way you can get rested XP in the game, and you can tailor it to your enjoyment. You can have NPC's, buildings, trees, crafting stations, mining nodes, things that give more more rested XP, mini-games, and the customization is leaps and bounds over what I've seen in other games (WoW garrison, GW2 guild hall, EQ2 guild hall, SWOTR space ship)
The game has a sense of humor, and even though some of the story is dead serious (I mean, HATE the other faction, serious) the gags, jokes, and subtle pokes at other games are enjoyable.
Tutorials. it's hard for a new player, starting a fresh character, to get lost in this game. You have a tutorial that shows you the game mechanics (WSAD, jump and double jump, riding a vehicle, combat, dodging, interrupts, etc...), gives you the plot, and a little bit of lore. Then you have arrows that point you in the right direction, quests that are linear when it needs to be (i.e.: leading you from one zone to another, and building a storyline), and quests that introduce you to new avialable aspects of the game (quests to show you around the city, introduce you to the Skyplot, tells you how to craft, etc..)
Scaling dungeons at level cap, means you can run dungeons with your lowbie friends.
XP after level 50 is converted into currency!
Rental Mounts! This is the first MMORPG, nay, first game that I've played with rental mounts, which are cheap (15 silver, cheap), that you can use for 1 hour.
The classes are interesting. There's 6 classes, all with unique animations, spell effects, rotations and so on. You have your usual, the Warrior and Stalker (or Rogue, if you play WoW), then you have the slightly unique classes: Engineer, a class with a big gun and a lot of pets (robots), but doesn't completely rely on those robots. The Esper, who's kind of like a mage, but uses mental powers, has the option to be long ranged or short ranged (melee range), and has temporary, but effective pets. The Spell Slinger, which is more like a mage, but with two pistols; and finally the Medic which you would think is the healer centric class, but shocks you with probably the most flashy spell effects in the game.
Friendly player base. This one's a double edged sword, but, because the current player base is so small, everybody seems to be more friendly, and are generally very helpful.
Daily rewards! Just for logging in you have a reward you can claim, that's mostly cosmetic, currency or crafting material.
Level up rewrds! Every couple levels you get a set of useful itmes like armor, weapons, buffs, boosts, etc, which helps you level up and becomes something else to look forward to while leveling.
Paths. Aside from your Class, you have Pathes which can be tailored to your gameplay: Soldier, if you like killing things; Settler, if you like clicking things and building things; Scientist, if you like lore and background info; and Explorer, if you like exploring (and jumping). AND they all come  with their own rewards and buffs.
Random (slightly) Challanges that are somewhat rewarding!
The Bad.
If you like the realistic graphics and proportions some MMO's are leaning towards (FFXIV, EOS, BDOL) then this game is gonna hurt your eyes.
The in-game cinematics are ok, not as good as PIXAR, but close to Disney's Fairies or Clone Wars. It's good, but the age of it is showing.
Low population (Steam Charts has it peaking at a little over a thousand players online, currently), which makes group activities hard to do, and group activities plays a HUGE part past level cap.
NCSoft.
If you make multiple Wildstar accounts (under different email addresses, of course) be prepared to go several days appealing bans with NCSoft, who doesn't seem to keep track of who they banned and who's ban they just recently lifted (in the last week, I've been banned maybe 10 times [being banned, having the ban lifted, then being banned again], and am currently appealing another ban.)
The UI gets a little cluttered, especially if you resize your window or UI.
Most of Wildstar's addons are outdated. It seems like most of the people managing the addons for Wildstar just up and left around 2014-2016.
Because most of Wildstar's player base left around 2014-2016ish, most of the guides for WIldstar is also that old and outdated.
BUGS: It's probably a good idea to macro /reloadui, because you'll be doing this more than you should have to. Sometimes the tooltips won't show correctly, /reloadui, sometimes you can't click on anything, /reloadui, sometimes you hit the "Exit Game" or "Switch Character" button but it doesn't let you log off...Alt+F4.
The directional arrows that point you in the direction of the quest is doing just that and only that, which means you have to find your own way there, even if that means running around a mountain, into a cave, pass the opposite faction's guards.
Wildstar's peaks (when the most people play) really matters. Because it's player base is so small, playing at 11am (populated) and playing at 11pm (not so populated) will have a big effect on your game play (as far as group content goes) if you're not in a good guild.
The Ugly.
Wildstar is still suffering from whatever happened between the developers and it's player base back in 2014ish, and so has a lot of people hating on the game, even if the game is (from what I hear) much MUCH better than it was back then.
"This is a dead game" is what everybody will tell you, driving you away from experiencing the game yourself.
Yes, it's a dying game, but the fact that you won't play the game because "it's a dead game" is actually what's killing it!
My verdict, as an average devoted casual gamer: Play Wildstar! I hated it (even marked it as "Not Interrested" in Steam) when it first came out, but after returning a few weeks ago, I've been having a blast! The kind of blast I haven't had since levelling in The Burning Crusade, when I started to seriously play WoW.
The leveling is rewarding, the rewards are satisfying, the zones are spectacular. It's like what the Narrator said in "Wildstar Features Trailor" on Youtube, "The only thing missing...is you."

So, I have to say a few things about the game itself before going on to speaking about the PC-port, so just hang in there and try to get through the whole review (or just read the interesting bits, your choice).
NieR Automata is a fantastic game and there's no denying that.
Not does it only feature a great story, beautiful soundtrack and gorgeous graphics, it's only got various kinds of different gameplay from different gaming genres mashed into one game, and it's actually done really well, creating a truly unique experience.
Even though the main action within the game may get a tad bit repetitious, it's still really fun and does stay fresh for the most part by introducing new sorts of enemies as you progress within the game. Yeah, there IS a rather annoying mini game that disturbs the combat sometimes, but I do not exactly see it being a problem myself. It's only a very small section of a otherwise great game full of all kinds of different content for you to explore, and who knows, maybe you'll actually like that section as well. At least I did every now and then when it wasn't in my face all the time.
I also really enjoyed NieR's interesting take on the usual skill tree mechanics with their rather unique Plug-In Chips, which basically work like items that affect your gameplay and you can buy or sell them. What I really personally found interesting was how these chips also included things related to your HUD and UI, which makes it possible to make it even more challenging for you if you feel like the game is too easy for you even on hard difficulty.
Speaking of difficulties, this game handles different difficulty levels really well. Not are they already very well balanced for what kind of challenge you might want to experience with the game, you can adjust it a bit more to your liking by editing the chips I mentioned before.
I could keep on going about how good this game is in several other ways as well, but I think you've already gotten the grasp on how I feel about this game and how it actually does have lots of good points, so I'll just leave the rest for you to experience yourself.
Honestly, this game is probably one of the best games I've gotten to play in a long time (or maybe even in my whole life), and it's definitely worth every cent that it costs.
Especially since you can easily get multiple dozens of hours of fun by playing through all the 26 endings (trust me, it couldn't be more worth it as together they complete the story and the first ending is just the beginning for the actual game).
But as you can see on the other reviews, the PC-port for this game isn't really the greatest port out there amongst all the games on Steam or PC in general.
It has lots of issues with it, and a few of them are not small issues at all.
Luckily, most of these issues might not even bother you (like they didn't me) and for the most part it runs very well with a stable FPS (There are some frame drops when there's lots of stuff happening at the same time), but you will definitely notice these four main issues that people seem to have with this game's PC-port.
1. You can not run this game 1080p in fullscreen mode.
Yes, this game actually suffers of this problem and it's probably the biggest issue I can see with this port. But don't worry, you can still get around it by either using an app called Windowed Borderless Gaming which makes it possible to technically run the game fullscreen by having the game on windowed mode without borders...
Or you can always download a mod called FAR (Fix Automata Resolution), which fixes this issue along with many other smaller ones.
So technically, this issue isn't too much of a problem in the end if you're willing to deal with it quickly yourself (though that doesn't make it any more acceptable for the PC-port to have an issue like this).
2. The cutscenes are very laggy and stuttery for some reason on the PC-port compared to the console versions.
This can break your immersion and damage your gaming experience quite a lot, but if you're like me, you might not actually care too much about that after playing it for some time.
3. The controls for PC are not exactly good.
The controls for gamers who prefer using a keyboard and mouse are not simple or good.
They'll most likely leave you confused for some time and make the action parts of the game also feel way less satisfying...
But I wouldn't really recommend playing this without a controller anyways, it's pretty obvious that the control schemes were designed with controllers in mind, so you definitely should play it with a controller if possible.
4. There's lots of graphics hiccups everywhere around the game that might annoy you quite a lot (at least it did annoy me). Good examples of these errors would be things turning invisible when they should be visible and some textures rendering badly and looking awful (and I know that it looks like that 'cause of a some kind of issue since in the same location at a different time and it looks great).
In the end, I feel like this game is overall a great purchase on every platform, but I would recommend to pick up the console version instead if you have a console.
Though even with all of it's smaller and bigger issues, it can be a great experience on the PC as well (especially since some of the flaws are fixable by mods already, and the rest will most likely be later on as well, or so I hope at least), so do try picking it up on at least some platform if you like games like this as I'm sure you'll love this game.

This is literally a masterpiece and certainly not only a GOTY but a game to be on the shortlist of best games ever. It manages to keep a very interesting plot (that spans multiple gameplays) and multiple game styles without getting too repetitive despite being a hack-an-slash at its core. I would probably like to have less "hacking" (second and third playthroughs) though.
Music, visuals, characters, plot and the incredible ever-changing perspective make this game unique, and the New Game+ is not really a repetition, but a NEW game, you NEED to play this game at least 3 times to really unlock all its secrets (you play as different characters on each New game, as well see things you didn't on the previous ones).
Seriously, how original can be a game that, if you die on the OPENING SEQUENCE (that takes around 1h and you cannot save), it says "You died, makind is lost" and ROLLS THE CREDITS AT FAST FOWARD and return to the opening screen, AWARDING you an "ending" (I think that is W ending). I was mad I died but immediatly laughed and new this was going to be an awesome game, and yes, it can happen anywhere in the game, you can permanently die and unlock a new ending (well, then you load the previous save game, but you get the gist).
Keyboard controls are OK too, would be best with a controler only because using the mouse on the 2D segments is weird, which is perfectly fixable by mapping the second stick to the keyboard too (right-side arrows is default already), but as you can see I clocked a lot on this game all on keyboard+mouse, I even came to prefer it (on controler it is hard to control your character, the camera and the pod simultaneously).
7/5 WILL play at 15 FPS the ending sequence on my 750 Ti over and over (yeah, it is a lower-than-minimum video card, yet the game plays beautiful on 720p and I had ZERO crashes on all that gameplay time you see above). I played over 85h and had zero crashes/bugs/issues, am I the exception? I don't think so.

People have mixed feelings about this game, understandable. It is buggy, glitchy and some of the systems are downright broken, but does that mean a game as fresh as this should be hated so badly? I sure as hell shouldn't think so. Brand new and green as grass, Warmachine: Tactics is a great RTS game, a turn based strategy set in the wonderful steampunk universe of the Iron Kingdoms, in particular detail, the amazing boardgame WARMACHINE. Whitemoon Dreams have evidently researched their stuff, or they've got a couple of players in their dev team; cos the attention to detail in the characters, scenery and system is fantastic.
Warmachine: Tactics has you play as one of the 4 main factions
- The imperial Khador
- The nation of Cygnar
- The divine Protectorate of Menoth
- And the nightmare empire of Cryx
Each with their own skills, attributes and tactics. WT has you re-live the game in digital form unlike any FPS could ever do. Gameplay-wise, it is fun, being turn based, you really need to think about placement and formation. No take-backs and you can easily be steamrolled by simply facing the wrong direction. This promoted challenge makes every game fun, and makes you feel like a boss once you've rick-rolled your opponent. The game brings to life all the aspects of the boardgame; hardass infantry, magically skilled warcaster and most importantly, the 12ft tall, steam-driven (soul-driven if its Cryx) and EXTREMELY p*ssed off mechs we lovingly call warjacks.
You create your own loadouts, out of any of the factions, assign it a controlling warcaster, then load it with whatever you want. Want loads of fast infantry? Go speedy! Want slow, but heavy dudes? It'll take weeks to advacne, but the effects will be so worth it. And if you want a list featuring only warjacks? That's the way to go; paint the map with scrap. The game has a great and simple interface system, allowing you to choose movement and combat actions and special abilities (if they have any). Warjacks even have power attacks from the board game too! That means you can push, slam, headbutt and even throw whichever target your warjack is in combat with and doesn't particularly like (which should be every one of the sorry b*stards). Graphics are unreal, I mayself play them on a lower setting so my PC can cope, but it can still run at 25-30fps. being a TB RTS, its kinds your saving grace, if it was like DoWII, you should have bought a new PC before getting this, but wither way, WT uses the Unreal 4 engine, making the game beautiful on my brother's PC.
The campaign is...meh. But then again, I haven't seen much of it, so I'll correct myself, its started off meh. Multiplayer is great and fun, and every player is known to be extremely friendly. Speaking of ciommunity, Whitemoon is literally commiting EVERYTHING to this game, meaning weekly patches, confirmed DLC units and armies even months before their release, and hundreds of FAQs answered and bugs treated per day. This game has been slandered as broken, unfinished and a misfire, I consider it more of a developing project, that will in time be absolutely outstanding. I myself have had no problems, so I can count myself lucky, but to all those Tacticians out there, just hold on, the game you deserve will be done soon.
Being a Warmachine player on the tabletop, along with my brothers, this game was an absolute steal. Even if you aren't a fan of Warmachine,. but have a love for tough, satisfying turn-based action, then this is for you, this is no-holds barred brutality! This is adrenaline injected metal-on-metal grinding hopped on steroids!
This is WARMACHINE: Tactics, the game that kicks so much a*s they had to name it in capitals!
(so far) 7/10

It's pretty good. Of course, this is early access or whatever you want to call it so there are a few bugs and the game isn't polished - the AI is very unpredictable and broken, the RNG is often massively frustrating, graphics are a bit flickery and so on - but the core is pretty solid.
I play the tabletop game and I can say for sure that although this isn't a 100% rule-for-rule stat-for-stat remake of the tabletop game, it captures the spirit of it very well. A few things are different here and there and a few of the most popular units in the tabletop game are unfortunately missing (Though, with the promise of paid-for (boo!) additional units and characters later) but overall it's pretty faithful to the spirit of the actual game.
The only thing that's not faithful to the spirit of the game is the very stingy microtransaction system that's being talked about. That's much more something I'd associate with Games Workshop than Privateer Press who are usually very good about being very inclusive with what you spend money. A bit of a shame but I suppose that's the age of gaming we live in. I will say that a Microtransaction system which will include characters and units, not just cosmetic items, is not something I would have expected to see in a Crowdfunded game and is not in the spirit of crowfunding.
TL;DR - Game is good. People exploiting crowdfunding and microtransactions is not.
Still recommended because it is solid. Might be worth waiting if you don't want to play an incomplete game, of course.

Also note the variety of faction units is pretty small at this stage of the game. Devs say they are trying to get all the units from the tabletop into the game when it's all said and done.
Game still has some work to be done but the developers seem like they are pretty hard at work with frequent updates and interaction with the forums.
Some of the work that needs to be done that really catches your attention is the cut scenes in between missions are not really animated at all. Characters don't move no facial expressions or anything, just still screen shots with voice overs. If you like turn based strategy games I would recommend this, even better if you are familiar with the game world.

First, I want to say who this game is NOT for. If you are impatient or like things done quickly, this game is not for you. By design everything takes time to do, and that is what makes it rewarding.
Wurm Online is one of the best sandbox games in the world, but I am one who does not like monthly subscription fees and believes that players should be the ones to host servers. For me Wurm Unlimited is a step in the right direction. The dedicated server was surprisingly easy to get set up and I had mine up and running about 45 minutes after the game launched on steam.
The actual gameplay is just as slow as Wurm Online, this is a plus in my book, but can be tweeked to speed up the skill rates. I have been waiting years for the standalone version of this game, and it's finally here. This game has been about so long parts of the terrain code were written by Notch before he left the project and later created minecraft. You can clearly see the influences that t left on minecraft too. Chopping trees, gaining resources, mining, defending yoursefl from enemies.

The big differences are the 3D graphics, the difficulty, and the levelling. The levelling is fabulously in depth, with over a hundred skills that you can level up. Want to climb a hill? Improve your climbing skill. Want to cook? Improve your cooking skill. Want to cook with dairy? Well, that's a seperate skill. Want to learn the yo-yo? Yep. There's a separate skill for that too.

And the difficultly is insane. The free starter items make it somewhat easier, but you have to craft everything you need, and you have a chance of success. Want to make a mallet? Well, you need to chop a tree down, so that depends on your skill at that, then your skill at making the logs into shafts, the shafts into mallet heads, etc, etc. And if you're not good enough you can mess these steps up. And you can mess up putting the parts together. At low skill there are dozens of ways you can fail.

On top of that, it's one of the few games where you can get properly lost. It avoids the easy "You are here" that we're all used to, and you just have to remember which way you went. It's incredibly refreshing, and it really makes it seem like you're exploring. Taken in the context of when that design choice was made, several years ago, it really stood out. It feels like a more hostile world when you can really get turned around and lose your bearings.

At first, you may well die a lot. If you see a lion, you've got about the odds you'd expect if you really saw a lion. Not much chance. If you walk up a hill, you lose stamina. If you run out, you fall. Many early games of mine saw me killed by a moderate hill. Then again, maybe you'll run into a 20 foot tall monster who will just stomp you into non existance.

The building is incredibly involved, and you can make wonderful structures with the tools in game. Now you can create a standalone world, you can keep them safely stored without any worry of them ever being deleted. You can create your own city, level your skills, and know it's all safe for you to come back to if you have to leave it a while, and that's well worth the wait.

I've been playing the MMO version of Wurm Unlimited (Wurm Online) on and off for a few years. We've been told that a singleplayer version of the game was extremely unlikely for a long time, so when WU was first announced I got a little overexcited. WO is and was an incredible game, but between not being able to consistently pay for premium (skills cap at 20 as a F2P, which is a ton of gameplay and you can play as long as you'd like, but as a F2P player your options are fairly limited) and the large amounts of time involved, I never could play too long.
I may not have played too much as of yet, but from what I have played (and I've done more than 2 hours - Steam didn't properly track the game on a session or two) I can honestly say that Wurm Unlimited is one of the best sandbox games out there right now. They literally took the MMO, and allowed you to create your own servers, alongside adding an optional adventure mode, AND you can customize the gameplay to suit your needs (skillgain multipliers and timer lengths are the big ones here). It's insane.
Wurm is a pretty strange game, however - even the MMO is odd. It's made in Java, the way terrain and building works can be unintuitive to newbies, and a lot of the mechanics and parts of the game can be unpolished or unintuitive even to this day. I started the Adventure mode and promptly died multiple times to wildlife and town guards because the game didn't give me a kingdom, so everyone was hostile towards me.
Even with its flaws, however, I strongly urge you to check out the game's wiki (google "Wurmpedia") and give the MMO a try - it's free, the tutorial in the MMO is much better than the one in WU, and if you decide you dislike the game you've lost nothing. The MMO plays differently, however - the skillgain system is slightly different, gameplay is a bit slower - there's a few differences that are hard to explain to someone who hasn't played the game before.
I would also suggest you bring friends - this game is amazing largely due to the players. I remember in the MMO I started on the free player server (now nonexistent - F2P players have a large variety of servers to choose from) where the map was incredibly tiny. After stumlbing about (and some minor drama involving the theft of a cart) I found a village run by some fans of the PC Gamer magazine (one of their staff members, an editor iirc, actually played from time to time, and he's written an article aobut the experience) and was taken in, fed, given a place to make a home, all that jazz - despite happening many years ago they're still some of the strongest memories I have from a game.
Wurm is pretty unforgiving and obtuse, but once you do, you'll find an incredibly deep game with tons to do. The MMO still has its own strengths and I honestly recommend you play whatever one you can - look past the janky aspects and set up a server with some friends, and you'll have a great sandbox game waiting.

This is not an easy game. It was never meant to be easy. But if you have the patience to learn, you'll be privy to the deepest sandbox experience available. There's a skill for everything: everything from bladesmithng and weapons head smithing, to toy making. You can change the land by terraforming... or sail to distant ones. Have the winds turn against you and be forced to tack to get where you are going. Build a bridge to nowhere or just explore what is around you already.
In Wurm you can interact with everything-water, the dirt, that bush, using either a right click menu, a selection bar, or many hundreds of hotkeys. This means that your "looking" has to be bound to the left mouse button. Many people are upset about this, and call it "clunky." Minecraft doesn't have this problem, they say. But Minecraft is a simple game, with only a few interactions: take, swing tool/weapon, fill bucket. But in Wurm you have literally hundreds of things you can do to tiles, objects, creatures, and plants depending on what you have active. This takes some getting used to, and there is no way you can get used to it in an hour.
My point is this: when people compain about the "UI" or "player interaction," they are actually complaining about the game's COMPLEXITY. They want a casual game, and Wurm is simply not that.
Regardless! You don't have to pay a thing to try Wurm! If you are still concerned about the game's complexity (pointed to as a flaw by haters), or If you are not sure if it's for you, you may want to try the free version, just do a search for Wurm Online. Keep in mind, though, that WO is much slower paced than WU, but it will give you a good idea if it's for you.
Things to consider:
1. Combat in this game is in the style of Dungeons & Dragons. That is, it is die roll based. Monsters are provided to add additional challenges to your exploration, but this is primarily a crafting/exploring game. Some have described it as more of a Medieval simulator.
2. If you play the slow version, it's important to know why it's slow. It's to encourage you to work as a team. This is to encourage realistic behavior in the players. Building a whole settlement should be a daunting task, and it is. If you decide to do it, you might get frustrated, but there is nothing like the feeling of finishing a grand building. The old expression is true: frustration fuels triumph.
3. Not everything is completely realistic, but it would be almost impossible to have complete realism. Digging fencepost holes is no fun. What Wurm does, rather, is attempt to give the *feeling* of doing it without taking you through every single step.

I'll start with the big point. It isn't pay to win, everything you need is available right from the get go, and anything extra you might want can be earned using the Omni-Bits currency. The only benefit you're going to get from paying is faster advancement, but the advancement isn't particularly slow anyways. Unless you can't handle working for your progression AT ALL (Which is core to any MMO) then you will never feel pressured to spend money.
Wildstar is, by and large, the most underrated MMO on the market that I've run across. The big con everyone is going to bring up is "ded gaem lul". This is simply not true. It is however, woefully underpopulated. That being said, the community is tightly knit and very active. The group finder isn't particularly useful for finding things to do, but spending a minute or two scanning the global chat has me finding something entertaining to do every time. If you're someone who is too lazy to take a minute to actually find players, and is reliant upon an automated system to match you with people that you will never speak with, then Wildstar is likely not for you. If you don't mind a bit of social interaction in your MMO's (That is kind of the point of them, isn't it..?) then you won't have any problems finding people to clear content with. Despite people saying there are only a couple hundred players in the entire game, I regularly see 40 man raids come together to stomp world bosses and events. PvP is admittedly lacking at the moment, but they have been adding incentives to get people to participate more.
Onto the game itself. The gameplay is somewhat similar to a couple other MMO's out there right now, TERA and Guild Wars 2 come to mind. The combat is this game gets intense. You won't be pressing tab and pounding out the same dull rotation while your tank does all the work in the endgame here. You'll be constantly forced to move and dodge brutal assaults once you get into the endgame dungeons, while aiming your own attacks and timing interrupts with the rest of your group to maximize your damage. It's refreshingly immersive, and I generally find dungeons keep me on my toes, instead of being the generic slaughterfest that it's become in some other games. I can only imagine how complex the raids get. (I haven't progressed that far myself) Gameplay aside, the game also looks quite pleasant with it's own brand of cartoonish art mixed with dark humor. Soundtrack is interesting enough, and some of the sound effects are top notch. (The announcer after a level-up gets me every time)
All in all, if you want an action style MMO that will test your reflexes and keep you amused, all for the low, low price of zero dollars, then I recommend Wildstar.

When I first saw this game I wasn't sure what to think, but I gave it a go, and I'm glad I did.
It's definitely worth the price. Even if you're not normally in to puzzle games (I'm not) it's still very fun. Though there is a puzzle element (okay, more than just an element) it's mostly a logic thing. There have only been a few "puzzles" that I've seen that have any distinct way of beating, and for the most part, it's just matching/moving things around so you can get to the children to rescue them, in whatever way ends up being the most efficient for you.
The good:
-Procedurally generated levels mean there's a lot of replay ability.
-You can make friends with the villagers and they'll give you gifts, and you can even get married! :3
-Challenging, in a good way. If you think and plan enough you should be able to overcome any challenges it throws at you.. and it will throw a lot at you.
-Adorable graphics (as I have come to expect from Spry Fox)
-The music and sound effects are perfect.
The bad:
-Eventually, constant failing gets aggrivating... though that could just be me.
-As far as I can tell, when the villagers get sick there's no way to make them better... I've pumped them full of medicine for DAYS and they stay sick... not really sure what to do about that.
-If you die, you lose your stuff, which isn't a problem (I'm aware that that's what Rogue-likes are like) except that there isn't really much of a way to get them back. You can become friends with the villagers, and they MIGHT give you an item.. but there's no way to really guarantee that you'll ever be able to get back the items you've lost (EG the "Fork of eating alone")
This game is amazing, the flaws aren't really flaws.. I mean, if you never fail then you never have to worry about losing your gear, or the heartbreak of losing (though you may have heartbreak of a different kind if the villager you want decides to leave you, and start dating a man...), it's more than worth the money that you pay for it, on sale or not.
