An excellent RPG.
The gameplay and mechanics are well thought out and have a logic that makes it fun to keep going through the game.
The battles are challenging enough to be engaging, and levelling up, crafting items, and doing side quests is very rewarding.
There are some personal disappointments.  These aren't really cons to the game, unless you agree with my own logic, I just feel they give room for improvement if a sequel is done, and I hope one is:
- Heavy re-use of assets.  Now pretty much all  j-style rpgs will have their blue slimes, green slimes, and gold slimes, but this game shows it had a budget with how relatively few unique kinds of monsters there are.  There's really only 3 'groups' or 'factions' of monsters.  All of the dungeons fall into these 3 categories or a mix of them.  The good news, is that even though assets are getting re-cycled, the abilities and how the monsters feel does change up, keeping the battles interesting regardless.
- Character development.  The characters are all awesome with good personalities, but there's not much real development between them and the world.  They're cool at the start, and they're cool at the end, that's it.  I guess you need to refer to the comics if you want to see growth in the characters, which I do recommend, they were quite good, albeit unfinished.
- Character Choice.  The characters only level when you fight with them.  And since you can only have 3 in a team, it basically means you might as well just pick 3 and stick with them.  Levelling the others turns out to be a chore with no real reward other than switching up playstyles, but because you have to fight more for each character you use, the switching up playstyles loses its value.  It's a 'change of pace' that ends up being slower than if you didn't change the pace at all.
- Dungeon Difficulties.  Another tell-tale sign of the limited budget these guys were working with.  You basically have to run each dungeon twice.  You run it once on normal, then again on hard, just to get enough levels to be ready for the next dungeon's normal difficulty.  I was hoping it was set up in a way where the hardest settings for the dungeons were intended as end-game content, but they're not, they're actually just bridging the gap in levels from one dungeon to the next, which I feel is a great example of making extra work for the player just to make the game longer and feel like it has 'more content', when really they're just making you play longer.
Even with these disappointments, all in all the game was awesome and I whole heartedly recommend it to any who enjoy the turn based battle genre, this was definitely one of the better ones I've played recently.

This is still the best Total War, and will continue to be the best Total War until Creative Assembly dumps the Warscape engine, which has become a serious handicap for every Total War after this one. That, and hiring competent AI programmers so they can stop oversimplifying and removing basic game mechanics just so that AI has less things to ♥♥♥♥ up.
Here's a short list of things M2TW does better than the later titles:
-To start, this is by far the most moddable Total War in the series. Everything from units to animations to the campaign and battle maps are completely moddable. Even the AI is moddable to a limited extent.
-Has by far the best recruitment system of any Total War game. Every unit has a limited pool to recruit from that replenishes at variable rates based on the building they're recruited from. Higher quality professional soldiers replenished slower than lower quality militia units, which prevents churning out stacks of elite units in quick order, atleast until you get to the point where you own half of Europe. I'm actually baffled as to why they moved away from this, but it was probably due to Creative Assembly being incapable of making the AI work with it.
-NO LIMITED BUILDING SLOT NONSENSE. And no idiotic food mechanics that further restricted your building choices either. In M2TW's cities/castles, you could pretty much build everything in every city/castle. BUT you can only build one building at a time, so to be optimal you still had to specialize each city/castle for a specific purpose early on.
-Agents that actually served a strategic purpose, rather than just being a general nuisance or generic regional stat buff.
-Battles that last more than 5 minutes. This is again probably due to CA's AI short comings, as the battle AI throughout the years has yet to evolve beyond "engage front line, flank with any extra cavaly, suicide general". The shorter the battles the are the less this is a problem, but the longer battles go it becomes easier for the player to out manuver and smash the AI.
-Soldiers have actual mass. Heavier units will actually force weaker units backwards in melee. In the later Warscape plagued titles, a few dozen of the weakest unit imaginable can literally prevent hundreds of heavy infantry from moving forwards.
-Sieges that were, at the very least, fun to defend and attack on. M2TW certainly has the most complicated siege battles, with the highest level castles having 3 sets of walls to overcome. The AI can have a tough time with it, but it usually does okay. Total War AI has always been a little extra special when it comes to siege battles, but other than Shogun 2 the AI has gotten significantly worse at them since M2TW, despite siege battles being significantly simplified.
As superior M2TW undoubtably is, there are a number of things later Total Wars do better:
-Graphics, an obvious one, though the graphics in M2TW still look pretty decent today.
-UI. M2TW's UI is big, ugly, and clunky, and scales poorly on widescreen resolutions. Definitely has not aged well.
-No ♥♥♥♥in diplomats. All diplomacy can be done instantly without the need of an agent running around all of Europe just to die of the plague right when you need him the most.

I am a huge fan of turn based strategy games such as XCOM, Civ, and Fire Emblem. I love me some board-games too, most recently I've been hooked on X-Wing miniatures.
This game scratches all of those itches. You have a very wide selection of units to choose from, and four factions at present that all feel very distinguished from each other. The depth of strategy in building a squad alone is immense, and it only gets more tactical when you actually have to deploy your units and do battle.
PROS:
*Proven gameplay taken from award winning tabletop game that's been around for a while
*Massive depth available for building and tailoring your army
*UI that is very helpful for n00bs (mouse over things to get them explained!)
*Animated "models" breathe life into a miniatures game
*Awesome rag-doll for corpses. Having a warjack hammer someone and watching a crumpled corpse get propelled backwards is always satisfying.
*Multiplayer Options (local, async online, etc)
*Well done single player campaign helps you learn units and gameplay rules
*True hit percentages.... you can have only a 20% chance to hit with a 5% chance to crit and successfully crit your target!
CONS:
*True hit percentages.... you can have  a 95% chance to hit with a 50% chance to crit and miss your target...
*Single player is only Cygnar Faction.  More please!
*Still being worked on. (not really a con, but some UI elements are a little rough still and things like the Army Painter are coming)
*No way to save skirmish games midgame. They do move pretty fast but if you need to do something else and you've got 2-3 rounds left it's going to be an issue.
*Camera can take a little getting used to
This game is a lot of fun. If you enjoy turn based strategy games, chances are this game will rock your world. It's not too hard to get into, but it'll take a few games to know what you're doiing enough to venture into the army creator.
As is 8/10
With  currently announced planned additional features: 9/10
Highly reccomended

Here we are in 2016, and we still have games without tutorials.
This game is a highly repetetive grind fest with a cumbersome, unintuitive UI (crafting, inventory, item use; all are as bad as it gets).
Roguelikes have replay value and a fresh experience each playthrough; Magicite is nigh identical every time you play, without interesting random generation.
Other things are a mess
Taking damage causes awkward things to happen: you recieve knockback and i-frames; while in i-frames you can still put out an attack animation, but it won't do any damage. Your attacks are very laggy, so getting hit while attacking means waiting for seconds before you can actually attack. Enemies also get i-frames, but they have contact damage during said i-frames. Enemies have attack animations, but always do contact damage even from behind. Enemies get knocked back by your character, but the knockback is ambiguous.
Jumps and aerial movement don't have tight controls, and the character moves with the gusto of a cement mixer.

Stellaris is a poor execution of a great idea. The premise is excellent: a Star Trek/Spore mashup, where you take your designer species to galactic dominance. There's a variety of interesting governments, societies, ethics and factions to pick from. Unfortunately, the game design is fatally flawed.
In empire-building games, you usually have a choice of goals: do you steamroll your competitors? Out-tech them? Form alliances? Build impressive centrepieces? Stellaris feigns the choice, but only aggression brings victory. You can try a peaceful route - forming a federation - but this ties you to the AI of the other federation factions. Which can lead to unwinnable war declarations. Or the careless loss of the federation fleet you've built, when the AI takes charge. You have to put up with a lot of frustration to win this way.
The other victory types are two flavours of conquest. If you don't want to wage constant war, you're out of luck. You and your allies might take out the warmongers. But you won't reach the victory target without turning on your friends.
Sadly, the poor game design shows elsewhere. There's a handful of ship types, often with choices of 2-3 modules, that you can fit with the weapons and defences of choice. In theory, it sounds great. Unfortunately, it falls apart the moment you discover the basic starter ship has the best return on investment. Tech is expensive. Upgrades cost resources. Armour, and better weapons, are expensive. Space stations and colonies are expensive. Resources lost that you could put to better use building more starter ships.
There's 3 main weapon types. They're supposed to be rock-paper-scissors. But one is completely useless (missiles). There's 3 main defences - but again, one is completely useless (armour plating). There's 4 ship types - but only the smallest (and maybe the lategame largest) are worth their cost. So for most of the game you'll choose the same weapons, the same defences, and the same ships.
Punishing the player is a recurrent Stellaris theme. Buildings cost maintenance. So rather than the choice of what to build on their planets, and being out-done by players making better choices (thus encouraging growth and better play), players are hit simply for building. Do you want to test out strategies? Try new things on easy? Good luck with that - there's no easy difficulty. Only normal, hard and insane. Do you want achievements? Then you better like ironman mode (only one autosave file) - pray that you don't hit one of the game's many frustrations.
There's some good in Stellaris. I loved the little sci-fi novellas, uncovering them as I explore the galaxy (of course, this only holds interest the first time). I like the planetary system variety, and the beautiful artwork of stars, black holes, and neutron stars. I like how factions in your species arise based on gameplay. I like the semi-random tech tree. It all makes the poor game design stand out for the worse.
If you want a space epic, get Star Wars: Empire at War, or even Spore, instead. Give Stellaris a miss.

The Binding Of Isaac is pitch-black and hard as hell. If you die in the middle of crawling the game’s randomly generated, Zelda-styled dungeons, you start the game from the beginning, armed only with the knowledge of the mistakes that led to your demise. Luck plays a factor: Stumbling upon the right magic weapons and power-ups can give a leg up. But persistence is the key. The necessity for masochistic patience in the face of terrible odds might be familiar to those who played Super Meat Boy, the brutal platformer Edmund McMillen co-created with Tommy Refenes. But here, the difficulty dovetails uncomfortably with a plot steeped in biblical lore, mommy issues, and scatology. Isaac, naked and unarmed, defends himself by spraying his aggressors with his own salty tears. It’s impossible to play The Binding Of Isaac without coming away with the feeling that McMillen could really use a hug. Don’t let that stop you…

This is a great naval game. It only lacks an active large player base, so there are many matches 10v10 or less.
Compared to World of Warships:
*Speed and handling more realistic (no ice skating ships while turning)
*Carriers require more skill and it is best to stay close to your heavy hitting Battleships.
*Subs (which WoWs doesn't have) are just plain fun, and they are not overpowered. You will run out of oxygen, get chased by Destroyers, Cruisers, and Planes. You must also manage your limited torp supply. The deck guns are good on subs that have them.
*Destroyers and Cruisers roles feel far better in this game. In fact it is recommeded that you play "with" your team and keep your ranges (radio, sonar, guns, spotting) in mind in relation to your team mates.
*Large artillary gains accuaracy with follow up shots in the same general area.
*The lack of pretty gfx that WoWs has is easily countered by the quality of the games mechanics.
*Night matches with flares. Need I say more?
TLDR: Give it a try!

This is a worthy game.
However, there are a few things that that could be implemented as a quality-of-life change.
1. EXP sharing
I wish exp was gained for those outside the immediate party. When I run into a boss that requires a party reformation, I have to spend a lot of extra time leveling them up.
2. Difficulty
Legendary mode does not live up to its name. Besides Deadwatch, which had those insane grave wardens running amok. It is also disturbing that the enemies in encounters are 4 levels higher but when I get to the boss he is 2 levels lower. Finally, I discovered you can escape a dungeon by doing "save and quit to main menu" and when you load it, it places you outside the dungeon. But that takes time. It would be easier if there was an escape rope kind of thing from pokemon.
3. Quick Save/Load
I don't see any other reviewers writing about this, so maybe I am missing something, but if there was a quick sdave/load feature it would be grand. For example, let's say I want to craft an epic item at 30%. If I fail, it would be cool if I could quick load and try again. This is a silly example, but you get what I mean.
4. World map, camera
Can we get some labels on there.
The camera does not go as far as I want when exploring the world
5. Fountains
I don't know if this is intended but I wish the fountains that give buffs tell you what those buffs do before you drink them.

Really enjoying this game. Large majority of RPGs today are action-based, which I enjoy but feels too common now. I was missing the feeling of the old school turn-based RPG like the older final fantasys, grandia, etc. This fulled that void very well. Only thing Is I wish you had the option to speed up attack animations just to increase the pace of fights after you have been playing for a while and have seen them all. Besides that, no complaints.

1st of all, I defeated the Final Boss in just 3 rounds......so anti climactic, but it was my own fault as i was using level Max(30) characters with 100+Perk Points and with Legendary Weapons + Max Gears (Debateable). I don't usually write a review for a game but because i like this game so much, gonna give it some hard love.
Story : 7/10
- If you really pay attention, the story and lore is quite good but as for me, there was a hit and miss at some times. Most of the time it's because of my mood or the music which i will talk about later. 70% of the time i just skipped the lores because i just want to collect them for the rewards.
Music : 5/10
- Its decent. Lets just say i turned off the master volume and put on spotify after 3 hours.
Voice Acting : 9/10
- It is really good! if i turned off the volume, i would replay the scene just to listen to the voice acting. All is good except Alumon which sometimes sounded like two different voice actors with different talents.
Mission : 10/10
- Its not open world so theres nothing wrong here. Get from Point A to Point B, plus you do get some side missions which are fun to do.
Characters : Interesting but "meh"
- I like the characters but they kinda felt flat. Example : Knolan, i don't know a thing about Knolan except that he is a angry old mage with a soft heart. that's all, theres nothing there to make the characters stand out to me. like if you ask me anything about the characters, i could only say the 1st impression i got from them and nothing more. Alumon, he is the one character i wanted to use since the 1st time i saw him in the intro but you get him in the late game and found out, he is not that much better than the 1st 3 characters that you used. thats another problem, when you get a new character, they are not the same level as the characters you are using, hence you need to level them up. i was level 15 when i 1st got Knolan which was level 9 like What The Furret? more on that later.
Dungeon : Fun but....
- The dungeons are fun because they procedurally generated and that makes grinding them less stressful but i will say that the Dungeon Events need fixing and 2 of the later Dungeons needs reworked or fixing.
RPG-ness : Its Good
- The Skill and Perk system is good and you can create a godlike character with a certain build with the correct types of equipments (I KO'ed the Final Boss using Garrison with 1 attack and 1 Burst Skill [Totalling in 3 Rounds])
Quest Logs : Needs adjustments
- Main Quest logs is fine but the side quest like the hunts needs to have some sort of log to read back on. Example : Legendary Weapons. You get all the clues for the weapons in 1 place at 1 time. so to remember all of them especially for the characters you don't use is kinda hard because theres no log or notes about them. Am i missing something here? because before the final boss i decided to collect the legendary weapons for the other characters but i can't seem to find anything to look back to. so the internet guide gods helped me there. not a big problem but something to improve upon.
Dungeon Skills :
- Monica and Knolan's dungeon skills is as useless as trying to use Calibretto's Cannon Shot at close range (and sometimes even at long range)
Visuals : 10/10
- Nice style and beautiful background
Others:
- The game is actualy pretty short IMHO for a rpg, i played for 67.3 Hours based on my Saved Game stats but thats filled with alt+tab-ing out to watch Youtube or do something else and lots of it are from grinding a certain early Dungeon Event item or trying to grind some parts (which i later found out it was easier to just move on to the next area). lets just say you could speed run this at less than half of my time. NOT SAYING IT IS A SHORT GAME but it is pretty short for me because it is a RPG adventure game.
- I wish there was more skins for the characters, i only used the 1st 3 characters that you got for the entire game. i tested and tried the other characters and felt that the main 3 is better. so to makes things not looking dull or boring, i bought the skins for the 3 main characters and yay it keeps things spicy, until you get bored of them too.
- The Collector, i avoided buying anything from him except fishing gears because i was afraid it would make the characters IMBA. which i was correct, i only bought fishing gears and the 3 skins (300) so i had lots of coins left, partly because i like grinding those airships. In the late game, because i have so many of the coins, i bought the perk books, i never bought anything else but only the perk books, and its only the perks books for the characters i was using. and man those perk books made my Garrison a God Of War type character that can dish out 4k damage crit, 2k damage regular attack, 4k confirmed damage on berserk. and thats how i breeze thru the late game. The Farseer i got 1 turn KO with Garrison and his level 3 burst skill.
- For the developers
: PLEASE FIX OR CHANGE THE EVENT DUNGEON WHERE THE EXCLAMATION MARK ON THE MAP GOES AWAY IF YOU DONE OR SOLVED THE DUNGEON EVENT
: *Spoiler Alert* Alumon using Blood Magic IS NOT A PLOT TWIST OR SHOCKING REVELATION
- The Ending was so-so with a sequel bait to add salt to the wound
Final Thoughts:
- Bought at a Discount, so that's a plus for me, at full price i could not recommend this game, sorry. but at a discount? HELL YEAH!
- Did i have fun?  Answer = Yes
- Will you play again for the NG+? Answer = Maybe, if im bored or have nothing else to do because the only thing they provide for NG+ is a new difficulty setting.
- Would you give this game an award? Answer = No, because it lacks something to make it stand out. Lets just say that i probably enjoy playing FF7 today than this game. Good Effort tho
- Does this game scratch that RGP itch? Answer = Yes, kinda.
- Are you interested in the sequal? Answer = Yes, kinda.

I absolutely love this game, but that does not keep me from recognizing that this a niche game for a niche audience. This is not your typical Platinum game like Bayonetta or Vanquish, most evidently shown by the game's director, Yoko Taro. So, I'll start off with my initial thoughts of the game so far given that the full campaign has only just been released.  *Warning* there will be some slight spoilers.
The good: I've just started to get into the tabletop version of Warmachine and so far what I've played does a good job of keeping to the core mechanics. The graphics are pretty good for a kickstarter game, some CG cutscenes would have been amazing (especially of the duel between Orsus and Sturgis) but that's really asking too much of a limited budget. The gameplay is well done, with actual thought being required so that you don't open yourself up to enemy charges or block your own movement and/or line of sight with an ill-timed activation. That's one aspect of the game I've really enjoyed so far which is good because there are a lot of minor areas that need at least a little improvement.
The bad: The story. The story is almost cringe worthy in its absolute lack of originality and, so far, bad presentation - I mean, another superweapon that could change the course of the war / end the world as we know it plot line? Really? Even the opening scene almost made me facepalm when Jakes stated that "I...I killed Commander Stugis". My reaction was no, no you didn't. I haven't even played the storyline yet and I know this, stop being a drama queen. Given the fluff available in the books I was really expecting better, even the game characters seem almost caracatures of themselves compared to their presentation in the books. There is one twist that might have been interesting but since anyone with even a nodding acquaintence with the game likely knows what happens to Stugis it's a moot point. I would have liked something more along the lines of the old Dark Omen game where your actions and decisions decided how the story progressed and what units were available.
The voice acting isn't bad, not great, but somewhere in the middle and they did seem to match their characters. However the pronounciation of Brisbane as Bris-bane really irritated me for some reason.
Since I haven't finished the campaign yet I can't say the storyline is difinitively horrible but I'm not hopeful for a turn around though if it does happen I will edit this review.
The mediocre: A couple of small issues that will likely be fixed in future patches, the UI really needs to be adjustable with at least a scale though being able to move, fade or remove selected elements in addition would be better. Having subtitles not take up almost a third of the screen would also be nice. The cost is about average for the standard edition but considering there's a lot of DLC in the works that you'll have to buy seperately... well maybe the DLC will reasonably priced.
I'd recommend this game if you're looking for something fun that will likely focus around multiplayer battles. I haven't come across many bugs at all so far, mainly just a few with speech and sound clips not playing or not playing quite right. Definetly no game breaking bugs which is great. Whatever you do you should not buy this game expecting a great or even good story but the gameplay is solid especially if you enjoy mulitplayer battles.

A decent strategy game for the price (got it a few months ago for $2 on Chrono.gg). Each game took me a little over an hour from beginning to end, playing at a leisurely pace. I played about three games before I got bored and felt I saw everything the game had to offer.
The most important thing to note is that you have no control over your units on the battlefield. The gameplay pretty much boils down to managing a very basic economy, deciding what structures to build and where to allocate resources.
On normal difficulty, it was smooth sailing until the midway point. After a fairly challenging battle around year 25, I found the game reverted back to being somewhat easy. That is until (what I assume is) the final battle in year 50. Thus far, I have been unable to overcome the insane number of units the CPU places on the battlefield, even with my own massive army of powerful knights, archers, druids, unicorns, tigers, and hydras. I'm sure it can be done, but I don't find the overall gameplay engaging enough to keep trying.
I recommend picking up the game if it's on sale. There isn't a lot to keep hardcore strategy gamers entertained for long, but it's fun while it lasts and makes for a nice, relaxing diversion.

A great casual strategy.
The gameplay is simple. You goal is to survive 50 years. Each year you get gold/wood/faith income which can be spent on hiring units and construction of buildings. Then you need to end the year. Before starting new year there is a big chance you will be attacked by enemies. If you survive it the next year starts. So the game is about good planning, you need to rise your army enough to stand against enemies, but if you will forgot about economy you will be outnumbered at the later stages.
Actually, this game could be passed in less than our. But you will start over and over again before you will find a strategy which brings you to the victory!
The economy part of the game is pretty linear. You can hire peasant. Each one gives 100 gold per year. For hiring any units you need food which can be granted by building Chicken farms. There is also a forester's hut which gives gold income and food. And there are buildings which gives wood and faith income. So, you need to hire as much peasants as possible during the early game and than choose your defense plan to concentrate on 1 resource.
There are 3 basic defenders: militiaman, swordsman and knight. They requires gold.
There are also other 3 different groups of units. First part is paladins, exorcists and angels. First two requires faith for hiring ( they also need a knight). Angel costs gold and improve paladins. To make a good army with them requires a lot of faith. The second part is mythical units. They are extremely strong and expensive. You can have only 1 such creature per 1 barrack. So you need a lot of gold for making the army of them. Finally, there is the third part of units, which requires wood for hiring, Archers, Druids and Unicorns. If you want to make them you need to change your economy from gold to wood.
There are also skill system. By killing enemies or buildings special buildings you get faith. If you save enough faith you will get skill levels. There are 25 skills divide by 5 groups. I won't describe them all, you can read it on your own. In my opinion the 3th group is the best.
Finally, there are dungeons. You need some years to unlock and then you can try to beat them. Each dungeon gives reward. Some of them are really useful, so you should destroy them all before 50 year.
It was really enjoyable to win this game. yYeah, sometimes it got pretty annoying starting new game right from the start. But it's OK because the game is fast passed. I made about 50 attempts until I found the strategy which brought to the victory and i got good feelings about it. Actually, I played on Very Hard. I think, it's much more easy to win on easier difficulties.
Pros
- Easy understanding gameplay
- High replayability. At least until you pass it :D
- A lot of ways of achieve victory. 11 nations with unique perks, 5 different skills tree, 3 different arny setups.
- Possibility to pass the game less than hour
- Relaxing graphics and music
Cons
- One mistake usually equals lose
- There is random in this game which could be devastated for the player
- No ability to save the game. Every time start from the beginning
- No ability to leave/restart the game during battle phase even if you realised you lose. Only Alt+F4
There are no great graphics or animations. But it's strategy game, it doesn't need it. So if you are fan of this genre, you should give it a try. I can recommend it.

This is a Flash Game.
It's one of the few Flash Games I've played that feels like more than a Flash Game. The control is good---deceptively simple---and even when it flakes out (sloooooows down), it' still addictive.
The RPG stuff is standard and executed well enough. The game reward you with perks to projectiles, traps, pets, movement, and health management, and uses an RNG to make each playthrough "different."
It plays like a warped Zelda, and there's something about navigating from screen-to-screen (room-to-room, except the rooms are locked in your view) that is really compelling. Maybe the room-structure juxtaposted with your having no idea what's next gives you motivation to go on. Other RNG dungeon crawler games I've played with simiar mechanics, but prettier and dynamic environments are more forgettable than Isaac.
The game has a grotesque, compelling setting that may offend some, but will entice others who think they have a rebellious streak. The power of the story is that it really makes you feel like you are descending lower and lower through the dungeon.
Lot's of fun, and highly recommended.

I noticed this game went on sale today (4/13/17), so I'm gonna throw out this quick review for anyone interested in the game.
It's good on PC, but only if you're gonna stick to singleplayer modes like MyCareer and not worry about MyPark and going online to search for games and such. There's two big reasons for this, Lack of players and Hackers. It's fine if you're gonna do a private game with a buddy, but searching for a public game is not really advised. If you're lucky, you'll fine some normal players on MyPark, but it's usually an empty wasteland. If you're gonna be playing online a lot, consoles might be a better option compared to PC. There's just not that many players on PC, and when there is, most of them are using hacked 99 rated players with 100% shooting accuracy.
In terms of MyCareer, it's a great mode, and easily my favorite mode right now. You'll need an online connection to access the 2K Store to buy clothes, shoes, custom bands to wear in NBA games, custom MyCourt floors and backboards, and much more. So if you're gonna be completely offline with no internet, MyCareer may be a bit lackluster and bland.
In terms of bugs, I haven't found anything extreme. There's quirks here and there that can easily be fixed by the devs, like opening the MyCourt pause menu pausing the music when it's not supposed to, but they just haven't fixed it yet for some odd reason. 2K puts PC in the minority compared to consoles, so keep that in mind when you buy this game.
I haven't played Seasons yet. I might give it a shot once I finish MyCareer.
The PC port is playable. The framerate will dip sometimes, but it never happens during gameplay, which is a godsend. There's a good video options menu that might be confusing, but it's better than Dark Souls 1's video options by a lightyear. It also supports borderless windowed mode, which is always a massive thumbs up as it's overlooked too much. Framerates higher than 60 are supported in singleplayer, but multiplayer is locked at 60, likely for balancing reasons.
Overall, I like NBA 2K17. It's a great and solid game, and I play it every day. I would recommend it.
I'll write a much longer review once I complete MyCareer and play the other modes.

My time with Loadout has been interesting. This 3rd-person Run-and-Gun f2p has really caught my attention and so far delivers a fantastic idea to how games can be. The idea of creating a 'Loadout' of two guns of one's creation and a side-tech really makes the possibilities take a 100 mile hike down a long road of creativity.
The game's idea of taking 4 base weapons and turning them into death dealing fire launchers or AoE Healers really makes for a great time. One could almost litteraly make a weapon suited to their playstyle and allows one to explore what gun they really like. This game takes the gun mechanics of Borderlands, the 'class' based system of Team Fortress 2 (in terms of abilities), and the humor of Drawn Together (look it up) into a game truly worth its weight in Blutonium.
Like all games, this one has its flaws. Character's base stats like speed, health, jump height, etc. arn't increasable and do not increase without the use of 'juice' (a type of buff). This can take some of the creativity out of making a custom class since one can't run super fast with a shotgun or jump really high to sniper possitions. A lot of mechanics still need tweeking, such as grenade strength, players committing suicide on their game mode 'Death Snatch' (players kill each other for a small vial of blutonium for points) to prevent the enemy team from obtaining points, and many other factors like these. This can cause certain aspects of the game to be exploitable and hard to counter. The match making system is non-existant at the moment of this review. Since the game is new (as of this review) there are many features that arn't implimented. I have had matches where I fight players that have weapons that can almost one hit kill in a single shot, and played matches where the entire team never customized a gun. Matchmaking is a feature needed for this game.
On a final note: I have had an absolute blast with this game. Playing against people of all skills and weapon types gives me an idea on what I want to do to further my weapon. I went from using a plasma rifle that shoots medicine to a rocket launcher that shoots clusters of healing bombs in a wide area. I went from using a full auto spikeball launcher to a spikeball shotgun with incredible hip fire accuracy. The possibilities for this game is endless and with all weapon upgrades available to everyone,  including f2p, this game's weapon balance is quite evident. All that is left is for you to get in the game and create your gun.
My Score: 8 / 10 (add matchmaking, f2p available clothing for purchase, and ingame mic chat and you got 9 / 10 from me)

I've been playing wildstar off and on since launch. I firmly beleive that it is the most fair and upfront f2p mmo's out there. With most of the cash shop items avaliable via an in game currency f2p players will have no problem standing side by side with subscribed players in any form of content.
Wildstar has a unique asthetic that seems to be love it or hate it and alongside that it has a combat system that truly does take some getting used to. So if you want a game that's familiar to what you've played in the past then this isn't the game for you. But if you want a high skill cieling game that has dark souls level of gratification after downing a boss this is the game for you!
Suggestions:
1. FIND A GUILD - The best place to find a guild is through the wildstar reddit. Head over there and try to find some people who are like minded. Having people to help you and guide you into Wildstar is an absolute must!
2. USE CHAT - Queing sucks in this game but the community is awesome! If you're trying to get something done do a /n to enter nexus chat and ask. Most of the time people are totally willing to help.
3. MAKE FRIENDS - This compounds with 1 and 2. Bolster your friends list with people to play with! Hell you can add me and hit me up if you need some help. IGN: Tearie Hex
4. TRY THE MOUSELOOK MODE - So this is a mode that makes the game feel more like Tera or Neverwinter turning your left and right mouse click into skills as well as locking your camera to your mouse. This little feature can make a HUGE difference for a lot of people and it could make the difference for you. To enable this go to the escape menu > Controls > and check the top 3 boxes in the mouselook mode section.
I hope these little tips help you when starting out! Head into nexus with an open mind and a willingness to play a game that approaches combat in a different way and you'll have a lot of fun!

I am not really the type for writing reviews, but this game deserves one. In my opinion one of the best games in this year 2017 for casual gamers! Thank you Airship Syndicate!
I read an article on gamestar about this game and put in my wishlist for serveral weeks. After it was in sale, I bought it and started playing it just by chance. That was right before christmas and after finishing the campaign (for the first time) today, I suppose it is a very fine christmas present!
I'm the type casual gamer, which starts playing a game, puts the entertainment to top priority and doesn't get sad when the game becomes boring and therefore gets dusty in my game library. I had my fun even if I didn't finish the game and it has been ages since I had a game which I urged to finish (due to irregularity in play time, too much content or too much grind). With Battle Chasers: Nightwar this changed in the last week. This game is so fun that I could not stop playing it until I saw the end.
Pro:
- right amount of grind for casual gamers: not so much that it gets annoying and not so little that it gets too easy and too fast earned
- right amount of complexity in character building: just deep enough that you have to think and spend some time about your builds but don't have to start a bachelor study of the game
- simple but entertaining and not too detailed story, perfect balance of linear and freedom-based gameplay (side quest, fishing, treasure hunt, arena, ultimate weapon building, boss hunting)
- beautiful graphics and art works
- good voice acting
- stable and almost (99,9%) bugfree (which is sadly not natural today)
Contra:
- Dungeon "Crimson Gardens" is way too long, especially if you have to play it multiple times for finding the right blood fountain (4 runs, after the 3rd I fought it was a bug)
- the difficulty level is fluctuating too much (gets it peek just until you find Alumon and after that it becomes too easy, especially after getting your first ultimate weapon)
I hope the developers will provide more content in the future and will trigger the rare occasion that I buy some DLCs ;). Again, thank you for the game and the fun!

Game has a great sense of humor and is a relatively straightforward RPG.
The main problem the game has is the combat system, or lack thereof.
Melee combat usually involves taking some small amount of damage per enemy, which quickly adds up.  Health regen is really slow and potions are the only way to heal otherwise.  Potions also have a cooldown.
This means that the main way to kill stuff is to run around casting ranged magic to avoid being hit.  The problem is that then the rate one can safely proceed without taking damage is limited by the mana regen rate.  This rate is not too bad for regular guys you are killing.  However, for bosses, this can be annoying since you end up only getting a few smal hits while trying to avoid all the boss attacks.  If you try and do a physical melee attack, you can often end up taking a fair amount of damage quickly in a boss fight.
Neither dodge nor the magic shield constitute a block or parry ability which is what is needed here to make melee combat more viable.  If you try to use melee combat, then you will be slowed down by the rate at which you can heal via potions, if you can keep enough in your inventory.
I think the game is trying to get you to use to some magic combination of range and melee with dodge and shielding, but in the end all that seems to be reliable and safe is just doing range damage and ignoring the rest.
My main other complaint is the lack of any options to control audio, graphics or anything.  It is unusal to see a game with this involved of a UI without providing something as basic as being able to change mappings on a controller.  The controller scheme is weird in that the main interaction button is the right button, which is odd, since every other game that is usually either A or X.  Even after playing for hours, I still kept getting missed up by this, since it is very odd.
Even given this weakness in the combat system, lack of options, and unnecessary tedium, I still recommend this game since it has a lot of charm and witty dialogue.

Zenith is an action-RPG in which the selling point is the humor. I must admit, there were a few gags that had me cracking a big smile. As a player, you sort of deal with the rough gameplay to see what sort of lunacy the game will throw at you next. There is an upgrade system and a loot system, but both are quite rudimentary. Zenith seems like the game I would've designed if I could've designed a game when I was 13 years old. Yes, it's quite silly, but it seems to have a lot of heart and passion behind it.
Initially, I was a bit annoyed with targeting enemies in melee. My character seemed like he was always punching or swinging his sword in the wrong direction and taking unnecessary hits. It's quite difficult to avoid hits in melee, period. However, enough potions were typically dropped that I could handle this combat awkwardness.
Next, I came to a large "open world" kind of section with this bouncy music in which you turn your character with your mouse instead of the keyboard (as you've done for the rest of the game). There are enemy encounters spread out everywhere in this section, and the way forward is not clear at all. I bumbled around for a while, fighting some encounters and running away from others without knowing where I was going. Eventually, I consulted a video walkthrough.
After this the game became tolerable again, until I ran into these jets of blue flame that instantly killed my character. The idea was for my character to pick up a large stone, and walk forward using it as a shield. However, this was easier said than done. My character seemed to continually revert to a "default" stance of holding the stone to his right, which made it impossible to block the flame. I eventually got through the first few flame jets by throwing the stone down to redirect the jets. Then, I ran into a rotating, spinning flame jet. I tried to actively block the flame with it, but my character kept holding the stone to the east while flames came at me from the north. I tried to drop the stone and hide behind it, but was killed (even though I appeared to be obviously behind the stone).
Eventually, the hit-or-miss humor of the game was no longer worth fighting the awful controls.

As far as HOGs go, this one is kind of mediocre.  The idea is that the game will hook you so that you spend real moneys to continue, but this is ultimately unnecessary, so the game can be enjoyed without paying a cent provided that you don't want to brute your way through it.  This is achieved by the mobile business model; you have a set 'stamina' that you can spend on solving various HOG rooms and when you run out, you can either hope that you earned enough premium currency to buy items to refresh your stamina or you can purchase premium currency via your Steam wallet.  Sometimes you get a freebie, so the game is not without generosity.  Fair enough.  I don't have anything against this model, so that's not really where the game heads south.
The issue is that the 'hook' isn't there because, well, the game is pretty grindy and very reluctant to hand out the rewards you need to progress through the game.  The basic set-up is that there are quite a number of HOG rooms, most locked behind an experience wall.  Solving a room gives you semi-random items (you know what you MIGHT get, but it's not guaranteed).  These items are used to complete missions which reward you with standard currency and experience points.  With more experience, you unlock more rooms and more missions and so on and so forth.  Except a) your experience reward is really tiny, so expect most of the rooms to be locked away for a looooong time and b) the only way to get a good amount of xp is to complete missions, but the game doesn't like to give you what you need.
At first, you might think this is easy peasy.  "What's this guy talking about?  I'm bashing out missions all the live long day."  That's true; there's a lot of simple missions that will show up and you'll get 'em done in no time.  It's when you get to the more complex missions that require several rare items that you can only get reliably from rooms you haven't unlocked yet is when you might start yanking at your hair.  Your alternatives are the wandering NPCs that never drop what you want or you can buy chests... which also never drop what you want.
The worst part is that since your unlock progression is really slow, you will be playing the same rooms repeatedly, over and over and over and over and over again and again and again.  This wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for a) there's only four or so variations per room and b) the object list never really changes.  Let's say each room as 20 objects and each time you attempt a room, you get a subset of those objects to find and one of the room variations - with only four (maybe five) variations on a room, you're going to quickly learn where everything is and there's never anything new to find.  The only difference is that the number of items to find increases as you 'level up' the room, but ultimately, when you know where everything is in a HOG, it stops being HOG, you see?
All that said, a patient player can have their fun with this game so long as they don't mind the slow-and-steady unlocks and repeatedly playing the same rooms.  Even paying for premium currency probably wouldn't solve Mystic Saga's grind problem as you're simply just not going to get what you want to move forward without putting a lot of time into it.  On the other hand, if you want to nab a whole lotta achievements in one sitting, the admission price is free and you can impress your friends in your activity feed... until they see what you've been up to.

On a more serious note: Steel Ocean functions like World of Tanks, (or World of Warships more rather,) but with slightly less graphic fidelity. The player base is a little small, but the community is hoping for more members soon.
It's a free to play game, so there's no risk to you by playing it, however there are micro-transactions. In reality, they shouldn't be considered when downloading this game because all you can really do with your real-world cash is buy gold for purchasing some exclusive ships and decorating your owned vessels in game. Some argue it's pay-to-win, but really it makes no difference, at least to me.
What I like most about Steel Ocean is the fact that there is a lot less grinding for EXP and Silver when compared to the WoT games, assuming you're a decent player. It's more historically accurate, there is a diverse selection of ships and ship types from multiple factions (though there are some factions with very few ships to choose from. USA and Japan are your best bets if you want a larger selection.) The game is easy to grasp but requires at least some skill to master and a good amount of teamwork. Ensure everyone plays their roles well.
You can choose from:
- Light Cuisers
- Heavy Cruisers
- Destroyers
- Submarines
- Battleships
and
- Aircraft Carriers
So there you have it. It's an all-around good multiplayer experience. I hope you enjoy your playtime if you choose to get Steel Oceans, and if you do, I will see you on the sea of battle!

Stellaris is fun, but it's one of those "just another turn" games like Civilization that can quickly snowball into playing for hours and hours... and hours. It's got an Option called "Ironman Mode" providing a single (latest) Save to prevent Save-Scumming that seems to be the preferred way to play and the only way to enable "Achievements", since the player has to live with the consequences of his actions. It's all for the better as it prevents you doing just that and Micromanaging situations for the best possible outcome. They still need to work on their Tutorial somewhat, since a few "Options" you have in the game are not obvious at all.
For instance for the first 10 or so hours I flew around the Galaxy with my unchanged starting ships because I had no idea you could actually Upgrade them manually, since they've hidden the Option in a menu called "Ship Design" in another menu and I didn't really feel like visually updating the design of my ships, which is what I initially thought it was for. I only found out that they don't self-upgrade with the newest tech you research after founding a Federation and getting the Federation fleet for a few turns, which had the Option to upgrade the ships automatically from the Fleet menu like I expected from my own ships.
There's also some other minor stuff that isn't exactly very obvious starting off, like how armies and invading other planets or the way in-game "Factions" and "Influence" as a resource works and how to increase it (I had my population nearly Revolt before having to start decimating my furthest outposts to quell it and got down to having only 3-4 Leaders left because of a lack of Influence for a while and a lot of the others dying due to age and being unable to replace them), or how to set up and properly manage Star Clusters to run themselves, since the player can directly manage just a limited number of core systems. Another minor issue is that the Technologies to Research pop up entirely randomly. I missed to upgrade the Starport responsible for allowing to choose higher ship classes the first time it showed up and it took rather long for it to reappear again, limiting me to Corvettes for large parts of the early game.
Nonetheless, once you get the game systems somewhat and push through the first few hurdles you'll have fun exploring the galaxy, dealing with other Empires out there, fighting Space Lizards and intergalactic wars, discovering the mysteries of the cosmos and dealing with late-game crises like invading Extradimensional beings and have dozens of hours of fun until the content runs out and you might want to start another campaign.

This is the perfect game for people who want to play Civilization but aren't hipster enough for Crusader Kings 2. The colonization and resource management mechanics are strong, and there is some light warfare strategy, but very little in the way of real time strategy or tactical action.
The story-driven dialogues are a welcome throwback to Alpha Centauri. However, the quests are more episodic, and therefore more open to replay value, if a bit less epic and memorable. The ideology and civ customization are deep, though systematically simpler than AC.
The retrowave soundtrack is also awesome, if a bit a short (hard to have the right expectations with a game that demands so many hours).
I expect that like other Paradox games the complexity will be further developed with time, so take my review as it applies to vanilla only.

Every mission starts with the camera in a stupid position and you need to adjust it, fighting with unacceptable camera controls: the camera turns around its own pivot instead of turning around the scene. It also can be zoomed in beyond the ground! It feels like a free floating debug camera. Also, the camera jumps back and forth in order to focus on every performed action, which turns out being very annoying. There are so many strategy games to look at for inspiration; I don't get how it can be like that.
The clumsy GUI requires some effort to get it (not the most intuitive one) and some of its elements are way too big, e.g. log and dialog texts (huge and blurry). I play PC games in front of my screen, no need to make texts readable to my neighbors ( ;
Last but not least, the interactions with the units and buttons are sometimes screwed up, so you need to deselect-reselect your unit.
So overall, the game shows some promise, but it feels like there's still a lot to polish. Some elements, such as the voice and dialogs, need even more than polishing: that should be shredded and redone.

I originally backed this on kickstarter because Privateer Press said they were going to bring the tabletop wargame experience to the video game world. As a long time fan, and former press ganger, nothing has stirred my imagination more than wanting to see these characters, machines, and beasts animated and actually interacting with each other. It does deliver that, to some degree... when it works.
I wanted to enjoy it, I tried to enjoy it. In some respects, I NEEDED to enjoy this, but I can't. It is continually bogged down by constant fatal errors, a conflicting design philosophy, an underutilized graphic engine, and; probably the most heartbreaking downside, a complete lack of soul.
Those of us that saw these problems and were deeply concerned tried to communicate these issues to the devs on the forums were shouted down. Our questions and concerns ignored until we just... gave up. They just don't want to hear it.
This game is not an accurate representation of what many fans would call a Warmachine experience.
It is a somber memorial to what could have been, and I am ashamed that I backed it.

This game looks like it might be funny, and I generally like the genre, but there are just so many design flaws that I can't get past to really get into the game. I'll preface this by pointing out that I haven't gotten past the first level after the prologue, but that's primarily because of these complaints.
1) The lack of sound controls in-game is a big deal. It doesn't seem like it would be, but the music is WAY too loud, repetitive, and overbearing. I checked the forums out of curiosity, and saw that the Developers actually saw the complaint, and responded that it was "too hard" to implement a feature that appears on about 95% of the games out there. Nice!
2) Health Potions have a *long* cooldown. So far I've found no way to avoid actually taking damage while attacking enemies in melee. Ranged attacks are weak and poorly aimed. Potions are plentiful, but the cooldown is really long. You can stop and wait for the cooldown after every fight to heal up, which is boring, or you can push ahead and keep dying. Maybe it gets better at higher levels, but I'll never find out.
3) I'm about an hour and a half in, beat the boss in the prologue, and a ways into the second area, and I still haven't even leveled up once. Admittedly, I take my time getting a feel for a game, but most games would have thrown at least one level up at me by now.
4) Looting is awkward, and bodies disappear really quickly, so you're going to miss out on loot.
5) Saving only at save spots. Why do game designers still think this is a good feature?
6) Graphics are... off. I can't put my finger on it really, but animation feels choppy and it gives me a headache.
7) It's a minor gripe, but since I'm already at it... The menus aren't designed with the player in mind. The "new game" button is the first option on the main menu, and "resume" is second. Most games have the "resume" or "continue" option first, and for good reason: people are going to want to keep playing where they left off. Not to mention accidentally hitting "New Game" will have you stuck clicking through dialogues for about 5 minutes before you can get back to the main menu. To close out the game, you have to go back to the main menu, but even then, it loads a "Press (button) to Start" screen... more jumping through hoops just to quit. Did the developers even try playing their game?
I wanted to like the game. Honestly. The sense of humor appeals to me. But it's just not fun to play.

This was a refreshing game for me as I usually avoided turn based games, feeling like it makes for stale combat. But it was actually quite good for the most part. Other parts of the game kept me well entertained, such as the art style and soundtrack, which paired together nicely. The story was told fairly well and made me interested in the world, though I feel like the plot devices that kept you constantly moving to other parts of the overworld harmed the games flow.
I can divide the game into 3 parts mentally. The beggining, where I felt enthralled and entertained by the world. The middle where I felt almost sad thinking that it could end soon. Then the final part where I wish it ended earlier. The game tended to drag at the end, where you are tempted by completion and upgrades that would ultimately make the end fight way too easy.
Looking back at the rest of the game, I'm glad I played it. It was full of charm and good intentions, would love to see the issues I raised addressed in a sequel. I think this game was pretty good for a modern turn based RPG, whereas before I thought it to be a dead and out-dated system. It changed my perspective on the genre and has hopefully opened me up to enjoying more games like it in the future.

When I first saw this game in the store I thought it looked like an uninspired ARPG school project.
After having played it for 30 hours I am happy to admit that my early and superficial judgement was 100% wrong.
The thing I am most baffled by is how in the world I managed to enjoy the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of an unfinished game with no story, uninspired graphics, no relatable characters and an uninteresting world.
The key here is how well Chronicon puts together its mechanics. It feels good to play, and has enough going on mechanically to make it fun for hours on end.
There is a real depth and complexity to every build, and you can tailor every item to your liking through an incredibly flexible enchanting system. The hunger for loot and xp, which drives any good ARPG, is present here, and it feels damn good to get new gear and skills to play around with all the way till lvl 100.
Don't expect to dedicate your life to it, though. At around 30 hours I am spent and probably won't be playing much more of it. It's rare to find an ARPG I feel satisfied quitting, but this is one of them. I got more than my money's worth, and if more content gets added, maybe i'll check in again. (like, add online multiplayer and i'll buy it for all my friends)
I like this game a lot, and would recommend it to anyone slightly intrigued by it.
EDIT: Turns out I got another 50 hours out of it after writing the review. Still good.

Try this game if you're any kind of fan of this genre.
I'm surprised at how solid the mechanics and loot system are.
For $10 dollars it is a total bargain.
The levelling system is satisfyingly deep without being overwhelming...builds seem to be very easy to imagine and implement. You can also respec at basically any time with an inexpensive potion.
I just finished Act 2 of 3 on Veteran difficulty and I haven't had to grind at all yet. That's a plus for me because it feels nicely balanced. I think in games like this, if you are putting a little thought into your levelling progression, you shouldn't need to grind until you get to the endgame stage.
Overall the game feels really nice to play with a few minor hangups...
I don't care for the art that much...I still play Diablo 2 and other pixel games so I'm not some big graphics snob; but I think the character models would be better served with smaller pixels and more detail. Right now things are kind of ugly.
I also don't like that most of the bosses I've seen so far are just larger versions of normal mobs. This is especially unsettling because of the pixel problem I described above.
I would also like to see some improvements to the mini map. I play Path of Exile and Diablo 2 with the minimap on almost all the time without problems but it just doesn't work as well in this game. It would be better if the map was smaller or relegated to a corner of the screen with a larger more detailed map being accessible through the menu or a hotkey.
All in all, this is a surprisingly good arpg, especially since it was made by ONE PERSON. That alone should get your money. Don't be afraid of this early access title, you'll be glad you picked it up.

There is an energy system where your actions cost energy and your energy can be refilled using in-system items, but there is no need for using any real money.  Your energy refills over time, at 2 mins per energy point, and each new level you achieve both refills and adds more total energy points.  You can even earn extra energy points by finding your items quickly.
I spent 3.5 hrs and went from level 1 to level 12 in one sitting- no money used at all. The energy bar system just forces you to evaluate your actions strategically- for instance, I have enough energy to play at the cabin, but not at the library- even though I need loot dropped from the library I will play the cabin, because that will give me enough energy to gain another level and my total energy will be refilled.
This is a casual type game, but it's just right mix of thinking and not thinking to be fairly addictive. I didn't mean to spend 3.5 hrs playing, yet I did.  There are various tricks the game implements to keep the game slightly different, but still pretty easy.  There's a nighttime mode, a silhouette mode, and around the time you get comfortable enough with a location to identify where certain objects will be, the game adds more items to your list. Also, there are achievements to gain.  I already have half the achievements with just a few hours gameplay. Finishing the game completely should give you all the achievements without need for any extra replays.
Please note, this is not a game that you will play through in one sitting unless you want to use a little real money to help. You will need to leave the game periodically to allow your energy bar enough time to refill. However, it is still a fun, slightly challenging,  fairly addicting hidden object game that will keep you occupied for a while.
It's free and doesn't use much space on your computer, so I definitely recommend at least trying it out to see whether you personally will like the game or not.

Mystic Saga reminds me a lot Lost Lands: A Hidden Object Adventure. Given the fact that it's Five-BN publishing, it's not a surprise. I don't know which one was the first but while Lost Lands was clearly based on a universe already developed with traditionnal games, Mystic Saga seems to have no counterpart.
The story isn't really the most important here but you're a young man that seems to have an extraordinary destiny: free the land from the Empress, who is evil.
You have an energy bar that will resplenish itself every 90 seconds. It's a reminder of the Facebook games, where you're limited to play because of that, which is also an incentive to buy energy. In Mystic Saga, like for Lost Lands, you can buy crystals that you can use to advance or buy items (like energizer) or the ingame money, used to buy items, mainly weapons or objects to exhange.
You have several quests to accomplish in order to advance: to do so, you need to visit locations with hidden objects scenes. You have three main modes: a list of words, a list of shapes and a night mode, where you have only a flashlight (or torch or choose anything that can light) to find items. Contrary to Lost Lands, Mystic Saga is showing you when it's day or when it's night in a location and which type of list you'll be confronted. I find it more interesting to have that data as you can cycle through the same location without asking yourself if it will take time to finally reach a night level.
When you complete a location, you're rewarded with items, money and experience. But it also means that energy is decreasing as each location costs energy (and it's increasing when you reach the upper level of the location - you have 10 - contrary to Lost Lands where you have 5 but it takes more or less the same time to reach the max). An unique feature in Mystic Saga (still compared to Lost Lands) is the fact that finding real fast items will give you bonus: experience, energy, coins but also items for collections like statues or unique coins. The game is still timed, so make sure not to be distracted like I was for a level, costing me 40 energy (or maybe half of it). I'll do the fail level achievement on my own with a low level energy.
You can also interact with people or creatures on the maps. In Lost Lands (Hidden Objects and Mahjong) and Clover Tales (a match-3 game based on the same mechanisms), you were scaring or killing enemies. Here, in Mystic Saga, you have people like a Merchant and a Sage with whom you'll exhange items. However, it's still the same item they need. But it's changing of spiders running around.
You can also collect items in a collection and exhange them once completed for tools, chests, experience, energizers or coins.
As it's implied that experience is used to level up, the fact to do it will increase your energy bar. Given the fact that some locations can cost 95 energy (I suppose that it will be the case, like in Lost Lands), increasing your bar is really advised.
The graphics are good but I'm just sad that clicking on the quest will make you leave the map and show you a full picture of the character concerned with their location. I prefer largerly how Lost Lands is handling it with just a pop-up. The soundtrack is also quite varied and nice.
Like Lost Lands or Clover Tales, Mystic Saga is free-to-play. However, as I've indicated, you can be tempted to buy money or crystals to advance faster in the game. And this is where you may be spending too much money if you're impatient. I will not point for a fourth time the hate I've for that kind of system.
But I will just give you a piece of advice: Mystic Saga will not disappear suddenly, at least, not now. Even if the stats of players aren't as high as a Killing Floor 2 or a Team Fortress, it's still enough for that kind of game. Besides, I suppose that from time to time, you'll be spending real money in the game, like I did for Lost Lands and Clover Tales. Thanks god, it's exceptionnal. In other words, you have time to complete the game. Just be patient and you'll see that you will not have the compulsion of buying more money or crystals.
In the end, I love Mystic Saga because it's similar to Lost Lands and yet so different and probably more adapted for me (an eastern setting, a soundtrack fitting and a better challenge). You can go ahead. Mystic Saga is really worthy.

At the time of this review, I have currently 2.9 hrs on record. I do not know if I'll get more or not because I have a few major reasons to dislike this game.
Single handly the biggest issue I faced, was not with the game at all but with the patching and account creation. Connecting to the patch servver was a gamble. Eventually I got tired of spam clicking 'Open wildstar' and waiting for it to fail. So I had to automate just running the game. So, on the rare chance that I am able to get the launcher going, I face another hurdle. Here the launcher while open, will try to connect to the servers once more. Repeat with the above and you'll begin to see why at this point, it becomes irksome. Spending time online to research solutions just to play a (Not my words) 'Dead MMO' is really off putting but I am open minded and was atleast willing to TRY the damn game. Adding dns entries to my host file, flushingdns, none of that works and it just comes down to luck. Will I be able to run Wildstar today? Well, probably not.
However, even before all of that can happen, I had to do the account creation for a 3rd party account. Apparently, Chrome, and firefox are too advanced a the site would keep throwing errors of failed creation. I had to actually switch Internet Explorer for it to work. At this point, morale is pretty low.
Right, so what about the game itself. Even after all that, I'm still willing to give it a chance. The game is a cutesy artstyle and I acatually enjoyed the world that I saw for briefly. The classes seem okay but does not seem like a lot of thought going into it. I picked soldier/stalker which may of been my problem but didn't see too much excitment out of it. The UI can be confusing for a bit you'll instantly be bombared with many ingame popup frames saying "DO THIS!" and it just becomes overwhelming to the point you'll click on everything just to get rid of them. The story was very intriguing, poor big tree -- just wanted to talk. Combat was okay I suppose, the telegraphying of attacks was super simple but I don't put that as a con since all MMOs make combat at a low level easy to understand, I imagine it gets worse as you level and you'd have to be much quicker on dodges. I mostly played by myself and only rarely saw other players. I suppose that is where the low population everyone chimes in about comes into play.
Overall, I just can't recommend a game that out of 2.9 hours, 1 hour is just trying to update/login without errors. Which is an honest shame too, it seems like the game would be atleast enjoyable and a refreshing attempt compared to other MMOs. Speaking of which, I consider myself to be a MMO veteran. World of Warcraft, Eve Online, Runescape, Guild Wars 2, Startrek Online, Realm of the Mad God, Warhammer 40,000: Eternal Crusade, and now Wildstar. Out of all those possible MMO's I've tried and played for years, Wildstar is the only one I've ever had this much trouble just trying to even start the game. Its a damn shame too

On a more serious note: Steel Ocean functions like World of Tanks, (or World of Warships more rather,) but with slightly less graphic fidelity. The player base is a little small, but the community is hoping for more members soon.
It's a free to play game, so there's no risk to you by playing it, however there are micro-transactions. In reality, they shouldn't be considered when downloading this game because all you can really do with your real-world cash is buy gold for purchasing some exclusive ships and decorating your owned vessels in game. Some argue it's pay-to-win, but really it makes no difference, at least to me.
What I like most about Steel Ocean is the fact that there is a lot less grinding for EXP and Silver when compared to the WoT games, assuming you're a decent player. It's more historically accurate, there is a diverse selection of ships and ship types from multiple factions (though there are some factions with very few ships to choose from. USA and Japan are your best bets if you want a larger selection.) The game is easy to grasp but requires at least some skill to master and a good amount of teamwork. Ensure everyone plays their roles well.
You can choose from:
- Light Cuisers
- Heavy Cruisers
- Destroyers
- Submarines
- Battleships
and
- Aircraft Carriers
So there you have it. It's an all-around good multiplayer experience. I hope you enjoy your playtime if you choose to get Steel Oceans, and if you do, I will see you on the sea of battle!

Please note that I am generally a harsh critic of games, so this positive review doesn't come lightly.
There are four classes: Templar, Berserker, Warden, Warlock.
Ok from those four you can make any class imaginable in every game, except perhaps a Floramancer from RIFT (a healer who heals others by damaging enemies).
Please note I have not yet played a Templar so I cannot comment. I will also add that playing the three classes of four there doesn't seem to be a healing class. If this game becomes super successful I can imagine a DLC or something to feel more immercive and team based. I believe the reason for the healer class being absent is that that's a hard job to do with leveling, as of course the game needs to function just as well in Single Player as well as Multiplayer.
Every class has 4-5 skill trees for maximum variety, mostly elemental variations of damage but the elements themselves are distinct from one another (cold tree is defensive and slows, fire tree burns stuff, etc.)
Warlock is my most experienced character. Your warlock is every mage, ever. He can dedicate himself to one strong element/tree, or spread out for more variety - for example a hellfire glass cannon, or a Necromancer gathering minions from all the trees.
The added variation is from the second experience bar - separately you gain levels in Masteries, which are pure passives and they augment your play even more. The masteries are quite varied and  I daresay they are yet another skill tree with many considerations.
The Skills are fantastic, I think a healing class or more co-operative skills would have made this game perfect, but it's a small loss and considering that would be hard to do with a controller skills are a solid 9/10
Finally there are the items - from common to unique you get your special things, even uniques roll random stats and you continue to find them at later levels - so your gear and drops are always around your level, but on the bright side it helps you better plan for the future.
Some items are also sets, bonus possibilities are even greater there, but still nothing unexpected.
There's also enchantments but I haven't played that far into the game yet.
LEGENDARY/Super Legendary(Lvl100+) Items - OOOOK here's the good stuff, these items start offering even weirder suffixes which apply directly to skills. You thought that passive looked cool, but the AoE explosion was too small? Well here comes a massive buff from these boots! Now it's a skill you can base your entire build around. Stuff like that.
Overall the itemisation could have gone even more interestingly, but as of Early Access, I consider it a 8/10
Random facts:
There's no hardcore mode.
The game keeps you mashing buttons and it's entertaining but if that's not fun enough you have to hold out until you get several skills to really feel like your character is being fleshed out.
Music is 6/10 - decent but nothing special.
Artwork 7/10
Graphics, well it's only the first area and this is E.Access but it looks a little dull. It's not annoying but it could be better 5/10
Game design - 8.5/10
The game is repetitive and some people don't like that but if you do enjoy Action RPGs then this will please you.
Local co-op, controller support, everything works great.
Hotkey economy - essentially you can only have around 6 active skills.
Controller support - I'm past my pro-gaming prime and I've comfortably settled for being a couch potato with an inferior instrument for gaming. This game is one of the best when it comes to controller support. For contrast I found Hero Siege very annoying.
On a final note I am seriously considering buying more copies of the game and sending it to random people, it's awesome and the devs deserve recognition for making great mechanics first, instead of a great looking broken P.o.s.
I hope this review has been helpful to you.

Perfectly timed jumps over jumps and if you miss the trajectory by even a micron you end up punished with death. Awful. Mark my words when you'll get to the "Vein of Helios" part of the game.
PRO
+ Borderlands, any version, is insanely fun.
+ Borderlands humour is unparallaled.
+ Pretty interesting story which cover the gaps between BL1 and BL2.
+ Plenty of different weapons and people to shoot at.
+ Vacuum and Low Grav scenarios are interesting.
CON
- Same engine and graphics of all other borderlands games.
- Way too many bugs.
- Story a little too short for Borderlands' standards.
- Pathetic Level Design in a few cases.

The story is amazing, at clocking around 55 hours to complete just about all the MAIN endings (there are a lot of side ones as well, which will hopefully provide a lot of replayability to this).
Unfortunately, as stated above, I said JUST ABOUT all the main endings. Unfortunately I had to look up ending E (which I believe is the canon ending to the game) on youtube.
THE GAME CRASHES EVERY TIME I HIT THE CREDIT SEQUENCE BEFORE ENDING E WILL PLAY.
I have checked the forums for a fix to this, unfortunately finding nothing that really helps. Sometimes I have gotten further along in the credit sequence before ending E will play than others. There is unfortunatly no rhyme or reason for why this happens, or when it happens, but it will crash during the credit sequence at one point or another before the ending is actually shown. This is without a doubt, one of the most irritating things I have ever experienced with a game. For it is an excellent game in nearly every aspect to me, and I had already reccomended this title personally to a few friends of mine.
But, on PC at least at this time I cannot recommend it due to this issue. If you don't mind having to look up just one of many endings to this game, I completly recommend this title. Otherwise, I advise you stay away until a patch is issued.
Outside of this, I have had no other issues with instability with Nier Automata on PC, but this is just one crash I cannot look past with how consistent it is.
