I have spent many hours in the Total War series. If I were to total all of them up (not including this, which only shows 61 hours currently), over all the computers I've owned and all the versions I've owned off of Steam, I would easily say that I've probably racked up well over 300-400 hours.
In that time, Medieval 2 has been my favorite. The depth of gameplay, the return of video assassinations, and the historical events, all masterfully done amidst the realistic religious strife...It makes it a complete game.
Become a Catholic nation whose neighbors war with you immediately. Send assassins to Rome to eliminate Popes with whom you have fallen out of favor. Continue your reign of terror until you can place one of your own Cardinals in the Vatican, firmly securing yourself in a position of favor within the Papacy.
Or strike hard and true as the hard-fighting Turks, with their naphta bomb throwers and their mastery of gunfire weaponry later. Call on your Muslim nations in a Jihad to reclaim lands lost, or to fight the infidels of lands far away.
Watch as your generals grow from young men to battle-hardened veterans, acquiring mercenary entourages as well as slave-women concubines -- until it turns out your general prefers men. Watch as he slips into madness and is cast off as a lunatic, all to see him claim the throne as his father dies of old age and he is next in line for the throne.
Master the art of the longbow or the crossbow, or the art of the heavy cavalry charge. Whatever your faction's strengths are, play them to their fullest and succeed on the field of battle.
Watch your provinces grow from small villages to mighty towns and cities, only to be wiped out by the Black Death. Watch your resources and money plummet as you go into severe debt (along with the rest of Europe and Africa and the Middle East), only to survive the ordeal and to find that, just as you are weak, so now are all your opponents, and you might just have enough strength to assail them in their moment of weakness.
The choice is yours. What kind of kingdom will you run?

At first the game is pretty good. There is a lot of customization you can put into your race, from species and ship type to starting planet and government. It really is good as a space rpg. The gameplay is solid as you recruit scientists and governors to research and build your empire. The research is also neatly done, with random choices appearing based on your empire and past decisions. To top off the RPG is a quest system called events, or an event chain. These can have minor results from getting more resources, or even change your empire completely.
So far, this has all been praise, but the game has a major fault. Namely, combat. The combat in this game is dull at best. There is some strategy involved based on what kind of armor and weaponry you use, as well as how you position your fleet. Beyond that, the combat work as such: Make as powerful a fleet as possible, send fleet at enemy. Once your fleet starts attacking, you lose all control of it. You have no say in anything they do after that point. This leads to really stupid combat choices, such as a large fleet of long range missiles going close range against enemies that have only close range  lasers. You also don't control who or how they target, so even if the enemy has a massive flagship, it's up to luck whether it'll be attacked or not.
The combat being so lackluster wouldn't be that big of a problem in any other 4x game. As such, the final nail in the coffin is this: The only way to win the game, is through combat. There are only two win conditions, wipe out all enemies, or own 40% of the galaxy. Since other empires spread out as much as possible, the only way to get that land is by fighting them. This ruins the roleplay of many races, gives isolationist empires disadvantages, and makes you slog your way through the combat.
Overall, a lot of the systems are fun and interesting, but only the most boring system can lead to victory. Not worth the 60$ or so you need to spend to get the game and dlc. Also, due to the long runtime of the games, you may end up in the same position I did, where you only find out how boring it is to try and win long after the time needed for a refund.
EDIT: As some people have pointed out, it is possible to get another empire as a vassal and then  integrate the vassal into your empire. This allows for a potential diplomacy type victory (still technically the expansion victory) by getting enough other empires integrated to reach the right size. As such, you may be able to win without having to get into wars, but it will be hard due to most empires distaste for servitude.
That said, it won't be very viable for my technocracy, stuck in a galaxy full of fanatic xenophobe spirtualists who hate my guts.

The Most Important thing in this game is Teamwork.
Destroyers are the Eyes and Battleships are the Hammers.
If play a Battleship and your destroyer lights up a target - Kill It.
If you play a CL or CA and your destroyer lights up a DD, CL or CA - Kill It.
If your destoyers are out of your gun range (You can't hit what they see), move up untill you can hit it and kill it.
That being said, Enemy Destroyers should be killed first as this gives your subs more room to play.
Then target enemy CL's. After this is done, your enemy BB's and CA's are blind.
Submarines are scouts too. They are also terrifying to BB's that are defenseless against them. Support your submarines and defend them from the DD that is trying to Torp and Depth Charge them.
DD's should SCOUT and ONLY SCOUT. Their PRIMARY JOB is to SCOUT. Their Secondary Job is to Kill UNSUPORTED Submarines (See above). DD's will get the occasional kill against lighter ships, but they should not charge in. This is a mistake that carries over from the T1 and T2 games.
Please understand that you cannot be Rambo in this game. You will die and your TEAM will lose.
Download it. Play it. Have fun.

This starts with an interesting concept, a time limited strategy game, in a rather minimalist style. However, that concept is marred by several design flaws that prevent this from being a truly fun experience.
While it is nice the game has different nations, religious bonuses, units, and building types, the simple fact is that nothing is balanced. At least two of the nations are unplayable except for those gamers looking for an excessive challenge. Two of the religions unlocked via play are 'must have', while the others can be safely ignored without impeding your enjoyment or effectiveness. The cost of buildings, expecially the higher level ones, are far too expensive for the comparative minimal benefits they grant.
The balance between the various units is better, although still lacking, especially considering the wholly random nature of attacks launched against you. This randomness also works against the game, as there is no true curve to the difficulty as the game progresses; it's simply a series of peaks and valleys. It is both annoying and frustrating to go from two millitiamen in one battle, to twenty knights and archers in the next. Since the game ends as soon as all of your units are defeated, and since you cannot predict, or even guess, what will be attacking you at any given time, you cannot stop focusing on developing your army, which, at mid to late game, limits what you are really able to do, where in most games with any type of upgrades, your options are more open and meaningful as you progress.
That said, I have put a decent amount of time into the game, and will likely play it for a few minutes here and there. I believe this is the best way to play this game, in small chunks, with plenty of time between sessions, when you have nothing else to do. As such, I will not fully recommend this game, since I assume the vast majority of gamers would rather play something that will hold their attention longer, or at least have slightly more long-term potential.

A 30 minute successful run of the game to show it off to viewers:
50 Years is a fun and quick game where you manage a small nation over 50 turns. You can do a run in 30 minutes; once you're done you'll try to think of other ways to do a run and want to play again.
The game: Over the course of 50 years (turns) you'll need to find a balance between economy and military might as you hire peasants and troops while building structures for varying purposes. At varying times, you'll come under attack from raids that will test your defenses and dungeons with special challenges/prizes will occur at timed points. There are 3 forms of currency: Gold/Wood/Faith. Each is important for different means, but you can focus on a specific economy depending on what nation you are using.
Gameplay: Solid and well balanced. At first you'll get run over, but in time you'll find strategies that work out. If the game feels too hard or easy, there are fortunately 5 levels of difficulty to allow you to do whatever you want.
Replayability: Because the game is so short and you have a variety of ways to go about playing, there are countless hours to play here. On top of that is the special modes and steam workshop.
Visuals/Music: Passable and servicable while you're having fun with the gameplay.
100% Recommend this game, wish it was on phone or tablet, it would be perfect for that.

Having played this game through and done a bit of skirmishing, I have to say I'm very optimistic. It's graphically beautiful with excellent animations, fun ragdolls and a boatload of fantastic effects. It's very clearly a labour of love too, visible in all the little details you can find in the textures and on the models. The boardgame rules translate flawlessly onto the PC as well, turning a game that can take hours to play into something you can play in half an hour or so. The abilities are cool, the units feel unique and powerful, and tactical play is just so genuinely satisfying.
I'm not seeing a lot of cons either. Most of my issues with the game as it stands come with the fact it's in Early Access. It's an incomplete, in progress game. It's got its crashes, its glitches, its frame drops and all that, but it's so easily forgivable. I don't regret a single minute spent on this game and I'm excited to return to it as it gets updated. This is also definitely a game that I could see myself gobbling down DLC for, getting new armies and units. The content you get with the main purchase is definitely, in my humble opinion, a full game's worth too, so I don't feel like it's unwarranted to do so. A solid singleplayer campaign and a nice selection of armies and units for multiplayer. It feels complete in that regard, and I'm certain they'll be adding onto it before the game comes out proper.
That being said, I do need to point out that this is a boardgame turned into a PC game, and thus the main crowd it attracts are the boardgamers, the war gamers, the tactical turn based gamers. It's methodical. It rewards understanding your units and their abilities, thinking through your actions, making smart plays and using positioning to your advantage. It's not for everyone, but boy oh boy, it's definitely for me.

Wildstar is a action-heavy cartoonish sci-fi mmorpg that is fully free to play with a fair business model letting you earn a currency that enables you to buy most vanity items by just playing the game with an optional subscription that enables you to progress a little faster and get some goodies on the side similar to TESO.
Pros:

- Fun freeform combat system (no 30 hotbars , no point and click)
- Classes all have at least 2 roles they can fulfill (makes grouping a lot nicer)
- Leveling at a moderate but fair pace
- Old WoW players like me that are kinda without an equivalent might rekindle old interest in mmos playing this
- Cross-faction grouping for instances and more
Cons:
- Playerbase while dedicated seems a bit small, dont expect to find low level pvp matches for example.
Note: Playerbase is more centered around the endgame where raiding and the like are fine though.
- A bit confusing at first, especially if this is your first mmo (crafting grid, several kinds of dungeons, amps etc.)

So I have to write a good review once and awhile just to prove to myself I'm not 100% a cynic.
This one will be short and sweet. With WildStar you won't get anything truly original or 100% AAA polished with this MMO. You won't get non generic quests or a story you will remember when somebody asks you about this game 5 years from now. However, what you will get is a truly beautiful artstyle driven game that scratches a particular itch that none of the MMOs out there has yet to try. Now, mind you that this is more like temporary relief for that itch but a relief non-the-less. And that itch is to have an adventure themed MMO with a light hearted cartoony style approach like the Jak and Daxter or Ratchet and Clank series.
Now, it has it's problems, mind you, and some pretty heavy ones at that. Those include: Game breaking bugs, no real party system for story game play, radical difficulty spikes, and a declining player base (for previous reasons). However, remember that this game is free and with that free game play, you get great music, fun story missions and side missions (not filler quests but voiced dialogue stories), and some interesting creativity with level design and player housing.
And for those who are wondering what will keep your attention, I say the game mechanics will. While it's certainly not new, and their are better mechanic MMO's like Black Desert, BnS, or Tera; WildStars mechanics are still faster paced skill shots and don't rely on the old MMO macro systems.
Bottome line is, if you've been looking for a quick to learn MMO to burn some freetime on, you should download WildStar. It's certainly worth the download and creating an account time, if not more.

Mystic Saga is a freemium hidden object point & click game. You can access a few locations at first like a cabin or blacksmith's house and you just have to find the objects it tells you to find. When you do finish a stage, you're rewarded with items to turn in to NPCs and they'll unlock more quest and so on. You'll also earn experience points so you can level up and access even more stages.
Here's the catch though. You get a certain amount of energy points. Every time you enter a stage it depletes your energy points and the only way to replenish them is by waiting minutes in real-time, finding energy repleneshing items from getting achievements or quest rewards, and by purchasing items from the in-game store with in-game currency. If you've run out of currency you can spend
as a shortcut just like any freemium game. You run out of energy very fast too since a stage only takes a minute or less.
The artwork is nice at least, it looks like the art department put effort into that. The game itself is very repetetive and unrewarding though, there are much better hidden object games on steam that are worth buying rather than sinking $ into microtransactions in this game. I'm sure you can complete the game by not spending a dime but that would take patience I don't have. I've only played for an hour but having to replay the same stages over and over killed any motivation I had to keep going.

Short version: Unless you REALLY like playing hidden object games, and you don't mind either spending money or lots of time waiting doing literally nothing, I cannot really recommend this game.
This game gives you quests which are "gather X amount of items", and you gather those items by going to the hidden object scenes, which you unlock by leveling up. Completing one rewards you with one or more random items. The game seems to give priority to those you need for your quests, which is good, as the amount of different items grows exponentially as you continue completing quests.
Now this wouldn't be so bad, but sadly, the game uses the classic browser/mobile game trick where you have "energy", which you spend doing the HO scenes. As you go to locations more and more, they level up and cost more energy to do.
Now, even all of that wouldn't be too bad, but then there's the "characters" you interact with. As you unlock more locales, more NPCs appear, roaming the map. There's several items that you can use with these NPCs to exchange for a random item out of their stock. Sadly, unlike with the HO scenes, the NPCs do not prioritize items you need, and some of these items are exclusive or just about exclusive to just these NPCs, meaning that if you have bad luck with rolls, you don't get the items you need or no needed collectibles at all. If you don't have the item you exchange for interacting with the NPCs, it costs in-game gold to interact with them.
For instance, I had a quest where I needed one item from the Wolf NPCs. It took me about 25 tries to finally get it off of him, and he only had 4 possible drops at the time (most of them didn't drop anything).
In other words, this game is very much designed to extort money from you by making you wait in order to play, and locking needed items behind the 100% random chance NPCs.
If you don't mind all of this, and like Hidden Object games, this game might be for you. Otherwise, though, I'd recommend looking at other ones.

The Steam Community will like this 'free to play' Hidden Object game far better then the last one (Lost Lands: A Hidden Object Adventure), for one, the achievements are far easier to get and are in sync with the area leveling.  Achievements are earned at the first level up.  Though I am sure many will still complain about microtransactions that NEVER, EVER have to be done.
The player levels up relatively fast giving the player a full energy bar to continue playing.  There are 38 locations in total to open.  There are also two nice features at the bottom of the page, a diary and main story quest log, so the player can keep track of the storyline.
The Hidden Object scenes start out with 3 items and the items increase at each level.  Also the player is encouraged to chain the object finds to increase the "prizes" of XP, money, items, and energy.  A special area feature is the little picture by each area name indicting the type of HO scene available.  "Sun" is straight find list.  "Hand and sun" Silhouette mode.  "Moon and stars" Night mode.  This makes it much easier to know, find and anticipate certain modes when needed for quests.
Much easier play style compared to other games of this type, with far less grinding then usual and who can beat the price of FREE, so give it a try if so inclined.

My wife and I have played through the existing campaign twice now, and will likely revisit it again once the next acts are added. It is enjoyable and accessible. The latest patches to overhaul the character progression have been particularly nice, as it felt like a much, much more broad set of builds became not only viable, but satisfying to play. The early game does suffer from some initial power creep, as abilities are introduced slowly to apply a learning curve, but this curve feels particularly slow. It will take several levels to get to the 'meat' of most any build, or even a reliable AoE ability.
Split screen coop was handled fairly well, with few glaring frustrations having been discovered through two playthroughs, the worst being a small bug that will likely be fixed. (When player one highlighted current items on the ground, player two was unable to attack while both were using gamepads. Minor, avoidable, and far from gamebreaking.)
I do not recall any crashes or other issues with the game, aside from the missing statue in act three, that is easily remedied by re-entering the area.
I'm quite certain I'll spend more time playing this than D2. It's a great game made by an awesome guy.

Steel Ocean is a Free to Play ocean-based World War 2 naval Simulation (that should be a tag, it just roles of the tongue).
With the amount of detail that is in this game, I am amazed it is free. Granted there are micro-transactions, but they are not game breaking or pay-to-win.
You fight against similar levelled foes in PVP battles. The ships have different roles in battle, sadly most people want a Battleship and then wonder why they can't see the bad guys. The Destroyers die quickly, the Subs can't stay underwater for too long and the Battleships sit and camp spawn while someone launches torpedos at them. Despite all of this, it is still good fun.
I would like to see a 'count as kill' option, as player 1 can do 99% damage to a ship then player 2 can take the credit for the kill. For ships with lower overall DPS this can get really frustrating when it comes to the scoreboard.
Friendly fire is on, this can be annoying as I have destroyed more friendly ships accidently with torpedos than I have opposing forces. This means that you can't just spam torpedos and hope for the best (well.... actually you can). If you kill a friendly player it counts as -1 on your score.
I would like to see a negative score for every hit a friendly makes on you, I have had players take my ships HP down then float away, making my ship pretty much useless.
Your ammo is limited, however you are only likely to run out of Torpedos quickly, or planes if you are on a carrier.
Carriers are quite vulnerable and are rarely protected, the AA fire from standard ships makes playing a carrier quite challenging. You also make a large fat stationary target for subs/fast ships to throw Torpedos at.
There are 2 types of currency; silver and gold coins. Silver is acquired through normal game mechanics and Gold is part of the micro-transaction system.
Your ship choices are defined via a tech tree which requires Silver coins and XP to unlock. XP is gained through battles and it does not take long to unlock the first few ships. Most aspects of the ship can be upgraded slightly through this tech-tree, but it won't make you invincible. Once a ship is fully upgraded it becomes an "elite" ship and there are extra bonuses around that.
Your ship receives it's own XP per match, but you also receive global XP which can be used on any ship in the tech tree upgrades.
Overall this is a fun game that can provide hours of fun for no cost. There are some lag issues which get really annoying, at first I thought this was my internet connection, but after playing it over fibre the problems are still there. The Euro proxy was supposed to make things better,  Ihaven't noticed.  This works fine (for me) on Windows 10. There are Steam Achievements including some rare ones if you are a collector.
I would recommend this, after all it is free.

This is roughly my third fourth attempt at muddling through writing this Zenith review, because there’s something very difficult in trying to talk about a game that gets so many of its base mechanics so hilariously wrong, yet still winds up being okay in the end. It manages that feat mostly because its sporadic highlights are based around something as subjective and intangible as humour.
You probably won’t laugh at every joke, but Zenith spreads them around with such a sense of reckless aplomb that it’ll be unlikely you’ll find nothing to appreciate inside its ten or so hour lifespan. It pokes fun at itself, at fantasy tropes, at the genre, at pop references, and even at its own reliance on pop references. Early in the game, you’ll meet caricatures of famous Final Fantasy protagonists whose overstated personality quirks openly annoy the people around them. There’s a sense that, even though the game has staples like a big evil trying to destroy the world, it’s incapable of taking anything all that seriously. The threat is never diminished; you’re under no doubt that something very powerful wants everything very dead and is very capable of making that happen. It’s just that it sometimes wanders by to casually chat and catch up on old times. Like how he was once thwarted by an elephant that you had to use as a substitute for a machine part, which has since been recognised as a holy symbol referenced throughout the game.
The problem Zenith has is that it can’t all be about stuffing elves into empty wine barrels and having a golem lob them up the side of a mountain. Sometimes, it has to make a sincere stab at being an action-RPG. The biggest issue there is that the only things weaker than Zenith’s particularly bland action are its barely-existent RPG elements.
It’s all very threadbare. You have an XP counter that you fill by taking on clunky real-time battles and, once you fill it, you can invest a point in a skill tree that is filled with barely useful skills. Oh, and there’s an awful, awful loot system that gives you the same small collection of armour over and over, just with a roman numeral attached so you can see what’s supposedly superior. It means you often come out of a dungeon with, for example, a handful of Earth Ring III accessories.

A very basic turn based strategy that involves building buildings to either gain more resources or grow your army. Every turn you stand the chance to get attacked. Limited opportunities for side quests and a maximum of 50 turns per game.
I can only recommend this game if you get it on sale and have extremely low expectations on tactical aspects of turn based strategies. Unless you enjoy figuring out what army comps are best for a specific starting situation and enjoy not having any form of control beyond that this game simply isn’t for you. Even the challenge modes that are available are best described by the word ‘meh’.
Hopefully it being early access will remedy some of the core issues over time but for now I can't really call this a 'good' turn based strategy.
At the 5 euro price point this game will deliver 10 hours worth of ‘fun’ at most provided you’re trying to get all achievements completed. The strategy aspects are too flat to give you real value for money.
is a basic tactical turn based combat game with a maximum of 50 turns per game.
You build buildings in your little ‘town’ which don’t actually appear in your town to unlock either more resources or capabilities to recruit different units into your armies. The more buildings you have of a single type the more units of that type you can have.
The building cost scale in such a fashion that you cannot build a lot of the same building more or less forcing you to decide on a basic army composition. Basic research is covered through a point system which you can collect through doing battles or building religious buildings.
You will be able to fill out about 10 research items in the course of the 50 turns you have making some research items infinitely more valuable than others.
Unfortunately, the user interface didn’t receive a lot of polish resulting in occasional overlaps, texts shifting slightly off screen and other annoying little tidbits that while absolutely not game breaking give it a very amateurish feel.
It's a good thing that there’s not too much text to read because what little ‘English’ there is, is barely recognizable as such.
The absolute downfall for this game however, at least for me, is the complete lack of tactical combat depth. Beyond the composition of your army (in which you can’t seem to dismiss any units to get a better sorting) you have no control on where on the battle field units are placed nor do you get any means to move units individually.
The two opposing forces just engage each other in a straight line giving you all the thrill of watching Tetris blocks trying to murder each other.
The game would’ve really benefitted from a little more polish and quite a bit more control options and could’ve really been worth the sticker price. As it stands however you’re likely to find a better turn based game without having to look too far.
Hopefully as the game grows out of early access there will be a lot more here and I will happily have another look at my review then.

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW: 9/25/14
With the latest patch from 9/23/14, you can finally play Skirmish mode, which means that you make your own army and play against someone else with their custom army, or against the PC (currently on Easy mode).  A typical skirmish game takes about 30-45 minutes.  For $40, I think that's a pretty fair price for what you'll eventually get when this game is complete, not to mention that there's going to be a 21-mission single player campaign too.
Fun is what it is, and it's pretty close to the tabletop miniature game.  It has so much ridiculous potential that if you're a fan of the Iron Kingdoms lore, miniature wargaming, and/or the X-Com style of turn-based strategy combat, then you'll have many hours of fun with this game in my opinion.

I purchased this game on Kickstarter and the beta is quite promising. Overall, the game is quite tactical as promised and the combat looks and feels visceral. Since it is still in beta, I will not comment of the bugs, lack of all playable features, etc. since that is to be expected from any beta. It is still too early to judge the single player storyline too. The gameplay, multiplayer-wise, is already quite fantastic even in beta.
I have 3 concerns. First, it is for a very high end computer. It barely runs on any computers from 3 years ago or older, especially laptops. I have confirmed this on a number of computers from the pre-2011 lineups. On lowest settings, I run at 3-4 fps. Don't expect to get any higher than 20 fps unless you bought the computer in the last two years with a mid-to-high-range (at the time) graphics card. Surprisingly high requirements should bar a good numbers of players, expecially at a time when PC/laptop sales are in a historic freefall.
Also, there are specific issues for the two major groups of players: those familiar with the tabletop game and those who aren't.For those who are familiar, they may be very turned off by the rules changes from the table top, namely that the units of infantry are much smaller in number and thus scaled so each infantry is considerably more powerful than the tabletop version. For those who aren't familiar, the price for the game on Steam, particularly for the digital deluxe, seems a bit of a gamble. If they aren't certain they will like the game's universe, that is asking for a lot. Thus, both groups face a major downside with the purchase of the game. I wish they at least catered to one of the groups, preferably the tabletop fans, who probably backed their kickstarter with capital already.

Wildstar is an incredible game for some, and for others just another stepping-stone while trying to find your next MMO home. Now let me be clear, no one should go into Wildstar expecting to settle down. Even ignoring the potential for the game to shutdown at any time they desire, it's just not an enriched world you'll want to spend your every moment in. It's a barren wasteland with friendly faces and incredible content spread out.
That's how you should approach Wildstar. In it's current iteration it takes about 8 hours for a new player to reach max level, and it's not the most fun journey. However once you get there, join a guild and the potential of the game is unlocked. Raids are incredible enough to warrant the other crap you'll have to put up with so long as you like the combat style (it's not for everyone).
Treat it like a singleplayer game (unless you go in with friends) until max level, and then find a guild with raid times that match your schedule. Once you get to that point, you're probably not going to play much outside of those raid hours ... but that's fine, because the raiding experience is so enjoyable.
Don't let the low population get you down - Wildstar is a really great experience, it's just not your traditional MMO where you'll log in every day for hours and hours with thousands of people around you to interact with. But that's fine, just know it going in, and experience it before its gone.
tl;dr - If you like raiding try the game for ~30 minutes. Try a few classes, and if you enjoy the combat then keep playing. Find a guild based on raid times, and treat it like a game that only exists during those hours (once you hit max level obviously). Then realize that's it, there's nothing left, but it was fun while it lasted.

PALADINS IS NOT OVERWATCH.
Okay, now that we've got that out of the way, let me unpack it a little bit.
While both games, Paladins and Overwatch, are team-based shooters in the vein of Team Fortress 2, they are both very different. Here are some of the ways they compare, as well as my personal opinions:
PROS:
+Paladins currently has over 30 playable characters (and counting!)
+Paladins uses an interesting card-based perks system that is generated uniquely per match, allowing you to tailor your damage or healing boosts to more effectively counter your opponents.
+For those of us who suck at FPS games (myself included), Paladins feels like it has a little bit of aim-assist to help you out--particularly compared with games such as CS:GO or Overwatch.
+The characters themselves feel really unique and clever--very rarely will I find two characters to feel the same as I'm playing them
+There is a built-in rewards system for accumulating gold and crystals (to unlock cosmetics/characters) the more successive days you play.
CONS:
-Microtransactions. I don't care how good the game is, I personally still don't care for microtransactions. It feels like the game doesn't trust itself.
-The game is still in beta, so some characters still aren't balanced very well (Evie and Jenos in particular)
Overall, though, I'd give this game a 9/10. Would recommend!

Another issue is the teamwork and team effort in this game. Compared to Overwatch and CSGO, its crap. In Overwatch and CSGO more people take the time to strategize to win and compete. Zenith is an irreverent take on the ARPG and fantasy genre with an interesting story that's unfortunately bogged down by the framework in which it lives. If you do play it, play it because the story is charming and witty, and mixes serious, silly, and sarcastic together in equal measure, while still telling a decently compelling tale. It's full of references to other games, and self-aware nods at the genre it settles in, and is pushed by a likeable cast with clear and relatable motivations.
The game itself, unfortunately, is nothing to sneeze at. The art is decent enough to carry it, but nothing amazing or spectacular. There are afew sceens with decent vistas, but for the most part you're just going to be staring at an isometric view of the usual scenic ARPG vistas, and that's by design.
The music is full of ups and downs. There's no volume control, so be sure to change the game's volume in Volume Mixer. It's way too loud. The music itself runs the gamut from jaunty tunes that match the lgihthearted theme of the game, to orchestral themes, to a few power metal themes for specific parts. The music sometimes feels out of place, and some of the tracks loop in awkward places that take you out of the game every time you catch the jarring loop end and begin. The good songs are pretty good, though, as are most of the main themes you hear throughout the game and in different remixes. There is no voice acting, so the songs and SFX are all you get here.  I don't consider the lack of voice acting a negative, though.
The ARPG combat itself is passable. There's 3 elements, and 3 weapons, 3 projectiles, and 3 AoE spells, one for each element. Levelling up is boring, and skill point effects should have been multiplied by about 10. I can't get excited about 2% more damage a rank when you can only put 2 ranks in it. The only ones that do an appreciable thing are the combo extenders. Definitely a missed opportunity. combat itself is very ARPG typical mobile stick and run against primarily melee enemies that attack with combos. So it's a lot of stick and move, and melee, until later in the game when you become an unstoppable juggernaut, is a dicey prospect. The game showers you in healing potions, but they're on a cooldown, so you can't be too over extended. Loot is OK: Mostly bigger numbers, slanted towards one of the three elements. Basically nothing gives physical resist, and I'm almost convinced this is on purpose as a nod at the fact that you're a robe wearing wizard all game.  Spells are all decent, but fire magic is bottom tier by a great deal: Ice magic hits multiple times and slows enemies, and earth magic creates pushing shockwaves and stone walls that pierce foes. Fire is just single target shot, middling damage. Fists and swords felt like they were way more powerful than hammers, with no appreciable difference in range or AoE. I stuck with fists pretty much the entire game.
Despite all this, I'd still recommend the game to people, if they're willing to look past its flaws. Nestled within a mostly passable ARPG with a lame overworld and "random encounter" map, no map system, and no quest log, is a genuinely interesting game with interesting world lore, and populated by a main cast of characters with motivations and aspirations that drive the story, rather than the story driving them. The ending leaves some questions unanswered, but they feel unimportant in the scope of the game - and this is made clear by the cast at the end as well, who also doesn't feel the need to ask the questions or seek answers for them. It's another nod to the genre.
Would recommend, but be aware the game is a bit clunky and may not appeal. I went through because I love ARPGs and I enjoyed the story - you may not be willing to go through it. It's roughlya 10-12 hour game.

I'm a long-time Kongregate member and so I played every Doodle God game many years ago; after much time I found this one on a big sale and I decided to play it even on Steam.
Graphics are awesome compared to the Flash games, I really loved the terraforming scenes and such, but the rest of the game consists - of course - of the usual combining of two elements in order to create a new one, or more, and you'll get every time a nice random quotation from some guy of sort.

Let's get the obvious out of the way: I understand that this is a beta, that they have yet to go through all the optimization steps, and that games on a mac usually don't run as smoothly as on the same windows machine.
So I know not to expect this game to be perfect. Yet I am disappointed. First off it runs incredibly slowly, meaning I have to lower the settings to abysmal levels in order to play. Then many standard features are lacking (like deactivating the hot corners in full screen, or having the escape bar unselect the current selection or close the current screen BEFORE it brings up the menu) which immediately give a first impression of amateurism. And finally the options are very scarce as it isn't possible to play a standard practice game vs. the AI.
Essentially this is the beta of a beta. Showing it to the public now satisfies the cravings of hardcore Warmachine fans who do not need any convincing to begin with, disappoints those who like the universe enough to know about this game and give it a shot but aren't necessarily blindly enjoying everything the company makes, and will definitely turn off gamers who know nothing about the IP but usually enjoy this kind of game.

50 years is addicting resource management game.Every few turns get attacked so you have to find a balance between building economy and military. There are several different modes but no endless at the time of this review. Considering that I like this game it really sucks that you can only play for 50 turns.
At the start of the game, you can choose between several nations that give starting bonuses. Some are better than other but you can always make it harder on yourself and pick a weaker one ( there are achievement for playing each nation )
Combat is automatic and has some luck attached to it because units hit random targets. I am not sure if its a good or bad thing but it least you can't 100% predict what happens. When playing on very hard it is very important to find right army composition and it will challenge you.
There are 3 different late game units that rely on different resources. You can commit to a specific unit type or find a balance between them. You can also go on random quests that may give units or buildings as a reward .
Skill tree has 25 perks. Last skill in each route requires 4 skills before it. You can either choose to commit to a specific skill path or find a balance between them.
Music is relaxing and does not distract from thinking. There is no much animation but in this genre, I look for decision making and not good looks.
Score : 7/10 . Very simple but enjoyable resource management game that can be played in different ways. Every wrong choice can snowball your loss so there is a good amount of decision making  .It took me about 4 hours to figure out how to beat very hard difficulty so I really wish there was endless mode and maybe leaderboards.

I picked this game up a couple of days ago after reading about it on the Grim Dawn forums.  I really wanted to hate it, I get a disturbing amount of joy out of disliking the indie craze that every dumb fan boy is jumping all over, but I can't.  This game really is killer for entertainment value.  I'll write a longer review when I get some time.
Suffice it to say, I'm a pretty fickle person when it comes to graphics.  When i first started looking at this game, I was disgusted with the graphical style, but it grew on me.  It actually has a bit of charm.
Balance seems to be a bit all over the place.  Both in terms of mobs and skills, but that's part of what makes the game fun.  I'm playing a lightning warden and this "Nimbus" Skill (a cloud that zooms around the map) is fantastic.  Cruises around, procs all my on attack effects, destroys the entire map.
What surprised me the most is the pace and responsiveness of combat.  It's excellent.  I'm playing with WASD and my mouse and I've been extremely pleased with the control of my character.  I'll probably crack out the gamepad tomorrow just to see how it compares, but it absolutely can be played with M+KB.
There isn't a ton in the way of a story, but in an action RPG about the loot hunt and explosively awesome build combinations, that doesn't bother me.  It's there if you want it to be, but isn't particularly intrusive.  I think the single developer has plans to rewrite some the dialogue to improve the overall lore.
The map overlay is a bit inconsistent as well.  In some areas, it's too dark (makes seeing your character/what's beneath the overlay difficult) and in others it is far too light.  This is pretty minor, but you might occassionally find yourself annoyed by it.  Note, there is a setting to change the opacity, but given the fast/frenetic gameplay it seems a bit obtuse to have to.
The class system/build system is excellent.  Kind of similar to Grim Dawn/Titan Quest, though not exactly, and leaves you with a lot of options.
Boss encounters are designed pretty well; I enjoyed them, just wish there were more.
Difficulty scaling could probably be tweaked.  I started in the middle, jumped to the second difficult around level 20, and by 50 I was playing on legendary after I had gotten some good gear.  I'm now level 100 and around ~60 anomaly and haven't had too many issues.  Occassionally run into a mob that has an absurd combination of affixes and wrecks me, but for the most part it is smoothe sailing.
Really looking forward to the next couple of acts.  I had a great time.

PALADINS IS NOT OVERWATCH.
Okay, now that we've got that out of the way, let me unpack it a little bit.
While both games, Paladins and Overwatch, are team-based shooters in the vein of Team Fortress 2, they are both very different. Here are some of the ways they compare, as well as my personal opinions:
PROS:
+Paladins currently has over 30 playable characters (and counting!)
+Paladins uses an interesting card-based perks system that is generated uniquely per match, allowing you to tailor your damage or healing boosts to more effectively counter your opponents.
+For those of us who suck at FPS games (myself included), Paladins feels like it has a little bit of aim-assist to help you out--particularly compared with games such as CS:GO or Overwatch.
+The characters themselves feel really unique and clever--very rarely will I find two characters to feel the same as I'm playing them
+There is a built-in rewards system for accumulating gold and crystals (to unlock cosmetics/characters) the more successive days you play.
CONS:
-Microtransactions. I don't care how good the game is, I personally still don't care for microtransactions. It feels like the game doesn't trust itself.
-The game is still in beta, so some characters still aren't balanced very well (Evie and Jenos in particular)
Overall, though, I'd give this game a 9/10. Would recommend!

Once upon a time, rocks fell and everyone died, because Voldemort took over the world...sort of.  You see, he didn't take over all of the world, so humanity fled beneath the surface to previously unexplored caves lush with life that requires sunlight to grow, including but not limited to plants, trees, T-Rexes, Shelob, Bilbo, and...wait, we're still talking about
, right?
Magicite is a side-scrolling roguelike, where you adventure through areas in pursuit of defeating The Scourge, because Arthas is a wuss...wait, we're still talking about Magicite right?
As you can tell, Magicite draws from various RPGs of yesteryear for its inspiration despite being a sidescroller.  Each Death is very important, because you can win new races with different starting loadouts, hats, and companions.
But is it good?
The 2D presentation is amped up by clever use of 3D techniques such as bloom shaders; the UI integrates seamlessly with the rest of the game.  Visually, there are really no faults to speak of in this title.
The controls are somewhat intuitive, and pressing Escape brings them up - left clicking 'attacks' with an item, while right click uses an item's special abilities (such as firing an arrow, firing a spell, etc.)  The in-game crafting in particular is well-suited to quickly creating things in order to defeat challenges.
The game's tempo is also good; after every area, you find a town, where you can do more in-depth crafting, sell spare items, buy items, and generally take a short breather.  This is good, because each area has a hidden time limit - if you stay too long, the Dungeon Guardian comes and deals you 9999 damage when it hits you...wait, we're still talking about
, right?
The first thing I noticed is that the physics are sort of wonky, if things land on top of you - they will sort of sit there and inhibit your ability to jump.  Sometimes it autoresolves, but not always - I've been able to blame a death on this particular physics bug.
Next, you can gain special abilities as you play through the game.  The controls for these abilities are obscure.  While you can see them with Escape, I find them forgettable and awkward to use.  I'm sure I would find the game more manageable if the special abilities unlocked by leveling up were more obvious, and easier to use.
Another thing at least for me is that after a few minutes of play, the audio for the game will mysteriously cut out for seemingly no reason at all.  This is very bad, because the game has a number of audio cues to telegraph certain things (like Scourge invasions).
While this is a Roguelite with all of the difficulty such a title entails, I find the game's difficulty curve a touch too high, actually - after a number of playthroughs, I've not managed to fight the final boss yet, and usually die well beforehand due to healing potions being too hard to come by.  While most 'traps' deal 1 damage, monsters usually deal 2, and strong monsters deal 4 damage per hit, in later screens it's possible to have the game more or less transition into a bullet hell game...which, this game is not tuned for.  I rarely say this due to games these days being too easy, but this one I feel is a touch too hard, but not due to my lack of skill, per se - increase the drop chance for Herbs (used to make Healing Potions), and try to tune the RNG to not spawn a bunch of projectile-spamming enemies.  The fact that I can hit more or less unwinnable screens is a Bad Thing™.
Lastly, decrease the dependence on the RNG.  I know, I know - Roguelite.  Much RNG is to be expected, but in this game, there are some really pointless randomizations on things - for instance, tools can grant HP gains, but only while you're using that tool.  If you're switched away from that tool, you can have full HP.  Due to the fact that there are no external healing sources, this means with a HP tool, you can never have full HP.  This isn't game-breaking, but it horribly inflames my OCD!  Stop doing that to me game!  Additionally, why give magic power to mundane tools like swords, axes, and pickaxes?  You can only use magic by using magic staves; if a staff has no Magic modifier, but a tool does, that's
!  WTF game!?
Should you buy Magicite?  Yes, absolutely recommended, it's a game worth your purchase, but it has problems that make it more frustrating than a Roguelite should be.  Still, these problems are often mild enough that you should still be able to enjoy the game as I am, and feel that you're getting your money's worth.

This is clearly and indie title, let's start with that.
3rd person fantasy/sci-fi action roleplaying game wiht plenty of satirical elements.  Takes about 10 hours to play through.
Strictly the game is as bare-bones as that, but it doesn't need to be more.
Let's start with the negatives:
The controller control scheme takes getting used to
Movement does not take analogue input
Graphics are ho-hum for 2016 (only a concern to some)
Lots of royalty-free music used in the soundtrack (they work, but original score would've worked nicely)
The overarching story is a bit cliche at times
Parrying is impossible when on the offensive
Oldschool camera
Story choices are illusions (was that the point?)
Sidekick doesn't do much anything in battle
Positives:
Sidekick doesn't get hurt in battle or hinder you
The writing is solid
The humor is spot-on
The setting is interesting
The monsters are varied (tenor-singing giant spiders)
The characters KNOW their adventure is cliche
All them pop-culture references (don't make a drinking game out of it; you gon die)
Weapons and powers make for easily costumisable gameplay (directed magic blast, empowered melee, magic AoE attack and dodge mechanic)
Oh, if the studio had had more resources for this along with talented voiceacting, the game would've been even better.
Still, as it stands, it's well above average for me.  And for an indie game that's a lot.
Looking forward to what the studio will make next.
EDIT: oh, almost forgot, a controller is basically a must to play this game, IMO.

No but in all seriousness here - This is not just a game. It is simply a piece of art.
A masterpiece
Most people seem only to be talking about butts - yeah there are butts as well. But it's not just a fanservice game. If you want that, go play Senran Kagura. There is more fanservice there.
This game is really a hidden treasure of the gaming world.
From the absolutely overwhelmingly great music to the extremely likeable characters, the extremely fun gameplay and the simply absolutely stunning story that I don't even have any words for anymore after finishing each of it's unique 5 main endings (not talking about the joke endings here) it was through and through a ride.
Yoko Taro's (the creator of the nier and it's sequel nier:automata) biggest issue with modern triple A titles were, that after you figured out these games for an hour or two they mostly remained the same for the next 20 or 30 hours - he wanted the mix of story and game to be surprising and always fresh and new for players and keep it interesting and exciting.

And he really managed to do that.
Nier:Automata - be it story and gameplay wise will give you one "wow moment" after the other. But it doesn't rest on these moments - no every time you think you've seen it all and think nothing can surprise you anymore this game will slap you in the face and leave you with a huge "wow" yet again.
And the characters.
The way it plays makes you feel more and more attached and familiar with the character you play, the dialogues and story slowly make you love and appreciate the characters and their unique personalities.
Seldom have I felt as much with the characters of a game as in Nier:Automata - joy, sadness, anger, hatred, love, pain - I felt so many different emotions while playing this game and when I had to stop playing I eagerly awaited the moment I could continue this adventure.
It might be one of the greatest games I have ever experienced - the game is incredibly expensive, yes, but what you get here for your money is an experience that you might never forget even.
The dialogue is so thought provoking that at some points I had to stop playing just to really think about the philosophic statements I had just heard.
The fights and the bossfights in this game are simply epic and they feel epic.
The voice acting is great and full of emotions - though I only play with japanese dub and english subs as I think the original dub is the one intended by the maker to be played like that. I always go with the original dub in games and for movies/series, so I can't say much for the english game dub.
I could go on here however Nier:Automata also comes with some drawbacks that have to be mentioned.
First of all the pc-version has several unfixed issue which is why I recommend you to install FAR - which you can find pinned in the community discussions as a download.
Also this game needs quite a powerful pc to run smoothly - if you don't have one it might be impossible for you to play this game with a desireable performance. In that case you might rather get yourself the playstation 4 version of the game and if you don't happen to have either simply have to wait till your pc is better or you own a ps4.
Gameplay wise there are some as well:
Some side-quests like the desert search with the scanner are incredibly frustrating and without some serious luck or the help of the internet can take you even hours to finish
As there is not much of a gameplay tutorial you will discover many possibilities in the game - and the way you can play and move probably only through playing - making some quests incredible difficult as you don't have a clear insight about what your character can do or not.
For example I did not realize that I can grab my pod and use it to throw myself farther - making it incredibly difficult or almost impossible to get to that chest and I only found out about that feature due to sheer luck.
The game is also clearly designed for console playing and I can't imagine someone having as much fun playing with a keyboard - from camera controls, dodging, options, self destruct - everything is completely fine-tuned for an amazing console play with your controller sometimes even vibrating at certain fitting story points, like when a giant stomps onto the ground, really making you feel the impact of the earth shaking
The pc version was probably just released on steam to have another platform they can sell it to and they clearly didn't put much effort in here.
As a last thing that might be taken as a drawback is that some people thought the game was kidding when it warned the player of a certain choice at the very end of the game - far behind everything else with the story already done.
The game warns you multiple times before making your choice and it is not kidding - so either back up your save or really think which option you want to choose as you can't undo that one!
Certain people who didn't think much about it seemingly ended up regretting it.
And also at a certain point at the very [E]nd that will make you want to give up, but don'T give up! Never give up! Keep going and DON'T give up under any circumstances or you will regret it and you will regret it for real!!! No matter how good or bad you are if you don't give up you won't regret it I promise you!
Overall except for some minor difficulties and drawbacks Nier:Automata has one of the best storylines in games I ever played, keeping me entertained from the beginning to the very last second.
Amazing characters , godly music that still haunts me to this day and a great story, very fun and entertaining gameplay, thought-provoking dialogues, every range of emotions - truly a piece of art.
Because of some of it's flaws I would probably give it a 9 out of 10 as a rating - even though it is truly nothing less than a 10 out of 10 experience.
I will never regret spending the amount of money that I spent for this and I wouldn't want to miss this game in my life.
Sidenote: If you have a PS3 or an XBox360 then I'd recommend you to play the first Nier before playing Automata. It will give you an even better playing experience and even many more breathtaking moments. Moments, that can only fully be appreciated if it's played as a sequel after the first Nier rather than as a standalone game.
Yes, Nier:Automata can be played without any knowledge of the first Nier, however it is in it's core still a sequel to that game, so if it's somehow possible for you then let it play that part.

This is a review of the early access version. That being said, I suspect that the Steam price of $65 is highly inflated and not at all worth the price of admission from what I have experienced so far. Assuming that everything is released, even with improvements, there will invariably be comparisons made between this game and other strategy games: Starcraft II being the most likely. If I were to compare Warmachine Tactics to Starcraft II at the price point at time of release, Starcraft II wins.
The performance of this game on my PC is fairly poor. While my PC is not a high end gaming machine, it beats the low end minimum specs while failing shy of the recommended specs. I have to play at the lowest resolution (1280x720) and low graphic settings to get 18 FPS. Compared to other strategy games, where I can get 30+ FPS, I'm a little troubled. Starcraft is real-time; Warmachine is turn-based. My performance is currently halved and that's at minimum quality. The UI is cluttered, though that isn't aided by playing at the lowest resolution the game allows. Which begs the question: how can an older RTS like Starcraft II perform so much better than a modern turn-based game? Were new DX features implemented because it was new and shiny?
All in all, as a (disappointed) backer, I get the game for $20.  Had I waited for release, I would pass on this title at full price, even when completed, because there are games out there with a lower cost of entry. There are _free_ games out there that perform better than the currently available game.
"That’s what we want you to experience in WARMACHINE: Tactics, the turn-based tactics game that, with your help, will bring the award-winning WARMACHINE miniatures game from the tabletop to your desktop PC or Mac." With all due respect, it does not:
- Imagine my surprise when a warrior model had hit points and didn't die when shot... This is not Warmachine. This is a turn-based strategy game that borrows from the Iron Kingdoms.
If this early access is a sign of things to come, "I have a bad feeling about this."

If you are reading this you are probably interested in purchasing The Binding of Isaac, either as a fan of rogue-likes or as not a fan of rogue-likes. Most rogue-like fans would be skeptical, seeing as it looks much more simple and user friendly than most rogue-likes, maybe even much easier. Otherwise non rogue like fans would be looking at this game from the perspective of one whom wants to enter into the genre and this seems to be the most user friendly. Either way, their expectations will be shatered. The Binding of Isaac is a rogue-like, maybe even a new breed you might say, which combines an excellent soundtrack with enemy designs which will only become more haunting as the game progresses. No, this is not a horror game, but many a time this game has filled me with terror. Maybe it was from the heart breaking cutscenes which involved the struggle for Isaac to escape from his brainwashed mother or from the hyper realisticness added which is not seen from just simply playing one floor of the game. Besides the enemies being there to spook, they also add depth to a combat system which on the surface seems too simple. "Okay, you just move around and shoot enemies with your tears?". But it is much deeper than this, if you wish to survive you can not only rely on your tactful key presses but also on the items which can be used strategically to build yourself up to take on the final rooms and then the boss. Though, if you believe once you beat the game it is all over, you are surely mistaken. I would not have so many hours in this game if it was not for the added replaybility which comes along with this product. Eveyr time you beta that boss, a new layer is added to the rooms, the game becomes more difficult, more rooms are added, tougher enemies are added earlier in a run. Soon enough you will realise it may be a most difficult task, completing this game over and over again, but that is what makes it so good.

The main idea of the game is great. You start out with 4 elements and you combine them to create more and more. At first it's fun coming up with possible combinations and logical solutions. Halfway through the game however, they throw all logic out the window. Combinations seem arbitrary or plain BS. How does grass+alcohol equal absinthe, and why is absinthe even an element? (Note that there's only about 250 elements to be discoveredand vodka and vodka and beer are already in there.) This takes all the fun out of the 'puzzles' as they become an excercise in trial and error, not logical thinking. In the beginning you'd feel stupid after using a hint, thinking stuff like: I should've guessed that, or why didn't I think of that. After halfway through the game you'll get mad after being revealed a combination; Really? That's the best you could come up with?
I personally don't mind the microtransactions, as you certainly don't need them. It's most fun working out the combinations by yourself and you get a supply of hints, of which one will rechare after its depleted. A game with a lot of potential, but poor execution.

- Endless mixing and matching of class skills (every class has 4 subclasses)
- Infinite progression on the alternate advancement/mastery window
- Shoot-and-loot bullet hell style gameplay. Think Diablo 2 meets Borderlands
- The graphics are simple enough to run well, yet relevant enough to feel like you're playing a modern game
-
battle system and progression mechanics!!
- Large, sprawling dungeons. Much bigger than most ARPGs; levels are longer the further in game you travel.
- Difficulties scale well, game is definitely a challenge on Heroic+
- Amazing class system allows for seemingly infinite customization and endless replayability.
- Character visuals don't change at all through out the game. The developer said he will get around to this when he's at a stage in the game's SDLC where he can afford the time to do so (this is a single person project, after all)
- Interface limitations: not being able to skip through/speed up quest dialogue, having everything relegated to subtabs on the inventory screen isn't very ergonomic.
- Can't move with inventory open. I think this is intended, however, so I can't really take points away from this since it's a mechanic that is intended to prevent you from spamming consumables/items/etc. to make boss encounters ez-mode.
- Game really needs a system that recycles unused loot. You will get so much loot in this game that if you were to pick it all up, you'd easily be going back to town every 5 minutes to vendor it. The game should give us a vendor or mechanic that allows us to break down an item into its corresponding essence (ie. uniques give soul essence, rares give crystal essence, and enchanted items give magic essence)

I'll start by saying that playing before the Steam release, I have spent far more time playing this game than I have recorded on Steam.
I hope this gives you some insight on how credible I am.
Definitely underrated, for starters. It is a small community, compared to other big MMOs, but I personally think that's due to a lot of people being unaware this game even exists. Despite the size, there seems to have been a curve of new players coming in within the past month or so, and it's really great!
It's an understatement that the creators have put hard work put into this game. Between mechanics, combat, story and lore, and cosmetics, it's unbelievable such a well-developed game is free-to-play. (And yes, slowly but surely, it is free-to-win.)
When it comes down to it, I feel like mostly anyone could find something to enjoy in this game. To start off, you have housing. The game supplies you with some pretty nice decor ranging from the essentials to small accents and details. But if even what they supply for you isn't enough for your housing needs, no worries. Housing gives you the options to link pieces of decor, so you can pick them up and put them down together and basically make your own piece of hybrid mesh decor! It also functions on a numerical grid/plane so that if you're not a drag-and-drop person, no worries, everything can be perfect.
Story: I have gone off on too many friends of mine about mordesh lore in this game, feel free to ask them. Every race and species have their own backstory, even the enemies (especially the enemies). Small journals and pieces of journals (TALES keys) can be found laying around an area that gives some insight on the history and background of that place, and what had happened recently that made it like how it is when you find it. Everything is just so interesting; the website even has a "loremaggedon" that fills players in on important people in the game to follow along with the story. I won't share spoilers, but in short I'll say I really am "that guy" who holds the team back to watch the cutscenes.
Cosmetics: I talked about the housing feature just before, and that was the most of what was going to be here. In other games, I'm a type of guy that'd sacrafice stats just because a lower piece of gear looked more pleasing with my character's outfit. Wildstar has armor pieces that, for the most part, have different looks from each other. Instead of keeping that one on you and suffering the consequences of beauty, you get this option that says "Unlock costume item" that sends it to your portable closet of pretty clothes. In fact, there's items that are specifically made just to be costume items. Basically, I don't perform well if my character doesn't look good.
Art: I guess this goes along with cosmetics, but I feel this needs it's own paragraph. I'm an artist. I like to paint, draw, doodle some things in my free time, I've taken a lot of classes and I'm pretty confident in my skills. Basically, it comes down to the fact that I really appreciate art when I see it. Now, this game caught my eye immediately when I found it. I was never a fan of sci-fi before this, admittedly. I'm still a bit iffy on it, but this game has definitely warmed me up to it. When I first downloaded the game, I was attracted solely based on the art. I played through the tutorial zone, which at the time, was set on a spaceship; big turn off for me. I got through half the tutorial, closed the game, and uninstalled it. Two days later, I found myself coming back to reinstall it*, thinking "hey, I'm not judging this book's cover hard enough." and then it stayed on my computer since then. All in all, the art is charming and adorable, and definitely a nice break from the dull, dark colors other MMOs have (even then, Wildstar still has some dreary colors, but it's done in the right places.)
(*I don't know about anyone else, but for me and multiple friends mentioned above, it took >4 hours for download JUST on Steam, then >4 hours to download on the launcher. I'd consider that some dedication.)
Combat: The raids are amazing. When you get yourself a good group, it really feels awesome being able to see all the different parts of the raid and all the functions. The loot isn't bad either. This is basically me about to go on about the story incorporation, so I'll stop myself. Open-world combat is great, for the most part. One thing I have to mention is that it's a bit frustrating just trying to cut by some mobs, and they aggro you and kill your auto-sprint. A bit bothersome, but not too hindering unless you pull more, and inevitably, get mauled to death.
TL;DR
PROS:
-Housing!!!!
-Costumes
-Art
-Raids
-Roleplay Community
-Devs come on every so often, it's nice to know that creators come on to hear what we have to say
-Community is pretty helpful**
-Free to play
-Free to win (at a slow rate, but still free)
-Pretty good humor
CONS:
-Fall damage system is kind of wonky
-"Ded gaem" conversation almost daily (It's really not, but trolls will be trolls)
-**Some people will just tell you "Google it" when you ask for help
-Requires a decent computer, not a problem if you've got a gaming rig; but it's not casual-friendly, to an extent (Regardless, I still run it on a potato, and the worst that happens to me is my computer rebooting every now and again)
-Most wikis and guides are outdated
-Inevitable trolls
-Download times (Again, not sure if me and my friends were the only ones that experienced this)
I really hope everyone considers this game, if not try it out. It's not for everyone, but I would recommend this to anyone who's looking for a break from a p2p MMO.

"What is best in life?"
"To crush God's enemies,
to see them converted before you,
and to hear the lamentations of their Imams."
-Conan the Barbarian (said during his stint as a mercenary for the Pope)
Seriously though, this game is still awesome, even after all these years later! In fact, M2:TW just celebrated its 10th birthday, this November 2016! And its still easily one of the best, if not the best, of the Total War series!
Improving upon, and outdoing most everything in the previous M:TW and Rome:TW (whose engine it uses) games, Medieval II was a triumph of RTS when it was first released. And a year later, it only got better with the best Total War expansion to date, Kingdoms. And thats not even considering all the many wonderful fan-made mods this title has available, thus extending its greatness even more so! Even fantasy lands are game! Want to wage war in Middle-Earth? There's a mod for that! Feel like fighting for The Elder Scrolls' Tamriel? There's a mod for that! How about waylaying the Warhammer world? Well, actually, that game was released earlier this year. But..there's still mods that predate that!
Caution: this game is a time consumer! You can EASILY spend 50+ hours on just one campaign alone, and given that there are 17 playable factions available (eventually) in just the base game alone, and that there is NO END DATE for any campaign (only an end to the campaign objectives, but the game still goes on, so you can play a medieval kingdom all the way into the 21st century and beyond, take that modernity! #ProgressIsForSuckers), you can rack up a kingdom's worth of time spent on this game! Rome wasn't built in a day, they say, but it sure was completed faster than this game is!
Whether it be conquering your back-stabbing neighbors (all the italian powers, always!!), managing your empire (where is the govenator when you need him?), retaking the Holy Land from the infidel (ya jerks!), converting the heathen (come on fellas, its "A.D." now, get with the program already!), or making a heroic last stand for all of Christendom against the rapacious onslaught of the Golden Horde (which is what you get when you don't tip the chinese food delivery guy on one too many occasions), yes sir, Medieval II has it all.
Even the possibility of having one of your generals get so cuckholded by his nakedly adulterous wife, that he loses it, becomes the most shameless man on earth, and shacks up with a tranny, thus bringing eternal shame to your kingdom! As I said, Medieval II has it all. Even things the developers really should have just left alone...*ahem*.
If your a strategy gaming fan, there are certain games in the genre you just have to have played in your lifetime, like Age of Empires II: Age of Kings. This is that kind of game. Don't miss out.
And here's to hoping that the developers go back on their "we don't make games with the number '3' in their titles" statement, and, once they are done with (the also fantastic, well-worth-your-time) Warhammer: Total War, they start developing Medieval III.
Deus Vult, Creative Assembly, Deus Vult!

I have played around 10 matches or so, and I admit it has been a few years since I have played the TT, but I feel PP did a fair job in bringing this game to the Online Game world.  The price as many have indicated is based on KickStrater, and for most people I would recomend waiting until release when the price will be much lower.  However, those who have played the TT will realize the $65 is nothing compared to how much money and time it takes to get a army up and running.  It appears the the Deluxe Ed. will grant some free additional units and that had me sold to get this game now!  This game will be riddled with "in-gmae purchases" so be aware!
I wont waste time with listing all the issues in this Beta, which there are a lot! But I remain confident the PP will grant us a game worthy of the title Warmachine.  A few major issues for newbies, is the lack of explainations of abilities.  Even myself had too look up some spells onine mid-game to remind myself of effects.  A minor detail now that I expect to be fixed, but those not used to the game will struggle.  For those TT players I say you will miss the in person interaction with your enemy.  You are forced to sit there for 3-10min per round in silence watching a turn go by and there is no chit chat.  I miss the cheers of "WHAT A HIT" or the cries of "YOU GOTTA BE KIDDING ME!" as the game played out.  A audio connection would be great or a chat box would be nice at least.
Units have moved from single point kills  to multi-point health, and that is nice, but I feel that this has greatly shifited the balance of power.  Now a few "solo" units can easily take down a  warjack in a turn or 2, and a Warjack can have 2-3 hits on a SINGLE unit and not kill it.  So when your Jack is ganged up on by 3 units, it has almost no chance!  Something needs fixed on that.
Overall this is a game to get.  For those who have played TT, now is a great time to buy, it's a low cost compared to what you have spent already on TT, and you'll get free stuff, Newbies its great to learn in a beta with few armies options, so the matches will be as even as they will ever be.   However, PP will try to sell the the moon with in-game upgrades, so if this game releases at $20 (and who knows!) the $45 you'll save may be better spent upgrading to the units you want, and not the freebies they'll give you in the Deluxe.

Nier: Automata is the long awaited collaboration between Yoko Taro and Platinum games. I was skeptical about this game since Taro's last game Drankengard 3 was a huge disappointment to me, it was as if he was spoofing his own work. Fortunately, Automata is the Yoko Taro game I've been waiting since the original Nier.
The gameplay in Automata is a great evolution from the original game, hacking, and slashing never felt so good in a Yoko Taro game before, there is a chip system where you could put chips with certain abilities into slots like high damage, regenerating heallth and even some time slowing ones, experimenting with these chips gives the combat variety and it's fun to try out various different combinations. You could also shoot projectiles, which is pretty useful in a lot of the bullet hell sections. Despite the fun combat, the game is severely undermined by the open world design.
The world of Nier: Automata feels empty in a lot of places, and many areas are needless large (the desert area, in particular, is mostly an empty space with some enemy encampments dotted here and there), traveling around the world is tedious and even with the teleport ability is just feels like a slog going through these areas over and over again. Admittedly, not all areas feel that way, but most of them do, and I wish the development team could have found some sort of compromise. Now with that out of the way, let's talk about the story.
The story of Nier: Automata focuses on three androids, 2B, 9S, and A2. These are YoRHa androids designed to aid humanity in their war against the machines which were created by aliens who invaded planet Earth, and humanity was forced to evacuate their home planet. 2B and 9S were sent on a mission on Earth and noticed that some of the machines have developed some human-like behavior and 2B starting to question whether or not these machines are evolving into more than just mindless automatons. While on Earth, they encounter A2, a YoRHa android that went rogue and Command ordering 2B and 9S to kill her.
The story of Nier: Automata deals with the themes of existentialism and identity and what it means to be human, the story does have some pretty emotional moments that will play on your heart strings, but it doesn't come nearly as good as the original game, in fact, a lot of the plot threads are taken directly for Nier and quite frankly Nier did it better, a lot better. While the story is far more thought provoking from the average game, as a Yoko Taro fan, I was left somewhat disappointed.
