It could have been such a nice game. Nice setting. Interesting visual design. And some nice riddles in the dungeons. But the game mechanics are just not fun to me. Firstly I do not like games where you are not utilizing half the heroes you get. Especially if those that you are not using during a dungeon are not getting any experience and thus hopelessly falling behind in level making them even less attractive to play to a point where you would need to farm hours to get them up to the same level as the rest of the party.
So you are somewhat doomed to pick some three guys, which you also meet at totally different points of the story and hope you liked them. If not you either start again or farm your♥♥♥♥♥off to get the ones you did not use back up. Additionally I don't like the world map. You are running on a 2D map either running into encounters or trying to avoid them. And sometimes you find a little extra on it. But generally it does not do much to the game.
Then there is those arcade like options of pickign a dungeon in three varieties of difficulty which, depending on the diffculty you chose, give you better rewards. However, either you simply always go for the highest difficulty or you do the same dungeon several times in a row to get all rewards. Coming back later is usually not worth it because of the items being level dependant.
This is also a system which i do not like overall. Items being attached to a character's attributes like strength, dexterity or whatever I understand. But why would I not be able to wear a ring because i am only level 4 and not 15? How much experience can wearing one ring over the other require? This adds just another very artificially feeling hurdle in the game, that makes it even more of a grind, so that you can finally get the good equipment, which you can already buy or have in your inventory to put to use.
I wish they had gone for a totally different levelling and item system. Because this just breaks down the whole fun for me and made me simply uninstall the game at some point.
Another thing that was tiresome for me was that I was not able to speed up the fights in anyway. Either by accelarating time, cancel animations or even deactivate animations. Sure at first the animations are nice, but at some point you just want to get over with the fights.
However if someone does not care about such things, the game might still be worth playing. I however won't waste any more time on it than I already did.

The game has beautiful graphics but It doesn't compensate its poor mechanisms:
1) It wants to extend the gameplay value with tedious xp grinding by using small parties of 3 characters and tedious combats.
2) Completely unimportant "side quests".
3) When you reach level 20 the game difficulty spikes to make you grind even worse.
4) Combat system doesn't bring anything new and it gets really boring.
Overall this is a tiresome and mediocre JRPG with beautiful graphics.

While the game is a lot of fun at the beginning it quickly becomes a bore; repeating the same dungeon over and over, acquiring new characters that are much lower level than your current ones and grinding them to match levels (really? why not just have them match levels), mundane crafting system, etc.  The bad turn based battle system is probably my biggest hang-up. The battle system is flawed in that it is not a true turn based game:  in this game, when you do ANYTHING other than a simple attack it puts you further down the turn list before anything happens, your hero just sits there "casting". These seemingly variable cast times make planning attacks, reacting to enemies, and complimenting other hero’s abilities extremely difficult. It should be that when you use any ability it is instant and the aforementioned ability you used reflects  your wait time until your next turn, with more powerful abilities putting you further down the waiting list (like almost all other turn based games such as FF10).
Overall I would recommend if you can pick up the game for a few bucks - it will undoubtedly entertain you for a few hours - but at its current price it just simply doesn’t deliver.

Let me start off by saying that me purchasing this game was sheer luck. I caught a streamer that I used to watch playing it and it immediately caught my attention and so I bought it... and boy am I glad that I did! My history with games alike? Well I play this genre quite 'religiously' you can say. I have played them since Diablo 2 first got me hooked to this genre. I have been through the Tochlight's, Grim Dawn, POE, D2-3, Titan Quest, Van Helsings and Victor Vran ect... you name it! And now we can add this gem to the list.
Without any sort of spoilers, I just wanted to create a little list instead of writing heaps of paragraphs.
PRO'S:
-This game pretty much has all that is good in arpg's alike and adds to that list, while leaving out the tedious/bad things.
-The skill tree's are super CUSTOMIZABLE, have ultimate abilities and masterys! Oh, and respeccs aren't gated nor a pain in the butt like with some other games.
-The combat is smooth as butter, something I was not expecting from game like this.
-The loot and itemization is fun and engaging, and you are always excited to find that next upgrade. Furthermore, you will constantly find pieces that cater to other specific build types, so get ready to set pieces aside end game and tinker with them.
-The content is still being updated obviously, but I can tell you that not ONCE was I bored or annoyed by the feel of and act. Other games tend to always have an act or 2 that are just dreadful, well not here!
-The game offers  a lot of Ui customization. So that the user can play how he/she prefers.
-The mobs are pretty engaging, all do different things and the areas are dense.
-Endgame offers 'anomolies' aka endless dungeons, where they progressively get more difficult.
also... music is great, atmosphere is well done and the game has crafting.
Cons:
-UGHH?... oh I guess no MP, but who can complain? It is a costly thing to implement.
There is so much more that I can say, but many others have covered quite a bit of this. I just wanted to further back those comments and this game in particular, because it is truly something special and I cannot wait to see what the future awaits. It is just a shame that only Inidie developers seem to have an ack in knowing how to make games great these days, in this case a super well done hack n slash arpg. This is probably why I have mostly given up on AAA titles.
9/10 Highly Recommend.

Before I start this review, I would like to say that I'm a level 27 player. I still have a lot to learn about the game, and have gotten tons of help from the community to get to where I'm at now.
A lot of people say... "this game is dead", the game is actually not dead it has many people playing but very few players go slow through early game. This fact alone makes the game a "everyone is level 50 and I'm all alone" experience. However lots of people help out beginners and more often then not you'll be able to find people to party with in dungeons.
The biggest problem with WildStar currently is that there are very little new players although I do see some people come to visit now and then.
When first playing this game I played with friends didn't do any research and went in blind, later my friends stopped playing the game however the games art style and cheesy humour got me hooked. I came back to the game a few months later deleted my character and started fresh, this time following a leveling guide.
That changed EVERYTHING, I actually felt like I was making real progress and quite quickly too in just 3 days of casually playing and messing around I got to level 20. (Many people tell me that leveling to 50, takes about 30-42 hours of gameplay depending on your play style.)
While leveling I noticed something I probably will never get used to... the trash mobs. I love the bosses, the adventures, and the way the game feels. However there are tons of trash mobs sprinkled all over the place that have little to no telegraphs and just wack you over and over, either forcing you to tank them, or spam heals. These mobs are really annoying and feel out of place in a game that has a combat system that uses tons of telegraphs. Usually if you're under leveled the mobs could pose a challenge and end up being quite fun. However if you're at the same level or higher then them they just feel like a burden attacking you on sight no matter what your level is compared to theirs, their attacks also feel like they slow you even though they only knock you out of auto-sprint.
The second thing I noticed and couldn't help talking about were the "tap with the metronome", Simon, and tap or hold down a key to get un-stunned. I'm sure many players would agree with me as there's even an addon that attempts to bypass most of these QTE like glorified "minigames".
But even with those flaws I have to recommend that people at least give this game a try, because there's a lot to love.
The dungeons, the expeditions, and the story are all very interesting and very fun. Not to mention that you can probably talk about the story alone for hours.
A lot of the dungeons/expeditions play out like little self contained stories and you find yourself almost seamlessly thrown into a wild adventure. I won't talk about the story because I'm afraid to spoil it.
The combat is amazing it can range from intense hold outs to really fast paced dynasty warriors style smash through tons of enemies gameplay. A lot of the bosses and unique enemies are really fun too and honestly there are bosses that I feel that I can go back and run again and again.
In the end the game is a little tough to get into especially because there aren't very many actually new players but once you crack through its hard shell you'll find something tasty. I think there is something here for everyone to enjoy you just have to give it a chance. So please do.
Negative Highlights:
[ Trash mobs forcing you to tank them, or spam heals. ]
[ Sudden enemy attacks also feel like they slow you even though they only knock you out of auto-sprint. ]
[ QTE like glorified "minigames" ]
Positive Highlights:
[ Great art, cheesy (in a good way) humour. ]
[ Leveling isn't too bad as long as you know what to do. ]
[ dungeons/expeditions play out like little self contained stories. ]
[ lots of people help out beginners. ]
[ Amazing combat is amazing, can be fast, can be slow, but always fun. ]

Stellaris is one of, if not the, best strategy games I have ever played. (Incidentally the other contenders are also Paradox games.) It blends traditional 4X gameplay with Paradox's own unique cocktail of grand strategy. (And the occasional wacky event.) Paradox's titles always have a strong sense of comunity and you know the devs realy care about their game and the user's experience with it.

I haven't had this much fun playing a 4X since Alpha Centuari...which wasn't that long ago. Let me try again.
It's the best 4X to be released in about 15 years.

The good:
If you're into games like civilization then you will like Stellaris. There's some solid depth here. If micromanaging the economy of a vast galactic civilization sounds like your thing then this is probably your game. I definitely found myself falling into the cycle of "just one more turn..." pretty often. If your attitude is more "less spreadsheets more pew pew" then you should probably give this one a pass.
The bad:
Enemy AI is simultaneously too dumb and too smart. In the too dumb category it is easy to trick it into making really simple mistakes, for example if you kill one of its armies, the fleet of ships sieging the planet will almost never give up even if there isn't another one anywhere nearby and you're slaughtering it's other fleets and planets one system over. In the "too smart" category it rarely declares war on you unless it has a clear numerical advantage at the time. It's something that's strategically wise but ultimately doesn't lead to compelling gameplay. In the same category if one of its fleets gets into a battle it can't win, rather than fight to the death it will always use an "emergency FTL" retreat option the moment it can, removing it from play for a short amount of time and returning it to one of its home bases. Again, technically the smart thing to do but really frustrating when you have to play "whack a mole".
The game also features your own AI helpers which control "sectors". This is basically the game's way of forcing you to cede direct control of your planets after your empire reaches a certain size (otherwise you could be individually managing hundreds of planets). Too bad these AIs are basically dumb as rocks too. Not really fun when you set them to create a "balanced" economy for the sector they control and they manage it in a way where they have 1000s of surplus (wasted) food and energy and a similar deficit in minerals.
The Mixed:
"Stellaris is not responding". Putting this in mixed becasue this is a problem I've been having since they pushed the 1.6 patch. I'm hoping they fix whatever they broke to make it lag so much more. More generally I'd prefer my approval before pushing a patch on me that changes a lot of things mid game.
Wars. The war system is fairly unique and that's overall a good thing. You set war demands and can only take about 8-10 planets per war even at the endgame. Good because it means every conflict doesn't turn into an all or nothing deathmatch. Bad becasue it turns the endgame into a real grind. Also a bit counter-intuitive, I was surprised when I got nothing the first time I fought a war and had to use google to figure out it was becasue I didn't set any demands. Also it can be used in really "trolly" ways which could be good or bad depending on your personality. E.g. you can conquer a bunch of frontier planets and then demand your enemy turn over their capital planet, or beat up the weakest memeber of an alliance and demand only concessions from the strongest member, who by the way never even managed to make it across the map before the war was over.
Summary:
Good strategy game, even if there are some parts that are a bit broken.

I'd like to start off immediately by saying that I do not play this game online. I'm well aware that cheating is a major issue that needs to be addressed, but online play in 2k (sports games in general honestly) has personally never been my thing. As I can't say anything about the pros/cons of online play for this game, this review will be purely based off of my experience playing the offline mods.
I really, really do enjoy this game. For starters, it looks great. 97% of the players look extremley realistic and the courts look amazing. The in game commentary is starting to get much better and you'll rarely hear repeated dialogue throughout a single game. Game mechanics seem like they're getting better too and the biggest update I've noticed about this from last year's game is that the player's movement seems much more fluent. On higher difficulties it can be very hard sometimes as making careless passes or taking bad shots will almost certainly put you in position to get blown out by the A.I.... you don't have a lot of room for error, but it's easy to catch on to this and break bad habits to run more efficent offenses and better defenses. There's plenty of plays and sets as well as defensive adjustments to either keep you in the lead or help you come back if you're trailing too. MyCareer is much better this year. I personally had a massive love/hate relationship with last year's MyCareer as the actual idea of it and the gameplay was fantastic, but the in depth story, cut scenes and drama made me almost stop playing it on more than one occasion. This year has less of a focus on your player's personal life and more about his basketball life and career, which is a very good thing. I haven't messed with MyTeam too much, but from the time I have spent in the mode it's pretty solid. The challenges are entertaining and I've had pretty fair luck (equal amount of good and bad pulls) with my pulls from card packs. MyLeague is pretty much the exact same thing it's been for years, which is a good thing in my opinion. Play games, trade/sign/cut players, scout rookies for the upcoming draft, etc... 2k didn't do anything to change this mode and that's perfectly fine with me. Why fix something that isn't broken? You also, as usual, have the ability to edit and update the rosters and then use those edited rosters in exhibition games, MyLeague, etc., which I find very useful because I tend to disagree with a lot of the ratings that 2k gives some of the players.
The game is not perfect though. Starting with in game issues.... I believe the shooting needs adjustment. When playing on All Star difficulty or higher, it can sometimes be extremley difficult to even make a shot.. and I'm talking like realistic NBA level shots. For instance, 8/10 times I will miss lightly contested mid range jumpers with Andre Iguodala. I'm well aware that he's not a premier shooter, but this is a shot that any NBA player would be able to hit at least 50% of the time, but unless you get a perfect shot release, it's most likely not going to go in. I can understand when Steph Curry misses 3s from near the half court logo.... but when he puts up brick after brick with light defense from 3 unless you get a perfect release? That needs adjustment, especially when the second your defense gets light, the A.I. will knock down shot after shot. A.I.'s ability to steal the ball compared to what you're capable of is also very lopsided. You make a lazy pass and it's definitely going to get stolen, yet there's times when I've actually had the A.I. pass the ball THROUGH my player and the ball didn't even get deflected. A.I,s on your team are pretty much useless compared to the ones you're facing and will regularly get burnt on defense (or do absaolutely nothing on offense) with you being able to do nothing about this. The game focuses too much on replays, interviews and the halftime report. The interviews with players that it shows 1-2 times a game look terrible and the halftime report is so overdone and unnecessary... While the overall player movement is very fluent, the one issue I have is that if you ever get to close to the sideline with a player that doesn't have the ball, then your player will most likely fall into the stands and be taken out of the play for a good 5-6 seconds... it's a very unnecessary and frustrating action that shouldn't even be put in the game. MyCareer is much better than last year, but the biggest issue I have is the upgrading system. At the beginning-ish time of your Career you'll select a play style for your player and you'll have corresponding attributes that are able to be upgraded higher and others that will seem to have a level cap. For instance, my player is more of a slashing PG, so I can pretty much max out my passing, agility, driving capabilities, defending, etc., but my mid range and three point shooting attributes can only be upgraded so high... I'm only done with one full season so I'm not sure if this can be adjusted or what at some point, but if it can't then that's really annoying as it makes it difficult for you to create a really well rounded player. You're also forced to actually attend your team practices during the week (you can however just quit the second your player gets into the gym with no penalty, but it still takes about a minute of your time for something you probably didn't want to do in the first place). If you miss practice, you'll get a nice text from your coach and then you'll lose minutes for the next game. Kind of annoying because all I want to do is you know, play in the games, but oh well... My game has on more than one occasion crashed when I left it paused to go do something (use the bathroom, make food, etc.). My computer has more than capable specs to run this game so I have no idea why this would happen, but it hasn't happened enough to really be that big of an issue to me. I'd like to address that regardless though for the sake of the review.
While it may seem like I focused more on the issues rather than the positives, that's simply because in my opinion this game doesn't have very many problems (again, only talking about the offline portion) so I tried to go as in detail as I could with the few issues I had with the game. Overall I'd give the game a 9/10. It looks great, plays very smooth and has a plethora of modes and things to do to keep you more than busy. Minor issues could definitely be fixed either through an update or by just addressing them in next year's game, but regardless it's still a great and fun game and I'll definitely be buying 2K18 as well.

This is where I'm kind of torn. Yes it's a Platinum Games slasher game alright but it's also an action-RPG which could lead to some complications.
The great things?
Phenomenal boss battles and combat system from Platinum Games with the weird and really creative direction from series creator Yoko Taro. The game gives you a lot of flexibilty in combat with tons of weapons and combinations that stems from those weapons, then add the pods which even gives you more flexibility since it is your main ranged weapon during bullet hell segments and it has extra abilities to give.
Thing I don't mind but does not add much to game variety.
The hacking sections I don't mind but it is just repetitive bullet hell sections that gets annoying after a couple hundred times you do it. Fan of bullet hells but it just saturated the game too much to my liking.
The problems?

You can cheese most enemies if you have tons of health items and healing plug-in chips (the games skill boost system) you won't die to most enemies.
The enemy variety on the other hand are just small robot, big robot, flying robot, and goliath robot in simple terms. We just get tiny variations to them but the boss battles as I have said are the most creative and fun bosses I have fought since Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance.
The music here is amazing. Emi Evans with her chaos language as the vocals of the song is enchanting, BUT one criticism to the music since this is also a Platinum Game is the music rarely matches the action like in Metal Gear Rising. A really missed opportunity but it does not detract that much from the game.
The sound design sound right, the clangs, explosions, blade slashes and hits sound perfect for this game and I have nothing to add more to that.
Before I go to the story I have to tackle the performance issues on PC. Yeah not that great unless you use a mod called FAR. Here are links to help you install it.
If you want a rundown on what happened last game click
and continue watching the series.
The story is where this game shines. It creatively and brilliantly mixes it's game elements and save system so deep in the story.  Since it's story heavy I will skip a lot of things in order to keep people from spoilers.
You will feel a lot of things with the story and expect the unexpected since the twists and turns here are unexpected and harrowing especially in the side quests. You will feel a lot for the main characters 2B, 9S and A2. The most I could tell you is you need many play throughs in order to have the full experience.
Yes all I said sounds vauge but the story is so interesting and overall great I greatly skimmed over a lot of the stuff that makes the experience as you should experience them yourself.

This game is a game like no other unless you count Yoko Taro's older work. A strong contender for Game of the Year. Bogged down by performance issues needing a mod to be fixed is my only true gripe. Worth the price in my opinion but if you are still on the fence wait for a sale, you won't regret your purchase. Plus there are also DLC waiting to be released so keep your eye on it.

Pretty nice simplified strategy, with short game sessions, and good replayability:
+Sound - good sound work, with nice ambient background music and sound effects.
+Visuals - is nothing out of the ordinary, but so what? They fit the simplified strategy concept after all.
+Gameplay - You have short time sessions - actually 50 turns (50 years :) ), to survive all the enemies attacks, and build your city and army to prepare for the final battle. Various countries offer various bonuses and allow different strategies to beat the game, Some countries seems easier to win, other offers more challenge if you want to get all the achievements.
+Steam achievements - pretty straightforward like a win on the hard and the hardest difficulties with each race + some other.
+Now with steam cards!
-No option to save your progress (+ and - of the short sessions), if you want to close the game or just go to the menu - your only option is to *restart* the game.
So one game session can be 30 minutes to 1 hour long depends on the speed of your decision making, the game is kinda cheap and pretty nice to spend a couple of evenings.

It's a very small text-based strategy game where you have to survive 50 turns as a township in a cruel morbidly eclectic fantasy world against constant random attacks from some unmotivated anonymous foes. You do it through budget planning - building and hiring workers & fighters, also you choose faith recieving divine bonuses for faith currency. The battles get resolved automatically in a plain field before your eyes - so when the stupid AI can't organize units' movement effectively & loose troops just because of poor pathfinding you only can clutch your teeth tighter. The art is rather bland in this one except the presentation screens, the music's quite repetative, an ok'ish mobile game.
Very addicting game with deep strategy and a real challenge in the higher difficulties. Try beating zombie chicken invasion on hard.

A simple, but entertaining, little time-waster.
50 Years comprises of trying to keep your village alive for 50 turns against progressively larger AI armies that attack randomly. You'll recruit peasants to earn gold, build barracks to recruit more swordsmen, logging cabins to get lumber for recruiting archers, stables to get knights, etc.
When a battle occurs you have the option to use a scroll (a consumable that typically debuffs the enemy in some fashion), or draft any number of your peasants to fight as militia (each peasant drafted will not produce any income for that turn, however). After you click to start the battle your involvement ends, and you watch helplessly as events play out and your preparations either prove sufficient, or woefully inadequate.
A single playthrough takes about 20-30 minutes at most. However, the game has several different factions, each with their own unique perk (some more useful than others), as well as several Faith/skill trees to experiment with and multiple difficulty settings to give the game a decent measure of replayability.
50 Years is best suited to being played in brief spurts when you have a little bit of time to kill, but not enough to dive into a more prolonged experience. To that end, I would like to see the devs add a Save & Resume function if possible, so you can stop and pick up where you left off even more easily. The game also seems well suited to mobile platforms - it could be the perfect thing for killing a little time on your phone while in the waiting room at the doctor's office.

A turn-based strategy which is surprisingly good. Game sessions are short, deep and spiced up with innovative mechanics. Generally, you have to effectively manage your budget to purchase buildings (which have various passive effects) and units (who will face enemy units at the end of the turn).
Replayability is right there - you can choose between ~10 factions, plus the games offers  achievements  and difficulty levels.  Even though it's Early Access, I haven't run into any unbalanced things or crashes.

The game presents you six options; Main Game, Quests, Artifacts, Puzzles, Tournament, and Encyclopedia. Naturally, Main Game is selected first and brings you in to a quick tutorial on the mechanics of the game. They're essentially the same as the old Doodle God - combine elements to make another, or several, elements to create other elements with.
You have a planet to watch over, which houses the elements you create. When you create Ash, the volcanoes will spew ash, et cetera. The graphics of the planet are strangely well done for a PC adaptation of a flash/mobile game, but this may be the only thing the game does right. I won't criticize the combinations of certain elements, as that is an original Doodle God game problem, right now.
Main game is the same as Doodle God. However, it does have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ energy bar mechanic which is to trick adults in their mid-life crises and/or little kids into giving up their money to not have to wait a minute to get one recharge (out of ten, maximum,) as well as quests.
Quests basically just require you to make an element. They're pretty unoriginal and could've been done in a lot more challenging and interesting ways. Most of them reward you with two officially unnamed tokens, but their provisional name with me is "Illuminati Tokens" because of the all-seeing-eye very clearly stamped on the front.
Artifacts give you a hundred attempts or so to guess the elements required to make an ancient construction or modern technology out of three elements of the ones you've made. So, obviously, not all of them are even unlocked until you've made everything. However, this doesn't stop some of them from being stupid,
but I guess they can't all be winners.
Puzzles are just "Try to create this with a limited amount of elements." At the time of writing this, there are only two -- go figure -- and they require you to make a Locomotive and a Tavern. Pretty standard, I guess.
Tournament is a ♥♥♥♥ing dumb♥♥♥♥♥♥measuring contest where you have to guess what element is made from two elements presented. You do this three times with a thirty-second time limit alongside two other players, whoever gets the most right in the least amount of time gets
literally nothing. It costs one Illuminati Token to play one round of this, and considering the lack of proper explanation on the mechanics of the Tournament, you'll likely never get the required amount of tokens to get into the top twenty (although my first time around I did get to thirty.)
Encyclopedia displays the elements you have unlocked, and provides quotes that have the elements' name in it. It doesn't show how it's made, it doesn't tell you what exactly it is, it's just unhelpful and there to add more megabytes to the game.
None of these "modes" are special in any way, other than the bafflingly stupid way in which they were executed. The game feels lacking in content, without substance. When you start it up, it feels like something you put down. It has no appeal, no originality, aside from the appeal and originality it ripped out of the original Doodle God to sway fans of the series into being trapped in clearly unnecessary microtransactions, masked under shallow, half-resurrected entertainment.
This game could've been a good remake of the original Doodle God, but instead it decided to be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

THIS REVIEW IS MY OWN UNBIASED OPINION - I was not compensated or rewarded for this review in any way.
Let me start off by saying I had this game on my Wishlist for 6+ months or so before it was released, and then for some reason (I don't remember why) I took it off, then found it on Steam again and immediately bought it post-release.  I feel like an idiot for ever taking it off my Wishlist; here's why:
If I had to pick just one game on Steam that I'd write a review for, it would be this one.  This game blew me out of the water.  Right from the start, watching the intro sequence and jamming to the amazing opening soundtrack, I was hooked.
The visual art and audio soundtracks for this game are top-notch in my opinion, and incredibly catchy.  Characters in the game are fully voiced for the important dialogues, which pulls you into the story even more.  The main set of characters as well as side characters (quest-givers, merchants, etc.) have fleshed out personalities and look very unique.
Gameplay is broken down into several parts.  First you have the overworld, essentially a guided map you run around on to collect loot and encounter enemies and enter towns (think games like old-school Final Fantasy or Golden Sun, if anyone remembers that title).  On the overworld, there's 2 different types of areas I've encountered: 1) Explorable Areas: These look like dungeons and play like dungeons, however there's no difficulty-select and they usually have something to do with the story or side missions. 2) Dungeons: Parts of the game you enter and choose a difficulty in order to receive a tiered chest reward at the end.
In both the Dungeons and Explorable areas, you can choose which of the characters in your party you actually run around with, and each of them has a special ability you can use to help yourself or hinder your enemies (or both in some cases).  For example, Garrison (the swordsman that's reminiscient of Guts) has a dash that helps you avoid trap damage, and if you initiate combat with an enemy using it, it gives Garrison a nice Haste buff.  Different characters have different abilities.  I love being able to run around as who I want and switch at-will.
Combat begins when you interact with an enemy either through using one of those special abilities I mentioned, simply walking into an enemy, or an enemy seeing you and running into you.  Combat is 100% turn-based (none of that ATB stuff where it's semi-timed), so you can take your time planning your strategy.  Your characters have regular abilities that generate Overcharge (mana that goes on top of your regular mana and gets used first), then special abilities that are more powerful and cost mana, you can also use items, and then there's Burst actions, but I don't want to spoil that for you.  As far as I've seen, you cannot skip through combat animations, but that didn't bother me much because they're pretty fast anyways.
There is quite a bit of character customization (not appearances though); you get to find different pieces and tiers of gear for each character, two different Perk trees you can invest points into to alter the core functionality of the characters, and from what I've seen equipping different weapons actually changes the way their weapons look in combat, which is a nice touch.
The game also features a fun fishing mini-game to collect fishing materials, lots of crafting items and things to craft, and tons of little pieces of lore you can find and read if you wish.  It even rewards you for finding all the lore pieces in a "set".  Additionally, as you battle enemies of the same type/genre, you gain knowledge of the enemy; their abilities, what they drop, etc. and you also gain permanent boosts to stats, which is pretty unique and cool.
The dialogues in the game are clever and fun to read, and the important dialogues are fully voiced, which I loved.  Less important dialogues are not voiced, which makes sense.
I honestly have no idea how anyone could not enjoy this game, or at least appreciate how much work went into it.  I will be putting LOTS of time into this game, especially since I'm a sucker for good turn-based RPGs.  I'm so happy I found this game on Steam.  If I could afford it, I'd buy 10 more copies and give it out to my friends, no joke.  If they ever make a sequel to this game, I'm buying it immediately.
Please developers, don't let this gem of a franchise be history - keep it alive!!

Fun, cartoony graphics and humor reminiscent of Team Fortress 2, this fast-paced arena shooter is probably one of the better free-to-play games out there, ranking only with Team Fortress 2. Weaponcrafting makes this a unique experience and coupled with the art style, you could almost think this was an arena version of Borderlands 2. And you'd probably be right, that's not a bad summary.
And I know what you're thinking. "Don't you mean pay-to-win?" Settle down there, hotshot, because that's what I thought at first, too. And the first thing I did?
Opened up the store.
Know how many weapons you can buy there?
Zero.
Everything you can buy is cosmetics (There ARE temporary xp/cash boosts you can buy, but again, these don't add that much AND you still have to play to earn your worth of that boost), meaning that all players are pretty much on the same field. Want to get better? Play more. Get a better weapon? Play more. Want to CRUSH YOUR OPPONENTS UNDER YOUR BOOTS?
Then come along and kill things with us.
(One small complaint: A few of the "vs Bots" matches are heavily one-sided, such as Blitz. Only once in a VERY long while do the humans beat the bots. However, the rest of the modes are fairly even-balanced.)

Before I start this review, I would like to say that I'm a level 27 player. I still have a lot to learn about the game, and have gotten tons of help from the community to get to where I'm at now.
A lot of people say... "this game is dead", the game is actually not dead it has many people playing but very few players go slow through early game. This fact alone makes the game a "everyone is level 50 and I'm all alone" experience. However lots of people help out beginners and more often then not you'll be able to find people to party with in dungeons.
The biggest problem with WildStar currently is that there are very little new players although I do see some people come to visit now and then.
When first playing this game I played with friends didn't do any research and went in blind, later my friends stopped playing the game however the games art style and cheesy humour got me hooked. I came back to the game a few months later deleted my character and started fresh, this time following a leveling guide.
That changed EVERYTHING, I actually felt like I was making real progress and quite quickly too in just 3 days of casually playing and messing around I got to level 20. (Many people tell me that leveling to 50, takes about 30-42 hours of gameplay depending on your play style.)
While leveling I noticed something I probably will never get used to... the trash mobs. I love the bosses, the adventures, and the way the game feels. However there are tons of trash mobs sprinkled all over the place that have little to no telegraphs and just wack you over and over, either forcing you to tank them, or spam heals. These mobs are really annoying and feel out of place in a game that has a combat system that uses tons of telegraphs. Usually if you're under leveled the mobs could pose a challenge and end up being quite fun. However if you're at the same level or higher then them they just feel like a burden attacking you on sight no matter what your level is compared to theirs, their attacks also feel like they slow you even though they only knock you out of auto-sprint.
The second thing I noticed and couldn't help talking about were the "tap with the metronome", Simon, and tap or hold down a key to get un-stunned. I'm sure many players would agree with me as there's even an addon that attempts to bypass most of these QTE like glorified "minigames".
But even with those flaws I have to recommend that people at least give this game a try, because there's a lot to love.
The dungeons, the expeditions, and the story are all very interesting and very fun. Not to mention that you can probably talk about the story alone for hours.
A lot of the dungeons/expeditions play out like little self contained stories and you find yourself almost seamlessly thrown into a wild adventure. I won't talk about the story because I'm afraid to spoil it.
The combat is amazing it can range from intense hold outs to really fast paced dynasty warriors style smash through tons of enemies gameplay. A lot of the bosses and unique enemies are really fun too and honestly there are bosses that I feel that I can go back and run again and again.
In the end the game is a little tough to get into especially because there aren't very many actually new players but once you crack through its hard shell you'll find something tasty. I think there is something here for everyone to enjoy you just have to give it a chance. So please do.
Negative Highlights:
[ Trash mobs forcing you to tank them, or spam heals. ]
[ Sudden enemy attacks also feel like they slow you even though they only knock you out of auto-sprint. ]
[ QTE like glorified "minigames" ]
Positive Highlights:
[ Great art, cheesy (in a good way) humour. ]
[ Leveling isn't too bad as long as you know what to do. ]
[ dungeons/expeditions play out like little self contained stories. ]
[ lots of people help out beginners. ]
[ Amazing combat is amazing, can be fast, can be slow, but always fun. ]

A very engaging, satisfying, and deep hack'n'slash/loot-based ARPG. If you enjoy Diablo-like games and you don't mind the pixelated graphics, it's a really awesome alternative. I typically shy away from indie games, but I can say without a doubt this game gives way more "bang for your buck" than (sadly) a lot of Early Access Steam games nowadays.
* Will run well on most computers.
* Tons of loot.
. Set items, uniques, class-specific, ability-modifying, etc.
* Satisfying spells/abilities that feel weighty when you upgrade them (and get better gear).
* Just updated with huge, customizable skill trees for every class. Just about everything feels viable.
* Updated frequently, with very frequent updates from the developer, as well as community interaction.
The only complaints I could muster, would be that there's a significant amount of loot sorting to deal with. The game has a filter option to prevent tiers of items lower than, say, "rare", tooltips from appearing at least. Also,
. But that's a small complaint, because I feel like a lot of Early Access games focus way too much on the multiplayer, and everything else suffers.
$10 is a bargain, and $8 (on sale) is a steal, if you really enjoy games like Diablo, Titan Quest, Grim Dawn, Path of Exile, etc.

Good game if you like JRPG-style games. No bugs that I noticed. Pros & Cons:
Pros:
- Animation of various attacks, characters, and enemies is consistent and high-quality. Some of the enemy designs caused me to stop playing and just look at them for a bit. Really well-done with a consistent art-style.
- Comic Book Influence: Characters and enemies have comic-book sytle speech bubble quips in combat. Boss fights and plot points are shown through illustrated comic-panel style movies.
- Six distinct characters, each with their own abilities you gain through levels. Each character also has two-perk trees where you can adjust point distribution every fight (if you wanted to).
- Combat: A well-implemented turn-based system. You have to watch which enemies are coming up and what attacks they are preparing. Buffs and debuffs matter, as does the rare strategic block.
- Pretty cool dungeon system. There are 8 "big" dungeons, semi-randomized each time you "run" them. They each have events and lore. To see most of the dungeon possiblities, you would have to run a dungeon two or three times. You can set the difficulty level for the dungeon at the start, which prevents you from just facerolling it the second time.
- Respectable loot system, which allows for multple character specializations. Each dungeon appears to have a pool of loot, and rng determines what you get on a given chest/enemy drop.
Cons:
- That high-quality animation? Yeah... you can't speed it up. On easy fights when you are over-leveled, nothing you can do to speed it up. Minor in the scheme of things, but there.
- You will have to repeat some content to stay leveled up. (I would think this is obvious, because its a JRPG-style game, but some people have no patience for any grinding.)
- Quibble: Movement on the overworld map is slower than it needs to be.

I wanted to like this game. The artwork and animation is very well done and fun. Combat has glimpses of challenge and creativity, but overall devolves into a grindfest. The graphics entertain, but the repeatitiveness gets very old very fast and results in a lot of filler beween anything engaging. In fact, much of the game seems geared to running up hours logged over actual interactions for the player.
I selected Insane difficulty for dungeons since otherwise it was already feeling monotonous, but unfortunately the general increase in interesting battles was all too frequently brought to a sudden halt when a seemingly unwinable encounter appeared with no discernable warning. 13 levels in, ability to win fights seems dramatically weighted towards levels over choices in battle, leaving a very small window where you are rewarded for attentiveness.
I think the developers have a lot of potential for future games, but this one was executed poorly when it comes to valuing the players time. Shorten it by 3/4, focusing on more challenging battles (quality over quantity), and I probably would have raved about it.

A very cluttered, mixed bag of flawed, underpolished gems.  There are great assets and innovations here, but the glacial pacing was a deal-breaker for me.  Luckily, another review pointed me to Cheat Engine's speed hack feature, where doubling the speed easily makes the game itself twice as good.  It is practically a requirement to keep Nightwar fun, since your characters run at the speed of frozen molasses and most combat is made of sitting even stiller.  Watching a slime slowly waddle over to a cahracter, smack them, and slowly waddle all the way back while everybody politely keeps quiet is almost a comedy act.  One that stops being funny after the 50th time when you can feel yourself aging to death.
Since bug fixes and improvements are still going, I'm hoping the pacing is something they'll tinker with.  And maybe give an official solution that keeps the sound effects in sync.  Another bad design choice is the inventory order.  Since every item, including consumables, has multiple tiers that aren't even kept next to each other, you end up with a shambling mess from which you'll never find that emergency healing item.  I guess the game being stingy with its money can help keep you from hoarding.  But that's not a real solution when juggling buffs through both consumables and equipment is an intended element.
If it sounds like I'm dwelling on the flaws, it's mainly to counterbalance the game's much more obvious first impression: its graphics and music are gorgeous.  Along with an innovative combat system, the developers really knocked those out of the park.  The combined atmosphere is enchanting and moody, and you'll definitely get your money's worth there.  It's just that the current flaws, it's hard to appreciate the beauty without a DIY solution.  With one, the dungeon crawling and resource gathering is fun enough to justify the price.  Since the great framework is already there, if the studio can keep polishing the system, this game might evolve into something amazing.  Here's hoping it turns into Super Battle Chasers Turbo, without being a separate purchase.
The fighting in the game shines because of the countless side effects every attack has, but I doubt I could express their appeals through words.  There's enough text on screen for each buff and debuff just playing the thing.  So instead, I'll point out that most of the writing outside those, is... not great.  BC's writing was never its appeal, being slammed for its cliches since the old days.  Most of the main cast isn't just made of broad stroke tropes, but are directly based on '90s anime and video game characters.  Gully even had Sephiroth for a brother, because for all his skill, Joe Mad's scripts were Deviantart accounts.
You won't see much originality in the plot or character interactions, since all the depth is in the mechanics.  Honestly, you won't find much of a story period, since everybody and everything just stays a collection of premises and homages that don't go anywhere.  The collectible dungeon flavor text somehow has more storytelling than the entire franchise after two decades.  As much as the soundtrack helps sell the stilted interactions, I do wish the writing improved, shedding some of the '90s excesses like Marureira's art did.  (Calibretto's robo-pants and Red Monika's watermelons used to look way more crammed in and out of place.)  That said, since the cast looks and plays great, it's not as distracting as it should be.  Nightwar knows to keep the focus on the gameplay, and the characters functions as a cool looking excuse for it.

Warmachine: Tactics is a turn-based strategy game, akin to XCOM and similar. While it is faithful to the tabletop game it is based upon, it currently offers little for the large price attached to it. I will go into more detail below.
- The game is set in the Iron Kingdoms, a high-fantasy world designed by Privateer Press that mixes magic and steampunk technology, resulting in the trademark multi-ton Warjacks of the franchise, and the Warcasters who control them. Each faction has a very distinctive design and colour palette (from the armoured and crimson Khador to the clean white and gothic-like Protectorate), so no matter what your taste one or several of the factions should appeal to you.
- In eight hours of gameplay, I have only suffered a single crash and malfunction in the game. The game seems to be in a surprisingly stable state. My only complaint about the preformance would be that on a low-medium setting, I am only getting 15-20 FPS. However, I am unsure weither this is because of the game being unoptimized or because my computer is getting a bit old. Nevertheless, if you have a somewhat modern rig, you shouldn't have any problems running the game at a pleasant FPS.
- Being a player of the tabletop Warmachine, the prospect of seeing the normally still and silent models come to life is very entertaining. Then watching the behemoth Warjacks swatting away infantry like insects is thrilling. The team behind Warmachine: Tactics has faithfully remade the tabletop units into the game. and they look, move and feel as they should. Add to this good sound and visual effects (I have no doubt these will be further improved upon) and satisfying ragdoll effects.
Even in its currently limited state, I have enjoyed every minute of the eight hours I have so far spent playing Warmachine Tactics, and I am certain that I will continue to play it for hours to come, both before and after the game's release.
- As it stands, the game is in a pretty unfinished state. While the game runs quite well (Only one crash in eight hours of gameplay, and no game-breaking glitches or bugs.), it is unoptimized. Alongside this, many of the features that are intended to be in the final release are not yet implemented. All four main factions (Khador, Cygnar, Protectorate, Cryx) have only one battlegroup of units available, and this battlegroup can't yet be modified. There are also only two multiplayer maps, and one singleplayer mission available.
The advantage of buying the game during the Early Access is the addition of the Digital Deluxe edition, which includes some future paid DLC for free.
- For what the game Currently offers, it is expensive. When the game is released it will be sold at a lower than current price, but at the disadvantage of not including some of the paid DLC that will be released after the game's release. By buying it now you will recieve the game, some future paid DLC for free And being able to play the game in it's current form.
According to the developers, the combined cost of the finished game and DLC will be higher than the current price for the Digital Deluxe edition on sale here.
- Before you make any purchase, you should look up some gameplay videos on YouTube. There are many to chose from, and don't be afraid of watching several before deciding weither or not this game is for you. I also need to stress that the game is Unfinished. It is clunky and rough around the edges (In addition to it being expensive for what it currently offers.)
But that should be expected from any Early Access title available on Steam. Do not buy this game expecting a finished product filled with content, because you wont find that here.
If you are fan of Warmachine and don't mind playing an unfinished and work-in-progress game, in addition to paying quite a bit for it, I can safely say you will enjoy Warmachine: Tactics. However if you aren't feeling the urge to immediately play it, you wont miss out on much by waiting for the full release and a cheaper price.
If you are less experienced about Warmachine, I again recommend you look it up properly before you make your purchase, else perhaps wait until the finished game is released, and along with it a lower price tag.

I don't normally write reviews of early access games, but I felt inspried to do so given the rather one sided nature of the current set of reviews.
Let me clarify one thing, the price of the game is a reflection of fairness regarding the price players paid during the kickstarter to access earier versions of the game. Contrary to most, this game will actually decrease in price as it gets clsoer to release, just like we have seen with Planetary Annihilation. Therefore this review is based on a 20$ game.
The game itself looks gorgeous. There does seem to be a little overemphasis on the glow effects, but other than that and a few graphical bugs expected during beta the game is a real beauty. There is a definite lack of features and areas to play in, but that again is also to be expect in the game's current stage of development.
Gameplay wise it could not be better. This game more than any other I have played brings the tabletop to the desktop. They have very succesfully transferred what is a very top quality tabletop boardgame and directly applied it in terms of look and gameplay to the PC. Players take turn moving their (now fully animated and awesome) miniatures and attacking, with all of the actions avaliable in a simple and effection fashion. The UI is clearly unfinished so we cannot take a good look at that yet, but the layout is very intuitive and the ability to move your camera right down into the heart of the action makes for some really exciting action moments rarely seen in the turn based genre.
Overally I conclude that the game is already enjoyable, but only about 50% feature complete and I very much look forward to the final product as all of the work so far is superb.

The pricing is unfortunate, but if they'd priced it lower than the kickstarter beta access, they'd have♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off early backers. But pricing it the same pisses off Steam users. Probably would have been better not to do a Steam Early Access, or at least do it closer to release at a more reasonable price point. At least there are goodies included with the extra price, which you won't get with the standard edition.
In conclusion, I'd like to give the game a 'sort of' recommendation. On the fence? Wait for release, buy it for $20 (I think that's what the final game will cost). Otherwise, think of this as preordering the digital deluxe edition, with a bonus included preview so you can try the game out.

It's a Steampunk XCOM: Enemy Unknown with extra mechanics!
No, but really. It is. But aside from that, Warmachine Tactics is a turn-based tile map strategy RPG set in the Iron Kingdoms world, and seems to be loosely based on the tabletop game of the same name. Even at this early beta stage, the game is showing a lot of polish and in the new and work-in-progress Unreal 4 Engine itself, runs fairly well. I was able to maintain 25-35FPS in the midrange settings. I have no doubt that this game will run like hot butter when it's optimisation is completed.
The game is very pretty, and the range of spells available between Warcasters, Warjacks and Infantry bring pretty interesting gameplay. However my initial impression of the 'direction' facing mechanic is that it is somewhat obtuse, but after some playing you get used to it. One of the things that also frustrated me some was that when you being taking actions with a unit, you can't 'save' actions for later in your turn. You must complete all possible actions or end that unit's turn in order to take action with another unit. That being said, the one single player scenario available in game is a lot of fun, and when it was completed I was only left with excitement for the next piece.
Closing this up, my only regret is that I don't have more time to play it RIGHT NOW. It IS a little bit prohibitively priced, but with the extras you get when the game goes into full release I'd say it's probably worth it. This is how Early Access should be done, and even in it's early beta state, with pretty solid gameplay I must give this game an 8/10.

This is a complete re-edit.
The steam version of this game started to stall at loading so I deleted it and downloaded Wildstar from the actual website for the game. This worked out much better, the game ran fine for a week then I started getting a memory error, this bug has been confirmed and around since 2014. This was the straw the broke the camels back. The inability to actually play the game anymore makes it difficult to enjoy.
Pros: the world is fairly large and engaging, the storyline was good and I really did enjoy most of my time in-game. The community was impressively friendly for an MMO, though there's always the "alt-f4 kids" offering their free advice, but over-all I was impressed. I think the average player tends to be older in wildstar, didn't run into any 12 yr olds rage quiting and swearing at me, so that was nice. You can get hoverboard mounts that are customizable, (can add parts to it) that was cool. Over-all the game itself is fine, there's plenty to do, the devs seems to still be supporting it, new content is coming out, etc. You can double jump! Combat is slighty more complex (need to understand the interrupt mechanic and dodging  is a factor), dungeons were actually quiet fun and challenging. It's actually F2P! Not P2W like Neverwinter. Everything is available and within reach without needing to fork over real money all day every day.
Cons: Crashes, not optimized for higher end computers, you literally have an advantage if your computer is older and a piece of crap. I have a gtx 760 and on default settings was still laggy and fps drops are a constant struggle. =/. You'll start recognizing the same people in barrens chat, because there's hardly anyone playing this game. Steam has given this game a slight breath of life but any dungeon/adventure/expedition that you might want to do pre-50 forget about queing, find people in chat otherwise the chances of that que popping is verrry low, not uncommon to sit in a low level que for 4+ hours during prime time. As a healer.
Over-all this game just falls short, it has so much potential, it was really enjoyable to play for the first week, one of the devs pops into nexus chat occasionally, there is a lot to like, but the lack of optimization, the constant crashing, never able to find a group even while in a "large guild" and the redundant quest system where you feel like a good dog cuz you can fetch crap like every other mmo. There really wasn't anything innovative about this game, I feel like everything this game has to offer I've seen it before somewhere else in another game.

Great board game conversion.
It has a Stratego style set up, but is much deeper with each piece having it's own powers and a numerical strength, piece placement is very important during board set up. You can see your opponents piece placement, but not what those pieces actually are.
Battles play out on a diamond shaped board with sixteen territories, your pieces can only move forward with some pieces and board spaces having powers that can allow exceptions to this. When you move into a territory with an opponent present, your opponents piece is revealed and a battle begins. Your strength and your opponents strength and power are revealed. You then play an additional card from your hand prior to the battle and then you and your opponent reveal cards simultaneously. Cards can generally only be used once and are not replenished until they have all been used. Your piece strength, special powers and the card you played determine the outcome. Get your Prince to the home territory of the shadow forces to win, or if your'e playing shadow forces, get three of your pieces to the light side home or kill the prince for the win.
Great game. Well implemented. I love seeing these great board games making their way to steam.
Mulitplayer games play out in real time (no async) and the game does have an integrated chat box.
I love it , Great price , fun strategy game. Well done.

A fun little game that has plenty of rough edges starting from a somewhat clunky combat system to a total lack of an options menu, but the story is interesting enough to make you push forward.
The story and the characters are the main reasons for you to play this game. Some of the jokes actually made me laugh out loud which is a rare thing for games these days... actually scratch that, most of the jokes made me laugh or at least have a sensible chuckle. Humor is subjective of course, I personally know a few people who love Borderlands 2 and I can't stand most of it, so your mileage may vary.
What I liked about the writing so far is that while it has a lot of gags and filled with easter eggs, there is an actual story happening and it's not half bad and I am curious to see what's going to happen. The only reason I stopped playing right now is because it's 4 AM, and even then it took some effort on my part to put the game down. I'd probably still be playing it if it didn't release so late but i guess that's irrelevant.
If you are here looking for a complex RPG with complex mechanics and smooth combat, then look elsewhere, the game barely does enough to be considered an RPG combat/upgrades/loot wise. It's not
, but I certainly wouldn't have kept playing the game if it wasn't a story focused experience.
Your hits lack impact and it feels like you are just swinging through your enemies, which in term just wail on you while you are trying to take them down. The game lacks some sort of stunlock mechanic I feel, if the enemies got momentarily stunned after a hit or two it would have made the whole thing a lot more satisfying otherwise it's just a flailing competition where you just hope that the enemy runs out of HP first.
Another issue is the lack of a proper options menu, you can't even change the sound options, that's just inexcusable.
In closing I will say that I don't regret the purchase, I am having a lot of fun even with all of the issues mentioned above. The game is rough, some areas of it look unprofessional as hell, but at the same time it has some beautiful areas, good (in my opinion) writing, and it costs less than some fast food I bought the other day.
EDIT: Finished the game, took me about 12-14 hours (don't mind the time played, Steam doesn't count offline mode time) and I will say that I think it was a good game. That said the gameplay is not good, if you didn't get interested in the story 1.9h - you may want to get a refund, the gameplay wont get much better.

When I first saw Zenith the thing that grabbed my attention was the trailer's take on the adventure RPG genre. I personally would consider Zenith to be a parody adventure RPG. Basically the game's storyline is goofy/cheesy regularly making jokes about video games while including a lot of pop culture references. So far I have found the game to be funny at times while some of the jokes fall flat.
With regards to combat I would say the game is quite average. The combat is not bad but I also wouldn't consider it to be anything that would make you want to play the game if you weren't interested in the story.
I encountered some technical issues while playing Zenith. First if your computer is near the recommended requirements I would highly recommend lowering settings (especially screen resolution) or the game's framerate is going to be terrible. Second the game has some pretty long load times. Finally the game has the occasional graphical glitches where characters were placed into the ground and items were highlighted when they shouldn't have been.
Basically my recommendation comes down to how interested you are in the story. If the story doesn't really interest you I don't think Zenith will be for you. If the idea of a parody adventure RPG sounds interesting to you I think you will enjoy the game.

(as it's not really a genre I've played)
The game's still good enough for me to play more of though, a very early judgement but I do wonder how the HC ARPG players would like it though, so far it seems fairly easy...trying Icewind Dale 2 a second run through (and even occassionally in the first - getting surrounded by spiders/bugs - certainly posted a whole lot more of a challenge than this...*so far*)

Negatives I have so far:
How to bind potions to the controllers D-pad is not apparent. (and no help is shown either)
Some things you "loot" still show the yellow outline around them if they're in reality triggers. (there was a table you should "loot" to trigger the contiuation of the game and after it had triggered it still had the yellow outline)
Purple and grey'ish text that's a part of the 3D visual right before you're about to enter the temple are a bit annoying due to the purple text becoming a bit smeared and hard to read, the grey'ish being a bit hard to read as the camera pans around and you're looking at a similarily coloured background. (it being part of the 3D visuals meas it becomes smaller as the camera moves away from the players it hovers over)
Some text (happened twice for me) gets cut very short due to something being triggered in the world.
Some corpses respawn very fast and at one incident I was stuck with text on the screen when enemies appeared and I had to smash the A-button 3-4 times to get out of it which meant they reached me. (the difficulty level still made that fine but....)
So as you can see my complaints so far are extremely far from game breaking and should in no way shape of form have you avoid the game...
What I could see as a potential put-off for lovers of the genre, you pro-Diablo'ers and such is that it's quite easy so far.

Full review:
Text:
Zenith tries so hard to be hip and cool and "in" that its reminds me of corporate managers using a comic sans to be "casual".
The constant immersion breaking references to other titles are so ham-fisted and forced that they not only lose any flavor, but actively detract from the game itself. Both visually and in writing (more below on that) the game breaks it's own world to make cheap puns and relishes in trying to be witty that it even breaks into combat and puzzle mechanics.
The writing is mostly to blame here with not only frequent, but badly written puns being the sole purpose of half the dialogue.. and the other half being a mix of a badly written fan-fiction and young-writer syndrome. It grinds and grates on the eyes, and in a game where you'll be doing a LOT of dialogue - that gets annoying and infuriating fast.
So lets even out the triforce of bad is sound design... which fits with the game about as well as a 90 year old grandmother fits with skydiving while having a heart attack. It doesn't mix, it doesn't switch well between gameplay (non combat / combat) and half the time they force puns into the damn game that serious and tension building moments are utterly ruined from it even from the audio side of things.
Now, having burned it to the ground... the gameplay is ok. the combat is mediocre and while interesting in its itemisation and character building, doesn't really do anything unique or new. The art syle is pretty cool, even if the game looks outdated and the animations are pretty poor.
But for a Narrative focus based RPG... ugh.

There's a lot to love about Chronicon. Like many other reviews, the comparison to oldschool Diablo is spot-on. Since its early days, a lot's been done to make the combat feel fluid and pleasant, and to add a little bit of variety to the game. On the upside, the game will shower you with loot and you'll never feel like you've been playing forever without changing some of your gear around, and there's never really a dull a moment in the game.
On the downside though, the animations are honestly servicable at best; they aren't /bad/ by any stretch, mind you, but they lack a little bit of fluidity. The game (as of the time of writing) does suffer from a little bit of jerkyness too; picking up currency often creates a really awkward stutter that's kind of hard to look past. Still, all of these things are minor gripes at best, and honestly very easy to look past.
The one thing that really brings the game down for me though, is just how completely overcrowded some of the earlier dungeons feel. Before level 10, you're reusing the same skill or two repeatedly to slowly cleave your way through enemies that are so cramped together, you barely get any time to go through your inventory to look at the loot you picked up. Some folks might enjoy this, but spending 1+ hour on the same dungeon level with 200+ enemies makes progressing through the game feel a little sluggish. Your mileage may vary.

I bought this game for my GPD Win because of its controller support. There aren't many ARPG's like this with xinput support. Sure Grim Dawn has some "meh" controller support, but it never felt right, and made menu navigation feel tedious. Then I saw Chronicon.
I had my doubts. I'm no graphics snob--it wasn't about the pixely style of the game. I'll take gameplay over visuals any day. It was mostly about this being such a little-known indie number. Loot/Grind/LevelUp/Repeat games are simple and addictive to play, but it's a beast to create a well balanced drip-feed of powerful items and rare enemies. Doing it right takes talent. There's no way this dinky little game was going to keep me interested for more than five minutes.
I was wrong.
First off, I've played waaaay more than the steam play record suggests. I've put considerable time in, basically since my GPD Win was first delivered. Chronicon has done more than surpass my expectations. It's one of those few examples of an early access game doing all the right things.
-It's what was promised. It's playable, fun, and scratches the "loot itch."
-Great, clear communication from the developer on what he's working on, and what to expect next.
-I actually find myself feeling excited for new content, rather than vaguely interested.
-Much deeper than it seems. Those first few hours, I was convinced I'd seen the gist of what Chronicon had to offer. There are small puzzles leading to decent gear, procedurally generated "events" and other stuff to shake up the game a little and distract you in between grinding and inventory management. "Yeah, okay, this IS a fun little game, but I don't know if I can play this forev--- OH, DEAR LORD, WHAT IS THAT?! HOLY SHI--"
-I'm not done yet. How am I NOT bored with this game? Sooo many indie and early access games out there and SO few keep my attention.
I love this game! Keep it coming!

Warmachine Tactics looks to be a potential great turn-based strategy game...if done correctly. The game is still in beta and is looking to be released in a month's time.
My gaming rig has a Intel i7 3770 @ 3.4Ghz, 16GB DDR3 1333MHz Kingston Value RAM, Gigabyte GTX660Ti 2GB, runs off a 1TB HDD 7200RPM. (I am getting a EVGA GTX780 very shortly so I'll edit for the difference in frames per second.)
Pricing: I'm not a Kickstarter Backer. When Warmachine Tactics was released on Steam for Early Access, I brought it immediately, didn't really care about the price. I had read what the game currently has for content. For a Digital Deluxe Edition, £49.99 is a decent price point for what players will be eventually getting when it's fully complete. I've paid more for other games but they were complete games, all content was there except for the future DLC with Season Passes. I didn't do any tutorials or play the Multiplayer yet, I wanted to see what the game could potential offer.
Game Performance: Moving onto the actual game itself, I pumped the settings up to max as high as they could go and played the Single-player scenario. The game was soild, running around 25-40fps @ 1920x1080 @60Hz, this is still beta and is subject to change until the release date for further optimization as well as future improvements. It played very nicely, no crashes or errors while playing the scenario. A bug with the units running through market food stands at the beginning of the level but that can be sorted out.
Visuals: The game looks very nicely crafted, the game models are very accurate to their original tabletop models and can individually pick out what warcaster or unit is. The map for the single-player scenario is beautifully created and solid representation of the Warmachine world, with the weathering effects are good so far, something you'd expect for the winter feel.
Interface: The UI is decent but large on a 1920x1080 though boarders and such aren't polished so they don't fit the role. I hope they are refined later on.
Sounds: As you'd expect, the sound effects for melee and range thus far a good. Background music is fitting.
Disclaminer. Just a reminder I've only played the Single Player scenario, that's all.
So the important question, is Warmachine Tactics worth it. Personal opinion, with the price now at £37.97 (£49.99 previous price) with the current content and now with an update (have yet to play), it feels a little more worth it but I'd rather wait till all the content for the Digital Deluxe there. So I'll say I do recommend the game but with a 'Buyer Beware' caution solely on the content to price ratio.

After tweeting and posting a message on Facebook. I really would like to know why the price changed since I did buy it for £49.99 from the developers and those who brought it for the higher price. Is there a possible chance of getting the difference refunded to the Steam Wallet?

As far as I am aware, I have never reviewed a game before.
Dunno why I decided to review this one out of the many I have purchased, but I figured why not. I need to put my thoughts into words for some closure on this game.
Just in case you were wondering, I have no experience with the previous NieR game, I did not complete all the quests, and I didn't unlock all of the achievements, I simply followed the main story, and did any sidequests that were tied to it.
Nier: Automata is without a doubt, one of the best games I have played as of late. The story was compelling from the start, and retained its great storytelling all of the way throughout. The gameplay was a breath of fresh air after having completed the most recent Mass Effect game. The game has varying play styles that it often transitions between. It has tight and responsive controls (with a controller), and its overall fun factor held strong throughout. Whenever something new was introduced, having previously thought I had seen all of the game's mechanics, put a smile on my face. I have never smiled so much while playing a game.
That's not to say it doesn't have issues, though. The game only crashed once for me, but it was still quite a setback as I had not saved in some time. Speaking of saving, the game's saving feature is forgettable (literally). It lacks an autosave function, only quick saving when out of combat. Factoring in the game's tendency to crash like a Russian driver with a windshield camera, it is more than likely the player will forget to save during the game's key moments, wind up killing themselves, breaking their immersion when they realize they have to do the last 30 minutes over again.
A few minor issues of mine would have to be the invisible walls placed around a seemingly open area during boss fights. I ran into these barriers countless amounts of times, resulting in me getting my android♥♥♥♥♥legitimately crushed. The enemies can also seem a bit like damage-sponges at times, whether that is to pad out the play time or a design oversight is beyond me, but it can become draining to wack a small robot with a fully upgraded sword around 30 times.
Overall, the game's story and frequently engaging gameplay mechanics kept my eyes glued to the screen so long I've now got dry eye syndrome. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes games of a similar genre, or anyone who is burnt out on playing the same game with a different skin every year.
