"It's like taking Lord of the Rings and mixing in the Wild West!"
Except there's nothing LotR about Steel & Steam, and the closest it comes to Wild West resides with the "evil desert" we're told about, and the guns that the characters use.
This is but an example of how S&S tries to pass itself off at something better than what the sum of its parts actually IS. "Great stories, awesome characters, and classic monsters, with a touch of steampunk!"
Or, slow-paced generic story involving a ton of back tracking and wasted time going through enormous barren towns. Characters that do get a decent bit of writing but fail to fully push the envelope or help to make the experience memorable. Classic monsters, or "RPG Maker monsters, with multiple pallet swaps for each", and steampunk again residing with only a few elements (guns, end-game enemy zeppelins, and Alyssa being from a family of tinkerer / sniper people).
The world map is horrible, entirely far too large for what little content there is; you could cut out everything but the two towns and nearby dungeons and wouldn't suffer a loss. Those two towns are, as other reviews complain, enormous and filled with empty space (kickstarter shoutouts) that hinder the game's fun.
Where the original character portraits and artwork are nice, the battle graphics are either lifted straight out of stock assets from RPGM, or are horribly muddy and blurry. Not even ripping off Phantasy Star IV's style of "behind the hero" can help it look any better than low res garbage.
And the meat of the game, the game play? An Enter / Space fest (because gamepad support is missing) where skills are basic, enemies have tons of HP, and the best/only strategy is "Mash attack until you win".
The sidequests are either this attack mashing or "find some thing in the giant world map / towns", and honestly triple the length of the game. Without the sidequests distracting you, S&S Ep 1 is quickly over.
Short, filled with ugly original and stock assets and tired gameplay mechanics, with little to break the tedium or really lift what had the potential for a really good game. Steel & Steam ain't worth the $9.99 they're asking for by a long shot. It's a shame; a lot more polish and tweaking and this could have been great.

RPG Maker game.  Need I say more?
Okay, so the game has some creativity, but it's shrouded in lame storytelling and terribly rushed game development.  The plot is interesting at times.  I like the premise of the story.  I wish it was told with more than bland RPG Maker text boxes.  There are some moments in the story which show off some nice but subtle art which distracts from the old school graphical style of RPG Maker, but I simply did not like the story and how it was told enough to overlook the awful visuals and terrible game design.
The game world is a bit blocky and obviously rushed.  The weird part is I did not know how to enter towns and other places once I arrived on the overworld level.  For the record, you reach the overworld just minutes into the story if you just walk right instead of left when you arrive at the first town.
I also did not like combat.  It consisted of simply pressing fight, selecting each character, and targetting the bear over and over again.  All I did was press space over and over. How is that fun?  It isn't fun.  It's an example of how generic this game really is.  The creator probably just threw together settings in RPG Maker and fit everything to his story.  It was rushed and not well thought out.  I would have given the player some combat strategy choices or something.  Don't make combat so pointless!  If combat is going to be so easy, you may as well not even have that gameplay element at all.
Redeeming factors are few and far between, but there are some good points in this game.  A lot of the NPCs have side quests and secret areas for you to explore.  There are a lot of ways you can venture off the main quest line to level up without grinding random battles, which is nice compared to games like Final Fantasy III. As I previously stated, the overworld is a little broken, and there are a lot of areas which are rushed and look horrible, but some areas look decent, and I appreciate the work that went into the combat sprite animations and emoticons and quest log and so on.
Overall, the game isn't worth buying, and the only reason I even tried it was it came with a bundle a while ago.  This isn't even a complete story.  It was never finished.  What reason do I have to continue playing it?  None.  I don't play it. This was certainly an interesting experience... and a tedious, frustrating one at the same time.
I must admit that I had a light craving for a JRPG lite like this one, before it showed up in a Humble Bundle, so I was all over it as soon as I got it, and finished it in something disturbingly close to "one go". And I can't say that I've enjoyed myself thoroughly, can't say I can recommend it. Why? Where do I start...
You are dumped way past some imaginary beginning of the story in a cartoonish steampunky/fantasyish world, without (m)any explanation(s) and with very vague suggestions about what needs to be done. So, you save some random old "famous hunter" from a rampaging bear. Which runs away.  And then you're told to go back, find it and kill it. Oh, and some friend of yours is looking for a professor who didn't show up. And there you are, level 1-2, in the middle of a city that's a veritable metropolis compared to most cities of the genre. With hope in your heart, you go exploring. And then all that boils down to a stream of mostly empty houses "belonging" to people who supported it on Kickstarter. Which is cool, but from a gamer's selfish perspective useless, boring, time consuming and lazy. You wander from house to house hoping that someone will be there and mention something questish - because when they do (in every... say... 10th house? 8th?), it can actually be cute & original. Not always though And that's the problem with the game in its entirety. The world map is very, very big. And very, VERY empty. 98% of your time, if you have ANY sort of completist or exploratory tendencies, will be spent wandering in the middle of nowhere with too frequent interruptions from random encounters, which soon become dull, mindless "enterfests". You click the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your enter key. Because there's generally no need, at least for a bigger part of the game, for much more. And it makes that huge empty (be it a forest or a plain) space even more irritating. And it feels completely unfinished. The ONLY other town you'll be able to access, Silverhead, is 3 times larger. And looks wrong and looks bad. It really could've been separated into 2-3 separate towns and make far more sense.
You'll find cute touches here & there, nice, sometimes even humorous little details/easter eggs if you wish, so it's not all that bad.
The game makes fun of stereotypes and illogical actions inherent to the genre, like, yeah, barging into people's homes and pillaging everything, or randomly dropped loot. It actually manages to be funny here & there. The two main characters (a fighter of sorts and a ranger of sorts) exchange cute banter - though you don't find much about them, their interaction IS charming in a way.
And the quests can be interesting, but the lack of a proper map/description renders them frustrating. So, you need to find a guy who lives in the south of Silverhand. Cute, there's only 40 nearly identical houses you need to check there. What fun. So, you have to travel to some mountains north of Silverhand. Well, guess what, there are NO mountains north of Silverhand - the ones in question are to the east. Another quest tells you to go south of those very mountains - but you get it far earlier in the game. So you don't really know where to look. Great. And those random encounters don't help. Trust me, if you're the exploring type, like I am, reaching one edge of the map, fighting increasingly hard battles only to find a place with "very good fishing" - with exactly the same 2 kinds of fish as everywhere else... You get disappointed. Though the minigame is cute. Oh, remember that bear I mentioned? You need to bait it with fish. But it doesn't tell you which kind. And, no, it's not the ones you catch, it's one you can only get from a single store in the nearby town. Great.
Back to the battles... Honestly, the only "close" battles I've had were @level 1-2, maybe a couple of random ones at the eastern edge of the map, aaand... maybe, just maybe the last battle. But I did do all the sidequests. I haven't used almost any item in battle apart from regular potions, maybe once or twice hi-potions. There's a third character, which you CAN ignore, I think, but he's a cleric of sorts, and even though the potions are plentiful, you'll need him. Items are OK enough, well balanced I guess, and you have multiple choices (the main caracter can use both swords and guns, and he has different specials for different weapons, you get to adjust which special(s) you find more usefull). Things get more interesting later on when/if you acquire summons for your two main characters, which go with prerendered animations that get boring very fast. Speaking of items... there's only one (1) shield in the entire game, and you get it through a quest. Wha?
Graphics are cute and adequate, if they are really generic, from RPG Maker (can't tell), then boo, but they do their job really. The music can really be nice, but the battle theme starts grating on your nerves soon enough.
I love this genre. I really do. That, and a bout of non-productive insomnia was what kept me going for hours at this game. And the promise of a story, that doesn't quite get fulfilled. Nothing more, nothing less. It's a hodgepodge of good and bad ideas, enjoyment and irritating frustration. Seemingly lazy/unfinished stuff and inspired details. Despite everything, I will likely try the Episode Two as well. But I can't recommend this to anyone outside of a bundle, especially at 10€.

I dropped Battle Chasers shortly after its initial release because it just felt painfully slow and while I liked the game as it is, it felt like wasting time. There is a reason that games like these get an optional speed up function these days. However, after picking it up again and using a little trick to speed up the game, I quickly realized what I have been missing out on.
As always, these are my own thoughts and opinions, please look at other reviews too before you make a purchase decision.
Let’s begin with my biggest problem; frequent battles who drag the games length out longer than it needs to be. While it was nice seeing those juicy animations the first few times, it quickly became a burden. This could easily be fixed with an optional speed up button, but so far they have not implemented one and I had to use Cheat Engine as a replacement.
The second problem I have has to do with the otherwise awesome crafting system in which you can only create one item at a time, making it a huge pain if you just want to craft a stack of potions for example. Also, your success chance gets reset after each crafted item and one has to to add materials each time when wanting to craft another epic potion, it’s annoying.
Battle Chasers’ combat offers a surprising amount of depth where each character has four primary attacks that are instant and generate overcharge, but what you build up is reset once the fight is over. Additionally, there are 12 primary skills per character that are much stronger but have casting time and need mana or overcharge resulting in a surprising amount of strategies at your disposal. Similarly to Final Fantasy’s limit breaks, Battle Chasers allows the use of three different Bursts per character that can be used as ultimate abilities for boss fights or quickly finishing of unpleasant foes, and they all share the same burst meter. You even have two skills for each character which can be used outside of combat to guard you from dangerous hazards or give you a buff for the fight you are about to enter. Furthermore, combat is done in a typical RPG manner but with not so typical RPG elements and the game combines all of them very well. Use status ailments like bleeding, chill, or haste that can positively or negatively effect combat and allow for some sick combos.
Battle Chasers offers a wide variety of interesting enemies even though most of them have, in typical old-school RPG manner, just different colors so one can tell them apart from each other. On the world map, monsters aren't encountered randomly like most RPGs do, they have fixed positions allowing one to skip some of them and you can even chose to skip lowly monsters entirely. While in exploration areas and dungeons you have the choice to separate enemies and fight them one at a time or rush in to take on the whole group at once. There are also fights with multiple waves of enemies which can be pretty harsh. This is used most notably in the arena where you have to fight many waves back to back until you reach the boss of that tier. Also, bonus streaks award more experience based on certain conditions met like one-hitting enemies or getting a double kill with one attack. Fights reward you with gold and crafting materials which are needed to craft, buy, and enhance equipment. Typical rarities often seen in RPGs, like uncommon, rare, epic and legendary, evoke the urge to constantly upgrade your gear and experiment with different stats.
Besides the deep combat, Battle Chasers utilizes a unique crafting system where you just have to get needed materials to craft something or simply take more materials from one component and increase your success chance without having all the materials you would normally need to craft it. You can increase your success chance up to 300% by giving it even more materials to craft rare or even epic gear, and the same can be done with weapon enhancements which grant passive bonuses to your equipment.

The bestiary rewards the player with passive unlocks for all characters by slaying monsters a given number of times and also provides information about health, attacks, and loot drops after a certain amount of kills which also changes the enemies health bars from ??? to their actual values and shows specific skills that they will be using next.
All of the six characters have two passive perk threes with 18 different passives each allowing for a specific role like tank, healer, or damage dealer, and you are free to mix between them. Moreover, customization towards your prefered playstyle starts to really open up mid-game where you have enough perk points to setup some nice combos. Perk points are earned through leveling or by buying/finding books that grant them.
There are eight dungeons stretched across the world map that may be played on Normal, Heroic, and Legendary, and they can be a real challenge the first time you visit them. While filled with loot and monsters, each dungeon also attempts to spice it up with puzzle elements here and there where you actually have to use your brain. A boss lies at the end of each dungeon and drops items that can be traded for tokens, which also come from a fun fishing minigame and bounties (“hunts”) you can take out on certain enemies. These tokens can be traded for many things like the perk books, random gear chests, or even different outfits for your characters.
While cutscenes are in 2D with awesome comic style drawings, Battle Chasers in-game visuals remind me very much of Torchlight but with way more polish and atmosphere. The world map is in a completely different style from the rest of the game, with a nice storybook feel to it.
Combat showcases gorgeous animations that feel both fluid and impactful, but at the same time tend to get old quickly and stay like that until later in the game. I do appreciate that each different weapon has its own unique visual style during combat and everywhere else, I just wish they would’ve done the same with armor.
While the story is alright as it is, I would’ve wished for far greater character development which was sadly lacking, apart from the little scenes while resting in an inn at night, that’s it. I do appreciate those little conversations though, they give you some sense of the characters’ personalities.
The soundtrack is beautiful, energetic and fits the tone of the game just right, often reminding me of Bastion’s greatness. I never got tired of hearing any of the songs over and over, they’re just that good!

I haven't played any Paradox grand strategy games at any depth, but I really enjoyed it. I feel like it needs more narrative content though which might be a bit more complicated than the historical grand strategy games (especially since this game takes place over centuries). End game events feel underwhelming though I read that they just gave Unbidden 4 times strength, so maybe I'm wrong at this point.

It's an extremely slow starter and days of patient empire building can be instantly wrecked through the slightest mistake in fight or flight. It doesn't help new players that achievements can only be made in ironman mode which could be seen as counter-intuitive as far as broaching the steep learning curve goes. But if you start with a "tiny" galaxy you will get the hang of all aspects more quickly than if you chose a larger map and this is definately where new players should start. It has levels of flavour and depth in deplomacy that other space 4X games, at best, nod towards and this is what makes it less of a "churn out units with little personality" game than all the others. Its slow-burning nature does not lend itself well to multiplayer situations as campaigns generally last a very long time. Trying to play with anyone but close and committed friends would be as pointless as creating a league made up of random player matchups in something like Football Manager.
Whilst it is certainly not for everyone those looking for an extended single player experience who persevere through the harsh learning curve will find that they are playing the most in-depth space 4X there is.

This is very much my style of game, so I was excited about it. Overall so far I think it is well done, but it does have its downsides too. I'm enjoying the story, the battle system is straightforward and more or less as expected. There are plenty of side quests available that don't particularly drag you away from the main story but provide enough xp that so far I haven't had to grind out any levels in classic RPG style.
I do have a few complaints, but nothing so serious that it has kept me from enjoying the game. The first is that there doesn't seem to be a world map, which can leave you floundering for town if you wandered too far from a road and aren't exactly sure where you are. The second is that the towns simply seem way too big, about 3 times as big as they need to be. The number of houses that have nothing in them is mind-blowing, yet for those of us familiar with RPG style games we know that we MUST check every one because the one missed have a unique item or quest. This can lead to frustration if you have a few quests you do at once because unless you've got an astounding memory you may not remember exactly where you need to go to turn it in.
The music isn't particularly riveting, and gets old with time. I don't mind this at all since I tend to turn game music off in favor of streaming anyway. The story seems to be unfolding at a good pace so far. There are occasional pop culture references that are fun. (Dr. Who, Eric Clapton) If you're an absolute fan of the genre, I definitely recommend the game. If not, I can't recommend getting it outside of a sale, but it is still worth trying.

CONs, The game is far too short. This is because it was a kickstarter game and with 8500 dollars being raised for this section and whatnot, this is what was finished. Straight storyline play in this game would be less than an hour or two, sidequests included this game can be completed in under 4 hours. My playtime is not terribly reflective of time spent in game. Also this game has some very underdeveloped character interactions between party members. All in all for a kickstarter effort it is good, which is why I will recommend it, but I would wait for a sale, I certainly wouldn't pay more than 5 dollars or so for the title. It is a good first effort and if you wish to support the people making it to hopefully add to it, then by all means, but if you are looking for something to fill up hours in an olde tyme JRPG style, get a FF game or something along those lines.

First try on Steel&Steam: Episode 1
The video is available here:
First off, the user defined tag "RPG Maker" is as accurate as a single tag can be. That does not necessesarily mean, you can't do great things with it as well. But first things first:
The options are not accessible via the main menu, but you can access them while playing the game. 3 different sliders for audio options are available, which is a plus.  Other than that you can change the default walking speed, the text speed from scrolling to instant and you can toggle battle animations on or off. Graphical options are not available, but this is not bothering in this case.
Into the game we go and we start off with a little tutorial in which movement, interaction, inventory manangement, as well as comat are shown to you. You move around using the arrow keys and interaction works via the spacebar or the enter button. You don't really need any more than that controlwise, since the combat is turnbased.
But the combat is not your typical run of the mill turnbased combat. Apart from critical hits, evasion and normal hits, there are different status conditions in which you can be set by the enemy or vice versa. For example, some hits or special abilities have the potential to knock you off balance which skips your turn until you regain balance.
So, after beating the first encounter you will be teleported into the first town. I didn't count each house and every npc individually, but I have to say that for a game of this format this has been one of the largest towns I've ever seen. The same applies to the second town as well.
In the town you can do what you can do in RPGs: Walk into some people's house, steal their stuff and talk to the people like nothing's ever happened. Sometimes it might occur that they give you some items or even quests as well.
And when you think that you have to listen(well, actually read) every dialogue, which by the way is recommended, because the dialogue is rather well written, you are mistaken. You can find the quests and their description in your controll panel.
In terms of the quest system I have to say the quests(side quests included) so far were rather enjoyable and I didn't expect to gain xp and gold from doing quests in a rpg like that, so I was positively surprised.
The control panel also includes your inventory and character information. Equipping your characters is relatively simple, since you have an autoequip button, which selects the best gear in terms of stats for you. Otherwise you can also equip the items yourself one by one. Other than that the inventory system is simple, but it fits its purpose.
So far there has been nothing negative to say, but as we progress through the main storyline we come to the point on which I start to scratch my head so hard that my scalp is coming off. By simply doing the necessary steps and encounters in the game, you gain 2-3 levels until that point, so you have your special ability. The game also gives you a healer, but not that it would matter in any way, because when you take on the 3rd quest(if I counted correctly) in the main storyline and venture towards the zone, the game suddenly turns around and gives you the finger.
From enemies which you killed in 2 to a maximum of 5 turns, the encounters suddenly take 10+ turns for no apparent reason. There are even some enemies which only take an average of 15-25 damage each turn while having 300-350 hp and not being the only enemy in an encounter. What spices things up even more is the fact that their attacks deal about 33-60% of your maximum hp. I've only done one encounter which took me 10 minutes and turned off the game, because I thought it was bs.
So, the tl:dr.... I cannot recommend it, I am sorry. The last point completely killed it for me.
If you can forgive the game for that, it might be right for you, but I can't be bothered. I might re-review it, if there is a solution to that, but at the current state, as much as it hurts, I have to give it a thumbs down.

I am going to make a comparison between Borderlands 2 and Pre-Sequel, because Pre-sequel is the sequel, and has borrowed a lot from 2.
Borderlands 2 and Pre-Sequel offer somewhat different experiences. Obviously this stuff is my opinion. I feel that Pre Sequel is superior in most categories, except for length. Borderlands 2 is much, much, much longer and has more of everything in every category (ie guns, monsters, quests etc), but I feel like it’s weaker in a lot of ways.
First Point: Story Quality and Humour
I am Australian so perhaps I preferred the Pre-Sequel humour better, but I really got sick of listening to the characters in Borderlands 2. 2 has more 'jokes' but they are without context most of the time. What I mean by this is that the jokes don't demonstrate anything about the person saying them, nor do they say something about the world, nor do they say anything about the plot. Anyone can say basically any line at any point in the story and they would work just as well.
Pre-Sequel's jokes are not as 'pop culture' as 2, but they fit into the story and the setting, and suit the character saying them much better. Not only that, but the dramatic parts of the Pre-Sequel story were actually excellent in my opinion. 2 constantly contradicted itself in terms of tone and its dramatic elements, and contains a rather basic hero saves the world type story. Any kind of tension it builds is immediately thrown away with the next pop culture reference.
The main villain of 2 talks for hours and hours and hours, but I don't feel like I have any understanding of their motivation besides vague hints, and none of the hints really gel together to produce a whole picture. There is a reason that an entire game can be made after 2 about the main villain of 2 even though 2 is so very long. Pre-Sequel provides a reasonable and dramatic 'Hero's journey' for the main Villain of 2, and provides a much greater understanding of both the Villain of 2, and also of the world the game inhabits.
Second Point: Enemies and Level Design
Pres-Sequel has many less enemy types than 2, however, I feel like the enemy AI is much improved. In Pre-Sequel you face a lot of human type enemies, but they use more tactics, plus the environments are much better designed around flanking and cover. Borderlands 2's enemies and areas always felt like a stats battle, where you both stand in a wide open area and walk towards each other until someone wins. The problem is that you will always lose unless you abuse level geometry to lessen the damage you take.
By abuse the level geometry I mean something different to using cover. I mean standing next to objects that cover a larger area than what the graphics show. So this would mean that you can shoot basically 'through' something that the enemies can't shoot through.
Pre-Sequel also makes each fight a 3d fight. You will face enemies above and below you constantly. And you will be able to take to the skies by virtue of the low gravity environment. This means attacks can come from a large variety of angles. And cover is only cover from certain angles.
Third Point: Character Skill Trees
I feel the character skill trees in Pre-Sequel are far superior to 2. Every character in Pre-Sequel has numerous interesting builds, and most skills will make actual gameplay alterations to how you play. 2 felt more like slight stat increases to basic abilities. So that at the end of 2 you are playing the same character as before, just more stats powerful. You don't gain any new game changing abilities. You don’t particularly change your behaviour in any way as you gain skills, you just increase your stats to compete with the enemies increasing their stats.
Second Point and Third Point Conclusion: The interaction of Enemies, Level design and Character Skill Trees
Now, to combine the second and third point together to provide a better description of the gameplay. In Pre-Sequel, you have a smaller range of enemies than in 2, but each enemy you face has greater AI, and more manoeuvrability. You will face these more interesting enemies in more interesting environments. These environments are more interesting because both you and the enemies will use the cover to fight, and the spaces to flank. The environments, being multi level, provide unique angle in relation to cover and flanking. Plus the skills your character learns over the course of the game will provide somewhat drastic changes to how you play.
Conclusion
So, in my opinion, Pre-Sequel is far superior to 2, and its only flaw is that it doesn't have as many environments to fight within and bosses to fight against with its superior skill sets and doesn’t have more story.

is probably a less accurate title than
. You play as an unfortunate pyjama-clad man trapped in his own room by the constant threat of elaborate
style death sequences and so, despite the titular warning, you have little choice to but to natter away online to 'Lucy', a malevolent and incredibly touchy spirit whose slightest agitation will result in you being stabbed to death or hung from the ceiling. Click the wrong thing, interrupt the sequence in any way and you die. Call the wrong number and you die. Go outside, you die. Go to sleep, you die. Tell Lucy that you don't have any hobbies, you die. does manage to conjure a very solid atmosphere with its art style, audio and creepy randomised glitches that drop themselves into the online chat but it's far too drainingly rigid as a puzzle game. successfully creates a creepy atmosphere and although most of the choices given seem either arbitrary or useless, there is a purpose, and there is a hidden pattern.This is a pixelated horror point-click puzzle adventure game with an excellent soundtrack, interesting lore, a permadeath mechanic and the best in-game arcade game since Galaga (ha!). This game pursues an interesting philosophy where the method by which the player explores or uncovers certain information that propels the game forwards is death. You click, you die, you learn something new about the puzzle (be it the about the stranger, the room or the story in general) and you start over until you know exactly what to do. That, or, you're an incredibly experienced gamer who mainly focuses on puzzle games and deduces exactly what to do from one or two attempts.
Most of the game is spent chatting with a strange woman online. Using simple point-and-click mechanics, you try to uncover the secrets behind this mysterious stranger. If you play your cards right, you'll get to have odd and surreal conversations with 'the stranger' that reveal interesting, yet puzzling bits of information that progress the story forward and clue you into what this is all about. If you don't, then you die, and have to start all over again. Your options are limited, yet you never feel trapped. You can walk back-and-forth in your room, interact with a few select objects, chat with the stranger or play minigames on your computer. However, the game is presented in a way by which every object has its place, and if you solve the puzzle, you will know exactly what to do and each objects purpose. The soundtrack is great. Especially the unknown piano song and the soundtrack to Mechs v. Fruits.
All in all, the game needs a few small patches but it is fun. Maybe extend the story with DLCs.

If you enjoy turn-based combat, dungeon crawls, and comic books you should buy this game.

If you’re a huge comic book fan, love Anime, and remember Joe Madureira Battle Chasers, yes 20 plus years ago, a book never quite completed. Then Battle Chasers may rekindle your love affair for that title. Battle Chasers: Nightwar tackles the tedium of traditional JRPG turn-based combat by turning the battles into epic tactical gameplay. As a parent, my reviews are always my experience only on a game for other parents and young gamers to review. Many new people come to Steam and may not know what to do with reviews, so here goes. There are some wonderful Pros and some annoying Cons.
PROS
• A: It is refined and a beautiful game with a great Anime feel to it. The Graphics are first rate in execution and gameplay.
• B: It does give you a comic icon tutorial as you make your way around to what is what, but mistakes will count.
• C: It has smooth controls for mouse or controller and the gameplay is smooth and clear cut. Save and Exit feature.
• D:  It will have a WOW this is cool first-time effect on all players as our in constant battles. You will at first get into every punch, every Bam! Pow! and Spell effect as debuff and buff stack, classic Tank, Shooter and Fighter type mechanism and clear animated visuals that will keep you invested.
• E: The parties can be altered too, so you can have your own builds based on their abilities to explore• and you have altering equipment crafting and RPG elements that you keep adjusting as you go.
CONS
• This has some spike balancing issues that I do think they will alter down the road with patches and I am sure future episode expansions.
• Grinding-Though the dungeon support replaying and you find ways to grind away. After a while those WOW effects can get tedious and hurt the game experience after a while. This I do think will change in time.
• Lack of Bestiality diversity-after a while you will get sick of the same enemies over and over. Beautifully done of not. The Codex of beast glossary is great, but if you’re going to grind you want 100’s of different enemies. Bats, Wolves, and Goo can get tedious again after a while. Something I do think they will expand on with expansions, but a small con for me.
Nuetral-Old Final Fanstasy Manga gameplay: Though I am sure the three party system is nothing new and sadly nothing they expanded from. True turn based tactical gamers like massive parties of 6-9 and much more expanded battles with plenty of tactical choices and outcomes. Unfortunatly your altering from 6 members to three small parties what developers miss is if you going to make extra members. Having them non active beats the purpose of a tactical turn base model.

OVERALL
UPDATE: I am giving Battle Chasers a positive review simply because I don't think they are near to being done. The effort and passion is clearly in display. The overworld map, encounter map, and dungeon maps are all done well and everything from an execution stand point is well done. Kids will love this game. Daughter adores the story telling and presentation. I do think they will adjust as they go and future episodes will build on the template created here. You may see more updates and events to improve the base game enough. Always See the VIDEO above discussions to preview the game prior to buying at a discount is wise. I would also advice getting this during sale events. If you love Disgaea for it's story telling presentation, Final Fantasy for it's 3 party encounters, Phantasy Star or classic Japanese 3 party rpg then Battle Chasers is right up your ally. A wonderful comic book rpg come to life. A nice start template to build on. My GRADE 3.9 stars out of 5.

I haven't played any Paradox grand strategy games at any depth, but I really enjoyed it. I feel like it needs more narrative content though which might be a bit more complicated than the historical grand strategy games (especially since this game takes place over centuries). End game events feel underwhelming though I read that they just gave Unbidden 4 times strength, so maybe I'm wrong at this point.

It's an extremely slow starter and days of patient empire building can be instantly wrecked through the slightest mistake in fight or flight. It doesn't help new players that achievements can only be made in ironman mode which could be seen as counter-intuitive as far as broaching the steep learning curve goes. But if you start with a "tiny" galaxy you will get the hang of all aspects more quickly than if you chose a larger map and this is definately where new players should start. It has levels of flavour and depth in deplomacy that other space 4X games, at best, nod towards and this is what makes it less of a "churn out units with little personality" game than all the others. Its slow-burning nature does not lend itself well to multiplayer situations as campaigns generally last a very long time. Trying to play with anyone but close and committed friends would be as pointless as creating a league made up of random player matchups in something like Football Manager.
Whilst it is certainly not for everyone those looking for an extended single player experience who persevere through the harsh learning curve will find that they are playing the most in-depth space 4X there is.

OK let me break it down for you.
When a game that you are genuinely interested in is released at a standard price point, for example £30 both on the web or via steam, I don't see anyone whine or anything, if you want it you buy it, if you don't want it you don't buy it, simples.
Take note of the above scenario, no whining, no complaining, no problems.
Buuuuuuuuuuut.......on the other hand, the scenario below is quite different.
When a game comes along that many people like the look of, they wanna play it, they are not sure if they would buy it in future or not, but regardless they still have some interest in it. Now in this case we have a game that is in late alpha/early beta stages of development, bugs, glitches and lack of content. During this period of time the game is open to those who wish to BUY INTO the beta testing phase for a higher fee which is matching that of the initial KS backers.
On top of this the deal is sweetened by the addition of extra content after the final release.
Now it must be made clear that the second option/scenario is INTENDED for one of 2 possible groups of individuals:
1) Die hard warmachine fans who simply cannot possibly stand the time of waiting and cost is no object to them in the face of not being able to play their treasured game franchise.
or
2) Those who do have some interest in the game, possibly not as much as a die hard fan, but nonetheless they are interested, however they have a very strong interest in shapeing the games continued development, learn more about the game, help find bugs and generally be part of the ongiong development process and are happy to pay the increased initial price of entry.
Now when we look at those complaining about the price point of this game, they clearly are either trolls, or people who should be waiting for the game to be released at the standard £30 price point and at that point either choose to purchase or back out and play something else.
However they are not.
It is clear to to us all then, that those who are whining (trolls/patient release purchasers) are simply making all of these whine posts because they are butthurt, they want the game NOW, but are not interested enough to pay the premium price, and hence they whine because they have to live with the fact they have to wait.
What can we take away from all of this?

This is a review of the early access version, which is a beta. I will update it depending on my time played and upon release.
Now then, the game:
Currently you have access to one single player mission and a limited multiplayer. Judging from that the game seems very promising, but still lacks a lot of polishing. The current interface is atrocious for example. Apart from that, we have a solid combat system, that's easy to understand. If you are familiar with the tabletop game that is, since there is as of yet no tutorial only a bunch of vids. But the tabletop rules seem to be translated faitfully into the game. Combos can be applied in the same way. Warjacks feel nice and stompy. Infantry give great utility.
The graphics are nice and very faithful to the originals. The sound effects are great and the animation looks nice, too.
So if you are a fan of Warmachine and don't mind paying for an early access, or just have to start playing right now, I recommend you get this game.
If you look for a tactical game, like steampunk and magitek and want to see the game grow, I recommend you get this game.
If you are looking for a fully fleshed out tactical game that will get you your money's worth immediately, I remmcomend you surf over to

I've been somewhat fanatical about basketball games since my earliest years. I've been through them all, Basket master on Spectrum, the legendary Lakers vs Celtics, the whole Nba live series (until it went sour) and ofcourse 2k's Nba 2k. I still can't wait to get my hands on each version, even at 35 years old i long for the release day like a child. I just love playing basketball. Real as well as virtual.
So how did 2k manage to ruin all this for me? You almost have to really try to ruin that kind of a relationship, but disregard for your player base will certainly drive away even the most religious fans. Before i start furiously ranting i still need to acknowledge the positives of the game. First and foremost, you need to realize that at its core the mechanics of the game are exceptionally good. The way the game flows, the way the players move, shoot or interact with the ball, collisions, shooting, dunking, you name it. I imagine recreating movement is one of the hardest things in game developement and 2k does its job brilliantly. You can easily distinguish players for their individual traits, like John Wall's handles, Durant's shot, MJ's up and unders. Whatever it is you're looking for, individuals are recreated to near perfection. Each team's strategy and playbook is very well done aswell and there's an integrated adapted a.i. engine that will adapt to how you play the game and it will counter and challenge your approach.Also the atmosphere in the arenas, sounds, commentary, almost everything about presentation is deliberate and exceptional. There are certain elements like the pregame show that are somewhat wooden, especially the halftime interviews, but a serious amount of dedication went into presentation of individual arenas, players, teams, the action, you name it. Granted some commentary about specific players gets annoyingly repetitive but that's mostly about the players on a team you are a part of (in my career), or you're playing mostly with. There's also a vast array of options as to what to do in this game.you literally do not have the time to explore all the game modes in depth, because the content is just massive. You can play exhibition games with current teams and rosters, you can play a story mode in my career and create your player there and play through his evolution with a story that goes along with it, you can create a fantasy team in My team, or you can play a manager type of mode if you're more into that sort of stuff. I don't have the time to go into in depth details of individual modes and i would also do some injustice since i don't play them. For the majority of people the game's most fun mode is to create a player, develop them and then play multiplayer games of streetball 3v3 in My park or 5v5 pick up games in pro-am. You can also pick a team and play in leagues with that team if you preffer that. Overall, if i would have to judge the game solely on its mechanics and presentation and the amount of content i would give it a strong 9.
As for the graphics i have to say that the game engine is getting outdated and could be better, but they did squeeze out a lot out of it, and it does still look solid.
So what's wrong?
Well first of all, it's the bugs. It's amazing to me how the game is still flawed with similar bugs that have plagued it for years like crashes, multiplayer games not starting, etc. each year the game is very flawed at release date and does get patched out eventually but it's just not tolerable in terms of approach. Then there's the animations. Each year they claim how you will no longer get stuck in animations of players, but in fact you still do and some are just crippling and annoying as *insert word*. And each year there are cetain cheese moves that people exploit and it literally makes you wanna strangle someone because it's something that will just not happen in real life basketball very often. The most annoying one this year are the charging fouls for example. They can drive you crazy. Then there's stuff that's just goofy, like other turnovers. Sometimes you pass to someone in the open lane who's 5 metres away and the pass will go out of bounds. God forbid you should attempt passes over half the court. Even with able playmakers. While i regularly make them in real life, half of them will be turnovers here. It's just unrealistic. And perhaps the worst if it all is the amount of steals the cpu makes. Makes you wanna cringe and explode from hate. It's just ridiculously hard to pass without the cpu intercepting the ball. Especially in proam games which regularly has some a.i. players since a lot of players disconnect or have some connection problems/crashes, etc. the cpu players are also ridiculously useless as teammates most of the times. Not so much in situations where you play against ai, but when you're stuck with cpu teammates against a made player squad, you're dead. They miss easy shots, are horrible on defense... basically the a.i. is just plain bad in this game. Granted, this kind of ai is MUCH more sophisticated to program than cpu opponents in some first person shooter, but still!  Also i have to touch on the story aspect of my career. Granted it's nowhere near as horrible as last years's Spike Lee debacle, but it's still downright ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I hate it. Period.
And now the main reason. The reason why i no longer yearn for the next year version and why i will no longer buy games from this developer/publisher.
CHEATERS! Cheaters everywhere. For the past few years now the community has been losing its mind. There's so many kids who use something called a Cheat engine to raise their individual player's attributes and abilities to godlike levels where they become unguardable, it's ridiculous. They effectively ruin your experience and all the fun, yet 2k sports either don't mind or are just completely arrogant to these facts. We literally flooded them with pleads,requests,petitions, flamed them, and then some. They just DON'T CARE. It's getting worse too. I can't stand for it, i will not support such bad practice and i've never felt so unappreciated as a customer in my life. Not only that, they're also insanely greedy with micro transactions. In order to really be able to compete against other players you have to really develop your player's stats and attributes. You either grind to earn ingame value known as VC or you pay real money to buy them. But it's gonna take you considerably longer if you decide to earn enough through grind. Ofcourse some will just hack this too. To be fair, they will ban people for that kind of hacking though, because god forbid 2k shouldn't earn money from you. Until 2k changes its attitude towards the pc community and implements some kind of anti hacking measure i cannot recommend this game. I highly advise you to not support this game. Then again, you have no alternative since it's the only real basketball game and this is exactly why they behave as they do. But sooner or later they will get competition. And i am very sure most of the community can't wait till that day comes because they will be willing to pay double just to shove it in 2k's face, as long as the other product is on par with it.  I really wish i could recommend this otherwise great product but they simply do not deserve it. Stay away!

Hello everybody, End World Gaming here to share an excerpt from my review for Battle Chasers: Nightwar by Airship Syndicate and THQNordic.
Battle Chasers Nightwar is a turn based RPG that’s not only based on a popular comic book series that originated in the 90’s but also heavily inspired by popular JRPG’s from the time period as well.
The story follows 5 unique characters named Gully, Knolan, Calibretto, Garrison and Red Monika. The story starts with our heroes arriving on a mysterious island and are immediately attacked by a group of bandits. Their airship is ultimately destroyed and they become entangled in the island’s troubles after they learn of an evil woman gathering the island’s artifacts for an unknown purpose. So, the heroes set out on a journey across the island to stop her.
The game features a turn based combat system, very similar in style to classic Final Fantasy games. You can take up to 3 party members into battle and each one has unique abilities which have various effects in a battle.
Attacks are split into two areas. The first are instant skills and the second is charge skills which take a turn or more to pull off. Skills also have buffs and debuffs that apply to enemies and party members. Enemies are also capable of applying these debuffs to your characters and they can easily alter a battle’s outcome.
There’s also special abilities that require the use of the boost bar. The boost bar fills up as you attack and use abilities. When it’s charged you can unleash a powerful ability. Some abilities purify and heal while others buff your party’s defenses. It’s a good idea to use them frequently, especially against stronger enemies.
The game also features an in-depth crafting system where you’re able to craft weapons, potions and enchant your items. You can purchase skill books from vendors to allow you to craft new and better equipment as well.
There’s also a beastiary in the game which actually has an effect on gameplay. There are beast perks which unlock as you reach milestones. For example, if you kill 50 bats you get a 1% increase in haste for all party members. So killing numerous enemies actually has a benefit to you during battles.
When your character’s level up they’ll sometimes get new skills as well as new perks (And perk points) to equip. Perks have a wide range of different effects such as increasing attack power or increasing haste or even defense.
One thing that I will admit about this game is that it’s better played in short sessions. I’ve played it for mostly long sessions in an attempt to complete the game but it gets quite boring after a while because there’s a lot of repetition in your actions throughout. You’ll be spending most of your time in battles no matter where you are in the game. Whether it be on the world map or inside of dungeons. There’s not much in the way of gameplay changes so it can’t keep my attention for over 2 hours.
Overall, Battle Chasers Nightwar has some excellent features and one of the best turn based battle systems that I’ve seen in a while. The only downside is that it does get pretty repetitive after 2 hours of play time so it’s best played in small chunks rather than long play sessions. If you’re in the market for a fun RPG with some great characters and a ton of battles then Battle Chasers Nightwar may be right up your alley.

This second chapter of the Silver Creek Falls series continue from the previous chapter where detective Sara Fitzgerald is assigned to a new partner from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Agent Valdez to investigate further into the unsolved mysteries of Silver Creek Falls. From the murder of Agent Valdez's former partner, Sara and Valdez investigate the disappearance of a hedge fund manager, attempt to locate an informant, search a suspicious bloodstained scene at a fisheries warehouse and follow a trail of clues back at Silver Creek Falls, a college campus, a pharmaceutical company's involvement and a secret research facility as a mystery adventure with thriller and comedic references.
Having played through most of the visual novels by Sapphire Dragon Productions, I would say the plot hook and story writing for mystery is better by having interesting plot hooks and development than the romance visual novels which seem rather short and rushed in comparison. I am recommending this chapter and the entire series because I know and hope Sapphire Dragon Productions do read through and take some of the player reviews and comments seriously and will consider my suggestion to focus more on mystery storylines and also consider adding comedic references in other titles in future. This chapter is recommended when at discount or in good bundle offer with chapter 3 as the game can be finished in less than 10 hours

One of my most anticipated releases of 2017; I decided to wait on it for a bit for a price drop but inevitably just went ahead and got it and BOY am I not dissappointed. Full disclosure, the game is really wierd; I ate a mackeral and 2B's circuits congealed and paralyzed her, ending the game with a credits sequence that played in fast motion and booted me out to the main menu. There's lot of funny things like that to be had here. Overall between the silk-smooth combat and the music (OMFG THAT SOUNDTRACK!!!) and all of the fun little tid bits here and there I can say with some confidence that this is my favorite game of the year so far! Even Horizon Zero Dawn didn't stick me quite as much as this one did. (I dig the whole 'robot post apocalypse' thing, clearly.)
For me, personally, it is one of the more perfect games I've played in recent years and with 14.1 hours as of time of writing I still have plenty of game left to go with new game+ storylines and that doesn't include playtime from starting from square one. I can tell this one will stick with me for some time. If you'd rather wait for a price drop I don't fault you one bit, but I for one am not dissappointed with where my $60 went so you'll so no complaints on my end either. (And it opens quite strong so you'll find out if you don't like it fast enough for a refund, at least.) In my own opinion this will be one of the few games in my library that I consider to be a masterpiece, and I don't say that lightly.
TL;DR: I highly recommend this game to anyone that likes anime and/or fast paced action combat.

I just didn't know that this would be what turned out to be one of the greatest games I have ever played.
Challenging the player even in the tutorial of this game, I started to see a grumpy Android Lady through a massive conflict with mental machines. And I was hopelessly immersed.
In short, here's what this game is:
It's a game that upsets all the run-of-the-mill gaming experiences you may have had so far.
It's a game that will have you reflect on the deeper meanings of life. (don't worry, you can still skip)

As far as I am aware, I have never reviewed a game before.
Dunno why I decided to review this one out of the many I have purchased, but I figured why not. I need to put my thoughts into words for some closure on this game.
Just in case you were wondering, I have no experience with the previous NieR game, I did not complete all the quests, and I didn't unlock all of the achievements, I simply followed the main story, and did any sidequests that were tied to it.
Nier: Automata is without a doubt, one of the best games I have played as of late. The story was compelling from the start, and retained its great storytelling all of the way throughout. The gameplay was a breath of fresh air after having completed the most recent Mass Effect game. The game has varying play styles that it often transitions between. It has tight and responsive controls (with a controller), and its overall fun factor held strong throughout. Whenever something new was introduced, having previously thought I had seen all of the game's mechanics, put a smile on my face. I have never smiled so much while playing a game.
That's not to say it doesn't have issues, though. The game only crashed once for me, but it was still quite a setback as I had not saved in some time. Speaking of saving, the game's saving feature is forgettable (literally). It lacks an autosave function, only quick saving when out of combat. Factoring in the game's tendency to crash like a Russian driver with a windshield camera, it is more than likely the player will forget to save during the game's key moments, wind up killing themselves, breaking their immersion when they realize they have to do the last 30 minutes over again.
A few minor issues of mine would have to be the invisible walls placed around a seemingly open area during boss fights. I ran into these barriers countless amounts of times, resulting in me getting my android♥♥♥♥♥legitimately crushed. The enemies can also seem a bit like damage-sponges at times, whether that is to pad out the play time or a design oversight is beyond me, but it can become draining to wack a small robot with a fully upgraded sword around 30 times.
Overall, the game's story and frequently engaging gameplay mechanics kept my eyes glued to the screen so long I've now got dry eye syndrome. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes games of a similar genre, or anyone who is burnt out on playing the same game with a different skin every year.

People - including me - often say that Yoko Taro doesn't like to make the same game twice. And this definitely holds true for Automata as well.
There are as many differences to Nier as there are common elements and there is no inherent guarantee that you'll like Automata's characters, themes or even the tone of the game just because you liked Nier's.
As a fan of Nier i'd have to say i'm disappointed that Automata did not hit the emotional drums for me quite as much as the original did (Not to say that Automata isn't emotional tho), but as a fan of Yoko Taro in general i can safely say that despite that, the story and themes are very intruiging nonetheless, including what has been a positive surprise for me, but i don't wanna spoil.
What i definitely do can say however is that Automata manages to make something unqiue and memorable out of what's in its core a fairly typical sci-fi trope.
There's quite a bit of fan service here and there - i'm not talking about the butt kind - but thankfully it doesn't feel forced and weaves for the most part perfectly into the game's story and lore.
Platinum took Nier's crazy genre mashup concept and did the best it could at polishing and expanding on a lot of it, especially the shmup/Bullethell aspect, but personally i kinda missed the non-action parts of Nier, while things like fishing are still there, the gameplay definitely got a bigger focus on fighting and action this time around.
But that's depending on what you prefer not a bad thing.
Platinum didn't just made more polished Nier gameplay, they expanded it with their own expertise in terms of set pieces, "event action", enemy variety and all other things you expect from Platinum.
Having what's in its core platinum action in a game that is not a Platinum typical 8 hours linear adventure also feels fairly refreshing and i very much hope they can expand on that in future games of theirs, wether it's a Yoko Taro game or something else.
I do feel that Yoko Taro did hold back a bit in terms of punishing/trolling gameplay elements compaired to past games, but within the context of the game as a whole i'd think that this was very much a decision coming from his side and not from P* or SE.
So overall i gotta say, Automata's gameplay is a bit less varied than Nier's, but what is there is a lot more polished and expanded upon.
The character designs are amazing and unique, tho i definitely can see why some people would have an issue with, you know, certain aspects of it.
The soundtrack doesn't quite come close to the first Nier's but is a big step up again from Drakengard 3's. You can definitely tell that Okabe tried to bring his A game again.
The only reason i'd even think of saying anything negative about Automata's OST is really just that it got Nier's soundtrack as it's predecessor. If it weren't for Nier, I'd call Automata's a unique and great masterpiece without a doubt.
All in all, i'd put it this way:
As a NieR Fan I'm happy but a tad disappoined.
As a Platinum Fan i thought it was great.
As a Yoko Taro fan i loved the game and do not regret having a BBE on preorder.
My advice is, do not approach Automata as a sequel to Nier, approach it open minded as a new Yoko Taro/Platinum IP "Automata", because just like Drakengard 1 and 3 are rather different games, so are Nier and Automata, despite many common elements.

About me: Long time MMO Player 13 solid years with Ultima Online, 10 years off and on with WoW, founder pack holder for other MMO's such as Revelation Online, Warhammer Online (rip) and tons more besides.
I absolutely despise the pay to win model, and in general, the free to play model, as it's about inconveniencing people to nickle and dime them to death, or about creating brick content walls that require 100$ or more to cross the hurdle and see the next portion of the game until the next brick wall is presented.
Wildstar has been reviewed very negatively here on steam, but if you actually dig into the play time and stats of the majority of the people writing the reviews, you'll find out that almost no one writing a negative review has actually made it to end game. Some of those negative reviews below have 6 hours of play time. A few have 1 or less. The steam achievement statistics bear that out, in fact with less than 1% of the entire steam playerbase having completed Genetic Archives, which is only the FIRST raid in the game. About half of the game content is tucked away either behind or around that one achievement alone. Frankly, almost no one writing these reviews has the experience necessary to give a comprehensive opinion on the matter. Please pay careful attention to your sourcing when looking for information. You all saw the bandwagon hop on the battlefield 1 vs cod infinite release videos. Yet BF1 is plagued with so many aimbots that I can't even name a friend that actually plays it, despite the "millions" of positive reviews for the trailer and the millions of "negative" reviews for CoD Infinite.
Pros of Wildstar:
It's not pay to win. I can't stress this enough, because it's been so, so long since I've seen a true non pay to win f2p game. You're not penalized in bag space, nor travel conveniences, beyond having to wait to use the "free" teleport almost anywhere system. There are store mounts and costumes, shortcuts (you can buy a max lvl character like other MMO's) and conveniences, but no true advantage that can't be earned for completely free in the game.
The combat. The glorious, glorious combat system. My only caution here is that if you play wildstar for a while, you're going to have a hard time going back to WoW or other "run to mob, stand and deliver rotation" style tab targetting games. Even random mobs of a comperable level can present a challenge to the solo player as telegraph dodging, successful camera rotation and awareness of your environment matter more than in any other MMO I've ever played. Any wildstar player can vouch for having rolled off the lip of a chasim dodging a telegraph from losing their awareness of their surroundings.
The game really begins at "end game". Many people complaining about low population never made it much past level 20 it appears. The lower end game content is primarily geared towards single player content, and exposure to the world story, which is complex and vast. The reason dungeon queues seem sparse at lower levels is because unlike WoW in which dungeons simply represent a short cut to quicker levelling, Wildstar dungeons are challenging and complex, sometimes taking hours to complete without a "carry". The single player content is solid enough that many feel the need to not even queue up at lower levels because after only a few dungeons, you'll completely outlevel a zone that you were enjoying the questing in and be forced to decide to abandon everything in the area, or to gain very little for seeing it through to completion.
The community. Although smaller than any other MMO I've ever played, it really speaks for itself, once you get beyond the "geam iz ded!" memes that circulate regularly though Nexus chat (think tradechat from WoW). To new players that are wondering why their dungeon queue time is an hour long, seeing the Wildstar inside joke of "gem iz ded!" spammed constantly across Nexus chat only confirms the bias the game is dead. I wish more than anything that meme would die. It's turned off so many players that don't want to invest their time or money into a "dead" game. Even I was reticent to plunk down any money at first as that was one of the first things I saw when making a new character.
The single player content. The questing here is more involved than any other MMO I've ever seen, and has none of that god forsaken autopathing you see in games like Allods Online, or Revelation Online. There are things to discover everywhere, and "challenges" that appear from stuff like just investigating a patch of dirt, killing a mob, or simply entering a location. You never really know what's around the corner for you in a zone and it keeps the content fresh, and occasionally frustrating while you see the timer ticking down for an objective you don't quite understand initially.
The multiplayer content. There are single to three player expeditions that are like mini dungeons that tell zone stories, 3 to 5 player adventures that expand upon zone content, conventional 5 man dungeons that can be 30 min affairs with a power team, or hours long skill tests if everyone is of comperable level and experience, end game 20+ man raids, battlegrounds (which generally only pop during core hours to be fair), arenas and more. There are 5 man open world quests (when a quest says 3-5 players in wildstar, fyi, it damned well means 3 to 5 players btw), world bosses that take an entire raid to take down and more besides.
Player housing. I can't speak much to this element of the game other than to say that I've seen some of the stuff people have created, and have been absolutely blown away with people's creativity and genius. This is the most robust housing system I've ever seen and you can literally create your own mini zone. I am told that housing is the true end game, but so far I've been too busy getting attuned for raiding, completing GA (just last night!) and learning about runeing my gear to have spent much time with it. When they say "housing" you might be thinking a chintzy pre-sized home from other MMO's versions of housing, and indeed, those exist, but they're just a toe dip into an ocean of possibilities the game provides.
Graphics are exactly what you would expect from the same team that was behind vanilla WoW. It's space WoW in this department. Shoulderpads aren't king, per-sey, but they damned sure help, and you can certainly spot the players with a WoW affinity as we are generally sporting the largest most gaudy set of shoulderpads we can find. If you have a rig that's capable of playing the game on its highest settings, you will be quite amazed frankly. The difference between even medium and "high" graphics is remarkable. When a friend of mine started playing on a laptop a few weeks ago, I looked over his shoulder one evening and asked him what game he was playing. At a glance, I didn't even recognize it. So if someone is complaining about graphics in a review, let me assure you, they're running something seriously subpar and should probably spend less time writing reviews and more time getting a job, as they simply haven't seen what it really looks like.
Character customization is as vast, if not more so than WoW. There is not only a vast array of actual gear that you can put into your holo-wardrobe, but there is a bewildering array of dyes to collect, and all your gear even has dye "channels" that you can turn off and on to customize your look in a way I've never seen in another MMO. In fact, WoW actually seems to have borrowed the holo-wardrobe idea from Wildstar with the release of Legion.
Cons of Wildstar
Player base. New players log in, don't see many folks around, see nexus chat spam saying "geam iz ded!" and uninstall.
It's probably not monetarily incintivized enough. Never thought I would say that, but it literally takes no money at all to enjoy to full end game. Purely cosmetic upgrades for money or conveniences.
"Gaem iz ded!" meme is making things worse.

A small caveat remains, however: The PC port, unfortunately, does not live up to expectations and players have yet to see a major patch for their issues. Do note, that kind souls in the community provide fixes for a plethora of these problems.

Awesome atmospheric soundtrack, tons of funny and interesting dialogue and a story that keeps you interested the whole way. Great amount of content for the price if you complete the entire game.

Do not be dissuaded by the rating steadily dropping; this is almost entirely due to poor performance and other port issues people are experiencing.  Look at other reviews for similar rigs and use your best judgment.

That's not the only issue. There is death-pits everywhere, and because the simple 6 colour palette of the maps, you can't tell the difference between cliff and saftey. Yet another issue is that the maps can become maze like. This game is advertised to be an action-packed-extreme-stupidness-blow-things-up-er, but you spend a good amout of the game just looking for people. When you do actually find people to shoot, the weapons are so hard to shoot. They fire slow, inaccurate, and when you hit someone a rock would be more effective. The weapons, the MAIN point of the ad campain, just don't work.
TL;DR Good to pick up and play for an hour or so. If you are looking for a similar game but much more polished I would reccomend Blacklight: Retribution.

This game is for sure a recommended game for anyone that plays either the TT games from Privateer Press or anyone that enjoys tactical games like X-Com.  While the game has bugs (this is beta after all) WhiteMoon Dream has always been very transparent about what is going on with the game.  Player issues are addressed, bugs are taken care of, and input is welcomed.  The game looks great and even with the current issue of low frames, its not choppy enough to be a deal breaker.  AI for the missions seem a little to hard scripted (very limited awareness) but we have only been give access to one mission and its the second mission of the campaign and I feel they are going easy on us.  The heart of this game is around the Multi-player mode.  Playing against real players with a diverse set of units and skills lends itself to making each MP game unique.  Replay will be very high even before all the DLC comes out in the months to years following(for those don't know the TT Warmachine has MANY MANY times the units currently planed for release).
A review for the game would not be complete without a comment or two about the current price of the game.  At $65 many people complain that its too much.  WMD has addressed its reasoning for the price and will not be changing it till after the game it out of Early Access.  The only important question left then about the price is this, is there VALUE of the game.  The short answer is Yes! How do i justify it beyond my above comments? Three little words..."Collectors Edition Release".  Many of us, myself included, have and do pay far more then $65 to pre-order collectors editions that don't have half the DLC that is being offered here.  Stop trying to look at this as a pay to play Beta and start looking at it like a Collectors Edition that happens to offer Beta access.  So if you are not a Collectors Edition buy just kick back and wait till normal release or a steam sale in any case it will be money well spent.

The $65 price tag is for the base game, plus a "season pass" of sorts for Mercenary units that are planned for later release, as well as the Apotheosis 'casters and 'jacks.  If you don't want to pay that much, wait for the full release, and don't get the mercs or Apotheosis units.
All that being said, the game does show a lot of promise in it's current stage. I had a dream, that one day I would make a kick♥♥♥♥♥aRPG in the spirit of Diablo but with pixel graphics.
Then I found Chronicon, and cried many different tears. Tears of joy that I had found exactly what I was looking for, tears of frustration that I didn't get to make the game, and tears of ...more... joy... joyful tears lots of joy and tears... and...
Okay enough onto the review.
This game is spectacular!
In scope, character builds, and OMG moments, both in frustration because of the difficulty and pure awe of the carnage and destruction.
This is not just your average Pixel aRPG - the sound is great, the pixel art is amazing, the boss fights are fun, and it has so many great things going for it's gameplay I don't know where to begin.
The control scheme works very well, weather you want to use a controller or you want to use keyboard and mouse...
hold on... chicken patties are done...
Thank's for waiting.
The loot drops are fun, and seem right on par with a diablo 3 as far as quality items dropping requent enough to enjoy the tons of loot that does drop.
There are additional portals that can spawn sometimes that take you to challenge areas such as an arena with waves of monsters, or an area with magical monsters that all have a global mod added onto them.
The progression is non-nonsense, you will be killing monsters 95% of the time, and the rest of the time you are back in town selling loot.
The 'town' is an efficiently layed out space that has the NPCs close by and the teleportation pad close by as well.
Almost evey level in a given 'Act' has a waypoint. So there is really not a lot of needless running around.
I have not played with friends, but I imagine it would be just as fun as any other aRPG is with friends.
All highlight points aside, if you are looking for a pixel art aRPG similar to Diablo, then just buy this right now, it is completely worth the full price, and if you see it on sale there should be no question at all.
It is so satisfying on so many levels it is hard to put into words.

If you like loot, and lots of it, you'll have more than you need. If you find yourself attracted to Mobs, you'll be in good company. As far as I am aware, I have never reviewed a game before.
Dunno why I decided to review this one out of the many I have purchased, but I figured why not. I need to put my thoughts into words for some closure on this game.
Just in case you were wondering, I have no experience with the previous NieR game, I did not complete all the quests, and I didn't unlock all of the achievements, I simply followed the main story, and did any sidequests that were tied to it.
Nier: Automata is without a doubt, one of the best games I have played as of late. The story was compelling from the start, and retained its great storytelling all of the way throughout. The gameplay was a breath of fresh air after having completed the most recent Mass Effect game. The game has varying play styles that it often transitions between. It has tight and responsive controls (with a controller), and its overall fun factor held strong throughout. Whenever something new was introduced, having previously thought I had seen all of the game's mechanics, put a smile on my face. I have never smiled so much while playing a game.
That's not to say it doesn't have issues, though. The game only crashed once for me, but it was still quite a setback as I had not saved in some time. Speaking of saving, the game's saving feature is forgettable (literally). It lacks an autosave function, only quick saving when out of combat. Factoring in the game's tendency to crash like a Russian driver with a windshield camera, it is more than likely the player will forget to save during the game's key moments, wind up killing themselves, breaking their immersion when they realize they have to do the last 30 minutes over again.
A few minor issues of mine would have to be the invisible walls placed around a seemingly open area during boss fights. I ran into these barriers countless amounts of times, resulting in me getting my android♥♥♥♥♥legitimately crushed. The enemies can also seem a bit like damage-sponges at times, whether that is to pad out the play time or a design oversight is beyond me, but it can become draining to wack a small robot with a fully upgraded sword around 30 times.
Overall, the game's story and frequently engaging gameplay mechanics kept my eyes glued to the screen so long I've now got dry eye syndrome. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes games of a similar genre, or anyone who is burnt out on playing the same game with a different skin every year.
