People - including me - often say that Yoko Taro doesn't like to make the same game twice. And this definitely holds true for Automata as well.
There are as many differences to Nier as there are common elements and there is no inherent guarantee that you'll like Automata's characters, themes or even the tone of the game just because you liked Nier's.
As a fan of Nier i'd have to say i'm disappointed that Automata did not hit the emotional drums for me quite as much as the original did (Not to say that Automata isn't emotional tho), but as a fan of Yoko Taro in general i can safely say that despite that, the story and themes are very intruiging nonetheless, including what has been a positive surprise for me, but i don't wanna spoil.
What i definitely do can say however is that Automata manages to make something unqiue and memorable out of what's in its core a fairly typical sci-fi trope.
There's quite a bit of fan service here and there - i'm not talking about the butt kind - but thankfully it doesn't feel forced and weaves for the most part perfectly into the game's story and lore.
Platinum took Nier's crazy genre mashup concept and did the best it could at polishing and expanding on a lot of it, especially the shmup/Bullethell aspect, but personally i kinda missed the non-action parts of Nier, while things like fishing are still there, the gameplay definitely got a bigger focus on fighting and action this time around.
But that's depending on what you prefer not a bad thing.
Platinum didn't just made more polished Nier gameplay, they expanded it with their own expertise in terms of set pieces, "event action", enemy variety and all other things you expect from Platinum.
Having what's in its core platinum action in a game that is not a Platinum typical 8 hours linear adventure also feels fairly refreshing and i very much hope they can expand on that in future games of theirs, wether it's a Yoko Taro game or something else.
I do feel that Yoko Taro did hold back a bit in terms of punishing/trolling gameplay elements compaired to past games, but within the context of the game as a whole i'd think that this was very much a decision coming from his side and not from P* or SE.
So overall i gotta say, Automata's gameplay is a bit less varied than Nier's, but what is there is a lot more polished and expanded upon.
The character designs are amazing and unique, tho i definitely can see why some people would have an issue with, you know, certain aspects of it.
The soundtrack doesn't quite come close to the first Nier's but is a big step up again from Drakengard 3's. You can definitely tell that Okabe tried to bring his A game again.
The only reason i'd even think of saying anything negative about Automata's OST is really just that it got Nier's soundtrack as it's predecessor. If it weren't for Nier, I'd call Automata's a unique and great masterpiece without a doubt.
All in all, i'd put it this way:
As a NieR Fan I'm happy but a tad disappoined.
As a Platinum Fan i thought it was great.
As a Yoko Taro fan i loved the game and do not regret having a BBE on preorder.
My advice is, do not approach Automata as a sequel to Nier, approach it open minded as a new Yoko Taro/Platinum IP "Automata", because just like Drakengard 1 and 3 are rather different games, so are Nier and Automata, despite many common elements.

Beta/Early Access Review:
If you are a fan of Warmachine table top game, or looking to get into a new tactical game with elements like X-Com, then this is a great game now, and going to get better.
Current build is a feature light, but everywhere you look are the signs and evidence that it will be feature strong. The game play even as it stand in this early build is, in my opinion, a perfect mix of the spirit of the table top rules combined with the realities of video games. I am very much looking forward to watching this game get better and better.
Side notes:
The $65 is a reasonable price point. That is the price point the kick starter had that provided beta/early access. It's also the price point for the digital deluxe edition of the game which provides extra content upon release. I'm happy to pay it and play it, both help the developers make this a better game. If you dont want to pay $65 to play an unfinished game, thats fine, dont pay it.

Steel Ocean is a naval warfare MMOG where you can control naval vessels that were built or were on paper before, during and shortly after WWII.
Pros:
-Control of the secondary battery on battleships and AA on all ships that have it. No RNG here, just who can shoot better.
-No aim assist for torpedoes, and you can fire torpedoes individually or in a salvo, this makes the the torpedo an area denial/ distraction weapon for the ships that have it.
-Arm time for torpedoes eliminates DD/CL suicide runs.
-The longer you focus your aim, the tighter the spread, again, no RNG here, the patient ones can hit a lot more than the one who is shooting wildly.
-The presence of submarines in the game (unrealistic as they are), forces destroyers and light cruisers to play a bigger role than just a scout, protecting the heavy cruisers and battleships and forces players to work as a cohesive unit.
-Premium items are hardly, if at all noticeable.
-Aircraft carriers can customize their wing, which can help players who wants to tune their wing to defense (fighters for escort) or offense (dive and torpedo bombers).
-Aircraft carriers can also take control of their main battery (DP cannons) which can give them a fighting chance against destroyers and light cruisers.
-Night battle mode, which has players using star shells and spotlights to spot and engage hostile warships. A very fun mode.
-More nations, though some of them are incomplete and mostly premium ships, though it will inevitably grow as the game develops.
-Movement of the ships affects accuracy, which is kinda realistic. This is especially true in the older warships and the Japanese ships which historically used optical rangefinders  (cannot include gun-laying radar ingame for obvious reasons). Zig- zagging while firing your cannons ain't gonna do much here.
-Faster shells, in WoWs, the shells feel more like guided missiles.
-Decent grinding to unlock ships and equipment.
-Commander system where the commanders assigned to ships give the ship a boost in certain stats (speed, firepower, reload time, durability) When a commander is assigned to become a captain, he can use a skill which can drastically increase a certain stat for a limited amount of time.
-Rewards for logging in consecutively for a number of days such as commanders and ships.
Cons:
-One server (NA) which presents difficulties for other players to enjoy the game, though if this game grows they will have to open new servers due to the player traffic.
-No seperate tech trees for light and heavy cruisers, forcing players to change playstyles frequently to play the cruisers.
-Price for premium ships are ridiculous.
-Wonky physics, with battleships getting up to speed in seconds.
-Game is dying, lack of players.
-Crashes up the wazoo.
EDIT: Now they have introduced a German proxy, does wonders to non-NA players. Still experiencing a lot of crashes.

TL;DR: Mystery crime adventure is a decent sequel to
but lacks focus.
I'll keep this as spoiler-free as possible.
Chapter 2 starts where the free-to-play
(
) ends: mysteries of murder and disappearances abound at Silver Creek Falls. Sara Fitzgerald gets reassigned to the case, this time with a laid-back FBI Special Agent Valdez.
Story is still the main attraction of the game. A murder rises new worries but there are fortunately new leads to follow, and more ominous parties join the fray. While
had minor puzzle elements,
ups the difficulty with a couple of potentially tough puzzles. Fortunately for the more casual players they can be skipped in story-fitting way or in some cases simply bruteforced.
Actually, puzzles in
are what I originally expected (but was disappointed in)) in
: you actually have to think for yourself and use the evidence to deduce the answers. I congratulate on succeeding in bringing this aspect of detective-work to play a real role in the adventure.
Speaking of puzzles: I especially liked the encrypted text puzzle that, while basic if you know some cryptography, made one think and even use pen&paper (or notepad), math and evidence in unison to properly solve it. In-game character would give clues or even solve it for you if you just wanted to get on with the story. This puzzle was very well done except for the long walks that ensued.
Long walks are due to the maps being large and sometimes you have to walk back and forth for errands. Also, the investigators walk fairly slowly. There are still no addresses of important places on the map so this emphasizes the issue. There are also long corridors everywhere. These things are probably the worst aspects of the game. Sure, some of the walking and wandering is reasonable, like in searching the campus for a certain person or the back-alley for a certain dude. Fortunately there is a fast-walking mode (by pressing Shift while walking) that mitigates the issue.
Also, in a late part of the game there's a maze of sorts that you have to solve. Not only do you have to solve it once, you have to also walk it back through again, which breaks the story flow. I think skipping the maze backwards would have been better (and the characters could have had a nice 4th-wall breaking dialogue or similar after the skip as well). In this way it seems that because of this and other long walks the game becomes artificially longer than it could be. For the story to flow, it is important to cut unnecessary walking or at least spice it up with interesting  interactions in the way.
There is lots of dialogue between Sara and agent Valdez when studying the case and this brings out their personalities very nicely. They even have different facial expressions for showing emotions in the dialogue. All side characters (aside from clerks) feel fleshed out and lively and also show emotions when appropriate. There are a few more people than in
, which is good, though the streets are still strangely devoid of human life. Personally, I would have liked to see more of Sara's hotheaded side that resurfaces only maybe twice during the whole
.
I encountered several non-gamebreaking bugs and one repeatable crash during my playthrough. Developers are great: all these bugs and issues were fixed quickly as the devs are active in the Steam forum and the game is now in a much more consistent and stable state than before the updates.
One annoying bug or feature was the cat in one of the hotels early in the game. If you tried to pass it, it would walk in the way and mock you by meowing. I was stuck there for some 10 minutes before I realized that the cat can be passed by walking past it while it's moving the other way. This was ridiculous but I'm not sure if it's considered a bug (and being fixed) or some kind of a meta-puzzle. I still find myself cursing at its stupidity. On my second playthrough (to see the fixes) it wasn't nearly as annoying so either it's fixed or I just knew how to deal with it.
For me the game lasted 4.5 hours to 100%, though the game records 2.5 hours. Some of my time went into reporting bugs and some for idling while solving the encryption puzzles online.
There was expectedly a cliffhanger at the end in anticipation of
, which finally released in spring 2016. All in all, I liked
: it has more content and it's more demanding than
. Still, it might have been better as a more compact and focused package, with less slow and aimless walking - in that
succeeded better. Story is still very interesting and it's the main driving force here: it makes you want to see how it continues.
I think the price of 5 € is adequate if you enjoyed
but mind that it's only about 2-4 hours long. If that feels too short for you, you might want to wait for a sale.
EDIT: Oh, I found a fast walk key! It's Shift (either). I'm not sure if it was there to begin with. Edited the review accordingly.

having been released, I updated the review slightly.

First of all, if you're debating whether to buy this game, JUST DO IT! Medival 2: Total War is basically a board game where you and other factions can preform activities such as build stuctures or train troops during a turn. There also is top-down style battles where you can order your army around, but you get the choice if you want to do it, or just let the computer auto-resolve the battle for you. If you fancy, there is also multiplayer mode in which you can play those top down battles online with other players, though I must say that sometimes the server list can be dead.
A brief overview of the game:
- You load into the game and choose one of the starting nations such as England, France, Roman Empire, etc. (When you take all the cities of one faction, you can then play them when you start a new campaign. Another way is just to complete the objective and unlock all the factions). The only differences between the factions are the kind of troops you can or will be able to produce, and the amount of land you start with and it's location. If you want something easy to start with I suggest playing England because once you take over the Scotish people, you are mostly safe from other factions on the island. All the special units in this game such as assassins, princesses, priests, generals and faction leader, all have special traits which make them better or worse at thier jobs. During your playthrough the game, these special units will gain trait, good or bad, and you must use them for what they are good at. With generals and factions leaders, you want to make sure whether you want to make the general more dreadfull or chivialrous early on in order to craft a good commander, as each have its own perks.
- You manage your cities and take on your first battle which is really easy. Too do well at the start of the game, build structures in your citites that will boost your economy such as roads and ports. If it is too overwhelming for you, you can turn on auto manage for the cities, which allows the computer to control cities if you do not have a govenor in that city.
- Can make alliances and agreements with other factions such as trade rights or military acess on other peoples land, or just demand money if thier weak. One thing I must point out though is diplomacy is one of the games weak points. It is way easier to just attack a faction than it it is to threaten them to give you thier cities. This may not fit under diplomacy, but you can spy on people to find out the traits they have. If there is someone important in another faction that may cause you troubles like a high level diplomat, you can attempt to assassinate someone. Key word is attempt because in this game, it is very difficult to level up spy's and assassins in this game, but it can be done. It is ussually best to spy of assassinate low level characters befoe actually moving up to the people you really are after.
- Like I said before, you can control your own army on what is called the battle map. You will get a notification saying someone is going to attack you. Sometimes you can run away from these fights but most of the time they will follow you until they can attack you. You can send spies into cities to slowly cause unrest in the cities, and to see what kind of troops are in the walls ( Word of warning thought, that if you do not have a high enough level spy, he has a high chance of dying). You can upgrade your troops armour in cities and all the units gain experience when they fight in battles. Each type of troop has a specials abillity/ies which are very helpful in battle, but can be fought without learning them, but will make difficults more costly in number of lives lost. A basic idea that will help in battle is this -
Stay friends with the pope!

Detailed Review:
Really enthralling for the first... 10-14 levels but then it's just becomes a thing of "meh". Basically the developers artificially increased the game's length to fit the pricetag, or whatever. It reflects in the story and character developement AND progression. Which is the most relevant thing to an RPG game. On sale - I don't know. If you have to. If it's like 5$ - you won't regret it.

Verdict- If you can get past the grind there is a lot to love here. Get it if you don't mind some grinding.
Pros:
-Amazing sound design. I can't think of a game that sounds better than this one.
-Great art direction. Everything looks really good.
-Interesting cast. I really like all the characters and I'm sad I can't use them all.
Cons:
-Grinding. You will grind xp and repeat dungeons and the game will expect you to be happy about it.
-Archaic xp. Characters you don't use do not get xp so even more grinding if you want to be able to adjust your party.
-Combat gets repetetive. I have yet to feel the need to change my tactics 17 hours in.
The first and most important thing you need to know about this game is that it is a grind. You will be grinding for xp. You will need to repeat the same dunegeons multiple times on harder difficulties. There are some roguelike aspects to it as diferent events will occur but they do not feel varied or interesting enough to make the dengeons feel worth clearing 3 times. Also enemies do not scale to you. You can be overlevelled and walk through a duneon with your eyes closed or you can be underlevelled and have no choice but to go back and grind more levels/better gear. If you can't deal with that don't buy this game. Combat is standard turn based combat with some minor twists like overcharge that lets you overcap your mana to cast abilities and lots of reliance on status effects to deal maximum damage. I have yet to feel the need to change up my tactics much after 17 hours so if you want deep, interesting battle mecahanics look elsewhere. Another frustration is using the outdated and not missed mechanic of not giving the party members who are not in your active party xp. They will sit in town and fall farther and farther behind necessitating that you either grind a ton more to keep everyone levelled or using the same 3 members for the entire game, making the already repetetive combat even more so as you can't change up your party. Exacerbating this problem even more is the fact that you don't get xp for fighting enemies too far below you. So if you want to leech up your lower level characters your high leveled ones will get little to no xp for it. Why they thought this was a good idea I will never know.
But everything else about this game is so good. The art style is beautiful and striking. The sound design is the best I have ever heard in a game. I can't remeber ever sitting there playing a game other than this one thinking "God damn this game sounds so cool." I can't praise this enough. The game sounds awesome. In addition, the characters are all interesting which makes it even more annoying that you can't use them all without tons of extra grinding. Despite its flaws the combat is not a weakness. Its just not a strength, but to be honest you can pretty much always know what to expect going into a game with turn based combat.

honestly i hate uncounterable instant kill mechanics. buy the game if you like the art thats about the only reason. this game only takes time to beat because the game requires an absolutely incredible amount of grinding to keep all the party members a high enough level to not get insta-gibbed when you have to inevitably rotate them out to help counter some instant kill mechanic some mob in the dungeon has. but hey it looks really good and the soundtrack is phenominal, kudos to the artists.

I wanted to try this game, mainly for the controversy, stayed for the gameplay and story. As it is a Square Enix game you should expect the music and story to be great and it is.
Story
This game has such an amazing story. If you watched Ghost in a Shell movies and series, and if the AI, androids, scfi setting interested you (like it did me) this will keep you wanting to know more of the story to the point you must complete it.
Music
Music is so powerful I had to go buy it on iTunes. Easy to listen to outside of the game if you’re working and need background music.
Gameplay
It’s mainly focused on 3d action RPG open world where you can do sides quest for more exp, with some parts turning into a top down shooter or a side-scroller (when attacking the castle in the forest). But whatever it changes to for a brief time it plays so well in all areas. You can upgrade stats, or effects and buy extra space for your android to slot more in later. You can also upgrade weapons and find new ones at shops or in the world. You switch between 2 weapons types for melee and you have a floating droid which shoots. You can also equip the droid too with skills too. Then you can also customise your looks as well as the driod.
I highly recommend this. I don’t want to talk too much about the story for spoiler reasons. It’s best to go in with very little knowledge and see for yourself.

While still in early access this game is nice hack'n'slack RPG that will satisfy your loot itch. The art style while definitely unique, it kinda feels a bit too simplistic for my taste but that doesn't take away from the fun. There's 3 Acts completed by the time of this review and the developer updates quite frequently with content and general fixes, there's 2 more acts in the works from what it seems which is quite exciting!
The combat might feel stiff at times but there's nothing too serious to hinder the player. There's lots of dungeons to explore, quests and optional quests, a quite decent story to unravel and the gear system is top notch. Legendaries, sets, you name it. There are several classes to choose from, each one with own specific talent tree and an important note is that you can actually change your talents at your leisure for dirt cheap.
There's some endgame content in the form of Anomalies (think of Diablo III rifts) and quite a few secrets within the main campaign.
Overall this is a very promising game, sort of like a diamond in the rough, quite worth its price compared to the hours of content provided, and there's replayability with playing different classes and doing anomalies. The game also supports local co-op however I did not had the chance to give it a go.
Recommended for experienced ARPG fans and even more so for those who might be new to genre.

Magicite was the lurker on my Wishlist (which is 189 games long now) and (somewhat) recently it went on a pretty sweet sale so I picked up the four-pack with some friends and I in mind. It had become a drug that I couldn’t kick and I had to get my fix almost nightly with one or two friends of course. Sharing is caring, right?
That’s not to say that Magicite isn’t a good single player game, but you know how some games are just more fun with other people? Well… this is “kind of” one of those games. I think, as opposed to some games where one mode stands out above the other, Magicite’s single and multiplayer modes have completely different feels and both want and get my attention.
When playing solo, you’ve got a bit more inventory management to deal with since everything is harvested and crafted by yourself. You can sell everything that doesn’t pertain to your build and get a decent bit money with some good speed. While running solo there’s no potions to split and there are no boar butts flying into your face after your buddies hit them in the face(the struggle is real). If you’re playing with three or more people, the inventory management gets pretty complicated with people arguing about whether or not “we should get the diamond upgrade first” or “what ore are we on with arrows, are we sure were done with rock arrows?” It takes us a long time in every town, but when playing with buds, it’s all fun. If I was playing Magicite with other people (read: online multiplayer servers), I think I wouldn’t enjoy the experience much, if at all.
While you get no support, the enemy AI acts funky when more than one person is on the screen. Bees are probably the worst offenders with their juking a completely different direction and hitting you. When you’re solo, it’s fairly easy to guess where most enemies are going to go. The boar is the one mob that has set up a melee = “solo only” policy with my buds and I. Hitting them knocks them back and a boar butt in the face has been known to be the kill-shot many times. All the mages and their casted magic can also cause some problems, but mostly if you’re melee. If you’re ranged, it’s not that difficult.
Each of the three modes of combat feel good, but they are not all equal. Like I’ve mentioned already, ranged is kind of like an “easy mode”. Once you’ve compiled a large enough some of arrows, you can just let them fly and not have a care while you go and frolic through all the loot there is to pick up. Magery can come off similarly, but with a perk. You can fire your Fire spell a little slower than one can shoot arrows, but fire goes through walls. (Whatever science; this is magic we’re dealing with here!) The issue with both is that sometimes getting the components necessary to build your arrows or your magic sticks can be more difficult in some runs than in others. That can be a great source of frustration because you can’t have easy arrow mode, if you can’t make a bow… or arrows.
Melee doesn’t tend to have that issue of ammo. You can always hit an enemy with something or if you are, for some reason or another, completely out of something to hit bad guys with, you can punch them. Melee is satisfying, but feels the most challenging. It’s tough to fight some monsters with their quirky movements or the fact that some just move faster than you. (I’m looking at you bats in the spider cave! … jerks…) Put that together with the two-handed weapons needing a sense wind-up timing and you can see where the going gets tough.
Score: Gewd
Magicite is possibly the game I would say you need to play if you want to have some good co-op fun with three buds. Even the single player has a place in my heart, even if I don’t enjoy the experience as much. Sure there are some single player games that do the platforming genre a little better, but with all the elements included in Magicite, this is a game that deserves to be in your library. Definitely money well spent.

, but in general the game is short, lacks variety between runs, and gets boring fast.
Multiplayer is where this game shines. It breaks up the monotony, allows you to specialize for a certain role in a team setting, and offers fun experiences with friends. The problem is that the multiplayer in this game is extremely buggy.
buggy. There is an ungodly amount of lag (even in a LAN), graphical glitches (your teammate may appear to be in one location on your screen, but is actually somewhere completely different) and game-breaking crashes/black screens. After several (at least 20+) multipler attempts, both on LAN and over the internet, me and my teammates were still unable to complete even one successful run. Every single time the town hub area in between levels would glitch out and completely break the game at some point, preventing progression and forcing a restart.
This game is not worth an outrageous $10, but itsn't trash. I was able to get a couple of hours of enjoyment out of it at least, but the the rest was just multiplayer frustration. If you want it, get it on sale (I think I picked it up for about $2.50). There is nothing in this game would give you a reason to buy it immediately.

After about 300 hours spent on this game I think I can give a fair review.
This game is fun, this game is addictive and.... did I say this game is fun??? Maybe I did.
Ok the framerate is not always the best especially on big battles populated with over 20 ships (and I mean huge supe detailed ships...) and yes there are some cheaters/hacker player. Still I would say 99% percent of the players are playing fair ...
Going in details you can chose a ship between those included in the lwoer classes of 4 Nations (UK, Japan, Germany and USA) and youc an improve that through experience (and silver) gained playing. The sips comes in different classes: Destroyers, Cruisers (light and heavy), Battleships, Carriers and Submarines. Each class has a different playstyle and a different use in the battle (like in a real fleet). Let me explain: like in real life Destroyers are made to be the eye of the fleet and to hunt down submarines. This doesn't mean they can't take down Battleships but be aware that if you try to simply charge a battleship like a ram you're heading for disaster. Submarines are made to hunt down big ships in the back of the fleet and they can cause a lot of pain and tears over there but be careful cause you usually have to avoid and /or defend yourself from Destroyers to get there and it's not going to be an easy task.
Because of the fact different ship are perfect to hunt down a different type of ship the matches tend to become either a big chess game or a total mess with everyone throwing all they have at everyone else and in the middle of the chaos, looking through the smoke of explasions, sinking ships or simply a smoke granade is very easy to miss your comms commander screaming "torpedo incoming" and end up (or better down) on the bottom of the sea to hang out with fishes.
Commanders are important: they add special skills to your ship (quicker reload time, more efficient use of oxygen for subs, better acceleration or steering and so on) and can be acquired through gold or merit (that you earn completing specific tasks like sinking three japanese ships every day or such).
When you reach level IV you can create your own fleet with your friends or you can joing an already exhisting one and make new ones.
The downside are (beside the frame rate at times dropping at 25 fps even on my eight core AMD) are:
- they are lacking servers. Apparently there are just 2: one in China only for chinese people (so I heard); and one in North America for the rest of the world. This determines ping value that can go from over 170 to well over 300 (ouch!);
- there aren't many players on level higher than 5 so if you're using a ship of level 6 or higher you might have to wait quite a few minutes to get a match (even more than 5 at times);
- the maps (depsite they get played in many different ways) are not as much as I wish they were;
- there a couple of well known Chinese players and another couple of players from aroudn the globe who think it's fun to use aimbots, invisibility and teleport... but thank God you won't meet them too often and the devs seems to be interested in trying to stop cheaters, hackers and bots so let's hope for the best.
Would I suggest to play this game: hell yeah  or I wouldn't have spent 300 hours on it.
P.S. at the moment the only British Ships available are the Destroyers and the HMS Repulse (a level 5 battleship) that coems as a Free DLC but will be retired from the store after january 10th so hurry up and claim your Battleship!

I really want to recommend this game because I'm a huge Warmachine/Hordes tabletop player (I backed the KS), but there is no way $65 is a justified price tag for this game in it's current state. Just to be clear, I do not think the early access is worth the extra money. The UI is unfinished which makes it frustrating to move warrior models around (and the lack of Units in the game makes moving 11 Mechanithralls "solos" a very time consuming process), game breaking bugs abound such as certain knockdown effects not affecting large base targets, some spells are listed on the UI but are not in the game yet, 20 FPS is about the max anyone can seem to get despite current gen computer hardware, and it is generally a painful rather than fun experience at the moment. I will happily create another review when the game is done, but as it stands I cannot recommend this purchase.
One thing I can say about the game in its beta state that will carry over to the final product is that this is *NOT* a clone of the tabletop game. Many spell effects and abilities differ, major effects like Disruption do not function the same, point costs have been changed since everything is now a solo, Warjack systems have been removed entirely so a jack with one box left functions just as well as a jack with 20 boxes, everything rolls three dice for attack and damage, and everything is grid based with an always-visible grid (read: pre-measuring). The devs have listed a full list of changes in the forums:
These changes may appeal to you or they may frustrate you, just don't buy this game thinking you will be getting the same experience as the tabletop.

Just bought it about a month ago on a steam promotion and until now there goes around 70 hours of heavy gameplay.
The game is a hard nut to crack for beginners on Paradox's strategy games, but once you get used to gameplay mechanics, and manage diplomacy and warfare on a reasonable parameter, you'll be able to start playing on larger galaxies, with many AIs and take over a couple of fallen empires.
About AI, it's really difficult to track it`s behaviour on the beginning, but as soon as you learn how the ethos' mechanic works, you'll know that most of them can be taken over by diplomacy, using the protectorade or vassalization system, unless they're fanatic zealots, in that case, just wipe those empires as fast as you can.
You'll learn that usually players with genocidal warmonger tendencies can be wiped out pretty easilly by other major races on the beginning of the game, expecially on higher difficulties.
War is always an option, nonetheless one that must be married with diplomacy and good alliances, since the warscore mechanics limits the conquest of other alien races.
The graphic is pretty reasonable for a strategy game, and it runs on most computers.
Oh, and yes, there are plenty of cheats available if you're not playing on iroman mode.
I must add that the variety of cheats available can make the game really enjoyable if you like to edit certain configurations or experience tons of events not available during a single gameplay, like endgame crisis (It doesn't work with leviathan's events, sadly).
About the support given to the game by Paradox, it's incredible, they make tons of patches for it, adjusting and balancing the gameplay, just like they already do to their other titles, which is, in my opinion, a really difference among game developers.
The only drawnback is the price on my region (Brazil), which makes the game a little bit prohibitive for most customers.
Neverthless, I heavily recommend it if you`re a big fan of 4x strategy games, and is used to micromanagement.

Let me start of by saying this, Stellaris is the first of this style of RTS that i have played, so this i coming from a new player's perspective.
Lets start with the good things
First off, the art style is beautiful. The game has a very realistic and yet diverse colour palet for ships, planets and stars. The graphics (who cares) are very nice too, and are very well optimized so in large space battles you will not lag so much.
Secondly, the ship design mechanic is... well to put it simply, the best of its kind ever implemented into an RTS. It allows for FULL customization to YOUR style of play, which for me is hit hard and fast, and dodge the big shots. Though more experienced players may disagree with me, i think the weapons are very well balanced, each type of weapon serving a very specific role on a ship, and that ship serving a role in an entire fleet.
Also, the more advanced mechanics like diplomacy, genetics, population ethics and empire creation, are f***ing glorious. The new mechanics introduced with the most recent patch and DLC have added SO much to the games total content. i won't go more in depth cos it would spoil a few things ;)
No game is perfect however
First off, the AI. I find myself looking at planets i took from the AI in a war that have about 5 or 6 populations unemployed. this is so stupid. sometimes populations may even be starving in AI empires.
Secondly, the early game is rather dull. its essentially, "Go survey there, research this and that, oh maybe i should colonise". I sometimes lose interest in games that start off VERY dull, such as games i start in a system where there is not any minerals... by far the biggest troll ever. The early-mid to mid-late game periods are very fun. you get interesting techs, fight wars and make other empires your subjects. Such tyranny, Much fun
overall, Stellaris is a very fun RTS that has a noticable learning curve. If you ask me, the price tag is a little high, considering most of the interesting content is locked behind DLC, but it is very much worth it when you start using mods. the workshop opens up entirely new ways to play. These can be Total Conversions, bug fixs made by independant modders or even mini expansions (Alpha Mod is the prime example of an excelent expansion-style mod)

Magicite 1.6, which, if I recall correctly is the latest version up until now, was released on February 28, 2015.
It's December right now.
Sadly, I can't say I recommend this game; it's just... Too boring. I should say first that I've played this game for quite a bit of time and had some fun with my friends, but I can't really say I've been enjoying it lately. No updates, slow and RNG-reliant unlocks, no sync between different computers, and the inability to save just make it an off-putting game to play after a while.
Frankly, I think that the game is hard, especially when you first start. There's no guide to help you, nor is there any threshold to keep you safe when you first start a game; it's all randomly generated, which can be a problem. It should be noted that usually you begin with anywhere from 3-6 HP, and most enemies in the starting biome do 1-2 damage.
Even then, a cluttered map due to RNG can take you out quickly in a few hits. I suppose the pause menu (or pressing 'ESC') brings up the controls, but the crafting recipes are all up to you to remember.
There's also no time for newbies to wait either; in the non-town districts, spending more than 5 minutes in there will prompt 5 'Scourge Guardians' to appear, which are basically unkillable enemies which do 9999 damage. Great.
Going back to the crafting recipes, the crafting mechanic is really... boring? Undeveloped? I mean, all you do is combine two things together and you get something else. There's not a lot of variety in what you can craft, at least now, anyway.
Meanwhile, your stats are randomly generated, and usually rerolled when you begin the game until you get a decent start. While it doesn't take too long, it's really an unnecessary time-waste, especially since if you die in that run, restarting gives you the same stats back. If anything, they should have less of an influence in the game.
Another thing to say is that games, especially those which progress pretty far, usually take up to an hour. Between that, there's no ability to save, and even if you do somehow manage to beat the game (which is actually an extremely hard feat the first time you do it, given that most of the good unlockables may be unlocked by beating the game in the first place), there's no telling that you'll unlock something useful. If you leave the game in the middle as well, you won't even unlock anything.
Finally, RNG is too relied upon in the game; many hats give you a % chance to gain an extra stat, all characters, hats and companions have a % chance to whether you'll unlock them (albeit some of them are 100%, but usually those requirements are a pain in the nether-regions to fulfill), the levels themselves are randomly generated, your character's stats and traits are rerolled, and even some of those traits include a % chance for extra resources.
Overall, I would recommend the game, but only if it's on sale. Really, unless you do multiplayer and exploit some glitch to beat the game and unlock a companion called 'Flame of Hope' (which is absurdly OP compared to what you need to do to unlock it), you're not going to have a very fun time with this game because of the difficulty and frustration that comes with it.

What I love about this game is how "Performance parts" perform just as what you expect in the real world and has real world consequences. For example, lets just say you just bought a worn out Sunstrip 1.5 (Honda Civic) and you see on the parts catalog Racing Sunstrip 2.0 springs and swaybar (Honda Civic SI), expecting the car to be glued onto the road. You install it into your crappy Civic then wonder why the car horribly understeers in corners as you crash into traffic and get ticketed...
Then you see others with amazing Sunstrip builds that hugs the road or does sweet drifts.
The game expects you to look up suspension tuning info used in real life to tune cars ingame, which is what makes this game great. Only downside is that the tire grip simulation isn't as good as other games.

Unlike Borderlands 2, this game is possible to complete while playing alone. Well, Borderlands 2 is also possible, but you die far more frequently there. You still benefit from having people to play with, but at least it is possible. The final enemy (no spoilers given) is moderately challenging alone, though.
Throw out half the laws of physics, then replace half of the remaining laws with the rule of Badass, and you've got a vague idea about what borderlands is all about. Fun times. Easily something one can return to later. So it definitely stands up to the test of time.

My first experience with this style of game was World of Tanks.  When the developers of that game announced that there was going to be a similar game that dealt with ship combat, I was very excited.  However, after playing World of Warships I found that game lacking in several respects.  Most noticably was with regards to battleships.  After losing interest with it, I had hoped to find something more engaging, more complex and more historical in it's feel.  Well, Steel Ocean is it!  It is what I envisioned for WoW, and then some!  Here are some specifics:
1) All ships have access to their full armament, including main batteries, secondary batteries, anti-aircraft guns, torpedos and even depth charges!  The weapons seem to be reasonably historically accurate, and the access to secondary batteries makes battleships absolutely devistating if you learn how to use them well!
2) Submarines!  These are in the game and done very well.  They are both playable, dangerous, and also very vulnerable if used badly!  You have the ability to operate at a shallow depth (equivalent to periscope depth) or dive deep.  Each depth has plusses and minuses, and you have to watch your oxygen and surface when it runs low.  Very nicely balanced and a great addition to the game.
3) Light and Heavy Cruisers!  The developers were smart enough to split cruisers into their real-life categories.  Much better than lumping them all together!
4) Night combat!!!  This is my favorite, favorite feature!  You have access to starshells and spotlights!  Too bad they don't have a historical map of Iron Bottom Sound...  If they did, I'd be in heaven!  Regardless, night combat is VERY VERY fun!
5) Better tech trees.  This may be totally subjective, but it seemed as if the tech trees are composed of better ship selections.  I'm still hoping they add more, but I am very happy with the selections for both the US Navy and Imperial Japanese Navy.  Also, I'm not seeing the changes that WoW felt necessary to balance the game - for example, the fictitious float versions of fighter aircraft that they added to between-the-wars ships to balance out their lack of AA.  Although a "float claude" was an attractive invention, it is totally developer fantasy - nothing else.
Okay, so I've given you a lot of upsides.  In fairness, I'll give you the few downsides I've found:
1)  The graphics, while still nice, aren't quite as eyepopping as WoW, although you can use the F8 key to toggle off the UI and make some nice screenshots.  The water looks good, as do the islands, but the ships are less detailed than WoW.
2)  The economy.  It uses a similar system to WoT, WoW, etc.  The problem is the gold.  Your ability to purchase gold is limited, if I read the instructions correctly, to a single purchase of each of the different gold packages.  For example, there is one package that costs you $1 and gives you a total of 1000 gold (again, if I read the instructions correctly), but you can only buy it once.  The next time you try to purchase gold, it will not be available.  There will still be the other packages of gold, which number less than ten, but they get quite pricey rather quickly.  I seriously doubt I'll ever purchase the last one, which is over $100.  Since gold is tied to purchasing ship slots this will be an issue for me early on.  There do seem to be other ways to get gold, including an "investment" program, which seems designed to keep you around until you reach the higher tiers.  I assume this was all done to prevent players from using cash to get too much of an advantage over other players.  Seems silly to me, since you can only play with one ship at a time, if this is the case.
In conclusion, I find Steel Ocean to be most of what was good with it's competition, World of Warships, plus much, much more!  Great game!

An extremelly underrated MMORPG, perhaps due to its horrific launch and cartoon-focused design which, despite not being a bad thing by itself, it is, just like anime, despised by many people.
Past happenings aside, this MMORPG nails too many points that other MMOs completelly fail as if they were to be launched 10 years ago. Wildstar though is a game fitting the next generation, or should we say, current generation.
Let's get on why this is a game worth your time, shall we?
Free-to-Play Without Butchering:
Main issue with F2P games is that they are made ok... And then the developers butcher and maim the game from a few fundamental parts and put them behind pay walls, because since the game is going to be free, you have to give people "some reason to pay for something", and that is making the game either frustrating or incomplete, and selling the relief or extra pieces. Well, Wildstar doesn't do that, and perhaps that is the reason why it is dying: It doesn't sell that well.
Which makes me wonder why did they go F2P in the first place? Yes it is an amazing game, but it is pretty much free at the moment, this is like charity... So it is worth your time while it lasts.
Fast Action Combat with Choices:
This is one of those rare MMOs in which the camera follows your mouse without you having to click and drag, and you can attack with your mouse buttons. Delish~ The kind of thing all MMORPGs should have at this point to be honest *cough* FF14?! *cough*, but I suppose to each their own.
The skill system is curious though. Your class may have 30 or so skills, but you can only have 8 at a time... Which means customization is for real. Have to add those skills can be upgraded as well. Most skills don't really have massive cooldowns, and so the game mainly focuses on spending your resources, that are built by attacking. Which means this game doesn't have the usual No Mana No Life kind of setting, which puts it above 95% of the market.
Arguably best Housing System to be ever made:
Perhaps too good for its own good, you get a land lot for free around some early level by following the main story. You can basically build a few speficic buildings in this land from a selection of collectable options (so you might wanna hunt down houses around the world, if that makes sense to you), and you can put furniture of all kinds in any size and orientation you want. I had a Turnip House with a massive Carrot Plushie in the front, a colossal tree behind it, and a giant mushroom growing on the roof as a final touch. All done manually. TAKE. THAT. CUSTOMIZATION.
Arguably best Wardrobe System to be ever made:
Nevermind GW2's wardrobe system that relies on some weird limited resources that might eventually require you to pay some cash, nay, nevermind FF14's glamour system that requires you to get a crafting class up to Lv.50, nevermind WoW's Transmog system that needs you to talk to NPCs.
Just freaking stop, we are in space now, and everyone got the gadgets. In Wildstar you can change your clothes immediatelly anytime. Got new equipment? You can save up to 350 pieces of equipment in your wardrobe and change to them immediatelly. Got all kinds of looks you wanna keep around? Yes you can have a few presets. All for free, that may cost a few in-game pennies, who cares, after a certain point the costs were irrelevant.
Universe Worth Exploring with Non-Linear Questing:
Some may disagree with me, but you don't really need to do much of the questing if you don't want to. Questing in this game is divided in a few categories, and those are related to the Regions. So you can get to some place and learn the story of that place, or you can get in, kill things and get out when you are tired.
There is an insane ammount of lore to explore, there is an insane ammount of collectables, quests, events and achievements to get, and overall a lot to see... If you want.
Cash Shop has good Stuff that you don't really need:
More slots for things that you don't really need, cool looking mounts that you don't really need, mount customizations that you don't really need, boosts of things that you don't really need, you know, a non-pay-to-win cash shop.
Conclusion:
This game tries to be fun and manages to do it. Sadly that's not how economy works, so it is dying. Nowadays you only get money from people's suffering, so in my opinion this game is like a test to the gaming industry. Wildstar dying means that making fun games is something developers are punished for, and making games that make players suffering is something rewarded for. I don't know what kind of curse will be casted upon all gamers when this game dies, but you can be sure it will follow this industry's decline.
Wildstar is the only MMO out there that doesn't want to hate you neither be hated by you, so try to give it some love, 'k? Have fun.

After being very disappointed with the lackluster at best titles 2K has put out for the past few years, including 2K16 last year for the PS4, I had no intention of buying 2K17.  The only reason I decided to play it was because of the free to play weekend on Steam.  It was a good chance to try out the game for free plus see how it ran on my newly built gaming PC as I make the transaction from console back to PC.
Keep in mind, I NEVER play online, due to cheaters and everyone choosing the Cavs or the Warriors every game.  I also won't review any mode that makes use of VC (myPlayer, myPark, etc).   I have never bought VC and don't plan to because I am very against micro transactions. Because of this, my review is only for offline quick play and offline franchise mode.  Also keep in mind this is my first NBA2K game on the PC so some things I mention may have already been here since I'm comparing it to 2K16 for PS4.
After finishing downloading the game I ran a quick play just to get a feel of the game and for the most part the game ran very smooth on my PC.  Graphics are good but since I never played this on my PS4 I don't have anything to compare it to.  Player models are great and look like their real-life counterparts.  There is great detail when you zoom closer and for the arenas I played it, they look true to life.  AI seems somewhat improved from last year, so it doesn't feel like the game is blatantly cheating you (i.e non stop offense rebounds for the CPU, constant missed layups, blocked shots always going back to the CPU, etc).  But I originally said the same thing about 2K16 until I started getting more games in then the cheating became more rampant.  There are still some shake my head moments that I've encountered, like knocking the ball away for an easy fast break score and the player I was controlling would just stop for no reason allowing the CPU to get the ball back.  Also some CPU rebounds seemed highly unlikely but for the most part these are toned down from last year. (so far)
I also like the ability to coach and run plays on the fly, it took some getting used to, but I finally started getting the hang of it at the end of my free to play period.
Another thing I really like about the presentation is how the game switches up the broadcasting crew.  Last year it was Kevin Harlan, Greg Anthony, and Clark Kellogg every single game, but this year they have random announcers each game, sometimes it would be the crew I mentioned above, other times it would be Doris Burke, Steve Smith, Chris Webber, and a couple of others.  Its a break from the monotonous broadcasting in previous years.  I suspect however if you play a lot of games, even the new broadcasting approach would get old.   The pregame, halftime and post game crew is still Kenny, Ernie, and Shaq and they have some new dialogue, but even during my free period they started repeating themselves.
Franchise mode is pretty much the same from last year.  So everything from 2K16 is still here including some problems:
1.)  Like 2K16, If you edit your team's jersey, you cannot easily go back to the default uniforms without downloading them back from the 2K community.
2.)  NBA Championship celebration is still lackluster as always.  No locker room celebrations from what I saw; just a few seconds of celebrations from the players, and then it just skips to the trophy presentation, then cuts to the MVP holding the MVP trophy.   I will say the ring ceremony the following season is a little better than 2K16.  In addition to my complaint on this, also if your team had won its first championship the previous season, they get no championship patch on the back of their jerseys like they do in real life.  Also, if your time adds a title, then the trophy count does not increment.  This may be hard to implement, so it is nitpicking, but at the minimum it should at least add the patch.
3.)  This year added the money ball rack to the All star weekend 3pt contest, but there is no way to place your money ball rack in the All star weekend 3 point competition like they can do in real life.  For every player its always the last rack.
4.)  Dunk contest is the same as last year with the exact same dunks.
5.)  All star game still shows Air Canada Centre on the center billboard, even though the court says New Orleans.  Also on All Star Saturday, the court is clearly still in Toronto.
6.)   In 2K16, the Raptors jerseys had the all star patch on them even when entering later years in your franchise, I didn't get to confirm that this still occurs this year with the Pelicans, but I am sure its still there.
Despite the issues, its a pretty good game offline speaking, but I feel I could get bored with it after a while.  As I said before, I'll never play online, and that is where it seems most of the issues lie.
The only way I can begin to recommend this game is if you are strictly offline and only if you can get it for around $30.  $60 is just too much to pay if you are only going to use it for off line play.  I enjoyed my free play but even with the $39 sale price this weekend, I still won't get it. If it comes down to $30 down the road, I may consider it
I'm on the fence with this one, aside from a few additions there is nothing really new here and many of the issues and oversights from last year carry over to this year.  If you do any online play, then I would say pass on this one.  If you are strictly offline play, then wait until it goes down to $30 or so because its not worth the full price tag.

Just bought it about a month ago on a steam promotion and until now there goes around 70 hours of heavy gameplay.
The game is a hard nut to crack for beginners on Paradox's strategy games, but once you get used to gameplay mechanics, and manage diplomacy and warfare on a reasonable parameter, you'll be able to start playing on larger galaxies, with many AIs and take over a couple of fallen empires.
About AI, it's really difficult to track it`s behaviour on the beginning, but as soon as you learn how the ethos' mechanic works, you'll know that most of them can be taken over by diplomacy, using the protectorade or vassalization system, unless they're fanatic zealots, in that case, just wipe those empires as fast as you can.
You'll learn that usually players with genocidal warmonger tendencies can be wiped out pretty easilly by other major races on the beginning of the game, expecially on higher difficulties.
War is always an option, nonetheless one that must be married with diplomacy and good alliances, since the warscore mechanics limits the conquest of other alien races.
The graphic is pretty reasonable for a strategy game, and it runs on most computers.
Oh, and yes, there are plenty of cheats available if you're not playing on iroman mode.
I must add that the variety of cheats available can make the game really enjoyable if you like to edit certain configurations or experience tons of events not available during a single gameplay, like endgame crisis (It doesn't work with leviathan's events, sadly).
About the support given to the game by Paradox, it's incredible, they make tons of patches for it, adjusting and balancing the gameplay, just like they already do to their other titles, which is, in my opinion, a really difference among game developers.
The only drawnback is the price on my region (Brazil), which makes the game a little bit prohibitive for most customers.
Neverthless, I heavily recommend it if you`re a big fan of 4x strategy games, and is used to micromanagement.

I first learnt about this game when I was just randomly searching up new games to download and play. Upon seeing the game cover and the trailer, I was determined to get this, so much so that I was even considering buying a PS4 just to play this. Luckily it came out on Steam a while later and so I got it. I did not even bat an eyelid at the $80 price tag.
So once it was downloaded and all that, I started playing it (duh). After some tweaking of the visual settings, it ran very smoothly on my PC (tried 2560x1440, but 1980x1080 is better). Bear in mind I played this game in Japanese audio with the English subs of course, which to me was better than the English Dub, but then again this is coming from someone who prefers subs over dubs, so for this language portion its whatever floats your boat.
The gameplay itself was stunning in my opinion. The combat was nice flashy and chaotic (in a good way), and it was a decent learning curve, though it would not be much of an issue for people who have played Final Fantasy or Dark Souls, like me. Be warned for those of you who havent seen any of the gameplay: the game changes platforms at times. One moment you are playing a third person view RPG, next it is a side scrolling platform, or one of a bird's eye view. I have seen the reviews of how some people apparently hate that.
During the game, the music is brilliant, to say the least. I have come to realise something as well: depending on how much you have played the game and how far you have progressed, the same song will make players react differently in terms of emotion. In one example, after completing one of the missions (rescuing some robot kid, you know, typical side quest stuff), the song Treasured Times started playing. At this point, because I had already completed the main storyline, it was a lot more powerful compared to those players that had done this quest without seeing all the Main Endings. Basically, prepare for tears.
At this point for those who dont like reading (why would you read this if you didnt anyway), I will try my best to summarise the Ups and Downs of the game.
Pros:
-Beautiful World, scenery and artwork
-The sexiness of 2B and A2 (two of the female main characters)
-Character development
-Combat control, especially slow-mo evasions once you get that ability
-Soundtrack, prepare for tears
-Great storyline, emotional at times, again prepare for tears
-A certain degree of plot twists (I predicted a few, but the main ones still blew me away)
-The idle animation, especially for 2B (I got goosebumps when she started stretching her arms out to enjoy the scenery)
-Causes you to bond with the characters emotionally (you feel for them)
Cons:
-The World is kinda open, though not as open and expansive as games such as Skyrim
-The general tone of the game may get a bit monotonous after a while
-Playing through the game again AFTER clearing the main storyline with your old save files, for the enemy is laughably easy then unless you stick it on Very Hard difficulty in which case you will be one-shot killed by ANYTHING
-2B and A2 can be VERY distracting at times
-The pod's lock-on function can be a bit annoying at times when they lock onto the wrong target (bear in mind Hard difficulties and above will have no lock-on function)
-Causes you to bond with the characters emotionally (I have crippling depression~)
All in all, I highly recommend this game for all, especially those who have played the previous NieR games. One word of warning: Try not to die within the first hour of the game. There is no save option for the first hour, though frankly it was not much of a challenge for me.
On a scale of 10, I rate this game a Yes.

A gorgeous, crisp, and fun hack'n'slash that rewards those with patience and those who are willing to see it through to the end.
[I'll start by saying that I won't bring up Yoko Taro, the man behind this series (and also keeping the game's loose connections to the original Nier and to Drakengard 1 / Drag-on Dragoon references to a minimum), outside of this small blurb. There is this bizarre celebrity worship of him as a mad genius that runs deep into those who follow his games, stories, and the associated material with it, and I feel as if that taints the perception of game discussion at hand, for better or for worse.]
NieR: Automata (henceforth abbreviated as NieR or Automata) is a sequel to NieR, or at least, on paper it is. Truth be told, one doesn't need to play the original to be able to play this game, but it does add to the experience through minor callbacks and references that otherwise come off as innocuous. As in previous titles, NieR follows a non-conventional story, where there are endings followed by another repetition of the story from a newer perspective, and then another, completely novel part of the story opens up after that.
The main characters in this game are androids - 2B and 9S are the main stars of the show, along with a third deuteragonist, A2 - which is not really a spoiler, considering that all three of them are on the front cover of the game. Automata is told primarily through small conversations, sidequests, archives you find, and directives given to you by YoRHa, an organization dedicated to fighting a never-ending series of wars with machines across the ruins of Earth for the glory of mankind.
The story itself is mired in a constant battle between highs and lows, where feelgood moments are shot down quick and things can always get worse. And yet, there's this sense of hope that's never abandoned, that the best is still yet to come. It's honestly hard to describe it in any detail without spoiling some aspect of it - it's best to go in knowing nothing about it, only that machines are going haywire and you are tasked to destroy them, buddy cop at your side and all. The only downside is that some of the sidequests can be boring and often are little more than glorified fetch quests, but the associated stories and lore compensate for it. The main story itself seems relatively straightforward at first, but it isn't until you're 10 - 15 hours into it that you realize that not everything is all it's cracked up to be. Even so, the biggest flaw of the game is the rather heavy backtracking at times that's partially remedied by fast travel stations - which don't kick in until you're about a quarter of the way through the game, but it is still nevertheless an open world game.
What really works in NieR's favor, however, is the impeccable marriage of gameplay and story togther into one cohesive unit. I might have lied a bit in the synopsis - Automata isn't strictly a hack'n'slash, as there are hacking (as in, computers) and fixed-perspective shooting segments, along with creative camera placement to spice up the gameplay of certain areas. For example, most areas are open and are freely 3D, but there are a couple of sequences that play like a Metroidvania, taking perspective only from one side as you go through it. Even so, the amount of combos, weapons, and upgrades you can get provides more than enough replayability and fun in itself to prevent the game from ever getting old. You can use two-handed swords, one-handed swords, lances, and even fisticuffs; they all have their own styles and unique twists to keep them entertaining and engaging, and you can use two of them in a set at once, alternating between the two in the middle of combat by just hitting another set of buttons. On top of this, you also have a pod that can shoot bullets or cast improved and special abilities to further your killing potential.
With all of this in mind, there is no fixed combination order or movelist to memorize to have fun. Rather, you can discover weapon differences by hitting a different button, hitting a couple at once, or just go wild and freestyling it. The game leaves the magic of discovery to you, and while there are minor protips and tutorials, it's ultimately up to the player to go about their business however they wish. Some may opt for simple and quick efficiency, killing their enemies in a handful of hits, while others go for the flashy factor, endlessly juggling cute robots and never letting them hit the ground until they so desire.
All of this is set to a fantastic soundtrack and gorgeous scoring, with certain tunes being gently sung by ethereal voices in a strange albeit familiar language and other songs just want to knock your socks off from the start. In my opinion, excellent sound direction is the most important part in guaranteeing the staying power of any game - it's why other games such as Morrowind and Chrono Trigger are remembered so fondly. It's that sense of nostalgia from hearing minor things like the overworld music or a specific character's theme that keeps those fond memories fresh in one's mind, even as the details of the plot and graphics, gameplay get fuzzier over time. NieR also has marvelous English voice acting, and in an odd twist of fate, I feel as it exceeds the original Japanese dub, especially on the part of 9S.
Graphically, the game is exceptionally pretty despite not having a large budget, but can be taxing on weaker systems - there are mods you can get that remedy a lot of these issues to make it smoothly run, which is rather unfortunate from a porting standpoint that this unoptimization exists in the base game. The animations are fantastic and there are a lot of cute details, be it idle animations or just minor background interactions, that show that a lot of love and diligence went into making this game feel as alive as it should be.
In previous titles and spiritual predecessors, the action was always the weak link, but this is honestly the first game that has made the combat truly enjoyable, which in turn, reinforces not only the plot, but the game's replayability on top of that. Keep in mind, however, that despite the world's run-down state, it still contains fantastical elements and not everything needs to be explained in excruciating detail. Keep an open mind and you'll find that Automata does a wonderful job in seeing creative vision pull through and knock it out of the park.
9.5/10! NieR: Automata is no doubt one of the best games to come out in 2017. Do yourself a favor and play it going in blind, since there is a lot more to it than what meets the eye.

It’s time to review another abstract title! Delirium delivers at least from this perspective, of a title that is puzzling and never explained properly. It sadly fails from nearly all other points of view, but not enough for me to demolish the efforts of a single developer at the start of his Steam journey. So yes, it is the Steam debut of Night Whale and many lessons shall be learned from Delirium’s narrative and even level design. You’ve been warned that this game shall not hold your hand and neither will I spoil its mysteries. I shall merely offer my own version of constructive criticism in regards to it.
How should I put this in mild terms…the story from Delirium makes other abstract titles run for the hills. How it received the Steam tag on its Store page with “Story Rich” is beyond my understanding. So what do we have? A nameless, genderless and silent protagonist who interacts with several objects within a house that looks more like an abandoned bunker in the middle of a war torn city. I’m inclined to consider the entire experience as a nightmare sequence since very little of it makes sense, even when compared to the many abstract or atmospheric games I played over the years.
Players are thus, steping in the shoes of a mysterious figure which tries to piece together, the life and most recent struggles of the house’s previous owner. Across the several rooms which may be explored, there are red journals which contain descriptions and the woes of an aging man coming to terms with his own mortality. May be cryptic drivel or perhaps there’s more to it. It’s very ambiguous and two words stand out: Samar and Innsmouth. The first is used in the books for someone’s name, so it’s not related to the island and provice from the Philippines but Innsmouth is an entirely different story. That’s a fictional town penned by H. P. Lovecraft. You just had to drag Cthulhu in this, didn’t you, Night Whale?
Delirium is powered by the Unity Engine, so I have no technical issues to complain about. It ran on 4K resolution and stable 60 frames per second. It’s not like there were any reasons to strain a GPU though, since the bunker is poorly lit and features relatively few objects to inspect or interact with. You can step outside the building and “admire” the desolate urban landscape in front of you. The textures and assets are of decent quality, but nothing special about them.
Sounds are severly lacking in diversity. Most of the time you’ll just hear footsteps made by the protagonist in search of some meaning to it all. Towards the end of the game, you’ll finally hear menacing whispers and that, along with a single jump scare, form the “horror elements” of Delirium. Take it as you will, I wasn’t impressed or scared by any of the game’s meagre efforts.
For a title that doesn’t save progress at all and expects you to finish it in one sitting, it all started on the wrong foot. A pitch-black room and facing a wall. I honestly thought that the game had frozen or something until I figured out that I had to open a door leading to the house’s first corridor. Pay close attention to all of the objects you see. Even if you can’t pick them up or zoom in, they may contain hints that will help you in your brief adventure. Read the books without skipping pages.
Two keypads require passwords that are hidden in a fairly subtle manner. You need to find and use them if you want to progress the story. I guess I could have finished Delirium in half the time it took me in the end, if only I wasn’t stubborn enough to figure things out on my own instead of relying on a solution from YouTube or whatever. That’s the low road of gaming and I strongly advise that you avoid it. The antagonist was a pleasant surprise, as was the endgame sequence. They’re also partially the reason why I still recommend you play Delirium eventually.
“Delirium” is a fascinating word by itself since it can represent both passion and temporary madness. It can still be better explained than the eponymous Steam game. The only reason why I’m willing to rate it just high enough to still recommend it, is that it shows promise from a developer who had the right ideas but lacked the means or skills to properly showcase them yet. This isn’t a lazy cash grab for a shoveleare platformer. Cthulhu is my witness that I had my share of those on Steam to last for two lifetimes.
So I’m not going to encourage you to steer clear from Delirium. Just be fully aware that it may not meet your expectations. Pick it up when bundled or heavily discounted and you won’t regret it. As for the developer, he really needs to add some Steam Achievements in his current and future projects. Sweetening the deal or not, it would show support for the potential player base and especially consideration for Steam collectors.

I cannot recommend this game for various reasons.
First of all, I want to point out that this game has been made by one person, which I admire. I know how much time and effort has to be put in a game for it to be released at all, and when one person pulls it off, I take my hat off to him.
Nevertheless, the experience I had with this game was unpleasant.
As we all got to learn, a first person horror game isn't gonna roll without loads of text for the player to read. In 'Delirium' however, you will spend as much time reading books than exploring the setting. The texts are too long and purple-prosey to enjoy them on their own, and they are the only means by which this game tries to tell a story. The H. P. Lovecraft allusion don't help.
The house itself is a few rooms, but there is nothing to discover there. The rooms are boring. Some textures are okay, but the huge difference between them is what breaks the immerson -- one is very sharp and detailed, others are blurred. Some even seem to be faulty, with big black pixels all over them. The lighting is, as usual with the more amateurish typed of horror games, unrealistic. It bends around corners, drops off after two meters and so on. I know this game has been made with the Personal Edition of Unity, but when there are two or more lamps burning in a room, this room won't have pitch black corners. This is not even a design thing anymore.
The sound is horrible. The constant background whispering gets annoying real fast. I believe that sound design might be more effective in a horror game than graphics. But the sound design in Delirium is lazy. Your footsteps all sound the same regardless of whether you're walking on wood or on sand or on grass. The ticking clock can be heard all the way outside the house, whereas a fire won't make a noise.
It's not free of bugs either. One time I got stuck between the table and the couch. On the other hand, in the yard, you can walk right through trash cans since they have no collision detection. That's sloppy.
I didn't care at all.
Note to the creator: Please don't give up. I really respect your work, but there is so much stuff that needs to be done or seems unfinished, the game shoudn't have been released yet.

Here are the things I regularly enjoy about the game and what keeps me coming back for more.
Housing - While I've never been one that is talented in the art of spatial-manipulation in games (such as The Sims), I've been able to build a low-key house for what I would enjoy hanging out in. This pales in comparison to the creativity of other players. The tools for housing are robust, and the housing community is always willing to help answer questions or make suggestions. Housing in and of itself is an end-game.
Soundtrack - This is the only game I play where I have not turned off the soundtrack. Jeff Kurtenacker is a talented composer, and his music is the highlight of this game. If you enjoy the soundtracks, purchasing them is hands-down worth your money. Sometimes I'll leave the game running in the background while I do other things just to play specific zone/housing tracks.
Graphics/Animation - While the graphics are not everybody's cup of tea, I enjoy the vibrancy and cartoony feel. They add humor to an otherwise dark story lore-wise. The animations are great, as well. All of the emotes are lots of fun, and unique based on race (the only gripe I have about animations is maybe the dance animations being the same!).
General Game Play (PvE/PvP) - The telegraph system is hands-down one of my favorites. While it can require more concentration, it keeps the game dynamic and fun. There is no lack of PvE content, though the PvP side of things is currently (sadly) lacking. Classes feel fairly balanced, which is a rarity in some MMOs. Content feels challenging, but rewarding and fun, even when you spend some time wiping. Working towards end-game PvE content can be a bit confusing, but has been streamlined much more than it initially was. (The rune system leaves something to be desired.) All of the zones you level through are engaging, and the leveling process goes fairly quickly. Tutorial Island is also a blast.
In-Game Events - The Holidays designed by Carbine are always interesting and fun, and provide lots of fun in-game rewards. They have fun lore and flavor that differ from other MMOs and help you feel more immersed in the world.
Community - This is the number one thing that keeps me coming back. Both the community of Developers and the community of Players.
Breaking Down of Faction Wall - This is newly implemented, but something that has helped to boost the community, allowing players of both factions to group together for content as desired. There are still some wonky bits to this, but it's a start, and a fun one.
No game is perfect, obviously, so give it a try before making a decision. The Devs do listen, and have been putting together "DevConnect" posts where they ask for community feedback on specific topics, and then work towards implementing changes in these topic choices.
