SUCH a fun game honestly, surprisingly so for a game that's just in early access, but I can guarantee you that this game is 100% worth the price; free!
So, the Pros -
- Runs REALLY well, even on computers with minimal features, such as mine, so you can enjoy the extra frames even on a toaster :)
- Decent Graphics - the game definitely isn't the best looking, but it really has its unique, quirky design that really does pull you into the game and makes the gameplay very immersive. It also helps you take the game not so seriously at times and just lets you enjoy it.
- Loads of heroes for you to play as - as of writing this, I think there are around 25-30ish heroes (don't quote me on that), and all of them have different abilities, of which each hero has 5. One is reserved for their movement and I can't get into this without taking a whole page up, but let's just say that the heroes have a LOT of diversity and uniqueness to them.
- Speaking of which, each hero has alternative voice lines, clothes, weapon skins, different emotes, sprays, etc. This really does individualise the heroes and lets the player, us, form a bond with them as we play with them more and more.
-!!NOT PAY TO WIN!!  I have played for around 52 hours as of writing, and not once have I been forced to pay for things to get a better chance at winning the game. No microtransactions have bothered me whilst playing and I haven't been forced to buy any sort of premium currency to progress. The only time I've thought about buying anything was of my own free will, and that was to get the founder's pack, just to unlock all the heroes, but that can be done EASILY through actually PLAYING THE GAME and actively setting a goal to get more heroes.
Those were the very BEST aspects of the game in my opinion, and to save time I'll just flash by the other goods of the game:
- Almost every game is fast paced, and if it isn't then you're not at the right spot or doing the right thing, especially in maps that FORCE teams to collide and battle all out.
- A Large variety of maps so you don't get bored, as each map has its own tactics.
- Heroes are relatively cheap and by the time you can afford another hero, you'll already have had gained quite a bit of experience with other heroes, and by default, you are given one hero from every class; DAMAGE, SUPPORT, FLANK and FRONT LINER, and with each, you have to play smart in order to win.
Now the Cons
- The matchmaking! The matchmaking in the game isn't the best, especially when it comes to Ranked/Competitive. I've been ranked up against people that have purple and diamond borders around their names despite me not having played half the matched required to reach the silver border. From my language, it's obvious that I don't know the official terms for these ranks but it is annoying to verse a level 20 Lian when you're just a level 8 Drogoz.
- The card system isn't very well explained and I don't know if this is just me being ignorant but if 52 hours hasn't taught me how to make a general or specified build for a hero, how are the new players going to get used to it? I had to ask my friend who has played the game for a while on tips for making the builds but I would really like to see that aspect worked on just a little more to provide a little more clarity for starting players.
- THE MATCH BEING CANCELLED WHEN A PLAYER DOESN'T JOIN ARGHHHH - This is one of the most annoying things I've witnessed in the game; when the other 9 people that HAVE pressed the "Join match" button, and there's just one guy, (or girl, can't be sexist), that doesn't press it and EVERYONE GETS PUT BACK INTO QUE FOR IT!! I honestly don't know why a bot doesn't replace them, because even if the bot causes them to lose, it's still better than waiting another 5 minutes for another "Join match" button to pop up. Maybe balancing the bots are hard, but it'd save me and a LOT of other players some valuable time, as I do have school and I'd rather play a game and lose due to a bot as opposed to waiting 3-5 mins TRYING to get into a game. This can and has happened multiple times in a row which really adds to the annoyance.
I am determined to play this game free to play, so as long as the devs don't focus on the business side of the game too much, and I mean, I get it, they're basically a business and their motive is to make money, but if you build a solid community through an excellently done game, that cash will honestly just come flowing in. I intend to get the Raeve Maeve skin by paying for it as I can see myself playing this game seriously for quite a while. Also, it's DEFINITELY NOT AN OVERWATCH CLONE JUST PLAY THE FKIN GAME AND YOU'LL SEE JUST HOW DIFFERENT IT REALLY IS!!!!
Sincerely, NafariousJafar

This showed up as a recommendation based on some of my other library titles and I'm glad it did. This is a damn fine little game and at 7.99 it's a steal. It scratches an itch for good old hack-n-slash loot-em-up gaming that I've had for a while now. Even as an Early Access title it's got a lot to offer.

Though not without it's issues and as someone who generally does NOT like JRPG style gameplay I have been playing this long enough that I definitely think it is a thumbs up rather than down.
This is a good, not great, game and is probably one of the most consistently gorgeous games I've ever played. I am stunned that they can maintain the art style while also giving us procedurally generated dungeon crawls. I tend to like the overall character design and stories even if Red Monika is basically every female game character trope rolled into one. I realize these are originally comic book characters but that isn't a far cry in terms of character archetypes.
The biggest problem, and this is probably something JRPG fans are used to living with, is the repetition. There is no autobattle for easy encounters, no way to skip or speed up animations, and it feels like the game is constantly pausing. Despite a fairly solid story, good characters, amazing setting, there is no flow to the game due to what feels like constant interruptions and tedious encounters. However, this is counterbalanced somewhat with the lack of necessary grinding most games of this type has.
Overall it was well worth the money even though I have not played all the way through as of this writing. I usually don't praise games for their visuals but this game is amazing in that department.

I backed this game when it first apepared on Kickstarter, but the final result has far exceeded my hopes. Nightwar is an awesome throwback to old-school JRPGs (travel on an overland map, with separate dungeons and combat screens), very satisfying turn-based combat and a lot of nice moments between the characters for all BattleChasers fans. And of course it all looks great thanks to Joe Mad's siognature art style and colors.

Probably the best 4x space game I have ever played.
Pros:
- Customize your race
- Plenty of customization options as you make your way through the game
- You can micromanage everything or not. Up to you.
- Tons of random events
- Caters to different playstyles very well
- Replayability
Cons:
- Sometimes annoying space combat
- AI seems to have psychic powers
- Sometimes lacking UI
- Tech queues seem completely random
- Terrible in-game help browser
I did spend a lot of time (about 300 hours) playing this game before I chose to review it. I also must admit I am biased because I am a huge fan of Paradox games. IMO they make the best strategy games. The only problem I have with them is their tendency to be a DLC factory, but they have to earn their money somehow and it is no different than other companies subsidizing their product to profit on content (e.g. Microsoft, Apple, etc.) That having been said, on with the review.
First of all the most impressive thing about this game is its replayability. I found myself restarting early games a lot just to explore the effects of all the different customizations you could make to your race and civilization until I found a combination I felt comfortable with. You can play as a warmongering slaver or peace-loving hippy but the good news is you are not locked into it. You can change this eventually simply by playing. In fact there is something to be said about strategically starting out one way and eventually moving your empire into a totally different role altogether.
I enjoyed the many racial customization options. The first time I encountered this was Master of Orion 2 and it seems like nobody got it right until this game. Later in the game you can even change this through genetic engineering and/or cybernetics.
You also have a lot of options for your civilizations policies. Hate aliens? You can be xenophobic which expands your borders. You can gain advantages from choosing your civics but each carries a disadvantage too. Want to be able to colonize 4 extra planets? Well you will also have to be pacifist. The good news is you can change these later by setting your policies.
You start the game with limited ability to expand. Once you fill up your "core systems" slots by settling planets you can still colonize by creating sectors, which are basically NPC-governed zones that give you half their production. You can also vasselize conquered civilizations which work in much the same way. The drawback to having a large empire though is more time will be required for research. The thing is, in this game you really don't have to expand if you don't want to. You can simply build upon what you already have and still be a contender.
There are many  options for micromanagement but these things can be left as is and won't really effect your game much. You can let many turns slide by just concentrating to your current war without having to worry much about anything else or you can spend a lot of time every turn making sure every little thing is going as planned.
Combat is probably the weakest part of this game but it is still pretty decent. I was enraged a few times when my fleet would lock in an engagement with a small mining operation while a much larger force was approaching. When you are locked into combat your fleets control themselves and there is little to do but just watch them die. After a (seemingly too long) amount of time you can retreat but risk losing ships. Your fleet disappears and reappears sometime later near one of your colonies.
I liked how this game handled wars. basically you can set your war demands in the beginning (such as ceding or liberating a planet) and you are given a score to attain. Once you attain that level of war score you are able to negotiate your terms. If you want to take over an enemy's planet you will need to declare war and set it as a war demand, then attack them and take over planets until you attain the given warscore and make your demand. You don't just go taking over planets and get to keep them.
I am not sure why there are turn speed controls in this game. I never used any setting but "very fast" because a lot of time I was just letting turns fly by waiting for something to happen.
One thing that really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off was that no matter how careful you are to hide your activities it seemed like every alien civilization had psychic powers to know exactly when you are weak enough to be attacked, and they would... every... single...time. If they hate you then they will immediately attack you when you are down. Well, at least it is predictable.
Another problem I had was the hotbar. You can set hotkeys for fleets and ships but you only get 10 keys to play with. This kind of sucks when you have 20 planets because it's not easy to get to them in the main window. There is a window that  shows all your planets but remembering them by name is usually not an option unless you name them yourself. I found it easier to place them in the hotbar by importance. There is no reason at all to set a fleet or ship on the hotbar because you already have a window showing all of these with clickable links. A second hotbar would have been a nice addition to this game.
The third thing I did not like was the seemingly arbitrary research queues. You get a list of things you can research but they appear to be completely random. Did you create your race and civilization to be terraformers? Well you could get the terraforming tech on turn 1 or turn 100,000. You won't know. It would have been nice if the research queues were based on your species and civics choices but they don't seem to be. Even if they had used procedural code based on your civ and species at least the researches would be in the same order all the time but if you restart the game they are completely different each and every  playthrough.
My last complaint is with the in-game browser. It's terrible. Might as well just alt-tab and use a real browser to see the same thing.
Anyway all-in-all this game was worth every penny and the frustration vs. fun ratio was very good.

Wow! This game is absolutely breathtaking in both its involvement and spontaneity. First, you make an Empire or choose a pre-created one. Then, your goal is to ascend into the stars, by diplomacy or by Force. Once you've ascended, your time is spent eliminating threats to the galaxy, discovering ancient secrets, and eventually repelling a galaxy-wide threat to your Empire or Alliance's well-being.
This game is one of the best strategy games I've played in a long time. Typically, there is not always one solution to all of your problems. You can be a violent and oppressive dictator and be hated galaxy-wide, or you can rule indirectly through superior diplomacy. You can enslave or exterminate entire species, or weave them into the fabric of your society... Even in tech, you can choose to become new-age evangelists, or technological ascendants.

After im close to Tier VII and played every Class to at Least Tier 5 i would like to share my Experiences so far with the Community.
First of, this game has, at least in my Eyes, no real Parallels to WoWS. If anything it would be more like Navy Field. It's more Arcade then WoWS (played about 1550 Matches in it, got a Tier X CV and BB). And for me, it does various things better.  I would say it rewards your personal Skills much more then wows because the game doesn't take you by the Hand. Let me elaborate:
- Torps are fired one by one and manually. This gives you much more Freedom about timing and placing, but can also be harder because you don't have an aim assist like in wows
- The BBs and CAs got an Artillery View for their Main Batteries which is pretty much like in WoT or AW, So you will have to Focus for a few secs instead of hit and run
- The whole Spotting mechanic is a lot different and rewards XP / Points for the Spotters. It also makes the Game much more Rock / Paper / Scissors.
- CVs are pretty well implemented right now. They did several things i critizied in WoWS over Months. A maximum Number of Planes that can be started at a time, a max of 3 squads a time, limited fuel and far less Spotting range. But also, you can chose manually what kind of Layout you want ( you can configurate the number of plane types you want aboard  in the Maintenance Screen)  Also, onward to my next point, your Planes will die more often because..
- You will have to aim your AA manually, and i love that Fact. If your Aim is good it allows you to annihalate Torp Sqads even before they can drop. Pretty much what i said at the start, it rewards personal Skill.
The only real Downside right now is that there are still not enough players, but hopefully my Review might change that :P If you liked Navy Field or WoWS you should at least give it a Try. It wont be your Harm. Right now, after 500+ games in it, i can't really see any Reason to go back to WoWS.

The thing is that you can find oxygen everywhere. From killing enemies, from the ground, in buidings, in chests, and even in buildings that already have oxygen. Action rpg's are my life blood. I love the loot pops, and the color coding and the whole hamster wheel. This game takes a lot of elements wholesale from diablo games. And it's often better off for it. I was shocked that a game that looked like this could literally be such a worthy contender in the genre.
Unfrotunately, I would rank this below such games as grim dawn, diablo 2, diablo 3, and even sacred 2. Some things about this game, despite having a ABSOLUTE TON of great content, are asthetic. The art style frustrates me. The sound effects lack any kind of crunch or grit. They all fall completely flat. And hitting enemies results in no explosion of bones or gibs or anything. It's just a sprite change from alive to dead.
A game like this needs crunchy impact. And right now , if i start a new game with a magic caster. Every single attack sound will irritate me. I could literally open up a free sound deposit website and find something better than the default attack sound. The visuals also lack that same gravity, they don't have to be 3d or gothic. If you want to use 2d lowbit sprites go ahead, just make them attractive.
Finally, the game itself has a lot of systems. And most of them, including combos, enchanting, skill trees, and loot stats are all quite good. The loot drop rate however is far too high. You go strait out the first gate in the game and it's nothing but blues. I think that needs to be inverted. Completely reverse the drop rate. And make a colored item, you know, rare. Make whites mostly drop.
Now, in order for this to work, you need to make the core combat without stats be crunchy. The entire reason why I think you have stats right away is because the raw combat never feels crunchy or satisfying. Make the core combat have crunch, sound plays a big role. Visuals and feedback and explosions play another role. You want the game to have a flow. to be quick and responsive, and to really focus on satisfying collision in all respects. - I know. It's very hard to get that right. But it's the most important thing. Go back. Fix that. Take that loot drop rate right down. Then let's see. For now it's merely a good game. I want it to become a great one.

I can only recommend Stellaris to those who enjoy games with little demand of thought or planning, though it is well made and receiving frequent updates (so far) there is little to do in Stellaris that doesn't involve watching numbers. This lightness of strategy does make it much easier to play online but if you are looking for something requiring deeper thought I would advise against buying Stellaris.
There are 8 total resources in Stellaris that control the might and capacity of your empire. Only Influence is uneffected by any form of building or resource collection.
is your primary "upkeep" pool, it is rarely spent except upon the creation of mechanical populations and private colony ships (if you have the tradition.)
are your "cash" used to build and upgrade everything, with the previous exceptions.
is shared across your empire, if you have none your population will be unhappy and won't grow, if you have surplus it grows quicker. I've not noticed any difference from having +1 excess to having +100.
dictates how fast you research stuff.
only used to purchase traditions, utterly worthless once you've unlocked everything.
is used to run policies, enact edicts, recruit leaders and hold defensive pacts, it's generated at a flat rate which can increased by factions and rivalries with opposing empires.
The key to almost any strategy game is the employment of your populace and I am thankful to say this in one area Stellaris does not skimp on. The planets you colonise have a number of tiles many of which have resources to be exploited and a structure that improves upon it however you are not forced to match the structure to the resource (Too much food? Replace your hydroponics with a science lab etc.) but will lose access to the over written resource.
Your controls over said populace, or "pops" as Paradox named them for some strange reason, range from slavery to full citizenship including robotic and chemically dependent species. The effectiveness of your workers is effected by the traits of each species (strong species gather more materials, intelligent species generate more research) and happiness which can be influenced by various factions that your population can join. The factions themselves usually align to a certain ethic and can be promoted or suppressed at the cost of influence.
In a word, boring. In two words, really boring.
There is only one control you have over combat and that is a single "Retreat" button. You select your fleet, click on an enemy fleet and watch a small bar turn either red or green depending on how the fight is progressing.
In a game where fighting is guaranteed to happen I would've thought more effort would be put into actually controlling it. There are no bonuses to flanking or splitting your fleet, no tactics beyond aggresive or passive, hell you can't even select a formation and don't get me started on trying to split your fleet into classes. It's blob (or Doomstacks as they are called) or nothing.
Sure you can design your ships to a variety of roles and weapons (Missiles, Energy or Mass Drivers) but in the end battleships are the only thing worth building, slap a spinal mounted gigacannon on the front and you've basically won.
To say the combat is disappointing would be a fantastic understatement.
Contact with any alien empire is influenced primarily by your
; Militarist or Pacifist, Authoritarian or Elagitarian, Materialist or Spiritualist, Xenophobe or Xenophile and Hive Minded.
Depending on what combination you have will influence that empire's opinion of you including policies, anything clashing will decrease opinion whilst shared will increase. Hive Minds, being more of a species type than an ethic only get a single reply and typically want to enslave or kill everything regardless.
The combination of opinion, policies and the comparitive strength of your empire will generate an
that will dictate how the opposing empire will respond to requests. Attitude can be changed by accepting requests or offering generous trade deals but some differences simply cannot be overcome.
Fallen Empires are the wildcards of the game, spawning fully teched and with huge fleets from the beginning, they are ticking time bombs of either protection or destruction depending on certain events and what type of fanatic ethos they've been given.
It's a functional system if not a little uninteresting, like everything else in Stellaris its just a numbers game though some of the insults are quite entertaining.
For the most part Stellaris is quite dull, the majority of your time will be spent watching/balancing your resource counters, building up your fleet and awaiting a random choice of technology to research. Things do tend to pick up when you start meeting other empires but again, dependent on the random selection that the game has chosen to populate your universe.
The various ship types are nice to look at but once you hit Battleships everything becomes obsolete and to take anything but Mass Drivers is simply pointless.
There are supposedly tradeoffs to using each kind of weapon type, Missiles being longest range and great tracking/accuracy but can be shot down, Lasers are accurate and powerful against armour but short range with less damage to shields whereas Mass Drivers are long range with poor tracking but have bonuses against armour and shields. In practice however the Mass Drivers simply devastate anything with sheer brute force.
Rather strangely, Energy and Mass Drivers get upgraded versions (Plasma/Disruptors/Matter Disintergrators and Autocannons/Artillery/Flak) yet missiles only get a medium slot only Swarm type and no spinal mount version at all.
The real meat comes with the end game events which so far I've only seen the Unbidden in my 200 hours of play but there are others that are triggered by certain research or anomolies that I won't spoil, those can be good fun and sometimes unnerving. Though its somewhat let down by the victory conditions, two of which are controlling planets (Federation, Conquest) or removing all other Empires (Domination.)
I've only played with the Utopia DLC but even that I feel was far too overpriced for what it added (£15 when the base game was £17.) The structures are all but worthless as the stage you unlock the technology is generally when the game is all but over and having extra populace or greater speed researching repeatable tech is meaningless. The Sentry Array can be useful for spotting enemy fleets and the Dyson Sphere for power, again if you've reach that point they're practically moot. I would advise holding off on any DLC purchases until they come down in price by at least half, to do otherwise is simply giving a thumbs up for overpriced content.
Putting it all together I'd say Stellaris is a medicore game, neither bad nor great at what it does. What good features it possesses are readily countered by its shortcomings. Still I would recommend this for anyone who enjoys 4X games or Empire builders, though if you are looking for greater depth I would suggest Sins of a Solar Empire or Civ 5 as Stellaris is far too shallow to keep the tactical mind engaged.

SLRR is a game about building, repairing and modifying cars. If you like cars or want an in-depth understanding on how cars work, buy this game.
The game starts by giving you a garage, a small sum of money and the ability to visit a used car lot/salvage yard to purchase your first wreck of a car.
Working on cars is the core element of the game. Vehicles are incredibly detailed with dozens of swappable components. You'll spend about 70% of your time in the garage trying to make your car go as fast as you can afford. The remaining 30% is spent on actually driving your car around a GTA-esque city, earning money by doing street races during the day and drag races at night (hint: drag races are more profitable by several orders of magnitude), running away from police if they try to pull you over as well as trying to keep the parts on your car that you spent the last 30 minutes saving up for from falling off.
By doing races, you gain 'reputation' and are able to move up the metaphorical ladder and compete with more challenging opponents at higher stakes. Your goal is to reach the top of this ladder. After about one in-game night of winning at drag races, you'll unlock professional track events. Track races can be done alongside street and drag races, but they're only available during the day. The game stops being GTA and (briefly) becomes almost like Gran Turismo, where you race around a dedicated racetrack with sports cars, rally cars and, towards the end of the game, racecars.
Understandably, there are parts of the game that have not aged so well from 2003. Graphics are sub-par at best, and crashes and hangs happen relatively often, and saves are sometimes corrupted by updates. The Steam edition comes with a different soundtrack than the original game, due to copyright issues. Very surprisingly, there is an active fan-based community that continuously implements new features as well as develops the game to support modern OSes. Updates come every month or so and there is extensive mod support for SLRR.
The price is $6. For a pretty fun game that is still being actively developed, this is a bargain.
8/10 from me.

I rarely review stuff, but this game merits it.
I'm not really a fan of JRPGs.  Generally, they're just not my thing.  It's also uncommon for me to pay full price for a game.  But something about it caught my eye (other than 2B's butt), and I can comfortably say it's worth every penny.
It has traditional RPG elements like leveling up, doing side quests, upgrading weapons, etc.  The combat is fairly fast-paced, and while not overly complicated, it held my interest.  At first, the changes from third person RPG to bullet hell to 2.5D side-scroller were kind of jarring, but you get used to them pretty quickly.
The director, Yoko Taro, is a pretty eccentric guy, and it shows.  The game has a lot of personality, from the ridiculous 21 joke endings to the witty dialogue.  Keep in mind, the game requires multiple playthroughs.  When you get Ending A, you're not even close to done.  Route B, playing through as 9S, is essentially the same thing with added bits of backstory to various things like bosses and areas that weren't explained in the initial playthrough.  Route C is where the story and characters really kick off.  The phrase "tragically beautiful" comes to mind.
In my opinion, where the game really shines is its story and characters.  The writing is wonderful, the characters are engaging, and by the end it's difficult not to be emotionally invested.
Speaking of which, fair warning:  this game will rip out your soul, curbstomp it, put it back together, throw glitter all over it, and hand it back to you.  No other game has made me cry like a little girl this many times.  Maybe I'm a softie, I dunno.  The ending sequence in particular hit me like a freight train, in part because of the music.
Speaking of the music, NieR's soundtrack is one of the best video game OSTs I've heard.  It's just plain awesome.
The PC port does have some technical issues that you may or may not encounter, though.  Originally, I had an issue with the game not displaying at 1920x1080, instead being a smaller screen with large black borders.  There's a very quick user-made fix for it, and after that I had no problems running it whatsoever.
Overall, it's a fantastic game, and has earned a place among my absolute favorites.
Come for 2B's butt-drying mechanics, stay for the soul-crushing story.

Very fun and well-made motocross simcade, but does have its drawbacks still very relevant to the first MXGP.
Pros:
-Bikes aren't as heavy anymore, better control is allowed overall.
-Bike customization is pretty great, in a genre where customization of your bike is fairly scarce.
-All licensed bikes/gear/aftermarket parts
-Tutorials can really help complete newbies get into it, which will help the series flourish and thus more revenue for a better title next time around.
-Stadium Series (supercross) are fun, albeit there's only 4 tracks.
But it's not without its glaring flaws, that the company -did- seem to not address because focus was immediately shifted to MXGP3.
Cons:
-No 2 strokes.
-AI are definitely on rails, the exact same rut gets horridly deep by lap 2 every race.
-AI weight seems to be 20x yours, you're very easily taken down by AI riders, making it much less enjoyable to be in the pack.
-Still performance issues/unoptimization, reflective surfaces flicker and isn't fixable, etc etc.
-Tracks are very obviously widened on the Stadium Series, and some Nationals even seem a little too wide.
-Bike physics, are honestly still pretty bad this time around. Mx Vs Atv Alive was better.
-Again, no 2 strokes. I know the reason for it but I'm still upset.
All in all, on sale, the game's definitely a fun pick-up motocross simcade racer, with a pretty in-depth career for what it is. Hopefully MXGP3 showcases what this team is capable of, and carries better support.

This game is not for everybody, and certainly has a specific player base. The player base of which I speak are those who play terraria and spelunky, for Magicite seems to bring with it characteristics found in both games. The player travels through a levels, gathering resources and using a simplified crafting system to quickly craft gear that will help the adventurer explore further, or if crafting isn't your thing there are periodically village levels that allow you sell and buy gear that you might not otherwise have access to until further in the game.
Each character in the game is unlocked through completion of certain tasks and acts almost as in an game trophy. All characters  belong to one of 3 classes, all of which have there perks and disadvantages. The game lacks an emersive story and develops itself more like an arcade game where the player competes with himself or friends to do better than his previous runs. The game is challanging and certainly takes a great deal of time to master, and complete, and for this reason Magicite can be very frustrating. It is, however, easy to control and easy to learn, just hard to master.
The game overall is fun especially if you enjoy adventure based 2D survival games, especially those related to terraria or spelunky. Though the game can very frustrating you can still have an amazing experience for hours on end just trying to earn new characters or beat the game, and for this reason I do recommend it to those already experienced with games in this genre, or those looking to get established and a feel for this genre of game.

This is a great RPG for people who embrace the New Game + grind.  NG + changes the game from an easy flowing overleveled experience into a more difficult battle feeling underleveled and undergeared at all times.  Rolling over the perk points might sound overpowered and easy but it will feel like the only thing keeping you alive for a good while.  I played every dungeon, as I got to them, on new highest difficulty and it was much more challenging and satisfying.  You will no longer be able to walk through normal mobs with ease and unlike the first playthrough you will need to think more about strategy and team compositions.  Even in the endgame dungeon you will be 3 to 4 levels lower than the mobs since you are capped at 30 and they are not.  Worthwhile time investment to get to NG + where the real challenge can begin.

Early Access Review
Well, early days yet for this game, and it's made by one guy, though despite this it shows much promise. However, I give it my recommendation because of this, and in spite of it's various flaws.
The skill system could use some work. A lot of it is cookie-cutter. Main Skill + Mana Reducing effect. I am not exageratting when I say every class follows this path, so the early hours of the game are mainly spamming a single skill. And why do I need to dump 10 skill points into that skill for it be usable? I should be spending those points on getting new abilities which will vary the game play.
The combat, outside of character building, is simple, but satisfying. Screen shakes, enemies explode all over the place, kill chains keep you moving (would love the timer bar from D3 in there!). That's all good stuff.
The itemization is also fairly solid, with some neat items to find, and while nothing mind blowing or game changing, there is a certain level of character customization to be found in what gear you decide to wear. Healing vs. Damage vs. Utility.
I give it a tentative recommendation. I will probably keep an eye out and keep playing, but hopefully over time, the skill system could get a closer look to enable more varied combat between classes and skill trees.
There is some stiff competition in terms of ARPGs these days, and even a tiny indie project must consider that, because you're fighting for that time. I would like to see this game do things a little differently, offer something fresh, as opposed to the same things found in AAA ARPGs, but at a smaller and pixelated scale.

Hello,
The main reason I'm givingthis a negative review is the mouse hit detection is very inaccurate. In other words, even if I click on a cell to move it, just as often as not, the cell will not move, as if the game refuses to register the hit. I've had to click a single cell multiple times to get it to register, and many times, it never does, only to turn into a virus.
The second reason is some of the sounds, at least to me, are VERY sad and depressing. Through the game, there's a sound that reminds me of a dog, or even a baby, crying, and this makes me sad. And game sounds basically NEVER make me sad. Only a few games, that I've ever even heard of, have sounds like this, and this game is very much one of them.
Not to mention that at any time during a game, things could cascade and the game could end very quickly, with nothing that can be done to at least try to from this.
My suggestions:
1) Get rid of, or replace the sad sounds with something not so sad.
2) Have the cell under the mouse cursor shimmer some, before it's even clicked, simply by being under the cursor. That way you know what will happen when you click.
3) Improve the mouse cursor hit detection.
4) Add some more variety in levels, etc. You could vary the color of the cells as well.

Is the title "Little Cells", or "Fully Bugged Little Cells"? Whatever. Little Hemorrhoid Donuts is a game where you rub two same colored one-eyed hockey pucks together to make them disappear. It has a wonderful art style and a motif that rivals Dr. Mario. It's also a one-handed, mouse only game, so if you're looking for something to do when you can't be bothered to get more than one hand involved, this could be the game for you.
There are three colors in total and any two differently colored cells that bump into each other will create another cell. Based on that alone, you would think you can just randomly throw the cells around and get a high score, but that's not the case. If a cell bumps into too many differently colored cells, it will die and you loose a lot of points. So kudos to the developer(s) for forcing the player to actually put some effort into it. A cell can also die if has been alive for too long. If it dies in this fashion, it will become a virus which will infect any cells that bump into it, and those cells will become viruses too. If too many viruses are on the screen, the game is over. It's a concept that is super easy to learn, but very difficult to master.
And that's pretty much where the praise ends. What makes Little Cells so difficult to master is the fact you simply can't win. You WILL lose each level. Period. The longer each level goes on, the faster new cells die and become viruses. As more viruses fill the screen, the darker it becomes which makes it very difficult to tell what color each a cell is, and even if it's a cell at all and not a virus.
There is also no objective, other than try to rack up as many points as possible before your inevitable failure. WHEN you lose a level, all of those points are dumped into upgrades. You get the first upgrade pretty quickly. After that Little Fails immediately turns into a MASSIVE grindfest. I've only been able to get the first two upgrades, the second of which was just an extension of the first and seemed completely ♥♥♥♥ing useless. I'm not saying all upgrades are useless, I'm just saying I wouldn't be surprised if that was the case.
What's really disappointing is it just seems like Little Smells is incomplete. It has a good enough gimmick going for it but not much is done with it. There's only one map, only one game mode, only one objective, only one reason to keep playing. The entire game is just one level you keep playing over and over and the only way to beat it is to quit and uninstall the game. There are tons of games with one very simple game mechanic, but they work with that mechanic to get the most out of it. Little Cells just gave up too soon.
But none of that is why I'm giving it a negative review. Nope. I'm giving Little Cells a negative review because I saw almost everything it had to offer in the first 5-10 minutes. I had to force myself to keep playing, at least long enough to get the second upgrade, and I was bored to death almost the entire time. I spent a dollar on it when it was on sale and I honestly still feel like I overpaid. Little Cells has potential to be so much more and I hope one day the developers will see that potential, too.

Cyber City is an experimental low-budget scifi horror retro visual novel.
The most striking aspect is its low-budget production: pixelated stock photos (perhaps so they can't be traced to the copyright holders?), sound effects reminiscent of the 8-bit era, soundtrack almost entirely from the free music site
, and the text is a very rough translation from the Russian original. All of this fails to obscure that the plot is disjointed and can't decide if it wants to be futuristic, medieval, calming, horror, or philosphical.
Technically, the game took me half an hour for the first runthrough, then another half hour to explore the other branches. The game has more save slots than it has decision points, and it autosaves at all of them. It runs windowed or fullscreen and works well on older systems. The game could be a third its size if it compressed its PNG files - and it is made with ren'Py, so it definitely can load them.
Like any experimental artwork, it is hard to make sense of this one. I simply can't decide whether the meaning got obscured by all the technical shortfalls mentioned above, or if there never was any to begin with. Maybe if the translation was better...
I do not recommend playing this game in English, and probably not in Russian, either.

I'd like to express how much I like this game but emotions are prohibited.
Time for an actual review:
Not having played the first NieR (on PS3 I think?) I was a bit skeptical regarding whether this game would be a direct continuation and I'd be lost - no worry, it's not, from what I can gather it hints and includes previous events but these aren't absolutely significant to the overall story in automata.
But thank god I've played this game. Actually playing a game where you can feel the passion and dedication of the developers is so refreshing, they really have pulled off a masterpiece here.
I'll begin with graffiks, firstly the port isn't absolutely amazing, it runs alright on my meme-tier rig of FX-6300 @3.7Ghz, R9 270x 4gb, 8Gb 1600Mhz RAM, 144hz monitor but know some have had issues. I generally hit 60fps all the time apart from very intense battles and cutscenes are set at 30fps.
The enemy character models are decent, good enough that you can tell♥♥♥♥♥♥from face but not groundbreaking which I don't mind - I'd rather have something run at 60fps than something that looks outstanding but is extra janky.
Friendly character models are a lot nicer, more detailed and higher quality than enemies (likely due to quantity of enemies at once), weapon particle effects are actually amazing, best use I've seen of the effect.
Environment is very pretty and immersive relative to the premise but the textures aren't groundbreaking again, it doesn't matter though the game itself is completely impelling and really gets you wrapped up in the world.
Gameplay is phenomenal, I mean absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant, I've just completed my first playthrough and can't wait to do it all again. Combat is never boring or repetitive, there's a real charm to the way the androids handle themselves and fling about compared to the janky movements of the machines.
Fighting mechanics maps light and heavy attacks (heavy swapped for hacking on scanner models), with certain weapons having better stats for each, although it's up to you what playstyle you want, I personally mapped two fast weapons but upgrading longswords makes them a lot faster.
The use of camera angles during set pieces is brilliant, I think it was in the first game as well but really mixes things up every so often and I've never seen it used in this way before.
There's also a POD function, so you have a gatling laser or missile system with a powerful special move (I kept the laser because it's OP but the chain looks coolest).
Now lets talk about the sound. My god. I genuinely think this has the best OST of any game ever (with Hotline Miami contending). There's a dynamic range for most tracks depending on whether you're fighting or running and softer melodic versions that really complement the world and make you think about what's happening - City Ruins (quiet) is quite simply beautiful and the language it's spoken in (which is a mix of a few different languages; Gaelic, East Euro, Asian and a bit of English/Dutch) is harmonic but difficult to understand yet makes you feel like you're in their world and really immerses you into the situation.
The story is also on par with the likes of Witcher 3 and Hotline Miami (my two favourite stories of a game - I know HM is weird but I love it) and is really open to interpretation which I think's brilliant, you don't just play the game once and leave. Some people may not like the format the story is told in but once you dig deep it really does blow you away.
The characters are loveable, it's not just generic dudebro and ditzy ho, there's kind of of a swap in roles as battle models are designed like female humans and recons as male although both are competant I found 9S can be a bit annoying but I am an unsociable♥♥♥♥♥♥
Overall this game deserves to be played by anyone who likes anything like an action/fighting game

I can only recommend Stellaris to those who enjoy games with little demand of thought or planning, though it is well made and receiving frequent updates (so far) there is little to do in Stellaris that doesn't involve watching numbers. This lightness of strategy does make it much easier to play online but if you are looking for something requiring deeper thought I would advise against buying Stellaris.
There are 8 total resources in Stellaris that control the might and capacity of your empire. Only Influence is uneffected by any form of building or resource collection.
is your primary "upkeep" pool, it is rarely spent except upon the creation of mechanical populations and private colony ships (if you have the tradition.)
are your "cash" used to build and upgrade everything, with the previous exceptions.
is shared across your empire, if you have none your population will be unhappy and won't grow, if you have surplus it grows quicker. I've not noticed any difference from having +1 excess to having +100.
dictates how fast you research stuff.
only used to purchase traditions, utterly worthless once you've unlocked everything.
is used to run policies, enact edicts, recruit leaders and hold defensive pacts, it's generated at a flat rate which can increased by factions and rivalries with opposing empires.
The key to almost any strategy game is the employment of your populace and I am thankful to say this in one area Stellaris does not skimp on. The planets you colonise have a number of tiles many of which have resources to be exploited and a structure that improves upon it however you are not forced to match the structure to the resource (Too much food? Replace your hydroponics with a science lab etc.) but will lose access to the over written resource.
Your controls over said populace, or "pops" as Paradox named them for some strange reason, range from slavery to full citizenship including robotic and chemically dependent species. The effectiveness of your workers is effected by the traits of each species (strong species gather more materials, intelligent species generate more research) and happiness which can be influenced by various factions that your population can join. The factions themselves usually align to a certain ethic and can be promoted or suppressed at the cost of influence.
In a word, boring. In two words, really boring.
There is only one control you have over combat and that is a single "Retreat" button. You select your fleet, click on an enemy fleet and watch a small bar turn either red or green depending on how the fight is progressing.
In a game where fighting is guaranteed to happen I would've thought more effort would be put into actually controlling it. There are no bonuses to flanking or splitting your fleet, no tactics beyond aggresive or passive, hell you can't even select a formation and don't get me started on trying to split your fleet into classes. It's blob (or Doomstacks as they are called) or nothing.
Sure you can design your ships to a variety of roles and weapons (Missiles, Energy or Mass Drivers) but in the end battleships are the only thing worth building, slap a spinal mounted gigacannon on the front and you've basically won.
To say the combat is disappointing would be a fantastic understatement.
Contact with any alien empire is influenced primarily by your
; Militarist or Pacifist, Authoritarian or Elagitarian, Materialist or Spiritualist, Xenophobe or Xenophile and Hive Minded.
Depending on what combination you have will influence that empire's opinion of you including policies, anything clashing will decrease opinion whilst shared will increase. Hive Minds, being more of a species type than an ethic only get a single reply and typically want to enslave or kill everything regardless.
The combination of opinion, policies and the comparitive strength of your empire will generate an
that will dictate how the opposing empire will respond to requests. Attitude can be changed by accepting requests or offering generous trade deals but some differences simply cannot be overcome.
Fallen Empires are the wildcards of the game, spawning fully teched and with huge fleets from the beginning, they are ticking time bombs of either protection or destruction depending on certain events and what type of fanatic ethos they've been given.
It's a functional system if not a little uninteresting, like everything else in Stellaris its just a numbers game though some of the insults are quite entertaining.
For the most part Stellaris is quite dull, the majority of your time will be spent watching/balancing your resource counters, building up your fleet and awaiting a random choice of technology to research. Things do tend to pick up when you start meeting other empires but again, dependent on the random selection that the game has chosen to populate your universe.
The various ship types are nice to look at but once you hit Battleships everything becomes obsolete and to take anything but Mass Drivers is simply pointless.
There are supposedly tradeoffs to using each kind of weapon type, Missiles being longest range and great tracking/accuracy but can be shot down, Lasers are accurate and powerful against armour but short range with less damage to shields whereas Mass Drivers are long range with poor tracking but have bonuses against armour and shields. In practice however the Mass Drivers simply devastate anything with sheer brute force.
Rather strangely, Energy and Mass Drivers get upgraded versions (Plasma/Disruptors/Matter Disintergrators and Autocannons/Artillery/Flak) yet missiles only get a medium slot only Swarm type and no spinal mount version at all.
The real meat comes with the end game events which so far I've only seen the Unbidden in my 200 hours of play but there are others that are triggered by certain research or anomolies that I won't spoil, those can be good fun and sometimes unnerving. Though its somewhat let down by the victory conditions, two of which are controlling planets (Federation, Conquest) or removing all other Empires (Domination.)
I've only played with the Utopia DLC but even that I feel was far too overpriced for what it added (£15 when the base game was £17.) The structures are all but worthless as the stage you unlock the technology is generally when the game is all but over and having extra populace or greater speed researching repeatable tech is meaningless. The Sentry Array can be useful for spotting enemy fleets and the Dyson Sphere for power, again if you've reach that point they're practically moot. I would advise holding off on any DLC purchases until they come down in price by at least half, to do otherwise is simply giving a thumbs up for overpriced content.
Putting it all together I'd say Stellaris is a medicore game, neither bad nor great at what it does. What good features it possesses are readily countered by its shortcomings. Still I would recommend this for anyone who enjoys 4X games or Empire builders, though if you are looking for greater depth I would suggest Sins of a Solar Empire or Civ 5 as Stellaris is far too shallow to keep the tactical mind engaged.

A fun action rpg of the Diablo/Torchlight variety with nostalgic graphics, random dungeons, lots of loot, and 4 distinct classes. Slightly clunky, but very well-developed for an early access title.
For maximum enjoyment: use a controller, turn up the ambient light in the settings, find a big screen, and invite three friends with three more controllers.
Edit: Having now played Chronicon for over 60 hours and reached level cap, I thought it worthwhile to expand this review.
Chronicon is easily one of the best Early Access titles I've played. The game is well balanced, the classes are already fleshed-out (with 4 skills trees each and plenty of legendaries to enhance each tree), and the level design is random enough that there's always an element of uncertainty (although the very small maps tend to just juggle around enemy variety and placement). The game has pretty solid controller support for both XBox 360 and Steam Controller; I mostly play with the latter.
The local co-op is one of Chronicon's strongest features. I've played a few hours with my brother and my girlfriend and it's a really enjoyable and straighforward experience. Just plug in another controller and go. Be prepared to spend a fair bit of downtown sorting through loot, though.
The updates have been very regular and significant so far. I worry about the amount of sleep the dev is getting. Bug fixes come very quickly and I haven't yet encountered a bug that ruined the game or cost me significant progress.
The plot isn't particularly rivetting, but I've never played an ARPG with an even remotely engaging plot, so this doesn't bother me. We're all here to kill monsters, after all, not read walls of text. And Chronicon's monster-slaying is highly satisfying. This is a game where you butcher hundreds of enemies in one go. The game includes a killstreak mechanic similar to D3's, except in Chronicon you'll quickly find yourself bringing in killstreaks that break 100. On higher levels, you'll find yourself getting closer to 1000.
I highly recommend Chronicon, especially if you're a fan of loot-heavy, dungeon crawling action rpgs but miss the controller support of older console titles like Dark Alliance and Champions of Norrath.

I am one of the MX vs ATV fans that has been waiting a decade for an upgraded Reflex. MVA Supercross was released, and it was garbage. So, I continued to wait. Then, a friend recommended this game. I checked it out on here, and it looked alright, but I held off on buying this game for awhile (admittedly because it is based on european MX). I didn't think that I would enjoy it, so I waited until the game was on sale.
Holy crap, was I suprised! This game is definitely not like the MVA franchise, but it turns out that that may not be a bad thing. Initially, you feel like you are "on rails" (can't turn easily). This was annoying, but I persevered. Also, the AI seemed to be "on rails" also, and they always seemed to win bar-banging incidents. Yet, I continued to give the game a chance...
Ultimately, I discovered the necessity of changing the settings to "Pro" and learning how to setup the bike. It just takes practice. Ultimately, I learned how to throw the bike around, scrub and whip, etc. I am happy I gave the game a chance, as I no longer have to play Reflex (thousands of laps on a dozen tracks gets old).
If you crank up the settings and difficulty, and learn how to control the bike, this game can be very fun! It is the most realistic MX game out there IMO. That being said, it isn't perfect!
Pros:
- Realistic physics
- Realistic career mode
- Real tracks, bikes and riders
- Sponsorships in career mode are a cool, immersive feature
- 250s are under-powered
- Rider customization is great
Cons:
- Number plate font is GOD AWFUL!!! 'Copperplate Gothic' or some crap like that... It's dated and ugly- worse than 'Impact'
- AI take the same EXACT line every lap of every race- always.
- You are easily taken out by AI from the outside during cornering (if you don't rewind and go straight during contact)
- Ruts do not develop anywhere except AI lines
- When riding for a team, you have to wear whatever brand/style of gear their real star rider wears (For example: Red Bull KTM, you have to wear Cairoli's AXO gear in Black/Orange ONLY)
- No american tracks (except Glen Helen), which is not a huge deal, but I am not a huge fan of European tracks and the style of riding they require
- Scrubbing results in you not being able to lean just before landing (which can force you off the course if you were not pointing straight towards your desired direction during take-off)
- Once mastered, the AI are no longer challenging enough (you just win every race, which is no fun)
Overall, this game is awsome! You will not regret buying it. Going back, I would've paid the full $50 USD (or whatever) for this when it first came out. If the developers would improve the AI to make them behave as realistically as the rest of the game, this would be the best MX game to date!

This visual novel has a ton of plot threads across multiple branches, and none of them, including the hook that begins the game, get resolved. It includes themes such as the creation of holographic AI copies of humans called "Molds", endless urbanization to the point where new locations appear without anyone noticing or caring, apathy to the point of confusing strangers for acquaintances, and a sun that, after an unexplained "incident", changes color by rotating in sections throughout the sky instead of setting; none of these ideas are ever fully expounded upon. The few characters that exist never have their arcs finished — sometimes their endings leave more questions than answers. Indeed, several of the story paths conclude on an "End of Side A" screen; if there is a Side B forthcoming, I've seen no evidence of that.
Coupled with photographs intentionally dithered to look like they're being displayed on an old computer monitor, as well as the English script that only barely rises above the cusp of Google Translated legibility, you'd think Cyber City 2157 could only be a project by people who spilled their stream of consciousness into an esoteric project to intentionally fleece and / or baffle anyone who stumbled across it. A quintessential Bad Game masquerading as Art.
Yet, even if that is actually the case, Cyber City 2157 somehow all comes together to create an experience that is strangely pleasing to read — and I use the word 'read' very loosely, as a lot of my amusement came from deciphering what the narrative was trying to communicate in words either too many or too few. The eccentric cast members, while most show up only for one scene, are genuinely compelling, and the eclectic soundtrack fits the journey perfectly. I wouldn't recommend Cyber City 2157 at the normal price, but if you can get it for cheap or free it is a truly unique excursion that I suspect a few of you may end up defining as your
.

Bought this game today, played almost 13 hours straight. Absolutely love it. I don't know what was promised to kickstarter people or whatever, but the fact of the matter is, this is a nice little game. Grab two or three friends and maybe  a few alcoholic beverages and get with it.  As it were, I cannot get enough of this game.
PROS:
Rougelike + multiplayer; it is surprisingly hard to find rogulelikes with good multiplayer.
Addictive: The levels and enemies change enough that each playthrough is just as challenging as the last. Sometimes you have to adapt your tactics because you couldn't find enough magic loot, sometimes you have way too much magic♥♥♥♥♥♥  Each playthrough is a new challenge.
Buggy:  Yeah bugs can be annoying at time, but honestly, most of the bugs we encountered were hilarious. Enemies launching themselves into the air at us using our allies downed bodies, and shops randomly opening when we hit the W key while in a dungeon were some of the more hilarious and sometimes useful ones.
Humor: There are a few fun little humorous easter eggs in the game.  Nothing says fun like TPK in a village safe zone because got a little too greedy with the village livestock.
Stuff: Theres lots of stuff in there, collectable stuff, races, hats, companions, hair-dos. And most of them benefit you in some way. Got a little ghost thing that lets me jump and infinite amount of times. That thing right there is the♥♥♥♥♥♥
Challenging: This game isn't for the light hearted. Get ready to die. A lot. Often right at the beginning. However, once you get going, you're usually golden, until somthing stupid happens and the entire party wipes because one person got downed in a bad spot.
Short: -ish? You can beat a playthrough in an hour if you're quick about it.  There's even an unlockable for it.
CONS:
Buggy:  Yeah some of the bugs were fun, but some were a little frustrating, like being instakilled for landing on a mob just the right way, but honestly, just don't directly on top of mob's heads. This is Super Mario Brothers.  Italian is not a race available for play.  There is not plumber hat.  There is not skinny brother companion. Forget about it.
Content: There is a nice bit of content in this game, but it would be nice to see more. However, I have no idea what the developer has planned for this game. If they just want to bug fix and call it a day, or actually continue adding stuff.
Overall, solid game. I hope to see much more come out of this game and from this developer.

Over 200 hours in and I realized that I haven't written a review yet! Holy cow. Okay, so I've always enjoyed really deep games. I'm not the type that goes for something as simplistic and repetative as Starcraft II. Sure, I'll play through the campaign and even enjoy it, but it's nothing I'll truly get my money's worth out of. Enter any game by Paradox ever. Right off the bat you're overwhelmed by mechanics and they keep adding things on top of that in the form of updates and DLC. This inevitably means there will be bugs, but that's to be expected (looking at you primitive notification spam!) But with the money I've spent on the game and two of the DLC's, it comes out to roughly 35 cents an hour (rounded up). I'd say that's money well spent! And those hours have been enjoyable. My favorite moment in this game, and this is out of many:
- In one of my first games, I'm building up my empire and expanding. I'm the United Nations of Earth, so I'm using my diplomatic skills to ensure all races get along. I'm not expanding my military beyond what I think I would need to defend my few colonies in time for my allies to make short work of the enemy. After all, I'm not a militarist. We need to expand our knowledge through science! What's this? A subspace signal? Interesting. Oh, the Unbidden? Cool looking... you want to feast? Maybe we can negotiate. No? I'm food? What's their military look like? WHAT? One of their fleets is bigger than my navy? Time to build up like crazy! They invade and crush empires that would have made me nervous had they gone to war with me like they were nothing but an annoying fly. The other empires turn a blind eye - they wouldn't dare invade us, so you're on your own. I stand alone. I send in my fleet to intercept and destroy one of theirs'. A small victory! Perhaps a glimpse of hope! Oh. There's four more fleets exactly that size. I retreat, lick my wounds, and pour what little resources I have into bolstering the fleet. I know where their portal is. Crucial intel while hunting for fleets that I could reliably kill to chip away at their military power. But now, knowing reinforcements come through that portal, I have to end this before all hope is lost. I send the fleet on multiple jumps through enemy territory and go straight for the portal. 3/4 health. 1/2 health. All four enemy fleets jump in and start to zero in on my only hope of saving the galaxy. My heart was racing (not being dramatic) and as my fleet engages fleet after fleet, we finally take down the portal. We've cut off their reinforcements. I retreat, and (again, not exaggerating) throw up my hands in excitement. Best gaming moment I've had in years. The underdog wins a desperate battle for all life in the galaxy, and comes out victorious. All I have to do now is go back to my original plan of chipping away at their fleet.
This was back when Stellaris first came out. Now it's more polished, has more features, and more ways things can either go really well or quickly go sideways. Think your empire is doing really well? Think again. This game has surprises in store for you.

Alright, so I've played nearly every Milestone motorcycle game since SBK 2001.
MXGP2 is at the top of the charts for their development history IMO, right up there with SBK 2001 and 2011.
Pros:
- Good graphics.
- Spot-on physics, better than Reflex.
- Great handling, after some practice - and you will need practice...
- Excellent "cockpit" camera view, very well done.
- Third person camera is also good, with adjustable distance (but not angle)
- Good career mode, if a bit bare bones. Choose Full Race Weekends, Qual + Double Race, or simply Double Race.
- Extra modes like MXoN (Moto-X of Nations), Real Events, etc. are nice.
- Bike and rider customization is excellent for the most part.
- Lots of settings for assists, but it's better and faster not to use them. Full sim with Pro physics all the way and don't look back.
- Rewind and Quick Restart features, both of which can be handy (pro tip: keep rewinds on for AI races, they WILL crash into you on occasion). Definitely handy for the holeshot against a pack of AI.
- Lots of tracks, all of them real-world, save the four or so imaginary stadiums which have you doing quasi-Supercross (which is cool).
- Fantastic replay system, but unfortunately you cannot save them to view later.
- You will spend hours in photo mode getting those photo-realistic screenshots (check mine out for examples). Or not, but it's there if you want to.
Cons:
- Typical Milestone "it's barely passable" bike sounds. There's hope for the future though because RIDE 2 just came out and has the best sounds I've heard so far from a Milestone game so maybe MXGP3 will sound better? Pray with me now to the God of MX...
- After whipping or scrubbing you lose air control and have to pray to the aforementioned God of MX that your initial trajectory wasn't garbage.
- When making contact with AI riders, there's a 90% chance to dismount you while they drive on. This can be mitigated somewhat by avoiding extra lean (right stick) while turning if other riders are elbow-to-elbow. Since discovering this I can now make light contact without being thrown off.
- No triple buffered v-sync. Must use Adaptive V-Sync on Nvidia for a tear-free image without terrible frame drops. Not sure what you could do on an AMD card, except suffer. Direct3D Overrider does NOT work as the game is 64-bit. :(
- A few bugs with the Test Track recording lap times, somehow one of my 450s has set a balls-on-fire 9.2 second time on the long track. Seems legit.
- Not many, if any at the time, people playing online. Pretty common with bike games unfortunately, but does support private lobbies for you and buddies.
- Can save and apply custom bike setups, but in typical Milestone fashion, will not apply them for you automatically come race time. Not a deal-breaker at all, but a constant small annoyance (another issue in all Milestone games).
Highly recommended for any and all MX fans. General bike fans will most likely dig it, and other racing fans may as well depending on their taste for realism and motocross. Basically, don't expect to jump on your bike and be fast in this game. Hell, don't expect to make it around your first turn fast and intact until you've got some practice time in. Even then you will get dismounted and ran over by a half dozen or so riders every other holeshot. ;)

This game was such a tasty donut for me. I haven't been so pleasantly surprised in a long time by a game, and I feel like it's necessary to explain how much. I had
interest in this game. The trailer seemed a little bland, although the art style was certainly distinctive, reminding me a bit of Darksiders (as it turns out, this is because they share a common art director in Joe Madeuira), but not enough to draw me in. The game came out, my friends raved about how good it was, but I remained unconvinced. One of them wound up buying the game for me, and then I begrudgingly tried it out... and didn't put it down for hours.
Battle Chasers is clearly a game made with love and is a better title in the classic Final Fantasy turn-based style of RPG than some Final Fantasy games. Combat is satisfying, with attacks having weight to them and half the fun being creating synergies of buffs and debuffs that make your party wildly powerful in combat. The art is gorgeous, with beautiful environments that I never tired of seeing and hand-drawn cutscenes that looked good and evoked Battle Chasers' origins as a comic series. The real gem in this package is the soundtrack, with Jesper Kyd creating perhaps his best work yet.
This game does have a few pitfalls: Combat difficulty can be a bit of a roller-coaster ride, spiking up and dropping down based on gear choices and whether or not you've done enough Arbitrary JRPG Grinding for the area you're in. Conversely, as XP gains are based on challenge, with trivial foes providing no XP at all, you can find yourself in a couple of spots where the answer is to either slam into the wall of difficult content or just grind, baby! The writing is a mixed bag: While there are some touching moments between characters, the greater plot is a Quest for the Magical Plot Device and its clever quips are YMMV: I
the idea that the town is literally called Harm's Way (get it?), but my friends appreciated it.
In short, Battle Chasers isn't reinventing anything, but it's damn good at what it tries to do, and is an excellent entry at the $30 mid-range price point that is well worth the price of admission.

Yeah, Battle Chasers isn't perfect but it's still worth picking up (in time).
Overall, the gameplay is solid.  Mechanics are well thought out and there's a lot of interesting interplay going on for some tactical depth.  There's some wonkiness with how turns work (Selecting abilities and when a non-instant ability fires off are considered two separate turns) which messes with how DoTs, Buffs, and Debuffs function in a way that I don't consider to be intuitive.  There are definitely issues game balance and it's mostly that you can make very simple side-by-side comparisons of abilities and pick a clear winner.  Some abilities don't seem to scale as well as others and its really obvious by the end of the game.  Other than that, Calibretto is Too Damn Good and I don't think he ever left my party.
Overcharge is a good mechanic.  I really appreciate that the game is proper turn-based and not some garbage ATB thing.
The biggest (and currently most commonly brought up) issue with the game is that battles are long and there's a lot of them and it makes dungeons and even overworld travel feel like a slog.  It also aggravates some other issues with the game.  XP isn't shared with non-active party members.  XP Gains are also relatively low for the time spent in battle.  Scaling in the game is fairly steep; damage and hit point values jump up significantly every couple of levels.  Underleveled and undergeared characters are literally dead weight if you bring them into a dungeon (with that said, even corpses in your active party will gain full xp... silver lining?).  All these things put together means that keeping all of your characters leveled up is a humongous chore.  I have just under 3 million games on my backlog, Knolan, I am not going to bother leveling you up old man.
Anyhow, the easiest fix is to have an option to speed up battle animations (2-3x).  I'd also like to see Any % amount of XP given to non-active party members... alternatively, removing level restrictions on equipment would do a lot to alleviate what I will dub as "The Knolan Problem."  Also, Also, I would like to see fewer but more significant fights.  Combo Battles are interesting and there aren't enough of them.
The game is very visually pleasing.  Each character and monster model are detailed and look great.  Attack animations have a real weight to them.  Colors are vibrant and delicious to my eyeballs.  Red Monica's boobs are fine, I don't understand why it's such a point of contention for some reviewers.
The music is okay.  I really like the boss track but the rest of the soundtrack is fairly generic.
The UI is fantastic as long as you're using a mouse to navigate through all the menus.  Otherwise, using your Keyboard or a Controller can be a bit of a hassle.  You can play the game with one hand with the keyboard, which I consider a positive.
Story is pretty sparse.  The character moments you get in the inn are good, but it'd be nice to see more stuff out in the world too.
Overall, I like the game and I like its potential and presentation.  This is the most solid old-school JRPG that I've played in years.  If there's a sequel, I'll kickstart that too.

==========
Chronicon is about a special magical device...a device that creates a link to the memories of the long-forgotten heroes of yore. A link that allows anyone who ventures forth to relive the past lives of those fallen heroes. You are chosen as one of the few this time...and being chosen is a great honor. What will you do now?
Chronicon is an action-adventure RPG, set in a (so far) small, Early Access world. Yes, Chronicon is in Early Access, but if you look past that tag, you might see the potential Chronicon has. Let's take a peek at what it has in store for you.
==========
So you've installed Chronicon and hit Play Game. You are greeted with a selection of 4 unique heroes: Templar, Berserker, Warden, and Warlock. Each one has a very distinct playstyle. The Templar and Berserker are melee characters, the difference being the Templar is defensive and the Berkserker is offensive. The Warden and Warlock are ranged, with their difference being physical offense (bow/arrows) and magical offense. Choose whichever playstyle suits you the best!
Each character has a small 'tree' of skills they can learn and assign to be used on the fly. You can access a new tier of skills every 5 levels. As you level up by killing monsters you gain skill points (1 per level), and you can invest these points into the skills of your choosing. The more points you invest into a particular skill, the more powerful or effective it becomes. Each character has unique skills and passives that can be learned, some offering great benefits, others offering new spells and actions.
At it's core, Chronicon is a dungeon crawler, similar to titles such as Diablo, Torchlight, or Titan's Quest. You explore a locale, kill monsters, collect loot, and level up. There are even some features in Chronicon that you may recall seeing in these other titles, such as the Portal Scroll which gives you a ticket back to the hub to sell your loot. There are also Waypoints, which you can use to traveI back and forth between predetermined points in each area. Speaking of areas, in the hub there are 5 Teleport Orbs, each one representing a dungeon/location. Only the Fallen Temple (first orb) is currently available, and during my 7-8 hours of play none of the other orbs were made available. The Store Page says these additional levels are coming in future updates. I played Chronicon with a controller, and the combat reminded me of a twin stick shooter. You move your character with the left stick, and aim your attacks with the right stick. It works, to be sure, but it was a little awkward for me at first to see this kind of control scheme in a game of this particular genre.
There are a lot of breakable objects, such as pots, urns, and baskets. These can be great for finding hidden loot and crystals (currency) but I felt like they served to padden the game a little bit. There are literally TONS of breakable objects in each stage, but only small groups of enemies scattered through each stage. I would much rather have mowed through hordes of enemies than break a room full of pots. This might be attributed to the fact that the game is still in Early Access, so I was able to look past it. When you did find monsters, it was fun to mow them down however you could, occasionally enjoying a slightly more prolonged encounter with a 'champion' monster. These are quite a bit more powerful than the normal monsters, and drop significantly more loot. Also spread throughout are small shrines, which take the form of statues. When activated, they may give you a buff or heal you, but they can also rarely spawn powerful creatures to attack you.
Certain loot can only be used by certain classes, and a lot of loot has its own special qualities. An item of one type can be very different than another item of the same type, depending on the quality. Try to stay outfitted with the best gear possible for the best chance of survival!
==========
Chronicon has a very distinct sprite-base design. They aren't what I'd call 'basic', but they aren't too terribly detailed either. Don't get me wrong, they look great for sprites, and animations are crisp, clear, and flow smoothly. But don't expect anything special as you play.
The Fallen Temple looked really good...very dark and creepy, as something 'fallen' should be! The monsters fit the theme of the area...ghouls, skeletons, and ghosts running around everywhere. Even some bats thrown in for good measure. All of these have the same quality as the character sprites, and are animated pretty well.
==========
This is easily the game's biggest downside. There is very little in the way of music or sound effects. The Fallen Temple has a low, somber tune that plays, but that's about it. Your attacks, breaking pots and urns, and hitting enemies have sound effects. But nothing else does. If it did, I hardly noticed. I also attribute this to the game being Early Access, so I was able to overlook it. Understanding that this is a very early Alpha build means that not all assets are implemented yet, and I'm sure they will be in the future!
==========
Chronicon ran without any hitches on my medium-tier rig. It should pose no issues to most players. It's not a very intense game, and I don't expect many people to run into any performance issues. Does your kitchen have a toaster? It can probably run Chronicon.
I played entirely with a controller, so I can confirm that it indeed has full controller support. The controls were very easy for me to use, even with the twin stick configuration combat has.
==========
At the end of the day, Chronicon is a decent entry into the action-adventure RPG genre. It's by no means the best, but it's not terrible. It's worth checking out and at least keeping an eye on as it develops further. With a handful of playable classes, lots of loot to collect, and small hordes of enemies to mow down, you should have a great time exploring the memories of past heroes. Future updates plan to include crafting, more quests, more items, a hardcore mode, and the 4 additional chapters currently missing from the hub. If you want to help this game out and see it suceed, please, by all means give it a purchase to support the devs! This is what Early Access is all about.
