Το MXGP2 πιθανώς είναι συνολικά το καλύτερο motocross videogame που έχουμε δει μέχρι σήμερα.
A perfect example of how one studio can improve a game, based on the players’ remarks, without ruining anything of the elements that worked well on its previous versions. MXGP2 is possibly the best motocross videogame until today.

Gameplay is more realistic when comparing to other motocross games such as Reflex, Alive, Supercross ENCORE, and MUD, etc. For example, you have control over the dirtbike's clutch, rear brake, front brake, and can shift gears manually. Also, use the left stick to control the bike and the right stick to control the rider's movements. All of these controls really matter as you approach certain parts of the tracks such as hairpin turns, berms, jumps, etc. Moving on, during a race, you have sessions such as practice or qualifying and then the actual race that conists of two heats.
Scrubs and whips look pretty good.
Use a Xbox controller to play.
Career mode is great. Compete in MX2 and MXGP with up to 18 national tracks. Also, create your own custom team or join an official team. If you create a custom team, earn a reputation and sponsers. Either route you take, you must meet certain expectations of that team/sponser or be fired. For example, your sponser may ask that you gain a certain amount of points or do better than a competitor during the current race week. Each race has two heats (as stated before) with each heat offering a maximum of 25 points. At the end, you will either move up or down in the MX2/MXGP season rankings.
BEST graphics seen for a motocross game. Check out my screenshot for example!
Customization is fun and awesome, but it would be nicer if there were more brands or things to choose from as far as gear goes and bike parts. I'm hoping for a modding community to start up to cover this.
There is a lovely test track for you to play around on or test your new customized bike.
You can now race on supercross tracks.
The A.I. can be challenging. Overall, they can make you feel like you're having a battle or that you have to work hard for first place.
There's cool stastitics tab within the main menu that shows your race results such as the number of times that you took first place, second, or third etc.
2560x1440p support, the first MXGP did not have offical support of this resolution.
There are some other neat modes like, "real events" that have you relive moments from real life MXGP 2015. Also, there's a game mode for monster energy FIM MXoN which is a "team event scheduled at the end of the FIM Motocross World Championship, in which the riders compete representing their own country."
The A.I. can be an unstoppable force. In other words, they will knock you off of your bike easily if they touch you while turning. Also, the A.I. (all of them) take the same lines while racing. Overall, these two issues with the A.I. can make playing singleplayer extremely annoying or frustrating.
When I tried multiplayer, the A.I. as well as real players were bugged. For example, the arms to their riders were moving awkwardly which was kind of distracting. I suggest racing without A.I. when online. Overall, the online gameplay was still playable. I had no lag issues.
I've noticed that certain A.I. riders always finish in the top 10 or 5 which can make the gameplay feel repetitive since I always know who to expect behind me or battling with me.
Falling off the track (even if you can easily hop back on) can reset your bike and rider making you loose your position in the race.
Attempting to clear doubles or triples can feel/look akward or tough. The same goes for turning. There's so many hairpin turns in this game and so much lack of legit berms to rail. Sometimes I get really frustrated since I have to really slow down to make some of these turn otherwise I will turn so wide that I loose ground against the other racers. Overall, turning in this game can feel realistic and unrealistic at times.
The sounds of the bikes are really terrible. Also, there's no great music within the menu or during a race. No real bands/singers or anything like that.
This game is worth it if you are a motocross fan. I believe that MXGP2 is the BEST motocross game to come out SINCE Reflex. (I never liked the first MXGP).

I will preface this by saying, I enjoy the game, I sing, and I'm well versed in the genre in my opinion.
Unfortunately this game is fairly questionable.  The pitch detection tends to be all over the place as it's picked up my non-vocalised coughing as a part of a song. On top of that the intros, and subsequently exits, for a lot of the lyrics could be greatly improved, in a lot of songs it can be from .2 to .5 seconds ahead where the actual music is.  There is a distinct lack of quality here in comparison to console karaoke games like SingStar.
Minor complaints:
-A handful of songs have non-sung parts that you still have to speak.
-The song menu has questionable UI, you have to click every song and you can't scroll or use arrow keys by default.
-Playing random songs in the pause menu is rather distracting and annoying, you tend to pause for a reason and putting a completely different song in someones head is not a good idea in a karoake game.
-The track list has a lot of good, but many terrible songs to sing, this is not a judgement of whether the song is good or bad but whether the song is good or bad to sing.  If the track list were, lets say, 100 songs this would be less of a problem, but the track list length isn't one of my complaints.
Overall I'd give it a 5/10, completely enjoyable but definitely not good, with it's glaring flaws, minor annoyances, and the fact things like Karaokeparty already exist online for the pc and things like singstar exist on consoles.  This is just a weak entry to the genre of karaoke games, and while it may be the 'PC's first' it's probably going to be end up being known as the PC's worst.

For a game that has combat completely unlike a World of Warcraft clone, almost everything else feels like you're playing WoW all over again. And mostly the BAD parts of WoW at that. Few gamers want to do the pointlessly tedious "press a button and wait for a few seconds, rinse and repeat" quest mechanics for hours on end. There are some seriously TERRIBLE quest mechanics that frequently have me walking away thinking "that's not fun at all, why the hell would you waste your time on that?"
Same with the challenge system: it sounds great at first. Walk around a map and you'll stumble on a side objective with some rewards. Usually it's just killing stuff like a quest, at best it might be something like using bouncy mushrooms to scale a cliff. Far too many challenges involve going up to objects, pressing F, waiting a second or two, and doing it again a few dozen times. Years ago, we all put up with that boring garbage when we played WoW because we were addicted, we loved the game, and we didn't really care. Now we care, and many of us don't feel compelled to waste our time on game mechanics that simply are not fun.
That basically sums up my thoughts on the crafting system, too: they tried to be clever by making a more-involved system to fine-tune your crafted gear, but when you're just trying to skill up or do crafting quests it makes for a lackluster time sink with way too much unnecessary clicking. Oh, and there's a salvage system so you can scrap old gear for raw materials which sounds great. But you have to salvage gear individually, and the UI literally "lags" for a second on the Salvage button which adds up to even MORE time staring at a screen and watching bars fill up. There's a fine line where nostalgia meets unfun game mechanics, and WildStar crosses that line far too many times than the devs probably realized.
Maps are incredibly detailed with lots to explore, unfortunately you aren't rewarded enough for actually exploring them so you have to do the boring quest system to actually level up at any reasonable pace. Don't be too surprised if you end up thinking about how you're going to have fun while leveling up in this game.
If you play this for a few hours, you'll see exactly why the player base has been dwindling, and it's a damn shame IMO. This game could have been THE next-best MMO, but they included too many bad aspects of World of Warcraft when they didn't need to at all. For every awesome part of this game there's something that makes you wonder what the heck the devs were thinking. If you try out WildStar you can have a lot of fun with the combat and player housing, just make sure you're actually having a good time and not just running around pressing F and questioning what the hell you're doing with your life.

Greetings!  I had hoped to review this game much sooner but at the same time wanted to play the game to conclusion.  So, 99 played hours later…what do I think?  Really?  99 hours played and you think what?  I didn’t like the game.  Silly reader… To be transparent I want to say that I backed this game on Kickstarter and am a huge fan of classic JRPG style games.  Suffice to say I played for 12 hours straight the day this game was released.
Haven’t seen your kind around here:  What we have here is a genuine classic RPG from the days of the early Final Fantasy’s with modern mechanics, graphics and storytelling from an indie development staff looking to accomplish this very task.  And…I love it.  The game is more difficult than many RPGs (and I enjoy this) overall, though many optional bosses in some games easily trump that.  The game also includes development for each of the 6 playable characters with equipment, perks, and abilities.  None of the characters play the same or even fulfill the roles in the way you’d typically see.  For example there are three characters with healing, each have minor mechanics that make them very unique despite having the goal of restoring hit points.  The game also explains things, not in a tutorial way (there is a small one and an online book) but in information provided through tooltips and having  clean, understandable mechanics giving you the ability to fine tune what you want your party to do and how best to attack an encounter.
Blood for the Blood God, Skulls for…wait what:  This game definitely draws from a lot of inspiration.  From items, plot points and even the music this game feels like it was made by a group that loves gaming in all its forms.  It was done so well, so seamless that I caught myself going ‘wait, is that a tribute or am I looking too deep’.  Every step of the game felt like a familiar game but fresh and exciting at the same time.  I can’t wait to see what they do for expansions and possibly sequels.  I wish more games would also use the same method to do conversations.  Yes, highly detailed cinematics are great and fun but let’s not waste the entire budget on them.  I’m perfectly okay with beautifully drawn characters in freeze frame talking across each other (though I would have like to have heard more voice over’s).
There's your problem:  So what are the problems?  To begin with (as of this review) there is an odd stuttering issue affecting many players.  It’s not a huge issue but the game will freeze for what is probably a millisecond or so but both Steam and other third party frame-rate programs don’t seem to detect it.  This seems to happen mostly on the world map and aside from that my computer ran the game at 35-60 fps without issue.  There are a few other minor issues:  The one I found the most annoying is what appears to be a lack of items throughout the game, primarily in the beginning levels.  Many times I’d have a level 6+ character running around with level 3 items.  Though not a huge issue I’d like to see more items released.  One slight annoyance is the game doesn’t seem to have any level 30 items, I found all the ultimate weapons (Gully’s quest for hers really needs to be revamped, I shouldn’t have to farm low level dungeons for random encounters).  I’d also like to see the way that rooms are randomized revamped, I think going through a dungeon three times should be more than enough to see every room, maybe I’m wrong.  The inventory manager could use an overhaul, makes no sense to have multiple locations for weapons, armor and accessories.  To be fair all these complaints are easily fixed and I am confident they will be, the developers are very vocal on the forums and are releasing patches frequently.
It’s not really complicated, if you like RPGs, especially those of the classic ATB style you need to get this game.  I’d argue you should buy it at full retail if nothing else than to support the developers with the hopes of more content down the road.  The game does have a few small bugs (I can’t complete the bestiary due to a choice I made much earlier in the game) and I’d like to see a few changes but the game is worth every penny that is asked, highly recommend.  I did want to note real fast that I have not begun the New Game+ my goal is to give the game a few months for new content, balances and bug hunting before starting a new game.

I had this game on wishlist since march 2016 so i wa a little hyped when it finally come out.
Maybe too much...
Dont get me wrong,i liked the game but some QOL improvements are really needed.
The game is a classic JRPG with a simple story and gorgeous art style.
If you dont care about achievements and 100% you'll get between 20-30 hours out of it, without the need to grind.
I completed each of the 8 dungeons 2 times for an achievement but with the latest patch you can select directly the hardest difficulty if you want.
Otherwise you'll be fine running them only 1 time, i was never severely underleved and if i was i just did some of Hunt sidequest with really no need for an insane grind.
The real time sink for me was the 100% : i spent almost 20 hours trying to find 2 monsters and 1 fish in the related minigame, it was really frustatring and almost took out of me the joy i had playing until then.
There is a nice crafting system for weapon/armor, potions and enchantments : a very simple "side job".
The major flaws for me were the speed of some things ( end of combat animation, nice  first time, really boring the 1000 times after, even mashing the skip button ... it doesnt skip enough ) like the movement on the map ( there's fast travel at least ), said map without any indication or names of places and your position.
Each of the six character is flexible and can do 2 roles ( usually everyone can dps and then make as tank or healer ) but once you have your party the non selected members dont level up at all. As i said i had no need to grind so i always kept the same 3 people til the end. And it's a pity cause each character has abilities that synergize well with othe teammates but you are not incentivized to experiment, unless you farm to level up unused characters.
NG+ was not challenging at all ( but i dont care, i'm not an hardcore player ) because even if you lose all gear and levels you start with all 6 characters from the start and with all the perk levels ( perk are like talents ) so if you played well on NG they'll be powerhouses on NG+.
It was a breeze and i only die 3 times on the final boss ( these were the only 3 deaths on Ng and NG+ combined ).
Even with these little problems the game is worth it, the combat is nice and the journey overall enjoyable.
Just keep in mind that If you want to 100% the achievement you'll face a lot of hours of boring grind at max level.

Best $5 I've ever spent. I only wish I knew about this game sooner. It's a bit buggy, but still one of the more rewarding and enjoyable racing games I have played.

The racing itself honestly feels pretty unbalanced, but I find that most of the fun here is to be had in the customization and tuning, and once you figure out how to build up a fast car, it becomes very easy to beat your opponents.
Overall, I think this is a must own for any racing game fan that wants to really get under the hood and personalize every single piece of their car, even though it's a bit old, the cars are unlicenced and the game is a bit unstable and buggy, it's still very easy to look past these issues and still have a very unique experience.
8.5/10.

This was a game i so badly wanted to enjoy, but didnt.
The art and animations are positively GORGEOUS and quite simply some of the best I've ever seen in an rpg.
But there are so many weird things holding it back that I just couldnt trudge forward anymore and bailed.
1. The combat is built around using basic attacks to build "overcharge" aka free mana, and mana recovery on its own is very very rare. This encourages kind of boring gameplay as you cant use abilities often or you risk running the mana dry long before you ever have a chance to get more.
2. skills are wildly imbalanced. Some heals will heal your group for literally like 1% of your health? Why is it so weak? Some shields are STRICTLY better than other shield skills, some attacks are STRICTLY better than a similar attack in your same arsenal, and its just oddly imbalanced and shows lack of attention to detail.
3. Exploration is a complete nightmare. You dont have access to a map except in designated spots, and even in the overworld nothing is labelled until you are on top of it, and you can only scroll the map in a small radius from where you are. There is also no legend for anything on the map so you dont have a clue what some of the icons indicate. This is the main reason i quit playing, as i was spending ungodly amounts of time just trying to figure out where the hell i needed to go.
4. Inbalanced difficulty. Some fights you can win in a couple hits, others will nearly knock a party member flat in a single turn, in the same spot in a dungeon or on the map. There are also some side-bosses with a recommended level notice, which is just plain wrong. I went to two of them at their "Recommended level" and they quite literally one-shot my entire team, through a group shield.
It's just not a good game. It drew me in with the gorgeous aesthetic and then let me down nearly everywhere else.

It took me a while to write this review.  I wanted to give the game ample time to get fun before I offered a knee-jerk reaction based on unreasonable expectations.  My assessment: NBA 2k17 is a supermodel.  Looks very good on the surface, but still the same dumb blonde underneath.  The most frustrating part about the game is that it comes so close to being a genuine basketball simulation, but then it decides "nah, I'd rather act like a video game."  There are moments when you pull of a great play and it works the way you intended and you pump your fist like it's a real basketball game.  Sadly, there are too many moments when the computer (on Superstar or higher) will simply not allow you to score and won't allow you to stop the other team when it decides "let's make the game close so we can build a false sense of suspense, because 2K fans are too stupid to notice that we make them struggle to score in EVERY 2nd and 3rd quarter, then we flip a switch and they hit everything and they feel excited when they come back.  Cool, right?"  No 2K, not cool.  Let me blow out teams that I should blow out based on my skill level and the level of talent on my team rather than making severely overmatched teams like Brooklyn and Philly play like the Spurs because you think I want to be challenged.  It defeats the purpose of trading and roster moves and training if my guys are going to play down to their opponent every game.  Also, we notice when the AI-controlled teammates in both My GM and My Player decide their going to stand in the lane and play off deadly shooters just so the CPU can get easy baskets.  We tell the guy to play him tight, and our teammates play off anyway, cause....suspense.  We pick the guy to stop that from happening and hope our PGs can contain enough to stop the other teams PG.  They fall asleep.  We get the PG on the Pick and Roll and our center runs in place as is man rolls and gets layup after layup.  It's not fun for those of us who like defense.
The presentation of this game is beautiful--the menus, the pregame, the stat tracking--and it was a smart move to take away the silly MyPlayer angles that made that mode convoluted.  But again, the AI is too stupid for this game to pretend it's a simulator.  It could possibly trick a casual fan who sees LeBron looks just like LeBron and says its the greatest game ever, but for us die-hard hoop fans, it's like watching that beautiful supermodel stumble off the runway right before she pulls off a perfect turn.
Will this game ever be on sale anytime soon?

A lot of talk is spread about hardcore gamers and casual ones. Some seem to really dislike casual games just because they are just that, casual. My opinion? A game can be "casual" and still be a solid experience as long as it does it's idea well. Peggle is one of those examples. From the get-go it's pleasant to look at and the sounds and music are satisfiying. The gameplay is simple. Fire a ball and try to hit all 25 pegs with only 10 balls. Yup, that's it. You do get diffrent powers from the characters availble, which vary on it's usefulness depending on the level. You can also get more shots by building points with one ball.
When it's all said and done, this is simple and fun. And that's all it needs to be. It also has plenty of content to keep you busy for a while. As for the cons, some of the powers are uninteresting. Tula for example gets rid of 20% of the orange pegs, and I only found a use for that power in the challenge mode levels with more orange pegs. Most are fun however, though I can see people loving the powers I do not and vice versa. Another issue is the gameplay does have a little bit of luck involved since it's difficult to know where the ball will go. Now this is fine overall as it's part of what makes it addictive. But the challenge modes can get frustrating due to this, since much of it requires you to do things that may not pan out for you. But overall this was a fun experience. I can see myself relaxing and playing it much more in the future.

Some games seem to be labelled into categories which don't quite do them justice...
While this is predominantly advertised as a casual puzzle game thanks to its rainbow jollies, it's cartoon critters each with their own unique garden gnome smile so wide that the joker would be jealous and its accompanying overture concerto that explode your eardrums with happy music every time you do something right. Make no mistake about it, this game is also one of the most ridiculously challenging puzzle games out there. More challenging than trying to find the G spot on a grizzly bear with the lights off, more challenging than trying to round up people at a sleep walkers convention, yes even more challenging than trying to keep a straight face when your spouse says "do I look fat in these jeans?"
Seriously so Hard-core is this game for those that like to 100% things, that nothing less than perfect skilled shot marksmanship will suffice. The casual side of the game only requires you to clear 25 orange pegs from 100 blue pegs placed in an assortment of novelty positions in correspondence to each levels background picture. Out of the 55 levels from the game's main "Adventure" mode, each level requires you to skilfully aim 1 of 10 balls from a ball launcher placed in the middle at the top of the screen and try and get all the orange pegs without losing all the balls at the bottom of the screen. To accomplish this it is crucial to either hit a number of orange pegs with each shot, hit 1 of the 2 green peggle masters pegs placed on the screen allowing you a special ball super power, or get the ball to be retrieved in a ball catcher which moves horizontally at the bottom of the screen. Failure to clear the board of all orange pegs will require the player to restart the level, while completing this objective will offcourse allow the player to progress forward to the next level.
Every five levels you will be introduced to a new peggle master, a cartoon character with a smile as wide as the Mariana Trench that can help the player with its unique special ability when the green pegs are struck. There is also a potential for the award of an extra ball if a high score is achieved with each shot. There are a number of ways to accomplish this… hit a large number of pegs on a given turn, strike two orange pegs quite some distance from each other, or hit a purple score multiplier peg.
Hard-core gamers though will be much more interested in the challenge mode requiring players to complete levels under strict excruciating requirements, for instance trying to score 750,000 on one level alone, or to beat the very tricky ai. Finally for those that have achieved all challenges in challenge mode can also attempt to clear 'ALL' Pegs on all 55 levels in Adventure mode giving them the coveted Ultra Extreme Fever peggle master trophy while Ode to joy victory cries through your loud speakers.

Peggle Deluxe is one of my favorite casual games and one of the few things EA could ever not mess up. Fun for all ages and a blessing for your wallet, this is definitely something you should check out if you're into casual experiences.
Story: As to be expected from a game like this, the story is quite minimal and unimportant. You play as a peggle student on their way to becoming a master at the game. Each time you pass through a phase of the game, you'll be instructed by a new professor who will give you a new power up in addition to levels. To be completely honest, while the story certainly doesn't ruin the game, it would be better off without it as there is no great conflict or question that drives the protagonist forward.
Overall Score for Story: 6/10
Gameplay: The gameplay is very simplistic yet requires much good strategy and sharp thinking. In each course, orange pegs are scattered randomly throughout a series of blue pegs. Eliminating the orange is how you pass each stage and you get additional points for any extra balls, combos, or extra score holes at the end of a successful completion of a stage. To do this you must aim and fire balls at each of them, lining up your shots so that each hits as many orange pegs as possible. Aiding you in you're peg massacre are a set of power-ups, each with their own perks and themes. As you progress through the game, you'll unlock more of these special abilities and eventually unlock them for all levels in the game including the late game challenge stages. All in all, this game is pretty fun whether you're in a 5 minute play session or an hour.
Overall Score for Gameplay: 9/10
Characters: The characters in this game reflect the same problems that the story does: their unnecessary and don't add too much. However they are quirky and colorful enough to add a little something unlike the overall "story". On top of this they teach you how to use the power ups instead of giving you a boring tutorial so thats a plus.
Overall Score for Characters: 8/10
Graphics: The art style in this game is very nice and vibrant, while fitting the mood of the game and its levels very well. Backgrounds are fun to look at and colorful while not becoming a liability to your performance. In addition to this there are some nice particle effects here that complement the game nicely.
Overall Score for Graphics: 9/10
Sound: The sound in this game is quite nice and fits in well with the graphics and gameplay. While it is minimal it performs its function which is all that is truly required in a game such as this.
Overall Score for Sound: 9/10
Soundtrack: While also minimal, the soundtrack in this game comes in at all the right times. From a slow and steady beat during gameplay, to the blasting version of "Ode to Joy" when you take down the last orange peg, the soundtrack is all you could really ask for.
Overall Score for Soundtrack:9/10
That just about sums it up folks. While an older casual game now, Peggle still brings a lot to the table and can be played by near anyone regardless of their age or previous experience. It has a fun and addicting premise while always sporting the low price tag which is pretty great.
Overall Score for Game: 8.2/10

There's a weird sort of nostalgia about Wildstar, mostly in the artistic choices of the retro-sci-fi goodness it offers. To me the company did a wonderful job of capturing the (kinda) Twilight Zone era of 1950/1960's grasp of future, where there was tech for every little thing and they all had goofy names and outlandish designs.
Unfortunately, that is quite literally the only thing this game had going for it, and the Fallout series did it better.
As a masochistic gamer, I tend to enjoy and latch onto MMORPGs far more than any other type of multiplayer game, I can be seen sitting for hours farming one piece of gear and wandering around zones under my level to help random people out, but I cannot for the life of me stomach this game for longer than thirty minutes.
Now, I seem like I'm just being a♥♥♥♥♥♥about this, and that's perfectly acceptable for someone who likes something to think about someone who dislikes the thing they like, but tell me this...
In the history of MMORPGS, at what point has any of them with the tagline "Action Combat" maintained a subscriber base of over 1 million people?
Now I'm sure you're leaping at the bit to♥♥♥♥♥♥on me here, how DARE I not know about such quality games as TERA or Guild War and Guild Wars 2? Or perhaps even Vindictus? Here's the main issue though. When people talk about mmos, or talk about the top mmos, those games aren't mentioned, and they never will be. Action combat is quite literally the death of an mmo, and often kills a game before it's even been out for six months. It's hard to play such games if you don't have strong internet, or are used to non-reactive games like World of Warcraft. Though, this is hardly the games only sin.
Beyond the combat system, the sheer amount of customization available from the skill points setup is enough to make a vanilla raider cringe. With very little community, the sudden dump of points to put into random nodes for minor buffs is terrifying, especially when ♥♥♥♥ing up those little nodes could lead to sub-par dps/healing/survivability later on down the line. Not only that, but the lock of 7 skills on a bar of which you can put even MORE points into is shocking to new players.
So we've basically just pointed out that the main mechanic (combat) is hard to get into skillwise, and difficult for those without exceptional internet.
Beyond this we're met with a handful of other issues, mostly in the form of extremely prevalent pushes for microtransactions, almost on par with SWOTOR, and the general game itself being slightly buggy and unoptimized. I'd go into more detail about these things but honestly there's a dozen articles able to word it better than me.
Final Score: Pick another MMO, this one's dead Jim.

Ok, so this may seem a bit premature and I'll update as I get farther along:
Out of the gate I have to say that I love the atmosphere and style that the developers chose to use for this game.  For anyone who's a fan of interesting environments and story I can already tell this game won't be lacking.
Mechanically, the game seems to already offer a more exciting take on a traditional MMO playstyle.  The dodge and aiming requirements are refreshing after so many "Target must be in front of you" messages.  The path quests are a nice side attraction during regular/story questing.  Controls are tight and mobility is definitely enjoyable.
My only and largest gripe so far is what appears to be the lackluster optimization.  I'm not playing this game on any sort of powerhouse of a laptop, but for a game that's over two years old I shouldn't be forced into almost universally "low" settings to keep a framerate ~30 fps.
I'm excited to dig into this game a lot more in the coming days/weeks, I just wish I could see everything the way the developers intended.

has the near-impossible task of following-up
after years of waiting and quality story-based DLC. It also didn't help the ending of
seemed to set up massive possibilities for a sequel. Save for the headhunter packs, all of the subsequent DLC included further additions to the story, without directly addressing the ending of its parent game (save for Tiny Tina's emotional storytelling finale). As a result, when
was announced, people were expecting much more from the game then what was given. So when the game came out, it was bound to receive its share of comparisons to its previous title. The problem is the game shorter and plays so similar to the previous title, it winds up feeling like an extra long DLC rather than a full-fledged follow-up.
Despite the failed comparisons to its previous title,
is an amazing and fun game that anyone should give a try. Although fun, it is a little lacking in content, so it is recommended to wait for a sale for the base game + season pass together. Since 2K Australia was closed down, there will be no more DLC, so no need to worry about future DLC not being included in the bundle.

A VERY tentative recommendation.  Here's the thing, I backed this on Kickstarter and was psyched for it and...that lasted for about the first 10 hours of 30.  The story here is pretty meh, but the game is slick as heck.  Battlechasers is a JRPG made by westerners and while the animation, combat systems, crafting, and world are all super cool, it falls prey to some really amateur mistakes that companies like Zeboyd got around almost a decade ago.  The grind is really aggravating.  There is no passive exp gain for characters not in your party, so prepare to grind or get locked into one party.  The enemies are either trash mob levels of annoying as they are not dangerous or mostly just stall, OR they are brutally broken and can one shot you.  This is a game that wants you to grind, but the gold, exp, and crafting materials you get are nowhere near enough to make it feel fun...it feels, like a GRIND without any meaningful reward.
Battlechasers is super slick, super cool, and can, when firing on all cylinders, offer a deep turn based JRPG experience mixed with a diablo style loot system.  At its worse, however, it is like the grindiest game to ever grind grind.  I want a sequel, which has been psuedo teased, but I want them to fix this crap for next time.

I really enjoy this game, but you have to know what you're getting into. This is what I would consider a game you can chill out and play while listening to podcasts or watching stuff on youtube. There are long periods of dungeon exploration and fighting lots of enemies on the way, and there will be some grinding involved.
The battle system is a lot like Final Fantasy X - turned based with a menu that shows which character gets to attack next, and the gameplay I'd compare to a roguelike dungeon crawler, where you go to a central town, take quests, dungeon crawl, get loot etc.
What makes this game stand out is its charm, its sleek design and interesting characters, its very engaging combat and fun dungeons, and it has quite a bit of content especially if you decide to redo each dungeon on higher difficulties.

Game is fun, but it feels like it runs at half speed.  Near the end of the game it becomes very tedious to have to wait through all the slow animations.  Even walking in the dungeons and on the map is very slow.  Some of the end game materials for legendary weapons are based on chance layouts in earlier dungeons.  If you don't get lucky you can waste a lot of time looking for those items.
I almost didn't make it to the end because of the speed problem and I wasn't looking forward to NG+, but someone said to try using cheat engine to speed the game up so I gave that a try.  The game at 2x speed feels normal.  I run it at about 3x to cut down on the animations, but with the speed increase it became a lot more fun.  The only annoying mechanic left was the random spawns in dungeons for a couple quest and crafting items.
NG+ started out difficult for the first 5 lvls or so, but it drops off a lot after that.  I found it easier from midway through the game because when you run the legendary dungeons you start to get so much xp that you out lvl the content.
The game is worth picking up.  You might cosider waiting until they patch in something to fix the speed or run a 3rd party tool to speed it up.  I ran into a lot of bugs in the end game dungeon, but that seems like it was patched in the first week so it looks like they're trying to fix these things.

Disclaimer: i finished everything what game had to offer. i LOVE joe Madureira's art (darksiders is anohter one). I did not grind a single dungeon. I played every dungeon exactly twice (for "Must Be Bored" achievement as legendary difficulty unlocks after beating dungeon for first time)... , someone may call it grind.
I found this game relatively easy, even on ng+. Map roamimg is quite stale, but dungeon, thats where this game shines. Dungeons are generated, but not Diablo-like. Game has predefine rooms and events for every dungeon, which are randomly connected each time a new instance of dungeon is started. Events are then randomly assigned to each room. Events varying from riddles, special monsters to side quests. Monsters are patrolling in rooms and will engage in combat (similar to HoMaM Series). Each dungeon contains Boss which require little bit of strategy, but i found every boss easy (Monika+Gully+Calibretto)!!
i loved everythig about combat, well except slow animations. Each characters gains xp which results in lvl up. After slvl up, certain amount of perk points is gained. These points can be spent to upgrade characters stats, alter characters skills by adding special effects. Spell are divided to 3 categories. Basic spells/actions cost no mana,are executed immediately and generate "overcharge"(can be used as mana, but it's lost after combat). Advanced skills use mana (or overcharge if available) and have casting time, which can be seen as preparation time and giving turn to following character or monster. Who played FF7 has sure understood what i mean.
crafting as it is has a nice feauture. adding basic amount of ingredients will grant you crafted item, but adding more igredients will improve quality of crafted item up to legendary (in ng+). As i progressed throufh my first playthrough i didn't find crafting necessary, well except of unique weapons for each character, which are best weapons in game. every chracter need unique legendary ingreddients for this weapon. These are acquired as side quests.
TLDR: if think thah u wouold love darksiders art with ff7 combat + humour, then get this game asap. otherwise buy it anyway. Gameplay time is about 40-50 hours per playthrough.

I played WOWS from Beta and loved it.
I think Steel Ocean is a better game.
Admittedly the graphics aren't quite as polished as the competition (especially the water) but the ships look fine to me during a battle and are more than pretty enough to blow up.
The things that put this above WOWS (for me):
Submarines - how easily they fit into the rest of the ship types and they work well in the game, not being too powerful or too easily countered but providing a tough challenge if you don't know what you are doing. They are a lot of fun to play.
They have a fleshed out German Navy tech tree already.
They have already added a CV and DD line of Royal Navy ships to the game (with the latest patch).
The Commander system provides an interesting bit of customisation beyond unlocking identical skills for every ship like in WOWS.
CVs don't seem as poweful, you can still get kills with your planes but it's more challenging, though you get complete freedom to launch whatever planes you want which is a nice bonus, no limits to one or two loadouts.
Being able to fire my own AA guns and Secondary batteries separately from my main batteries, a massive bonus on BBs.
There are a wide variety of maps, a number of different game types including deathmatch style Competition mode and a massive array of ships to collect. Considering the game has only been out for a month I am very opptimistic about the future and look forward to seeing what will come.
The only downside to me at the moment is the fact I have to play on a NA server meaning the lag is a bit annoying but even so the game is still playable enough and I've not had any major connection issues.

So far I can't recommend this game enough to any MMO nerd. The only negative feedback I'm hearing is that there's a bug with the patcher and that the population isn't as high as it should be.
This game was designed by former WoW devs who got bored after Burning Crusade, and their experience shows.
-No other MMO I've played has as much to do while leveling as this one. There's virtually no downtime, unless you choose to take things slow. The path system creates a ton of variety, much in the way Guild Wars 2 gives you a lot of freedom to do what you like.
-The style and tone of the game is cartoony and full of character. If you dig WoW's aesthetic you'll feel right at home.
-The combat is the best you'll find in a hotkey MMO. It's the most mobile and action-focused you can get outside of Eastern MMOs like Tera or Blade & Soul. Everything feels smooth, and both ally and enemy abilities are telegraphed clearly, so you never feel like you were cheated by invisible hitboxes.
-The business model is the most generous I've ever seen in any F2P game. Nothing you buy in the store is mandatory, and you can earn a fair amount of currency to buy things like Bank and Character slots by simply playing.
-Lots of opportunity to be a try-hard since the devs know their hardcore audience and bring on the challenging raid content.
-There are a million little things like UI design and quality of life choices that feel great after years of playing MMOs. It's something I really appreciate, knowing how many hours you can lose over the years to minor examples of poor design.
This game is worth your time if you're into this genre. When Legion loses a bit of its luster or you're tired of how user-unfriendly Korean MMOs can be, give it a shot!

Still pre-alpha as of Feb 4, 2017.  It's got a lot of issues, but a lot of potential.  I was happy to spend 10 bucks on this game, and I've put in a lot of time for those 10 dollars.  There's supposed to be an update soon, and the developer is somewhat active on the forums.  I'm hoping the next update vastly improves the camp management part of the game, which is the section that is the least fun at the moment.
Basically the ideas are good.  Scavenge for supplies and look for other survivors.  Build up a camp.  Defend it from zombies.  It's the execution of the core game mechanics that need work, and unfortunately the game suffers for it.
The camp related parts of the game need a lot of love.  The interface is hard to read due to the font and backgrounds they use.  The menu system in camp is very clunky right now, and bloated.  There are too many sub-categories, and it could easily be streamlined.  Production and construction can also be streamlined, and for some reason construction of certain parts of the camp are separate from the camp upgrades even though it's basically the same thing.  It could, and should, all be in the same menu.
The exploration and scavenging is a fairly decent third-person shooter, given the early stage of the development cycle.  It's kind of fun to run around and collect stuff, shoot zeds in the head and try to deal with the two stronger types of zeds.  Okay, okay, "Infected".  They're zombies, no matter what you call them.  The game has rare and legendary items, they're simply better quality items, and weapon mods that you can find.  They have a good variety of guns, however they all kind of feel similar except for a few exceptions.  Headshots are your friend, and even the worst weapons can kill with one or two head shots, unless you face the tougher infected.  Those take anywhere from 8 to 30 or 40 head hits depending on what you're using to shoot them.
Currently the enemies aren't too bright.  The human enemies will take cover and shoot at you, by far the most dangerous thing in the game so far, however even the "parasite" infected, which is very tough and will chase you rather quickly, can be easily defeated by anyone.  They're also too dumb to climb, so if you can get up on a truck or a van, they won't attack you and can't reach you.  Yet.  I think this is eventually going to change, but there's a lot more work to be done.
Hit detection is wonky.  Often with a clear line of sight you can't hit what you're shooting at, the bullets strike some invisible thing somewhere between you and the target.  A few guns are buggy, if crouched you can't shoot properly.  Combat is fairly simple right now, but if you're not careful you can still be taken down.  Some of the infected tend to sneak up on you when you're not paying attention.  If you access your inventory the game does not pause.  You have to pay attention.
The most frustrating part, and most tedious part, is building kits for your scouts, scavengers, etc.  I absolutely hate this part of the game.  You have to go back and forth too many times in the menu system just to build one simple item, and each kit takes several items.  There's no indication on the production screen to tell you how many of any resource you have, it simply lets you build the item if you have enough but doesn't tell you what you're missing if you don't.  You have to go back to the main camp screen, go into the inventory screen, click around in there a bunch of times because there are several categories and buttons you can click, then look around to find what you have.  It's just way too time consuming and clunky to be fun.
The base defence is terrible.  Zombies come at your base to attack it.  The game puts up a very poorly designed screen with a few buttons at the bottom.  It shows on the left how many survivors you have in camp, excluding your four heavily armed heroes - for some inexplicable reason they can't help with this - and the zeds on the right with one icon each.  Combat is turn based, and you pick a combat "stance", and your tactics, then click a button.  You have a bunch of numbers representing initiative, power, defence and so do the zeds, but it seems to matter very little that you have numbers 10 or 20 times larger than theirs.  You can, at most, kill one or two of them per turn.  Click, click.  Bang.  An icon gets an X over it in red.  Next turn.  Click, click... bang.  Another zed gets an X.  It's uninspired, boring and takes forever.  I really hope they completely overhaul this part of the game.  At least make it a tower defence style sequence where your survivors, and heroes, can defend an actual camp.  Better yet, use the same third person perspective and gameplay that the exploration part of the game has.  That might actually be fun!
For an EA game, despite my complaints, I've been drawn in.  I like a lot of things here, and I truly believe that the game will only continue to improve.
It's imperfect, but still very early Alpha.  I put enough time in so far, and had enough fun, that it's very worth the roughly $10.00 price.  I am looking forward to some significant changes, and multiplayer.
Despite my gripes and the issues with the game, I recommend giving it a shot, and supporting these devs.  It's got potential, and I would like to see it continue to improve.

MXGP2 is the best MX game to date! And I've played pretty much every MX game going back to excite bike on the NES to having 277 hours in Reflex on the Steam/PC version alone (double that counting time spent on the Xbox 360 version). They really nailed it with physics, gameplay, graphics, and detail. There's so much detail you can even see the welds in the swingarm! I came in expecting just a MXGP1 re-hash with some added tracks but it feels and looks totally overhauled with the exception of sounds which the rest is so good I can almost completely forgive the the sound which falls behind the quality of the rest of the game.
But just to be warned, there's a learning curve with the updated physics. Like I said, I was expecting just a re-hash of MXGP and thought my same techniques would all carry over but it turned out to be quite different! And it's all for the better! Now to powerslide corners, or rail the inside line and blast out of the corners ripping you have to utilise the clutch and leaning where as in the first game I almost never had to use the lean much and never used the clutch. The bike has a much softer feel now as well. Gone are the days when it looked and sounded so stiff almost to where you had no suspension when landing or blasting whoops. The suspension has a real plush feel to it now.
The replay system is also much improved. You can fast forward and rewind at varying speeds using the RT and LT on a xbox controller. You can really get some sick screenshots with the replay! I can really go on and on about all the improvements and how good the game is, but just take it from someone who used to race in real life and has played nearly every MX game to date going back to the 80's, this is the best one by a long shot! I'm glad to see so many developers of racing games steering more towards realism these days instead of arcade physics and Milestone won't dissapoint you if you're looking for realism! Real tracks, real riders, realistic graphics and handling, what else could you possibly want? Plus for us older guys that used to race for real, this satisfies the MX racing crave but is so much safer, i.e. no broken bones to deal with, lol. Of yea, the MX of Nations mode is another nice added bonus!

Having played MXGP and loved it, I was very excited to play MXGP 2. Several swear words and a broken controller later, I have some conclusions.
It is great. It's better than the first. The handling is different and at times can seem a touch too sensitive, but once you get used to it, it really is nice. The whips and scrubs are slightly improved. The new layout is a bit add at first, but again, once you get used to it, it's fine.
The game runs pretty smoothly, with only a slight hiccup here and there. It is nowhere near as bad as MX vs ATV Encore was (that game did get a decent patch to fix most problems).
There are new tracks and some from the previous game have been removed.  Of course, most Americans (like myself) will probably wish there were more US tracks, but this is MXGP after all and not Lucas Oil Nationals. Thankfully Glen Helen is now on the schedule and most of the removed tracks are ones I didn't care much for anyway. The addition of the MXON is nice, although I'm a little disappointed that I cannot use my custom team in it. Oh well, at least I can represent USA and create the ending I would have preferred for last year's race. The indoor races are more Arenacross than Supercross. They are very tight and by the end of it you will probably hate Nagl, Febvre, and Gajser. Maybe it's a good thing they don't have the license for the US series.
The AI is improved and takes much better lines. I still have yet to bump it back up to the highest setting, but they are definitely more aggresive. Again, you'll probably end up hating quite a few guys. The only problem is a lot of times inside passes result in tipovers from the AI, although this seems to be true in most MX games.
Overall, I wish there were a few things different, such as first-person starts and the clutch assignment not locking up the game, but this series is well on it's way and with any luck, maybe, just maybe, one day there will be an installment for the US series.

My playthrough is still in progress - but I'm at a point where I want to voice my dissatisfaction.
Firstly, I never played a game like this (3rd person brawler) before so this was new. Ultimately I did not really like the mechanics. I was able to learn the basics but it just did not click with me (I think one of my biggest problem was that I could not find a satisfying camera setting that let me focus where I wanted to in combat mode), so I set everything to auto after a while when I finally gave up on the challenge part - after that the game thankfully just pretty much played itself during fights.
I did this because even though one of my reasons for getting the game was to try something from the genre - the bigger draw was the intriguing story/world. Sadly, it didn't do anything for me in this regard either.
All I can see is pointless sentimentalism. I don't much care for metaphores and symbolism and I suspect this game is full of them and I just can't pick up on it.
The setting is that of a kind of generic post apocaliptic open world rpg (desert, forest, overgrown city and abandoned factory) filled with uninteresting samey mooks. I found no meaningful story so far (I did not go through all the endings yet), things just happened in a particular order without much influence on or link to one another. It's fascinating for a while but it got boring - nobody really learned anything or went anywhere. Well, sometimes people died (in uninteresting ways and without much reason). It tried to do the usual tricks to pull my heartstrings - but without my investment in the characters or the world that just did not work on me.
Overall, it's not bad at all, it's just ...meh. I'm happy for all the people who managed to get something out of it but it seems it is not really for me. (I still intend to finish all the 3(?) main endings but I don't know if I can push myself through with my quickly waning interest.)

I dont normally write reviews, in fact this may even be my first. But I feel compelled to after playing Nier: Automata.
This is probably one of the best games I have ever played. I don't say this lightly, I am a harsh critic and it takes a lot to impress me. I dont normally buy games on the first day of release due to the price, but I took a chance on this and I am so glad that I did because it is worth every penny.
The story is engaging and gripping to the point where I was up all night playing it and then had to go to work on 3 hours sleep. Also, I am not an emotional man, in fact I am much like the protagonist :P but there were certain parts that had me sobbing like a baby. Make no mistake, this game has some very dark themes to it which is bound to affect you in one way or another.
The graphics and visuals are amazing, the fights are exciting, the music is epic and really adds to range of emotions you will go through when playing this game.
Sure there are a few things I felt could have been done better, it's not without it's flaws. The overall world that you play in feels a little small once you've explored the whole map, I wish there could have been more zones, more places and people to visit. There were some technical issues when it was first released and the game sometimes crashes on me, I wont lie. The cut scenes are very choppy in terms of frame rate. For some reason it caps the cutscenes at 30fps. During gameplay it goes back to 60fps. I dont know if this will ever get fixed. But all of these things are completely eclipsed by the game's good points that it doesnt bother me. It's not enough to keep me from giving this game a 10/10.

I think this game is actually pretty fun. Get it if you like to engage in naval Battles in the countries of the US, Japan, And Germany. You have the choice between destroyers, Battleships, Light and Heavy Cruisers, Submarines, And aircraft carriers. I think those of you who tried might actually like it.

This is a naval game where every part of the fleet is important.
Oh, and they have British Battleships, and German Battleships. The whole line.  So yes, you can actually play sink the Bismarck!
Let me get the negative out of the way first: Visually this game is a bit dated. The ship controls are a bit arcadeish (but still fun and in a way, doesn't ruing the immersion if that makes sense.
That's it.  The rest is all positive.
This game actualy manages to get that rock paper scissors gameplay correct.  Submarines are incredibly deadly to battleships, but are countered by DDs and CLs.  DDs can wreck BBs if they get in close, but CLs tear them to pieces.  CLs and BBs are the primary targets for BBs, and the BBs main advantage (range and firepower) are modelled nicely.  CVs take a lot of skill to work right, but a tight fleet formation can ruin an air attack's day.
I like that the heavy weapons are not unlimited ammo.  You can't spam torps all the time, you have to be careful.  Torps have a minimum arming range, making suicide rushes a thing of the past.  There is no real aim assist for guns or torps, making both fair.  Heavier ships can switch to lighter secondary armament for taking on enemy light vessels and aircraft, giving a smart player a modicum of protection close in.
The game tracks your ability to help your team.  Are you a stealthy DD spotting for your fleet?  You get points and experience for that.  Radio Ranges and radar ranges become important, since if you scout too far ahead, no one will get your data, and your fleet can't rain down fire on the enemy.
Overall, the co-operative nature of the fleet based gameplay makes this a solid choice in my view.  There's tons of ships and lines to unlock, each type of ship has its own unique feel and gameplay style meaning that there should be something for everyone.  The game rewards teamwork and skill, and punishes lone wolfing (unless you are a sub, in which case that's your gameplay style).
It's frankly great fun.  I'm sure that as the playerbase keeps growing (never less then 30 seconds for a match for me)  the game will become even better with updates to the visuals.  As it stands, it's probably the most naval fun you can have these days.
It's basically like Navy Field if it didn't suck.

After the wild success and fun of
, the announcement of a full-fledged follow-up was pretty exciting.
fills in the gaps between the first and second game through the story telling by the main characters after the events of the second game (hence, The Pre-Sequel). Although the game is brings back all of the amazing fun of Borderlands 2, coupled with some extra features like low gravity, OZ boost kits, and lasers, it does tend to fall a little short of the immense popularity of the second game. The reason why it falls short can be subjective, but what it comes down to is
falls victim to being a follow-up of an amazing game without introducing anything ground-breakingly new.
has the near-impossible task of following-up
after years of waiting and quality story-based DLC. It also didn't help the ending of
seemed to set up massive possibilities for a sequel. Save for the headhunter packs, all of the subsequent DLC included further additions to the story, without directly addressing the ending of its parent game (save for Tiny Tina's emotional storytelling finale). As a result, when
was announced, people were expecting much more from the game then what was given. So when the game came out, it was bound to receive its share of comparisons to its previous title. The problem is the game shorter and plays so similar to the previous title, it winds up feeling like an extra long DLC rather than a full-fledged follow-up.
Despite the failed comparisons to its previous title,
is an amazing and fun game that anyone should give a try. Although fun, it is a little lacking in content, so it is recommended to wait for a sale for the base game + season pass together. Since 2K Australia was closed down, there will be no more DLC, so no need to worry about future DLC not being included in the bundle.

This is kind of a hard review to write, because ultimately Battle Chasers delivered on everything it promised. I think ultimately the fact that I didn't enjoy it is because I want it to be more than it is.
The Good: Battle Chasers is gorgeous, and visually very satisfying. Every hit from my team was visceral and brutal, and for a while, it tricked me in to thinking I was enjoying the combat. The special effects are gorgeous, the music is good, the animation is stellar. Honestly, if you're just looking for a relatively mindless game that is very pretty, ignore my review and go try it. It's not without its merits.
The Bad: Combat is staid and bland, with not a lot of choices. Ultimately, its limited customization means that combat just boils down to a pretty easy to beat efficiency simulator, with an attached over extension gambling module. I looked through the various abilities, and while I was able to spot some interesting combo possibilities, it more felt to me like it was a game where you find your first order strategy and spam it over and over again. In a world with Darkest Dungeon in it, there's no excuse for a combat system this static. The "overcharge" system *helped*, but it wasn't doing enough differently to entice me. Crafting is a joke- Like many games, crafting boils down to "input items, get output item." The gambling system for getting higher rarity is... nice... but like in combat, it doesn't make up for just how straight forward crafting is.
The Ugly: Ultimately, an RPG sells itself on one of two things: A great plot, or a deep, highly customizable system that puts power in the players' hands. Battle Chasers fails at both of these. The story seems like a pretty generic collection of comedy relief anti-hero tropes put in to stock fantasy situation 664: The airship crashes on a dangerous island. While they performed their tropes decently, I couldn't help but to start thinking about where I'd seen these characters before. As far as customization goes... There is none. Equipment lets you choose stats, but this is just a lever for the aforementioned efficiency simulator. I know that all JRPGs essentially boil down to "Make the numbers on the bad guy go down faster than yours", but so many recent games have done so much of a better job of hiding that fact.
There's a lot of "nostalgia" in this game that harkens back to the way JRPGs used to be, and that might be enough for some turn based die hards, but not for me. Call me spoiled by the likes of Disgaea and Darkest Dungeon and XCOM, but I want some customization and agency meat on this bare bones of a combat system.

This analysis is based on latest version which tweaks some issues. So you might expect different criticism from early review or if you're uncomfortable with the length, you can skip to other brief review.
BC: Nightwar is turn-based RPG game from Kickstarter campaign in 2015. Developed by Airship Syndicate using Unity engine. The game represents world of ’90 Joe Madureira’s comic with refreshed JRPG turn-based combat and interesting features. The design is diverse from the comic dialogue and 2D multi-layered world map, shifted into isometric view in dungeon and fully-animated turn based section. It’s subjective design if you enjoy arcanepunk, but well-polished production.
---------------------------------------------------------
Story of Nightwar serves as a continuation of ’90 popular Battle Chasers series. You don’t need to read comic to understand the story, because Nightwar has its own separate storyline for main characters. Your airship is shot down into one island during your main journey. As you progress through story, you recruit your crew and reveal the dark secret of the island.
Every dungeon and landmark has bit of lore and NPC that provide additional background of the world. You also learn character development by bit in cutscene and resting in Inn which is nice touch. The main story isn’t much spectacular, but the writer did great job on dialogue and lore description.
Not just because interesting character design, but how well they tie each character with original personality and combat ability which most fit in right place.
---------------------------------------------------------
The design of combat system gives strong vibes of old school turn-based RPGs. In-game manual and UIs are friendly for newbie as you gain access more advanced skills and perks by leveling and visiting NPCs.
In combat, each turn allows you to perform 3 main options (Actions / Abilities / Burst). Actions are instant action with overcharge bonus. Abilities are advanced actions that require casting time. “Overcharge” serves as temporary mana (action point) or enhance some abilities depends on how much overcharge you have. This unique mechanic adds layer of combat and encourage player to analyze their best output of next turn. Finally, Burst is ultimate skills that can turn the tide, but require gauge gain by performing action. Every basic action and skill has extra function (buff, debuff, etc.) and designed on purpose to be support by some perks or chained combo skill. Even character stats do matter, to boost chance of extra turn or completely evade the attack. It’s combination of well-design elements and emphasizes player’s experiment which can be huge advantaged in most encounters.
Progression allows freedom of playstyle based on you build. No holding hand to specific method, but encourage you to try out all 6 different playable character (assigned as 3-man party). You can extend based existing skills or create hybrid characters by simply switching perks and enhancement which I personally love this dynamic design. Moreover, each action is well animated and gives you strong feedback.
---------------------------------------------------------
BC: Nightwar doesn’t have a large world, but it’s dense with complexity and side features. Dungeon design is distinguished from each other with polished details, logical puzzles, and randomization. Debuff from traps will carry over the combat and events will offers you random loots or bonus. You can use character’s dungeon skill to gain initial advantage in combat as well.
Teleport cube in dungeon is a nice touch, allow you to insert weapon and search where the cube is teleported. You gain higher grade weapon as reward.
Crafting and enchanting are simple but fixable, missing ingredient give you lower chance of success and excess materials can craft higher grade item.
Bestiary contains information of all enemies (stats, drop, special move), it’s a small feature but motivate player to hunt and gain beast perk as permanent party bonus.
Fishing is optional fun mini-game as you trade fish for Shadow Coin (special currency to trade special item, skins, and perk books). Even you dislike fishing; Shadow Coin can still be obtained via dungeon, special enemies, and side quests.
---------------------------------------------------------
From the character action to enemy movement, BC: Nightwar delivers fantastic and satisfied sound design. Great overall voice acting even the game isn’t fully voice acting which miss opportunity for other interesting dialogues. Atmospheric soundtracks by talented Jesper Kyd and Clark Powell fit properly in each area (subjective).
---------------------------------------------------------
While the combat is by far strongest point. BC: Nightwar suffers from inconsistent difficulty due to awkward enemy design. The level has an impact in combat. Fighting with higher 1-2 level foes can be really rough due to damage scale. Same-leveled foes in mid game can take character down by 1-2 action. This quite unfair design as you forced to grind to access better perk and gears. Legendary difficult in dungeon can be challenge, but mostly rewards under leveled items once you revisit and might give you unsatisfied accomplish. It’s issue that breaks the flow of game progression.
The game also lacks of passive leveling process, only active party member will gain EXP from combat. So, you might expect grinding if you want to try other characters (at least it’s not huge grind compare to some of JRPG), and watch same animation over and over can become tedious.
In addition, other issues like lack of key binding, world map description, various enemy type (most are reskin with different abilities), and unmotivated endless arena mode can be discomfort and inconvenient for some players.
---------------------------------------------------------
This topic is very subjective based on different PC build. The game is made in Unity engine and well-optimized as I experience no fatal bugs / glitches in 80 hrs. of 100% completed playthrough. Delay gap of enemy wave and few frame drops in raining areas are noticeable.
---------------------------------------------------------
Post playthrough unlocks New Game+ featuring faster leveling, tougher enemies and Mythical dungeon which give highest great items. You have to start over with level and gear progression, but you keep all skills, perk, beast perk, collectable, and some special items from you first playthrough. If you like this approach, NG+ is best choice for any completionists.
---------------------------------------------------------
Although, the game structure might be stumble and conflicted at some points, but BC: Nightwar is one of most satisfied experience and entertainment for old school turn-based RPG. Each element is well-designed and fall into place.
I recommend anyone who loves JRPG or people who start looking for different RPG experience. The developers are responsive for player feedback and I hope they continue to extend world of Battle Chasers or similar project.

So far I can't recommend this game enough to any MMO nerd. The only negative feedback I'm hearing is that there's a bug with the patcher and that the population isn't as high as it should be.
This game was designed by former WoW devs who got bored after Burning Crusade, and their experience shows.
-No other MMO I've played has as much to do while leveling as this one. There's virtually no downtime, unless you choose to take things slow. The path system creates a ton of variety, much in the way Guild Wars 2 gives you a lot of freedom to do what you like.
-The style and tone of the game is cartoony and full of character. If you dig WoW's aesthetic you'll feel right at home.
-The combat is the best you'll find in a hotkey MMO. It's the most mobile and action-focused you can get outside of Eastern MMOs like Tera or Blade & Soul. Everything feels smooth, and both ally and enemy abilities are telegraphed clearly, so you never feel like you were cheated by invisible hitboxes.
-The business model is the most generous I've ever seen in any F2P game. Nothing you buy in the store is mandatory, and you can earn a fair amount of currency to buy things like Bank and Character slots by simply playing.
-Lots of opportunity to be a try-hard since the devs know their hardcore audience and bring on the challenging raid content.
-There are a million little things like UI design and quality of life choices that feel great after years of playing MMOs. It's something I really appreciate, knowing how many hours you can lose over the years to minor examples of poor design.
This game is worth your time if you're into this genre. When Legion loses a bit of its luster or you're tired of how user-unfriendly Korean MMOs can be, give it a shot!

I just realized, I haven't written a positive review for this game, even though it is my second most played game in my library!
Even with the obviously superior Rebirth out now, the original Flash-Isaac is still a very compelling, yet rock hard experience. As far as flash games go, this is probably one of the very best - if not THE very best - positive example. Like many roguelites (is this the correct classification for purists?) it is brutally hard and unforgiving in the beginning, but the more you play it, the more you get the hang of it, the further you will get, until eventually, you can start a run and know "okay, I will most probably finish it after an hour, if the items I get aren't COMPLETELY garbage."
Now, with the new "eternal edition" update out, it's worth revisiting the old times.
I recommend buying the original, IF you are already through with Rebirth and:
-Want to see, where Rebirth came from and how the original incarnation played differently
-Want to listen to an, in my humble opinion, slightly better soundtrack - but that's highly subjective!
Otherwise, if you haven't played any of Isaac at all yet, you might want to skip this and start with Rebirth instead, except if you want to relive the process of improvement.
Recommended.

I'll update this review as the game changes.
MXGP2 is better than its predecessor in a lot of ways but ultimately feels less realistic than the first game did.You begin the game on a stock 250cc bike (MX2) that can't clear anything and on realistic difficulty every NPC is faster than you. After upgrading some parts its a little better but it's not until you get on the 450cc (MXGP) that the game is fun. Even then, if you came to race AI NPCs you're going to be dissapointed. There is no bar banging like in the first MXGP. The NPCs don't make any attempts to pass or avoid you, they're very clearly on rails and don't fall down often. The pack never splits up like in real motocross or in the first MXGP, its just a horrifying train of bikes that take basically the same line for the entire moto. What's worse is that when they inevitably barrel into you from behind you WILL fall, and they probably won't. Still, when you aren't racing with unstoppable machines piledriving your swingarm into the dirt, the riding is a blast! Suspension feels nice and bouncy and cornering, although not as satisfying as the first game is a fun technique to learn. Furthermore, THE BERMS WORK NOW! You can absolutely RAIL some corners on the outside line, and what is motocross about if not railing corners? The suspension tuning and gear ratios do make a noticeable difference and I personally find it really fun to tweak with different setups while running practice laps.
Anyway, this is getting too long so I'll get to the point. MXGP2 isn't great and it probably isn't going to get better but it is a realistic and fun experience in genre where only one new game hits the market every 2-3 years. If you're not interested in multiplayer, check out the original MXGP. If you're not interested in realism and just want to freeride dirt bikes with friends, go get MXvxATV Reflex. If you want to play a realistic motocross game with friends, I recommend this one.
Milestone has made decent games in the past like Ride and the MotoGP series, unfortunately MXGP and MXGP2 don't live up to the same level of quality as their other titles. The first mXGP was released with a lot of bugs and support was ultimately dropped leaving the multiplayer unplayable and the game performance very low quality. I recommend that you take Milestone's poor history into account while reading this review. Hopefully I'm wrong, but it's unlikely that we will see any bugs being fixed let alone any requested features added to the game. The only DLC planned are additional rider gear and TWO more tracks, nothing to get excited over.
Apprehensively Recommended
The first impressions of MXGP2 will leave you wanting a refund but after toying with bike tuning, upgrading to a 450cc and rebinding your controls, you'll learn to love it.
The game is more polished than the first MXGP but feels less gritty and more arcadey.
If you're looking for realism this game blows the MX vs ATV series out of the water standing as the ONLY decent offroad motorcycle game with manual transmission and clutch controls.
This game wins most improved in a genre with very few competitors.
The first MXGP is better and more fun in a lot of ways but this game feels more finished.
If you're a fan of realistic motocross games and want to play alone, I recommend the first MXGP.
If you want to play a fun motocross game with friends, get MX Vs ATV Reflex.
If you want a realistic motocross game to play with friends, this is your best (and only) bet.
P.S. Milestone please add more Stadium courses!

I dont normally write reviews, in fact this may even be my first. But I feel compelled to after playing Nier: Automata.
This is probably one of the best games I have ever played. I don't say this lightly, I am a harsh critic and it takes a lot to impress me. I dont normally buy games on the first day of release due to the price, but I took a chance on this and I am so glad that I did because it is worth every penny.
The story is engaging and gripping to the point where I was up all night playing it and then had to go to work on 3 hours sleep. Also, I am not an emotional man, in fact I am much like the protagonist :P but there were certain parts that had me sobbing like a baby. Make no mistake, this game has some very dark themes to it which is bound to affect you in one way or another.
The graphics and visuals are amazing, the fights are exciting, the music is epic and really adds to range of emotions you will go through when playing this game.
Sure there are a few things I felt could have been done better, it's not without it's flaws. The overall world that you play in feels a little small once you've explored the whole map, I wish there could have been more zones, more places and people to visit. There were some technical issues when it was first released and the game sometimes crashes on me, I wont lie. The cut scenes are very choppy in terms of frame rate. For some reason it caps the cutscenes at 30fps. During gameplay it goes back to 60fps. I dont know if this will ever get fixed. But all of these things are completely eclipsed by the game's good points that it doesnt bother me. It's not enough to keep me from giving this game a 10/10.
