I decided that my first Stellaris playthough would be on Ironman mode, with no prior knowledge of the game whatsoever. What follows is three of the most interesting points in a campaign that has thus far spanned 180 years.
Background:
I named my empire "The Galactic Empire" and began the game as a militarist, materialist, and authoritarian.
The Celimy Conflict:
Early on, around the 50 year mark, I encounter a species of strange, fungal creatures. They call themselves the "Celimy States". They are fanatic spiritualists and pacifists. Fools.
After a series of insults and the declaration of a rivalry, the Celimy declare war on me.
My navy, christened the "Grand Imperial Navy", departs the Coruscant System to engage the Celimy "Mycelium Carriers", as they called themselves.
A short time later, the Imperial Navy reaches the Celimy home system.
Imperial transports land armies on their capital.
The takeover is rapid, and at the end of the war the Celimy States has splintered into 3 separate nations: The Celimy Hegemony, the Celimy Confederacy and the Celimy Associates.
Later on, the Associates would become my vassal. The Confederacy was a long standing enemy.
The Galactic Civil War:
Around 120 years in, the galaxy is almost fully filled with about 20 separate empires, and two distinct sides begin to form.
On one side is myself and a federation called the "Stellar Entente", along with various other small empires.
The other side is comprised of a vast array of small nations, led by the "Karabnar Nations".
War breaks out, with the Karabnar declaring war on the Galactic Empire.
I now have 3 fleets: The Star Corps, the Shock Battalion, and the Grand Imperial Navy. The Star Corps and Shock Battalion are relatively small shock forces, whereas the Grand Imperial Navy is my main force.
A massive space battle in the Ocheron system involves over 1000 ships, with almost every known nation being present.
The battle (which was beautiful to watch) was relatively even until the arrival of the Star Corps and Shock Battalion, who tipped the balance with fresh ships.
The combined fleet of myself and my allies (yes, the AI is THAT good) eventually reaches Karab, the Karabnar Nations capital, and takes the system with the help of two Titanic Beasts recruited from the outer systems of the Empire.
On the verge of victory, I am notified that a massive fleet is currently in orbit over Coruscant.
Sent by the Hjaarthi Syndicate, one of our enemies, the fleet is in position to take our homeworld.
My own fleets cannot reach Coruscant in time. All seems lost.
A mere few days before Coruscant's fortifications would've failed, a fleet from one of my allies, the Verulian Compact, comes out of hyperspace above Coruscant and annihlates the enemy fleet.
The Karabnar Nation and their allies surrender, and the war is won.
The Fallen Empire (150 years in):
A fallen empire (which is a fully developed but stagnant state) exists above me. They call themselves the Yz'Vorak Remnant (which I shortened to Y Remnant).
They are military isolationists, and hate my empire with a special intensity.
They insult mea and shortly afterwards declare war on my empire. This sort of war is usually a death sentence, so I move large numbers of people away from the Frontier and prepare to submit.
At this point I've got 3 vassals. All are weak, but they are extremely loyal.
The vassals join me in the war.
All 3 of my fleets meet above Coruscant, along with Transports for my Droid Army (Irony, much)
I deploy my entire military to the Jahab system, where we meet the Fallen Empire's forces.
Their ships are unlike anything we've ever seen, and are incredibly powerful.
We are losing the battle. Things are not looking good.
Suddenly, out of hyperspace, come 3 fleets; my 3 vassals have brought everything they have to assist the effort.
With their help, we drive back the Fallen Empire forces.
Fastforward about 3 years.
Through intense naval strategy and economic strain, Imperial forces have out matched the Y Remnant's fleet.
The Grand Imperial Navy and the fleets of my vassals orbit above their capital: The Core.
I don't have enough strength left to invade their planets, so I offer them a white peace.
Fallen Empires cannot build new fleets, so this seemed logical enough.
I recieve a notification:
"Peace Accords on Coruscant"
While signing the peace accords on Coruscant, two V Remnant agents who were standing next to the Emperor (of the Galactic Empire) killed him and mutilated his body.
Furious, the Imperial Navy and the combined fleets of all of the Empire's vassals and allies immediately attack the Y Remnant Capital.
Out of nowhere, a massive army from the Fallen Empire comes out of hyperspace over The Core (I still am not entirely sure where this army actually came from).
In the epic battle that ensues, the Grand Imperial Navy defeats and destroys the Y Remnant's fleet, allowing the ground invasion of The Core to take place.
With The Core fallen, the Fallen Empire cowers and begs for peace.
The Y Remnant is annexed by the Galactic Empire.
Peace reigns across the galaxy.
Around 20 years later...
Subspace energy surges indicate something we have not encountered before. A new being from out of our dimension makes contact. Their signal is not unlike a hunting call.....
BY POPULAR REQUEST, AN UPDATE:
Their name is the Unbidden and they make an immediate point.
A transmission appears on my screen, depicting some kind of strange, ethereal being.
They say something about prey and then the transmission cuts out.
The Unbidden fleet is marked by science ship in the bottom part of the galaxy, below myself and the "Qix'Lufran Combine".
The Qix'Lufran are isolationist authoritarians, but decide to deploy their entire fleet, the sole largest fleet in the galaxy, to immediately engage this extraterrestrial threat.
The Qix'Lufran fleet reaches the Unbidden's position, and is utterly destroyed.
This shocks the entire galaxy.
Interestingly enough, these "Unbidden" would remain effectively dormant in their small region at the bottom of the galaxy. Not sure if it was because of the Fallen Empire bordering them, or simply because they were waiting for reinforcements. Either way, the Unbidden hold their position for the time being.
The Great Intergalactic War:
The Galactic Empire has become the most powerful and largest state in the galaxy. Above us, the "Hjannarthi Syndicate" exists, which nearly equals my own power. To our left is the "Stellar Entente" federation. To the right is the Njalax High Kingdom, and the Uriy Republic. Below us, the Zuifvan Imperium, the Qix'Lufran, and the Unbidden.
Although there is a period of peace, there is great unrest in the galaxy.
The Qix'Lufran and Njalax grow closer and closer every year.
Eventually, they declare a defensive pact and close their borders to myself, the Stellar Entente and the Hjannarthi Syndicate.
Their combined power rivals my own; they are dangerous.
They undergo a combined massive military buildup, and begin to become increasingly aggressive.
In mid july of 2412 (212 years in) the tensions boil over. The Njalax and the Qix'Lufran declare war on the Galactic Empire, the Hjannarthi, and the Stellar Entente.
The galaxy is divided.
A line is drawn essentially down the middle of the galaxy, dividing the left(Qix'Lufran and Njalax) from the right(Galactic Empire and Allies).
I issue an immediate order to deploy the fleet. The long dormant Grand Imperial Navy assembles over Coruscant.
Admiral Cognat leads the navy.
My ever-reliable vassals send everything they have to join the Imperial Navy. I love those guys.
The Stellar Entente's federation fleet strikes first. They use their wormhole stations to attack directly at the heart of the Njalax.
My own fleet reaches the Qix'Lufran capital with relative ease, meeting almost no resistance.
We confront a vastly outmatched Qix'Lufran force of 2 battleships and 18 corvettes.
MAX REV LENGTH

After not playing for several months, I recently decided to return to the game with the release of Utopia. However, if you want a more comprehensive review of Utopia, I would suggest reading the reviews on its own page. Suffice it to say that it greatly expands on Stellaris's initially lacking late game, and if you do chose to buy Stellaris, I would highly recommend you also purchase Utopia. Regardless of the new content that the various DLC's bring to the game, Stellaris remains let down by its one major flaw: War.
Victory in Stellaris comes down to one thing, and one thing alone: the size of your military. You could create a race of pacifist bird-people, as an expample of Stellaris's impressive scope for diversity, but you'll probably end up conquered almost immediately. What about a race of reptilian scientists, deades ahead of the rest of the galaxy? Sure thing! But watch your back, if someone with a bigger navy comes rolling into town, you're probably not going to stand a chance! What about a humble democracy of Humans? You could do that too, but have fun getting penned in! From my 135 hours spent in-game, at least at the times of this writting, the only way I've found to not only rule the galaxy, but merely to survive in it as a sovereign state, is to play as a militaristic conqueror - or as a Hive Mind, one of the new forms of government added in the Utopia expansion.
I would have no problem with this, as both EU and HOI are two of my personal favorite grand strategy franchises at the moment, and both are built around the concept of military conquest. However, war in Stellaris is much less nuanced and, frankly, over simplified than it is in either of those aforementioned games. As hinted at above, it comes down to "He who has the biggest fleet wins." "So why not just build more ships?" you ask. Well, let me tell you: the number of ships you can have in your navy at any one time is limited. It can, however, be increased by constructing orbital space stations around your colonized worlds, or through various technologies. The key then becomes colonizing worlds faster than your opponents, something easier said than done, given that colonization, at least in the early game, is a massive drain on your exonomy.

Therefore, a balance must be struck durring the early game and maintained throughout the rest of the game: on one hand you must expand your empire, witch is expensive, and in the mid to late game - when most of the galaxy has already been claimed by one empire or another - requires and impressive navy. You must also invest in science facilities on planets, along side research stations in orbit, to ensure your technological supremacy. Not to mention power generation facilities - the main currency in Stellaris is, of course, "Energy Credits" - and mines. All of which consume the same resources that you need for the expansion and maintenance of your navy.
This is an EXTREMELY brief overview of war in Stellaris. In short, I find it a tedious nightmare to manage. But this is, after all, a Paradox game. I have every confidence that in another year - not to mention in another two or three years - Stellaris will be a fantastic game. Right now, it's little more than a foundation. In time, something spectacular could be built here. It just hasn't been built yet.

Stellaris os an overall fun game, but the game play can get stale, and the dlc strategy of paradox is less than ideal.
I would describe Stellaris as a 4X RTS game and would not consider it grand strategy in its current state (1.5 at the time of review) due to lack of depth in diplomacy.
Having come from gal civ and civ V, the game feels pretty intuitive and easy to get into. I had hear that this was the easiest paradox strategy game to get into. Having only played the tutorial of ck2, I would agree. Time will tell if the starting ease will disappear as the game develops.
Speaking of game development, the developers are very active in development and transparency. I started playing ok 1.4.1, currently on 1.5, anD 1.6 has been announced. The devs are active on social media.
Species creation is acceptable. It's not a big factor in my opinion, but I am satisfied with it.
Game setup is decent, too. Before 1.5, all new game setup settings revetted to native defaults, and making tweaks was tedious. I would recommend playing 1 FTL allowed. Also before 1.5, the game would not explicitly tell you if the game setup is eligible for achievements.
The game is definitely fun to play. There are missions that you can play early and somewhat mid game to add excitement. Very Early game is pretty straightforward ward for a 4X: explore and expand.
War game play is in need of improvement. When war is declared, you set "war goals" which dictate your spoils should you win. Winning a war is done by achieving 100% "warscore" which is determined by winning space battles, and conquering planets.
The AI is not the best and they are pretty predictable; they will always prioritize defense. A human can easily judge and engage in winning battles, or turtle by scattering your fleet offensively. Most of the strategy of war comes well before war is declared in the ship designer.
As far as ship designer goes, there is some balance issues that should be addressed. Missiles are horrible. They are the least likely to hit, and they overkill. The 3 standard types of weapons were designed to have strengths and weaknesses, but missiles strengths are grossly outclassed by their weaknesses.
Game play style, I have only played wide. Without utopia dlc, playing tall holds no to very little advantages. Playing wide increases population, production, and naval capacity at the cost of higher science requirements for technologies and more sectors.
The player may only control a small number of planets directly. When there are too many planets, you create sectors, which are AI controlled systems. These are beneficial because they reduce tedious micromanagement, and bad because the AI is dumb. As of 1.5, resource management sucks. The player only receives 75% max of resources. Excess resources are effectively lost. You tax both resources equally, so specialized sectors may be resource deficient. That scenario is counterproductive to the micromanagement doffusion. That all being said, 1.6 is confirmed to fix the resource issue.
As far as DLC goes, there are features that are DLC exclusive that IMO should not be. Things like war in heaven, or slavery/purging options come to mind. Those features could be added to the base game, but are not. Having only played leviathins dlc (planetoid is aesthetic iirc), the leviathans and nomads are sufficient enough for a DLC.
Overall, I'd recommend this game. Wait for a sale.
At this time, Stellar is Paradox's best game. Great replayability and the graphics are on a higher level than their other games. The consistant updates and expansions are also a big plus.

So my review will be fairly short. If you like MMOs you should like this game. After 15years of MMO gameplay you really should have seen it all by now even if you are new and watching YouTube. 1. Questing is fun and like normal questing. A good variety at the lower levels.
2. There are quests that activate as you move through the world as a bonus.
3. Things are easy to locate and the quest log is fairly clear.
4. Easy to learn new things as you go. It is explained if you read.
5. Along with your class you can pick a profession like explorer, scientist, etc. I don't remember the rest.
6. The game is cartoony but beautiful at the same time. Reminds me of Guild Wars 2 but more cartoony like borderlands.
7. You can accumulate coin and buy stuff from teh store.
8. If you like building you can build a house or residence from scratch or from prefab stuff.
9. I was questing with a friend and we had good fun together.
10. Customization of characters is very in depth. Check out my screenshots of you want to see some.
If anyone wants to play let me know and add me to your friends list. But I only like to play for fun. I don't care for power leveling. I enjoy my games because they are games. Not because they make me special in some way. I prefer using teamspeak as well.

The Moon Silver is a psychologial horror game that I can't talk much about without spoiling. Without any spoilers the story talks about the fate of four friends that lived in a island under the protection of a holy artifact that kept a Demon away. During the entirety of the game you will be walking around a small deserted island piecing together a story and getting to know who the four friends were and what happened on the last few days on the island,  and everytime the story progresses a certain amount of time passes. When night falls you must return to the mountain.
The game is to be played in one sitting and its duration is of about 1 hour long, so if you are looking for a quick piece of story with some horror added to it. The graphics aren't the best but the soundtrack and the story make it for a great game. I recommed it for people that enjoy these kind of psychological horrors.

All in all, The Moon Sliver is a great, short experience for those looking for a calmer, story-based game.

I bought this game out of my love for horror games, pixel graphics, and puzzles, but I was let down. The puzzles have, in classic point-and-click fashion, insane solutions. Solving a problem does not so much depend on figuring out a solution as it depends on scouring all the pixels and places for the items you need.
The story is what seems to be the most important part of this game, but it is thoroughly incoherent. Told purely from our main character and whatever he sees, there is never a sense that there is a world outside of him. Perhaps intentional, perhaps not. Who knows? Certainly not me, because this story is interpretational and has different endings based on some things you need to do/not do. ( Kill all the monsters, don't kill all the monsters, make a choice in a hospital or something...)
All the horror classics are here, with none of the refinement or horror. Spooky girl who may or may not be part of your past. Clear signals that not-all-is-right and that your main character might be in a coma/delusion/dream/death. Monsters whose existence are never explained...
Perhaps if the sound design had been better, and the gameplay smoother and more refined, I could have loved this game. As it was, it failed to be scary. It also failed to be fun to play, or intruiging. I do not understand the positive reviews at all - for a horror indie-title with more atmosphere, better monsters, and similarly awkward controls, just download Cry of Fear.

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is another loot shooter that's a way too similar to Borderlands 2 for its own good.
The game is set between the two main Borderlands games and follows Handsome Jack's rise to power. Unfortunately the story is rather poorly written and the jokes are not nearly as funny as in Borderlands 2.
Most of the action takes place on Pandora's moon Elpis. This means low gravity combat and oxygen managament for outdoor environments. In practice I didn't really care too much for either mechanic. Oxygen management in particular felt rather tedious without really adding anything to the game.
The weakest part of the game, however, is the poor map and mission design. On outdoor maps it's way too easy to fall into holes and cracks that will insta-kill you. Furthermore, a lot of the missions require extensive backtracking. Combined, these two problems get old really quickly.
The core gameplay is still fun, but overall it's hard to recommend the Pre-Sequel unless you have already played Borderlands 2 to death and are still left craving for more.

The game is quite old. It was released in 2003 by Invictus Games. Invictus Games finally named it abandonedware and moved on. Imagecode managed to revive the game and put it on steam. Even till this day, They slowly update this game. What makes it unique is that this is a game using an engine from the late 1990s and was released in 2003, but is still being updated as of 2017.
The game is quite fun with tons of tuning and racing. You can tune up a car and take it to a street race, drag race, or another racing event. Career mode can be challenging as you have little funds to buy a functioning car and start racing. If you accidentally crash, the effects can be devastating. You will lose parts and your chassis will become mangled up. And worse yet, crash damage is permanent unless repaired with money. Once you get enough cash and a good car, you can fine-tune your car and decorate it with your heart's desire.
The game also uses workshop integration as well as having a large modding community online. There are thousands of mods that add cosmetics, performance parts, cars, and even new tracks.
Sadly, the game is NOT stable. Crashes are more than common and can lead to deletion of progress. Every button click makes you cross your fingers in hope that the game wont crash. But luckily, the game is still being updated and patches are still rolling out.
Pros:
+Classic
+Still indev
+Indepth tuning
+Racing
+Challenging
+Workshop integration and mods.
Cons:
-Unstable
9/10

This game has the potential to be a lot of fun, but about half a dozen glaring issues makes this hard to recommend.
1) There are a lot of situations that'll force you into starting a new career, the most obvious one is running out of money. Even buying the cheapest car will only leave you enough money for a few races, if you don't make headway with that you'll be out of money with no option but to start a new career.
2) The game has about a 1/3 chance of crashing whenever you return to your garage from city mode and if it crashes while entering your garage your car will disappear never to be seen again. I've gone through 3 careers and had this put an end to each one before finally putting the game away. When you enter the game again you'll have all of your progress and cash but your garage will be empty and you'll be prompted to buy another car.
3) Night racing scales too quickly and doesn't give you enough chances to make money before your opponents start blowing your car out of the water. I've started with the 19k sports car twice now and it'll carry me through about 4-5 races to the point where drivers start betting 4k each and after that I get pounded into the ground with (seemingly) no option to challenge weaker racers. This leaves you stuck in the position of doing track races (if you can with your car, the sports car only qualifies for like.. 2? out of 59 to begin with.)
4) From what I can tell you can't jack up your car in the garage, which causes you to be unable to take certain parts off your car if you want to repair them piece by piece, this isn't a HUGE issue because there's an option to repair everything on your car, but if you have some expensive repairs and want to be selective about what you repair this could cause a problem.
5) The early track races get repetitive fast and don't reward enough money to make them feel satisfying. If you start with the $17k wagon you'll qualify for a race that costs $100 to enter and rewards $500 for first place. It'll take about 3 minutes to clear, meaning you'll make roughly $1200 in about 10 minutes of racing the same track. I don't expect to be given 3k per race and have an amazing car grinding the first race, but it does make it a bit too grindy to get to a satisfying place. Also, if you plan on night racing at all, having that grind wiped away by issue #2 makes things even worse.
6) The parts catalogue does little to help you in picking out parts for your car. I was thankful that it would at least tell you if you could install certain parts in your car when you went to buy them, but didn't do much to tell you what was compatible with what, and if you couldn't buy it it wouldn't tell you anything at all which makes planning for future upgrades difficult. I'd like to see some sort of part comparison later on that'll make it a bit easier to tell what's compatible with your vehicle in its current state.
Those are the glaring issues I see with the game in its current state, but I did have a lot of fun before #2 became a roadblock for me. The customization has the potential to be really enjoyable, I like being able to sell off parts of my car that I don't use for a little extra cash (who needs a passenger seat or doors!?) and the painting booth seems like it could be nice as well even though I never really had the spare cash to use it. As a guy that doesn't personally have a whole lot of experience with cars I could see myself having a lot of fun with this game once it gets a bit more polished, it's pretty approachable already.

The short:
This game is beautiful and the soundtrack is fantastic. Unfortunately it is bogged down by a dated combat system that makes fights a chore rather than a challenge. The combat loop just isn't interesting enough to carry the player through the game without outstaying its welcome.
The ramble:
The art style is beautiful. Everything from the vibrant colors to the fluid animations with weight and punch on heavy characters and finesse and elegance on the roguey-types. Cutscenes are equally stylistic with a comicbook aesthetic. Watching a giant Hulkbuster Iron Man looking robot dash up, wind up, and PAWNCH looks and sounds fantastic.
Complimenting the art is the music. The fluid animations at the start of each fight is coupled with music that punctuate the movements of the party members as they ready for the fight for each area. Boss fights have their own tense yet oddly calming at the same time. The soundtrack is great in the background for concentration. It elevates the fights without being in the spotlight of attention.
The loot system is pretty decent with items that have effects beyond pure stat boosts. Some give you a chance to heal on hit, others more attack as you attack, or others that have chance to apply different statuses oh hit or crits. Crafting potions and upgrading gear feels rewarding as it can make an impossible fight possible and a hard fight no sweat.
Sadly, the core combat loop feels dated, slow, clunky, tedious, and a chore. The animations while beautiful and not as long and drawn out as some other games- is just long enough to get that urge to mash the confirm button even though it does absolutely nothing to speed up the animations but short enough that you can't go grab a cup of tea while it's playing. The core combat loop is balanced in a way that most fights are either trivial via outleveling/gearing the encounter, or you die. Most combos you can set up either kill the targets so fast it's not completely setup or last so short that by the time you set up a combo, the fight's over. Most fights that last long enough for a combo to be worth setting up ends up doing too much damage to actually setup an offensive combo and results in a healing loop leading to a slow death. The way that resurrection works (at least in the early game) is frustrating. If a member falls a bit of timing and luck is requires to resurrect that member and KEEP them up. More often than not something hits the recently revived member and they keel over again. The inability to queue up a single target heal/shield limits the options to revive said member.
Long story short, there is very little room for actual strategy in a given fight. You either overpower the fight, die a quick death. Fights are pretty braindead. All in all, it was not my cup of tea but some may find it a good wind down game at the end of the day with the fantastic soundtrack.

I've been playing Wildstar casually for a while now, I never played this game when it first came out, but I know people that did. I'm told that it was a completely different experience to how it is now. I try a lot of MMOs because I'm on an eternal quest to fill the gaping hole WoW left in my heart. This one I'd heard a lot about so I thought, hey why not give it a try and see.
I never expected to be so charmed, but by the time I finished the tutorial I was ready to drop some money and support this game. It has a vibrant charm which reminds me of the appeal of WoW. The slightly more skill-based combat is engaging and more involved than your standard "hit and be hit" format. I enjoy exploring the Nexus and I like the addition of secondary objectives to complete based on your profession. Voice acting is great, characters and lore are interesting too.
Although great, the game isn't perfect. I'm not a fan of the faction split. While it does give some context to the events I don't like the way the exiles are painted as these all loving good guys, while the dominion as these almost 'Sith-esque' levels of evil. Other MMOs are good at making the factions feel balanced but I don't get that here, it feels like the exiles are the real favourites. It's a matter of taste really, but it has bugged me that the Exiles feel like the main focus.
The questing is also not very engaging I'm sad to say. The game does the standard MMO thing of leading you one quest to another until you hit a hub and pick up a handful which lead you to the next area, etc. While nothing is strictly wrong with that, it would have been nice to see some innovation. There is variation in the exact stuff you have to do, and the gathering quests make you spam a button or do a simple skill based action to complete, but it's still a case of grab quest, do quest, turn in quest. I find myself running around to all the '!' symbols on the map, grabbing all the quests, then opening my map to find out where to go, rather than stop to read any of it. Which is a shame.
If you like your standard MMO experience then Wildstar is definitely worth your time. It's charming, and fun to play. Best of all it's free so you can play with friends. While I don't agree with everything that you can purchase for real money, it's safe to say that no purchases are "required" to play and enjoy the game. If you played the game when it first came out I would recommend giving it another go because it's certainly changed in a good way.
TL;DR - Only some gameplay innovation over other MMOs (mostly combat), but lots of charm and polish. Worth trying.

My favorite part of the horror genre isn't the monsters but the build up to the monsters. In my opinion, that is what this game does well: build-up. There are no jump scares, no running or fighting for your life, and no clear, linear order in which the exploration needs to happen. Only that it does need to happen. Honestly, if I had to give one 'con' to this game, it's that the exploration aspect is a little unclear--there was a section I really didn't want to go through because of how (let's be honest) scary it was. I ended up going through it twice, partially because I hadn't investigated it all, and partly because I didn't realize that the last location I needed was actually on the other side of the island. Whoops!
[Spoilers!]
The shifting narrative is wonderfully done, especially at the end. There is definitely an 'oh crap!' moment at the big reveal. I probably stood staring at the wall for a good fifteen seconds when I reached the chair and the lamp, just laughing at myself because of how much I genuinely didn't want to turn around. I love the reveal (or, more accurately, un-reveal) of the 'monster' at the end, though. The shadowed figure in the distance gave the perfect mixture of dread and relief. Dread, because omg a shadow monster. Relief, because by the time we reach that point we know that it's what we want.
I never let my flashlight run out of battery (but it was a super close thing in the tunnels), so I don't know if it's possible to be snatched up before the actual ending. Honestly, I don't think I want to give it a try.
Overall, this was a nice narrative experience. I probably won't play it again, but it was definitely worth the ~$1 price.

For everything Delver does right, it does one to three things incredibly wrong.  And for almost 4 years in Early Access, you'd think there'd be... more.  And better.  Here's hoping the relatively recent workshop implementation isn't just "I'm done with the game, you guys make stuff for it".
First playthrough, the game is cool.  Things to discover, things to find out, the novelty of the new and unexplored.  The cute art style, the charming ambience and music, the question of "how lethal is all of this" upon first discovering things.  A simple yet effective gear system, manageable weapon durability, just enough inventory space, and just enough tools to get the job done.  A decent flow of experience and leveling, a health system based on regeneration except for the rarer instant heal potion, and some magic.  All of this creates a nice adventure and roguelike environment.  Right up until you become familiar with it all.
!!! There will be "mechanics spoilers" below.  If you want to find these out for yourself, do not read the rest.  !!!
About half of the enemies in the game apply a Damage over Time effect when they hit you.  Nearly HALF.  Nothing counters this damage except healing, so it doesn't matter how much Defense or AC (armor) you have, you simply have to outheal it or step in water if you're on fire.  Or, if you're poisoned, sucks to be you.
All healing items are consumables.  All healing items are completely random and you may get a lot or you may get none.  None of those healing items stack in the same part of your inventory.  I believe a piece of food heals for 12 points of health over time because all different food heals the same amount for some reason.  You start with 8 health.  I believe both Burning and Poison do 6 points of damage.  So, in order for your healing to be efficient you have to be missing at least 12 points of health otherwise you're wasting part of the food, or the amount healed post-DoT has to be worth it.  It's messy and annoying.
Flying enemies have awful hitboxes and extremely annoying, unpredictable AI.  On the contrary, melee enemies all engage you in the exact same way unless they jump, then they jump the exact same way.  Mage enemies cast Fire spells that burn you from afar.  There is a flying mage enemy common throughout half of the floors.  What all of this equates to is melee enemies are a joke, never a threat as long as you're looking at them, and are just bags of experience.  Unless they have poison, which means if you get tagged you lose 7 health minimum.  This also means that flying enemies and mages are extremely un-fun to fight as they have both a ranged and a melee attack and the ranged attack is very likely to  Burn you.  Did I mention the hitboxes of your weapon, when swung vertically, are garbage and wonky?
Speaking of weapons, they're powerful enough in their own right that you don't -really- need additional attack as long as you can keep finding newer weapons with decent stats, because all weapons degrade.  Magic is absolute garbage, either having very low damage or very low sustainability, or both.  Archery is strong but the arrows have a chance to break upon impact and you don't get very many.  On a good run, the highest amount I had at once was around 30.
Since the weapons are powerful in themselves, melee enemies are a joke and flying enemies are always faster than you, magic is garbage, and DoT's are wildly overpowered, this makes the stats you want to take on leveling very, very limited.  There is Attack, Agility, Speed, Defense, Health, and Magic.  None of those level up on their own, you have to choose them.  Except you can only pick from 1 of 3 of those, at random, when you level.  If you don't take Health multiple times, you basically can't play the game because you'll die instantly.
The problem with the levels themselves is that they don't really offer anything new from one another.  All of the loot, plus and minus some minor numbers, can be found anywhere, and all of the enemies operate extremely similarly.  The last world is also pretty unbalanced.  All the spike traps work the exact same and do the same damage and are basically just an inconvenience rather than any kind of trap.
Also there's a shop system that pretty much sucks.  Gold is really rare, even if your "save file" keeps it, not just that life, but there's only about 3 different locations for shops, the inventory is random, and things cost a LOT.  So, pretty much useless.
*deep breath*
Right, then.  That's a lot of nonsense, and it all collapses in on itself to make your runs just one big frustration.  Half of it is good and half of it is awful.  The things that are easy are a joke and a waste of time, and the things that are hard are just wildly frustrating and not satisfying or rewarding to overcome.  My final few runs were just sprinting through as fast as I could, conserving melee weapons, healing items, and the health stat because anything else just wasn't worth it.  Then, when I was really prepared for the special "event" that happens at the final world, I got screwed over and saw no way to be anywhere near able to beat it.  Then I stopped for good.
Unfortunate.
Edit:  Forgot to mention that the game invariably crashed if I had it open for too long, and there was constant stuttering with my mouse movements.

Lone survivor is an amazing psychological Silent Hill like horror game. It has a vary appropriate UI and keyboard layout making it so that you don’t ever use your mouse to let you immerse yourself in the game without any hiccups. You got to keep in mind that this is, in a way; a role-playing game and you may have a greater experience if you treat the character as a human being instead of just a character sprite. The 8bit style applied in this game is great and truly works well with the whole feel of the game. In the end, this is a truly well made game with great use of the medium that successfully conveys the theme and tone of the game. In fact this is the game that got me to truly appreciate 8bit games!

Lone survivor may at first seems like a normal horror game that you have played times and times before, but it's not. It got the thing that made Silent Hill 2 and IMSCARED Great.
The main character is a nameless person and seems like he doesn't care for anything, not even his life. But he have a past and through the game you might get an idea of what the story is about if you took a close look. you will start to wonder if anything is real or if he just imagining everything because of his loneliness and depression, he's not crazy by any means but I think the game is symbolic for how he feel inside.
There is a lot of optional quests to do in the game, but by the time you beat the game you will realise you haven't done a single quest, you will be lucky if you at least finished one quest. You will eventually know about the thing you missed after you finished your first run.
The game is difficult because of the rarity of the bullets and batterys. I had to start the game from the beginning multiple times because I lost a lot of them and they are necessary to progress through the game.
The Atmosphere in the game is one of the strongest in any video game I've ever played in my life. the soundtrack alone will give you the scares. I'll say the OST alone is enough reason to play the game. The game has one of the best soundtrack in all of video game history, It's not a surprise since the Composer/Designer is Jaspert Byrne, the same guy who made some of the music in Hotline Miami 1&2.
The pixel art in the game is foggy and gloomy in the best possible way which helps the atmosphere and make it stronger.
The game has ZERO Jumpscare which make the horror real and much more effective.
You also have a sanity and a hunger meter that you can't see it but you can take care of it by taking care of the Lone Survivor by giving him food and letting him sleep when it's nesasary, but be careful for the food is rare and sleeping (or the lack of it) will have an effect on the ending you will get.
There is Multiple Endings to the game but there is no Good or Bad ending, it's all about the things you see and how you take care of The Lone survivor.
I won't spoile to much of the game I already said enough.
All in All, the game is nothing short of a masterpiece and you can tell it was made with love and Jasper really loved survivor Horror games. It's heavily inspired by Silent Hill 2 and that's not a bad thing at all, the game gose for the old school survivor Horror rots and that's the best thing about it. You will enjoy the game especially if you like horror games or games that tells a surreal story in general.
Definitely Play it       10/10

Super stylish RPG. Actual battles are turn based like the JRPGs of yore, but there is a lot of strategy. The first hour or so it may seem kind of simple, but once your characters hit around lvl 5 or 6 a wealth of options open up for them. Each character has 4 'basic' attacks that you pull off instantly, then a bunch of magical spells that take a bit of time to pull off (modified by the 'Haste" stat, the higher your Haste, the quicker you use your spell.) Then there is a burst move which each character shares, some are offensive and some are defensive. You can only use the burst move once the gauge fills up, a la FF. You also earn perk points to invest in one of two trees for each character. Combat starts somewhat simplistic and aquires a lot of depth quickly.
A pretty cool crafting system, replayable dungeons with higher difficulties that yield higher rewards, a great selection of monsters to fight, and absolutely gorgeous artwork/character design/graphics in the Joe Mad style. Take every character or enemy, draw them completely over the top, and keep going until they just explode onto your screen as the ultimate action hero or super villain.
Also has some pretty good voice acting and, like every great JRPG before it, a fun fishing minigame. There are many other things that make this fun, I just can't type em all.
Only cons (which don't bother me, but might bother some) sometimes it can seem a bit grindy. I haven't needed to grind yet, but I lucked out with two incredible weapons for two of my three main heroes I use.  When you're fighting low level enemies sometimes you'll wish for a fast forward option for battles, but the graphics and animation are so good it's not a major concern. Laslty, the overall movement speed of your characters in the overworld and the dungeon maps is a bit slow, it'd be nice if they would speed it up a bit or add a run button or something, but still, minor quibbles.
If you like old school RPGs or if you want to try something a bit different than the recent slew of cookie cutter western RPGs, you can't go wrong with this.
Also... dat art. Whew.

The Battle Chasers franchise is a niche one, evidently. I've never heard of this comic nor read it when it was released. According to the wikipage, it was extremely popular, hence the game. It actually continues the story from where issue #9 left off and will bridge the gap between issue #9 and issue #10... so get reading I suppose?
It seems like an entry level comic book, something for the kids, you won't have to go mining deep for an enthralling plot because there isn't one to be found. They took a note from their own page, so to speak, because the game itself is also an entry level RPG with zero depth. Read On.
The presentation is great. I love the art style, I wasn't a huge fan of it in Darksiders because let's face it, Darksiders is pretty lame as far as serious gaming goes... It's one of those franchises that just takes itself too seriously and ends up just being dumb in the end... there's a bit of that here as well. It was a fitting marriage to hire the art designer for Darksiders on this project... I'm a stickler for JRPG's so the "mechanics" saved it for me.
If you know JRPG's the rest is self explainitory. There's nothing new or innovative here. You choose an attack, the character carry's out the attack, you wait for the enemies to attack, then the cycle repeats. They placed a turn tracking bar so you know which characters turn is up next, which was a nice touch, it adds a bit of tactical element to your choices. Some attacks require more time to perform but I'm so used to the guessing game it made the choices even easier, there's such a huge margin of error in this game you'd have to be trying hard to actually die in a fight.
On top of that, there's a Street Fighter style battle burst bar that everyone in the party shares. Not quite sure what fills it, seems like just carrying out attacks, I never really paid attention, it fills so fast and frequently it almost trivializes the "super moves". In a lot of fights I almost forgot I even had the option because I was breezing through things, I'd always just leave it full for those moments where I just wanted to slaughter a boss.
You walk around a map, there's only a single town (HUB) and 8 fully explorable dungeons with about 5 or 6 small side areas to carry out extra quests. The map is linear, it runs on a node system like Super Mario World and doors block your path, so you never have full control of where you can explore. The game basically just holds your hand and every area is locked until it's time to go there when following the main story. There are warp points though but honestly, there should of been more of them. Your characters walk insanely slow and when you're forced to walk along a winding road to your destination instead of taking the shortest direct path, it can get tedious and frustrating.
The dungeons themselves are pure RNG, just randomness. You never know what you're going to encounter and what order you're going to encounter it in. You can replay dungeons on different difficulty modes, on the first playthrough there's 3 modes, on New Game+ there's 4 although from what I've heard there isn't much difference between the 3rd and 4th difficulty levels.
The side quests are insanely cryptic and require lots of reading and checking inventory items, or you know, the internet. The game is mediocrity at it's finest but then there's these insanely cryptic, almost impossible to figure out, side quests plugged in to the game but it's strictly due to how random some of the games elements are... there's nothing difficult about them, just shoddy craftsmanship when designing this game. There's a few really annoying random events in some of the dungeons that are linked to obtaining some of the characters ultimate weapons but without a walkthrough of sorts, you'd never figure them out... and even when you have discovered what to do, it's all based on your own personal luck... pretty bad system honestly.
So rather than just completely♥♥♥♥♥♥all over this game and tell you to stay clear, I'll just say, it served it's purpose. It ate up a lot of my time unnecessarily, a giant gripe of mine is artifical game extension and this game is just chalk full of it... and before I hear in the comments "but it's an RPG, it's supposed to waste your time" .... it's doing it in the wrong ways... Forcing me to complete the same dungeon over and over again multiple times to try and get a random room to spawn or find some enemy so I can get more rare drops is not my idea of good game design.
The game loses it's charm about 60% of the way in and by the end you just want it to all be over but you can't let it end because you have to catch every fish in the game and fight every enemy 25 times each so you can get all their bestiary information... I seriously started getting a headache because of this.
By the end of the game you'll literally be 1 shotting every enemy, including the final boss... yes, I used a level 3 burst attack and killed the last boss in a single hit... I never even saw it do a single attack.
I've also never seen an RPG where the enemys are so anxious to run head first in to death... Even when you're 20+ levels higher than the enemies, they all come charging in full force ready to waste more of your time with pointless battle animations. You figure the dev's would of implemented a system where the enemies would flee from you if you could kill them in a single hit but no, on the world map they give you the option to fight them, in dungeons, you're forced to fight everything... logic? None.
So yadda yadda yadda, was it terrible? No... was it trivial? Yeah. Should you buy it? Sure, if you're bored and have nothing to do. It was fun, it served it's purpose (RPG fix) but I don't want to play through it again, and considering there's a NG+ option that basically just piles on more redundant game play it's a huge turn off in my books.
Great entry level turn based RPG for the kids with a great artistic style (subjective, I like it) But is unfortunately marred by poor game design choices, graphical bugs and redudant and boring gimmicks to keep you grinding, but not for power, just for junk items to fill up collectors log books. If you're looking for a compelling plot, game play depth or even a remote challenge, you need to look elsewhere.
Otherwise, it's a 7 / 10.
It needs some patch work and over all leaves much to be desired... but if you can grab it on sale and have about 50 hours of your time to kill, it's a decent game to mess around with.

For the most part this game plays like a classic JRPG, with a few twists. Instead of random encounters 'randomly' popping up, they occur at intervals along your path in the overworld, or visible enemies in dungeons. Either one triggers an old school turn based battle, again with a couple twists. You have a few actions at your disposal that act instantly, as well as spells that have varying delays until they activate. Actions can also build overcharge, which is temporary exta mana that lasts for the duration of the battle, and will be consumed first when you have both. I particularly like this mechanic as it allows me to be a little more liberal with spells than I would otherwise be, and eliminates the need for hoarding a lot of mana potions for working through a dungeon or longer trips in the overworld. The characters each have unique combat abilities, and a bunch have secondary effects that you can combine with other characters' abilities to increase in strength. They also have abilities that can be used outside combat with a effects ranging from healing the party, to navigating or exploring dungeons, to starting a round of combat with a buff.
So far the game has been all around fun, and I have no complaints.

Recommendations don't come much easier than this tbh.
Nier is an exceptional title that is not only super fun to play, but does a lot of unique and creative things with its narrative that deserve much love and praise. In an age when every title is derivative of another -which in and of itself is not condemnation, it is simply difficult these days for devs to truly innovate - Nier comes along and manages to do just that, innovate. What's more, that innovation lends itself to some truly excellent story telling and impressively smooth transitions between multiple different play-styles.
I'm not going to go too deep here on describing the game, I'd imagine anyone who is interested in it will do their due diligence and read multiple reviews etc from the major gaming publications, which will explain the mechanics and all that jazz. I also don't really wanna give anything away, as I went in pretty unspoiled and enjoyed it immensely, I think if I'd known more it may have taken away from that sense of discovery a tad. Not enough to be ruinous or anything of course, but yeah, best to go in knowing the bare minimum and strap in for one hell of a ride.
I'll leave this portion by saying this:
This game wasnt even on my radar, yet currently it is my Number 1 GOTY contender. The only game I actually think will beat it for me is Red Dead Redemption 2 if it manages to keep on schedule, and that's because I adore the first and the GTA franchise.
I recently played, and platinum'd, Horizon Zero Dawn, and enjoyed it a lot. But this title was easily superior imo, and gave me a far more memorable experience.
The thing is I expected HZD to be great, I expect RDR to be amazing, but Nier came out of nowhere for me, I'd never even heard of the original, and it turned out being something very special and a truly wonderful surprise as I was not in any way following this games development. It's also great to see Platinum Games well and truly back on track with this stellar title.
Platinum, Yoko Taro, ‎Keiichi Okabe, and everyone else involved should be very proud of this title.
TECHNICAL PERFORMANCE:
I'll keep this brief, I had absolutely no issues with this title except one.
The one thing is the full screen/resolution issue. It was a super easy fix using the mod linked in the games steam forum, but I cannot deny that it is also inexcusable that Square Enix have not addressed this with an official patch fix still! It took a mere couple of minutes to resolve but still...c'mon guys support the product properly.
Beyond that though, my experience was incredibly stable.
I ran it at 1440p resolution, every setting maxed except AA (4X instead of 8x) and i can count on one hand the amount of times it dropped below its 60fps cap. Excepting the cut scenes of course which are at 30fps.
I also had no issues with cutscene choppiness like some have reported, and the game crashed on me ZERO times, which I consider impressive for any game in this day and age when I'm approaching 40 hours played.
So, not to discount others who have had a rougher time of it, but if your configuration is similar to mine you hopefully should have a very nice experience with this title.

I started playing 4x games back in the early 90's when I bought my first overpriced Acer computer from Best Buy. The first one was called "ascendancy" and it is still a great game but very ancient. Of course I played gal civ 1-3 and several others. Inevitably I would grow either bored, too frustrated, or just disapointed with nearly every 4x game that over promised and vastly under-delivered. I bought Stellaris with fairly low expectations thinking it would be just another shallow, tedious, or impossibly hard piece of garbage, but I was WRONG. This is THE BEST 4x game that I have ever played hands down. It has everything that I find enjoyable and none of the crap that ruins 4x games. It has random encounters with story threads that can be followed for extra bonuses (and sometimes doesn't always turn out for the best which is just fine). It has a very deep and intuitive UI and the AI seems to be spot on as far as difficulty. A lot of recent 4x games have been impossibly hard even on easiest levels, but Stellaris gets it just right. It has a lot of choices for customization and flavor and it isn't all just window dressing- the choices you make developing your species and empire flavor the universe and reactions to you, etc. I haven't exhausted nearly half of what the game has to offer and that is also rare. I just started looking at mods and playing around with them, but the vanilla game right out of the box is spot on as is. Not one time has this game crashed on me either which I must admit is rare for a Paradox game. This is well worth the full price and is wat 4x games should have always been. I can honestly say that there is not one misstep. I give this game my highest recommendation.

The biggest con with this game would probably be the fact that any time you switch your weapon type- for example, going from a rifle to a beam weapon- any upgrades you had on that rifle to use on the beam weapon are not available and you are forced to rebuy them. What's even worse is that if you ever want to switch back to the rifle weapon type you still can't use your original upgrades. In a game so heavily focused on changing and customizing your loadout, the fact that you essentially throw away all of your credits that you have invested in your gun whenever you just want to change your current weapon to a different type is incredibly frustrating.
Aside from that, the game is incredibly fun. There is plenty of customization to be had, the wide variety of combinations you can have in your weapons is excellent, and all of the humorous stuff in it never ceases to be funny. I'd say try it.

It won't swallow your very soul and social life like I expect from a good online shooter, but there's lots of fun to be had.
It's an arena shooter with standard modes and the lighting, animation, and graphics look absolutely GORGEOUS!
From there, it adopts its own style. When you get experience fighting effectively in matches, you get the "blute" currency, with which you can customize several different types of guns and skill trees in a variety of effective ways. While the guns don't seem entirely tested and balanced... (COUGH COUGH rocket launchers, COUGH COUGH incendiary rounds), they're a whole load of fun to use and it's addicting to level them up. Also, there's a myriad of death and damage animations that are cringe-inducingly gruesome to flat out Loony Toons-style hilarious.
The character customization is where the game shows its cartoony sense of humor. You exchange real world money for the "spacebux" currency to buy anything from hardcore military, to sci-fi, to saggy rapper jeans, to biker vests, to hair metal band t-shirts, to the infamous "Axl's Rod" for one of the three mercs. While these items have no effect on gameplay, they are INSANELY expensive. One average cosmetic will set you back an equivilent of four or five bucks in real life. It would be nice to either increase the amount of spacebux you get for your dollar or have some way of earning spacebux ingame.
It's new, so some infrequent bugs might occur. It's also clearly an indie-game. The match "announcer"'s voice is done with some sort of Microsoft Windows 98 Speak-and-Spell potato or something like that. For this to be a released game and not even have a real voice actor for combat commands is truely pathetic.
The spacebux and "indie-ness" of the game aside, the insane and totally-customizable weapons are an addicting feature that have kept me playing this game in order to buff my favorite guns to the top. The repetition of maps and the overall un-diverse gameplay will only make it enthralling enough to play it an hour or so at a time, but for a free-to-play game, it's definitely a must-play.

I've been playing Wildstar casually for a while now, I never played this game when it first came out, but I know people that did. I'm told that it was a completely different experience to how it is now. I try a lot of MMOs because I'm on an eternal quest to fill the gaping hole WoW left in my heart. This one I'd heard a lot about so I thought, hey why not give it a try and see.
I never expected to be so charmed, but by the time I finished the tutorial I was ready to drop some money and support this game. It has a vibrant charm which reminds me of the appeal of WoW. The slightly more skill-based combat is engaging and more involved than your standard "hit and be hit" format. I enjoy exploring the Nexus and I like the addition of secondary objectives to complete based on your profession. Voice acting is great, characters and lore are interesting too.
Although great, the game isn't perfect. I'm not a fan of the faction split. While it does give some context to the events I don't like the way the exiles are painted as these all loving good guys, while the dominion as these almost 'Sith-esque' levels of evil. Other MMOs are good at making the factions feel balanced but I don't get that here, it feels like the exiles are the real favourites. It's a matter of taste really, but it has bugged me that the Exiles feel like the main focus.
The questing is also not very engaging I'm sad to say. The game does the standard MMO thing of leading you one quest to another until you hit a hub and pick up a handful which lead you to the next area, etc. While nothing is strictly wrong with that, it would have been nice to see some innovation. There is variation in the exact stuff you have to do, and the gathering quests make you spam a button or do a simple skill based action to complete, but it's still a case of grab quest, do quest, turn in quest. I find myself running around to all the '!' symbols on the map, grabbing all the quests, then opening my map to find out where to go, rather than stop to read any of it. Which is a shame.
If you like your standard MMO experience then Wildstar is definitely worth your time. It's charming, and fun to play. Best of all it's free so you can play with friends. While I don't agree with everything that you can purchase for real money, it's safe to say that no purchases are "required" to play and enjoy the game. If you played the game when it first came out I would recommend giving it another go because it's certainly changed in a good way.
TL;DR - Only some gameplay innovation over other MMOs (mostly combat), but lots of charm and polish. Worth trying.

Trigger Runners is a marriage of endless runner and 2D shooter, presented well but ultimately a pretty average game that barely squeaks by with the addition of some ridiculously fun bosses. The sprite artwork is nice, but the artwork during the cutscenes is a little amateurish. The chiptune soundtrack is good. Gameplay, however, is mostly underwhelming: You run automatically through the level, jumping over chasms and aiming your gun to shoot the enemies before they can attack you. Jumping in this game is pretty wonky, so a significant part of the game's challenge lies in a couple of particularly tricky sections that require precise jumps that the game really doesn't let you perform. Trigger Runners' greatest shortcoming, though, is that it lacks a good balance of difficulty. Normal mode is really very easy, but Hard mode might well be too difficult to finish the game on, forcing you to decide between a course of gameplay that is either unsatisfying or frustrating.
That said, the thing that really redeems this game, the aspect that saves it from mediocrity, is the boss battles. Boss design in Trigger Runners is incredible, requiring the player to juggle attacking the boss's main body to kill it with attacking the parts that will cause it to run you over or shoot back at you. The bosses in this game are just really, really fun to fight. That doesn't make all of the general "meh"-ness go away, but it definitely makes it a safe recommendation, if only by a nose.

Short, simple, sweet, sentimental. These are the words I would use to sum up Trigger Runners. Done in a retro style, its music and graphics hearkening back to the games of yesteryear, it's a pleasant throwback compared to what we usually see.
Gameplay is brief, only about thirty minutes, but it does strike me as reasonably replayable, obviously needed in this format. The story, told via cutscenes, is basic but endearing.
The biggest flaw I see is that the jumps should take a heart away rather than automatically kill you, as they really seem to be the hardest opponents in the game. Besides that, the gun needs to have a broader angle - you should be able to shoot all around you. Shooting stuff just under you is impossible at present. The only other issue is a part where, with the "barrier" shooting on one level, the little bombs you couldn't blow up blocked your shots, making it nigh impossible to not get hit. It also needs a volume control on the options menu, as well as the ability to pause when a boss is loading.
Does this have particularly engaging gameplay? No. Most bosses are very easy and lack defining traits. But it is a fun, quaint little game to just kick back with and enjoy. Retro, cheap, and has trading cards? I'll take it. Especially recommended if on sale.

I'll be honest, as a borderlands fan I hated this one.  The odd neon color scheme was too much for me.  It's an absolute eye sore, literally.  I played for maybe an hour or so and I was done.  I tried to like it but I don't care for it.

First of all: This game seems to be a mobile port. There's a controls menu, but instead of telling you to press spacebar to jump and the left mouse button to shoot (which is everything you do in this game) it only tells you to touch.
The game was fun in the beginning but it got repetetive really quickly. You aim, shoot, sometimes jump over a gap and that's it. Most enemies don't do anything besides flying towards the left-hand side of the screen and often you don't even have to shoot because they wouldn't hit you anyway, but of course you want some points. I never died because of the enemies, I only died because I fell down a gap while shooting at things for points.
There are some really nice-looking bosses. But seriously, what's the point of them? They sometimes spawn a small enemy or shoot a cannonball at you - you can destory the cannonball with a single hit - and that's it. You can even disable the weapons by shooting at them. The bosses are easier than the rest of the game because they don't throw gaps and enemy swarms at you.
I stopped during stage 4-2 because it was exactly the same thing as in 1-1, except for the multitude of gaps that made my keep dying. Oh, did I mention that minutes of shooting at small enemies isn't challenging or fun and that there are no checkpoints?
Seriously, Trigger Runners has some great ideas and it can be fun for 30 minutes, but that's it.

After playing this game for over six hours straight, I have no choice but to reccomend this game. I enjoy the crafting system and ability to find raw materials to construct greater weapons and armor, as well as the need for the different playstyles to gather different materials for their own unique items. When paired up with multiplayer, this makes for very fun co-operative experience. On the topic of multiplayer, I see many people complain about game ending bugs in the multiplayer mode; Yes, they do exist. Perhaps I've been lucky, or the developer has just patched this since I've started playing, but in my experience, around 1 in 15 of the multiplayer games you play will have some sort of issue, some more debilitating than others. I cannot really speak for the game in terms of singleplayer performance as I play this game almost entirely multiplayer with friends, but I really do like the mechanics and gameplay. It does become a tad repetitive once you play for hours at a time, and I'd love to see more content in the game, but it's a very fun exploratory rogue-like adventure. The art-style is very bright and quirky, and is very visually appealing. The game's soundtrack is equally wonderful as it really sets the mood for the area you're exploring, and it's just fun to bob your head to as you shoot giant red mushroom warriors. I often see on forums and such that controller support is a large complaint, however, I was unaware of this at the time of purchase and didn't expect controller support so I suppose that was an issue that didn't really apply to me. When chilling out at friend's houses and trying to find something to play, Magicite is almost always one of the top three picks due to the fact that the game has a relatively low cost, it runs smoothly on almost any computer, and the fact that it seems almost designed to be played in groups where players can exchange items and trade weapons and gear.  Ultimately, if you're on the fence about getting this game, I recommend it very strongly, but if you're not sure, go to YouTube and check out some gameplay videos, see for yourself what kind of game you're getting into.

This is one of those games that I HATE, because it clearly has a good concept, but it's too flawed to really make use of it at all. At its heart, it's good, difficult, classic Castlvania-esque platforming action, complete with button-delay combat (which is a GOOD thing, I assure you) but it's just soooo poorly executed.
Here's a couple examples:
-Armor increases max health but not current health, and there's very few ways to restore health, so armor is mostly worthless.
-Food can't be eaten unless you are slightly hungry, but cooked food is one of the best ways to restore health, so high-tier strategy involves "hunger grinding" to get those precious health points back.
-The crafting system is convoluted and out of place. Combined with the hunger, it feels like a cash grab at emulating Minecraft.
-New characters' stats cannot be chosen, only randomised, so starting a new char means clicking "randomise" until you get the stats you want.
-Many things cannot be unlocked until you beat the game.
-Lockmaster trait no longer does anything, but the creators never bothered taking it out, so your character may randomly have one trait instead of two if they get Lockmaster.
I try to look past the problems and focus on the music and the pixel scenery and the core combat stuff, but all the bad things bog it down too much. It all just makes me want to remake the whole game from the ground up and make it work better.

If you came here for a game review, you've come to the wrong place.
But if you came here for an outstanding chocolate cake recipe, you've come to the right place.
Chocolate Cake Ingredients:
-3/4 cups butter or margarine, softened
-3 eggs
-2 cups sugar
-2 cups flour
-3/4 cup unsweetened cocoa powder
-1 teaspoon baking soda
-3/4 teaspoon baking powder
-2 teaspoon vanilla
-1 1/2 cup milk
How to make Chocolate Cake:
-Pre-heat oven to 350 degrees.
-Grease and flour three 6" X 1 1/2" round cake pans.
-Mix together flour, cocoa powder, baking powder and baking soda. Set aside.
-In a large bowl, beat butter, eggs and vanilla.
-Gradually add sugar.
-Beat on medium to high speed for about 3-4 minutes until well mixed
-Alternately combine in flour mixture and milk to batter while beating.
-Continue to beat until batter is smooth.
-Pour equal amounts of batter into greased and floured round cake pans.
-Bake 30 to 35 minutes.
-Check with a toothpick to se if it is done. Bake a few minutes more, if needed.
-Remove from oven and allow cakes to cool in pans for a few minutes.
-Place cakes on a wire rack, to them allow to completely cool.
Frosting Cakes:
-Place one round cake on a cake plate.
-Spread frosting on top.
-Repeat this for the third cake.
-Frost top of the third cake.
-Frost the side for the cake.

This had such a massive potential to be the best Silent Hill game since Silent Hill 2. Everything from the art direction, music, sound and story are inspired by that series and are very well made. Unfortunately the game ends suddenly. I was expecting the final location to be a whole new chapter with new areas to explore, that would build on the ideas presented earlier and nicely wrap up the story... but it just triggered a final cut-scene. Even though it is short and has some minor flaws, I highly recommend this game.
Pros:
+ Interesting story.
+ Great atmosphere, music and sound design inspired by Silent Hill games.
+ Option to kill everything or completely avoid all confrontations.
+ Side quests.
+ Boss encounters.
Cons:
- Very short.
- Infinite resources make the game too easy after a certain point.
- Expert mode doesn't increase difficulty or change the game in any significant way.
- Super low resolution graphics. The game's native resolution is around 160x100 pixels. For comparison, even NES supported up to 256x240. Sometimes it is hard to tell what you are looking at.
- The game is dark and is recommended to be played in a dark room, but all the speech text is very big and bright when played in fullscreen, causing me eye strain and headaches.

I bought this game in 2012 (5 years ago at the time of writing this review). I tried to play it before, but was put off by it for some reason. Now, after I mustered up the strength to go through it and finish it, I know why that was.
Due to the overall presentation (highly pixelated 2D side scroller) I could not, for the life of me, feel any kind of tension or even much of any atmosphere. This leads to the complete inability to be scared.
However, there are other issues abound:
- opening the inventory screen does not pause the game,
- the mental health system the game gives almost no clues about and which is the main factor for the ending the player receives,
- navigating the basement of the apartment building is a complete chore,
- the chase sequence in this basement is a case of the main character going full retard and conveniently forgetting about the shortcuts (or, to be more precise, not allowing the player to use them) just for the sake of the chase,
- the constant need to eat and sleep every 10 minutes just to pad out the length of the game,
and last but not least,
- the fact that the whole game is a tribute to Silent Hill without a sliver of its own identity; it even follows the same story cliches.
The whole time through I was thinking how much I would prefer to play an actual Silent Hill game over this.

How much of this game I've played: 12 Hours, 35 minutes
How I've played so much: I had a pre-ordered non-steam copy.
Completed Main story, not the super secret boss area.
Here's why you'd be interested in this game: Good rhymes, good story, old school gameplay.
Good rhymes: If you haven't heard of BeNeVoLeNcE, you might have heard of Mega Ran - he's known for clean nerdcore rhymes over chiptune beats and melodies. Hip Hop by both is featured in the game, and it's not an "afterthought" like it might be in some games - the music is interwoven in with the story - it's actually rewarding to gain access to the rhymes that go along with the instrumentals in different parts of the game.
Good Story: There's a lot of heart in this story, and one can feel like it really draws on some current feelings in real life. The story told here is indeed good vs. evil, but it also touches on how evil can flourish because of indifference, and greed.  And also how some things a person might want to do with good motives...have to be put off for one reason or another. A person can really be drawn into this story.
Old School Gameplay: If you've played a Shining Star game, or Secret of Mana/Evermore, the game plays similar to that. Very reminiscent of old school SNES games. Some of the items/skills in the game are implemented in the same way as games in the past.
---------------------------------------
Here's why a person may not like it: Old school graphics; mostly stupid AI party members, sometimes frustrating movement/attack aim
Old school graphics isn't really something I have beef with at all, but if someone expects the latest Ys from this game, this is not it.
Mostly stupid AI party members: This issue had me yelling at the screen a few times. AI party members are dumb, and will charge to their death often. Best advice here is to not worry about spending items reviving them, unless you need them as cannon fodder. This goes into the third issue.
Sometimes frustrating movement/attack positioning: This is very much a game where you need to take a few seconds to learn boss patterns. Once you have an idea of where to stand and when, you will not take a scratch on boss fights. It's Dark Souls-y in that way. Get greedy, and you will get punished. Many times on certain characters your attack skill will put you in harm's way, so often learning how to be cheap about your own attacks will serve you well.
Score: 9/10. This is a solid, enjoyable game, and I look forward to the next chapter.

I’ve had a lot of fun playing this and really like what I have seen.  Early access or not this game has a lot in it to keep you entertained for hours at a time.  When I first started it took me a bit to find a decent weapon in the town so those karate kicks, however expertly delivered, took a while to take those buggers down.  I eventually found a crowbar which made scavenging the town a much more enjoyable experience.  From there I built my inventory of weapons/ammo and other goodies and really found it interesting to explore the town.  What I enjoy in these types of games is some suspense and this game definitely delivers that.  There were a number of times when the sun started to go down and the light got a little dimmer and I would be focusing on one thing or another and then have some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sneak up on me.  Made me jump a little especially with the creepy/suspenseful music playing.  Music for me is a big part of any good game and I liked what I heard so far.
I really like the combination and balance between the live action scavenging and camp management.  It was fun to go out and scavenge for things you needed for that next building, camp upgrade, or new weapon I wanted to make.  It would be nice to be able to see specifically what materials you are picking up so you could decide what to keep or drop since you can only carry so much.  You can for guns, ammo, meds, etc. but not for some reason not materials.  I tried dropping some stuff in specific locations to come pick them up the next time but no luck.  It would also be nice to be able to hide items in a trunk or locker so you could get them the next time you’re in town.
There is a lot to enjoy in this one so I don’t want to give too much away.  Overall I have had a lot of fun so far and am really looking forward to seeing what comes next.  As a side note, I have been impressed with the level of involvement the developers have had in the community and the rate at which updates/fixes have been coming out.  Keep up the good work!

If you want to experience lovable characters, beautiful worlds, insane leaps of logic, and sudden shifts in perspective, then pick up a controller and get ready to have your heart broken. It's worth it.
EDIT: I almost forgot the soundtrack! Unobtrusive and yet still somehow the star of the show, the music is a huge part of what makes this game impactful. It takes just as many chances as the rest of the game, and consistently delivers in ways I would never have expected.
Easily one of the best games ever made. It's a work of art, and you're doing yourself a disservice if you don't play it.
