For an Early Access game I'd say CM Softworks nailed it! This game has features that most games don't implement until the Beta stage. They may be small features, but they're still there! This game has provided me with 10 hours of suspense, and zombie slaying fun! If you like games where you get to kill zombies, earn/spend skill points (on three attributes at the moment) and manage your own survival shelter then this game is perfect for you. Not many zombie games give you the ability to loot cities in real time, and manage a camp where you can build Farms to have a food supply, and a Radio Tower so you can communicate with other known camps! There are many more things to create that help your camp grow and survive. You can even simulate the ability to search for other areas to loot, and you can choose to loot them in real time or simulate the loot phase.  This game has you make some serious decisions too. An example: "There is a horde of zombies spotted near your camp. This will conclude in Two Phases". So you have to think; Is the camp ready? Is your defense rating where it needs to be? Should you run out into the city to grab supplies before they get to the camp? If there is no one at your camp to fight off the horde of zombies then they overrun it and you lose it so you have to get everything done in the alotted time given. There are different types of zombies as well. They're not just your standard infected walking around. Currently there is "The Crawler" (The nickname I gave her; She can be spotted with her blonde hair) and "The Boss" (He's easily recognizable. These zombies have the chance to drop rare loot, but take excessive amounts of damage so I recommend a weapon with a good amount of ammo. Randomly throughout the game you will see a bright shinging light (Red or Green so far) and that spawns a loot crate. Green Flare=Resources Red Flare= Weapons. Where will you put all this loot? There is a Storage system at your camp that can be upgraded to hold more things! You just need the right materials.  There is a small part to the camp management that I haven't used personally yet but it's there. The ability to craft "Homemade" weapons and ammo using materials that are looted.   Here's my Pros and Cons list so far:
Pros
-Zombies
-Looting System
-Different Type of Zombies
-Camp Management
-EXP System
-Unique Zombie/Player Animations
-Weapon Rarity System
-Durability Ratings for Weapons/Clothing (Although Clothing doesn't decay yet)
-Ability to Rescue/Recruit Survivors
-Working Random Loot System (No location is the same)
-Small Material Crafting System
-You can Slide
Cons
-Hit Boxes for Zombies are not the Greatest (You might take a hit when you shouldn't have)
-Camera Movement is a bit Funky/Takes awhile to get used to
-Finding Survivors is sometimes a pain
*****The time it takes to get from "Morning" to "Night" is Really Short***** (Fixed in Last Patch)
-There's not an Easier way to Find Survivors
-Ability to Control Where your Attack Goes (It just follows in one direction until the animation is done)
So all in all there is some Pros and Cons. The Cons can/will be fixed. The company is pushing out updates every few days. They listen to the consumer, and act on what everyone would like to see. You can currently vote on different additions that you would like to see in the game and that is checked daily by the developers. I recommend this game at it's current (on sale and base price) and with where it's headed this game will be an amazing addition to the zombie era of gaming.

A game that was stunning. A very long play for me, and my go to for any kind of good horror game I have, disincluding Silent Hill.
Speaking of Silent Hill, while the storyline of Lone Survivor is not as detailed, the storyline of Lone Survivor relies on a similar gameplay mechanic of Silent Hill, rather than relying on jumpscares. For the majority of the game, it's only going to be you and your gun. The gameplay itself when it comes to shooting is simple and easy to use. However some parts of the gameplay is definitely lacking. You'll find yourself using lures that barely work at times, and as the game progresses, you find yourself stuck with that one weapon. The pacing is slow, and good for a person who likes slow paced and Silent-Esque games.
The storyline however, is somewhat awkward and fails to fully establish itself. The storyline jumps all over the place and gets hard to understand from a person who picks up the game. There's no distinction on what is and isn't real, or what is good and bad to the survivor. There are few things clear at what happens, and who is and isn't real. There's not as much to say about the storyline, as it is lacking at best, however there are certain parts that exceeded lacking.
The soundtrack is extremely good. Made also by Jasper Bryne, the soundtrack is absolutely stunning, and really helps immerse the player at points. However, despite the soundtrack being amazing, there are parts where the soundtrack fails to really immerse, and sometimes seems out of place at some points. The sound effects are very well made and placed perfectly. There's not a lot to complain about the soundtrack or sound effects, only that songs from the soundtrack sometimes feels out of place.
The graphics, despite looking pixelated, exceeded my expectations, and really killed it in that department. It really shines in this department, and sometimes doesn't even feel as if it's pixelated, and more of a more detailed game.
Overall, if you're looking for a game that has pixel-graphics, a Silent-Hill esque game, or a game with a good soundtrack and some good gameplay, I'd recommend this. However if you're looking for a linear story that isn't vague or doesn't really jump around, I'd recommend passing up on this.

I have to respect this game's particular pixel art style, but in terms of what it's trying to accomplish, I find that it fails.
I haven't read any reviews or interviews with the creator, but I got an incredibly huge feeling that it was inspired by Silent Hill. It's so much of an hommage that it looks like more than that, it's almost as if it was intended totally as a new Silent Hill. The psychological horror, the look of the monsters, the lack of lighting, a main character that is hiding something, all of it and even an area that was previously normal looking suddenly turning nightmarish.
It works artistically and I have to say it's a huge thing to accomplish to have a truly scary looking environment in a 2D pixel art game. But the way it plays, I had no sense of stress, of being scared, of not knowing what was hiding from me.
The fights are too simple in that the enemies are simply moving towards you and you just press the shooting key and hope to have enough bullets. Aiming is usually not necessary and if you stock up on bullets, it's just pressing the shooting key when you see an enemy with no strategy implied. The enemies' strategy is mostly always just moving towards you, as simple as that.
If you play the stealth way, it's a matter of having enough rotten meat with you and placing it at the beginning of a section where you can hide in the background and get on your enemies' left or right while they're busy eating, but there's not enough of figuring out how to get past those sections. In the end, the strategy is having enough bullets or enough meat on you, at least in my experience.
I would then guess this game relies on the psychological element and the atmosphere, but without the feeling of stress, no matter how you achieve it, the way a Silent Hll type game is specifically designed will never feel like true horror in my opinion. Which is a shame, because I loved the concept of Silent Hill as the series was even better than Resident Evil for me (true uncomfortable horror compared to jump scares).
This game seems to be made by a talented person and there is a lot of good to be said about what it feels like outside of how it plays. I would have to see a similar game with better mechanics, it could be a very good replacement to Silent Hill if this game was improved upon. I certainly don't expect to play a real Silen Hill any time soon anyway.

Gamers who like retro survival adventures, gameplay that has to be figured out (a bit like Don't Starve), and old skool UI probably feel right at home. For me this was too retro.
I think there is no excuse not to have an ESC menu where you can do basic setup and look at key commands: what key does what, to get you started and see what can be done in the game, especially with one that has so little to no explanation to start with. But the ESC menu is mostly empty. To look at key commands, you have to go into your apartment, into a specific room, and look at some random note hanging around in that room to see the key bindings. If you forget some and head out and are in the middle of something, you're out of luck, leave everything and go back to your room to look at the key bindings. This should be in the ESC menu somewhere, some kind of basic help. I don't want to memorize or write that down myself.
Also the visuals are extremely blocky. Retro adventure and pixel graphic all nice and good, but to me this looks extremely raw. You almost don't see what the objects are because it's just 2 pixels glued together. It's like having really bad vision. You go to some pixel pie and see if you can interact with it. Sometimes it's nothing, sometimes it's something important, a note, some object. But you can never tell in advance if this is something or just a block of randomly colored pixels that is dirt on a table. Visual readability is very low.
If you like finding out how to play a game the hard way, it probably is enjoyable. If you're looking for an adventure that is more streamlined, go somewhere else.

DISCLAIMER: As a veteran of the Borderlands franchise, this review will most definitely be debated based on the content reviewed in this review. Nonetheless, enjoy! :)
Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is a good game that tells the story that would lead in to its beloved predecessor, Borderlands 2. While some people says that Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel was a failure as a game, it's no slouch to me. I definitely shout out Gearbox for implementing my favorite BTPS gun aka the Laser Disker. While BTPS fixed some issues that was in Borderlands 2 such as the uneven UVHM endgame balance, there were some very questionable patches to the game after the release such as the nerfs of the Ol' Rosie, Kaneda's Laser, and the Probe. To set some pros and cons out there, like my Borderlands 2 review, I'll put out a chart out there listing both. Hope the chart would help.
Pros:
-Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode is balanced compared to Borderlands 2 (BL2's UVHM balance is extremely off)
-Weapons returning from Borderlands 2 are proven to be more effective in BTPS due to the game balance (weapons such as the Nukem, Mongol, and Pitchfork)
-Jack the Doppleganger (my personal favorite character to play as)
-Fills the gap of the story told in Borderlands 2
-Claptastic Voyage DLC (I really love the setting and concept)
-Cryo element (it can compliment Torgue weapons)
-Some weapons and gear returning from Borderlands 2 still retain the power that makes them beloved in Borderlands 2 (Lady Fist, Maggie, Sham)
-Some skills of characters proves to be as effective as similar skills from Borderlands 2 (Example: Aurelia's I Never Miss Skill = Zer0's Critical Ascension)
-Skills of many characters (Athena's Malestrom, Jack's Leadership, Nisha's Tombstone, etc.)
-Luneshine (interesting buffs to weapons that also appear without a Luneshine effect)
-The Jakobs Pepperbox (likely cut from Borderlands 2 but appears in BTPS only in Glitch rarity in the Claptastic Voyage DLC)
-The talking weapons in BTPS isn't as annoying as the Bane seen in Borderlands 2 and some are incredible when used
Cons:
-The questionable nerfs of some weapons after release (Ol' Rosie, Kaneda's Laser, Probe)
-Some weapons are either reskins or renames of weapons seen in Borderlands 2 (not much of a con but still not as creative)
-The Holodome DLC (criminally difficult)
-The Holodome weapons (the weapons received in the DLC aren't worth really the effort that it takes to beat all the rounds of the Holodome)
-No Bee Shield </3 (I'm not that mad or sad about this one since we have the Rerouter but it would've been nice to see the Bee return)
-Tales from the Borderlands weapons cannot drop in the game and can only be claimed once (it's a shame because I really love the Company Man and Fast Talker)
-A lot of weapons in the game cannot crit without assistance from Nisha's Tombstone skill
-Not as much DLCs as Borderlands 1 or Borderlands 2
-Many weapons in BTPS is a major downgrade to amazing weapons seen in Borderlands 2 (Example: Snowball is not as good as the Fastball seen in Borderlands 2)
-Some weapons that can be farmed from only one boss can't be farmed again for the rest of the playthrough unless you alt + f4
-Eclipse/EOS at the end of the Claptastic Voyage DLC (not as mad about this one, annoyingly difficult to beat but does have a guaranteed legendary drop at the end which is worth it)
The chart above is only my opinion and can be debated among the community. While I think that the game served its purpose, some people just don't like the game. Now, I'll leave it up to you if you think it's worth the money to buy this game. In my opinion, I think it's a good game to tell the Borderlands storyline. I think I can definitely recommend this game to those who continue to play the Borderlands franchise. Hope this review helped you to make a decision if you think it's worth it to buy the game. I tried to play this game, I really did. Nothing inside really held my interest. This game feels like a soulless MMO with no personality to it. Storyline is absolutely dull and uninteresting. Why are those guys my enemy? Because the game says so? Why should I care about any of these factions, races, and characters?
Nothing is inspired, nothing is unique, nothing is new or exciting. I'd almost describe this as a WoW clone, and that is both an insult to WoW and an insult to this game. I can't think of a single thing which would interest me enough to keep playing.
This game is like that kid who tries too hard to fit in with the crowd and falls flat. Lots of pretty graphics, no substance behind any of it. It's as if the devs blew their entire budget on pretty graphics and art designed, then realized they forgot the story and hastily slapped together a plotline.
Truth be told, I can't even tell what demographic this game is aimed towards. It has a LOOOOOT of immaturity and childish humor, yet also has some adult themes (not that kind of adult themes).
This game reminds me a lot of Sony's MMO called Free Realms (now canceled). The cartoonish nature of the game, the lack of meaningful content, no real story, mindless gameplay, and the pointless repetition.
It's not a terrible game, it's just not interesting or compelling in any way. If I had to summarize this game, I'd say "Meh" and shrug in disinterest.
I'd ask the devs a simple question: Why should anyone play your MMO? Seriously, why should anyone play this game?
Customizable player housing? - Lots of other games have this.
Cool looking mounts? - Lots of other games have this.
Unique gameplay? - Hardly.
Faction vs faction warfare? - Lots of other games have this.
Story line? - What story line?
Cartoonish graphics? - Lots of other games have this.
Y'all need to take a good hard look at what you offer gamers in regards to gameplay, story, and content because you're falling behind.

I love paradox games, I spend several hours playing their games like Victoria II and Stellaris feeds into my sci-fi interest fusing my desire of being a space sovereignty. You must lead your destined empire to greatness. Destroying empires that deny your glorious empires reign and subjugated them to brutality. Perhaps you wish not to supress the galactic empires and find peaceful cooperation or isolate yourself while keeping a nationals idealogy clean from interlopers? The choice is yours on how you lead your people, for greatness or self-mutilated yourself to fall and be eradicated or assimilated by another galactic power.

Too often find myself getting attacked by fleets 5x my size at the beginning of the game and having to restart, even after learning how to play a lot better. Poor guidance on how to cross galactic spiral arms. I'm fine with a high learning curve, but this game legitimately doesn't give guidance where it's needed. Early game is too hard, late game is too easy, and it's almost never effective to run around with multiple fleets so war strategy against equal opponents gets reduced to amassing and attacking singular points.
Stellaris is a complex, involved game. Approach at your own risk.

It is a good game.  It is heavier on the 4x side of things, but mods easilly fix that.
Honestly, I was hoping for Vicky II in space, but on release was a little disapointed.  Diplomacy was pretty bland, and politics was non-existant.  The pops system and economics as a whole is very dumbed down.  It makes sense why they did this though.
Recent patches and mods have improved the game vastly.  Now, I'm running a mostly human empire that has different sides to it.  Half the population is xenophobic, and half is egalitarian.  I am running a heavily modded game though, so the way government works is different, the ethics are different, so on and so forth.
Compared to a similarily priced game, distant worlds universe, it has a drastically simplified economy.  The politics are much better though, especially with mods.  The game is in 3D, rather than 2D, although I consider graphics Skub.
There are other options, both free and paid for that are MUCH cheaper than this game, for example Space Empires IV and V or Star Ruler 2.  I'd wait until it goes on sale, or the price goes down.
Final point is that I think resources are a bit too sparse for me, and I've downloaded some mods that fix that.
I will put this as a yes for I do not regret buying this game.  I do not own any of the DLC.  I don't think it is worth it at this point.  Just buy the base game and play with mods.

This why I highly recommend this product if you enjoy 4x or strategy games.

The Moon Sliver is a short, "literary" walking-sim game that isn't overwhelming in its presentation or design, yet still challenging enough to be engaging. By "challenging," I don't mean in the traditional gaming sense: this is challenging because you have to think about the story being told as it's given to you, and how to conserve your "energy." It could have been♥♥♥♥♥♥if the ending didn't pay off, but one hour later I am still thinking about and still getting a chill from it, though I can't decide whether its from the horror or elegance of delivery, or both. It's very minimal, using a few assets from Unity over and over again, but always to a great pretty, weird, "moony" aesthetic, emphasizing many "slivers." Minimalism works to its advantage, especially the scenes where you have to think wisely about the "energy" mechanics, how it's upturned later on. I wouldn't have believed it before playing either, but this is also an imaginitive parable with interesting things to say, or at least ask about humans, which is cool because lots of games don't get that far in 80x the hours.

Some of the screenshots feature fireplaces - as you read in the darkness of these rooms while the shadows dance on the walls thanks to the light it can certainly create an amazing atmosphere. At the same time it is haunting; you can go as far as to say that your loneliness is horrifying. What is this place? These small houses built on an island that has long been away from society. Where are your friends? Who did you come here with?

The Moon Sliver is one of those 'visual novels' or 'interactive stories', so it's not a game. And there are two more heads-ups here:
- it's very short, 30 to 40 minutes, so it's more of a short story than a novel;
- the interactivity is pretty limited. I wanted to elaborate a bit on that but then I considered that might be a spoiler so I decided against it.
The story presented here is pretty basic stuff. It's also told in a peculiar way, but I suppose that's due to translation issues rather than intended. The graphics are ok for the purpose they serve, but they are certainly not impressive in a way that they would improve upon the story or the overall experience.
I went back and forth between recommending The Moon Sliver or not, but in the end I went with 'No' because of the following facts:
1. What you're getting here is a very short story/experience, and not an overly impressive one at that. "It's ok" is the most enthousiastic phrase that comes to mind, really.
2. Only when it's on sale for less than 50 cents could one consider recommending The Moon Sliver. At its full price it's definitely a 'No Way'!
3. Yes, the game has Steam Trading Cards but it's too short for that. When you\'re finished, you will usually have received one of three cards. This means everyone needs to let the game run idly in the background for at least an hour to get the other cards.

Lone Survivor has some interesting ideas, but fails to execute most of them in a satisfying manner.
Let's start with the pretentious story.  In the first 5-10 minutes of the game, you'll get that all of this may or may not be real.  The problem is the story never progresses or reveals anything.  The best you'll get is 1 of 5 vague unsatisfying endings that are designed to let you interpret the story however you want.  It's not my job to come up with the story or interpret it, that's the designers job.  I wouldn't mind it so much if the rest of the game made up for it, but it doesn't.  Which ending you get is dependent on your mental health.  You have no way of knowing what things you can and can't do that contribute positively or negatively to your mental health, so unless you go in having looked up how to get good endings in advance, enjoy one of the bad endings.  After you finish the game, it does give you some idea about what's affecting your mental health, but it's a sizable list (including how much you eat/don't eat, what you eat, whether you sleep too much, not enough, how many enemies you kill, how many pills you take, etc), and there're things unlisted that you have to do in order to get the “best” ending.  I'm not bothering to play through this again.
There're a couple characters in the game, but they never develop into anything and you're never given a reason to care about them.  Characters, including your own, speak in cryptic messages that serve no point other than to frustrate the player.  Also, some dialogue makes no sense.  Cut-scene dialogue often moves at an absurdly slow rate considering there are usually only 6 or 7 words on the screen.  I don't need 5-10 seconds to read each set of 4 - 8 words.
Combat isn't very good either.  There are only 2 types of enemies throughout the game, along with 2 bosses.  You can kill enemies, sneak by them, blind them with flares, or place meat to distract them.  The limited enemy types as well as the limited options means enemy encounters get repetitive pretty quickly.  Both of the bosses are fairly lackluster as well, considering you don't even fight one of them.  I got somewhat annoyed going through the game killing monsters, I can't imagine how annoying the game must be going through while avoiding killing monsters to get the “better” endings.  Without going into detail, the combat mechanics are clunky, and I'd imagine even people who love this game would be hard pressed to say they're good.
Your character gets hungry and sleepy throughout the game about every 5 minutes and will constantly spam messages up about how hungry and sleepy he is every 30 seconds until you satisfy these.  Especially fun is when he's doing it while you're fighting enemies.  You can eat pretty much anywhere, but sleeping requires you to go back to your room, and you don't get good sleep if your character is hungry, so you need to make sure you eat right before you go to sleep unless you enjoy getting spammed messages about how sleepy you are a minute after you've finished sleeping.  It doesn't help that the game provides no bars to gauge how hungry or sleepy your character is, so you never have any idea how much certain food is decreasing your hunger or how much rest your character got from sleeping.
The game also has an inventory system divided into 3 layers (health/tools/notes) that gets increasingly big throughout your playthrough as you find more items.  It's clunky to go through and isn't very well managed, especially when items you think should be in one section are found in another.  For instance, if my gun is in the tools section, why is my ammo for it found in the health section?  Some items are pretty easy to determine what they do, but others are left very vague.  Naturally you will attempt to experiment with them or even play around with them (you know I'm going to try eating that rotten meat).  The developer though decided that doing such things should be a punished, so you'll lose mental health using some items or fooling around with them, but you won't know this until after you finish the game.  Thank you!
The game does have a couple good qualities.  I enjoyed exploring (though the map can be confusing), some of the weird stuff you run into, and the music is alright.  There's also more I could complain about, but I'll stop here.  I don't hate this game, but the best I can say about it is that it's ok at times.  The game usually ranges from playable to annoying.  It rarely did anything that got me excited or really wanting to continue on.  Your time is better spent playing something else.

DISCLAIMER: As a veteran of the Borderlands franchise, this review will most definitely be debated based on the content reviewed in this review. Nonetheless, enjoy! :)
Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is a good game that tells the story that would lead in to its beloved predecessor, Borderlands 2. While some people says that Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel was a failure as a game, it's no slouch to me. I definitely shout out Gearbox for implementing my favorite BTPS gun aka the Laser Disker. While BTPS fixed some issues that was in Borderlands 2 such as the uneven UVHM endgame balance, there were some very questionable patches to the game after the release such as the nerfs of the Ol' Rosie, Kaneda's Laser, and the Probe. To set some pros and cons out there, like my Borderlands 2 review, I'll put out a chart out there listing both. Hope the chart would help.
Pros:
-Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode is balanced compared to Borderlands 2 (BL2's UVHM balance is extremely off)
-Weapons returning from Borderlands 2 are proven to be more effective in BTPS due to the game balance (weapons such as the Nukem, Mongol, and Pitchfork)
-Jack the Doppleganger (my personal favorite character to play as)
-Fills the gap of the story told in Borderlands 2
-Claptastic Voyage DLC (I really love the setting and concept)
-Cryo element (it can compliment Torgue weapons)
-Some weapons and gear returning from Borderlands 2 still retain the power that makes them beloved in Borderlands 2 (Lady Fist, Maggie, Sham)
-Some skills of characters proves to be as effective as similar skills from Borderlands 2 (Example: Aurelia's I Never Miss Skill = Zer0's Critical Ascension)
-Skills of many characters (Athena's Malestrom, Jack's Leadership, Nisha's Tombstone, etc.)
-Luneshine (interesting buffs to weapons that also appear without a Luneshine effect)
-The Jakobs Pepperbox (likely cut from Borderlands 2 but appears in BTPS only in Glitch rarity in the Claptastic Voyage DLC)
-The talking weapons in BTPS isn't as annoying as the Bane seen in Borderlands 2 and some are incredible when used
Cons:
-The questionable nerfs of some weapons after release (Ol' Rosie, Kaneda's Laser, Probe)
-Some weapons are either reskins or renames of weapons seen in Borderlands 2 (not much of a con but still not as creative)
-The Holodome DLC (criminally difficult)
-The Holodome weapons (the weapons received in the DLC aren't worth really the effort that it takes to beat all the rounds of the Holodome)
-No Bee Shield </3 (I'm not that mad or sad about this one since we have the Rerouter but it would've been nice to see the Bee return)
-Tales from the Borderlands weapons cannot drop in the game and can only be claimed once (it's a shame because I really love the Company Man and Fast Talker)
-A lot of weapons in the game cannot crit without assistance from Nisha's Tombstone skill
-Not as much DLCs as Borderlands 1 or Borderlands 2
-Many weapons in BTPS is a major downgrade to amazing weapons seen in Borderlands 2 (Example: Snowball is not as good as the Fastball seen in Borderlands 2)
-Some weapons that can be farmed from only one boss can't be farmed again for the rest of the playthrough unless you alt + f4
-Eclipse/EOS at the end of the Claptastic Voyage DLC (not as mad about this one, annoyingly difficult to beat but does have a guaranteed legendary drop at the end which is worth it)
The chart above is only my opinion and can be debated among the community. While I think that the game served its purpose, some people just don't like the game. Now, I'll leave it up to you if you think it's worth the money to buy this game. In my opinion, I think it's a good game to tell the Borderlands storyline. I think I can definitely recommend this game to those who continue to play the Borderlands franchise. Hope this review helped you to make a decision if you think it's worth it to buy the game. Bye :)

This is a fun, addicting game. I've barely had it for a day and I'm already hooked on it. There's plenty to explore, collect, loot, kill, and just look at. Given that this game is in Beta I believe, I'm expecting much more in the future. The pixelated art style is charming and adds a certain quality that makes it kind of light hearted and not too serious. That's also a good way to describe the game as well, since this game is pretty easy as far as Roguelikes go. The combat isn't anything special, but it's balanced and deep enough to keep it interesting while playing. I never found it to be tedious, and it was fun timing and landing charged attacks. The menus are a bit confusing though. Nothing really goes in depth in explaining them and I'm still not sure if I've got it all figured out. The default button for your inventory is "I" which is a bit out of the way and inconvenient considering that the main form of movement is WSAD. If there's more movement options or a way to change the controls, I am unaware of those at this time. Another problem I had with the menus was using items. There's no indication of what button does what, nor is there any explanation as to what anything does. I had a potion in my hot bar so I could drink it. Instead, I threw it on the ground, and it exploded. It took me a minute to realize that to use some items, you had to be in your inventory, which can be a hindrance in tense moments of battle where you need something from your inventory and quickly. There's definitely room for improvements to menu functionality and more, even if small and brief, tutorials. A note saying "Drink potions from your inventory and put them on your belt to throw them!" would be just fine. Other than those, this game is pretty solid and simple, and has room to expand upon in the future. If you're looking for your next short addiction (or maybe even a long one) this is a good game to look into.

text:
So what can I say, I've played this game maybe 400-500 hours outside of Steam before, and now I felt the need to come back and it is still the great game I've known for a long time now. From a history of playing Perfect World, Jade Dynasty and other f2p MMORPGs, and also World of Warcraft and Guild Wars 2 I feel that it is time to give this a try again. I loved it before, and I still love it. This is right now, along with Guild Wars 2 the best free2play MMORPGs out there, maybe because both used to be pay2play games. I started playing Jade Dynasty in early 2008, and somewhat after Perfect World, and that is my history of Free2Play MMORPGs, and I quit Jade Dynasty in 2012, and from then til now I've been playing everything from World of Warcraft to Guild Wars 2 and also some Final Fantasy, but after plays here and there, I've come to the conclusion that even tho World of Warcraft is the "greatest" of all MMORPGs out there, I must say Wildstar is the best in my opinion.
So with my history out of the way, what makes the game you might think by now, right?
Firstly, you see reviews on Steam,
, and they are not wrong at all. The game is first of all,
. No hidden locked content if you don't buy a special item for 9,99$, or a hidden ultimate armor for another 9,99$. The graphics is absolutely stunning, PVE doesn't take forever and grinding isn't much of a issue like in WoW where you run same instance over and over to get loot. That's just boring and takes away the fun of player interacting. That's where I feel that WildStar has succeeded alot. The combat is also different from every other Free 2 Play, and Pay 2 Play MMORPG. I won't spoil it, you've got alot to find out by yourself. Play the game, and help make it the best Free MMORPG on Steam.

NieR: Automata is one of the best games I've played in a long time, and that's saying a lot in a year that has already had a number of other great games come out.
The gameplay is top-notch, exactly what you'd expect the developers of Bayonetta to be capable of, but it's even better when it's paired with a story by Yoko Taro.  If you're new to the Taro experience, don't be fooled when you're 15 hours into the game, see the credits scroll by, and think you know what the story is about; you're only 1/3 of the way done with the game, and there are multiple layers of complexity to go through.  There are tons of interesting side quests, well-developed characters, and a fantastic soundtrack by Keiichi Okabe.
The only negative thing I can say about the game, if you'd call it that, is that the system requirements are no joke; this is a GPU-intensive game.  The listed minimum requirements really are the lowest you should try to get away with, and even then, expect to be playing on low settings.  You'll need serious hardware if you want to play this in 1080p at a solid 60 fps.

The Moon Sliver... Well, that was an interesting thirty minutes.
There's not much I can say without spoiling the story, so I'm keeping this review short.
David Szymanski seems to love making these 'artsy', story-driven short games; and honestly, I love playing them. Well, Szymanski's games never truly felt like games to me; they feel more like vessels for the stories he wants to tell. This story is one of darkness, sadness, death, and the end of days.
As you walk through the bleak environment, exploring the remnants of the old world, you'll find snippets of the conversations and thoughts which the story is told through. In the notes are combinations needed to access new areas, and hints on where to go next.
If you're not into walking simulators, or games focused on dialogue, then I'd just skip this one. But if you're in any way curious, it's worth the $1.99.
Curator page:

A genuinely creepy wander through an unsettling location - the rising tension is brilliant, and you start to feel an unwillingness to move around for fear of what you will find. This will definitely appeal to people who love a story over action.

First and foremost, I'm definitely interested in seeing more from this indie creator.
However, don't go into this expecting a "game" - there are interactive elements, but they aren't terribly challenging or an important component of the experience. A better description might be something more like visual, interactive fiction. Where The Moon Sliver shines is the storytelling, which is done in an incredibly creative way that is largely non-linear. And I definitely got the heebies playing this late at night (though I'm easily scared).
Someone reviewing this program as a "game" is likely to give it a lower score than it necessarily deserves, but a player who doesn't go in expecting a gameplay experience is likely to enjoy the experience for what it is, and enjoy it a lot more.
My one criticism is that the maps in the underground section were not terribly imaginative. I feel they could have been put together more efficiently and less predictably.

The Moon Sliver is wandering an island finding random clues that don't make any sense. Upon completing the game it creates a clear picture. My character appeared and began to walk through the desert. He could only go forward. He continued on in a straight line, and I clicked to pick up grass and pebbles as he went. This was all I could do, other than make him rest, or choose between having him stop, walk, or run. Then, very quickly, the game began to throw random events into the mix. Something would appear in the path ahead, and it would be unavoidable.
Mostly, "random events" meant encountering aggro, lone wolf cubs. At first, I thought that these encounters were ridiculous and tedious. A baby animal, which was all alone, was attacking a grown man and he couldn't scare it off? He kept missing when he tried to hit it, and did little damage to it, despite the fact that it was a small baby? That was silly. However, it soon became an annoying, frequent occurence. I wanted to skip these silly battles, but there was no option to. (I also think that fighting might have been glitchy for me. His arm stuttered when I clicked for him to strike, but the game's trailer shows clean, simple blows for its animation.)
The other random events didn't enliven the gameplay for me. For example, sometimes a human would show up, and this was the most interactive random event that I got. If she/he wasn't hostile then I could click "talk, trade, beg, rob."
Yet, "talk" was a brief line of dialogue with no importance. Each line was the NPC saying something bland:  'I can tell you're suffering', 'if you're overloaded then you'll need to drop things,' or whatever else. (I can barely remember the lines enough to paraphrase them.) Meanwhile, my own character didn't seem to say anything back to them.
"Trade" meant that they wanted something odd like a snowglobe, and I didn't have it yet.
"Beg" is self-explanatory, but begging for things had a low percentage chance to work. It didn't work each time I tried it. When it didn't work, my character said, 'I couldn't move them', and the word "failed" popped up. It seemed like a robotic, dull interaction.
I didn't bother to rob anybody. I didn't like the battle system, and I didn't want to randomly attack passerby. Besides that, for most of the time, I didn't have a weapon. I had a knife at one point, but it strangely disappeared.
And that was the MOST interactive that the game was in my almost-40-minutes of playtime. Other events did occur, but they were even less interesting.
For example, an oasis would turn up, and I could click "drink, refill bottle, fish/scavenge." "Drink" meant that a slurp sound played, and my character's thirst was quenched; "refill bottle" meant that a sound played, a full bottle sprite popped up, and a bottle got filled in the inventory; "fish" (clean water) meant a single click might get a fish, and "scavenge" (dirty water) meant a single click might get random items.
The game likely gets better when someone's deep into hours of playtime, because then crafting would open up more as more items were found, etc. However, I wasn't enjoying playing. I didn't want to invest hours of time in it to get to a possible, future fun point.

Delver is pretty decent. I'm not floored by much of anything but it's managed to keep my attention for more than 10 minutes, and with all the un-played games in my library that's a compliment. Visually it's fine to look at, the art style is a mix of 3D environments that have a definite Minecraft vibe, whereas enemies and items are 2D sprites - although the animation on them is well done and actually useful in predicting attacks to get timing down.
The soundtrack is great although turning off the music can be useful as almost every enemy gives away it's position with some basic sounds. Combat is alright, although it feels a little sluggish - even when you're wielding something light and quick like a dagger. Magic is much more satisfying and useful, but there's not a lot of it. The same can be said of bows and arrows. I think the game would be a lot more enjoyable and replayable if both magic and archery were viable "builds" on their own and not just supplements to melee.
Nothing too fancy here, I would recommend this only if you were really looking for something in this style of game.

I understand that this is not similar to the average game and that it's purpose is somehow different, I see "The Moon Silver" somehow as an "experience" portrayed through a graphical novel in some way, but there were some elements that, in my opinion, interfered with the author's purpose.
The main story is portrayed to you in the form of procedural texts, that more often than not, get in the way and instead of letting you enjoy the reading along the gameplay, they'll end blocking your field of view for a few seconds making the experience a little bit, or very much, frustrating.
The Moon Silver made me feel I was reading a paperback attempt that was left unfinished and forgotten, and then transformed into a lackluster visual novel. The "unfinished" feeling gets reinforced with the soundtrack (available as a DLC) because it is conformed by six pieces that does not even contain iD3 tags nor relevant information, and even worse, each one is "cut" at the end abruptly.
Graphics are pretty basic for todays standards, I would compare them to those present on Quake I, or even simpler than that, but that's not a disadvantage at all given the style of the game. I would recommend playing "The Music Machine" instead, it's by far a much better approach to this type of games despite its simplicity.
I would say even a game as old as "Samorost I" gives you a more fulfilling, satisfying and professional experience.

I've always loved an interesting story, and the non linear snatches of dialogue and text scattered throughout this experience left me wanting more. What we have here is not a game, it's an existential short story with a solid streak of atmospheric horror brought to life. There is no combat, and the gameplay consists solely of walking and exploring while piecing together bits of narrative to gain an understanding of what happened to the island's inhabitants. I finished it the first time in around 25 minutes (missing a bit of the story, yet knowing enough to get the gist of it) and all I want now is to find out if the full story exists somewhere online, so I can read through it again.
With regards to the horror part of the experience, it does an excellent job of creating tension and unease. At one point in the tunnels, my light started to go as I heard some creature growl in the distance and I started to panic a little.
In terms of what I didn't like, the non linear storytelling approach that drew me in has also frustrated me a bit as I've missed out on some things and don't quite know how it all fits together. The regular price is a bit much, don't bother unless it's on sale for around a dollar or less.
In summary, it's a thoughtful journey that leaves me uneasy and wanting more. I'll be thinking about this one for a good while tonight.

Every side quest was fulfilling.  Every new game mechanic added something interesting and changed up the gameplay.  Every character felt well-written, with unexpected depths.
I feel like the developers took a lot of chances, had a lot of fun, and delivered a remarkably compelling experience.
Disclaimer: If you want your stories strongly supported, and your endings to tie up all the loose ends, you may not find Nier:Automata satisfying.
If you want to experience lovable characters, beautiful worlds, insane leaps of logic, and sudden shifts in perspective, then pick up a controller and get ready to have your heart broken. It's worth it.
EDIT: I almost forgot the soundtrack! Unobtrusive and yet still somehow the star of the show, the music is a huge part of what makes this game impactful. It takes just as many chances as the rest of the game, and consistently delivers in ways I would never have expected.
Easily one of the best games ever made. It's a work of art, and you're doing yourself a disservice if you don't play it.

The real star of the show in The Pre-Sequel is Jack. In Borderlands 2 he was perhaps the most gleefully sadistic, and effective video game villain since Final Fantasy 6's Kefka. Seeing his journey from hero to maniac is perhaps the biggest reason to make the 20-or-so-hour trek across Pandora’s moon, Elpis. Writer Anthony Burch shows a real knack for storytelling here, drawing a more sympathetic portrait of Jack without ever making him into the clichéd misunderstood villain. He's every bit the hilarious, ego-centric asshat here that we remember him as, and his excellently written and delivered dialogue is responsible for the lion's share of the laughs.
It’s a good thing too, because those laughs were often all there was to carry me through the long stretches of purposeless wandering around with barely anything to fight. This is part of a problem Borderlands has had since the beginning, and The Pre-Sequel hasn’t solved it. The inadequate waypoint system that doesn’t save you from going in circles while looking for your next objective, the boring trek back to your quest-giver at mission’s end… it’s all still here. The early hours on the moon were particularly trying, since everything is incredibly spread out, and every low-gravity jump takes seemingly forever. I just don’t want to walk towards a diamond on my mini-map for god knows how long to get to where the fun is.
And I really don’t want to go on a multi-step wild switch hunt to trigger said fun once I get there. The Pre-Sequel is cardinally guilty of this one. Apparently neither the Hyperion or Dahl corporations know how to make doors in space, because almost every single one you need to go through requires you to throw a breaker or manual override somewhere back in the area you just slogged through. In a game about shooting and looting, I should be doing those things almost constantly, but in The Pre-Sequel there were times when 10 or more minutes could easily pass without me doing much of either. Things do pick up in the latter half of the campaign, but this sort of buck-and-stall pacing has plagued the series for years, and it gets harder to forgive with each iteration.
But once The Pre-Sequel hits its stride, we get down to what Borderlands has always done best: the bullets start flying, the loot starts dropping, and joyful chaos ensues. The Pre-Sequel delivers a whole lot of that, starting with its four new playable characters and their positively nutty skill trees. Their action skills feel wildly different from one another, and from any of the vault hunters that have preceded them.
Wilhelm’s flying drone duo, Wolf and Saint, really stands out. Not only does one of them go on automated bombing runs against nearby enemies, but the other hangs back to heal him, or even your allies with the proper skill points invested. Nisha’s washes the screen in classic Western sepia, turning her into a godless, gunslinging killing machine for a short while, which is a bit more straightforward, but no less satisfying. Athena’s shield allows her to go all Captain America on fools, but Claptrap’s is by far the craziest, granting him different abilities depending on the situation at hand. Those who love a more anarchic, unpredictable approach to combat will get all the mayhem they’d like out of it.
In fact, everyone’s  skill trees are flush with abilities that reward specific playstyles with powerful temporary effects, like mini achievements you unlock over and over. Borderlands’ mascot robot Claptrap, now playable for the first time, is the best example. I happen to be a compulsive reloader with a mild death wish, so his Boomtrap skill tree seems to have been made just for me. By rapidly reloading, I can get a variety of big buffs that have explosive results, but at the cost of some health and accuracy. Oh and I have chance of actually griefing my teammates with my action skill (serves you right for joining my game without an invite...jerk). Just reading some of the other characters’ high-level skills made me think, “How does THAT work?” A copy of whatever gun I’m holding appears in my off-hand? I turn into a walking nuclear bomb? I just had to try this stuff out.
The Pre-Sequel has a few other tricks up its sleeve too, and most of them work out. Not the new Stingray hovercraft – which handles like a wet mop with a ceiling fan strapped to it – but the new low-gravity mechanics are a success. Coming to grips with my elongated jumps took a while, but once it clicked, I started using my new freedom to deadly effect. It becomes so easy to put space between you and your enemies that sniping becomes a more viable option, and being able to bound over cover to slam down behind your foes’ cover makes getting up close and personal easier, and more satisfying than ever.
The new gearing options are a blast too. Freezing enemies solid with cold-based attacks and burning them to a crisp with the new laser-class weapons feels great, but just wait until you see some of the mods that come on the Oz kits that keep you breathing in space. Some grant you accuracy and damage bonuses while airborne, while others give you an entirely different set of buffs depending on whether you’re in vacuum or atmosphere. The Pre-Sequel is really generous with loot, too, so you’ll have plenty of opportunities to shape your character in interesting ways. I mean, my Claptrap basically waltzes into the middle of groups of enemies and decimates them exclusively by reloading and dying. I can’t think of another game I can do that in.
Despite its tendency to make you jump through hoops before getting to the good stuff, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel delivers where I expect it to as a Borderlands fan. The new gear and low-gravity mechanics mixed with the zany skill trees makes for a fresh experience, and with Jack at the center driving the story forward, you get a deeper dive into the always entertaining, if well-traveled universe of Borderlands.

I have been a fan of Borderlands since the 2nd one. I never went back and played the first but I loved Borderlands 2 so I purchased this to try it out. I love it. If you have played Borderlands 2 then you would love this game. Everything is the same HUD, equipment type, skill tree (the concept not the skills. All new skills and classes), chest that you can open using shift account/gold keys, and etc. There are new things such as the "OZ kits" as they are called which are oxygen kits. You need these to breath on Elpis (Pandora's moon) in areas where there is no atomosphere. For the most part when you are on missions where you enter a fort/base there are breathable areas. Some people do not like this but grant it if you are fast at killing things then you will be fine because enemies drop Hyperion O2 refill that each one refills 25% of your max oxygen supported by your Oxygen kit. Also your oxygen does not deplete really fast. I am currently level 18 and most of the oxygen kits I have found are ~150 O2, which will last me about 2.5 minutes if I'm just standing there. There are plenty of oxygen sources as well through out Elpis. There are little square patches through out the outside of Elpis that contantly spew out oxygen that you can just walk over and refill your oxygen kit in a second or two.
Anyway I reccommend this game to any Borderlands fan and any FPS lover that likes a little fun in their games. Borderlands is a comedy in a FPS. I love the little jokes they make and crazy character personalities. I hope you found this review helpful and please rate it :D.

If you are looking for a polished, free to play MMO with great visuals and sound loook no further. There is absolutley no reason not to install this game. I'll admit the art style didn't jump out at me as attractive when it first came out, but after sinking hours into it, I can really see the wonderful style for what it is.
Ok now for the PROS:
-Character creation - offer enough variety to make a truly customizable character that looks cool
-Tutorials - Great option to do the tutuorial mode at the beginning, makes getting into the game alot easier.
-Character Development - The way that skill are leveled up and character progresses is very unique and exciting.
-Sound - The sounds are impressive (im big on sound in games) The soundtrack is truly fantastic
-Graphics - I am running a nVidia 760gtx and can run the game on or near full and maintain my 60fps. Loading times are nice and short , game overall runs very smooth
-Combat System - This is really where the game shines. Sucha  unique way to make it an Action RPG and not a buttton masher. You have to be present during battles against AI. The skills must be aimed and enemy skilles are telegraphed allowing you to either dodge roll our interupt in avariety of ways. Overall the combat is the best in any MMO i've ever played. And I've played almost every MMO starting with Ultima Online.
-Questing - The quests are fun and engaging, there are a variety of ways to level up.
The Cons:
-U.I. -  the ui is a bit clunky at first but once you get used to it, its fine. It is customizable so take some time and do so.
-Art style - some people will not like the cartoony art style that is present. I think you need to play for a few hours before you make your decision. It makes immersion a bit more of a challange. You have to play for several levels before you become immersed. I would give it until level 10 before making the decision.
In closing I haven't been able to test out PVP system yet so there is no review for that portion. And also end game. I just haven't played long enough to know. Overall I think if you are looking for an MMO you should give WildStar a try, it is truly fee to play and you risk nothing.

I have been a vivid MMO player for so many years, and I was looking forward to Wildstar and its release. (I actually bought the deluxe version while it was in beta, so my 150+ hours of gameplay doesnt get counted in Steam)
The game plays excellently and has very fluid movement along with cool combat along with the housing system wich is probably the best on the market.
However, I feel like the game is reserved for younger people, as it is a very "kiddyfied" game, wich made me feel like I was way too old for playing it.
The shop was an excellent way for Carbine to keep some income, and as experienced from TERA, the cosmetics in the shop should be very very cool.
This was the polar opposite of my expectations though, as the shop cosmetics look like complete garbage on your character in most cases, and I cant make myself believe they actually make a good revenue from cosmetics at all.
The hud bugs out way too much and gave me errors from a fresh install when I booted up the game, much of the text looks like crap wich is often borderline unreadable, and the chat system is unfortunately still bad.
I wanted to like the game as the combat is VERY fun, but all the other downsides unfortunately just ruins it.

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Future Soldier is a third person shooter from 2012 featuring a cooperative campaign which can be played with up to four different players. The game also supports competitive multiplayer modes and of course, a singleplayer variant of the campaign. It's a cover based shooter so the way taking damage works means that if you're in cover, you're almost invincible even on the hardest difficulties. If you're out of cover? You die in three seconds even on the easiest difficulties.
The graphics of this game are decent. For a game released back in 2012, they were far from revolutionary. But combined this with the game's severe lack of optimization on PC, the lack of a properly functioning vsync option, and a frame cap of 60 fps? The graphics and performance of this game are far from a reason to buy this game. Speaking strictly of performance, it's actually a reason not to buy this game. As for the animations, they're pretty damn good I think for the main characters, but for the rest of the world? They're....bad.
The soundtrack of this game is simply decent for the most part, but on occasion, and by occasion I mean about one time in the entire game, it can make something the most amazing thing you've ever experienced. The actual sound effects of the game are severely lacking and very often, at least twice per mission, you'll run into an instance where you feel like at least half of the sound effects are simply...missing.
The story is another thing that's just decent. Throughout half of the game I personally found it difficult to care very much about anything happening because after you complete a mission, everything that happened a mission or two ago is now completely irrelevant, never to be brought up again (With the exception of the prologue). The game even sports a highly gruesome cutscene which is likely the reason for the game's age restriction, but that scene adds literally nothing to the game. It was weird to watch because it was so random, and it was never mentioned again after the mission that followed it. It's like it exists solely to get shock value, and if you've played video games for awhile, it's really not all that shocking.
The gameplay is where my biggest gripes with this game lie. The core mechanics of hiding behind cover and shooting are alright. Unfortunately while you're looking around your character likes to switch which over the shoulder perspective he's using, occasionally messing up your aim or making you unable to see your target. Sprinting is annoying to control at best, feeling very bulky and clunky; and they put your character model right in your face and fog out part of your screen while you sprint, making it impossible to see anything that is straight ahead or to your left side. Controlling missiles is just..horrible. You try to line up a straight aim and your missile actually just jerks around like it's having a seizure mid-flight. The game also features many on-rails portions that some gamers may object to. It does contribute to having a more cinematic experience I think, but it does sort of break immersion when you go from having freedom of movement to suddenly not being able to look two inches to your left because they want player 3 to kill that target, not you. You have two options to approach each mission usually. Stealth or going loud. But it's important to note that there are no free stealth mechanics in this game. There is a stealth MODE. Once you break that stealth mode every enemy immediately knows your location even if you're cloaked and you cannot get stealth mode back until you kill every last enemy in your current objective.
There's something else very important to note if you're here for the campaign. This game was designed as a coop game. No dev ever seemed to expect anyone to play it without a full group of four, because let me tell you, your friendly AI are the most unrealistic companions I have ever seen in a game. They completely lack stealth mechanics. They run around and get hindered like they're trying to be stealthy, but once you see them literally run past enemies or stand right next to them you realize that's just for show. They do not exist during the stealth mode of the game. I repeat. They DO NOT EXIST. To support that claim allow me to highlight another point. They CANNOT SHOOT in stealth mode. While you CAN Q up targets and order them to shoot them, guess what? They're not actually shooting them. It's an instant lock on and kill mechanic that is not hindered by any physical barriers. Hence in the video you can see my teammate one shot an enemy THROUGH A PLANE.
As a side note, and that's all this other portion of the game really feels like, a side note. The multiplayer of future soldier will only appeal to a very specific type of player.  If you are not a Call of Duty run and gunning lover who is tolerant of occasionally taking cover, then you will not like this game's multiplayer. I tried playing it tactically like the campaign and I did alright. Once you turn it into a run and gunner, you come out on top of the leaderboard by miles ahead of anyone else. Miles.
Overall Ghost Recon Future Soldier is a good example of how NOT to do a Ghost Recon game. While it did have some awesome moments in it, that's all they were, moments.  Ghost Recon Future Soldier is not worth your attention unless you get it on a sale and have three other friends to play the campaign with. It is a below average game and earns a 4/10 because of that. There were much better games to play in 2012, and are far more better games to play now. It was fun, but the fun mostly came from laughing at just how bad it was. (With the exception of one amazing mission halfway into the game)

I took a break from Stellaris nine months ago because it was just too under-developed. Its diplomacy, warfare, mid-game monotony, and clunky interface were just too draining. Research, exploration, species customization, and the aesthetics had me playing for such a long time, but eventually I was burnt out in a bad way.
The dlc Utopia and the latest patch were released recently, so I decided to wade back into the waters. With the new customization, building, and internal political options, I was hooked back in for another absurdly long stretch. However, I'm burnt out again by the same unresolved, under-developed systems. I've played this game way too long to be able to tell you it's a bad game or that you shouldn't buy it. But I kept playing wanting to get over the things that I can't stand. I don't think I'll be playing again until the next update, and I don't want people who just have a passing interest to  take the risk on this. It's certainly not Paradox's best or most complete game. One year in, it feels like it still shouldn't have been released. I'll update as it updates.

First, a warning to anyone who does get this game:  Watch your stat numbers.  On more than one occasion, I have noted that they will seemingly drop for no reason.  If one invests the starting stat points before the first battle of the game, they seem to disappear immediately after that battle.  This is the most common time I have observed this, but I have seen it at other times as well.
This game is horribly unbalanced to a great degree of luck.  _If_ a playthrough has a decent balance of materials to continue upgrading equipment, only then can a player make real progress.  The combat system is otherwise horribly flawed so that only three or four wolves in a row will automatically be the end.  There is no good way to heal unless, again, one is sufficiently lucky to find that the generated map happens to include large numbers of herbs.
I love a challenging game.  This game is not challenging.  It is pointlessly turned toward 'luck of the draw' so that skill and analysis and careful planning for expenditures of valuable resources mean nothing.
The 'Mood' mechanic is hopelessly broken.  For each rare event that increases the character's mood, there are twenty others that drop it near to nothing.  Rest barely improves mood or health, and that is assuming the player opts to rest at all - because those rebels are always right behind.
I want to be challenged in a game, not held hostage to the whims of the random number generator that decides if I will happen to find sufficient wood to improve a weapon.  Balancing the use of limited wood and forcing me to make a difficult choice is fun; having a useless weapon against the alpha wolf after four regular wolves have already taken my health down to naught and I have no method by which to heal myself is absurd.
I strongly recommend passing on this one.

I discovered this game about two weeks before it was released.  I knew nothing about the Battle Chasers comic book, but the teaser video with the sweet music lured me in.  It isn't too hard to find an online version of the comic book.  Reading it inspired me to purchase the game given that the series ended abruptly.  I was hoping that the game would continue where the comics left off.  Unfortunately it does not.
That's not a bad thing, but for the first several hours, you're stuck with only the first three characters.  The most challenging part of the game is keeping it from crashing.  I have crashed in every ... single ... dungeon ... at least once ... forcing me to run through them again.  Walking around the map is agonizingly slow ... there is no excuse.
The actual gameplay is fine, but repetitive.  After unlocking the last character, it seems to have opened up some more variety with critters to battle.  That's a good thing because I was getting bored out of my mind fighting slimes, werewolves, bats, and tanks.  Yes, tanks ... sentient tanks ...
Crafting is done well, but unfortunately there isn't a real convenient place to actually craft.  Unless this changes at some point in the game, there is only a potion crafting station in the main town.  You're forced to walk to dungeons to find other crafting stations.  Did I mention walking anywhere is pure agony?
I think the developers can improve the quality of life and allow the characters on the overmap to move at least double-time.  Fixing the crashes wouldn't hurt either.  Oh, and maybe kicking up the gold rewards in random chests?  One of my characters is level 17 and I'm still finding a pittance in gold.
I recommend this game if you're a fan of JRPGs.  I would wait for a steam sale and, hopefully, by that time the developers will have made the game more stable.
**UPDATE**
I'm removing my recommendation due to the constant crashing.  The developers claim that the fault lies with Unity.  They recommend running the game in Safe Mode DX9.  When/if they ever fix the constant crashing I'll recommnd the game again.  As it stands, to blame the game engine (when countless thousands of high-quality games run on Unity) is a pretty lame excuse.

Update 2: Now that it's the following day and I am less frustrated about the whole thing, I have to say that so far this was the only major issue with otherwise thoughtful design and beautiful game. The impression I had when I walked away from this game is that it should have been done in a different medium. The story may have been good, but I approached it as a game, involving first-person atmospheric horror, and the story was being presented to me as on-screen text, which felt like an intrusion.
I didn't finish it, because the mountain can only be entered once the player has discovered all the pieces of the story. Having missed some piece somewhere, I wasn't too interested in wandering around for who knows how long before I found it and could advance.
I have no criticism for the graphics of the game, as it was obviously a labor of love by probably only one person, and production value takes man-hours. What I was disappointed by was the fact that it didn't convey its story through gameplay, which is kind of why you make something in this particular medium. Stories, especially ones being told in a horror-esque setting are best conveyed visually, where the player see, hears, and interacts with the environment. In this, portions of the story are told out of order when the player interacts with objects that may have nothing to do with the story section being told. That, and the various clips found in a room can start overlapping, making it impossible to read.
I don't regret the money spent to support new developers, but I would suggest to creator to give some thought to the medium you're creating in. If you want to tell a story, find ways to convey it to the player without resorting solely to text.

Do I recommend this game? If you:
Like walking, story-centric horrors
Have an hour to spare
Have the cash to spare
Then yes, I do.
Did this game blow my mind? No, of course not. The walking, story heavy horror has a lot to offer, but it takes a lot to really tap into the potential. This game gently caressed the surface. Given that it was made by one person, however, I think it did a fair job. The story was easy enough to piece together, so long as you're able to understand subtle clues. And there was a nice, rounded twist at the end that explained, without a wall of text, what your purpose for the exploration was. I found that was a nice touch and it made the completion of the game satisfying.
Unless I missed a portion of story (which is possible, as I guessed one puzzle so unless that was what I was supposed to do, I may have missed some minor reveals) then most of the questions were answered in some formatm which was nice.
The praise being said, this game doesn't have any replayability, aside from having a friend who doesn't handle horror well playing it while you watch and snicker in the background. A nice soundtrack and fair but not amazing graphics. However, again referencing to the fact that it was made by one man. Making a game isn't easy, after all.
Save your money and wait for a sale.

Ignore the people who are hate bombing the game because of SE's business practices, it says nothing of the game itself. I do not support or condem said practice, which is SEA pricing for the game. I will not facetously claim to have knowledge of the conditions and arguments on either side, but it is the simple truth that the pricing issues are a business-side issue and have nothing to do with the game itself.
The easiest way to sum up NieR: Automata is that it is a game that was obviously made with a lot of love and care. The game's producer (Yoko Taro) doesn't get the manpower and budget of other games, until now and it shows greatly in what is in my opinion, one of the best and most impactful games ever made.
In the past few years we've been seeing an upswing in games that have developers who actually take pride in their work and put their heart and soul into their projects. We have also seen many creators push out unambitous products with only the minimal amount of effort and with very little polish or care. NieR: Automata is one of the best examples ever of the former. I won't dull you with the back story, but people were threatening to quit if they didn't get a chance to work with Yoko Taro on a game with adeequate resources.
For background the last Yoko Taro game I played was in college: Drakengard 1 back in the early 2000's. Me and my friends who watched me play still remember the insanity of said game and the impression it left, especially with the final ending. Nier: Automata has that impact in spades. Onto the bullets.
-The game is very beautiful visually. Not much to say there but it's very well done. The only detraction I can give it is that some optimization issues are there for the PC port. (FAR helps with this as I describe below)
-The music is arguably the best ever from a game. I have nothing to add to that. It is simply that good.
-Combat is fun and well done, as well as effectively combining different genres of games into one (bullet hell and melee action game play). The combat never feels like a chore, not even after my 50+ hours. If you played Metal Gear Rising, it will feel similar in a lot of aspects. You can dive deeper into it if you desire (fighting things while severly overleved and/or hard difficulty), but it's not so compliacted that you can't pick it up and go. Difficulty can be changed on the fly.
-Upgrading and customizing your abilites is well-done and enjoyable, and it gives you 3 Configurations to save for easy switching. There is a lot to play around with concerning the chips, and a great deal of fun to be had.
-The game is very aware of itself through it's humor. There is a lot of humor in this game, however, it doesn't break the 4th wall excessively and does not detract from the story or the immersion.
-While the rest of the game is excellently done, it is the story and the way it is experienced (not told) that is the strongest feature of this game. The story sucks you in little by little, then before you realize it, it has smacked you in the face. Lucky for you, it doesn't stop smacking you in the face until the end credits, which is better described as a violent assault by an unruly mob at that point. The ending to the game is one of the strongest ever if not the.
-The difficulty never gets in the way of the story, so long as you get familiar and decent at the combat system. The one area it DOES get in the way, there's an out and its a truly beautiful thing that you owe it to yourself to experience.
I would have to implore that you do your homework on whether or not your system can handle it, as certain graphics cards are known to not work well with the game (if at all). The program "F.A.R." exists and it helps the game's performance tremendously. I have a GTX 970 and I use FAR. I only experienced slow down once in 50+ hours using FAR.
Buying this on console may be a safer bet giving some of the technical misgivings, just remember that people who are playing the game and enjoying it don't commonly frequent the discussions, so again: do your homework as you should with any game on PC.
Outside of all of that, I highly recommend this game.

Stellaris is a sci-fi 4x game. It may perhaps be
sci-fi 4x game. It covers very many angles of science fiction, you can re-create almost any sci-fi scenario in Stellaris. If it's not available in the base game, it's probably in a DLC or someone's modded it in. If you like galactic-scale science fiction and/or 4x games, you're going to like this game.
+ Good soundtrack of space music. You don't know what space music is? It's this kind of stuff.
+ Sound effects are good. Nothing too outstanding here, but it's appropriate.
+ A lot of love went into the graphics for the stellar bodies, and it's soothing to watch pulsars or black holes or planets spin on their axis.
+ Good writing. Since most events and diplomacy are conveyed through writing, this is good. You can ignore it if you hate reading, but you'll miss out on the feel of being part of a novel.
+ Strong early game with lots of exploration events.
+ Lots of attention to detail everywhere.
? Notable lack of graphics for a lot of in-game events, or a small number of still images are re-used. Don't expect unique art every time something happens, but to compensate a lot of stuff seems to happen.
? Endgame is a bit nebulous (hah). One of several end-game events that will happen if you have the setting turned on, and these are alright. There's some fun end-game shenanigans you can do with genetic manipulation or building mega-structures, but by the time you get to them, you'll already either won or lost.
- Graphics engine chugs during the endgame with lots of on-screen ships.
- Emaciated middle. I hope you're ready to put the game on the fastest speed and just churn though technologies while you micromanage your holdings and build up a blob fleet of death. Slightly alleviated with the Leviathans DLC, but it's not enough.
- Diplomacy is almost nonexistent.
- Federations (large alliances) are a huge waste of time thanks to the way the AI flounders with the federation fleet.
- No espionage or intrigue between empires. You can infiltrate pre-FTL worlds, but empires can't touch each other.
- The game attempts to discourage you from micromanaging your planets and heavily penalizes you if you go over your Core World limit, but the sector AI that you're supposed to use instead is inscrutable and dumb. This ironically results in more and more frustrating micromanagement.
- Space combat consists entirely of throwing as large a fleet as possible at the enemy. There are no tactics, there are no formations, just balls of death.
- Ground combat is even worse because it's also a blob, but you don't even see the lasers and missiles, just numbers and HP bars on a screen.
- War in general is a slog due to how demands work. It can take several wars with a 10-year truce between to conquer or eradicate an enemy, because the game won't allow you to take more from the enemy than it deems fit.
- Tall empires are not feasible because by the time you research the technologies that allow construction of tall empires you've already lost because of the huge disadvantage you have of spending the first two thirds of the game as a small empire.
- Despite all the different aliens feeling different because of appearance and ethical attitudes, they all have the same weapons on their ships, they all have the same hydroponic farms, and they all have the same mining stations.
That looks like a lot of cons, huh? Well, there's a lot of other mechanics that do work and will keep you busy so that it's still fun for a while before you start noticing the downsides.

Ok, I'm hooked. Haven't had a 4x space game reel me in like this in a very long time.
The interface isn't great. Certain information and game functions are buried in the various windows and tabs, and are not explained well.
The tutorial is severely lacking, and the learning curve is vast. I made MANY visits to various online sources to figure out what I was doing.
The graphics & sound are passable, nothing spectacular but they get the job done.
But the scope... Wow, the scope! Complex diplomacy, deep and varied government options, a very clever sector system that lets you hand over control of parts of your empire to AI governors (which took some getting used to but now I like it...) This is a complex game that really rewards taking the time to learn the various systems. Once those systems are familiar, it all starts to make sense.
The game concepts themselves are all very familiar. Grow your empire. Deal with alien races. Choose and assign your governors & leaders. Design your fleets. But it's the way these tried & true mechanics are presented that set Stellaris apart. For example, your leadership will actually advance in rank, grow old, and die. Your prized engineering researcher may suddenly find herself elected president. With her expertise now elsewhere you'll need to fill that role. Do you move an experienced survey ship captain to fill her spot, or recruit a fresh face? (which can be further complicated when that newly elected president dies of old age 2 years later, creating a new series of power shifts...)
As somebody who played the hell out of classic games from the golden age of grand 4x space conquest from the 90s (Master of Orion, Pax Imperia, Galactic Civ, etc) this is a worthy addition.
