The real star of the show in The Pre-Sequel is Jack. In Borderlands 2 he was perhaps the most gleefully sadistic, and effective video game villain since Final Fantasy 6's Kefka. Seeing his journey from hero to maniac is perhaps the biggest reason to make the 20-or-so-hour trek across Pandora’s moon, Elpis. Writer Anthony Burch shows a real knack for storytelling here, drawing a more sympathetic portrait of Jack without ever making him into the clichéd misunderstood villain. He's every bit the hilarious, ego-centric asshat here that we remember him as, and his excellently written and delivered dialogue is responsible for the lion's share of the laughs.
It’s a good thing too, because those laughs were often all there was to carry me through the long stretches of purposeless wandering around with barely anything to fight. This is part of a problem Borderlands has had since the beginning, and The Pre-Sequel hasn’t solved it. The inadequate waypoint system that doesn’t save you from going in circles while looking for your next objective, the boring trek back to your quest-giver at mission’s end… it’s all still here. The early hours on the moon were particularly trying, since everything is incredibly spread out, and every low-gravity jump takes seemingly forever. I just don’t want to walk towards a diamond on my mini-map for god knows how long to get to where the fun is.
And I really don’t want to go on a multi-step wild switch hunt to trigger said fun once I get there. The Pre-Sequel is cardinally guilty of this one. Apparently neither the Hyperion or Dahl corporations know how to make doors in space, because almost every single one you need to go through requires you to throw a breaker or manual override somewhere back in the area you just slogged through. In a game about shooting and looting, I should be doing those things almost constantly, but in The Pre-Sequel there were times when 10 or more minutes could easily pass without me doing much of either. Things do pick up in the latter half of the campaign, but this sort of buck-and-stall pacing has plagued the series for years, and it gets harder to forgive with each iteration.
But once The Pre-Sequel hits its stride, we get down to what Borderlands has always done best: the bullets start flying, the loot starts dropping, and joyful chaos ensues. The Pre-Sequel delivers a whole lot of that, starting with its four new playable characters and their positively nutty skill trees. Their action skills feel wildly different from one another, and from any of the vault hunters that have preceded them.
Wilhelm’s flying drone duo, Wolf and Saint, really stands out. Not only does one of them go on automated bombing runs against nearby enemies, but the other hangs back to heal him, or even your allies with the proper skill points invested. Nisha’s washes the screen in classic Western sepia, turning her into a godless, gunslinging killing machine for a short while, which is a bit more straightforward, but no less satisfying. Athena’s shield allows her to go all Captain America on fools, but Claptrap’s is by far the craziest, granting him different abilities depending on the situation at hand. Those who love a more anarchic, unpredictable approach to combat will get all the mayhem they’d like out of it.
In fact, everyone’s  skill trees are flush with abilities that reward specific playstyles with powerful temporary effects, like mini achievements you unlock over and over. Borderlands’ mascot robot Claptrap, now playable for the first time, is the best example. I happen to be a compulsive reloader with a mild death wish, so his Boomtrap skill tree seems to have been made just for me. By rapidly reloading, I can get a variety of big buffs that have explosive results, but at the cost of some health and accuracy. Oh and I have chance of actually griefing my teammates with my action skill (serves you right for joining my game without an invite...jerk). Just reading some of the other characters’ high-level skills made me think, “How does THAT work?” A copy of whatever gun I’m holding appears in my off-hand? I turn into a walking nuclear bomb? I just had to try this stuff out.
The Pre-Sequel has a few other tricks up its sleeve too, and most of them work out. Not the new Stingray hovercraft – which handles like a wet mop with a ceiling fan strapped to it – but the new low-gravity mechanics are a success. Coming to grips with my elongated jumps took a while, but once it clicked, I started using my new freedom to deadly effect. It becomes so easy to put space between you and your enemies that sniping becomes a more viable option, and being able to bound over cover to slam down behind your foes’ cover makes getting up close and personal easier, and more satisfying than ever.
The new gearing options are a blast too. Freezing enemies solid with cold-based attacks and burning them to a crisp with the new laser-class weapons feels great, but just wait until you see some of the mods that come on the Oz kits that keep you breathing in space. Some grant you accuracy and damage bonuses while airborne, while others give you an entirely different set of buffs depending on whether you’re in vacuum or atmosphere. The Pre-Sequel is really generous with loot, too, so you’ll have plenty of opportunities to shape your character in interesting ways. I mean, my Claptrap basically waltzes into the middle of groups of enemies and decimates them exclusively by reloading and dying. I can’t think of another game I can do that in.
Despite its tendency to make you jump through hoops before getting to the good stuff, Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel delivers where I expect it to as a Borderlands fan. The new gear and low-gravity mechanics mixed with the zany skill trees makes for a fresh experience, and with Jack at the center driving the story forward, you get a deeper dive into the always entertaining, if well-traveled universe of Borderlands.

You need these to breath on Elpis (Pandora's moon) in areas where there is no atomosphere. For the most part when you are on missions where you enter a fort/base there are breathable areas. Some people do not like this but grant it if you are fast at killing things then you will be fine because enemies drop Hyperion O2 refill that each one refills 25% of your max oxygen supported by your Oxygen kit. Also your oxygen does not deplete really fast. I am currently level 18 and most of the oxygen kits I have found are ~150 O2, which will last me about 2.5 minutes if I'm just standing there. There are plenty of oxygen sources as well through out Elpis. There are little square patches through out the outside of Elpis that contantly spew out oxygen that you can just walk over and refill your oxygen kit in a second or two.
Anyway I reccommend this game to any Borderlands fan and any FPS lover that likes a little fun in their games. Borderlands is a comedy in a FPS. I love the little jokes they make and crazy character personalities. I hope you found this review helpful and please rate it :D.

I just got this game and alsready put 10 hours into it. It's a charming, colourful TBC RPG. It can be challenging in some places, which is what I was hoping for, so don't let the cartoony visuals throw you off.

There's fishing too, which I haven't figured out what to do with my catches yet, but it's a relaxing little mini game if you need a breather.

Plus points first...
This offers a level of customisation I haven't seen in any other street racing game. For example, you don't just upgrade a stage 1 engine to a stage 2 engine. You buy individual engine components and assemble them. In the right order. Do you know the optimal air/fuel ratio for a specific type of fuel and engine configuration? You'll need to find out if you want to get the best from your car. What spring rate is best for the suspension setup you have and the intended use of the car? What shock absorber settings? It really is that detailed and it has a strong effect on how a car handles.
There's a Roguelike philosophy in this game, in that game over is game over. I had to restart half a dozen times. You start with only one car. If it's damaged and you can't afford to repair it to a working state, game over. Start again. That will probably happen to you because damage is heavy. You're not going to get away with minor damage after clipping a post at 60 mph. Angry or incompetent AI opponents might well ram you. You won $1000 in the race...and they rammed you into a lampost, causing $5000 of non-cosmetic damage. You only have $2400? Game over, start again.
And now the negative points:
Bugs. The developer of this new version is doing a good job, but they were starting from a game that had more bugs than a square mile of the Amazon rainforest. There are still a lot of bugs (this is true for build 920, the latest build at the moment). Some are irritating. Some are gamebreaking. Some are odd (e.g. on my PC fullscreen is currently effectively broken because the framerate is so low, but windowed mode at the same settings can reach hundreds of FPS)

Change one front suspension setting...exit garage...drive around ring...make a pass...return to garage...change the setting again...exit garage...drive around ring...make a pass...return to garage...etc. By the way, if you try the mile time on the test track with all but the slowest cars you will run out of track before you can brake and you will ram a wall and you will do a lot of damage, probably destroying your engine. Bugs. So bugged that it's worth mentioning twice. This is not a finished game (and it's clearly stated as being unfinished and unstable).

I really like the optics, the athmosphere and the basic gameplay of Delver.
It has four main problems:
1: Arrows stack. Well, that is some do some don't. Arrows you buy at a marchant can only stack up to two arrows wich is not very helpfull at all. Some other arrows do stack though and sometimes it looks like arrows you pickd up again (a feature i really like) stack with arrows they haven't stacked with before. No idea what is going on there but it isn't very helpfull.
2: Collision Detection for Arrows is terribble. That means that on several of enemys hitting the Sprite doesn't actually hit the enemy. On other enemys it's a game of luck if the arrow damages the enemy upon contact or just flys trough. This is seriously frustrat5ing especially when you want to concentrate on playing with bows and because you need to use all reserves avaiable to you to get trough the game. This leads to problem two.
3: This game sooner or later is a game of attrition. Sooner or later you are going to die simply because the ressources like food and or potions aren't nearly enough to get you trough. Especially potions are superrare and you need at least one to even find out what they do because the potions change functions between attempts to master the dungeon. What in one session was a health potion could be poison or a magepotion in the next session. Together with problem one, the lacking collision detection this leads to a slow grind to death.
4: The roquelike elements aren't good enough because they aren't really persistent. The point of games like these is that although you die you gain somethinmg from your try at the dungeon that helps you within your next attempt.
In Delver this is gold, if you die you get to use the gold you had in your inventorey on the next cahracter and nothing else. This is a problem.
Logically you could say that it would bring you forward for your next character so you can buy items to maybe master the dungeon this time.
The problem is that you can only buy temporary items that dissapear with your next death. This would mean that you have to do several runs just to grind out gold for that on round that you maybe, maybe not, get trough the dungeon with. That would be if the avaiable items could make a hug impact, wich they don't because they are standart items you could easily find in the dungeon itself.
A seller a few levels down selss actually experience potions wich practically means you are buying levels. But they cost 250 Gold per potion and that means a whole lot of goldgrinding runs to maybe be able to buy enough so that it has an impact.
Delver clearly needs more persistent rewards that carry over between deaths.
Now, why do i still recommend this game?
Well, as Delver is kinda in endless Early Access there is hope these things can change.
But my bigger reason is that despite the mentioned flaws i honestly have to say that i had a lot of fun for the money the game has cost and that i still feel that i will come back to the game here and there to have some atmospheric, simple fun playing it.

Indie games have something of a problem when it comes to wearing their inspirations on their sleeves. Time and again you'll hear touted roots in Legend of Zelda, Earthbound, 90s platformers - and in this case, Silent Hill. Lone Survivor hasn't so much said it's been inspired by Silent Hill as much as it has carved off James Sunderland's face and is proudly displaying it for the world to see.
Especially fitting considering how paper thin and two-dimensional this game is compared to the real deal.
Every part of this game is bad so we're going to break it down in steps.
It's ugly. While predating the worldwide novelty of low resolution pixel art coming to a screeching halt, Lone Survivor manages to be ugly on its own merit. Filters, overlays and soft shading don't disguise the absolute amateur attempts at anything resembling human characters, to the point where it's legitimately hard to make out overall shapes, nevermind details.
"What the hell is that?" is usually a response you want to body horror, not to regular bodies.
This isn't aided by self defeating gameplay. You actually have 4 ways to deal with enemies:
Problem is that the entire game is divided and dictated by a moral choice system that means you will only ever use two of these at a time. And with only two main enemy types in the game, this means that even with a 2-3 hour playtime, you're going to get bored. 2 hours and it manages to be a repetitive mess.
Somehow even the sound direction manages to unimpress - the constant static that the zombies emit has beaten records in how quickly it gets annoying, and your classic Silent Hill "panic tunes" constantly trigger when there's nothing happening.
Walking down an empty hallway? Time for some heartbeats and tempo. In a crowded room, 3 Thin Men and a Fatso right up your rear? No room for tunes, baby, not over all this ear-bending, monotonous screeching static.
That's one Silent Hill classic element tossed to the winds. What about the other, what about the narrative? Good question. What about it?
Every single character, plot line, ending, and interaction is obfuscated and muddled to the point of absurdity. Everything is a metaphor, or not really there, or is speaking in riddles with no answers that nothing prompted, and it all ends in a lovely "Was it ever really real?".
It's pretentious trash. Everything is so completely convinced that it's all so deep and meaningful and smart, with every plot thread busy jamming its thumb up its colon.
With the amount of theory-baiting this game does, the developer could have just thrown up a blank canvas with "May as make up your own story, frankly we're not interested" with a bullet point list of prompts to get you started. Who is "her"? Why does the man wear a box? How many of these lines are just references to other, better games? You decide.
All five endings over 9 hours. Three distinct ones, one incredibly minute variation, one joke ending. That represents 3.5 playthroughs, all done to explore if there really is any merit behind this game.
Lone Survivor is for one niche - Silent Hill fans who are desperate for more similar content and don't mind a massive quality drop in everything. Made by a fan who couldn't see the forest for the trees, it's low grade imitation beef.
The soundtrack is nice. You can buy that on bandcamp. Anything else, you're looking in the wrong place. I don't recommend this game to anyone.

Originally a 2012 title and later updated to the Director's Cut version free of charge in 2013, Lone Survivor tells a story about a nameless man trying to survive in a world ravaged by a disease that turns almost, if not, all of it's inhabitants into mindless zombie-like monsters. Supplies dried, he's forced to leave his apartment behind after so long to forage provision and find other survivors while constantly trying to keep his sanity in check.
This game is a purely a throwback to the survival horror goodness that games nowadays lack. The writing and visuals works excellent in portraying the madness of how the new world has become and the lines between reality and insanity becomes blurred with each passing day. The game plays in a 2D manner and you can navigate the masked man right and left, also facing the front and the back. Every level will have a map which you have to find and it's vital to keep your bearings intact because not only does the area looks vaguely similar at times but there's a chance that the room will appear differently when you came back. While exploring, you have to keep your hunger and tiredness in check, which are noted by dialogue cues. Items can be combine and cook to provide more significant bonuses when consumed. Lone Survivor also relies heavily on the pocket flashlight (Silent Hill, anyone?) which uses battery when lit. You can't examine things if there's no light so there's a need in moderation. Same goes with the handgun you'll find early on in the game. As you can already guess, ammo are scarce so more often then not, sneaking your way through would be the best course of action.
The pixelated graphics works surprisingly well for the game! That, added with the amazing sounds and creepy lighting, will keep you on your toes whenever you enter a new area. Even though the monsters appear blocky at time, I can guarantee you that pants will be♥♥♥♥♥♥(or at least a little scream) when the thing suddenly lunges or jump up to the ceiling! The game also dealt with psychological horror aspects so do expect some disturbing scenes while playing.
Despite the praises, Lone Survivor is no where a perfect title. The problem particularly arises from the controls in my view which I'll list them in a bit down below.
Personally, I think the price tag of $15 is a bit too steep for a 4 years old game but the game itself is pure gold and any survival horror enthusiasts shouldn't missed out on this. If you ever managed to find it on sale, then by all means, go for it. Money well spent, I say.

1. I wish there were some sort of neutral rating on Steam. This game is worth starting but not really worth finishing.
2. The standout quality of this is sound design, which is simply as good as it gets. The sound effects almost feel like a natural extension of the music, which is excellent in its own right.
3. The art style, I am not in love with. It is just sort of a pixely blur. It works well enough but something about it just looks like you have resolution on your monitor set incorrectly.
4. The atmosphere--see number 3--is enticing at first. Very immersive. This isn't really scary exactly but there is a menacing quality that is very foreboding and appealing all at once.
5. Gameplay is a survival horror game boiled down to 2D. While the giants of this genre are rotting away into AAA action games, it is nice to see an indie dev do something that stayed true to what people love about survival horror while adding their own twist.
6. 2D survivor horror works fine. The third D is overrated in gaming.
7.  Number 5  is why I really, really wanted to like this game and why it's been on my to-play list for years. Unfortunately, this works only as a proof of concept. See number 6.
8. Once you absorb the atmosphere, the gameplay starts to wear thin. There is nothing wrong w/ it inherently but the whole thing seems to lack polish. You are backtracking all over the place. You have to rest and go through the same little clip scenes over and over. There is a mild puzzle solving element but it's just like, "You need to cook? Find a pot, I guess."
9. Yes, backtracking and an overall slower pace are hallmarks of survivor horror and I just praised this game for being a true survivor horror game. What can I say? This game is both good and bad. It's a paradox.
10. *the sound of minds blowing*
11. There are multiple endings. Multiple endings are overrated in gaming.
12. Like, seriously, are you so full of yourself that you think your game is worth playing like five times over and over? Sorry, I got things to do.
13. In all honestly, I didn't finish this thing even once. I was just bored to death after picking it up the second day for another hour. Tried again on a third day and still bored, I set down my trusty Steam controller, and thought, yep that's all I'm ever playing of this game for the rest of my life and I feel good about it. I will totally buy a sequel or preferably a new IP in a similar style if the developer makes one. There is promise here but unfulfilled.

Lone Survivor is a 2D survival horror game. You play the role of You who lost in the abandoned apartment block must make his way out. It won't be easy though. You don't have much food, medicine, ammo and you have to pass countless corridors full of danger.

The game has a great soundtrack. It doesn't consist of many tracks but they all contribute to a nice lonely, unsettling atmosphere. It's also got an openly interpretated plot. The story may seem confusing. No, actually it is very confusing.
You don't know who you (he?) really are. Was it all just a dream or?

Moon Sliver (or Moon Silver that I bet many of us read at first :), is pretty simplistic, atmospheric game, that focuses on exploaration (small but nevertheless very intriquing island) and it's story..
In first person view, "armed" with only a flashlight that you need to recharge once in a while (which is no problem) and curiosity about the island and the world around it..
It takes about one hour to beat the game, but even though it's arquably very short, it tells pretty decent story about existence, meaning of life, desperation, fear, false happiness and all other psycho/phylosophical themes that surrounds human nature..
There will be few questions left unanswered which, in my opinion, works very well because gives you the freedom to fill in the blanks.. Graphics ain't great, it's pretty simple but it really doesn't matter since the atmosphere of the game prevails right from beginning..
PRO:
- interesting story,
- doable in under one hour (when you don't have much time, but want to play something cool),
- decent graphics and surrounding sounds,
- sense of being followed, having a feeling of unease,
- writing, it gives you just about info to make some sense out of this island and it's habitants, but few infos are missing (for me, even better)
- ending! (which left me pretty surprised)
CONS:
- no save game (not really a con, since game can be beaten in less than one hour),
- graphics (yea, I listed graphics in PRO section, but just because it's an indie game, if you compare this game to some "bigger fish" result will be "damn, this game sucks graphic♥♥♥♥♥quot;..
CONCLUSION:
Very good game, interesting and "catchy" story, little controls to worry about.. I recommend this game if you wanna take break from crazy action driven games and want to enjoy a somewhat scary and frightening story about destiny of few people that were/are on that island..

The difficulty: It's rather challenging if you "just" do story missions. You might have to grind a bit of XP to be able to beat the bosses and elite mobs. And you lose gold, which is hard to come by if you just do story missions. You get where I'm going with this. My point is this: Do everything in the game, all the time. And you might be able to kill the bosses without having to grind (an awful lot).
The only thing that really bothers me, are the difficulty levels of dungeons. Normal, Heroic and Legendary. So let's say you did the first dungeon when you HAVE to do it. Which means when the story arrives at that very dungeon. The difficulties will say: Normal = Average, Heroic = Hard, Legendary = Locked. You can do it on heroic. It won't be that easy, but you can do it. You beat it. You now unlock the legendary difficulty. Because you JUST did the dungeon, you don't do it again right away, so you progress in the story.
You come back a couple of levels later. You click on the dungeon and you can still choose the difficulty setting. It will say: Normal = Very Easy (Duh..), Heroic = Very Easy (Duh?), Legendary = Very Easy (Wait a second..)
Exactly, THAT is my only complaint about this game (up to this point that is, ~15h in). WHY DON'T THE DUNGEONS SCALE WITH YOUR LEVEL ON LEGENDARY DIFFICULTY? If you come back to a dungeon and do it on legendary, you don't get♥♥♥♥♥♥for it!♥♥♥♥♥♥gear,♥♥♥♥♥♥XP, you don't even have fun clearing it.
Please fix this soon. Because I love this game and I wanna neglect my social life some more..

Battle Chasers: Nightwar is based off of the late 90's comic book series simply titled "Battle Chasers". Battle Chasers: Nightwar follows the original cast from the comic book series through a new and mysterious land of which there is little known. This game seeks to capture the old styles of turn-based RPG's and does such with flying colors, making the combat a tense and fun experience. Now, before I begin to gush about the game for hours, shall we get on with the pros and cons?
Pros:
- Wonderfully done turn-based RPG style. Introducing a variety of elements from the genre and including some of its own twists upon the genre. I personally am not a turn-based RPG fan, but this game has been an absolute blast so far!
- Outstanding OST. Simply wonderful with haunting tracks which are fitting for various engagements. One of the few game OST's I'll go back and listen to whilst not playing the game.
- Gorgeous art style, with a theme based around a modern comic book vibe.
- Simple and powerful perks and progression. Upon leveling up your character you will gain perks which you can assign skill points to. Perks grant various passive bonuses including leveling up various attacks, or allowing for you to grant them stat bonuses such as crit chance % and so on.
- The ability to reassign skill points at any time! This is such an important feature within this game, as Skills begin requiring upwards of 10 skill points at a specific point within the game. Allowing players to respec their skill trees at any time allows for various theorycrafting builds, and synergizing builds between characters.
- Interesting overworld and dungeon exploration. Overworld exploration consists of a somewhat linear map which marks various caches of supplies, crafting ingredients, loot boxes, and also enemies. Dungeon exploration allows for the usage of one of the three player characters, each coming with various skills you may use in the dungeon to either escape enemies or give yourself an edge when getting into a fight.
- Fantastic worldbuilding. One of my favorite parts of this game are the very well done lore pieces you can find scattered amongst the dungeons and the overworld. Along with lore pieces, characters will interact with one another when resting at an Inn, further developing their relationships and their interpersonal stories/background information.
- Extremely varied enemies, with the inclusion of a bestiary to read further into the monsters and bandits scattered along the world.
- Interesting shopkeeps and supporting characters! This has always been a big gripe I've had with games. Most games have characters which aren't interesting for shopkeepers and supporting characters. Each character within the game has been given a particular personality, with each one having their own quirks, interests, and traits. From the simple Blacksmith to the mysterious Collector, each character is so very well done.
- Fishing! With a large variety of fish able to be caught, including mechanical fish.
- Inclusion of multiple difficulty settings on Dungeons before delving into them. Upon first encountering a dungeon the difficulty is maxed at Very Hard, however upon defeating a Dungeon it can be explored once more on Legendary difficulty. Each difficulty grants various bonuses and risks, with each giving its own treasure chest to the player at the end. Rarity is determined by difficulty.
- Support for a wide array of monitor resolitions, including 2560x1080 and beyond!
- Interesting boss fights, with each boss being its own unique entity with a haunting soundtrack accompanying it!
- The Battle Burst System. Through various actions within a battle you can gain what is known as "Burst". Burst allows you to unleash various devestating attacks upon your enemies, or extraordinary buffs upon your allies, and in some cases both damaging enemies AND buffing allies. Various bosses/minibosses within the game can use Bursts as well, so some precaution is needed when facing down tough adversaries.
- Days progress whilst adventuring within dungeons, thus allowing for enemies to repopulate the overworld and shops to restock. Don't want to wait in an inn and would rather do something productive until shop stock changes? Go crack some skulls with the team.
- Inclusion of a system that allows you to ignore/avoid all lesser enemy fights upon the overworld if you'd like. See an enemy that is an extremely low level compared to you? Walk right past it and pay it no mind!
Cons:
- The inevitable grind. Whilst Battle Chasers: Nightwar does have a great leveling system, the games difficulty spikes up very quick in the later levels, resulting in having to grind for gear and levels in places you've already visited.
- Non-chosen party characters do not gain experience with you. While this may seem like a weird con, the characters are considered with you within the game world, coming out and conversing with other party characters at critical junctures within the game. Having to juggle between six characters means that each character must be meticulously leveled to keep up with the other characters, which lends itself to the grind and feels like an artificial way to pad the games playtime.
- Lack of optimization for specific GPU's, mainly being the Nvidia GTX 900 series. GTX 980 results in stuttering and frameskips whilst exploring the overworld map. This isn't an entirely HUGE issue, as it does not ruin the game, however it does heavily break immersion which is not a good thing for an RPG.
- A lack of pertinent information in battle pertaining to enemies. Various fights within the game seem to have imposed difficulty curves just for the sake of making them "more challenging" without giving the player any information as to what is going on behind the scenes. A good example of this is how an enemy with a seemingly two-staged attack (one turn to charge, then one to attack) can change to being a single stage attack for seemingly no reason without ANY haste buffs or the like. Most likely mechanics to make specific fights more difficult, however insight should be given to players regarding their adversaries.
- An extremely limited overworld map. Sporting very little in the way of random adventuring and so on, causing the player to be generally forced along. As far as RPG's go, this one has very little exploration outside of the main questline.
- Some enemies within the game are unable to be one shot. This is quite an off-the-wall con, however some enemies are placed within time-trial modes in the game that require the quick execution of enemies. Some enemies have mechanics which will split them into two enemies or so on upon receiving X amount of damage, and upon playing yesterday I learned the game locks them at 1 HP and then splits them with a large amount of HP (4960) regardless of how much you hurt them.
Overall: I personally love this game and would rate it a rather high 9 out of 10. Gameplay elements are great and the game is just highly enjoyable with extremely good music. Most likely going to be one of my favorite 2017 release games.
Worth $30? Yes. Very much yes, however it will most likely go on sale at some point, so if you're not sold after this review, would suggest waiting until such.

This game takes me back to the good ol' Final Fantasy games.... ill try to keep this review short, but just so i make myself clear, its not perfect. There are various little annoying details that try to gnaw at your ankles as your go through this game, but the experience in general is worth the tolerance to said details.
A very strong point of this game and that im sure is the one that reeled a lot of people in, it's the amazing artwork, and yes it truly is... and it remains constant throught it entirely, there's some ocassional voice acting that is well done and very welcome.
Story (6/10):
This is and adaptation-sequel to Joe Madureira's fantasy comic book series "Battle Chasers". The main story is nothing you haven't heard of. You gather some dudes that are sworn protectors of the main-ish protagonist who has this great power that everybody wants (although nobody really gives a sh*t, the story so far revolves elswere), ill have to finish the game to see if this changes but i have a pretty good idea of where this is going.
Characters (7/10):
There are 6 heroes, each of them with their unique set of abilities and skill trees. Theres the main hero Gully; she's by far my favorite character, her character design, role and abilities so damn cool. Theres this big ol' war golem (that ill talk about in a second) that you'd think is the team's tank... you'd be wrong, the main tank is actually the 9 year-old kid. She can EAT through so much enemy damage that its almost ludicrous.
Then theres the war golem Calibretto; another bird-loving robot with a conscience, he's quite squishy (all heroes aside from gully are, this is an important point i'll talk about in a second), and it's the main and only reliable support of the team, he can bring everybody back to 100% hp in a jiffy as well as dispel a lot of dire ailments in battles.
Moving on the the main DPS Garrison, he will be the one landing most of the kills in battles, once again, he can take like 3-4 direct hits before he's laid out cold so you have to make sure gully keeps him well protected. He's the classic warrior with a gruesome past and f****d up decisions seeking some sort of redemption by helping the daughter (Gully) of his once upon a time brother-in-arms, Aramus. I like this character a lot as well, he's got some nice abilities that you can patiently combine in battles for some absolutely anihilating profit.
And that's all i really want to say about the characters; the other 3 are quite dull, having even more bland and cookie-cutted backstories and personalities.
Combat (7/10):
There are mixed feelings here... overall its very fun and so far i haven´t got bored of it, even if at some times battles can turn into xp and crafting material grinds (yes, crafting is a thing here, and it is very useful). It's very similar to Final Fantasy's turn-based combat, but here you have to traverse through dungeons to progress through the story, making sure you have ample supplies in case of emergencies.
You can only have 3 heroes in your group at any and all times and you have to go back to town to be able to switch to other heroes (which is garbage, it would have been better to be able to switch on the fly), speaking of heroes... you don´t really need to switch to anyone else aside from the 3 first heroes i mentioned (lets call it the Gully-Calibretto-Garrison team comp, GCG for shorts). The other 3 have some overly complicated abilities (in my opinion that is) and nothing you can't do better with GCG comp, which is sad because youre cutting in half the combat experience of this game. For me this is arguably the game's biggest fault, and one i can overlook because of how good everything else is....
I wanted to point out the things i was mostly concerned about in this game... i could write an entire document about it and still feel like im missing content to describe. So for my sake i'll skip to my conclusion.
Battle Chasers; Nightwar is a great game, i was left with a carving for more, so much more. There's a lot of room for improvement on this fun little game.

The story is pretty typical "save the world" fare but it takes you across a variety of landscapes.  You'll find yourself in the arctic, deserts of Africa and forests & cities in Russia. The maps and models look really good. Everything is very detailed.  The maps are nicely designed and they seem pretty huge but in fact, they're pretty linear. The teammate AI wasn't too bad. They kill stuff & heal you so it always isn't up to you (just mostly). Enemy AI is pretty hit or miss. They're pretty quick to see you which can trigger some long fire fights. It was a bit infuriating watching enemies walk right into your cloaked teammates though.  This is a console port with auto saves. One screw up and prepare to lose a bunch of progress.  The gameplay is at times tactical though it's more of a cover shooter than anything else. I will say one thing I disliked though
. I can only played the single player campaign so that's the only goodness I can attest to. Overall I really enjoyed nearly every minute of the 11 or so hours I put into GR: Future Soldier. If I paid MSRP of $20, I'd sleep easy. Get this on sale and you'll sleep easier.

It’s really been a while since I last wrote a negative review. Not because I couldn’t find dozens, if not hundreds of poor examples from my own Steam collection, but for a reason that is far more simple. I outright refuse to write about most games I deem as detrimental to my patience/spare time/overall mood. Sadly, my gut feeling does fail from time to time and I end up with a “masterpiece” such as the game I’m writing about today.
Where to begin? Home Behind looks, controls and feels just like the type of video game you’d play for free on your smartphone or other mobile devices. And I just remembered exactly why I avoid this type of time wasters, since I won’t acknowledge the vast majority of them as proper games. TPP Studio, started on the wrong foot, as far as I can regard their Steam debut. Perhaps they’ll learn from past mistakes and their second project might be an improvement. It can’t really be much worse than Home Behind.
At least I was thankful that the antagonists in this title aren’t zombies. Had my fill of those for the next month at least. The storyline in Home Behind shows signs that the dev team at least aimed for something decent. Players shall unravel the tragic tale and journey of a father desperately looking for his kidnapped daughter. A civil war is being waged in a nameless country and the Rebels in this game, much like in real life, aren’t portrayed as noble freedom fighters but as savages with a penchant for killing people, regardless of what “side of the fence” they’re on. I really did appreciate this perspective onto civil war. Just cause or not, it’s as merciless and pointless as any type of conflagration.
Our hapless protagonist has witnessed the murder of his wife and siblings, so his daughter is literally, the only person still keeping him alive and determined to survive. The desire to rescue and protect her once more. I can respect that. What I cannot tolerate though, is the manner in which the story is being conveyed. A side-scrolling experience that is randomized in the wrong manner. On one hand, it’s obviously intended as to avoid even more repetitiveness but on the other, you soon realize that you can die of thirst/hunger at any time and reloading a previous save file, won’t guarantee increased odds of survivability.
I have no idea what graphics engine  is powering Home Behind but I sincerely hope it’s not Unity, for the simple reason that Unity Engine has never disappointed me so far. Don’t be quick to judge me for disliking Home Behind’s simplistic 2D looks. I play and enjoy writing about countless indie games which manage to impress without 3D acceleration. Home Behind features hand drawn assets which annoyed me through the perspective of their repetition. Let’s assume you come across a village or refugee camp in your long and liniar journey. The villagers/refugees, even if they’re 5 or 20 of them, will have just two sprite variations. One for male and one for female. That’s it. No extra beard styles/hair color variation or even clothing differences to set them apart. It’s like a nightmare sequence (as if, the silent hero hasn’t endured enough already) in which you’re surrounded by clones and even the scenery makes you feel like being stuck in a time loop.
It ran in my monitor’s native resolution plus 60fps, as if that was a surprise. I think that I’d be able to run Home Behind, even on my first PC and I still wouldn’t be able to tell the difference. The Steam Overlay allowed me to take screenshots, like I always like doing for my review projects. I can tell you that the ones from Home Behind won’t become desktop wallpapers for me anytime soon. It doesn’t look abysmal, since those 2D assets are still light years away from what I’d be able to “draw”. They were just far too repetitive to the point of recycled parody. While searching for his daughter, I was almost lead to believe that the heroic father had passed away and was now walking  across some literal hellscape, almost like a trip to Dante’s Inferno. Minus the “fun” within those Nine Circles.
The soundtrack presented itself to me with next to no in-game sound whatsoever. Can’t really judge something I never got to hear. I bet that some funny voices or any voice acting at all, no matter how unskilled, would have at least put a smile on my face enough to overlook some of Home Behind’s other weak points. So the sound effects are few and far between. They really insisted on cementing my already negative impression on this title.
Let me think of what more can be said of Home Behind. If only I could come up with something truly positive about it. I tried. I pushed myself through its simplistic and repetitive gameplay, despite not enjoying it one bit. It was like watching an episode of Family Guy’s latest seasons. The train of originality and fun has left the station a very long time ago. Yet I was still clinging onto the hope of finding a redeeming point. It always ended prematurely, with my valiant survivor, succumbing to his wounds or hunger/thirst despite gorging on resources, like a Skyrim character after a battle. You gotta eat all of those cabbages and potatoes. And then you still die, since they didn’t add enough hitpoints and/or decrease the hunger meter.
Yes, meter. More than one, in fact. This side-scroller really wants to punish you further by only increasing the rate at which you shall perish if you run instead of walking. So don’t run. You’ll only die tired and with diarrhea from that camel corpse you thought would be a good idea to consume as a last ditch effort. Just kick the bucket, pal. It’ll all be over as soon as you uninstall. I was just glancing over Home Behind’s designated genres from its Steam Store page. Adventure and casual, it is not. Survival, perhaps and yet you’ll find the trip almost not worth it.
One of the gameplay’s few bright ideas, has to be the crafting system. Too bad it gets spoiled from the scarcity of the required components. Home Behind allows you to trade with the NPCs you meet along your lethal odyssey. But there’s always a fly in the ointment, right? Those friendly refugees won’t trade their stuff with you for just anything or some form of currency at least, as in every RPG I have ever played so far. They want specific goods. You want  a can of sardines from Refugee Girl Clone #2? You better offer her iguana-on-a-stick. Nevermind the fact you never met that kind of commodity before. You don’t have that, you can’t trade, sorry. Now move along and die from hunger.
I definitely recommend you purchase (if at all) Home Behind under a heavy discount or pick it up when bundled with far more attractive titles. Perhaps it might entertain you for a limited time, but it failed this basic task, in my case. There are countless examples of Steam games which simulate the struggles for survival in a more complex or pleasant manner. No need to torture yourself playing Home Behind unless you are fully aware of its inherent repetitiveness and difficulty just for the random sake of it. You have been warned, the ultimate decision is as always, yours to make and live with it.

To gain a greater appreciation for this review, let me roll the calendar year back 3 years, to the last quarter of 2012 when I signed into the World of Warships forum.
-
At this point, my first impressions of the community in its infancy was relatively positive, largely due to the objective nature of both the users and the developers.  Granted, there was very little information regarding the status of the game development, however, there was sense of community that our input was being received, and to some degree, acted upon.  One of the discussion that surfaced was the inclusion of submarines, and while the community embraced the possibility of testing said model, behind the scenes that topic had been shelved, and forgotten.  The community on the other hand, frequently raised the question, to which either mods were instructed to avoid it altogether, or Wargaming simply did not respond.
-
Eventually, as the game developed, Closed testing began, the truth of there being no subs came to life in a very public manner with Wargaming’s own spokesman stating ‘there will be no subs in the game’, and other statements regarding how they don’t fit in the game – period.
-
I have been a Closed Alpha tester for World of Warships, and from the very first day I signed up in 2012, I have always maintained that submarines do fit, and properly balanced, the game would attract every possible sort of player.  Of course, this didn’t sit well with those carrying water for the devs, nor for anyone else for that matter, that aligned themselves with the status quo.
-
For them, it was a creative decision.  For the fans, it would be a marketing disaster waiting to happen.
-
In enters, Steel Ocean.
-
From a pure standpoint of marketing, this title brings relief to a specific market, players that have conceded that WoWs was the only fruit in the vineyard, the only game that provided some soft resemblance of our long departed Navy Field, and settled for WoWs.  In the back of mind, playing destroyers in a limited role, there was always that desire to use the fan tail, drop depth charges, chase submarines, and fully embrace naval combat both in surface warfare, and Anti Sub Warfare.
-
Steel Ocean delivers on all these points, and then some.
-
Not only is the gameplay fluid, dynamic, and challenging, the game provides every possible component that a full-cycle player would want, from diving to avoid bombers and torps, to hiding and ambushing passing ships, the game excels in these regards.
-
The balance consideration is perfect, giving submarine commanders’ room to risk it all on the surface, dive to avoid contact, and lay in wait for an unsuspecting enemy contact.  There is a sense of drama that is what inspires many sub drivers to play this role, the challenge of supporting a push, guarding a choke point, or watching the base.  Besides these points, the full spectrum experience of having the ability to engage the enemy on the surface, below the surface, adds so much more strategic and tactical reasoning to the game, something the developers took time to develop, and get it right.
-
For me, the simple inclusion of submarines into a massive player online experience is the icing on the cake.  For me, Steel Ocean is now my harbor away from home, preparing my submarine for combat, and having a place to have my cake, and eat it, too.
-

A quite fun roguelike dungeon crawler, even though it has a very high frustration level involved.
The premise is simple: you start a game, go in the dungeon, fight monsters, avoid traps, level up, find items and gear, then use what you have to get to the end of the dungeon, grab the orb and come back. Dungeons are randomly generated each time you go into a new level and even the potion effects are random each time you start a new game. It's simple enough, but not as easy to actually beat - could be perhaps described as "easy to play, hard to master", as you have to learn what stats work better for your play style, learn more about enemy behavior, wands and plan ahead to beat the game.
As fun as the game is, there is a huge frustration level involved, not just because it's a roguelike game but also because of how the game works. The first reason is that the only thing carried over when you die is your money, which you can use to buy some starting gear, though that doesn't help much since gear will degrade with usage (specially weapons). The best thing you can buy is a potion that gives you an instant stat point to spend, but obviously it only lasts for one playthrough. The second reason is that sometimes the game can overwhelm you all of a sudden - maybe you're having a perfect playthrough, finding lots of good items and dealing with enemies one by one, then all of a sudden you find yourself in a situation where your health bar drops so quickly, you don't even notice it until you're dead. These sudden difficulty spikes make the game extremely frustrating at times.
The game is currently on early access, so perhaps this issue will be addressed in the future, which might make the game a lot better than it currently is. Nonetheless, it's a fun and well made roguelike game.

An online survival shooter set in a post apocalyptic world, this is the theme of Desertland 2115, a game that is in Early Access on Steam and that I could test for a few hours today.
To begin with, the game drinks a little from the source of games devoted to this theme, and remembers a few games like RAGE, Mad Max and Fallout 3, with destroyed places, debris, human enemies and futuristic machines that can destroy you in a few seconds if you do not take care.
The game does well the part of survival and exploration with indicators of ammunition, water and energy, which makes you have that urgency in collecting resources to always maintain high levels. It is totally online so you will find other players between your wanderings on the map, which is pretty big by the way.
I thought the game would be more impressive if it had a singleplayer mode, with remarkable characters and a storyline that invites you to play more. After a while playing I lost a sense of purpose, and just wanted to keep my character alive as much as possible.
The game is good, yes, you will entertain yourself for a few hours and reward you for exploring, but the absence of a singleplayer mode and small character animation bugs can take you away from the immersion of being present in a dystopic and post apocalyptic world like this.

Each game needs a bit of mystery. Gamers don't need an entire game devoted to all this stuff. There's no more mystery with this stuff in Borderlands 2 anymore, which is a real shame. The gameplay, is Borderlands 2 but with low gravity and the ability to use the air in an oxygen tank to boost to higher areas, and get an edge over opponents. Virtually the same game.
Characters are varied here,but I don't find most that interesting. Jack doppleganger is cool, but I don't care much for the other ones.
Laser guns are cool. Just replaces E-Tech though, so...
Final boss is cool, but the enemies are lame. Most are politcally corrected variations of existing enemies (Midget=Lil' Scav). No need for this change.
If you like Borderlands 2, you'll love The Pre-Sequel. Just don't dig too deep, or you'll fall into a deep, spikey pit.

I have no doubt in my mind that this game was created to "cut losses" from the gigantic financial and critical bomb that was A:CM, and to show that Gearbox "still has it"

After our victory over the English and the Danish, taking many miles of northern coastline, Scotland was settled as a new, prosperous kingdom. Many alliances, trade agreements, and marriages flourished. But the Pope called a crusade against Jerusalem, and I raised an army for the cause. My noble swordsmen clad in plate embarked for a long voyage through the Bay of Biscay, along the Iberian Coast, and then followed the North African coastline to take Cairo as a staging ground to move armies against Jerusalem. We were successful; my army took Cairo in the name of the Pope. I raised a new army and sent them northeast, deciding to take more land for the Pope. But, to my dismay, I saw that no other nations were joining the crusade. Complicating matters further, the Mongols joined the Turkish and Egyptian cause, and a three nation army destroyed my own in the field. Left with my original crusading army, in Cairo, we withstood one assault after the other. My fleet had returned home, evacuation wouldn't be here in time. After many assaults, my army broke through their coalition lines and we took Alexandira, watching Cairo fall back into enemy hands. There, we raised a fleet and sailed away from our enemies. But they pursed my fleet, and shadowed and raided us at every opportunity. Going back the original way would be too long. France had declared war, so I made the decision to invade southern France. We landed and razed the fortress to the ground. My army was thin, we wouldn't be able to hold it. We burned our ships and pushed north. We fought off raiding Frenchmen several times, and were forced to raze another fortress to the ground. Finally, my army of crusaders, diminished to less than fifteen men per unit, bloodied, muddied, exhuasted from years of combat, arrived in Caen, part of our continental territory. I put them on ships, and sent them home.
Did that actually happen? Yes. Yes it did. This is the best, most complicated, challenging, and entertaining installment of the Total War series.

Lone Survivor is a sidescrolling 2D survival horror game, largely inspired by Silent Hill. It's set in a zombie apocalypse of sorts and the story starts with the unnamed protagonist venturing out of his apartment for the first time since the infection started. Gameplay is fairly typical for the genre with a heavy emphasis on resource management and exploration. Unfortunately, I never really found the game that scary as health and ammo pickups were relatively common and I usually found it easier to just shoot mutants rather than trying to sneak by them.
I also found the survival aspects somewhat underdeveloped. While having to worry about eating and sleeping in a horror game is interesting, it just became tedious because the character can barely leave his room without getting tired and hungry and you can't really craft much to help with it. I was never able to reach a place of sustainability in the game where survival became easier, which just felt unsatisfying.
However, I did enjoy the level design, exploring, interacting with other survivors, and the general atmosphere of the game. Overall, I would recommend Lone Survivor to survival horror fans (especially those who like psychological horror games) but not to those seeking a game with good survival or action gameplay.

I really admire what this game managed to accomplish with the limitations of 2D side-scrolling. The design, atmosphere, and music are well rendered tributes to the Silent Hill games it was clearly modelled on. This is a long review, and what I've said many have already mentioned, but I felt this game was just too close to the mark of being brilliant that it needed to be given justice.
That said there are weak points, some minor and some not so, and these for me made the game a real chore to play and enough reason to not finish it. Yes, reviewing a game you haven't even finished is laughable, but for me it serves as a statement about it's appeal and playability.
For one thing, the lack of being able to access the title screen to quickly reload a game when you screw up (and you will), means having to either find monsters to finish you off (if they're still alive) or exit the game completely and restart it. And that takes just long enough to be a real pain, not least because the sequences you can't skip (like the Game Over sequence and the first loading screen) go on for longer than is necessary or desirable. This becomes a major problem by the way when facing the first "boss", which was the point in the game where I waved the white flag and stopped playing due to much bigger problems.
The fact the character can't last ten minutes without needing a nap means either backtracking to your apartment (albeit facilitated with "mirrors" - itself a nice nod to Silent Hill), or drinking coffee (although you still need to go back to your apartment to brew it), or taking "booster" pills which you run out of way too quickly. It should be mentioned that sleeping in your apartment is how you save the game. I am not kidding when it is literally about ten minutes before you need to "nap" for 24 hours and lose another day in the game. What would take any normal person a couple of hours to complete took far too long for it to be enjoyable. Instead of fighting monsters, I spent most of my time sleeping and eating, backtracking to my apartment again and again. I'm grateful they didn't program in the need for the character to go potty and floss.
Then there's the healing process. As with most other games, you do so by eating and drinking. Problem is, the character gets hungry, regardless of your health level. And if you don't have food, you die. Same goes for water. And sleep. And yes, foraging for food takes just as much time and effort as satisfying the need for the character to sleep. Which means going back to the apartment. Over. And Over.
My final criticism is the plot. Not the main story, i.e. trying to escape a city suffering the ravages of an infectious outbreak, but the special characters injected into the game to add mystery to the hero's back-story. It's difficult to say what exactly feels wrong about them. But I guess it's the fact they speak so vaguely that very little is revealed about who you are, and who they are, until later in the game. Long enough to lose interest with all the sleeping, cooking and foraging you'll be doing while apparently playing a survival-horror game where a quick getaway from an apocalyptic scenario is key. What they do say is cliched and generic to the point of being another reason to quit the game and apply for a refund.
I really wanted to like this game. What is has accomplished is impressive, and it is by no means a bad game in terms of potential. But the gameplay issues I had with it marred what I hoped would be a memorable experience. As a casual, no-frills (and not very competent) player, it's more effort than it's worth for me to persevere with it.

'Lone Survivor: The Director’s Cut' is one of these little games that shows how good indie titles can be.
This little pixelated horror adventure suceeds where many huge (Horror-)AAA-titles fail nowadays: Creating a deep and atmospheric experience full of creepy and mysterious situations without relying too much on (cheap) tricks like e.g. jumps scares behind every corner.
After the outbreak of an unknown disease the nameless protagonist – only called 'You' – tries to survive in this harsh and cruel world. He lives withdrawn in a lost apartment building, unsure if he is still sane or if everything he sees is only a hallucination. Due to the questionable mental stability and the omnipresent problem of starvation he doesn't know how long he may be able to stay alive. First of alll 'You' doesn’t want to die alone – therefore he starts exploring the apartments and looking for other survivors of the catastrophe.
While exploring the remnants of the 'good old times', 'You' will be confrontend with deep fears and mysterious situations, monsters and hallucinations, unsure what is real and what is just a trick of his own mind. Armed with a flaslight, batteries and a gun with very limited ammunition he makes his way into the unknown depths of the apartments, facing mysterious horrors while trying to keep the rest of his sanity and finding enough food to eat and time to sleep. The only 'true‘ friends he has in this apocalyptic world are a plant and a plush doll – but is it really a sign of sanity to talk to them? Who knows…
The story is short but well done and the dialogues make you actually care about the characters, their well-being and their behavior, questioning the situations that 'You' has to face in and what’s really happening in front of him as everything may change in the blink of an eye. And in the end every step and decision you‘ve taken may affect him.
Until 'You' will see the end of his journey it will take approximately four up to maybe five hours (I finished the game already two times outside of Steam, therefore my short gaming time is no sign of lacking experience). Fortunately the replay value is quite high due to many different endings based on your choices during 'You‘s' journey and a NG+ Mode with some additional content.
__________________________________________
To cut it short: It’s a pixelated game based on Flash Engine so you shouldn’t expect too
much – but for this it does quite a good job. The games‘ soundtrack is fantastic and fits most of the times absolutely perfect. It’s creepy and catchy at the same time, giving you the chills in the right moments.
The pixelated graphics are well done and you can see that the different appartmens, rooms and scenes were crafted carefully and with a love for details. The game feels like a great trip in good old 2D-Horror Games and has a deeper atmosphere than many huge titles nowadays.
__________________________________________
Unfortunately 'Lone Survivor' somehow feels bulky and using the inventory or selecting items can be quite annoying from time to time (just as using your gun in my opinion). The controls aren’t very comfortable despite some hotkeys, remapping them isn‘t possible and due to the restrictions of flash games there is no easy solution for controller support aside from third party software – a fact where the game would benefit from heavily. That’s kind of sad as the PS3-version has both controller support and achievements (that are somehow missing in the PC version).

Overall campaign is fun to play. Typical Russian bad guys vs the American good guys plot, typical ending, but no one really plays a tactical shooter like this for the story, it's more about how the game plays.
First off, you can definitely tell this game is ported from the console version as at times controls are clunky and button callouts are that of the Xbox controller instead of your Keyboard/Mouse callouts. This in itself does not make it a bad game but at times it can be frustrating because you're used to having PC functionality in a PC game.
In terms of gameplay, I thought it felt true to other games in the franchise and of course other Tom Clancy's games. Weapons are realistic, one-shot headshots are a thing, and you will die instantly if you peek enemies without thinking (playing on Hardcore difficulty). This is a game that relies heavily on your ability to think critically in the middle of a mission. You will want to stealth through but sometimes you need to take out enemies without alarming others, and this can lead to retrying at the checkpoint, or just outright dying because you weren't able to control your engagements.
I was able to complete the single player campaign solo on Hardcore (hardest difficulty) in about 14 hours of gameplay, with there being about 11 missions, that is just over an hour per mission, with multiple retries on some missions that are frustrating to run.
Overall I'd give this game an objective 7/10 simply because it wasn't bad, but it wasn't amazing. The gameplay feels rewarding when you complete  missions, but the cinematics look grainy, the console feel of the game even when playing on a high-end PC. If you are into tactical shooters and have a couple of friends to run co-op on, I'd say grab the game for a cheap price as it will hold you over until Wildlands drops in 2017, if you are a Ghost Recon fan, I would recommend it as well but if you're just a FPS/TPS player who is looking for a new game - do not focus on this game, instead get Rainbow Six Siege or Wildlands when it comes out in 2017.

Home Behind is an interesting rogue-like game with a light political sensitivity to current events.  You play as a refugee that walks from left to right on the screen, and things pass by.  Once you have pass them, you can't ever go back, so you want to enure you are thorough. But the game has a built-in tension that rebels are heading your way, and if you wait too long they will catch up to you.  So you are constantly trying to things like build stuff, explore, talk to people, and fighting that takes times off the clock.  Meanwhile, the rebels are relentlessly movign behind you and taking everything over.  Now, like a Rogulilke, there is just one save, you have to continue from where you start, and teh RNG can be your friend or enemy. It's also a hard game on the normal mode of difficulty, and there is no (real) tutorial, you are just thrown in.  But it certainly is a good game, with things to unlock and and understand as you play through.  Sucessful playthrough should be 6-7 hours, assuming you don't die.  Unlike normal Roguelikes, you can restart from your pervious save when you bite it .  I enjoy the game and I think's well done and packaged for just 6 bucks, and the only things I would add to the the game are minor nitpicks (A few key dialogues happen in pull away scenes adn don;t take time off the clock, others happen on the screen and do.  The further yo go, the more stuff you have to craft to make crafting things, and I'd love some shortcuts so I don't have to make four ropes to turn into a heavy rope each time I need a heavy rope fo rsoemthign and I have the reources for the lesser ropes) .  Those minor concerns aside, this is a very strong game.  Enjoy!

A lot of times we are hesitant to buy unknown indie games that are short and sometimes, a waste of money and time, and this happened to me just before buying The moon sliver. I pondered a lot of time sitting and thinking wether I wanted to buy this game. I did it. However, instead of getting a simply indie game, I recieved a beautiful interactive fairy tale, a dark one, but a fairy tale at last. The moon sliver is an experience, not entirely a game, which you have to go through. Even though is short and basically a walking simulator, it is worth giving it a look, mainly because of its solid story and its amazing atmosphere. The graphics could be better but you completely overlook that while you're playing because of how invested you're in the story. What this game does great is that it makes you hunt for little pieces of the story, turning it into a kind of a "story-driven-puzzle". It's not offered to you served in silver platter. That's why I could see people getting confused with the story, shouldn't they pay enough attention. As regard to the characters, I give props to the developer for doing everything with writing, and no voice acting, given that it accentures the tone of the game. Nevertheless, I feel that all that reading could put off some players. Of course it has its faults (like the flashlight system that is a little bit clunky or the maze thing that I believed unnecesary) but overall it is a beautiful game that I could see myself playing again. Definitely give this one a chance.

This is a short story, presented in an interactive format. The Moon Silver's "gameplay" almost entirely consists of using exploration to put the story to its intended pace.  Emptiness and tedium that would easily doom similar games, instead serves to expound the motifs and themes of the story, and rarely does any facet of the experience come across as forced or unnecessary.
While you'd be forgiven for thinking otherwise at first glance, The Moon Silver is far from clueless; It knows exactly what it's doing and why, ensuring that any who entrust it with even a modicum of faith will be rewarded.
Definitely worth the price of admission.

Ok, firstly this game is early access (ie, effectively a public beta) and as such has several bugs that i've noticed so far. That said, the concept is original, the gameworld is huge, and there is a lot of potential. On the basis that the dev(s) continue to update on as regular a basis as they have been doing, i'm minded to reccomend it.
Easter egg to spot:
If you look carefully explore the ruined vehicles in the spawn town/city, you will notice that one appears to be the APC from Aliens. No facehugger though.
Problems noted so far, that you should be aware of:
1/ Sniper rifle is a one shot kill weapon against all PC and NPC targets - even if you only hit an extremity (tail or hand).
2/Whilst there is a facility for in game chat - by pressing enter - the in game key assignment screen doesn't currently show it. Although it does show an entry for a score screen, that doesn't appear to be functional yet.

NieR: Automata is one of the best games I've played in a long time, and that's saying a lot in a year that has already had a number of other great games come out.
The gameplay is top-notch, exactly what you'd expect the developers of Bayonetta to be capable of, but it's even better when it's paired with a story by Yoko Taro.  If you're new to the Taro experience, don't be fooled when you're 15 hours into the game, see the credits scroll by, and think you know what the story is about; you're only 1/3 of the way done with the game, and there are multiple layers of complexity to go through.  There are tons of interesting side quests, well-developed characters, and a fantastic soundtrack by Keiichi Okabe.
The only negative thing I can say about the game, if you'd call it that, is that the system requirements are no joke; this is a GPU-intensive game.  The listed minimum requirements really are the lowest you should try to get away with, and even then, expect to be playing on low settings.  You'll need serious hardware if you want to play this in 1080p at a solid 60 fps.

Stellaris is an early alpha game that is to be finished in DLC. If you buy it now, you get to enjoy all the placeholder mechanics that they will ask you money for to replace with something resembling an actually thought out game. And even then it will be half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and with minimum effort because you're already invested (See also the Sunk Cost Fallacy). You'll have to buy it or be stuck with an unfinished version that isn't really good at anything.
And it's that version I will review here. Stellaris attempts to merge Grand Strategy games and 4X games, managing to take only the worst of both worlds in a nice looking jacket to hide the lack of things to do. To begin, the early game plays much like a 4X game. You explore, you look for places to expand and colonize, and you work on your planets. After everything is mostly claimed and you've met a fair amount of alien empires the grand strategy game is supposed to take over, but it never does. This leaves you with a rather poorly done 4X game that has no real mid or late game. Once you've finished exploring, you build up a military until it's bigger than your neighbour and throw it at them until you have no more neighbours.
To begin with the good things about it, it looks pretty decent, as screenshots will show you. And the events have decent flavour to them, and a few stories that actually made me want to follow up on them only to be disappointed when it results in an anticlimactic "+500 energy credits" for finishing the entire storyline. Many events and anomalies imply you'll be able to do great things once you end up with highly advanced technology, but you never do, and the simple events and anomalies start repeating before you're even done with one game. Most of these storylines and events do not seem to matter whatsoever, with all of them being self-contained minor effects that do not interact with anything outside of them.
Nearly everything in the game is, I would hope, a placeholder mechanic- Technology ends in the mid game and you research repeatable technologies that give you a slight numbers bonus, military matters are simple with no depth to them whatsoever, species are all interchangeable except for a few fringe cases, diplomacy doesn't really exist, just like many options to control your empire don't seem to exist and there is no real grand strategy part of this. It offers you three ways to travel the stars with FTL technology, yet two of these are completely useless.
The AI, in all ways, is completely incapable. Diplomatically it doesn't do anything of real note, often remaining passive until a certain value just happens to rise by coincidence and triggers it to do something. Militarily it doesn't do anything- It makes ships that are poorly planned and optimized by just putting on whatever seems like the latest technology, even if it's terrible. It develops its lands randomly, completely ignoring any sort of planning or goals it may be able to do, and in general feels much less like it's trying to emulate an opponent and more like they just hooked up an RNG to the controls.
The military and combat stuff is, in one word, bad. While there is a minimum of customization to try to counter your opponent, in the end everything comes down to who just has the bigger stack. The entire military game is essentially a♥♥♥♥♥♥measuring content. If yours is bigger then you win, take your opponent's stuff and move on to measure against the next guy. There is no strategy, no tactics, and no maneuvering. You do not even get to control what your ships do and do not engage. Planetary invasions are a joke- You leave some ships above the place and then bring in a big stack of armies to wipe out the defenders. It's more of a formality at that point, because you have the bigger naval♥♥♥♥♥♥from the earlier measuring contest so it's not like you can't just wait a few years to bring in more armies
As mentioned earlier, technology is a joke past the early game, but even at the early game you will find a large amount of completely useless technologies that will never be even a little bit useful. You get a choice of a few randomly selected technologies to research, and while I like the idea of it, all it really means is that you're going to just research the cheapest technology of the set until something actually useful comes up.
Most of Stellaris is set up to be pretty and to pretend it has depth, but if you look even a little bit at it you will find that most of it is empty and flat. Past the initial experience of the early game and expanding there is nothing to do except waiting or continued♥♥♥♥♥♥measuring competition with your neighbours, and then moving on to measure against the next guy.
Is it worth getting? Maybe if you can get it really cheap on sale. Maybe in a few years when they've finished it.

In Lone survivor, you control the titular survivor of some kind of apocalypse that has left the majority of the population as faceless monsters that wander around searching for prey. "You," as the game refers to the player character, wake up in your apartment and seek a way out into the surrounding city streets. The problem is the apartment building You are in is in shambles, leaving doors locked, hallways in ruins, and more than a few monsters running around.
Right from the get go, this feels like an early Silent Hill game. Despite the very simple pixel based graphics and the side scrolling perspective, the game manages to hav a good atmosphere of tension and dread. It uses its limited perspective to its advantage, leading to a lot of atmospheric touches.
It's a good thing that it has atmosphere, too, because the story is a bit all over the place. You run across a few different characters throughout your journey, and they usually serve as some sort of source of goods and supplies, while also asking You cryptic questions that don't make a whole lot of sense. Unfortunately, this is one of those games that, I have a feeling, needs to be played through numerous times in order to fully grasp what's going on, because the ending I got was anticlimactic at best and confusing at worst. I'm not someone who needs everything spelled out for me, but the vague nature of the game is a tad frustrating.
Still, this is a worthwhile survival horror game. As mentioned above, it's very creepy and manages to feel old school thanks to its hunger and ammo systems. You must constantly explore to find more supplies and ammo, meaning conservation and planning are a must. Give this game a shot if you like games such as Silent Hill or are itching for something highly atmospheric.
Such an awesome game! Made with love and great music!

If, like me, you are not a big fan of survival horror games, this game may not convince you to become one. I enjoyed the atmosphere invoked by the graphical and audio design, but the gameplay and plot often took me out of the experience. I kept asking questions that I'm not sure the game wanted me to ask. Why is this man selling items in this back room? Why am I given so many unexplained, unnecessary items? Why is backtracking more boring than tense?
It's very likely that this game requires players to be more willing to experiment, fail, and try again, but I never felt rewarded for the experimentation I did. ("Oh look, I just wasted something I didn't know I needed. Better reload an old save.") If I had been more invested in the early exploration, I might have been able to forgive some of the less-optimal moments later in the game.
This game wasn't for me, and if you can identify with my gaming preferences, maybe you should stay away, too.
